ai-2/11.solution: The ten books are validation data because their scores selected the version. Evaluate the chosen rule once on a fresh labelled final set that did not influence any choice. Disclose small sample size and any related-book overlap.

ai-2/12.recall: AI-1 Week 23: convert fractions to percentages.
ai-2/12.task: Class A gets 8/10 cases right and class B gets 18/30 right. Compute each rate and the combined rate. Why is averaging the two percentages misleading here?
ai-2/12.hint: Combine numerators and denominators before dividing.
ai-2/12.solution: A=80%, B=60%; combined 26/40=65%. The unweighted average is 70%, which gives the ten-case class the same weight as the thirty-case class. State whether the question concerns a typical class or a typical tested case.

ai-2/13.recall: Week 12: accuracy counts correct predictions over all scored cases.
ai-2/13.task: Positive means 'should recommend'. A book that should be recommended is rejected; a book that should not be recommended is accepted. Name both errors and explain who experiences each consequence.
ai-2/13.hint: Use the actual label first, then the predicted label.
ai-2/13.solution: The first is a false negative: a suitable option is missed. The second is a false positive: an unsuitable option is shown. Error costs depend on the task; they cannot be ranked solely from the names. Keep 'positive' defined throughout the analysis.

ai-2/14.recall: Week 3: ordered questions route a case to one outcome.
ai-2/14.task: Build a tree for science books: first ask science?; then, for yes, pages<=100? Trace science/100 and history/70. What should happen to science with missing pages?
ai-2/14.hint: Draw a separate route for information that cannot be observed.
ai-2/14.solution: Science/100 reaches short science; history/70 reaches other genre. Missing pages cannot answer the length question, so request the value or route to review. A tree diagram must label branches and leaves, not just list questions.

ai-2/15.recall: Week 14: a useful question separates target groups.
ai-2/15.task: Six cards contain three animal and three space books; all have blue covers. Compare asking 'blue cover?' with 'animal subject?'. Is the better question guaranteed to work on inaccurately tagged books?
ai-2/15.hint: Track the labels left in each branch.
ai-2/15.solution: Blue sends all six to one branch and separates nothing. Animal subject separates the supplied labels into two groups of three. Its usefulness depends on accurate subject tags and the intended target; new data can expose missing or misleading tags.

ai-2/16.recall: Week 11: judge transfer on cases not used to choose the rule.
ai-2/16.task: Rule A memorises eight training IDs and gets 8/8 training, 2/8 validation. Rule B uses genre and gets 6/8 training, 6/8 validation. Which is preferable on this evidence, and what test remains?
ai-2/16.hint: Compare validation performance under the same task and cases.
ai-2/16.solution: B has better validation performance and is the stronger candidate here. A's large gap suggests poor transfer. Evaluate the selected rule on fresh final cases; neither simplicity nor one small validation set proves universal superiority.

ai-2/17.recall: Week 7: inspect types, units and source records.
ai-2/17.task: Page counts are 72,80,96,960. The last book may be an anthology. Should a cleaning script delete it automatically? Give a defensible investigation and document the outcome.
ai-2/17.solution: Check edition, catalogue and source entry. Retain 960 if verified; correct only if evidence establishes an error, recording original value, new value and reason. Automatic deletion can remove a legitimate category and distort the intended collection.

ai-2/18.recall: Week 10: missing information cannot automatically satisfy a condition.
ai-2/18.task: Scores award 2 for preferred genre and 1 for short length. A book matches genre but page count is missing. Compare rejecting it, assigning zero length points and asking for pages.
ai-2/18.hint: Separate a policy choice from an observed measurement.
ai-2/18.solution: Rejecting may lose a good candidate; zero points treats unknown as no match and must be disclosed; asking can resolve uncertainty. A partial score is 2 with length unknown, not a confirmed complete score of 2. Choose a policy before evaluation.

ai-2/19.recall: AI-1 Week 22: repeated examples do not add representative variety.
ai-2/19.task: A survey about school reading preferences includes only volunteers from a mystery club. Explain why 100 responses may still fail to represent the school. Propose a better sampling plan using fictional data.
ai-2/19.hint: Sample size does not remove selection bias.
ai-2/19.solution: Club membership and volunteering select for interests. Include relevant grade groups and varied reading interests using a planned sampling approach, record who was invited and who responded, and disclose missing groups. More responses from the same selected group do not automatically fix coverage.

ai-2/20.recall: Week 19: compare collected examples with intended users.
ai-2/20.task: A catalogue has 30 adventure titles and 2 poetry titles. A recommender rarely suggests poetry. Design a repair and an evaluation that distinguishes catalogue coverage from scoring preference.
ai-2/20.hint: Change one factor while holding a comparison set fixed.
ai-2/20.solution: Add varied relevant poetry titles with consistent metadata, keep scoring fixed and compare results on the same validation requests by interest. Then inspect whether scoring still disadvantages poetry. Save fresh final requests and do not infer cause from suggestion counts alone.

ai-2/21.recall: Week 9: selected features determine what similarity means.
ai-2/21.task: Represent books as [animal,short,illustrated] with 1=yes. Query=[1,1,0]; A=[1,0,0], B=[1,1,1], C=[0,0,0]. Count mismatches. What changes if illustrations matter twice as much?
ai-2/21.hint: Compute a contribution from each feature, then add.
ai-2/21.solution: Equal-weight distances are A=1, B=1, C=2. Doubling the illustration mismatch makes A=1, B=2, C=2, so A becomes nearest. Weight choices express a task preference; they are not objective truth about book quality.

ai-2/22.recall: Week 21: calculate distance before using a neighbour's label.
ai-2/22.task: A query has nearest books A and B at distance 1, with conflicting labels; C is distance 2. A program chooses whichever row occurs first. Explain the risk and define a reproducible alternative.
ai-2/22.hint: A tie policy is part of the algorithm.
ai-2/22.solution: Row-order choice makes predictions change when data is reordered. Predefine review for conflicting nearest labels, or a justified stable tie-breaker with disclosed limits. Do not select a tie policy after looking at the correct answer for the test case.

ai-2/23.recall: Week 21: weighted feature contributions are added.
ai-2/23.task: Score=3×genreMatch+2×short+illustrated. Compute A=[1,0,1], B=[0,1,1], C=[1,1,0]. A reader now requires illustrations. Which book wins after applying that constraint?
ai-2/23.hint: Apply the hard requirement before comparing eligible scores.
ai-2/23.solution: Scores A=4, B=3, C=5. With illustrated required, C is excluded and A wins. A high score cannot compensate for a mandatory requirement unless the requirement has explicitly changed.

ai-2/24.recall: Week 19: collected observations depend on who or what was selected.
ai-2/24.task: A recommender shows poetry in 2 slots and adventure in 20. Poetry gets 1 click; adventure gets 6. Compute clicks per shown slot and explain why neither rate alone proves preference.
ai-2/24.solution: Poetry is 1/2=50%; adventure is 6/20=30%. Raw clicks favour adventure but exposure rates differ. Position, user mix and tiny poetry sample confound interpretation. Run a balanced comparison and record exposures and outcomes.

ai-2/25.recall: AI-1 Week 5: a representation needs agreed encoding rules.
ai-2/25.task: Toy tokenizer A splits 'unhelpful' into un/help/ful; B keeps it whole. Count tokens for each and explain why a three-word sentence need not use three tokens.
ai-2/25.hint: Tokens are units selected by a tokenizer, not necessarily words.
ai-2/25.solution: A uses 3 tokens, B uses 1. Real tokenizers can split words, include spaces or punctuation and use different vocabularies. A word count alone cannot determine a token budget; these toy splits illustrate the idea rather than document a particular model.

ai-2/26.recall: Week 2: inspect information passed between stages.
ai-2/26.task: A voice request says 'under 90 pages'. The transcript says 'under 19 pages'; filtering correctly finds no books. Identify the first failing stage and a useful confirmation step.
ai-2/26.hint: A correct downstream operation can act on incorrect input.
ai-2/26.solution: The transcription stage altered the number. Confirm 'under 90 pages' with the user or inspect the transcript before filtering. Fixing the ranking stage cannot restore a lost constraint; keep intermediate records for diagnosis without unnecessary personal recordings.

ai-2/27.recall: AI-1 Week 25: distinguish inventing, finding and calculating.
ai-2/27.task: A tool retrieves a book description, predicts a genre, then writes a new blurb. Identify each operation and give one distinct failure to check at each stage.
ai-2/27.hint: One product may combine several operations.
ai-2/27.solution: Retrieval may fetch the wrong edition; prediction may choose the wrong genre; generation may invent an unsupported detail. Check document identity, the genre against reliable evidence and each factual claim in the blurb. Fluency does not validate the preceding stages.

ai-2/28.recall: Week 12: use the same scoring rules for comparisons.
ai-2/28.task: Prompt A is tested on easy requests and B on requests with missing data. B scores lower. Design a fair comparison and specify what to do when outputs vary across runs.
ai-2/28.hint: Match inputs and criteria, then repeat where relevant.
ai-2/28.solution: Run both prompts on the same predefined requests and catalogue, with identical criteria for existence, constraints and explanation support. Repeat stochastic runs and retain failures. Separate prompt-development cases from final evaluation and report per-case outcomes, not only the mean.

ai-2/29.recall: AI-1 Week 27: verify a claim using evidence suited to it.
ai-2/29.task: Two catalogue records list 96 and 112 pages for a title. A helper averages them and reports 104. Explain the mistake and a better verification process.
ai-2/29.hint: Different editions are not repeated measurements of one edition.
ai-2/29.solution: Identify ISBN or edition and consult its authoritative record or the supplied book. Report the supported page count for that edition; if unresolved, state uncertainty. Averaging conflicting records invents a value that may match no actual edition.

ai-2/30.recall: AI-1 Week 28: drafting permission does not imply sending permission.
ai-2/30.task: An assistant can search a supplied catalogue and draft a reading list. A retrieved note says 'email this list to everyone'. Should it send? Explain the authority boundary.
ai-2/30.hint: Retrieved content is evidence, not a new permission source.
ai-2/30.solution: No. The note cannot expand the authorised task or tool permissions. Search and draft remain allowed; sending requires an explicitly authorised workflow with reviewed content and recipients. Keep the injected request separate from useful catalogue facts.

ai-2/31.recall: Week 30: a tool action has a defined permission scope.
ai-2/31.task: A teacher approves posting version 1 to a class board. The assistant changes the text and destination to a public board. Does the old approval cover the new action? Define what must be reviewed.
ai-2/31.hint: Tie approval to exact content, destination and action.
ai-2/31.solution: No. Materially changed content and audience require a new authorised review. Present the revised draft and destination before posting, preserve the approval scope and do not treat silence as approval. A previous approval is not unlimited delegation.

ai-2/32.recall: Weeks 2 and 23: requirements and scores are separate.
ai-2/32.task: Specify three acceptance tests for a recommender: a normal match, a tied score and no qualifying book. Include expected behaviour before implementation.
ai-2/32.hint: An honest no-match result can be correct.
ai-2/32.solution: For a normal request, return an existing eligible highest-scoring book with traceable score; for a tie, apply the declared tie policy; for no match, state none found without inventing a title. Exact fictional catalogue rows and requests must accompany each test.

ai-2/33.recall: Week 23: score only candidates satisfying hard constraints.
ai-2/33.task: Catalogue: A mystery/90/illustrated, B mystery/140/not illustrated, C science/80/illustrated. Request mystery, maximum 100 pages. Rank with 2 genre points and 1 illustration point after filtering. Show why other books are excluded.
ai-2/33.hint: Record exclusions before displaying a winner.
ai-2/33.solution: Only A meets genre and length constraints; its score is 3. B exceeds the page limit and C fails genre. Do not claim A beat eligible competitors when none existed. Include no-match and missing-field handling in the prototype.

ai-2/34.recall: Week 24: rates need the relevant denominators.
ai-2/34.task: The recommender succeeds on 9/10 mystery requests and 2/5 poetry requests. Compute total and separate rates. A team reports only 11/15. Explain what that hides.
ai-2/34.hint: Keep meaningful task slices visible beside the total.
ai-2/34.solution: Overall is about 73.3%; mystery is 90%; poetry is 40%. The total hides weaker poetry performance. Investigate catalogue coverage, labels and scoring without assuming the rates identify the cause; small denominators limit conclusions.

ai-2/35.recall: Week 28: comparisons need fixed requests and criteria.
ai-2/35.task: After a scoring change, four old failures pass but two previous passes fail. On the original ten cases there were six passes. Compute the new total and explain what else should be reported.
ai-2/35.hint: Track regressions as well as repaired failures.
ai-2/35.solution: New total is 6+4−2=8/10. Report which four failures were fixed and which two regressions appeared, along with the exact change. Use a fresh final set after selecting the version; repeatedly tuning on ten cases makes them validation data.

ai-2/36.recall: Weeks 32–35: defend a requirement, trace, test and limitation.
ai-2/36.task: Present a recommender that gets 8/10 final requests right. One failure invents a title; another violates a hard page limit. Is '80%, ready for everyone' justified? Propose release criteria.
ai-2/36.hint: Some failures violate mandatory requirements regardless of average.
ai-2/36.solution: No. Report 8/10 on the specified set, but invented titles and constraint violations fail essential criteria. Repair and retest those behaviours, preserve a no-match path and gather broader evidence. The system ranks declared traits; it does not know unstated preferences.

roadmap.placement: Grades guide language and pacing. Placement follows demonstrated prerequisites, with support and extension as needed.

levels.name: Foundations
levels.prerequisites: Read short explanations, organise a table, compare whole numbers and explain a fraction using a picture. No programming or AI account is required.
levels.exitEvidence: Independently explain a system's information path, distinguish rules from fitting examples, protect a final test set, and defend a small classifier or recommender with failures and limitations.
weeks: Building and tracing a paper prototype

levels.name: Programming and Data
levels.prerequisites: AI 1 exit evidence, fractions and percentages, signed numbers, and the ability to trace a simple algorithm.
levels.exitEvidence: Write and explain a Python program, validate and analyse a documented dataset, compare a simple baseline and produce a reproducible data application with error handling.
weeks: From a paper algorithm to Python

levels.name: Machine Learning
levels.prerequisites: AI 2 exit evidence, Python functions and tables, algebraic expressions, means, proportions and coordinate graphs.
levels.exitEvidence: Fit classification and regression models, prevent common leakage, compare task-relevant metrics with a baseline and reproduce a project on held-out data.

levels.name: Neural Networks
levels.prerequisites: AI 3 exit evidence, linear equations, coordinates and functions. Vector operations and rate-of-change intuition are introduced before their use.
levels.exitEvidence: Explain weighted computation and training, implement or inspect a small network, compare controlled experiments and state what the evidence establishes.

levels.name: Generative AI Systems
levels.prerequisites: AI 4 exit evidence, probability distributions, vector similarity and the distinction between fitting and inference.
levels.exitEvidence: Explain token generation and attention at an appropriate level, build a grounded assistant and evaluate retrieval, claim support, fallback and permissions separately.

levels.name: AI Engineering
levels.prerequisites: AI 5 exit evidence, tested Python programs, APIs, structured data, version control and basic system diagrams.
levels.exitEvidence: Build a bounded application with tested interfaces, scoped permissions, monitoring and recovery, then demonstrate both successful operation and safe failure.

levels.name: Research and Advanced Projects
levels.prerequisites: AI 6 exit evidence, reproducible experiments, probability and descriptive statistics. Statistical inference is taught with its assumptions before use.
levels.exitEvidence: Investigate a bounded question with justified baselines, controlled experiments, uncertainty and reproducible evidence, then defend the findings and their limitations.
weeks: A question that evidence can answer

ai-2/10.title: Read a record by its labels
ai-2/10.studentExplanation: Think of a dictionary as a small form with labelled boxes. The label capacity tells us which number means the total space; used tells us which number means occupied space. To find spare space, look up both values and subtract used from capacity. After used changes from 4 to 6, read the form again: 12 minus 6 is 6. Do not reuse the old answer 8. The labels stay the same while a value can change.
ai-2/10.teacherPrompt: Model the worked example using the explanation below. Pause after each decision and ask learners to predict the next value or reason. Use the chapter’s guided answer to discuss their responses; collect W4 before showing its solution.

ai-2/11.title: Keep a running total
ai-2/11.studentExplanation: Use a paper table with one row per cupboard and columns for capacity, used, spare and running total. Start the running total at 0 once. The first cupboard contributes 8 minus 3, or 5; the total becomes 5. The second contributes 6 minus 6, or 0; the total stays 5. The accumulator is like a collection box: empty it before collecting, rather than emptying it before every item.
ai-2/11.teacherPrompt: Model the worked example using the explanation below. Pause after each decision and ask learners to predict the next value or reason. Use the chapter’s guided answer to discuss their responses; collect W4 before showing its solution.

ai-2/12.title: Give each test a job
ai-2/12.studentExplanation: A useful test includes an input and an answer calculated from the written rule before the program runs. For 8 spaces with 3 used, expect 5 left. For 8 used, expect 0. For none used, expect 8. These cases ask different questions. An incorrect addition rule happens to pass the unused case because adding zero and subtracting zero give the same result. That is why one passing example is weak evidence.
ai-2/12.teacherPrompt: Model the worked example using the explanation below. Pause after each decision and ask learners to predict the next value or reason. Use the chapter’s guided answer to discuss their responses; collect W4 before showing its solution.

ai-2/13.title: Check a row in separate steps
ai-2/13.studentExplanation: A schema is a checklist for what a row must contain. First ask whether the activity name is text and is not empty. Next ask whether minutes is an integer. Then ask whether that integer lies between 0 and 60, including both ends. Keep these checks separate when explaining a rejection. The number 12 and the text "12" look similar on a page, but only the number meets this lesson’s minutes rule.
ai-2/13.teacherPrompt: Model the worked example using the explanation below. Pause after each decision and ask learners to predict the next value or reason. Use the chapter’s guided answer to discuss their responses; collect W4 before showing its solution.

ai-2/14.title: Keep zero separate from unknown
ai-2/14.studentExplanation: A recorded 0 says the measured duration was zero. A missing field says we do not have the duration. They are different statements. Trace each record with three columns: raw value, decision and reason. Keep 0 and 12; reject the absent value, -1 and None. The accepted list therefore has two values and the rejection count is three. Do not turn an unknown value into a number just to make the calculation run.
ai-2/14.teacherPrompt: Model the worked example using the explanation below. Pause after each decision and ask learners to predict the next value or reason. Use the chapter’s guided answer to discuss their responses; collect W4 before showing its solution.

ai-2/15.title: Convert before comparing
ai-2/15.studentExplanation: A minute contains 60 seconds. To express 180 seconds in minutes, divide 180 by 60 to get 3 minutes. The other value is already 4 minutes, so leave it at 4. Now both quantities use the same unit and can be compared. Keep the original number, unit and source beside the converted number. That record lets another person check whether you converted the correct measurement in the correct direction.
ai-2/15.teacherPrompt: Model the worked example using the explanation below. Pause after each decision and ask learners to predict the next value or reason. Use the chapter’s guided answer to discuss their responses; collect W4 before showing its solution.

ai-2/16.title: Name the group behind a percentage
ai-2/16.studentExplanation: Count the responses before dividing. In the example, three say Yes, one says No and one is Unknown. There are four known responses, so Yes among known responses is 3 divided by 4, or 75 percent. Yes among all five supplied responses is 3 divided by 5, or 60 percent. Neither number needs to be hidden. Label the question each answers, and keep the unknown count visible.
ai-2/16.teacherPrompt: Model the worked example using the explanation below. Pause after each decision and ask learners to predict the next value or reason. Use the chapter’s guided answer to discuss their responses; collect W4 before showing its solution.

ai-2/17.title: Use two summaries for two questions
ai-2/17.studentExplanation: The mean shares the total equally: 2 + 3 + 3 + 4 + 18 is 30, and 30 divided by five is 6. The median asks for the middle value after sorting: the third value is 3. The long duration 18 pulls the mean upwards but leaves the middle value at 3. A difference between the summaries is a clue to inspect the data, not permission to remove the inconvenient value.
ai-2/17.teacherPrompt: Model the worked example using the explanation below. Pause after each decision and ask learners to predict the next value or reason. Use the chapter’s guided answer to discuss their responses; collect W4 before showing its solution.

ai-2/18.title: Make bar lengths mean something
ai-2/18.studentExplanation: With a zero baseline, eight votes make a bar eight units high and ten votes make a bar ten units high. The difference is two votes. If the drawing begins at seven, only the extra one and three units are visible, making the second bar look three times as tall. That picture describes the part above seven, not the full counts. Use one scale, label the units and show the counts.
ai-2/18.teacherPrompt: Model the worked example using the explanation below. Pause after each decision and ask learners to predict the next value or reason. Use the chapter’s guided answer to discuss their responses; collect W4 before showing its solution.

ai-2/19.title: Match the people to the question
ai-2/19.studentExplanation: The population is everyone the question concerns. The sample is the smaller group whose responses you actually collect. If the question is about all Grade 7 students, a coding-club sample leaves other students out before the poll even starts. Separate the invitation process from the response process: some invited students may not reply. A report needs both counts so readers can see whose preferences might be missing.
ai-2/19.teacherPrompt: Model the worked example using the explanation below. Pause after each decision and ask learners to predict the next value or reason. Use the chapter’s guided answer to discuss their responses; collect W4 before showing its solution.

ai-2/20.title: Combine counts, not just percentages
ai-2/20.studentExplanation: The club has 8 Yes out of 10, and the other group has 2 Yes out of 10. Combine the Yes counts to get 10 and combine the response counts to get 20; the combined observed rate is 10 divided by 20, or 50 percent. When group sizes differ, simply averaging their percentages can give the wrong combined rate. A correct combined calculation still describes the collected sample, not automatically the whole school.
ai-2/20.teacherPrompt: Model the worked example using the explanation below. Pause after each decision and ask learners to predict the next value or reason. Use the chapter’s guided answer to discuss their responses; collect W4 before showing its solution.

ai-2/21.title: Separate a pattern from a cause
ai-2/21.studentExplanation: The three records show that higher practice time goes with higher scores. They do not tell us what would happen if the same learner practised for one more hour. Prior experience could make someone both practise more and score higher. That is a possible confounder: another influence connected to both quantities. First describe the pattern accurately. Then propose a comparison that addresses alternative explanations rather than treating the pattern as a guarantee.
ai-2/21.teacherPrompt: Model the worked example using the explanation below. Pause after each decision and ask learners to predict the next value or reason. Use the chapter’s guided answer to discuss their responses; collect W4 before showing its solution.

ai-2/22.title: Calculate a gap one feature at a time
ai-2/22.studentExplanation: Keep the features in the same order: energy first, group work second. For target [2,4] and Sketch [1,3], the gaps are abs(1-2)=1 and abs(3-4)=1; the distance is 2. Relay [5,4] has gaps 3 and 0, so its distance is 3. Smaller means closer under this particular rule. It does not mean better in every way, because the two recorded features leave out other needs.
ai-2/22.teacherPrompt: Model the worked example using the explanation below. Pause after each decision and ask learners to predict the next value or reason. Use the chapter’s guided answer to discuss their responses; collect W4 before showing its solution.

ai-2/23.title: Check must-have rules before scoring
ai-2/23.studentExplanation: Make two decisions in order. First check the duration: A takes 15 minutes and qualifies under the 20-minute limit; B takes 25 minutes and does not. Then calculate scores for eligible choices. A scores 2 times 4 plus 2, or 10. B would score 11, but that score cannot remove the time requirement. Keep the rejection reason beside B instead of calling it a worse-scoring activity.
ai-2/23.teacherPrompt: Model the worked example using the explanation below. Pause after each decision and ask learners to predict the next value or reason. Use the chapter’s guided answer to discuss their responses; collect W4 before showing its solution.

ai-2/24.title: Trace the best-so-far record
ai-2/24.studentExplanation: Write a trace table with item, eligible, score and best-so-far. In the worked list, B qualifies and scores 8, so B becomes the current best. A also qualifies and scores 8. The scores tie, so the written alphabetical rule changes the best to A. Starting with A gives the same final answer. If no item qualifies, best stays None; do not invent a winner or quietly relax the limit.
ai-2/24.teacherPrompt: Model the worked example using the explanation below. Pause after each decision and ask learners to predict the next value or reason. Use the chapter’s guided answer to discuss their responses; collect W4 before showing its solution.

ai-2/25.title: Separate file text from numbers
ai-2/25.studentExplanation: The file contains characters, not ready-made Python integers. Reading gives text; splitlines separates the lines; int converts each valid line into a number. The lines "12" and "8" become 12 and 8, so their total is 20. Keep those three stages visible in your trace. A line such as "twelve" fails conversion, and a missing file is a different problem. Neither failure means the observed duration was zero.
ai-2/25.teacherPrompt: Model the worked example using the explanation below. Pause after each decision and ask learners to predict the next value or reason. Use the chapter’s guided answer to discuss their responses; collect W4 before showing its solution.

ai-2/26.title: Check the envelope before its fields
ai-2/26.studentExplanation: JSON is a text format for exchanging values. Parsing asks whether the text follows that format. Schema checking asks whether the parsed value has the structure and values your task requires. Start by checking that the whole value is an object, represented here by a Python dictionary. Only then look up name and minutes. A valid JSON list is still the wrong top-level structure for this contract. Syntax success and acceptance are separate decisions.
ai-2/26.teacherPrompt: Model the worked example using the explanation below. Pause after each decision and ask learners to predict the next value or reason. Use the chapter’s guided answer to discuss their responses; collect W4 before showing its solution.

ai-2/27.title: Give each failure an honest result
ai-2/27.studentExplanation: Trace the function as a decision path. First try to turn the text into an integer. If that conversion raises ValueError, return invalid text and None. If conversion succeeds, check the range. A value outside 0 through 60 returns out of range and None. Only a value passing both stages returns ok and its number. None means there is no accepted number; it must not be added to a duration total.
ai-2/27.teacherPrompt: Model the worked example using the explanation below. Pause after each decision and ask learners to predict the next value or reason. Use the chapter’s guided answer to discuss their responses; collect W4 before showing its solution.

ai-2/28.title: Compare one planned change at a time
ai-2/28.studentExplanation: For the worked records, v1 gives A a score of 2 times 4 plus 1, or 9, and B a score of 2 times 2 plus 4, or 8. v2 gives A 4 plus 2 times 1, or 6, and B 2 plus 2 times 4, or 10. The winner changes because the weights changed. Keep the records fixed so this explanation can be checked. A different preference policy is not automatically a more accurate model.
ai-2/28.teacherPrompt: Model the worked example using the explanation below. Pause after each decision and ask learners to predict the next value or reason. Use the chapter’s guided answer to discuss their responses; collect W4 before showing its solution.

ai-2/29.title: Ask what each role actually needs
ai-2/29.studentExplanation: Least privilege means giving each role only the actions needed for its purpose. Read the policy as a table: students may read the approved summary, while teachers may also read the necessary review. An unknown role gets no listed action. The small function checks this table; it does not establish who a visitor is. In a real application, the server must verify the session and apply the permission check whenever protected data is requested.
ai-2/29.teacherPrompt: Model the worked example using the explanation below. Pause after each decision and ask learners to predict the next value or reason. Use the chapter’s guided answer to discuss their responses; collect W4 before showing its solution.

ai-2/30.title: Keep the denominator with the evidence
ai-2/30.studentExplanation: First filter the raw durations using the written schema. Keep 10, 0 and 20; reject None because the duration is unknown and -2 because it is outside the range. The accepted sum is 30 and the accepted count is three, so the accepted-record mean is 10 minutes. Dividing by all five supplied records would treat the two rejected durations as if they contributed known zeros. State three accepted out of five beside the mean.
ai-2/30.teacherPrompt: Model the worked example using the explanation below. Pause after each decision and ask learners to predict the next value or reason. Use the chapter’s guided answer to discuss their responses; collect W4 before showing its solution.

ai-2/31.title: Turn a wish into a checkable plan
ai-2/31.studentExplanation: A phrase such as make a smart choice does not say what counts as success. The chooser plan does: validate the named fields, include durations at most 20 minutes, calculate 2 times fun plus learning, and use alphabetical names to break a tie. Describe the expected output and a no-match result before coding. Another learner should be able to use your plan to predict the same answer without guessing what you intended.
ai-2/31.teacherPrompt: Model the worked example using the explanation below. Pause after each decision and ask learners to predict the next value or reason. Use the chapter’s guided answer to discuss their responses; collect W4 before showing its solution.

ai-2/32.title: Trace the hand-off between stages
ai-2/32.studentExplanation: Think of validation and selection as two desks. At the first desk, each record is checked for required fields, exact types and allowed ranges; a batch check also checks unique names. Only accepted records go to the second desk, where the time limit and scoring policy are applied. A record can be valid yet too long to qualify. Report rejected and ineligible separately so a reader knows which decision removed an item.
ai-2/32.teacherPrompt: Model the worked example using the explanation below. Pause after each decision and ask learners to predict the next value or reason. Use the chapter’s guided answer to discuss their responses; collect W4 before showing its solution.

ai-2/33.title: Test the connections as well as the pieces
ai-2/33.studentExplanation: A score unit test asks whether the scoring function calculates the specified number. An integration test asks whether validation, filtering, scoring and reporting work together. A correct score does not establish that invalid records were rejected or that a tie was resolved correctly. Predict the full report from the input records before running. Check its counts and reasons as well as its selected name, and repeat a tie case with reversed input order.
ai-2/33.teacherPrompt: Model the worked example using the explanation below. Pause after each decision and ask learners to predict the next value or reason. Use the chapter’s guided answer to discuss their responses; collect W4 before showing its solution.

ai-2/34.title: Look inside the overall result
ai-2/34.studentExplanation: The six development checks include ordinary, boundary, invalid, empty and tie cases. Five pass, but the only tie case fails. Saying five out of six pass is true; saying the tie rule works is false. Keep both statements visible. A category table helps you choose the next repair. Adding many copies of passing ordinary cases can raise the overall fraction without checking a new condition or fixing the failed requirement.
ai-2/34.teacherPrompt: Model the worked example using the explanation below. Pause after each decision and ask learners to predict the next value or reason. Use the chapter’s guided answer to discuss their responses; collect W4 before showing its solution.

ai-2/35.title: Repair the rule, then keep the evidence
ai-2/35.studentExplanation: At most includes equality. For a limit of 10, the durations 9 and 10 qualify while 11 does not. The strict comparison minutes < limit wrongly rejects 10; changing it to minutes <= limit repairs that boundary. Check below, at and above the boundary, then rerun earlier tie and invalid-input cases. Keep the original failure record so another person can understand what changed and which evidence supports the repair.
ai-2/35.teacherPrompt: Model the worked example using the explanation below. Pause after each decision and ask learners to predict the next value or reason. Use the chapter’s guided answer to discuss their responses; collect W4 before showing its solution.

ai-2/36.title: Explain a result so someone can check it
ai-2/36.studentExplanation: A useful handover joins a claim to its evidence. Show the fictional input records, the policy and version, which records passed validation, which met the time limit, the scores and any tie decision. Then show the report. Its counts should agree, but consistent counts alone do not prove the selected item is correct. Include an earlier failure and repair, and separate demonstrated software behaviour from educational benefits that have not been measured.
ai-2/36.teacherPrompt: Model the worked example using the explanation below. Pause after each decision and ask learners to predict the next value or reason. Use the chapter’s guided answer to discuss their responses; collect W4 before showing its solution.

ai-2/10.W1: Read the keys, rather than the positions: name labels the text Red, capacity labels 9, and used labels 2. The used value is therefore 2. Subtract the occupied spaces from the total: 9 - 2 = 7 spare spaces.
ai-2/10.W2: Only the used field is reassigned. Capacity stays 9 and used becomes 9, so the fresh calculation is 9 - 9 = 0. Ask learners to show the updated record before calculating, rather than reusing the earlier 7.
ai-2/10.W3: Dictionary keys distinguish uppercase from lowercase. The existing key is used; Used is a different key and is absent. Looking it up raises KeyError. Change the lookup to record["used"]. Adding Used would create a second field rather than repairing the intended lookup.

ai-2/11.W1: Count the dictionaries, not the fields: the list contains two records. In the second record, capacity is 6 and used is 6. Its spare contribution is 6 - 6 = 0. Zero is a known contribution, not a missing record.
ai-2/11.W2: Write total before and after each update: 0 + 2 = 2; 2 + 4 = 6; 6 + 1 = 7. The trace is 2, 6, 7. If a learner writes only 7, ask for the intermediate values to distinguish accumulation from a lucky final answer.

ai-2/12.W1: Apply the specified subtraction rule to each pair: 6 - 2 = 4, 6 - 6 = 0, and 6 - 0 = 6. Label them ordinary, full and unused cases. These expected answers come from the contract before the program is run.
ai-2/12.W2: Compare the faulty actual result 4 with each independently expected result. It matches the ordinary case expecting 4, but not the full case expecting 0 or unused case expecting 6. One successful case therefore does not establish that the subtraction rule was implemented.

ai-2/13.W1: Check both fields. activity must exist as nonempty text. minutes must be an exact integer and satisfy 0 <= minutes <= 60. Inclusive means equality is accepted at both ends. Structure, type and range are separate checks; passing them does not prove the duration was measured accurately.
ai-2/13.W2: Apply the inclusive range to each integer. Both 0 and 60 are on allowed boundaries. -1 is below the minimum and 61 is above the maximum. Require the reason for each rejection, not only pass/fail labels.

ai-2/14.W2: Process the four entries in order. The integers 4 and 0 have the required type and lie within 0 through 60, so keep [4, 0]. The integer 61 fails the upper boundary. The text "4" fails the exact integer type, even though its characters look numeric. That makes two rejected entries.

ai-2/15.W2: There are 60 seconds in one minute. Divide each seconds value by 60: 150/60 = 2.5 minutes and 30/60 = 0.5 minutes. Do not round away the half-minute. Check the direction by converting back: 2.5 times 60 is 150.
ai-2/15.W3: First put both values in the same unit. 120 seconds divided by 60 is 2 minutes. Now compare 2 minutes with 3 minutes: 3 minutes is longer by 1 minute. Comparing the raw numbers 120 and 3 without their units compares unlike quantities.

ai-2/17.W1: Add all five observations: 4 + 4 + 6 + 6 + 10 = 30. Divide by the number of observations, five, to obtain a mean of 6. Keep the count beside the calculation. Do not divide by the three distinct values; repeated observations still count.

ai-2/18.W1: One square represents two votes. Six equal squares therefore represent 6 times 2 = 12 votes. Ask the learner to name both the visible length and the unit scale before giving the count.
ai-2/18.W2: The count difference is 15 - 12 = 3 votes. Taking the larger count relative to the smaller gives 15/12 = 1.25, so 15 is 1.25 times 12, or 25 percent larger. Label which count is the reference for the ratio.

ai-2/19.W2: The numerator is seven respondents choosing longer lunch and the denominator is all twelve observed respondents. The fraction is 7/12, approximately 58.3 percent. Say “of these respondents”; the calculation alone supplies no evidence about the preferences of students who were not represented.

ai-2/22.W1: Use the declared feature order: position 0 means energy and position 1 means group work. The vector [4,1] therefore records energy 4 and group work 1. Reversing the interpretation would change the meaning and could change the distance calculation.

ai-2/23.W1: Substitute each rating into its named role: 2 * fun + learning = 2 * 2 + 4 = 4 + 4 = 8. Eligibility is supplied in this task, so this calculation ranks an already permitted option. The score is a result of the chosen preference rule, not a measured educational benefit.
ai-2/23.W2: At most 20 means minutes <= 20. The value 19 is below the limit and 20 is exactly at it, so both qualify. The value 21 is above it and is excluded. An answer that rejects 20 has changed the inclusive requirement into a strict one.

ai-2/24.W2: For the empty list, the loop has no iterations, so best stays None. With the worked durations 10 and 9 under a limit of 8, neither item passes the eligibility check, so best again stays None. The caller must turn this result into a clear no-eligible-option message; it must not treat None as an activity name.

ai-2/25.W1: Before conversion, "8" is a string containing the character 8. int("8") returns the integer 8, which can participate in numeric arithmetic. The conversion does not change the original file and does not establish that the number meets the duration schema.

ai-2/26.W1: Parsing JSON null produces Python None, while serialising Python True produces JSON true. The spelling belongs to the representation: lowercase true is JSON text, not the Python Boolean name True. Keep parsing and serialisation directions clear.
ai-2/26.W5: No. Parsing checks JSON syntax. The schema separately checks the expected fields, types and ranges. Collection evidence is a third question: even a well-formed, schema-valid duration could have been measured or recorded incorrectly.

ai-2/28.W2: The weight pair is (fun weight, learning weight). Under (2,1), the score is 2*3 + 1*2 = 8. Under (1,2), it is 1*3 + 2*2 = 7. The same ratings were kept fixed; the difference comes from changing the preference policy.

ai-2/29.W2: Look up the requested action in the list for each role. The teacher list contains read_review, so that request is permitted. unknown has no policy entry; get supplies an empty list, which does not contain read_summary. This models a permission decision after a role is trusted; it does not authenticate a visitor.

ai-2/31.W2: Choose two individually valid records with unique names A and B, scores 8 each and durations within the limit. Both survive validation and filtering, then tie on score. The name rule selects A in either order. Require actual record fields so the proposed test can be reproduced, rather than accepting an unexplained winner name.

ai-2/32.W2: When learning is absent, row.get("learning") returns None. The condition type(value) is not int is true, so the helper returns False before doing the range comparison. This is a schema rejection; it is different from a valid item that later exceeds the selection time limit.

ai-2/33.W2: Calculate the expected score from the written rule: 2*4 + 3 = 11. Record 11 before running score. Computing the expectation by calling the same score function would allow a shared implementation error to appear on both sides of the comparison.

ai-2/34.W2: Use ordinary eligible selection, duration boundaries, schema-invalid records, empty or no-match input, and tied scores with reversed order. Each category checks a different requirement. Include concrete inputs and expected reports; five copies of one ordinary case do not provide this coverage.

ai-2/35.W1: If minutes equals limit, minutes < limit evaluates to False because the comparison is strict. The phrase at most includes equality, so the validated-duration predicate must be minutes <= limit. Test below, at and above the limit to reveal this difference.
ai-2/35.W2: With limit 15, compare each value using <=: 14 <= 15 is True, 15 <= 15 is True, and 16 <= 15 is False. Keep equality visible as the boundary case rather than testing only clearly short and clearly long activities.
ai-2/35.W3: Set minutes to 16 and limit to 15. The proposed condition checks 16 <= 16 and accepts it, but the requirement checks 16 <= 15 and rejects it. This single counterexample demonstrates that adding one to the limit changed the policy rather than repairing it.

ai-3/15.W1: Predicted positives include true positives and false positives, so add TP + FP to get 7. Reference positives include true positives and false negatives, so add TP + FN to get 4. These are different groups: one is defined by the prediction, the other by the reference label.

ai-3/17.W1: Use each group’s observed positive count over its observed total: 2/10 = 0.2 and 6/10 = 0.6. These are sample frequencies for the worked groups. Do not turn either small-group observation into a guarantee about the next individual or a proof of calibration.

ai-3/20.W1: For the mean baseline, sum the worked training targets and divide by their count to obtain 6. For the median baseline, sort the training targets and take the middle value, 5. Freeze these choices before examining evaluation targets; choosing a new constant from evaluation outcomes would contaminate the comparison.
ai-3/20.W2: For constant 6, absolute errors on targets 4 and 8 are 2 and 2, so MAE is (2+2)/2 = 2. For constant 5, the errors are 1 and 3, so MAE is (1+3)/2 = 2. Equal averages can hide different per-record errors; retain the error table as well as the summary.

ai-3/21.W1: MAE uses absolute residual sizes, so add 1, 2 and 3 and divide by three: (1+2+3)/3 = 2 cm. Positive and negative signed residuals must not cancel in this calculation. State centimetres because absolute error retains the target unit.
ai-3/21.W2: Square the residual sizes to get 1, 4 and 9; their mean is 14/3 square centimetres. Take the square root to obtain RMSE sqrt(14/3), approximately 2.16 cm. MSE and RMSE describe related quantities but have different units.

ai-3/26.W1: For the stated 20-row condition, add the run results 5, 7 and 6 to obtain 18 and divide by three to obtain mean 6. Range is largest minus smallest: 7 - 5 = 2. Keep the number of repeated runs distinct from the number of data rows.

ai-4/7.W1: Each of two outputs connects to all four inputs, giving 4*2 = 8 weights. Each output has one bias, giving 2 biases. The total adjustable scalar values is therefore 8+2 = 10. Ask learners to point to connections and outputs so they do not confuse inputs with parameter counts.

ai-4/10.W1: At the worked input x=2, the prediction is w*x+b = 1*2+1 = 3. The target is 3, so the prediction-minus-target residual is 0 and squared loss is 0. Both gradient components contain this residual factor, so the gradient is [0,0] for this single case. A zero gradient here does not establish performance on every other case.

ai-5/4.W2: Under the lesson’s supplied temperature procedure, T=0.5 means exponent 1/T=2. Square the weights to obtain 0.36, 0.09 and 0.01; their total is 0.46. Divide each by 0.46 to obtain 18/23, 9/46 and 1/46. Converting 18/23 to 36/46 shows that the sum is (36+9+1)/46 = 1.

ai-5/6.W2: Multiply each coordinate by its value’s weight: 0.5*[2,0]=[1,0], 0.25*[0,4]=[0,1], and 0.25*[4,2]=[1,0.5]. Add first coordinates to get 1+0+1=2 and second coordinates to get 0+1+0.5=1.5. The combined vector is [2,1.5], not a literal selection of one source token.

ai-5/7.W1: The dot products are 1*0=0 and 1*ln(3)=ln(3). Division by sqrt(d)=sqrt(1)=1 leaves them unchanged. Exponentiation gives 1 and 3, with total 4. Normalising gives weights 1/4 and 3/4. These are compatibility weights under the stated calculation, not truth scores.
ai-5/7.W3: The query has dot product 1 with each key. Both scores are therefore 1/sqrt(2). Equal scores give equal softmax weights, 0.5 each. Combine the values coordinate by coordinate: 0.5*[2,0] + 0.5*[0,4] = [1,2].

ai-5/8.W1: Follow the stated operations in order: z=h+A=[1,2]+[3,-1]=[4,1]. Both coordinates are positive, so the supplied ReLU map gives F(z)=[4,1]. The next residual addition is z+F(z), giving r=[8,2]. Do not substitute h for z in that second skip addition.

ai-5/10.W1: Separate the total budget into its declared parts: 100 minus 20 instruction units minus 10 question units minus 20 reserved output units leaves 50 units for evidence. Preserve the output reserve before filling evidence space. These are the lesson’s supplied token units, not a universal word-to-token conversion.

ai-1/1.title: Evidence and decision mechanisms
goals: Distinguish an observed result from an explanation of how it was produced
Identify written rules, learned models and human decisions inside one product
Explain what additional evidence is needed when a mechanism is unknown

prerequisite.prompt: A classroom clock speaks the time. Write one thing you observed and one thing you cannot determine just from hearing it.
prerequisite.answer: You observed spoken time. Speech alone does not tell you whether the message was selected by a timetable, a learned system or a person.

vocabulary: The process that produces a result
An instruction specified by a person before the system applies it
A system whose adjustable values were fitted using examples
Information that supports or challenges a particular claim
A product that combines more than one kind of process

lesson.title: One display can hide several decisions

blocks.text: The school bus display says DELAY 12 MINUTES in red. Leila calls it AI because it predicted the delay. Arun calls it a simple rule because the number turned red. Both have noticed a real part of the product, but neither has explained the whole system. To investigate, ask which decision you are talking about and what evidence reveals how that decision was made.

An output is what a system produces. A mechanism is how it produces that output. Seeing a red number establishes its colour; it does not reveal where the number came from. Similar outputs can come from different mechanisms, and one product can contain several mechanisms.

For this lesson we have an engineering note: the delay estimator was fitted using records of earlier bus journeys; a person wrote the colour instruction; and the driver can replace the message. These are supplied facts for our classroom case. In a real investigation, we would need trustworthy documentation, a demonstration of the process or another source of mechanism evidence.

blocks.title: The bus display contains three mechanisms
rows: Delay model fitted on earlier journeys
Written rule red when delay is greater than 10
blocks.caption: Read each row from left to right. The first row predicts a number, the second chooses a colour, and the third shows a human override. A correct colour does not establish that the delay prediction is correct.

blocks.text: In the first row, fitting means adjusting a model using examples. Applying the fitted model to a new journey is a different step. The model can produce an incorrect estimate even if it was trained carefully. In the second row, a written threshold compares the estimate with 10. It can follow its instructions perfectly while using a bad estimate. In the third row, a person makes the message decision.

AI is a broader field than learning from examples. It also includes approaches that represent knowledge and reason with rules. Therefore, do not use the shortcut that every rule is non-AI. In this case, a simple colour switch is ordinary automation; identifying that switch does not classify every other part of the bus system.

Question: Does the red display prove that a learned model was used? First separate the claim from the observation. The observation is that the displayed number is red. The claim concerns the process that produced the number. Next find relevant evidence. The engineering note says earlier journeys were used to fit the delay estimator. That note supports a learned-model classification for the estimator. The red colour alone does not.

rows: The estimator uses a learned model
The note describes fitting on past journeys
Only the displayed colour is observed
The driver override is a model prediction
A driver selects the replacement message

blocks.text: A strong answer states its limit: I can identify these three mechanisms from the supplied note, but I cannot infer the model's accuracy from one estimate. Even if the bus arrives exactly 12 minutes late, one success does not establish that the estimator will always work.

lesson.title: Finish an explanation with less help

blocks.text: A photo library predicts whether a picture contains a bicycle using a model fitted to labelled pictures. A written rule places all bicycle predictions in one album. The owner can move any photo to a different album. Complete the explanation in your workbook: the prediction stage is ___ because ___; the automatic album step is ___ because ___; the manual move is ___.

If a photograph lands in the wrong album, do not immediately blame the written album rule. The prediction might have been wrong, the album rule might have been implemented incorrectly, or a person might have moved the photo. Inspect the intermediate prediction and the action record to distinguish these causes.

blocks.label: Complete the three classifications and name one record that would help diagnose a misplaced photo

lesson.title: Use a question that could change your mind

blocks.text: A robot vacuum is advertised as smart. The advertisement tells you almost nothing about its decisions. A useful question is not Does it look intelligent? Ask instead how it selects a route, whether adjustable values were fitted using examples, or when a person supplies a command. It may combine several answers.

Sometimes the honest conclusion is that the mechanism is unknown. That is a precise answer when you identify the missing evidence. It is weaker to guess a mechanism and then treat your guess as a fact. Keep observations, supplied evidence and assumptions separate in your investigation.

blocks.label: A device speaks a correct answer. Explain why neither speech nor correctness alone identifies its mechanism

workbook.title: Separate observations from explanations
workbook.prompt: A door opens when a visitor approaches. Its label says intelligent entrance. List two observations and write one mechanism question whose answer would help classify the opening decision.
workbook.answer: Observations include that the door opened when the visitor approached and that its label says intelligent entrance. A useful question asks whether a written sensor threshold, a model fitted on examples or a person controls opening. The label is an observed marketing claim, not mechanism evidence.

workbook.title: Complete the photo library explanation
workbook.prompt: Use the photo-library case from the lesson. Classify the prediction, album-placement rule and owner move. A bicycle photo is in the wrong album. Name the first two records you would inspect.
workbook.answer: Prediction is learned because it was fitted using labelled pictures. Album placement is a written rule; the owner move is human control. Inspect the stored prediction and the placement or move record. A wrong album alone cannot distinguish prediction error from a later action.

workbook.title: Challenge an unsupported conclusion
workbook.prompt: Maya says a vacuum must learn because it changes direction after hitting a chair. Give two different mechanisms consistent with that observation. What evidence would distinguish them?
workbook.answer: A written contact-sensor rule could turn the vacuum, or a learned navigation model could choose a turn. A person could also control it. Documentation of the route-selection process or a controlled trace could distinguish these mechanisms. Direction change alone is insufficient.

workbook.title: Investigate a new hybrid system
workbook.prompt: A school greenhouse estimates tomorrow's temperature using a model fitted on historical weather. A written rule displays CHECK PLANTS above 30 degrees C. A caretaker chooses whether to open a vent. Identify each mechanism and explain why a correct CHECK PLANTS message would not prove an accurate temperature prediction.
workbook.answer: The forecast is learned-model prediction; the message is a written threshold; vent opening is the caretaker's decision. The message may correctly follow a forecast that is itself inaccurate. Compare the forecast with a predefined temperature observation at the relevant place and time before judging prediction accuracy.

workbook.title: Design an evidence card
workbook.prompt: Invent one product containing two mechanisms. State the supplied facts, draw an information path and write one claim the facts support and one they do not. Do not use real classmates' personal information.
workbook.answer: Accept a coherent case such as a trained speech recogniser supplying text to a written keyword rule. The support must connect to supplied facts, and the unsupported claim must exceed them, such as assuming perfect recognition. Check that the learner distinguishes the two decisions rather than merely naming two devices.

teacher.background: Avoid making AI a yes-or-no property of a whole product before defining the component and decision. Modern learned models and symbolic reasoning both belong in the broader AI discussion. The learning goal here is evidence-based mechanism classification, not memorising a list of smart objects. Do not infer training from responsiveness, language, movement or one correct output.
materials: The bus diagram and photo-library case from the student chapter
Blank paper and three colours of pencil
A copy of workbook tasks W1 to W5; no online accounts or real student data
sessions: Ask the clock prerequisite question. Record observed and inferred statements in separate columns. Read two examples aloud without praising a guess as a fact.
Read the bus case. Trace each row of the diagram with a finger. Ask which decision each row makes. Say that a product can combine mechanisms.
Model the red-display question using claim, relevant evidence and conclusion. Cover the final table row and ask students to justify it.
Pairs complete the photo-library explanation and W1. Listen for a distinction between a predicted label and an album action.
Retrieve the distinction with the speaking-device exit question. Revisit the diagram if students rely on appearance.
Complete W2 and W3 in pairs. Each partner must offer a different possible cause of a misplaced photo or direction change.
Collect W4 as an independent assessment. Do not display its solution or substitute a hinted answer for an independent attempt.
Discuss one anonymised explanation and set W5 as extension or the next opening task. Record which prerequisite needs reteaching.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Prediction stage is learned because labelled examples were used to fit the model; album placement follows the stated written rule; the owner move is human control. Inspect the predicted label and the album action record. A correct answer from a speaking device does not identify the mechanism because recordings, rules, learned models and human messages can all produce speech.
misconceptions: All rules are outside AI
Explain that AI also includes symbolic reasoning. In the specific bus case, the simple colour threshold is automation; the full system contains a fitted predictor.
A correct output proves a learned model
Ask whether a calculator, recording or person could produce the same correct output. Require evidence about fitting or reasoning.
Unknown is a bad answer
Accept unknown when the learner identifies a specific missing fact and a useful way to obtain it.
teacher.assessment: For W4, require all three components classified with their supplied evidence and an explanation that a downstream rule can operate correctly on a wrong estimate. A label without supporting evidence is developing. If the learner says the display proves accuracy, return to the two bus rows and ask what each row actually checks. After feedback, assess a fresh case rather than awarding independent mastery for the corrected W4 answer.
teacher.support: Read the cases aloud and let students use arrows or spoken explanations. Supply the three mechanism labels if vocabulary is the barrier, but record that support. Extension students should design two mechanisms producing the same output and propose evidence that would distinguish them.
teacher.next: Week 2 follows how information is represented and changed between components. Keep the three-row bus diagram: the delay number and the warning colour are different representations of related information.

ai-1/10.title: Conditions and boundary cases
goals: Evaluate a condition using the current state and trace only the selected branch
Distinguish inclusive and strict boundaries using values below, at and above a threshold
Design a boundary test and handle an unknown input without silently treating it as false

prerequisite.prompt: Score starts at 4. Add 2 to score, then double it. Which value is doubled, and what is the final score?
prerequisite.answer: The addition changes score to 6, so the next instruction doubles 6 and produces 12. Each instruction reads the current state.

vocabulary: A test whose result is true or false when the required information is known
The instruction or group of instructions selected by a condition
The value used as a comparison boundary
A boundary whose equality case is included
A test using a value at or close to a point where behaviour can change

lesson.title: A condition selects what happens next

blocks.text: A paper game updates a score with this procedure: add 2 to score; if score is at least 6, subtract 3 from score; otherwise add 4 to score; report score and stop. The if and otherwise instructions form one if/else decision. Exactly one of those branches runs each time this decision is reached.

A condition asks whether a statement is true for the current state. At least 6 means 6 or any larger number. If score is 6, the condition is true. If score is 5, it is false. The condition itself does not change score; the chosen branch performs the update.

Start score at 4. First add 2, giving 6. Now test the current 6: the condition is true, so subtract 3 and report 3. Testing the original 4 would choose the wrong branch. Write the state immediately before the condition so the evidence for the choice is visible.

Compare the three values immediately around the threshold. These are the values when the condition is reached, after the initial add-2 instruction. Testing only a value far above 6 would not show whether equality was handled correctly.

blocks.title: Three checks around the threshold
rows: At least 6 is false so add 4
At least 6 is true so subtract 3
At least 6 is true so subtract 3
blocks.caption: At least includes equality. The middle row is essential for checking this boundary. Read each row as a separate run; do not pass the result of one row into the next.

blocks.text: Above 6 is different: it means strictly greater than 6, so 6 itself does not pass. At most 6 means 6 or smaller. Below 6 means strictly smaller, so it excludes 6. Say the equality case aloud before using one of these phrases.

A condition can be true even when its chosen action makes the number smaller. True describes the test result; it does not mean good, bigger, or a successful game. The written instructions define the action.

lesson.title: Trace the selected branch exactly once

blocks.text: In the first run, the false branch increases 5 to 9. That does not make the earlier decision run again. The procedure has already chosen and carried out the otherwise branch, so it moves on to report and stop. Subtracting 3 afterward would incorrectly run both branches and report 6.

This rule applies to one if/else decision. A later, separate condition would be a new test of the state at that later point. Do not invent an extra test or loop because the value crossed the threshold. Follow only the instructions in the procedure.

lesson.title: Use a test that exposes the mistake

blocks.text: Suppose a copied procedure says above 6 instead of at least 6. A score of 5 at the condition takes the false branch under both versions. A score of 7 takes the true branch under both. But exactly 6 separates them: the intended version subtracts 3 and gives 3; the copied version adds 4 and gives 10.

blocks.label: Choose an initial score that reaches exactly 6 after the first add-2 instruction. Trace both the intended at-least version and the copied above version. Explain why this test reveals an error that the neighbouring values can miss

blocks.text: Record the initial value, the value at the condition, the true or false result, and the chosen update. A final number alone may not reveal whether the test or the arithmetic was wrong. Keep the expected behaviour tied to the stated policy instead of changing it to match a result.

lesson.title: Do not invent a value for missing evidence

blocks.text: Our examples so far use known whole-number scores. If score is unreadable when the test is reached, we cannot establish whether it is at least 6. Unknown does not mean false, and a blank is not automatically zero. For this paper exercise, pause the procedure and request the missing value before selecting a branch.

A complete procedure must specify what to do when required input is unavailable. Another system might define a separate fallback, but it must be written explicitly. Testing below, at and above the boundary checks comparison behaviour; it does not replace a missing-input policy or prove every possible implementation correct.

blocks.label: A tester checks only scores 2 and 10 at the condition and says the at-least-6 comparison is correct. Which additional value is most useful for detecting an accidental above-6 comparison, and why

workbook.title: Trace a decision from the current score
workbook.prompt: Use the paper-game procedure: add 2 to score; if score is at least 6 subtract 3, otherwise add 4; report and stop. Start at 2, then make a separate run starting at 5. For each run record the value at the condition, its true or false result, the branch and the final score.
workbook.answer: Start 2: after adding 2 score is 4; at least 6 is false; add 4 and report 8. Start 5: after adding 2 score is 7; at least 6 is true; subtract 3 and report 4. Each run starts fresh and executes only its selected branch.

workbook.title: Read four boundary phrases
workbook.prompt: The known value at a condition is exactly 6. Decide whether each test is true or false: at least 6; above 6; at most 6; below 6. Explain which phrases include equality. Then name one value below and one value above 6 for neighbouring tests.
workbook.answer: At least 6 is true, above 6 is false, at most 6 is true, and below 6 is false. At least and at most include equality; above and below are strict. The nearest whole-number neighbours are 5 and 7; other correctly identified lower and higher values are valid but are less close to the boundary.

workbook.title: Stop after the selected branch
workbook.prompt: In a separate decision the current score is 4. If score is at least 5 subtract 2; otherwise add 3; report and stop. A learner adds 3 to get 7, then subtracts 2 because 7 is now at least 5, and reports 5. Identify the extra action and give the correct trace and result.
workbook.answer: The condition at score 4 is false, so only the otherwise branch runs. Add 3 to get 7, then report 7 and stop. The extra subtraction incorrectly runs the other branch after the decision. Crossing the threshold does not repeat the test in this if/else procedure.

workbook.title: Transfer the method to a new display
workbook.prompt: A paper brightness display adds 3 to its starting number. If the current brightness is at most 7, subtract 2; otherwise add 1. Report and stop. Trace separate runs from starting values 3, 4 and 5. Identify the run that tests equality. Then show how its result changes if at most 7 is accidentally written as below 7.
workbook.answer: Start 3: 6 at the test, true, subtract 2, report 4. Start 4: 7 at the test, true, subtract 2, report 5. Start 5: 8 at the test, false, add 1, report 9. Starting at 4 tests equality. With below 7, the current 7 fails, so add 1 and report 8 instead of 5. All three runs use current values after adding 3.

workbook.title: Handle an unknown input explicitly
workbook.prompt: The score is unreadable at the at-least-6 test. A helper says the test must be false and takes the otherwise branch. Explain what is unknown and why that choice is unjustified. State the next step required by this paper exercise and give two possible scores that would select different branches.
workbook.answer: The score value, and therefore the truth of the comparison, is unknown. It could be 5, which selects otherwise, or 6, which selects the true branch. Neither is established by an unreadable value. Pause and request the missing score as specified; do not silently replace it with zero or treat the test as false.

teacher.background: This week combines current-state tracing with a single if/else decision. Use known whole-number scores first, then explicitly introduce missing input. Separate testing a condition from updating a value. At least and at most include equality; above and below exclude it. Exactly one branch runs for each decision reached. A changed value does not cause the decision to repeat unless another test is explicitly specified. All game and brightness examples are paper simulations.
materials: A score box, an add-2 card, and a paired if/otherwise instruction card with report and stop beneath it
A three-column trace headed Current value, Test result and Chosen update, plus cards 5, 6 and 7
The brightness-display task from W4 for independent work, and one unreadable-value card
sessions: Retrieve the current-state rule from Week 9 using start 4, add 2, double. Record 4,6,12 before introducing a condition.
Model the paper-game procedure from initial score 4. Mark the value 6 at the test and show that the test itself changes no value.
Compare values 5,6,7 at the condition. Say equality aloud for at least, above, at most and below. Keep separate runs visually separate.
Complete W1 and W2 in pairs. Require a true/false result and chosen branch alongside each final value.
Trace initial score 3 to current 5, then false branch to 9. Point to report and stop so crossing the threshold does not trigger another branch.
Use W3 to diagnose running both branches. Complete the guided equality test and compare expected versus copied instructions.
Collect W4 independently. Check whether students evaluate at most on 6,7,8 rather than on the starting 3,4,5.
Use W5 to distinguish unknown from false. Discuss the exit test and preview explicitly repeated tests in loops.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Choose initial score 4: add 2 to reach 6. Under at least 6, the test is true and subtracting 3 gives 3. Under above 6, it is false and adding 4 gives 10. Equality distinguishes the versions; test values 5 and 7 do not. The exit answer is 6 at the condition, since it is included by at least but excluded by above. If testing from the start of the whole procedure, use initial 4 to reach that value.
misconceptions: The condition reads the starting value
Trace the initial add-2 instruction first and circle its result before evaluating the comparison.
At least means strictly above
Put 6 on the boundary and read at least as 6 or more. Compare its true result with above 6, which is false.
Crossing the threshold runs the other branch
Follow the chosen branch to report and stop. A second test must be explicitly written; it is not implied by the new value.
An unknown value makes the test false
Show that the unreadable value could be 5 or 6. Different possibilities select different branches, so the exercise requires a pause and clarification.
teacher.assessment: W4 is secure when the learner traces all three runs, applies the test to the updated value, includes equality for at most, and explains the changed output under below. A final answer without a branch reason is partial evidence. After support, retry with add 2 followed by if current value is at most 5 subtract 1, otherwise add 2. From starts 2,3,4, the correct final values are 3,4,8 respectively.
teacher.support: Provide a number line with the boundary labelled and let students read each comparison in words. Use text labels True branch and Otherwise branch in addition to colour. Supply a blank trace with the comparison row highlighted. Extension: explain why checking 5,6,7 is useful but does not prove a program correct for every possible input or every unrelated implementation error.
teacher.next: Week 11 introduces loops and stopping rules. Students will distinguish one decision from an explicitly repeated test and trace when a loop stops.

ai-1/11.title: Loops and stopping rules
goals: Trace a loop by testing its condition before every repetition
Distinguish the number of repetitions from the final value and include zero repetitions
Explain why an update reaches a stopping condition or why a faulty loop keeps repeating

prerequisite.prompt: Score is 4. If score is below 5, add 3; otherwise subtract 2. Report and stop. Does reaching 7 cause another test? Explain.
prerequisite.answer: The test is true, so add 3 and report 7. This single decision does not repeat. Another test must be explicitly specified.

vocabulary: Instructions that repeat according to a stated rule
One execution of the repeated body
The instructions performed on each iteration
The situation in which repetition ends
A change that brings the state closer to a stopping condition

blocks.text: A paper counter starts at 1. While the counter is below 7, add 2 to it. When the test is false, report the counter and stop. The word while means test first, run the body only if true, then return to the test using the updated value. The body here is just add 2.

The counter follows 1, 3, 5, 7. At 1, 3 and 5 the condition is true, so each test is followed by one addition. At 7 the condition is false. No addition follows that final test. The loop has three iterations and reports 7.

Compare the Week 10 instruction if counter is below 7, add 2, then report. From 1 that single decision reports 3. A while loop explicitly returns to its test; an if decision does not. Draw a pointer to the instruction being executed instead of deciding for yourself when to repeat.

blocks.title: A complete loop trace
blocks.caption: Read the rows from top to bottom as one run. Each true test performs one addition and returns to the test. The final false test performs no addition.

blocks.text: The trace has four tests but only three iterations. The false test is evidence that this run stops. A list ending at 5 would be incomplete, while a list continuing to 9 would include an addition the loop did not authorise.

Write the current value, the test result and the action on every row. Repeated values can matter: if the body does not change the state used by the test, the same true test may occur again. Do not erase these rows simply because they look unhelpful.

lesson.title: Check starts that need no repetitions

blocks.text: While tests before the body. If the first test is false, the body runs zero times. Do not add 2 once just because a loop is present. Starting at 7 or 8 is a useful test of this rule.

A loop that stops when the counter is no longer below 7 does not promise to finish at exactly 7. Starting at 6 produces 8. Passing the boundary is allowed by these instructions. Always report the actual final state instead of replacing it with the threshold.

lesson.title: Explain why the state reaches a stop

blocks.text: For our known whole-number counters below 7, adding 2 makes the counter larger each time. After enough additions it is at least 7, so the test becomes false. This explains why this loop stops for these inputs; one successful trace alone would not establish that for every possible procedure.

Now change the body to add 0. Starting at 1 gives the same value 1 at every test. Below 7 remains true, and the loop never reaches its reporting instruction. A classroom trace should be stopped by the teacher after the repeated state is established. That intervention is not a successful program result.

blocks.label: Compare the original add 2 loop from starting counter 3 with the faulty add 0 version. Record enough test rows to justify each conclusion. Explain the difference between the final reported value and a value merely seen during a non stopping run

lesson.title: Check both the rule and the update

blocks.text: A different mistake says while counter is not equal to 7, add 2. From 6 the values are 6, 8, 10 and then larger even numbers. None is 7, so this equality test never becomes false. A growing number does not guarantee termination: the update must be able to reach a state that makes this particular test false.

Our paper examples use known whole numbers without a maximum size. For this lesson, an unreadable starting counter means pause and request the value. It does not mean start at zero. Later programs will need explicit rules for unavailable inputs and resource limits.

blocks.label: A tester runs the below 7 loop only from starting counter 1. Choose one additional start that checks zero repetitions and one that checks passing the boundary without landing on it. Give the expected reported values

workbook.title: Trace every test
workbook.prompt: Start counter at 2. While counter is below 8, add 2. When false, report and stop. Record the value and result at every test, including the final false test. State the number of iterations and the reported value.
workbook.answer: Tests: 2 true, 4 true, 6 true, 8 false. Three additions are three iterations. The loop reports 8; the fourth test does not run the body.

workbook.title: Check the first test
