workbook.prompt: Use the same below 8 loop with add 2. Make separate runs from 8 and 9. Explain how many times the body runs and what each run reports. Why would adding 2 once be an error?
workbook.answer: Both first tests are false. Each run has zero iterations, reporting its unchanged starting value: 8 or 9. Adding 2 once would execute the body despite a false first test.

workbook.title: Find the extra repetition
workbook.prompt: Start counter at 3. While counter is below 8, add 2. A learner writes values 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 and reports 11. Identify the first unauthorised update. Give the correct final test, reported value and iteration count.
workbook.answer: After 7 becomes 9, the next test 9 below 8 is false. The update from 9 to 11 is unauthorised. Report 9 after three iterations, with test rows 3 true, 5 true, 7 true, 9 false.

workbook.title: Transfer to a countdown
workbook.prompt: A paper countdown starts at 7. While remaining is above 1, subtract 2. When false, report and stop. Trace the run and count iterations. Repeat from 6 and from 1. Explain why the final value need not equal 1. What happens from 7 if subtract 2 is replaced by subtract 0?
workbook.answer: From 7: 7 true, 5 true, 3 true, 1 false; three iterations, report 1. From 6: 6 true, 4 true, 2 true, 0 false; three iterations, report 0. From 1: first test false, zero iterations, report 1. Above 1 stops at 1 or below. Subtracting 0 from 7 leaves every test true, so that faulty run never reports.

workbook.title: Test a proposed stopping rule
workbook.prompt: A procedure says start at 4; while counter is not equal to 9, add 2; report and stop. Write the first four values tested. Explain why the loop will not reach 9 using whole numbers. Suggest a changed condition that would stop once the counter reaches or passes 9, and trace that repaired run.
workbook.answer: The first four values are 4, 6, 8, 10. Adding 2 to an even number always gives another even number, so the counter cannot become the odd number 9. Change the condition to while counter is below 9. Then 4 true, 6 true, 8 true, 10 false; three iterations and report 10.

teacher.background: Teach a pretest while loop with exact whole-number arithmetic. Track the instruction pointer, current state, test result and body count separately. Use both zero-iteration and boundary-crossing cases. The termination explanations depend on the stated update and condition; do not claim that every increasing counter terminates. Faulty loops are paper traces, stopped by the teacher once the reason for repetition is clear.
materials: A counter card, a while condition card and a separate body card with an arrow back to the condition
A trace sheet with current value, true or false and action columns, plus a separate iteration tally
Starting-value cards including 1, 6, 7 and 8, and an add 0 fault card
sessions: Retrieve the single-decision example from Week 10. Establish that reaching a different value does not create repetition without an instruction to return.
Model start 1, while below 7 add 2. Move a pointer between test and body and include the final false test at 7. Tally only body executions.
Compare starts 6, 7 and 8. Require students to predict before tracing. Explain overshoot and zero iterations using the written condition.
Complete W1 and W2 in pairs. Check that learners distinguish four tests from three iterations and never run the body after a false first test.
Use W3 to retrieve stopping behaviour. Ask students to identify the first extra update before discussing the final answer.
Complete the guided comparison of add 2 and add 0. Stop the physical demonstration after repeated identical states and ask whether the program itself reached report.
Collect W4 independently. A decreasing countdown checks transfer beyond the upward counter. Require the final false test on each finite run.
Discuss W5 and the exit tests. Explain why exact equality may be unreachable. Preview finding the first step where expected and observed behaviour differ.
teacher.guidedAnswer: From 3 under add 2: 3 true, 5 true, 7 false; two iterations and report 7. Under add 0: 3 true repeatedly, with no change and no report. Seeing 3 during that faulty run is not a returned result. For the exit, start 7 or any larger whole number checks zero iterations and reports that start. Start 6 checks crossing the boundary and reports 8 after one iteration.
misconceptions: Every loop runs at least once
Point to the test before the body. From 7 under below 7 the first test is false, so no update is permitted.
The final value must equal the threshold
Trace start 6 under add 2 and below 7. The loop reports 8 because the stopping requirement is no longer below 7.
Tests and iterations are the same count
Count body executions separately and show the last false test with no body action.
A changing number guarantees a stop
Compare below 7 with not equal to 7 from 6 under add 2. Even numbers pass 7 without equalling it.
teacher.assessment: W4 is secure when the learner traces the decrementing loop, includes zero iterations, accepts 0 as a valid final result from 6 and explains why subtract 0 cannot end the run from 7. After support, retry start 8, while above 2 subtract 3: tests 8, 5, 2; two iterations and report 2. A correct final number without test reasoning is incomplete evidence.
teacher.support: Let students move a token from the test card to the body and back. Use written true and false labels as well as arrows. Provide a separate tally box for body executions. Extension: explain why start 2, while not equal to 7 add 2 never reaches its reporting instruction with exact whole-number arithmetic.
teacher.next: Week 12 develops debugging from traces. Students will compare expected steps with observed steps, identify the first divergence and retest a repair.

ai-1/12.title: Debugging with revealing tests
goals: Compare expected and observed traces to locate the first difference
Choose a test that distinguishes competing explanations of a fault
Repair a stated instruction and rerun both the failing case and earlier passing cases

prerequisite.prompt: Start at 3. While counter is below 7, add 2. List the values at every test and state when the body stops running.
prerequisite.answer: The tests see 3 true, 5 true and 7 false. Two iterations occur; the body does not run after the false test. Report 7.

vocabulary: A statement of what a system is required to do
The result worked out from the specification before running a test
The result actually recorded during a test
The earliest step where observed behaviour differs from expected behaviour
A repeated check that previously correct behaviour still works after a change

blocks.text: A paper points machine must add 3 to its starting score, double the updated score, then subtract 2 and report. From 4 the expected values are 4, 7, 14 and 12. These instructions are the specification. Calculate the expected result from them before looking at the machine output.

An observed run instead records 4, 7, 11 and 9. The final result is wrong, but changing the report from 9 to 12 would only hide this particular failure. Compare the intermediate values to find where the behaviour first stopped matching the instructions.

The first difference is after the doubling instruction: expected 14, observed 11. The final subtraction is consistent with the observed 11, since 11 minus 2 is 9. That later difference can be a consequence of the earlier fault rather than a second faulty subtraction. A trace narrows the investigation; it does not automatically reveal every cause.

lesson.title: Keep expected and observed evidence together

blocks.title: Locate the first mismatch
blocks.caption: Each row compares the same checkpoint in two traces. Arrows lead from the checkpoint to its comparison and interpretation; they do not represent arithmetic between columns.

blocks.text: Record the input, the exact instruction version, expected values, observed values and first mismatch. This makes the failure reproducible: someone else can follow the same procedure with the same starting value and check your observation.

Do not rewrite the expected column to match the observed result. If the specification itself seems ambiguous, clarify it first and record that change openly. A test can judge an implementation only against a stated expectation.

lesson.title: Choose a test that separates explanations

blocks.text: For the faulty doubling step, two explanations fit the observed change from 7 to 11. Perhaps the step adds 4. Perhaps it adds the original starting score, which was 4. Repeating the same start 4 cannot separate those explanations because they make the same prediction.

headers: If step adds 4 or original start
rows: 7 if add 4 or 5 if add original 2
10 if add 4 or 11 if add original 5

blocks.text: Starting at 2 produces 5 after the first addition. The intended double gives 10 and then reports 8. Adding 4 would give 9 and report 7. Adding the original 2 would give 7 and report 5. The different predictions make this a revealing test.

If the observed final result is 7, it supports add 4 over add original among these two explanations. Other faults could still give 7, so inspect the actual instruction or more checkpoints before claiming a unique cause.

lesson.title: Repair the instruction and rerun the evidence

blocks.text: Suppose inspection confirms that the second instruction says add 4. Replace that instruction with double the current score. Keep the original failing test, then rerun other inputs. From starts 4, 2 and 5, the corrected final results should be 12, 8 and 14.

blocks.label: A copied machine reports 9 from start 4 and 7 from start 2. Which of the two proposed explanations is consistent with both results? State what to inspect, the repair if confirmed, and the expected results to record after the repair

blocks.text: Change the suspected instruction while keeping the test inputs fixed. If you change several instructions and inputs together, it is harder to tell which change mattered. Rerun previously passing cases as regression tests, because a repair can accidentally break other behaviour.

lesson.title: Match each test to a reason

blocks.text: For an arithmetic step, choose inputs that produce different predictions under plausible faults. For a condition, test its equality case as well as values on each side. For a loop, include a false first test and a run that crosses its stopping boundary. A test list is stronger when you can explain what each case checks.

A useful bug report names the version and input, says what should happen, records what did happen, and identifies the first known difference. Include the repair and retest evidence once available. Passing a finite collection of tests increases confidence in those behaviours; it does not prove every possible input correct.

blocks.label: A repaired below 7 loop is checked only from start 1. Name a regression test that would reveal an accidental change from below 7 to at most 7, give both expected outcomes with add 2, and explain why the test is revealing

workbook.title: Locate the first difference
workbook.prompt: A procedure must add 2, double the updated value, then subtract 1. Starting at 3, an observed trace is 3, 5, 8, 7. Write the expected trace, identify the first difference and explain why the final subtraction is not necessarily a separate fault.
workbook.answer: Expected trace: 3, 5, 10, 9. First difference is the doubling checkpoint: 10 expected versus 8 observed. The later 8 minus 1 equals 7, so the observed subtraction is consistent with its input. Investigate the earlier step before claiming another fault.

workbook.title: Choose between two explanations
workbook.prompt: In W1 the faulty middle step may add 3, or add the original starting value. Both explain 5 becoming 8 when the start is 3. Choose start 1 or start 3 for a revealing new test. Predict the final result under each explanation and under the intended procedure.
workbook.answer: Choose start 1. After add 2 the value is 3. Adding 3 then subtracting 1 reports 5; adding original 1 then subtracting 1 reports 3. Doubling then subtracting 1 should report 5. This separates the two fault explanations, but a final 5 alone cannot separate add 3 from correct doubling on this input; retain the original failing start 3.

workbook.title: Reject a repair that hides the symptom
workbook.prompt: A learner repairs the original points machine by reporting 12 for every input, because 12 is correct from start 4. Give a different starting input and its expected output under add 3, double, subtract 2. Explain why the constant report is not a valid repair and what earlier evidence should be preserved.
workbook.answer: Start 2 should report 8, with trace 2, 5, 10, 8; other correctly calculated starts with a different output also work. Always reporting 12 breaks the specification. Preserve the original input and observed intermediate trace as evidence, then correct the faulty instruction and rerun the cases.

workbook.title: Debug a new ticket rule
workbook.prompt: A paper ticket rule must add 1 to the input count. If the updated count is at least 5, report Group; otherwise report Single. A copied version says above 5. Choose the smallest three consecutive nonnegative starting counts that test just below, exactly at and just above the comparison boundary. Predict both versions, identify the revealing start and state the repair and retests.
workbook.answer: Use starts 3, 4 and 5, which reach 4, 5 and 6. Intended results are Single, Group, Group. Copied results are Single, Single, Group. Start 4 exposes the equality fault. Restore at least 5 and rerun all three, retaining starts 3 and 5 as previously passing regression cases.

workbook.title: Make a defensible completion claim
workbook.prompt: After repairing W4, all three chosen tests pass. Write a short report with the fault, the exact repair, the three inputs and expected outputs, and what those passing tests establish. Explain why saying every possible error is now impossible would go beyond the evidence.
workbook.answer: The copied rule excluded equality. Change above 5 to at least 5 after the add 1 step. Tests 3, 4 and 5 now report Single, Group and Group. The repair passes these checks around this boundary and retains the tested neighbouring behaviour. Other inputs, missing values or unrelated implementation faults were not established by these three tests.

teacher.background: Use debugging as evidence-based investigation of a stated procedure. Distinguish finding the first observed divergence from establishing a unique root cause. The arithmetic examples show that two faults can fit one result and that a test may separate two explanations while still missing a different fault. Use paper traces and preserve the original failing case throughout repair.
materials: The points-machine specification and its observed trace on separate cards
An expected and observed trace sheet with an instruction-version field
Cards for add 4 and add original start, plus the ticket rule for independent assessment
sessions: Retrieve the complete loop trace. Emphasise that the false test is a checkpoint that must be recorded.
Work the points-machine specification before revealing the observed run. Align checkpoints and find the first mismatch at the doubling step.
Compare add 4 with add original start. Predict outcomes from 2 before showing any observations. Explain the limits of choosing between two proposed causes.
Complete W1 and W2 in pairs. Ask why a passing result from start 1 does not remove the failure from start 3.
Use W3 to distinguish repairing an instruction from replacing a reported answer. Retrieve the need for an unchanged specification.
Complete the guided repair and write expected retest results. Keep a record of the original failing case and prior passing cases.
Collect W4 independently. Check that starts are chosen before the add 1 step, so equality is reached from start 4.
Use W5 and the exit to practise a limited, evidence-based completion claim. Preview fitting a rule from examples next week.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Add 4 fits both reported results: from 4, 7 plus 4 minus 2 is 9; from 2, 5 plus 4 minus 2 is 7. Adding the original start predicts 5 on the second run and is inconsistent. Inspect the actual middle instruction. If it says add 4, restore double the current score and expect 12 from start 4 and 8 from start 2; also check start 5 gives 14. This distinguishes the proposed faults without claiming no other cause exists. Exit: start 7. Below 7 runs zero times and reports 7; at most 7 adds 2 once and reports 9.
misconceptions: The last wrong number locates the fault
Compare every aligned checkpoint; an early mismatch can cause several later wrong values.
One revealing test proves the only possible cause
List the explanations actually compared. A different, untested fault may make the same prediction.
A correct answer on one input proves the repair
Use the constant-report example and rerun original failing and previously passing cases.
Expected results should follow observed results
Calculate expectations from the specification first. Clarify genuine specification changes explicitly rather than hiding a failure.
teacher.assessment: W4 is secure when the learner chooses starts 3, 4, 5, tests the updated values, explains equality, repairs the comparator and retains both neighbouring cases. W5 must limit the claim to the tested evidence. After support, retry add 2 then if current is at most 6 report A otherwise B, with a below 6 fault. Starts 3, 4, 5 should produce A, A, B; the fault produces A, B, B.
teacher.support: Provide aligned expected and observed columns and ask learners to point to the first unequal pair. Separate predicting a result from running the procedure. Extension: explain why start 1 in W2 is useful for comparing the two faults but cannot alone prove correct doubling.
teacher.next: Week 13 introduces fitting a pattern from examples. Students will carry forward the need to state candidate rules, compare their predictions and keep fitting evidence distinct from later evaluation.

ai-1/13.title: Fitting a pattern from examples
goals: Fit a threshold by tracing predictions and counting disagreements for every candidate
Apply an explicit tie rule while recording what the fitting examples leave unresolved
Use a selected rule on a new input and explain why fit alone does not establish future correctness

prerequisite.prompt: A rule predicts tall when height is at least 5 cm. What does it predict at 4, 5 and 6 cm? Why is 5 a useful boundary test?
prerequisite.answer: Predictions are short, tall and tall. At 5 the at least rule includes equality; an accidental greater than rule would instead predict short.

vocabulary: One possible rule being compared during fitting
The examples used to choose or adjust a model
The number of predictions that differ from their comparison labels
An explicit method for choosing between equally scoring candidates
How well a fitted model works on new cases beyond its fitting examples

lesson.title: Turn an example comparison into a procedure

blocks.text: Four imaginary paper towers have heights 2, 4, 6 and 8 centimetres. Their supplied labels are short, short, tall and tall. These labels belong to this classroom task; they are not a universal definition of tall. We will fit a rule using height as its only input.

Every candidate predicts tall when height is at least its threshold and short otherwise. Compare thresholds 3, 5, 6 and 7 centimetres. The fitting procedure chooses the fewest disagreements with the four labels. If candidates tie, choose the smaller threshold. Write these choices before comparing results.

For each candidate, start its count at zero. For each example, predict with that candidate, compare with the supplied label, and add one only for a disagreement. After all four examples, record the count. Then move to the next candidate with a fresh count. This uses the conditions and repetition you have already traced.

blocks.title: Disagreements on the four fitting examples
blocks.axis: Number of label disagreements out of four examples
blocks.caption: All candidates use the same four examples and the same zero to four scale. Thresholds 5 and 6 have zero-length bars. They tie; our stated smaller-threshold rule selects 5.

blocks.text: Threshold 3 incorrectly calls the height 4 tower tall. Threshold 7 incorrectly calls the height 6 tower short. Thresholds 5 and 6 agree with all four supplied labels. Check each disagreement against the individual example instead of trusting a total without its trace.

The bar chart compares disagreement counts, so a shorter bar is better on this fitting set. Zero is a measured count here, not missing data. This chart says nothing yet about the error count on new towers.

The first four rows are fitting examples. The final row asks what the two tied candidates predict at a height missing from that set. Our tie rule selects 5, so the selected model predicts tall at 5. The fitting examples alone do not tell us whether that new prediction matches the task label.

A tie rule makes the selection reproducible. It does not prove that the chosen threshold is the true boundary. Record that 6 tied with 5 and that they disagree at height 5. Hiding the tie would hide a real limitation of the available evidence.

lesson.title: Record how added evidence changes fitting

blocks.text: Suppose the task designer supplies an additional fitting example: height 5 centimetres, label short. Compare thresholds 5 and 6 again using all five fitting examples. Do not discard the original four when adding the new example.

blocks.label: List the prediction at the added height 5 under each candidate and update both total disagreement counts. Select between 5 and 6 under the fitting procedure. Explain why the added example is now fitting evidence rather than an independent final test

blocks.text: A label that helps choose the threshold participates in fitting. This is allowed, but it changes what the example can establish. We must use separate evidence to evaluate the selected model beyond the examples that shaped it. Week 15 will develop that separation in detail.

lesson.title: State the limits of the fitted pattern

blocks.text: The best candidate means best among the candidates compared, using this counting rule and these recorded labels. A different candidate family, feature or label policy might give a different result. People chose those ingredients; fitting does not remove those choices.

If two records with identical input height have different labels, any deterministic rule using only that height gives them the same prediction. It must disagree with at least one label. Investigate the records and task definition instead of silently changing a label to make the model look perfect.

blocks.label: The selected threshold has zero disagreements on four fitting examples. A learner claims it will label every future tower correctly. Write a more accurate claim and name evidence that is still needed

workbook.title: Count each candidate from zero
workbook.prompt: Heights 2, 4, 6 and 8 cm have labels short, short, tall and tall. Predict all four labels under threshold 3, then under threshold 7, using tall when height is at least the threshold. List the disagreeing examples and separate totals.
workbook.answer: Threshold 3 predicts short, tall, tall, tall, disagreeing only at 4 cm: count 1. Threshold 7 predicts short, short, short, tall, disagreeing only at 6 cm: count 1. Reset the tally for each candidate.

workbook.title: Explain a tied fit
workbook.prompt: Thresholds 5 and 6 both have zero disagreements on the W1 fitting set. The tie rule chooses the smaller threshold. Which is selected? Give a whole-number height where the two candidates disagree and both predictions. Explain what the tie rule does not prove.
workbook.answer: Select 5. At height 5 cm, threshold 5 predicts tall and threshold 6 predicts short. Choosing the smaller threshold makes the procedure definite; it does not prove which prediction matches a label not supplied by the fitting set.

workbook.title: Update with an added example
workbook.prompt: Add height 5 cm labelled short to the four fitting examples. Recompute the disagreement totals for thresholds 3, 5, 6 and 7. Select the candidate with the fewest disagreements, keeping the smaller-threshold tie rule. Explain why the new label is part of fitting.
workbook.answer: Totals are 2, 1, 0 and 1 respectively. Threshold 3 now disagrees at 4 and 5; threshold 5 at 5; threshold 6 nowhere; threshold 7 at 6. Select 6. The new label influenced selection, so it is fitting evidence.

workbook.title: Fit a new distance task
workbook.prompt: Imaginary map markers have distances 1, 3, 5 and 7 units, with supplied labels near, far, far and far. Compare candidates that predict far when distance is at least 2, 4 or 6 units. List every prediction and error count, select the lowest-error candidate, then predict at distance 2 before any comparison label is supplied. Limit your conclusion.
workbook.answer: Threshold 2 predicts near, far, far, far with 0 errors. Threshold 4 predicts near, near, far, far with 1 error at 3. Threshold 6 predicts near, near, near, far with 2 errors at 3 and 5. Select 2 and predict far at exactly 2. This fits the four labels among these candidates; it does not establish the unknown label at 2 or all future distances.

workbook.title: Keep conflicting records visible
workbook.prompt: Two fitting records both have height 6 cm. One is labelled short and the other tall. A learner says a clever height-only rule can agree with both on every run. Explain the problem for a deterministic rule and name two checks to make before changing either record.
workbook.answer: The same input must receive the same prediction from this deterministic height-only rule, so at least one of the two labels disagrees. Check the original measurements and units, and check whether both labels used the same task policy; also investigate an omitted relevant feature. Do not edit a label merely to improve the score.

teacher.background: Extend Week 4 from a small candidate comparison to an explicit fitting algorithm, recorded tie handling and a changed fitting set. Use the same examples for every candidate and reset counts. The chart deliberately includes zero errors and a tie. Do not present the supplied classroom labels as natural truth or the selected threshold as a discovered universal law.
materials: Four tower cards showing height on the front and supplied label on the back
Candidate cards 3, 5, 6 and 7, a separate tally for each, and the smaller-threshold tie rule
An additional 5 cm short card, the independent distance examples and two conflicting 6 cm records
sessions: Retrieve at least and its equality case. Ask what information is available when predicting a new label.
Model threshold 3 with a fresh zero tally. Predict each example before comparing its label. Record the single disagreement at height 4.
Complete all four candidates. Interpret the shared-scale chart and emphasise that zero-length bars represent zero disagreements.
Complete W1 and W2 in pairs. Apply the tie rule but preserve the record of both tied candidates and their prediction difference at height 5.
Retrieve the selected threshold and ask whether the tie rule proves its missing boundary label.
Use the guided task and W3 to add height 5 short. Recompute on all five examples and explicitly reclassify the added evidence as fitting data.
Collect W4 independently. Require all prediction lists and counts, then cover the new label while students predict at distance 2.
Discuss W5 and the exit. Separate record investigation from changing labels to flatter the model. Preview constructing a complete classifier.
teacher.guidedAnswer: At height 5, threshold 5 predicts tall and adds one disagreement; its total is 1. Threshold 6 predicts short and adds none; its total remains 0. Select 6 between these candidates. The new label affected selection and is therefore fitting evidence. Exit: the threshold agrees with these four supplied labels under this procedure, but future performance remains unestablished. Check predictions on appropriate new labelled examples kept separate from selection and inspect their coverage.
misconceptions: The lowest error count is added across candidates
Reset to zero for each candidate so all totals describe the same examples under one rule.
A tie rule proves the selected boundary is correct
Compare tied thresholds at height 5, which was absent from the original fitting set.
Zero fitting errors guarantee future correctness
Separate the evidence used to choose the rule from new labelled cases used to evaluate it.
Disagreeing labels should be changed to match the model
Inspect original measurements, units, omitted information and label definitions; model agreement is not sufficient grounds for editing a record.
teacher.assessment: W4 is secure when the learner lists the three prediction sequences, obtains counts 0, 1, 2, selects 2, includes equality in the new prediction and limits the claim. After support, retry values 2, 4, 6, 8 labelled near, near, far, far with thresholds 4 and 6: counts 1 and 0, select 6. Ask about an unseen distance 5 to check that prediction is not confused with verified correctness.
teacher.support: Use counters for disagreements and a number line with a closed threshold dot. Let students read labels aloud after committing predictions. Extension: identify all positive whole-number thresholds with zero disagreements on the original tower set and explain why the available labels do not select uniquely between them.
teacher.next: Week 14 constructs a classifier as a complete procedure with defined inputs, a selected model and explicit handling of invalid or missing records.

ai-1/14.title: Constructing a classifier
goals: Construct a classifier with a stated input format, selected rule and recorded output
Trace valid, boundary and invalid inputs through different paths
Distinguish an input check from evidence that a prediction is correct

prerequisite.prompt: A fitted rule predicts tall at a height of at least 6 cm and short otherwise. Predict at 5 and 6 cm. What should you check before applying it to a blank height?
prerequisite.answer: At 5 predict short; at 6 predict tall. Check that a height was supplied. A blank is missing information, not the number zero.

vocabulary: A procedure that assigns a predicted category to an input
The format and conditions an input must satisfy for a procedure to accept it
Checking whether an input satisfies the stated contract
An explicit outcome when the classifier does not assign a category
A name that identifies the particular model used for a prediction

lesson.title: Build the procedure around the fitted rule

blocks.text: Your task is to build a paper classifier that another learner can operate without guessing your instructions. It will predict short or tall for imaginary towers. Use the threshold of 6 centimetres selected after adding the height 5 short example in Week 13. Name this selected model Tower1.

Write an input contract: one height recorded as a whole number of centimetres from 1 through 10, including both endpoints. Require the unit cm to be shown. This is a classroom design choice about what the procedure accepts. It is not a claim that every accepted height appeared in fitting or that towers outside this range cannot exist.

A complete classifier needs instructions for checking the input, applying Tower1 when the input is accepted, and recording the outcome. It must also say what happens when the input fails a check. The threshold alone does not provide these surrounding instructions.

lesson.title: Trace the paths before constructing your own

blocks.title: Three records through the Tower1 classifier
blocks.caption: Read each row from left to right. An accepted input reaches the threshold rule. A missing input stops before that rule and receives an explicit no prediction outcome.

blocks.text: For every record, first check that a height is present and its stated unit is cm. Then check that it is a whole number from 1 through 10. If any check fails, record no prediction and the reason, then stop processing that record. Do not continue into the threshold comparison.

If all checks pass, compare the height with 6. At least 6 gives the prediction tall; otherwise give short. Record the original input, model version Tower1 and the prediction. For a rejected record, record the original input, Tower1, no prediction and a reason. Tower1 identifies the intended model even when its threshold was not used.

A valid 9 cm input receives a tall prediction, but the input check does not establish that the prediction matches its comparison label. Validation checks the contract. Evaluation checks predictions against appropriate evidence. Keep these questions separate.

Sixty millimetres equals six centimetres, but this version accepts cm records only. It does not contain a conversion step. Ask for a correctly recorded cm measurement or deliberately design and check a conversion step in a new version. Do not silently treat the digits 60 as centimetres. A missing height must not become an invented zero either.

lesson.title: Make another learner operate your instructions

blocks.text: Write the procedure as numbered steps or connected boxes with labelled branches. Give it to a partner who follows only what you wrote. The partner should record each check and stop point, including equality at the threshold and at both accepted range endpoints.

blocks.label: Construct Tower1 in your own words. Have a partner trace 1 cm, 6 cm, 10 cm, 11 cm and a blank height. Record each outcome and any instruction you had to clarify. Explain why the accepted 10 cm case still needs separate evidence of correctness

blocks.text: A partner finding an unclear branch gives useful design feedback. Revise the instruction and retrace the affected examples. Keep the model name and threshold visible so a change to the fitted rule is not confused with a correction to an instruction.

lesson.title: Separate the predicted category from the next action

blocks.text: The classifier reports a prediction or no prediction. It does not decide what a person must do with a tower. A separate classroom procedure might ask someone to remeasure a rejected input or compare a prediction with a recorded label. Write that action separately from the predicted category.

No prediction is not a third tower size. It records that this procedure did not assign short or tall. Count and investigate such records when evaluating the whole system; hiding them could make a system look more useful than it is.

blocks.label: A classifier accepts 9 cm and predicts tall. A learner says the input passed, so the label is definitely right. Correct the claim. Then explain why reporting short for a blank height would violate the Tower1 procedure

workbook.title: Write an input contract
workbook.prompt: Write the complete Tower1 input contract. Give one accepted example and three different rejected examples, each with its reason. Explain why an accepted input does not have to be one of the examples used to fit the threshold.
workbook.answer: Require a present height, unit cm, a whole number and range 1 through 10 inclusive. For example, 7 cm is accepted; blank is missing, 60 mm has the wrong unit and 11 cm is outside the range. Fractional values such as 4.5 cm also fail. The contract defines accepted inputs; it does not list only the fitting records or establish prediction correctness.

workbook.title: Construct both outcome paths
workbook.prompt: Write numbered instructions for Tower1, including input checks, the stopping path after a failed check, the threshold rule and the record to keep. Your partner must be able to use them without supplying an unstated rule.
workbook.answer: Check present height and cm unit, then whole number in 1 through 10. On failure, record original input, Tower1, no prediction and the reason; stop that record. Otherwise predict tall if height is at least 6, short otherwise. Record original input, Tower1 and prediction. Equivalent clear branches are acceptable.

workbook.title: Trace boundaries and a broken path
workbook.prompt: Trace 1 cm, 5 cm, 6 cm, 10 cm and 11 cm using Tower1. A faulty procedure records no prediction for a blank, then continues and treats the blank as zero to report short. Identify the missing instruction and the proper final outcome.
workbook.answer: The first four are accepted and predict short, short, tall and tall. At 11 cm reject for being outside the range. The faulty path lacks stopping after failure; a blank must end as no prediction with reason missing height. It must not be converted to zero or reach the threshold rule.

workbook.title: Build an independent ribbon classifier
workbook.prompt: Design Ribbon1 for ribbon lengths recorded as whole centimetres from 1 through 12 inclusive, with unit cm required. Predict long at 8 cm or more and short otherwise. Write complete instructions and trace 7 cm, 8 cm, a blank length and 13 cm. Include reasons for no prediction and the model version in each record.
workbook.answer: Check present length, cm unit, whole number and range 1 through 12; otherwise record no prediction with reason and stop. For accepted inputs, use at least 8 for long, otherwise short. Ribbon1 at 7 cm predicts short; at 8 cm predicts long; blank gives no prediction because length is missing; 13 cm gives no prediction because outside range. Each record includes original input, Ribbon1 and outcome, plus reason when rejected.

workbook.title: Explain what your procedure establishes
workbook.prompt: Ribbon1 accepts 12 cm and predicts long. No comparison label has been supplied for that record. State what has been checked and what remains unknown. Explain why changing a blank to 1 cm just to produce a category would be a mistake.
workbook.answer: The value satisfies the input contract and the stated rule predicts long. Agreement with an appropriate comparison label has not been checked. Replacing a blank with 1 invents a measurement, conceals missing information and violates the stated rejection path. Ask for the measurement instead.

teacher.background: Students construct a paper procedure around a fitted threshold, joining input checks, conditions, stopping and recorded output. Separate input validation, predictive correctness and subsequent human action. Tower1’s range and whole-number requirement are classroom restrictions, not general requirements for classifiers.
materials: Input cards with 1, 5, 6, 9, 10 and 11 cm, a blank, 60 mm and 4.5 cm
Blank paper for numbered steps or branch diagrams and a record with input, version, outcome and reason
Separate Ribbon1 task cards; no accounts, devices or personal measurements required
sessions: Retrieve threshold equality and the difference between missing and zero. Introduce the goal of instructions another learner can execute.
Read the Tower1 contract and model aloud. Trace 5 cm, 6 cm and blank through the diagram. Stop physically before comparing the rejected card.
Compare valid boundaries and rejected units or fractions. Complete W1 and explain why acceptance is not proof of a correct label.
Start W2 in pairs. One learner writes, the other follows only the written instructions. Require an explicit stop after a failed check.
Retrieve the output record and both paths. Ask whether no prediction is a tower size.
Use the guided task and W3 to test partners’ procedures at endpoints, threshold and missing input. Record and repair ambiguity.
Collect W4 independently before support. Look for transfer to the new range, threshold, labels and version instead of copied Tower1 constants.
Use W5 and the exit to separate contract checks from correctness evidence. Preview final tests kept apart from model selection.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Check presence, cm unit, whole number and range 1 through 10 before comparing. At 1, 6 and 10 cm predict short, tall and tall. At 11 cm record no prediction, outside range; at blank record no prediction, missing height. Record Tower1 throughout. Acceptance of 10 cm does not verify its label. Exit: 9 cm passes the contract and predicts tall, but correctness still needs evidence. A blank must stop as no prediction.
misconceptions: Any numeric input must receive a category
Check the stated unit, whole-number condition and supported range before comparing the threshold.
An accepted input proves a correct prediction
Ask separately whether the input satisfies the contract and whether the prediction agrees with evaluation evidence.
No prediction means a third category of tower
It is a system outcome indicating that no short or tall category was assigned.
Writing a rejection is enough even if processing continues
Follow the failed path to an explicit stop so the later rule cannot overwrite the outcome.
teacher.assessment: W4 is secure with both paths, range 1 through 12, threshold 8 including equality, explicit stops and Ribbon1 records. After support retry Flag1: whole cm from 1 through 9, unit cm, large at least 5 otherwise small. At 4, 5, blank and 10 cm expect small, large, no prediction for missing and no prediction for range.
teacher.support: Use separate check, compare and record cards with arrows. Let partners move each input physically and read the branch aloud. Extension: propose a separate mm-to-cm conversion stage; state what extra cases would need checking, including a conversion that yields a fractional centimetre.
teacher.next: Week 15 keeps final evaluation examples unseen during fitting and explains why repeated changes based on their labels weaken the independence of that test.

ai-1/15.title: Keeping final tests unseen
goals: Separate examples used to choose a model from examples reserved for its final evaluation
Record a fixed model and its predictions before revealing comparison labels
Explain how test feedback changes the evidence available for a revised model

prerequisite.prompt: A height passes the input contract and the model predicts tall. What is still needed to check that prediction? If its comparison label changes your threshold choice, what role has that example played?
prerequisite.answer: Compare the prediction with an appropriate recorded label. If the label helps choose the threshold, that example has participated in fitting or model selection; it is not independent evaluation evidence for the resulting model.

vocabulary: Examples available for fitting, comparing or revising a model
Examples reserved from development for evaluating a fixed model
Record a model and stop changing it for a particular evaluation
Information from a reserved test influencing model development
A record of the tested model, predictions, comparison labels and results

lesson.title: Give development and testing different jobs

blocks.text: A rule chosen to fit examples may work differently on new cases. To investigate that difference, reserve a set of examples before development. Use the development examples to choose the model. Keep the final test examples separate until the model is fixed, then evaluate that recorded model.

In this paper activity, a teacher keeps the reserved examples in an envelope. Record the input contract, feature, category rule and model version before opening it. Once the input values are revealed, predict using the frozen model before revealing their comparison labels. This prevents copying the labels into the predictions.

The worked example below describes a completed experiment, so its test labels are visible for discussion. It is not an unseen test for you. In the workbook experiment, the teacher will supply a separate set of comparison labels after you have saved your predictions. All data are imaginary classroom records.

lesson.title: Follow the evidence through a completed experiment

blocks.title: Different roles for development and final testing
blocks.caption: Read the rows in order. Information from the final comparison must not travel back into model selection while the result is still described as an independent final test of that model.

blocks.text: In the completed experiment, development towers at heights 2, 4, 6 and 8 cm have labels short, short, tall and tall. Candidates predict tall at or above 5 or 6 cm. Both fit all four labels; the stated smaller-threshold tie rule selects 5. The team freezes model TowerA with threshold 5.

The reserved inputs are different records at heights 3, 5, 7 and 9 cm. TowerA accepts whole cm heights from 1 through 10. It predicts short, tall, tall and tall. These predictions are saved before the reserved labels are opened. The comparison below records what happened, including the failure.

lesson.title: Report the original test before making improvements

blocks.text: TowerA agrees on three of these four reserved examples and disagrees at 5 cm. That is evidence about this fixed model on this small set. It does not prove a success rate for every future tower. The labels, range of examples and way records were selected also matter.

After seeing the 5 cm label, the team changes the threshold to 6 and names the revision TowerB. TowerB agrees on all four of these now-seen examples. The change may be useful, but those examples have influenced its development. Four agreements on them are not an independent final test result for TowerB. Keep TowerA’s original three-of-four record.

Improvement after a test is allowed. State that the old test informed the revision, preserve both versions, and reserve fresh appropriate examples to evaluate the revised model independently. If none are available, report that limitation instead of inventing a fresh test result.

blocks.label: Write two result statements: one for TowerA on the original reserved set, and one for TowerB after the revision. Explain what must happen before a new independent evaluation of TowerB. Would shuffling the four old records make them unseen again

blocks.text: A test can lose independence even when you never copy its labels into a training table. Repeatedly trying thresholds and choosing the one with the best test score also uses test information to choose the model. Separate development comparisons from the final check.

lesson.title: Check the limits of the reserved set

blocks.text: Keeping a set unseen is necessary for this kind of independent check, but secrecy alone does not make it a good test. Four near-identical easy cases provide little evidence about varied cases. Copies of development records can also make a reserved set misleading even if their file names differ.

Define what future cases the model is meant to handle and choose evaluation examples that address that use. Keep related or copied records together when separating sets. Record invalid inputs and no prediction outcomes separately instead of quietly dropping them from the report. Later weeks examine coverage and performance comparisons in more detail.

blocks.label: A team tries ten thresholds, reads the reserved test score for each, and reports only the best score as its final unseen test. Explain the problem and give an honest description of what it has measured

workbook.title: Assign the evidence its role
workbook.prompt: For each event, state whether examples are being used for development or independent evaluation of a fixed model: comparing candidates on fitting labels; scoring a frozen model on previously reserved examples once; changing a threshold after reading a test score. Explain your last choice.
workbook.answer: Comparing candidates is development. Scoring a frozen model on previously reserved examples is evaluation, provided they did not influence its development. Changing a threshold after reading the test score uses that test information for development of the revision; the same set is no longer independent of that revision.

workbook.title: Preserve the original result
workbook.prompt: TowerA uses threshold 5 on reserved heights 3, 5, 7 and 9 cm. The labels are short, short, tall and tall. Write its predictions, agreements and disagreement. Then state why TowerB with threshold 6, selected after seeing these labels, cannot claim four independent test successes on these same records.
workbook.answer: TowerA predicts short, tall, tall, tall: three agreements and one disagreement at 5. TowerB predicts short, short, tall, tall, matching all four, but the revealed labels influenced its selection. Report its four agreements as a result on examples used in development, preserving TowerA’s original test record.

workbook.title: Detect a less visible leak
workbook.prompt: A team leaves reserved labels out of its fitting table but tries six rules and reads a test score for each. It chooses the highest-scoring rule. Explain how information still reached model selection. Would renaming or reordering the same test records repair the problem?
workbook.answer: The scores depend on the reserved labels and guide the choice among rules, so test information influences selection indirectly. Omitting the labels from a fitting table is insufficient. Renaming or reordering records does not remove that information; reserve new appropriate examples for an independent final check.

workbook.title: Run a separate ribbon experiment
workbook.prompt: Before receiving any test labels, freeze RibbonA: whole cm lengths 1 through 12, long at least 6 cm and short otherwise. Save predictions for 5, 7, 9 and 11 cm. Ask your teacher to reveal the reserved labels, then record agreements, disagreements and a limited result statement. If you later choose threshold 8 after seeing these labels, explain how you must describe its result on the same records.
workbook.answer: Saved predictions are short, long, long, long. Reveal labels only after predictions are saved: short, short, long, long. RibbonA has three agreements and one disagreement at 7 on four reserved records. Threshold 8 then gives short, short, long, long, but it was chosen after feedback. Its four agreements are on now-seen development examples, not a new independent test. Do not alter the saved RibbonA predictions.

workbook.title: Audit a proposed final set
workbook.prompt: A class reserves ten copies of one easy development example in a new file. The model agrees with all ten labels. Explain two reasons this gives weak evidence about new cases, and propose a better final evaluation plan without promising perfect future performance.
workbook.answer: Copies repeat a case already used in development and provide almost no variety; a new file does not make them new evidence. Reserve distinct relevant cases before model choices, keep related copies together, freeze the model, save predictions, reveal labels and report every outcome. Include cases relevant to intended use and state that a finite test cannot guarantee all future results.

teacher.background: Make the order of evidence visible. The lesson table is a retrospective worked example, not an unseen student test. W4 is a separate staged exercise: do not reveal its labels before predictions are committed. Avoid calling ordinary input validation a validation set here; the focus is development versus a held-out final check.
materials: Development and reserved tower cards from the worked example, marked as a completed experiment
RibbonA input cards 5, 7, 9, 11 cm and a covered label sheet: short, short, long, long
Paper for a dated frozen-rule record and separate predictions, labels and outcome columns
sessions: Retrieve the difference between accepted input and checked prediction. Ask when a label becomes part of development.
Trace the three evidence stages in the diagram. Explicitly identify the lesson table as an already completed experiment.
Compare TowerA predictions and revealed labels. Complete W1 and W2, preserving the original failure when TowerB is introduced.
Use W3 to show how a score can influence model selection without exposing individual labels. Discuss why shuffling is not a repair.
Retrieve the frozen-model and saved-prediction requirements. Keep the RibbonA label sheet covered.
Complete the guided task and plan the two statements for TowerA and TowerB. Describe what fresh evidence would be needed.
Collect W4 predictions independently before revealing short, short, long, long. Students append results without erasing predictions, then explain the revised threshold.
Use W5 and the exit to distinguish independence from coverage. Keep original and revised result claims side by side.
teacher.guidedAnswer: TowerA agreed on three of four original reserved records, failing at 5 cm. TowerB agreed on all four after their labels informed its revision; this is performance on development evidence. Freeze TowerB before evaluating fresh appropriate reserved examples. Shuffling cannot undo prior use. Exit: the team selected using test scores, so it measured a development comparison and still lacks an independent final check of the winner.
misconceptions: A new file makes old records unseen
Trace whether records or copies already influenced development, regardless of their file names.
Only labels copied into training can leak
A test score can guide rule selection even when individual labels remain hidden.
Testing means the model can never improve
Improve openly, preserve the original result, and obtain fresh independent evidence for the revision.
A perfect reserved score proves universal correctness
Check sample size, variety, relation to development records and intended use; keep the conclusion within the evidence.
teacher.assessment: W4 is secure with saved predictions, three agreements, the 7 cm failure, a limited claim and a correct account of post-test revision. If labels were seen early, record the exercise as coached practice. For an uncoached retry freeze BandA at long at least 4, use inputs 2, 4, 6, 8, then reveal short, short, long, long: three agreements, failure at 4.
teacher.support: Use two envelopes and a timeline with a clear freeze point. Read the steps aloud, preserving the learner’s original predictions. Extension: explain why selecting the best of many test scores may give a flattering result even without deliberate cheating.
teacher.next: Week 16 develops explicit uncertainty and review paths when available evidence does not justify a confident category or action.

ai-1/16.title: Uncertainty and review
goals: Identify a specific source of uncertainty and explain how it affects a prediction
Compare predictions across stated possible inputs without inventing a missing value
Design a review step with relevant evidence and an explicit unresolved outcome

prerequisite.prompt: A model predicts tall at a height of at least 6 cm. What would it predict if an unclear record could mean either 5 or 6 cm? Does a good result on a small final test settle this particular input?
prerequisite.answer: At 5 it predicts short; at 6 it predicts tall. The unclear input leaves two different possible predictions. A previous test result does not tell us which height this record contains.

vocabulary: Something relevant that the available evidence does not settle
An input still compatible with the stated information
A stated condition that sends a case for an additional check
Information gathered to investigate the reason a case was referred
Still not settled after the available checks

lesson.title: Name what is unknown before choosing a check

blocks.text: An unclear measurement, a missing feature and a weakly tested model create different problems. Saying the AI is unsure does not identify which one matters. Write what is known, what remains unknown and how the unknown could change the result. Then choose a check that addresses that specific gap.

Use the familiar tower model: tall at a height of at least 6 cm, short otherwise, for whole-number heights from 1 through 10. A smudged card could read 5 cm or 6 cm. The threshold is known; the input is unclear. Repeating the same calculation cannot recover the missing digit.

For this paper investigation, treat the listed possibilities as the complete set allowed by the exercise. In real use, that assumption would itself need evidence. We will compare the model’s predictions under each possibility; we are not changing Tower1 to accept an invented exact measurement.

blocks.title: Possible heights can change the prediction
blocks.caption: A shared prediction across the listed possibilities does not identify the exact input or prove the category correct. Different predictions show that the unknown input can change this model’s result.

blocks.text: At either 5 or 6 cm, one possibility predicts short and the other tall. Record no single category yet and ask for the original record or a new measurement. Do not select the more convenient digit. Averaging the two readings would introduce a different input that neither possibility stated.

At either 8 or 9 cm, the model predicts tall in both cases. You can state that the prediction stays tall under these two possibilities. Keep the exact-height uncertainty visible. This agreement does not check the model against a correct task label or establish that the list of possible heights is complete.

lesson.title: Match the review to the cause

rows: Check how the record was made
Check the label policy and sources

blocks.text: A review request should carry the original input, model version, unresolved issue and any predictions already made. Name the evidence to seek and the person responsible for checking it. A reviewer needs access to relevant evidence and a clear task; being human does not make an unsupported guess correct.

After review, record what was checked and what changed. If a reliable new reading establishes 6 cm, the model predicts tall. If the record is still unreadable, keep no prediction with reason unresolved height. Do not replace the original record without retaining the reason for the correction.

lesson.title: Construct a review path with a stopping point

blocks.text: Use a written review policy: if stated possible valid heights lead to different predictions, pause the single-category output and request a measurement check. If a required input or its unit is missing, request that information. After the check, apply the model only to a supported valid input; otherwise retain an unresolved outcome.

blocks.label: A card could mean 5 or 6 cm. Write the record sent for review, the check requested and two possible endings: a new measurement establishes 6 cm, or no reliable height can be obtained. Explain what each ending permits you to report

blocks.text: A review path needs an ending even when evidence cannot be obtained. Repeating the same unsuccessful request forever does not resolve the uncertainty. Record that the case remains unresolved and follow the agreed next step, such as holding the classroom sorting decision until the missing record is supplied.

A deterministic model repeats the same prediction for the same input and settings. Ten identical runs do not give ten independent measurements of a smudged digit. Several models can also share a feature gap, training examples or mistaken assumption. Agreement alone is not proof that the prediction is correct.

Keep the claim specific: tall under both listed heights, input still unclear, or no category until the measurement is checked. Do not attach a made-up confidence percentage. Evidence about correctness and the meaning of confidence will be developed in Weeks 17 and 18.

blocks.label: A learner runs the same model ten times on a guessed height and gets tall every time. They say review is no longer needed. Explain what the repetitions establish and name the evidence still needed

workbook.title: Describe the uncertainty precisely
workbook.prompt: For a smudged height that could be 5 or 6 cm, state what is known, what is unknown and the two predictions under tall at least 6. Choose a check that could distinguish the heights. Explain why rerunning the threshold comparison cannot do that.
workbook.answer: The rule and two stated possibilities are known; the actual height is unresolved. At 5 predict short, at 6 predict tall. Inspect the original readable record or remeasure. Repeating a calculation supplies no new information about which height was recorded.

workbook.title: Keep a stable prediction within its limits
workbook.prompt: Assume the only possible heights are 8 and 9 cm. Apply tall at least 6 to each. Write a justified result statement and two things it does not establish. Do not invent a confidence percentage.
workbook.answer: Both inputs predict tall, so the prediction is tall under both listed possibilities. This does not identify whether the exact height is 8 or 9 and does not establish agreement with the correct task label. Outside the exercise, completeness of the possibilities also needs evidence.

workbook.title: Choose useful review evidence
workbook.prompt: A record says 60 but omits the unit. A reviewer suggests reading it as 60 cm because the model needs cm. Explain the problem, name the evidence to request and state the outcome if the unit cannot be established.
workbook.answer: The required input format does not prove the original measurement’s unit. Ask for the original measurement record, instrument scale or recording instructions. If the unit cannot be established, retain no prediction with reason unresolved unit; do not silently assume cm or convert from an assumed unit.

workbook.title: Transfer the method to distance
workbook.prompt: A paper model predicts far at a distance of at least 4 units, otherwise near, for whole-number distances 1 through 8. For each complete possibility set, compare predictions: 2 or 3; 3 or 4; 4 or 5. Identify the set requiring review before a single category can be stated. Design a relevant check and an unresolved ending. Limit the claims for the other two sets.
workbook.answer: At 2 or 3 both predict near. At 3 predict near and at 4 far, so that set leaves the category unresolved. At 4 or 5 both predict far. Request a reliable distance reading in the stated units for the disputed set; if unavailable retain no single category and reason unresolved distance. The other two predictions are stable only across their listed possibilities, not verified as correct labels or exact distances.

workbook.title: Review the reviewer’s conclusion
workbook.prompt: A reviewer cannot read the original tower card but chooses 6 cm because two models both predict tall when given 6. Explain why this fails to resolve the input. Write a more defensible review record and a next step.
workbook.answer: Both models were given the same guessed input, so their agreement does not establish the actual measurement. Record that the original remains unreadable, the height is unresolved and no supported single-category output is available. Request a reliable new measurement or keep the sorting decision on hold under the stated policy.

teacher.background: Develop uncertainty as a specific evidence gap with a matching review path. The possible-input comparison is a reasoning exercise, not a probability calculation. Assume the listed possibilities are complete for the paper tasks; do not imply that a model normally knows all possible inputs or that shared predictions verify correctness.
materials: Tower cards labelled either 5 or 6 cm, either 8 or 9 cm, and height missing
A review record with original input, model version, issue, requested evidence and outcome
Distance possibility cards from W4; use fictional measurements and no personal data
sessions: Retrieve the two threshold outcomes for 5 and 6. Distinguish an unclear input from a known model rule.
Trace every diagram row. State the complete-possibilities assumption and retain exact-height uncertainty even when predictions agree.
Complete W1 and W2. Ask students to identify which claim follows from both possible inputs and which claims still lack evidence.
Use W3 and the review table to match each missing fact to a useful source. Reject an assumed unit as a repair.
Retrieve the difference between a new measurement and another run on an unchanged input.
Construct the guided review record and both endings. Require the unresolved path to stop without inventing a height.
Collect W4 independently. Look for all three possibility comparisons, an appropriate measurement check and limited claims.
Discuss W5 and the exit. A reviewer can preserve an unknown; human involvement alone is not correctness evidence.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Record the original 5-or-6 cm card, threshold-6 model version, possible predictions short and tall, and unresolved height. Request a reliable original reading or remeasurement. A supported 6 cm reading permits a tall prediction, with the correction documented. If no reliable value is obtained, retain no prediction and hold sorting under the policy. Exit: repeated runs show consistent computation on the guessed input; a reliable height is still needed.
misconceptions: Two possible values imply equal probabilities
A list of possibilities supplies no probabilities unless further evidence states them.
Averaging guesses recovers the missing input
A calculated average is a new assumption, not an observed measurement.
Repeated identical outputs remove input uncertainty
Re-running unchanged information does not reveal a missing digit or unit.
A human reviewer can always settle the case
Require relevant evidence and allow an explicit unresolved outcome.
teacher.assessment: W4 is secure with near/near, near/far and far/far comparisons, review of the middle set, useful evidence and an unresolved ending. After support retry long at least 7 for whole cm lengths 1 through 10 using 4 or 5, 6 or 7, and 8 or 9: short/short, short/long, long/long. Require limits as well as labels.
teacher.support: Use a number line and a separate card for each possibility. Keep known, unknown and requested evidence in three columns. Extension: add a third possibility that changes an apparently stable result and explain why completeness of the possibility list matters.
teacher.next: Week 17 separates a prediction from the later observation or comparison evidence used to judge it, preserving both records.

ai-1/17.title: Predictions and observations
goals: Separate a recorded prediction from the observation used to check it
Compare matching cases using a stated outcome rule and preserve unresolved evidence
Report checked results without counting missing observations as successes or failures

prerequisite.prompt: A model predicts far, but the distance record is unreadable. Can this case be called correct? What evidence would let you check it?
prerequisite.answer: It remains unassessed. Obtain a reliable distance record for the same trial, with units and the rule defining far. Repeating the prediction does not provide the missing observation.

vocabulary: A model output recorded before consulting the comparison outcome
A recorded measurement or event used as evidence
The agreed method for turning observed evidence into the category being checked
A prediction that differs from an established comparison outcome
A case whose prediction has not yet been judged against adequate outcome evidence

lesson.title: Keep two records for two different jobs

blocks.text: A prediction states what a model outputs. An observation records what was measured or happened. To check a prediction, keep both records and compare the same case under the same outcome rule. Writing a prediction into the observation column would make the check circular.

Use a fictional ramp investigation. Before each trial, Ramp1 predicts far for a ramp height of at least 6 cm and near otherwise. Its allowed heights are whole centimetres from 1 through 10. After a toy rolls, a learner measures its travel distance. The outcome rule is far for a distance of at least 4 floor units and near otherwise. Ramp height and travel distance are different quantities.

The values in this lesson are invented practice records, not a physical law about ramps. Ramp1 is a fixed paper model for learning how to check predictions. Each trial has an ID so that its height, prediction and later measurement stay together. Keep the model version and record the prediction before opening the observation card.

lesson.title: Follow the prediction and the observation separately

blocks.title: Two records meet at a comparison
blocks.caption: Ramp1 predicts from height: A near, B far, C far. The observation is travel distance. Apply the distance outcome rule separately, then compare categories for the same trial.

blocks.text: For B, the input 6 cm produces the prediction far. The later distance of 3 units produces the observed category near. This is a mismatch. Retain far as the original prediction and near as the observed category. Changing the old prediction to near would hide the mistake rather than improve the original result.

For A and C, the categories match. These two matches provide evidence about these trials. They do not show that every future prediction will be correct. Even a correctly computed prediction can disagree with an observation because following the model rule and matching the world are different checks.

lesson.title: Decide whether the evidence supports a comparison

blocks.text: For E, 3 units means near and 4 units means far. The disagreement can change the judgment. Check the trial ID, original measurement and recording procedure. Do not choose the distance that makes Ramp1 look better. If the conflict cannot be resolved, retain both reports and mark the comparison unassessed.

An observation is evidence, not an automatic guarantee of truth. A wrong trial ID, unclear unit or copying error can make the comparison unreliable. If a supported correction is made, retain the original entry, the correction, its source and the reason. Remeasuring a new trial does not reveal what happened in the old one.

lesson.title: Report the denominator and the unresolved cases

blocks.text: Consider only trials A through E. Three have established outcomes: A, B and C. Two of those three predictions match and one does not. D and E are unassessed. Report two matches out of three assessed trials, with two more trials unassessed. Do not report four successes by treating the unknowns as correct, or two out of five as if every trial had a known outcome.

blocks.label: Write a results record for A through E. Include each prediction, its observed category or unresolved evidence, its comparison status, and a summary that names both assessed and unassessed counts. Explain why D and E cannot be counted as correct

blocks.text: The missing cases might be different from the checked cases. The result describes the assessed group; it does not settle performance on all five or on future trials. Collect the missing evidence where possible, document what remains unknown, and keep the original model version visible. Week 23 will develop performance fractions more fully.

lesson.title: Investigate a mismatch without rewriting history

blocks.text: Start a mismatch investigation by checking the input, trial ID, prediction calculation and observation procedure. A mismatch alone does not identify which part caused the problem. If all records are sound, this case is evidence that the model prediction did not match the outcome.

If you revise the model after seeing B, record a new version. A new prediction for B can help explain the change, but it is no longer a check on an unseen case. Preserve Ramp1’s result and use new reserved trials to evaluate the revised version, following Week 15’s method.

blocks.label: A learner changes B’s old prediction from far to near after reading its distance, then reports three matches out of three. Explain what is wrong with the report and how to preserve an honest record

workbook.title: Separate inputs from observed outcomes
workbook.prompt: For Ramp1 trial B, height is 6 cm and the later travel distance is 3 units. State the input, prediction, observation, observed category and comparison status. Explain why the prediction rule and outcome rule use different measurements.
workbook.answer: Input height 6 cm; prediction far because 6 is at least 6; observed distance 3 units; observed category near because 3 is below 4; mismatch. Height is available to the model before the trial, while travel distance is measured afterward to check its prediction.

workbook.title: Check a boundary without changing the rule
workbook.prompt: Trial F has height 6 cm and verified travel distance exactly 4 units. Apply Ramp1 and the outcome rule. A partner says exactly 4 is near because far means greater than 4. Use the stated rule to resolve the disagreement.
workbook.answer: Ramp1 predicts far at height 6. The observation is far because the stated outcome rule is at least 4, including equality. The prediction matches. Greater than 4 would be a different rule and must not replace the agreed one after viewing the result.

workbook.title: Keep incomplete evidence visible
workbook.prompt: D predicts near but has no distance record. E predicts far but its two distance records say 3 and 4 units. State each comparison status, request useful evidence, and explain why neither guessing nor a new trial can establish the old trial’s outcome.
workbook.answer: Both are unassessed. For D request the original distance record for D with units. For E inspect the trial IDs, original measurement and recording procedure to resolve 3 versus 4. Guesses supply no observation; a new trial produces a new outcome. Retain unresolved evidence if the old result cannot be established.

workbook.title: Transfer the check to drying predictions
workbook.prompt: In a fictional paper test, Dry1 predicts slow for a moisture score of at least 7, quick otherwise. Allowed scores are whole numbers 1 through 10. The observed outcome is slow if drying time is greater than 10 minutes, quick otherwise. Records are P: score 6, time 12; Q: score 7, time 10; R: score 9, time 14; S: score 5, time missing. Record all predictions, observed categories and comparison statuses. Summarise matches out of assessed cases, name the unassessed count, and limit the conclusion.
workbook.answer: P predicts quick, observed slow, mismatch. Q predicts slow, observed quick because exactly 10 is not greater than 10, mismatch. R predicts slow, observed slow, match. S predicts quick, observed outcome unavailable, unassessed. One match out of three assessed cases, with one unassessed. This describes the assessed cases and does not establish the result for S or future trials.

workbook.title: Correct a report without erasing evidence
workbook.prompt: After seeing B’s observed near category, a learner replaces Ramp1’s far prediction with near. They call the new entry a corrected observation and report a perfect result for A through C. Explain the two record-keeping errors and write a defensible replacement report.
workbook.answer: They changed a prediction after seeing the outcome and mislabelled that change as an observation correction. Restore the original far prediction for B and retain the observed near category. Report two matches out of three assessed Ramp1 trials A through C, including B’s mismatch. Any revised model needs a new version and new reserved cases for evaluation.

teacher.background: Teach comparison as an evidence procedure. The ramp and drying records are fictional; do not present either predictor as a scientific law. Distinguish predictor inputs from outcome measurements, correct rule execution from outcome agreement, and an unassessed case from a failure. Keep observation quality open to documented review.
materials: Ramp trial cards A through F with heights and separate distance cards from the lesson
A record sheet with trial ID, model version, input, prediction, observation, outcome category and status
Drying records P through S from W4; paper only and no personal data
sessions: Retrieve why a missing observation prevents judgment even when a prediction is available.
Model A, B and C with separate height and distance cards. Record predictions before revealing distances. Explain that the lesson shows a worked retrospective example.
Complete W1 and W2. Require both numerical rules and include the exact-distance boundary at 4.
Discuss D and E and complete W3. Ask which evidence could establish the old trial outcome and why a new trial cannot do so.
Retrieve input, prediction, observation and outcome category with four labelled spaces.
Complete the guided A-through-E results record. Make assessed and unassessed counts visible before forming a result fraction.
Collect W4 independently. Watch for the different greater-than boundary at 10 minutes and the missing S outcome.
Discuss W5 and the exit. Preserve old predictions, distinguish documented observation corrections, and connect model revision to new reserved tests.
teacher.guidedAnswer: A predicts near, observed near, match; B far, observed near, mismatch; C far, observed far, match. D predicts near with missing distance; E predicts far with conflicting 3 and 4; both unassessed. Two matches out of three assessed, two unassessed. Exit: changing B after reading the outcome hides a mismatch; retain its original far prediction and observed near outcome, and identify any revised model separately.
misconceptions: Running the rule correctly proves the prediction correct
Rule execution and agreement with the observed outcome are separate checks.
A missing outcome is a success or a failure
Mark it unassessed and report the missing count alongside assessed results.
Every recorded observation must be true
Check the trial identity, units and evidence; document supported corrections.
A new trial repairs the old observation
A new trial has its own ID and result; the old outcome may remain unknown.
teacher.assessment: W4 is secure with quick/slow/slow/quick predictions, slow/quick/slow/unknown outcomes, two mismatches, one match and one unassessed case. Require one of three assessed and limited claims. After support retry scores 5, 8, 4 with times 9, 10, missing: quick/slow/quick predictions, quick/quick/unknown outcomes; one match, one mismatch, one unassessed.
teacher.support: Use separate coloured cards for predictions and observations and pair them by trial ID. Read at least and greater than aloud on number lines. Extension: investigate how selective missing records could make the assessed cases an incomplete picture of model performance.
teacher.next: Week 18 distinguishes confidence from correctness and asks what evidence could support a confidence claim.

ai-1/18.title: Confidence and correctness
goals: Distinguish a confidence claim from evidence that a prediction was correct
Compare recorded confidence claims with observed outcomes for a group
Explain why a score, a confident sentence and repeated agreement need different checks

prerequisite.prompt: A prediction says far and sounds very certain. No travel distance has been recorded. Can you mark it correct? Explain what is missing.
prerequisite.answer: No. The case is unassessed until adequate outcome evidence is available. The strength of the wording supplies no observed distance.

vocabulary: A statement or number expressing how strongly a prediction is supported according to a stated method
Whether a prediction agrees with an adequately established outcome for the task
A numerical estimate of how likely a specified event is
Agreement between probability estimates and observed frequencies across relevant groups of cases
The definition explaining what a reported number measures

lesson.title: Ask what a confidence claim means
