blocks.text: A prediction can be expressed strongly and still be wrong. Confidence describes a claim about support or likelihood; correctness is checked against evidence. Keep the prediction, the confidence claim and the observed outcome in separate columns. None can replace the others.

A display reading 80 might mean 80 out of 100 points for matching features, an estimated 80 percent chance of a specified event, or something else. Read its definition before interpreting it. The number alone does not tell you which meaning applies. A sentence such as definitely far is not a measured probability.

Ramp1 from Week 17 produced categories using a threshold. It supplied no probability estimates. We must not attach a probability merely because the height is far from that threshold. This week uses fictional forecast records with an explicitly stated probability claim; we are checking those claims, not inventing them for Ramp1.

lesson.title: Compare a claim with a group of outcomes

blocks.title: Claims and results are separate records
blocks.caption: Here each percentage claims the probability that its chosen category will be correct. The two ten-case groups are fictional examples. A group comparison cannot identify an unknown individual outcome.

blocks.text: An 80 percent claim means an estimated chance of 80 out of 100, for the event that was named. Across many relevant cases carrying that claim, a well-calibrated method should be correct about that often. It does not promise exactly eight successes in every ten cases or tell us which cases will fail.

Eight correct out of ten agrees numerically with 80 percent in this small group. Five out of ten is lower. Both are observations worth reporting; neither small group alone establishes how dependable the method will be. Larger relevant checks, independent of model fitting and score adjustment, give a stronger basis for judging the claim.

lesson.title: Check individual cases without changing their scores

blocks.text: A high-confidence error and a lower-confidence success can occur even when a probability method is useful. One error does not prove that all confidence estimates are worthless, and one success does not validate a method. Keep the original scores and investigate patterns across relevant cases.

Record the task, model version, event being assigned a probability, score definition and evidence used for checking. If outcomes are missing, report that count. Do not quietly remove difficult cases or change the confidence values after reading the answers. Adjustments belong to a new recorded method and need a fresh evaluation.

lesson.title: Make a limited report from complete records

blocks.text: A fictional classifier records an 80 percent probability that each selected category will be correct on ten reserved cases. All ten outcomes are later established: eight correct and two incorrect. The report should preserve both the claim and the observed counts. The group supports a comparison, not a guarantee about the next case.

blocks.label: Write a short report for this ten-case group. State the event claimed, the recorded probability, both outcome counts and one limitation. Explain why the next prediction at 80 percent cannot be marked correct before its outcome is checked

blocks.text: Now suppose two of the ten outcomes were missing. You would need to report which cases were assessed and how many remained unknown, as in Week 17. A confident-looking percentage does not repair missing observations or make an incomplete sample representative.

lesson.title: Choose evidence instead of confident wording

blocks.text: Before relying on a confidence display, ask what its number means, how it was checked on relevant cases and what happens when it is wrong. A feature-match score may help rank options without being a probability. A generated sentence may sound certain without supplying either a defined score or supporting evidence.

Repeating a claim does not establish its truth. Several tools can share information and mistakes. Useful checks seek relevant independent evidence and preserve unresolved outcomes. Review decisions also depend on the consequences of an error; a probability alone does not grant permission to act.

blocks.label: A tool says definitely correct and repeats the same answer five times. A learner writes 100 percent confidence and skips the outcome check. Explain two unsupported steps and name evidence that would be more useful

workbook.title: Read the score definition
workbook.prompt: A card sorter gives a match score of 80 out of 100 points. Its documentation says the score counts weighted feature matches and is not a probability. A learner calls this an 80 percent chance of correctness. Explain the error and write an accurate description.
workbook.answer: The learner replaced the documented score meaning with a probability interpretation. Report 80 of 100 feature-match points. To claim a chance of correctness, a defined probability method and relevant outcome evaluation would be needed.

workbook.title: Judge cases using outcomes
workbook.prompt: Use cases A, B and C from the lesson table. State which is correct, incorrect and unassessed. Explain why ordering them by confidence cannot replace checking their outcomes.
workbook.answer: A is incorrect, B correct and C unassessed. The score is a prior claim; the observed category determines agreement for an assessable case. A larger claim does not supply a missing outcome or override a conflicting one.

workbook.title: Interpret a small group carefully
workbook.prompt: Ten predictions each claim an 80 percent probability that their chosen category is correct. Five later prove correct and five incorrect. State the claimed probability and observed fraction separately. Does this prove every future prediction will be wrong, or that each next prediction has exactly a 50 percent chance? Explain.
workbook.answer: Claim 80 percent; observed five correct out of ten, or 50 percent in this group. This group falls below the claim but is small. It proves neither all future failures nor a precisely known 50 percent chance for each next case. More relevant independent evidence is needed.

workbook.title: Audit a different probability claim
workbook.prompt: A fictional leaf sorter claims a 75 percent probability of correctness for each of eight chosen labels. Later evidence establishes six correct labels, one incorrect label and one missing outcome. A report says six out of eight proves perfect calibration and guarantees the next label. Repair the report, state the assessed and unassessed counts, and describe a better follow-up check.
workbook.answer: Seven cases are assessed: six correct and one incorrect; one is unassessed. Report six out of seven assessed alongside the missing count, and preserve the original 75 percent claims. Six out of eight treats the missing outcome as known. The small incomplete group proves neither calibration nor the next label. Seek the missing outcome and evaluate the unchanged method on more relevant reserved cases.

workbook.title: Keep repetition separate from evidence
workbook.prompt: A learner copies the same 90 percent prediction into ten rows and calls this ten independent tests. No new outcomes were obtained. Explain why the evidence has not grown and propose a useful check.
workbook.answer: The rows duplicate one prediction, not ten independently assessed cases. No new outcome evidence was obtained. Preserve the original record, establish its outcome where possible, and gather distinct relevant reserved cases with their own predictions and verified outcomes.

teacher.background: Keep confidence, numerical scores and correctness separate. Calibration is introduced as a group comparison, without formal estimation. Small exact matches do not prove calibration. Concept reference: scikit-learn probability calibration documentation at https://scikit-learn.org/1.8/modules/calibration.html. All classroom examples here are fictional.
materials: Separate cards for probability claims and later outcomes
Ten counters to show observed correct and incorrect cases
W4 leaf-sorter records, with one outcome deliberately missing
sessions: Retrieve the need for an observed outcome before judging correctness.
Contrast a feature-match score, a defined probability estimate and confident wording. Explain each diagram row.
Complete W1 and W2. Require score meanings and outcome evidence in separate statements.
Use ten counters for W3. Compare the recorded claim with the observed fraction without turning the fraction into a guarantee.
Retrieve why a high-confidence prediction can be wrong.
Complete the guided group report. Discuss the difference between numerical agreement in a small group and evidence about a wider method.
Collect W4 independently. Check that the missing outcome stays visible and the denominator is seven assessed cases.
Discuss W5 and the exit. End with the evidence needed for a meaningful confidence claim.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Each score claims an 80 percent chance that the chosen category is correct. Observed results are eight correct and two incorrect out of ten assessed. This small group matches the claim numerically but cannot guarantee future performance or identify the next result. Exit: confident language is not a defined probability, and repeated wording does not establish correctness; seek relevant outcome evidence and documented score evaluation.
misconceptions: An 80 point score always means an 80 percent probability
Read the documented quantity before interpreting it.
An 80 percent method must succeed exactly eight times in every ten
A probability describes likelihood; small groups can vary.
A high-confidence error disproves all probabilities
Investigate many relevant cases while preserving individual errors.
A missing outcome can be counted as a failure to finish the fraction
Report assessed results and missing counts separately.
teacher.assessment: W4 requires six of seven assessed, one unassessed, the original 75 percent claim, no calibration guarantee and a relevant follow-up. After support retry ten 80 percent claims with seven correct, two incorrect and one missing: seven of nine assessed and one unassessed, with the same limits.
teacher.support: Use counters and separate headings for claim and outcome. Read 80 percent as 80 out of 100 before comparing fractions. Extension: explain why checking only easy cases might make the confidence method appear more dependable than it is.
teacher.next: Week 19 investigates how selected features change similarity and the examples a system considers close.

ai-1/19.title: Similarity and selected features
goals: Calculate similarity using explicitly selected features and a stated scoring rule
Explain how a change in feature weights can change the highest scoring item
Handle ties and missing features without claiming that a similarity score proves suitability

prerequisite.prompt: A system gives an item two matching-feature points. Does that mean a two-thirds chance that the item is suitable? What must you read first?
prerequisite.answer: No. Read the score definition and selected features. Matching-feature points describe a comparison rule, not a probability of suitability.

vocabulary: Closeness under a stated choice of features and comparison rule
Agreement between two recorded values for a selected feature
The number of points assigned to a feature match in this scoring rule
Two or more candidates sharing the same score
An item being considered in a comparison

lesson.title: Define similar for a particular purpose

blocks.text: Two objects can be alike in colour and different in shape. A computer comparison needs a precise answer to similar in what way. Select features, state how their values are compared, and define what a larger score means. The result belongs to that rule; it is not a universal judgment about the objects.

Our target card is red, round and smooth. Three candidate cards are A: red, round, rough; B: blue, square, smooth; C: red, square, rough. First give one point for each feature that exactly matches the target and zero for each known mismatch. Add the points. Colour, shape and texture are the only selected features.

This paper exercise uses complete category values with agreed spelling. Real records can be missing or uncertain. Do not silently treat an unknown texture as a known mismatch or copy a value from the target. First identify whether the information supports the comparison.

lesson.title: Trace every part of the score

blocks.title: Three features contribute to a score
blocks.caption: The target is red, round and smooth. A has the largest score under equal weights. These points count selected feature matches; they are not probabilities or evidence that A suits every purpose.

blocks.text: A receives 1 for colour, 1 for shape and 0 for texture: total 2. B receives 0, 0 and 1: total 1. C receives 1, 0 and 0: total 1. Record the contributions, not just the totals, so another learner can check the computation.

A is most similar among these three candidates under this rule. That sentence names the candidate set and the rule. It does not say A is identical to the target, has the right texture or will be the best choice for a task that needs smooth material.

lesson.title: Change one scoring choice and compare again

blocks.text: Suppose texture matters more for the stated comparison. Keep colour and shape worth one point each, but give three points for a texture match. B now scores 3 and becomes the unique highest scoring candidate. No card changed; the rule changed. Record both versions rather than overwriting the first result.

Weights express priorities in this designed rule. They need a reason connected to the task and should be set before inspecting the final evaluation results. A convenient winner does not justify a weight. If smooth texture is required without exception, use a requirement check rather than hoping a weighted score will always enforce it.

Add candidate D: blue, round, smooth. Under the original one-point rule, D scores 2, tying A. Our policy is to return every candidate with the largest score, so the result is A and D. Returning only the first row would silently introduce a different policy.

blocks.label: Using A, B, C and D, calculate the four totals under the original rule and then under texture worth 3. Return every highest scoring candidate each time. Explain which matches caused the change and why neither result establishes a probability of suitability

blocks.text: If a required comparison value is missing, our classroom policy pauses the final ranking and requests the missing value. Retain the known contributions and the reason for the pause. A different policy could be designed, but it would need to be explicit and checked for its effects. Unknown and different are separate states.

lesson.title: Keep the task bigger than the score

blocks.text: Feature selection leaves information out. A card comparison ignores size and material unless those are included. A book comparison using topic and format may ignore language or reading difficulty. More features are not automatically better: irrelevant or repeatedly copied features can change a score without improving the decision.

A useful report states the purpose, candidates, selected features, weights, missing-value policy and tie policy. Check the proposed method on relevant cases that include ties and imperfect records. If it supports a recommendation, keep the explanation limited to what was actually compared.

blocks.label: A learner says A is objectively the closest card because it won the original comparison. Use the changed texture weight and the added candidate D to explain why the claim needs qualification

workbook.title: Show the contributions before the total
workbook.prompt: For the red round smooth target and candidates A, B and C in the lesson, record the colour, shape and texture contributions under one point per match. Give each total and identify every highest scoring candidate.
workbook.answer: A: 1, 1, 0 gives 2. B: 0, 0, 1 gives 1. C: 1, 0, 0 gives 1. A is the only highest scoring candidate among A, B and C under equal weights.

workbook.title: Explain a changed winner
workbook.prompt: Keep the same target and candidates but make texture worth 3 points, with colour and shape worth 1 each. Recalculate A, B and C. Explain what changed and what stayed the same.
workbook.answer: A stays at 2, B becomes 3 and C stays at 1, so B wins. Only the texture weight changed; candidate values, target and other weights stayed the same. The result is specific to this new comparison rule.

workbook.title: Keep unknown separate from different
workbook.prompt: Candidate E is red and round but its texture is missing. A learner assigns zero for texture and declares E fully scored. Apply our classroom policy. State the known contributions, the missing information and what must happen before a final ranking.
workbook.answer: Colour and shape contribute 1 each, giving a known subtotal of 2 under the original rule. Texture is unknown, not a known mismatch. Pause the final ranking, request E’s texture, and record the unresolved feature if it cannot be obtained.

workbook.title: Transfer the comparison to books
workbook.prompt: A target book has topic space, format comic and language English. Candidates are J: space, prose, English; K: animals, comic, English; L: space, comic, Spanish. Give 1 point per exact match and return all tied highest scorers. Then make topic worth 3 points while keeping the other weights at 1. Report both sets of totals and winners. Explain why a winner may still fail a requirement to read English.
workbook.answer: Equal weights: J 2, K 2, L 2; all three tie. Topic weighted 3: J 4, K 2, L 4; J and L tie. L remains a highest scorer despite Spanish language, so weighted similarity does not enforce the English requirement. Check language eligibility separately if English is required.

workbook.title: Notice an accidental extra weight
workbook.prompt: A designer adds a second colour column that copies the first and gives both columns one point. They say no feature has been given extra importance because every column has equal weight. Explain the problem and propose a clearer rule.
workbook.answer: Colour now contributes twice for one underlying match, so it has effective weight 2 while other features have weight 1. Remove the duplicate or state and justify colour’s weight explicitly. Equal column weights do not guarantee equal importance for the underlying features.

teacher.background: Treat similarity as a defined computation with a purpose. This week uses exact category matching and whole-number weights, avoiding formal distance geometry. Keep ranking, probability and eligibility distinct. Students should be able to explain changes in results from the feature contributions rather than memorise a winning item.
materials: Target and candidate card records from the lesson, with D and incomplete E added later
Counters for colour, shape and texture contributions
Book records J, K and L from W4 with feature headings
sessions: Retrieve why a point score is not automatically a probability.
Trace the three diagram rows with one counter per match. State the target and candidates aloud.
Complete W1 and W2. Change only the texture weight and compare the two recorded results.
Use W3 to distinguish a missing value from a known mismatch. Require a recorded pause under the classroom policy.
Retrieve the scoring rule and why it depends on selected features.
Introduce D and complete the guided task. Return all tied maximum scores and explain the weighted result.
Collect W4 independently. Look for all ties and the distinction between similarity and a required language.
Discuss W5 and the exit. End with the need to document feature choices and effective weights.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Original totals A 2, B 1, C 1, D 2, so return A and D. With texture worth 3: A 2, B 3, C 1, D 4, so return D. D combines shape and texture. Scores count weighted matches, not observed chances of suitability. Exit: the winner depends on weights and candidate set; A’s first result is not a universal fact.
misconceptions: Similar has one objective meaning for every task
Name the features, comparison rule and purpose.
The highest score proves all requirements are met
Check mandatory requirements separately.
Equal scores can be resolved by whichever row appears first
Use the stated tie policy; here return all highest scorers.
Missing texture deserves zero as if it were rough
Retain an unknown and apply the stated missing-value policy.
teacher.assessment: W4 is secure with 2/2/2 then 4/2/4, all candidates then J and L as winners, and a separate English eligibility check. After support retry topic weight 2: totals 3/2/3, J and L still tie. Require contribution explanations, not only totals.
teacher.support: Place one row of counters under each feature heading. Keep the target visible while checking candidates. Extension: add a feature that is irrelevant to the stated purpose and show how it could change the winner without improving usefulness.
teacher.next: Week 20 uses explicit scores and requirements to form recommendations, then examines what feedback can and cannot establish.

ai-1/2.title: Representations and information paths
goals: Trace information through a system without confusing information with a physical action
Explain which details a representation preserves or discards
Locate the earliest stage at which an incorrect result could have arisen

prerequisite.prompt: In last week's bus case, the forecast number and the display colour came from different decisions. Which decision produced each output?
prerequisite.answer: The fitted model produced the delay estimate; the written greater-than-10 rule selected the colour. A caretaker or driver decision is a separate action.

vocabulary: A way of recording information so that it can be stored, communicated or processed
Information supplied to a particular process
An operation that changes, selects or interprets information
The result produced by a process
Details that cannot be recovered from the retained representation

lesson.title: A display does not do every part of a task

blocks.text: A library kiosk asks Sam for a genre. Sam selects mystery. The kiosk compares that preference with catalogue tags and displays three book titles. Sam says the kiosk has read three books aloud. That conclusion adds an action that the description never supplied: displaying a title is different from producing spoken audio.

An information path names what enters each stage, what happens there and what leaves it. Treat input and output as roles relative to a stage. A list of titles is the output of the search, but it could become the input to a separate text-to-speech stage. A component can therefore receive the output of another component without doing the same job.

The kiosk's genre-matching operation can be implemented with a written rule. Nothing in this description establishes that a model was trained. This connects to Week 1: tracing information tells us what a process needs to do, while mechanism evidence tells us how it does it.

blocks.title: Two possible library information paths
rows: Genre request mystery and catalogue tags
Three titles from the first stage
A separate speech system if available
Spoken titles rather than whole books
A selected title and an available copy
A person completes the borrowing process
A recorded loan and a borrowed copy
blocks.caption: The first row is the kiosk as described. The later rows require additional components and actions. Arrows show information dependencies; they do not establish that every stage has actually run.

blocks.text: Notice the difference between a title, a description and an entire book. All three can be text, but they represent different amounts of information. Even a speech stage receiving three titles can speak only those supplied titles; it has not thereby read the full books. Always identify the content of an input, not just its data type.

A recommendation is also different from a loan. Selecting a title does not reserve a copy unless an authorised reservation step exists. Keeping these distinctions clear prevents us from crediting a system with actions it did not take.

Consider two catalogue records. Book A has 90 pages and is about a child solving a seaside mystery. Book B has 90 pages and is about a lost spaceship. If we keep only page count, both become the number 90. The number is useful for a length limit, but it cannot tell us which story is a mystery. Information that was never retained cannot be recovered just by calculating harder.

rows: Does it match a mystery request?
Will this particular reader enjoy it?
What does the description say happens?
What exact sentence occurs on page 42?

blocks.text: The phrase cannot settle alone matters. A genre tag might be inaccurate, and a reader might enjoy an unfamiliar genre. A representation is useful only in relation to a question and its limits. More detail is not automatically better: unnecessary personal information can add risk without helping the task.

A greenhouse records morning temperatures of 18, 22 and 26 degrees C, then retains only the largest value, 26. Can the stored value prove that the temperature rose steadily? No. The sequence 22, 18, 26 has the same largest value but includes a decrease. These two sequences form a counterexample to the claim that the largest value determines the order.

To solve this, first state exactly what was kept: one maximum. Then ask what the claim requires: the order of several readings. Finally construct two possible originals that share the retained value but give different answers to the claim. If both originals fit the record, the record alone cannot decide between them.

blocks.label: A record keeps only a visitor count of 3. Give two different arrival schedules consistent with it and name one fact the count cannot reveal

blocks.text: The kiosk is asked for mystery books under 100 pages but displays a 140-page mystery. Before changing everything, inspect the intermediate records. Was the maximum entered as 100? Did the catalogue say 140? Did filtering preserve the wrong record? Did the display show a title different from the filtered result? The first mismatch between the intended and actual path helps locate the problem.

A correct-looking final screen can hide an earlier error. A calculator can correctly multiply a number that was transcribed incorrectly, and a warning rule can correctly use an incorrect forecast. Write down intermediate values so you can test each connection.

blocks.label: Explain why a system that displays a book title has not necessarily spoken, reserved or read the book

workbook.title: Trace a request
workbook.prompt: The kiosk receives genre=science and maximum pages=120. The catalogue contains A science 80 pages, B science 150 pages and C mystery 90 pages. It keeps records with the requested genre and no more than 120 pages. Draw the input, process and output, naming the surviving record.
workbook.answer: Input includes both request fields and all three catalogue records. The process checks science AND pages<=120. Output contains A only; B fails the length condition and C fails the genre condition. Listing A does not establish that a copy was reserved.

workbook.title: Finish the visitor example
workbook.prompt: A record stores only total visitors=3. Give two different arrival schedules that produce this total. Can the total tell us the busiest hour? Explain.
workbook.answer: Examples: three visitors at 09:00, or one each at 09:00, 10:00 and 11:00. Both total 3, but their busiest-hour patterns differ. The total lacks arrival-time information, so the busiest hour cannot be recovered from it alone.

workbook.title: Choose a sufficient representation
workbook.prompt: For each task, choose the information needed: decide whether a book is under 120 pages; quote its first sentence exactly; decide whether a copy is available now. Explain why a genre tag alone is insufficient for all three.
workbook.answer: Use the page count for the length condition, the actual first sentence from the correct edition for an exact quote, and a current copy-availability record for availability. Genre supplies none of those facts. Even suitable records must be checked for the correct edition or time.

workbook.title: Investigate a new loss of information
workbook.prompt: A classroom device receives four scores and stores only their total, 20. A student claims that every score must be 5. Give two different lists of four nonnegative whole-number scores with total 20. Explain precisely what the stored total establishes and what it does not.
workbook.answer: For example [5,5,5,5] and [2,4,6,8] both total 20. The stored total establishes the sum under the stated recording process, but not the individual scores or their equality. A list with fewer than four entries or a different total is not a valid counterexample.

workbook.title: Diagnose before repairing
workbook.prompt: A voice calculator receives a spoken request for 16 divided by 4. Its transcript says 60 divided by 4 and its calculator returns 15. Identify the first incorrect stage, show the intended result and propose a check before calculation.
workbook.answer: Transcription first changes 16 to 60. The calculator correctly computes the wrong supplied expression. The intended result is 4. Display or confirm the interpreted numbers before calculating, rather than changing the arithmetic code to force the expected answer.

teacher.background: Teach input and output as relative to a stage. Avoid claiming that representations are inherently truthful or complete. This lesson introduces information loss through counterexamples, without requiring formal information theory. The two-originals method is the important reasoning move: if two source records map to one stored result but imply different answers, the stored result cannot decide that question alone.
materials: Catalogue records A science 80, B science 150 and C mystery 90 written on cards
The information-path diagram and blank arrow diagrams
Paper for two four-number lists; no devices or accounts are needed
sessions: Retrieve the bus stages from Week 1. Ask which result becomes a later input.
Read the kiosk case and trace the first diagram row. Cover later rows, then reveal them as additional operations rather than assumed capabilities.
Use the two 90-page book descriptions. Ask which question survives when only 90 is kept. Model one counterexample.
Pairs complete W1 and the visitor example. Require exact input fields and outputs.
Ask whether a largest temperature proves a rising sequence. Have two students construct alternative sequences.
Complete W2 and W3. Separate current records, exact source text and summary tags.
Collect W4 independently. Give no example list until the attempt is saved.
Use W5 to connect information loss with stage diagnosis. Review the exit explanation and preview measurement.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Visitor schedules can be three at 09:00 or one each at 09:00, 10:00 and 11:00. The total does not reveal timing or busiest hour. Displaying a book title produces text on a screen; speaking needs audio generation, reserving needs an authorised availability update and reading the whole book needs its full content.
misconceptions: Every output is the final action
Trace an output entering the next stage. Ask whether the borrowing or speech stage exists and has run.
More calculation can recover discarded details
Ask students to distinguish two original records with the same retained value. No deterministic calculation of that value alone can know which original occurred.
A data type tells us what the data means
Compare a title, a summary and a full chapter. All can be text while supporting different questions.
teacher.assessment: W4 is secure when both lists contain four nonnegative whole numbers, both sum to 20, at least one is not all fives, and the explanation distinguishes sum from individual values. If the learner offers only one list, request another record consistent with the same total. Use a different total for the uncoached retry.
teacher.support: Provide four empty boxes and counters for learners who need arithmetic support. Let them explain information loss orally. Extension: ask which extra field, such as minimum score, would rule out one of their lists and whether it would uniquely determine the original list.
teacher.next: Week 3 examines how physical signals become measurements, including the units and conditions needed to interpret recorded values.

ai-1/20.title: Recommendations and feedback
goals: Apply eligibility requirements before ranking candidates by preferences
Explain a recommendation using its actual scoring rule and limits
Interpret feedback in the context of what was shown and distinguish clicks from satisfaction

prerequisite.prompt: A book has the highest similarity score but is in a language the reader cannot use. Should the score override the language requirement? Explain.
prerequisite.answer: No. Eligibility requirements must be checked separately. A high preference score does not make an ineligible item suitable.

vocabulary: Whether an item meets the requirements for consideration
A desired feature used to rank eligible choices
A suggested option produced under a stated process
An opportunity for a person to see an item
A process in which earlier recommendations influence the feedback used for later recommendations

blocks.text: A recommendation suggests an option for a particular purpose. Start with requirements: conditions every suggested item must meet. Then use preferences to rank the eligible options. An item that fails a requirement cannot make up for it by collecting more preference points.

A fictional reader needs an available English book. The reader prefers topic space and format comic. BookRec1 gives eligible books 2 points for space and 1 for comic; a known mismatch gives 0. It returns every eligible book tied for the highest score. If none are eligible, it reports no eligible option rather than ignoring a requirement.

The candidates are J: space, prose, English, available; K: animals, comic, English, available; L: space, comic, Spanish, available; M: space, comic, English, unavailable. These are invented records. The purpose is to trace a recommendation, not to infer anything about real students or collect their personal preferences.

lesson.title: Trace the decision before writing the explanation

blocks.title: Requirements come before preference scores
blocks.caption: BookRec1 recommends J from this candidate set. L and M match both preferences but fail a requirement. The recommendation does not guarantee that the reader will enjoy J.

blocks.text: J passes both requirements and scores 2. K passes and scores 1. L fails the English requirement; M fails availability. Do not place L or M above J because they would earn 3 preference points. They are excluded before the eligible scores are compared.

A faithful explanation says J is available in English and has the highest eligible score because its space topic matches the stated preference. It should also mention that J is prose, not comic. Claiming that the system knows the reader will love J would go beyond the computation and the evidence.

lesson.title: Read feedback without inventing a motive

rows: The reader noticed or liked it
Reader said J was too long
A stated reason in this context

blocks.text: A click can reflect interest, curiosity or a mistaken tap. No click can reflect a missed display, lack of time or a decision not to choose it. Preserve the observed event separately from any interpretation. More direct feedback may clarify a reason, but one response still describes one person and occasion.

Useful feedback records name the item, what was shown, the system version, the event and any stated reason. Use only information needed for the task. Our paper exercises use invented feedback; they do not require accounts or recording classmates’ browsing behaviour.

lesson.title: Follow how exposure can shape later records

blocks.text: Suppose a system shows only space books, then collects clicks only on those books. If it treats those clicks as proof that space is the only wanted topic, it may keep showing space. Its choices helped produce the evidence it later uses. The absence of animal-book clicks says little when animal books were never shown.

blocks.label: A log says J was shown and clicked; K was never shown. A designer wants to label J enjoyed and K disliked. Write the two defensible records, identify the unsupported labels, and propose a useful way to ask for feedback without assuming the answer

blocks.text: A better investigation can ask the fictional reader directly or offer a small set of eligible alternatives with clear choice and optional feedback. Record what was offered as well as the response. Such a comparison still needs care: order, context and missing responses can affect what is observed. Do not call an unseen item rejected.

lesson.title: Revise the process without rewriting feedback

blocks.text: If feedback says J is too long, length may be a relevant missing feature. Ask what limit matters before adding a requirement. Do not automatically remove all space books or silently turn one comment into a permanent preference. Keep the original feedback and document any change to the recommendation rules.

Check a revised version on reserved paper cases, including ties, no eligible choices and missing required information. If a required fact is unknown, mark that candidate pending verification and report the limitation; do not assume it passes. If all candidates are pending or excluded, return no verified eligible option. A recommendation leaves the final choice with the reader.

blocks.label: A system recommends only the books it showed last week because those are the only books with clicks. Explain how its own display choices could keep other books out of consideration and name one improvement to the evidence collection

workbook.title: Filter before scoring
workbook.prompt: Apply BookRec1 to J, K, L and M from the lesson. State eligibility or exclusion reason for each, the scores of eligible books and the recommendation. Explain why L’s two preference matches do not make it the winner.
workbook.answer: J eligible scores 2; K eligible scores 1; L excluded for Spanish; M excluded because unavailable. Recommend J. Preference matches cannot compensate for failing the English requirement.

workbook.title: Explain a recommendation honestly
workbook.prompt: Write an explanation of why J was recommended that mentions one preference it does not match. A marketer adds guaranteed enjoyment. Explain why that phrase is unsupported.
workbook.answer: J is available in English and its space topic earns 2, the highest score among eligible choices; it is prose rather than the preferred comic. The rule supplies a ranking, not evidence guaranteeing enjoyment.

workbook.title: Do not label an unseen item rejected
workbook.prompt: J was shown and clicked. K was never shown. Separate the observed records from the labels enjoyed and disliked. Write a question that could gather a stated reason while allowing no answer.
workbook.answer: Record J shown and clicked; K not shown. Enjoyment of J and dislike of K remain unsupported. An optional question such as Did this suggestion suit what you wanted, and why or why not? seeks a reason without presuming satisfaction. No answer remains missing feedback.

workbook.title: Transfer the process to activities
workbook.prompt: A fictional learner needs an indoor activity lasting at most 20 minutes. Preferences score 2 for drawing and 1 for solo. Candidates: A drawing, solo, outdoor, 10 minutes; B drawing, group, indoor, 20 minutes; C music, solo, indoor, 15 minutes; D drawing, group, indoor, 18 minutes. Filter, score and return all highest scorers. Only B is then shown and selected; C and D are not shown. State what the feedback establishes and what remains unknown.
workbook.answer: A excluded because outdoor. B eligible scores 2; C eligible scores 1; D eligible scores 2. Return B and D. Exactly 20 minutes passes at most 20. The log establishes B shown and selected, not enjoyment. Preferences about unshown C and D are unknown; selecting B does not prove rejection of D or validate the choice to hide it.

workbook.title: Handle an empty eligible set
workbook.prompt: Return to BookRec1. J and K become unavailable, L remains Spanish, and M’s availability becomes unknown. A designer proposes recommending M anyway because it matches both preferences. Apply the requirements and propose an honest response.
workbook.answer: J and K are excluded as unavailable, L for language. M is pending availability verification and cannot yet count as eligible. Report no verified eligible option, identify the missing availability fact, and request confirmation or let the reader revise requirements explicitly.

teacher.background: This is an explicit paper recommender, not a claim that all recommenders use the same algorithm. Separate eligibility, scoring, exposure and feedback meaning. The feedback-loop concept is supported by the primary research Degenerate Feedback Loops in Recommender Systems, https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.10730. All task records are fictional.
materials: Book records J through M and requirement and preference cards
A feedback log with item, exposure, event and optional stated reason
Activity records A through D for the independent task
sessions: Retrieve why a similarity score cannot override a requirement.
Trace BookRec1 eligibility and scoring. Ask why L and M never enter the eligible ranking.
Complete W1 and W2. Compare a faithful explanation with a claim of guaranteed enjoyment.
Read the feedback table and complete W3. Preserve what was observed without guessing motives.
Retrieve the difference between an unseen item and a rejected item.
Complete the guided feedback record and trace the space-only display loop. Discuss an optional, neutral feedback question.
Collect W4 independently. Require the tie, the 20-minute boundary and limits on the selection log.
Discuss W5 and the exit. Test no eligible option and unknown availability without relaxing requirements silently.
teacher.guidedAnswer: J: shown and clicked; enjoyment not established. K: never shown; dislike not established. Ask an optional neutral question about suitability and reason, or offer eligible alternatives and record exposure and response. Exit: only showing prior clicked items restricts opportunities for other feedback; include eligible alternatives and preserve which options were actually shown.
misconceptions: A high score can cancel a failed requirement
Filter on requirements before ranking preferences.
A click proves enjoyment
It is an interaction; motive and satisfaction need further evidence.
No clicks means dislike even without exposure
An unseen option has not received a meaningful opportunity for a response.
No eligible result means the system must choose anyway
Return no verified eligible option and explain exclusions or missing facts.
teacher.assessment: W4 requires excluding A, scores B 2 C 1 D 2, both B and D returned, and no inferred enjoyment or rejection from unshown items. After support change the time limit to at most 18: B becomes excluded, D wins with 2 over C’s 1. Keep feedback limits unchanged.
teacher.support: Use separate trays for excluded, pending and eligible items. Score only the eligible tray. Extension: change the display order while keeping scores fixed and explain why different clicks would not automatically show changed preferences.
teacher.next: Week 21 investigates data quality and how to repair a record with evidence while preserving its history.

ai-1/21.title: Data quality and documented repair
goals: Check records against a stated format, unit and meaning before using them
Distinguish an evidence-based correction from an unsupported guess
Keep original values and a change log, then report what remains unresolved

prerequisite.prompt: A recommender needs availability, but that field is blank. Can the highest preference score establish that the item is available? Explain.
prerequisite.answer: No. The score does not supply the missing fact. Keep availability unknown and seek evidence before counting the item as eligible.

vocabulary: A description of required fields, formats, units and allowed values
Checking a record against stated requirements
A record of where information came from
A change supported by evidence about the intended value
A record of what changed, why, when and on what evidence

lesson.title: Decide what each field means before checking it

blocks.text: A tidy table can still contain wrong information. Validation checks whether a record follows a schema. A schema says which fields are required and what their values mean. Passing these checks makes a record usable for a stated task; it does not prove that the measurement or claim is true.

Our fictional RampLog records one ramp trial per trial ID. The fields are trial ID, height in centimetres, travel in centimetres and source card. Height must be a whole number from 1 through 10. Travel must be a whole number from 0 through 10. The source card identifies the original observation. Repeated trial IDs need investigation before counting trials.

The purpose is to count trials whose travel is at least 4 cm. A measured zero means no travel; a blank means no value was recorded. Never silently replace a blank by zero. Use only the invented records here; no personal information is needed.

lesson.title: Follow the evidence from original to corrected record

blocks.title: Preserve the original and explain each decision
blocks.caption: C2 supports correcting T2. C3 cannot supply a missing measurement. C4 shows that zero is a recorded observation, not a placeholder for missing data.

blocks.text: The complete raw table is T1: height 4, travel 3, card C1; T2: height 60, travel 5, card C2; T3: height 5, travel blank, card C3; T4: height 6, travel 0, card C4. A second export row repeats T1 with height 4, travel 3 and C1. C1 confirms one trial T1, not two. C2 reads height 6 and travel 5. C3 has no travel measurement. C4 reads height 6 and travel 0.

Work in a separate corrected copy. Record T2 height 60 to 6, evidence C2, transcription error, reviewer and review date. Link the repeated T1 export row to the first T1; count that single trial once and keep both raw rows. Do not remove two different trials merely because their measured numbers match.

lesson.title: Choose an action that the evidence supports

rows: Confirm one trial on C1; count once
Treat every repeated number as a duplicate
Pick the value that improves the result

blocks.text: A conversion changes units while preserving the quantity. If an authorised source records 50 mm, that is 5 cm because 10 mm equals 1 cm. Write the original unit, conversion and resulting unit in the log. A bare value 50 without a known unit does not justify assuming millimetres.

A plausible value can still be a transcription error: 7 would pass the height rule even if its source said 6. Conversely, an unusual but supported value is not automatically wrong. Checking format and checking agreement with a source are different jobs. A source can itself contain an error, so retain its identity and any unresolved concern.

lesson.title: Count only after describing the repaired records

blocks.text: After the documented correction and confirmed duplicate handling, RampLog contains four distinct trials: T1, T2, T3 and T4. Three have recorded travel. T1 has 3 cm, T2 has 5 cm and T4 has 0 cm. Only T2 meets at least 4 cm, so the result is 1 of 3 assessed trials, with 1 trial missing travel. Do not report T3 as a failure or hide it from the account.

blocks.label: A reviewer fills T3 travel with 4 because it makes the results look more balanced. Identify the unsupported change, write an honest report using the recorded evidence, and name the source information still needed

blocks.text: Describe which records entered the calculation and why. Keep unresolved records visible in a separate status list. A new measurement is a new observation with its own time and identity; it should not be passed off as the missing observation from an earlier trial.

lesson.title: Check the repair and preserve the uncertainty

blocks.text: After changing a value, run the schema checks again and compare the corrected copy with the raw copy and log. Recount distinct trials. Check that every correction has evidence and that zero, missing and conflict remain separate. A repair can introduce a new mistake if a value is changed in the wrong row.

The corrected RampLog supports a statement about its three assessed trials. It does not establish how every ramp or future trial behaves. Better formatting cannot create missing observations or broaden what was sampled. Next week asks which cases a dataset actually covers.

blocks.label: A table now has no blank cells because a designer guessed all missing measurements. Explain why this does not establish better evidence, and state what a trustworthy repair record should retain

workbook.title: Check a schema without guessing
workbook.prompt: Use the RampLog schema. State the issue or valid status for height 60, travel blank and travel 0. Give the range allowed for each numeric field and explain why a blank and zero require different treatment.
workbook.answer: Height 60 fails the whole-number range 1 through 10. Travel blank is missing; its value cannot be inferred. Travel 0 is valid in the whole-number range 0 through 10 and can represent observed no travel. Zero is a measurement, not a replacement for a blank.

workbook.title: Write a traceable correction
workbook.prompt: C2 says T2 height is 6 cm and travel is 5 cm; the export says height 60 cm. Write a change-log entry with ID, field, old and new values with units, evidence, reason, reviewer and date. Use a fictional reviewer and date. Explain where the raw export is kept.
workbook.answer: Example: T2; height; 60 cm to 6 cm; source C2; transcription error; reviewer R; review date 16 September 2026. Preserve the original export unchanged and apply the correction to a separate working copy. The source supports 6; the invalid 60 alone would not reveal the intended number.

workbook.title: Distinguish duplicate rows from similar trials
workbook.prompt: The export repeats T1 with the same source C1, which confirms one trial. A different trial T5 also has height 4 and travel 3, with its own source C5 confirming a separate trial. Explain which rows count once and why T5 must remain separate.
workbook.answer: The two export rows for T1 represent one confirmed trial and count once, with a link explaining the duplicate. T5 is another confirmed trial and stays separate even though its measurements equal T1. Matching numeric values alone do not establish duplication.

workbook.title: Audit an independent paper-plane log
workbook.prompt: Each flight ID must be unique; distance is a whole number from 0 through 20 cm. Raw rows: F1 8 cm; F2 120 cm; F3 blank; F4 0 cm; another F1 8 cm. Source S1 confirms one F1 flight. S2 says F2 travelled 12 cm. S3 is blank. S4 confirms zero. Preserve the raw rows, describe supported repairs and give the number of distinct flights. Report how many assessed flights travelled at least 10 cm, including missing records separately.
workbook.answer: Correct F2 distance from 120 to 12 cm using S2 and log the change. Link the duplicate F1 row using S1 and count F1 once. Keep F3 missing and F4 at measured zero. Four distinct flights remain; three have recorded distances 8, 12 and 0. Only F2 meets at least 10 cm: 1 of 3 assessed, with 1 missing. Retain all five raw rows and the evidence for both repair actions.

workbook.title: Handle conflicting and converted evidence
workbook.prompt: Two signed cards disagree about the same F3 flight: one says 9 cm and the other 11 cm. Neither is established as the correction. What can you report for the at-least-10-cm question? Separately, a source for a new F5 flight explicitly records 100 mm. Convert it to centimetres and state the conversion evidence to retain.
workbook.answer: Keep F3 unresolved because 9 would fail and 11 would meet the threshold; do not choose whichever improves the result. Flag both sources and request resolution; the known F1, F2 and F4 results still give 1 of 3 assessed with F3 unresolved. F5 is 10 cm because 100 divided by 10 equals 10. Preserve 100 mm, the source ID and the 10-mm-per-cm conversion. F5 is a new flight, not a repair of F3.

teacher.background: This paper investigation separates validation, source checking, correction and reporting. The schema is a classroom contract, not a universal range for real ramps or flights. Preserve raw records and treat a repair as an evidence claim. No spreadsheet, AI account or collection of student data is required.
materials: The five raw RampLog rows and source-card statements printed in the lesson
A blank change log with ID, field, old value, new value, evidence, reason, reviewer and date
The five independent flight rows and source statements printed in W4
sessions: Retrieve why a preference score cannot supply an unknown required fact.
Read the schema and distinguish a measured zero from a blank. Complete W1.
Trace the diagram and source cards. Model a correction in a separate copy, then complete W2.
Complete W3. Compare a duplicate export row with a separate trial that happens to have matching values.
Retrieve the evidence needed for a correction and the reason to keep the raw copy.
Complete the guided report. Require 1 of 3 assessed and 1 missing, with no invented T3 measurement.
Collect W4 independently. Check the repair log, distinct-flight count and denominator.
Discuss W5 and the exit. Distinguish unresolved conflicting sources, supported unit conversion and a new observation.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Filling T3 with 4 has no observational support. Keep travel missing; T1 3, T2 5 and T4 0 give 1 of 3 assessed at least 4 cm, with 1 missing trial. Seek an original travel observation for T3; C3 currently supplies none. Exit: guessed completeness is not evidence of accuracy. Retain raw values, source identity, supported changes, reviewer, date and unresolved statuses.
misconceptions: Every valid value is true
Schema compliance does not prove agreement with an observation or establish that the source was accurate.
A blank means zero
Zero is a known value; a blank is missing information.
Matching measurements must be duplicates
Distinct trials can have equal measurements; investigate identity and provenance.
A repair should make the result look better
Corrections follow evidence, regardless of whether the result improves.
teacher.assessment: W4 requires the supported 120-to-12 correction, one count for the repeated F1, four distinct flights, measured zero retained and 1 of 3 assessed with 1 missing. After support change F1 to 10 cm with confirming S1: the numerator becomes 2 of the same 3 assessed; the missing count remains 1. Do not award independent mastery for copying the original report.
teacher.support: Use three cards labelled measured zero, missing and conflicting. Provide a change-log frame while requiring students to supply the evidence. Extension: show a value that passes the schema but disagrees with its source, and ask which check reveals the problem.
teacher.next: Week 22 examines sampling and coverage: which cases supplied the records, which are absent, and how that limits a conclusion.

ai-1/22.title: Sampling and coverage
goals: Name the target collection, selection list and cases actually assessed
Use a coverage table to identify missing conditions before making a claim
Propose a selection plan that addresses a stated gap without promising certainty

prerequisite.prompt: A table has been checked and every recorded value matches its source. Does that prove it includes all the conditions in which a system will be used? Explain.
prerequisite.answer: No. Correct records can still describe only a narrow set of conditions. Source checking does not establish coverage of unrecorded cases.

vocabulary: The whole collection of cases a question is about
The selected cases used to investigate a larger collection
The list or source from which cases can be selected
Which relevant kinds of cases the list or sample includes
Systematic distortion caused by how cases enter an investigation

lesson.title: Name the collection before reporting a result

blocks.text: Suppose a shape recogniser will be evaluated on a fixed collection of 24 invented picture cards. This target population has 6 bright circles, 6 dim circles, 6 bright squares and 6 dim squares. Each card has its own ID and an independently checked circle or square label. We want to know how often the recogniser gives the correct label across these 24 cards.

A tester takes the 6 bright-circle cards nearest the front of the box. Those 6 cards form the sample; the other 18 have not been assessed. The recogniser is correct on 5 of the 6 sampled cards. That is a result for these assessed bright circles. It does not establish correctness on the squares or dim cards.

A sampling frame is the list or source available for selection. A complete list of all 24 IDs could give every card a chance of selection. A list containing only bright-circle IDs cannot select dim cards or squares, even if the choice from that list is random. These fictional picture cards do not contain personal information.

blocks.title: Coverage is about cases as well as counts
blocks.caption: All 6 assessed cases come from one of four conditions. An assessed count of zero means no evidence for that condition; it does not mean the recogniser failed every case in it.

blocks.text: The target has 24 distinct cards, but the sample covers only the 6 bright circles. Photographing each sampled card twice would create 12 image records without adding a new card or covering a missing condition. Record the identity of the underlying case as well as the number of files.

Both shape and lighting matter to this question. A sample with bright circles and dim squares includes each shape and each lighting label, yet still misses dim circles and bright squares. Check combinations when the interaction could matter, not just whether each individual label appears somewhere.

lesson.title: Match the selection plan to the purpose

rows: Draw from all 24 IDs by chance
Every listed card can be selected
A small draw need not balance conditions
8 cards do not establish all 24 outcomes
Does not prove performance on future images

blocks.text: For a broad estimate, a chance-based plan should start from a suitable complete list and use a documented selection procedure. For investigating missing conditions, deliberately selecting cases from each condition can be useful. State which purpose you chose. A set built to expose problems is not automatically a faithful miniature of everyday use.

Selection bias is about a systematic feature of the selection process, not whether a person had bad intentions. Choosing only easy-to-reach, bright cards can leave harder conditions out. More cases from the same narrow source may repeat that gap. A larger sample cannot by itself repair a frame that excludes relevant cases.

lesson.title: Keep selected, assessed and unassessed separate

blocks.text: Imagine a new plan selects 2 distinct cards from each of the four conditions: 8 cards in total. One selected dim-square file cannot be opened. Only 7 have assessed outcomes. Record the missing file and its condition; do not call it a recognition error or pretend all 8 outcomes were checked. This exercise evaluates recognition only, so file availability is reported separately.

blocks.label: A report says the original recogniser is correct on 5 of 6 cards, so it works on all shapes and lighting. Rewrite the claim using the original sample, identify the three missing conditions, and propose a selection plan to investigate them

blocks.text: Choose and document cases before seeing their outcomes. If you use the results to revise the recogniser, keep a separate unseen final test as in Week 15. Coverage and an unseen test solve different problems: one asks which conditions appear; the other asks whether the evaluation cases influenced the revision.

lesson.title: Describe what the evidence can reach

blocks.text: A careful report identifies the target, frame, selection method, distinct cases, assessed outcomes and gaps. For the original sample: 5 of 6 selected bright-circle cards were correct; the 18 cards in other conditions were not assessed. This is useful evidence with a narrow reach, not a score for all future images.

Even checking all 24 cards answers a question about that fixed collection and that recogniser version. New image sources, different lighting or other shapes introduce new cases. Revisit the target and the coverage plan when the intended use changes.

blocks.label: A tester collects 100 more bright-circle images and says the absence of dim-square tests no longer matters. Explain what increased and what coverage gap remains

workbook.title: Name target, frame and sample
workbook.prompt: Use the 24-card investigation. State the target collection, the original six-card sample and the three absent conditions. If the selection list contains only bright-circle IDs, explain why random selection from that list cannot reach every target condition.
workbook.answer: The target is all 24 specified cards across four conditions. The sample is the 6 bright-circle cards. Dim circles, bright squares and dim squares are absent. A frame containing only bright-circle IDs excludes every other condition, regardless of how randomly IDs are drawn from it.

workbook.title: Separate files from distinct cases
workbook.prompt: Each of the six original sampled cards is photographed twice. State the number of image files and distinct cards. Has this covered a new shape or lighting condition? Explain why the counts need different labels.
workbook.answer: There are 12 image files but still 6 distinct cards, all bright circles. No new shape or lighting condition has been covered. Multiple records of the same cases are not 12 distinct sampled cards and do not resolve the missing conditions.

workbook.title: Read a coverage table in combinations
workbook.prompt: A different test includes 3 bright circles and 3 dim squares. A designer says it covers both shapes and both lighting conditions, so no combinations are missing. Identify the missing combinations and propose six additional distinct cards to investigate them.
workbook.answer: Dim circles and bright squares are missing, even though circle, square, bright and dim each occur somewhere. Add 3 distinct dim circles and 3 distinct bright squares from the target collection. This addresses those combination gaps but does not establish every unassessed card outcome.

workbook.title: Audit a new sound-recognition claim
workbook.prompt: A fixed target has 20 invented clips: 5 quiet bells, 5 noisy bells, 5 quiet claps and 5 noisy claps. A tester selects 4 distinct quiet bells from a quiet-bell-only list; 3 are correctly labelled and 1 is wrong. Write a supported result, name missing conditions and explain why the result is not established for all 20 clips. Propose an 8-clip plan that includes every condition, with no clip selected twice.
workbook.answer: The recogniser is correct on 3 of 4 assessed quiet-bell clips. No noisy bells, quiet claps or noisy claps were assessed; even one quiet-bell clip remains unassessed. The restricted frame and sample cannot establish the all-20 result. Select 2 distinct clips from each of the four conditions using the complete target list, document selection before outcomes and report remaining limits. Eight clips improve condition coverage but are not all 20.

workbook.title: Report a selected case without an outcome
workbook.prompt: An 8-clip plan selects 2 from each sound condition. One selected noisy-clap file cannot be opened. The task measures recognition correctness only. State selected and assessed counts and the assessed count for each condition. Explain why a report of all 8 checked is wrong, and how to handle the missing file transparently.
workbook.answer: Eight clips were selected; seven were assessed. Quiet bells, noisy bells and quiet claps each have 2 assessed; noisy claps have 1 assessed and 1 unassessed file. No recognition outcome is available for the unopened file. Log its ID and reason, recover it if possible, and document any replacement rule without choosing on outcomes. Do not label its recognition result correct or wrong or hide its absence.

teacher.background: Teach the difference between accurate records and adequate coverage. The populations here are finite invented card and clip collections, so students can account for every selected and unselected case. Avoid presenting equal group counts as a universal sampling rule: this target has equal groups, and the proposed balanced plan investigates condition coverage. It does not guarantee an unbiased estimate in every application.
materials: A paper inventory with 6 IDs for each of the four picture-card conditions
A four-row coverage table with target, selected, assessed and missing columns
Twenty paper clip IDs grouped into the four fictional sound conditions; no audio recording needed
sessions: Retrieve why source-checked data can still omit relevant conditions.
Model target, frame and sample using the picture-card inventory. Complete W1.
Read the coverage diagram. Complete W2 and distinguish file count from distinct cases.
Complete W3 and compare individual features with their combinations.
Retrieve the three absent conditions in the original investigation.
Compare selection plans and complete the guided claim rewrite. Use shuffled paper IDs to show that a small chance draw need not balance conditions.
Collect W4 independently. Require a bounded result and a feasible plan with distinct clips.
Discuss W5 and the exit. Keep selected, assessed and unavailable counts separate.
teacher.guidedAnswer: The original recogniser correctly labelled 5 of 6 assessed bright-circle cards. Dim circles, bright squares and dim squares were not assessed. A documented plan selecting 2 distinct cards per condition from all 24 IDs would include each condition without claiming to establish every outcome. Exit: the image count grew, but the absence of dim-square tests remains; more bright-circle data cannot supply dim-square evidence.
misconceptions: More records always remove bias
A restricted source can keep excluding the same conditions as its record count grows.
Random selection repairs an incomplete list
Excluded cases cannot be selected from a list that does not contain them.
Every feature value appears, so every combination appears
Bright circles and dim squares still omit dim circles and bright squares.
Zero assessed means every case failed
Zero assessed means no observed recognition outcomes for that group.
teacher.assessment: W4 requires 3 of 4 quiet bells, all three missing conditions, recognition that the all-20 result is unestablished, and an 8-clip plan with distinct cases from all four conditions; 2 per condition is one valid plan. After support use a sample of 4 noisy claps with 2 correct: the supported result is 2 of 4 noisy claps, and quiet bells, noisy bells and quiet claps are absent. Require a fresh explanation, not a copied list.
teacher.support: Place paper IDs in four labelled boxes and physically mark selected and assessed cards. Provide the column headings while students fill the counts. Extension: explain why a full assessment of this fixed 24-card population still would not prove correctness on every future photograph.
teacher.next: Week 23 compares performance fractions while keeping denominators, missing outcomes and evaluation conditions explicit.

ai-1/23.title: Fractions and performance comparisons
goals: Compute a correct-out-of-assessed fraction and explain its denominator
Compare systems on shared cases while checking performance within conditions
Combine counts correctly and keep missing outcomes separate from assessed errors

prerequisite.prompt: Eight cases were selected, but one has no assessed outcome. How many have assessed outcomes, and what must a performance report say about the remaining case?
prerequisite.answer: Seven are assessed. Report the one unassessed case separately and explain why its outcome is unavailable; do not silently count it as correct or incorrect.

vocabulary: The count above the fraction line; here, assessed correct cases
The count below the fraction line; here, all assessed cases
Different written fractions that represent the same proportion
The fraction of assessed classification cases labelled correctly under a stated rule
A result formed by combining the counts of several groups

lesson.title: Name what goes above and below the fraction line

blocks.text: For this week, accuracy means the number of correctly labelled cases divided by the number of assessed cases. Every assessed case has a system label and a checked reference label, so its result can be judged correct or incorrect. State the system version, cases and scoring rule with the fraction. Cases without an assessable outcome are reported separately.

Two fixed shape-recognition versions, A and B, label the same 12 previously unseen picture cards. Eight cards are bright and four are dim; each has a checked circle or square reference label. Both versions return labels for all 12. A is correct on 8 bright and 1 dim card. B is correct on 6 bright and 2 dim cards.

A therefore has 9 correct out of 12 assessed, written 9/12. Dividing numerator and denominator by 3 gives 3/4. Three quarters equals 75 out of 100, or 75%. B has 8/12, equal to 2/3. For this comparison keep B as an exact fraction; a rounded percentage is unnecessary.

lesson.title: Use the same denominator for a direct comparison

blocks.title: Combine correct and assessed counts
blocks.caption: A has the higher overall accuracy on these same 12 cards, while B has the higher accuracy on the 4 dim cards. The overall fraction does not describe every condition equally.

blocks.text: With the same denominator 12, compare the numerators: 9 is greater than 8. A is correct on one more of these cards. This establishes the ordering on this test under this scoring rule; it does not prove that A will always outperform B on future cards.

To compare fractions with different denominators, rewrite them as equivalent fractions with a common denominator. For example, 3/4 equals 9/12 and 2/3 equals 8/12. Changing the written denominator does not create new test cases: it only helps compare the proportions.

lesson.title: Look inside a total before choosing a system

blocks.text: The bright group has twice as many assessed cards as the dim group. Each individual card counts once in the combined result, so add correct counts and assessed counts. Do not simply average the two group percentages and call it the all-card accuracy: that would give each group equal weight despite their different sizes.

If the intended task especially needs dim-card performance, inspect that result and gather suitable additional evidence before choosing. An overall leader can still be weaker in a relevant condition. This table alone also does not tell us whether particular mistakes have different consequences. The scoring rule must match the purpose.

lesson.title: Keep comparison conditions and missing outcomes visible

blocks.text: A third version C is run on the same 12 cards, but two results are lost before they can be judged. Among its 10 assessed outcomes, 9 are correct and 1 is wrong: 9/10 = 90% assessed accuracy, with 2 outcomes unassessed. Do not call this 90% on all 12. Its assessed subset differs from A and B, so the headline fractions do not give the same complete-case comparison.

blocks.label: A report declares C best because 90% exceeds A’s 75%. Write the fraction and missing count for C, explain the comparison problem, and propose an evaluation step that would make the evidence easier to compare

blocks.text: Recover and assess the two lost results if possible, without changing the versions. Another clearly labelled comparison can use the exact same cases with known outcomes for every version; disclose which cases it excludes and why. The current totals do not tell us how A performed on C’s ten assessed cases. Never invent that subset score.

lesson.title: Write a claim that preserves the counts

blocks.text: A useful performance statement gives the correct count, assessed count, missing count and evaluation conditions. For A: 9/12 correct, no missing outcomes, on the shared test of 8 bright and 4 dim cards. Follow it with the important contrast: 8/8 bright and 1/4 dim. Percentages are optional shorthand, not replacements for these counts.

A score of 3/4 and a score of 75/100 are equal proportions, but they describe different quantities of evidence if they come from different tests. The collection method and case coverage still matter. Neither fraction is an individual prediction confidence or a guarantee about the next case.

blocks.label: A system has 2 correct of 2 in one group and 4 correct of 8 in another. Write the combined correct and assessed counts. Explain why averaging 100% and 50% would answer a different question

workbook.title: Explain both parts of a performance fraction
workbook.prompt: For version A in the lesson, write correct and assessed counts, simplify the accuracy fraction and express it as a percentage. Explain what its denominator includes and why 9/9 would be misleading.
workbook.answer: A has 9 correct out of 12 assessed: 9/12 = 3/4 = 75%. The denominator includes all 12 judged outcomes, including 3 incorrect ones. Using 9/9 would exclude the errors and falsely report perfect assessed accuracy.

workbook.title: Compare totals and conditions
workbook.prompt: Compare A and B on the shared 12-card test and on its bright and dim groups. State the leader in each and explain why the overall result does not imply that one version wins in every condition.
workbook.answer: Overall A leads 9/12 to B’s 8/12. On bright cards A leads 8/8 to 6/8. On dim cards B leads 2/4 to A’s 1/4. The overall count combines unequal groups; A’s overall lead does not mean a lead in the dim group or a guarantee for future cards.

workbook.title: Do not hide unassessed outcomes
workbook.prompt: C has 9 correct and 1 incorrect assessed outcome, with 2 other selected cases unassessed. Write its assessed accuracy and missing count. A reviewer reports 9/12 as assessed accuracy; another reports 90% on all 12. Explain the problem with each label.
workbook.answer: C has 9/10 = 90% assessed accuracy and 2 unassessed outcomes. The denominator 12 includes cases not assessed, so 9/12 is the fraction of selected cases with verified correct outcomes, not assessed accuracy. Reporting 90% on all 12 incorrectly extends the assessed-subset fraction to missing outcomes.

workbook.title: Compare a new shared sound test
workbook.prompt: Versions X and Y label the same 20 previously unseen clips: 12 quiet and 8 noisy, with no missing outcomes. X is correct on 10 quiet and 2 noisy clips; Y on 9 quiet and 5 noisy clips. Calculate each combined fraction and percentage, identify the overall leader and compare the leaders within each group. Explain why an overall result cannot guarantee the next clip’s outcome.
workbook.answer: X has (10 + 2)/(12 + 8) = 12/20 = 3/5 = 60%. Y has (9 + 5)/20 = 14/20 = 7/10 = 70%, so Y leads overall. X leads quiet clips 10/12 to 9/12, while Y leads noisy clips 5/8 to 2/8. These are observed results on this shared test; they do not determine the outcome of the next clip or show that Y is better in every condition.

workbook.title: Combine counts rather than group percentages
workbook.prompt: A separate test has 2 correct out of 2 assessed in group P and 4 correct out of 8 assessed in group Q. Calculate combined accuracy as a fraction and percentage. A chart reports 75% by averaging the group percentages. Explain why that is not the accuracy over all assessed cases.
workbook.answer: There are 6 correct out of 10 assessed: 6/10 = 3/5 = 60%. The unweighted mean of 100% and 50% is 75%, but it treats the two differently sized groups equally. All-case accuracy counts each case once, so the larger group contributes 8 of the 10 cases.

teacher.background: Keep the metric definition visible: this lesson measures accuracy among assessed classification outcomes and separately reports unassessed selected cases. It does not teach that missing system outputs should always be removed from every real evaluation; an end-to-end task may define output failure as a failure. Here, the scoring scope and unavailable records are explicit. Fractions compare observed proportions, not certainty or individual confidence.
materials: The shared A/B card counts from the lesson and two colours of counters for correct and incorrect outcomes
Paper fraction strips partitioned into 4 and 12 equal parts
The independent X/Y sound counts in W4 and a place to record missing outcomes separately
sessions: Retrieve selected versus assessed counts from Week 22.
Model 9 correct and 3 incorrect counters. Explain denominator 12 and complete W1.
Use fraction strips to compare 3/4 and 2/3 in twelfths. Trace the diagram.
Complete W2 and discuss the overall and dim-condition leaders.
Retrieve why the incorrect cases stay in the assessed denominator.
Complete the guided C comparison and W3. Keep unknown cases separate and avoid inventing A’s subset score.
Collect W4 independently. Require totals, percentages, condition comparisons and a bounded claim.
Complete W5 and the exit. Use counters to show why combined case counts differ from an equal-group average.
teacher.guidedAnswer: C has 9/10 correct among assessed outcomes, with 2 unassessed out of 12 selected. A has 9/12 across all 12. The assessed sets differ, so recover C’s lost results or compare all versions on an explicitly documented common assessed subset using case-level records. A’s score on that subset cannot be inferred from the totals. Exit: 6/10 = 60% across cases; averaging 100% and 50% gives 75% with equal weight to the two groups, a different summary.
misconceptions: Only correct cases belong in the denominator
All assessed cases, including errors, belong in the assessed-accuracy denominator.
Equivalent fractions mean equal test sizes
The proportions match, but 4 assessed cases are not 100 assessed cases; preserve actual counts.
The overall leader wins in every condition
The lesson’s dim group and W4’s quiet group provide counterexamples.
Average group percentages to get all-case accuracy
Add correct counts and assessed counts when each individual case is weighted equally.
teacher.assessment: W4 requires X 12/20 = 60%, Y 14/20 = 70%, Y overall, X quiet, Y noisy and no next-case guarantee. After support change Y’s noisy correct count to 3: Y becomes 12/20 = 60%, tying X overall while X still leads quiet and Y still leads noisy. Require the changed conclusion with unchanged denominators.
teacher.support: Use counters and equal-sized fraction strips before percentage notation. Accept exact fractions for group comparisons; rounding is not required. Extension: describe what per-case records are needed to compare A fairly on C’s ten assessed cases, and why the group totals cannot recover them.
