teacher.next: Week 24 asks which information a task actually needs and how to reduce unnecessary collection and exposure of personal data.

ai-1/24.title: Privacy and data minimisation
goals: Justify which information a stated task needs and remove unnecessary fields
Distinguish reducing personal data from hiding a name
Design a simple access, retention and deletion plan for a classroom activity

prerequisite.prompt: A report needs the number of correct answers out of 20 fictional test cards. Does that calculation require a student’s name or home address? Explain.
prerequisite.answer: No. It needs the assessed outcomes and counts, not a student’s identity or home address. The required information depends on the purpose.

vocabulary: Information about an identifiable person, including combinations that can identify someone
The specific job information is collected or used to do
Using only the information needed for a stated purpose
A rule and mechanism deciding who can see or use information
How long information is kept before an agreed deletion or other approved action

lesson.title: Begin with the job, not the collection form

blocks.text: Privacy includes having appropriate boundaries around information about people. A useful first question is: what exact job are we trying to do? A second is: what is the least information that can do that job? Collecting extra details just because a form has room for them creates more information to protect.

Our fictional class wants to choose one of three workshop topics for Friday: drawing, music or coding. It needs a total for each topic, not a list of who chose what. Each fictional pupil gets one paper slip and marks one topic. No real class survey is needed for this lesson. The teacher counts the choices and uses the largest total; a tie goes to a class discussion.

A proposed form asks for name, full date of birth, home address, photograph and topic choice. For the stated counting task only the topic choice is needed. Remove the other fields before collection. Do not fill them in and promise to ignore them later. If the purpose changes to individual attendance, design and justify that separate task with the teacher rather than silently reusing the survey.

lesson.title: Follow the information from collection to deletion

blocks.title: A small information plan for a fictional vote
blocks.caption: Purpose: choose a workshop topic. Collect the minimum, limit access, share the required result and agree how long the source slips are kept.

blocks.text: Suppose the fictional counts are drawing 8, music 7 and coding 5. These totals support the choice of drawing. There is no need to publish each slip or a photograph of a child holding it. The teacher checks the total of 20 against the number of slips and then follows the agreed school process for disposing of the slips after verification.

A retention plan needs a clear trigger and a responsible person: for example, the teacher disposes of the fictional vote slips after the totals are checked and the activity closes. Real classroom records must follow the school’s approved process. Deleting one visible copy does not prove that every backup, screenshot or previously shared copy is gone.

lesson.title: Removing a name is only one change

rows: Hides the name on this sheet
A separate key can reconnect the code
Small or unusual groups may still reveal a choice

blocks.text: A code is not a promise of anonymity. If a teacher keeps a key connecting P07 to a pupil, the coded record can still be linked to that pupil. Even without a key, a combination such as an exact birthday, a team and a photograph may identify someone. Ask whether a reader could connect the information to a person, not just whether the name column is blank.

Totals also need context. A report saying that the only member of a tiny club chose music reveals that member’s choice. Our whole-class topic totals reveal less detail than individual rows, but we should not describe every possible total as automatically anonymous. Share only what the audience needs for the purpose.

lesson.title: Check access before sending information to a tool

blocks.text: An AI tool is another place where information may be sent. Before using it for schoolwork, follow the teacher’s approved tool and data rules. Do not paste real names, contact details, photos, passwords or private messages into an unapproved service. For this lesson, use the provided fictional counts or work entirely on paper. An AI tool is not needed to add 8 + 7 + 5.

blocks.label: A classmate proposes uploading the named vote spreadsheet to an AI tool to make a chart. The required chart shows only three topic totals. Propose a smaller input, explain what must be checked before tool use, and name a way to complete the task without uploading data

blocks.text: A student may need the lesson and their own work; a teacher may need restricted teaching records. Access should match these jobs. A hidden link or a hard-to-guess filename is not a substitute for an access check. When information is shared more widely, it may be copied beyond the original audience. Decide the audience before sharing.

lesson.title: Write a plan someone can actually follow

blocks.text: A useful data plan answers five questions: what is the purpose; which fields are necessary; who needs access; what result will be shared; and when will the source information be disposed of under the agreed process? It also names who is responsible. “Keep everything safe forever” answers neither the collection question nor the retention question.

If you accidentally share personal information, stop sharing it and tell the teacher or another trusted adult promptly. Do not repost it to ask classmates for help. An adult can follow the school’s process and decide what action is appropriate. Avoid promising that deleting a message has removed every copy.

blocks.label: For the fictional workshop vote, name one field to collect and two to remove. State the audience for the totals and a clear trigger for the teacher to dispose of the slips under the agreed process

workbook.title: Trim a form to its purpose
workbook.prompt: The fictional workshop vote asks for name, full date of birth, address, photograph and topic choice. Its only purpose is to count votes for drawing, music and coding. State which field to keep, which to remove and why. Explain why collecting the extra fields first is different from never collecting them.
workbook.answer: Keep topic choice; remove name, full date of birth, address and photograph. The totals do not require identity or contact details. Collecting extra fields creates copies and exposure to manage even if those fields are later ignored or deleted.

workbook.title: Challenge a claim of anonymity
workbook.prompt: A teacher replaces names with codes and keeps a separate code-to-name key. A pupil calls the records anonymous. Explain the problem. Then explain why removing names while leaving photographs would not settle the question either.
workbook.answer: The key can reconnect each code to a person, so the coded records are not anonymous just because names are absent. Restricting the key helps limit access but does not erase the link. Photographs can identify people even if the name field is removed.

workbook.title: Share the result the audience needs
workbook.prompt: The fictional class has drawing 8, music 7 and coding 5. Write the result needed to choose a workshop. A pupil suggests posting every vote slip online as proof. Explain a lower-exposure way to check and share the result. Why can a total about a one-person club still reveal a choice?
workbook.answer: Drawing leads with 8; totals are 8, 7 and 5, adding to 20. The teacher checks the slips and totals, then shares the three totals with the class rather than public individual slips. A one-person club total can be linked to its only member, revealing that person’s choice.

workbook.title: Design a different minimal-data task
workbook.prompt: A fictional library wants only the total number of books needing repair in each category: cover, page or binding. It does not need to contact borrowers. A draft repair sheet asks for borrower name, home address, book repair category and borrower photograph. Design a plan: state the purpose, required and removed fields, who handles source sheets, what totals are shared with the librarian, and who disposes of sheets at what agreed point. Use no real borrower details.
workbook.answer: Purpose: count repair needs by category. Keep repair category; remove borrower name, address and photograph because no borrower contact is required. An assigned teacher or librarian handles the source sheets, checks counts and shares category totals with the librarian. Name that adult as responsible for disposal after totals are verified and the counting task closes, following the agreed school process. Other justified restricted roles and clear disposal triggers are acceptable.

workbook.title: Respond to an unnecessary upload
workbook.prompt: Someone plans to upload the library repair sheet with borrower details to an unapproved AI tool to add three totals. Explain a smaller-input alternative and a no-upload method. If the sheet was already shared, state a suitable first response and one claim you must not make about deleting it.
workbook.answer: Use only fictional category counts in this lesson; for real work check teacher-approved tools and data rules before any upload. Add totals on paper or with an approved local calculator. If shared, stop further sharing and tell the teacher or trusted adult promptly so the school process can be followed. Do not claim that deleting the visible message removes all copies or backups.

teacher.background: Teach privacy as purposeful information design, not a demand that pupils disclose private experiences. Use fictional paper examples throughout; no account creation, real survey or upload is necessary. These examples are classroom design exercises, not legal advice or a substitute for school policy. Coded records with a re-identification key remain linkable. Aggregation reduces individual detail but does not guarantee anonymity in every context.
materials: Fictional topic slips or counters marked drawing, music and coding
A sample form containing only the fictional field labels in W1
Paper for the five-question data plan; no real pupil or borrower records
sessions: Retrieve which fields a performance count actually needs. Establish fictional examples only.
Define the vote purpose. Complete W1 and remove unnecessary fields before collection.
Trace collection, access, sharing and disposal on the diagram. Check the totals.
Complete W2. Contrast coded records with a claim of anonymity.
Retrieve why a blank name column does not prove anonymity.
Complete W3 and the guided chart task. Discuss small-group inference and approved tool rules.
Collect W4 independently. Check that purpose, fields, access, output and disposal align.
Complete W5 and the exit. Rehearse telling a trusted adult without repeating exposed information.
teacher.guidedAnswer: A chart needs the three topic totals, not the named spreadsheet. Use the fictional counts provided here. Before any real tool use, check teacher approval for both tool and data; a smaller input does not itself authorize an upload. Draw bars on paper or use an approved local chart tool. Exit: collect topic choice; remove any two identity/contact fields. Share totals with the class. The teacher disposes of slips after verification and task closure under the agreed school process.
misconceptions: More data always improves a task
Unnecessary identity fields do not improve a category count and create more information to manage.
Codes or missing names mean anonymous
A key or other identifying fields may reconnect records to a person.
Every total is safe to publish
A small or distinctive group may allow a reader to infer a person’s choice.
Deleting one copy proves all copies are gone
Other copies, screenshots or backups may remain; follow the adult-led school process.
teacher.assessment: W4 requires a category-count purpose, repair category only from the listed fields, removal of all three borrower fields, a restricted responsible adult, category totals for the librarian and an actionable disposal trigger under the agreed process. After support change the task to contacting borrowers about repairs. Ask the pupil to explain that the old minimal field set no longer performs the new task and that an adult must design an approved contact workflow; do not request real contact details.
teacher.support: Offer a five-box planning frame: purpose, fields, access, shared result, disposal. Accept spoken explanations of why each field is or is not needed. Avoid asking children to describe past privacy incidents. Extension: construct a fictional small-group total that reveals one choice and suggest a less detailed output.
teacher.next: Week 25 distinguishes generating a plausible response, retrieving an existing record and calculating a result from explicit rules.

ai-1/25.title: Generation retrieval and calculation
goals: Distinguish retrieving a record, calculating from inputs and generating wording
Trace a task that combines these operations and check each step
Identify unsupported details and explain why output appearance does not reveal its method

prerequisite.prompt: You need a chart of three fictional topic totals. Why should a named pupil spreadsheet not be the default input?
prerequisite.answer: The task needs the three totals, not pupil identities. Use the least information needed and follow the teacher’s approved tool and data rules.

vocabulary: Finding and returning existing information from a collection
Applying specified mathematical operations to input values
Producing content using a model and its input context
An existing item whose content and origin can be inspected
A record of the inputs, operations and outputs used in a task

lesson.title: Ask what operation produced the answer

blocks.text: Three tasks can produce similar-looking text while doing different work. Retrieval finds existing information. Calculation applies mathematical operations to input values. Generation produces content using a model and the context it receives. A single application can combine all three, so the label AI does not tell you which step happened.

Our fictional makers club has a current notice N2: Wednesday, Room 4, six tables with four places at each table, and three places reserved for helpers. An older notice N1 says Room 2. N2 explicitly replaces N1 for this event. These records are invented for this lesson; no search, account or real booking is needed.

To answer “Which room does the current notice list?”, find N2 and return Room 4 with the record identifier. That is retrieval. To answer “How many places remain after the helper reservation?”, use 6 × 4 − 3 = 21. That is calculation. To suggest a friendly invitation, generate wording and check that its factual details agree with N2.

lesson.title: Follow three operations with three different checks

blocks.title: One club task with three kinds of work
blocks.caption: Retrieval supplies recorded information; calculation derives a result; generation drafts wording. Each operation needs a check suited to what it does.

blocks.text: Retrieving N1 accurately would still give an outdated room for this task. Successful retrieval means finding a record, not proving that every record is correct or current. Check the event, source and version. Here the explicit replacement statement tells us which notice governs the classroom example.

A calculator given 6 × 4 correctly returns 24, but 24 is the total capacity, not the number remaining after three reserved places. Correct arithmetic on an incomplete expression answers the wrong question. Explain the input values, units and operations before accepting a number.

lesson.title: Generated wording needs evidence for factual details

blocks.text: A generated invitation might add free snacks because that detail fits a familiar invitation pattern. Plausible wording is not evidence that snacks are provided. Remove that claim or obtain an appropriate confirming source before including it. Generated content can be useful and can contain correct facts; its fluent style alone does not verify those facts.

Generation also does not guarantee originality. A response may repeat wording already present in its context or elsewhere. Retrieval and calculation can feed a generator, and a generator can propose a calculation for another tool. Keep the evidence path visible instead of assuming that every sentence came from the same operation.

lesson.title: Use a trace instead of guessing from the final sentence

blocks.text: Two applications display “21 places remain.” One trace shows retrieval of N2 followed by a calculator call for 6 × 4 − 3 and a sentence built from the result. The other gives no record or tool trace. Their identical visible answers do not establish identical methods. The second answer may be right, but its appearance does not prove retrieval or calculation took place.

blocks.label: A draft says “Join us Thursday in Room 4 for free snacks; 24 places remain.” Use N2 to identify which claims need correction or removal. Write a corrected factual sentence and state the retrieval and calculation steps that support it

blocks.text: Check the record yourself and independently recompute 6 × 4 − 3. A displayed trace is useful evidence, but it should refer to an inspectable record and the actual tool result. A sentence saying “I checked” is not the same as a check you can inspect. If evidence is unavailable, say what remains unverified.

lesson.title: Choose the work needed for the question

blocks.text: For an existing meeting time, retrieve the relevant notice. For a total, calculate using the right inputs and units. For a draft title or invitation, generation can offer wording, followed by review. You can also do these classroom tasks on paper. Choose the operation because it fits the question, not because a tool is described as intelligent.

A complete answer keeps source facts, derived results and suggested wording distinguishable. It marks missing facts instead of inventing them, preserves the source identifier and explains the arithmetic. This makes a later change easier to handle: if the number of reserved places changes, recompute the result and update the sentence.

blocks.label: If N2 now reserves five helper places, calculate the remaining places. State which existing source facts stay the same and why the old answer of 21 must be revised

workbook.title: Name the operation and its evidence
workbook.prompt: For each task name the main operation and a suitable check: find the room listed in N2; work out six tables of four places minus three reserved places; suggest an inviting title for the event. Can an application combine these operations?
workbook.answer: Room: retrieval, checked against the right source N2 and event. Remaining places: calculation, checked as 6 × 4 − 3 = 21 with correct inputs. Title: generation, checked for the requested style and unsupported factual details. An application can combine them; the labels describe operations rather than exclusive types of application.

workbook.title: Separate a correct sum from a correct answer
workbook.prompt: A calculator correctly returns 24 for 6 × 4. A pupil reports this as the number of non-helper places available. Explain the problem and write the correct expression, result and meaning.
workbook.answer: 24 is total capacity before the three helper places are reserved. The requested remaining count is 6 × 4 − 3 = 21 non-helper places. The calculator can execute the supplied expression correctly while that expression omits a required step.

workbook.title: Inspect a record and a draft
workbook.prompt: N1 lists Room 2. N2 explicitly replaces N1 for this event and lists Wednesday in Room 4. A draft says Thursday in Room 2 with free snacks. Identify the supported corrections and the unsupported detail. Explain why finding N1 successfully would not settle the current-room question.
workbook.answer: Use Wednesday and Room 4 from N2. Free snacks are unsupported and should be removed or verified with a suitable source. N1 is an existing record but is superseded for this event, so retrieving it does not establish the current room.

workbook.title: Trace a new library workshop
workbook.prompt: Current fictional record B lists a library workshop on Friday in Room 5: five tables with six places each, with four places reserved for helpers. B replaces old record A, which lists Room 3. A draft says “Thursday in Room 3, with 30 places remaining and a free bus home.” Retrieve the current day and room, calculate the non-helper places, write a corrected factual sentence and identify the detail that cannot be supported by B.
workbook.answer: Retrieve Friday and Room 5 from B. Calculate 5 × 6 − 4 = 26 non-helper places. A suitable sentence is: The workshop is Friday in Room 5 with 26 places after the helper reservation, according to B and the capacity calculation. The free bus is unsupported and must be removed or verified separately. The draft’s 30 is total capacity before reservation.

workbook.title: Do not infer a method from its output
workbook.prompt: Two applications both display “26 places remain.” Only one provides record B and a trace showing 5 × 6 − 4. What can and cannot be concluded from their matching sentences? Describe how you would check the numerical claim without relying on either application’s assurance.
workbook.answer: The visible numerical outputs match, but that alone does not reveal the second application’s method or prove that either checked the right task. Inspect current B, confirm the inputs and independently calculate 5 × 6 − 4 = 26. The first trace supports inspection; a verbal assurance of checking is not equivalent to inspectable evidence.

teacher.background: Keep operations distinct without presenting three mutually exclusive product categories. A modern system can retrieve records, call a calculator and generate a final response. Lewis and colleagues provide a primary example combining retrieval and generation: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks (2020), https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401. Use this as teacher background, not required pupil reading. The fictional notices and arithmetic here are independent classroom examples.
materials: The fictional N1 and N2 notice details printed in the student lesson
Paper for three-column traces labelled source facts, calculation and wording
The independent library record B in W4; no online account is needed
sessions: Retrieve the minimal-input principle from Week 24.
Compare the three operations using N2 and complete W1.
Trace the diagram and complete W2. Ask what the result’s unit and meaning are.
Complete W3 and separate a retrieved record from a current record.
Retrieve why correct arithmetic can still answer the wrong question.
Complete the guided correction. Require evidence for each factual claim.
Collect W4 independently, with source, expression, result and unsupported detail.
Complete W5 and the exit. Discuss identical outputs with different or unknown methods.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Correct Thursday to Wednesday using N2; Room 4 is supported. Remove free snacks unless independently verified. Replace 24 remaining with 21 from 6 × 4 − 3. One sentence: The makers club meets Wednesday in Room 4, with 21 places after the helper reservation. Exit: 6 × 4 − 5 = 19; day, room, table count and places per table stay the same. The changed reservation invalidates the old remaining count.
misconceptions: Retrieving a record proves it is current
Check event and version; N1 is superseded by N2 in this example.
A correct calculator result always answers the task
The expression must include the required reservation and correct units.
Fluent generated details are verified facts
Free snacks and transport need evidence; wording alone is insufficient.
The final sentence reveals the method
Matching outputs do not establish matching operations; inspect records and traces.
teacher.assessment: W4 requires Friday, Room 5, record B, 5 × 6 − 4 = 26, a consistent corrected sentence and rejection of the unsupported free bus. After support change B to reserve seven helper places: require 23 remaining with the same day and room, and continued rejection of the transport claim. A numerical result without its source and expression is incomplete evidence.
teacher.support: Use three coloured cards for recorded fact, derived quantity and suggested wording. Work with counters for total and reserved places. Extension: explain which steps should be repeated if only the room changes versus if the number of tables changes.
teacher.next: Week 26 turns a vague request into a clear prompt with supplied evidence, output requirements and tests.

ai-1/26.title: Specifying and testing prompts
goals: Write a prompt with a clear task, supplied evidence and checkable output requirements
Test a response against criteria chosen before seeing it
Revise a prompt using observed failures while preserving missing and conflicting information

prerequisite.prompt: A generated invitation adds a meeting time that is absent from its source. Does fluent wording make that time supported? What should happen next?
prerequisite.answer: No. Remove the unsupported time or verify it from an appropriate source. A plausible sentence is not evidence for a missing fact.

vocabulary: Instructions and context supplied to a model for a task
A requirement that an acceptable response must satisfy
A stated rule used to judge a response
A particular input with expected behaviour used to check a process
A documented change intended to address a specific problem

lesson.title: Turn a vague request into a checkable task

blocks.text: “Write something good about our club” leaves many decisions unstated. Who will read it? Which facts may be used? What must the output contain? A more useful prompt states the job, audience, evidence and requirements. This makes it easier to judge the result rather than choosing the answer that sounds most confident.

Use this fictional source C: the paper modelling club meets Monday in Room 7, and participants bring paper. C gives no start time. Our task is a short information card for Grade 6 readers. It must report day, time, place and what to bring, using only C. There is no need to supply names or private information.

Prompt P1: Using only source C, produce an information card for Grade 6 readers. Return exactly four labelled lines in this order: Day, Time, Place, Bring. Copy or faithfully restate each supported value. For a missing value write “not stated”. Add no other details. Source C: the paper modelling club meets Monday in Room 7; bring paper.

lesson.title: Connect each instruction to a test

blocks.title: From prompt requirement to evidence of success
blocks.caption: Choose these checks before reading a response. A response must satisfy all required criteria, not merely look tidy.

blocks.text: For P1, an acceptable card has Day: Monday; Time: not stated; Place: Room 7; Bring: paper, each on its own line. The semicolons here separate lines for discussion. A correct format with an invented 3 pm time still fails the evidence requirement. Accurate facts inside a long paragraph still fail the requested four-line format.

These are classroom response examples written for inspection, not measurements from a live AI system. You can test the instructions by asking a partner to follow them on paper. That checks how clear the instructions are, but it does not prove that a model will always follow them.

lesson.title: Test missing and conflicting information deliberately

rows: C plus a stated 3 pm time
Does not fill a gap by guessing
C and D disagree on room
Does not silently choose a record

blocks.text: For the third case, D describes the same event as C but gives Room 9, and neither record is marked as replacing the other. P1 explains missing values but says nothing about disagreement. Revise that weakness: if supplied records conflict about a requested field and no priority is given, write “conflicting information” for that field. Preserve values that do not conflict.

Call the revision P2 and keep the rest of P1 unchanged, except that it now refers to the supplied records rather than C alone. The place field should flag the conflict; it must not silently choose Room 7, choose Room 9 or combine them into Room 79. A later authoritative correction may resolve the conflict, but this input does not provide one.

lesson.title: Record failures before changing the instructions

blocks.text: A small test log can record prompt version, input case, output, each criterion’s result and the reason for failure. If you use an approved model, also record the model and available settings. Compare prompt versions on the same cases under the same recorded conditions. Keep all observed outputs rather than only the best-looking attempt.

blocks.label: For original C, an example response has four lines: Day: Monday; Time: 3 pm; Place: Room 7; Bring: paper. Identify the criteria it passes and fails. Explain why adding “be accurate” alone is not enough, and propose a missing-value test to rerun after a revision

blocks.text: P1 already tells the model not to invent missing values. A failed output can therefore be a failure to follow an adequate instruction, not necessarily a missing instruction. Inspect the actual output, retain the failure and try targeted changes if useful. Clear prompting helps communicate requirements but cannot guarantee correctness, remove the need for checks or grant permission to use restricted data.

lesson.title: Make a bounded claim about an improvement

blocks.text: Suppose a revised prompt handles three classroom examples correctly. You can report that it passed those examples under the recorded conditions. You cannot conclude that it will always work. If outputs can vary between runs, plan repeated trials and keep every result. A single good response is not a reliability guarantee.

Use the failures to improve the specification and add revealing cases. Keep the same evaluation criteria when comparing versions; changing both the prompt and the scoring rule makes the comparison hard to interpret. A new requirement may justify a new criterion, but document that change rather than pretending the results used the same test.

blocks.label: Two prompts are compared: P1 receives a complete record and P2 receives a record with a missing time. Why is that insufficient to attribute different results to the prompt change? Describe a fairer comparison

workbook.title: Find what the vague request leaves open
workbook.prompt: The request says “Write something good about our club.” Name four decisions it leaves open. Then explain how source C, the Grade 6 audience and four labelled lines make the task easier to check.
workbook.answer: Possible omissions include audience, source facts, required fields, format, missing-value behaviour and limits on extra claims. C supplies evidence, Grade 6 specifies readers, and four labelled lines define visible fields and structure. These requirements support checks but do not guarantee compliance.

workbook.title: Score a response by separate criteria
workbook.prompt: For original C, a card gives four correctly labelled lines but says Time: 3 pm. All other values match C. State which format and evidence checks pass or fail. Is the card acceptable overall? Explain.
workbook.answer: The four-line label and order checks pass; day, place and bring values match. The time and no-unsupported-details checks fail because C gives no time; Time should be not stated. It is not acceptable overall because every required criterion must pass.

workbook.title: Handle disagreement without choosing a favourite
workbook.prompt: C gives Room 7 and D gives Room 9 for the same club event, with no replacement or priority stated. Both agree on Monday and paper, and neither gives a time. Under P2, write the four output values and explain why the room cannot be selected from confidence or wording alone.
workbook.answer: Day: Monday; Time: not stated; Place: conflicting information; Bring: paper. Neither source is given priority, so choosing one room from style or confidence would invent a resolution. The other fields can still preserve their supported values.

workbook.title: Specify and test a new exhibit card
workbook.prompt: Fictional record X says an exhibit is called Shadow Pairs and is in Hall 2; no opening time is given. Write a complete prompt for a Grade 6 card with exactly three labelled lines: Title, Location, Opening. Limit facts to supplied records, define missing and conflicting values and prohibit added claims. Give two test inputs and expected outputs: original X, then X with an opening time of 10 am added.
workbook.answer: A valid prompt names the Grade 6 card task, supplied records only, exactly three lines in Title/Location/Opening order, not stated for missing values, conflicting information for unresolved disagreements and no added details. It includes X. Original X gives Title: Shadow Pairs; Location: Hall 2; Opening: not stated. Adding 10 am gives the same title and location with Opening: 10 am. Equivalent clear wording is acceptable.

workbook.title: Preserve the comparison evidence
workbook.prompt: A pupil tries P1 once and P2 five times, then compares the P1 response only with the best P2 response and declares P2 always reliable. Identify two problems and design a fairer small comparison. State a conclusion the evidence could support.
workbook.answer: Selecting only the best P2 output hides failures; unequal trial counts and an always-reliable claim also undermine the comparison. Use the same cases, criteria and recorded model conditions, with the same planned number of runs for each version. Keep all outputs and report pass counts and failures. The evidence can describe performance on these trials, not guarantee all future outputs.

teacher.background: This is a specification and evaluation lesson, not a live model benchmark or a collection of magic prompt phrases. All example responses are authored classroom cases. A partner following instructions on paper is useful for finding ambiguity but does not establish model reliability. If an approved tool is used, record the exact prompt, inputs, model and available settings; keep failures as well as successes.
materials: Fictional C and D records from the lesson, with D sharing the event but giving Room 9
A four-criterion checklist for supported values, missing/conflicting handling, format and no additions
Paper for a prompt-version and test-case log; optional teacher-approved model only
sessions: Retrieve why an unsupported time must not be accepted from fluent wording.
Compare the vague request with P1 and complete W1.
Trace requirement-to-check links in the diagram. Complete W2.
Introduce C/D disagreement and P2. Complete W3.
Retrieve why format success cannot cancel a factual failure.
Complete the guided criterion check. Distinguish inadequate instructions from failed compliance.
Collect W4 independently, requiring both prompt and expected test outcomes.
Complete W5 and the exit. Preserve all trial results and bound the conclusion.
teacher.guidedAnswer: The response passes four-line structure and the three supported values. It fails the missing-time requirement and introduces an unsupported time. Be accurate does not specify how to handle absence; P1 already gives that rule, so this is a compliance failure. Rerun a record lacking a time, expecting not stated, and also a record with a time, expecting that value. Exit: input completeness differs as well as the prompt. Compare both versions on both inputs with the same criteria and recorded conditions.
misconceptions: A tidy response is a correct response
Score facts and missing-value handling separately from layout.
A better prompt guarantees correct output
Inspect actual responses; even explicit requirements can be violated.
A conflict can be resolved by choosing the confident record
Without authority or priority, flag the unresolved field.
The best attempt represents every attempt
Keep all planned trials and report failures rather than selecting only a success.
teacher.assessment: W4 requires a complete task, audience, X, three labels and their order, evidence restriction, no additions, missing and conflict rules, and both expected outputs. After support add Y for the same exhibit giving Hall 4, with no priority and no opening time. Require unchanged title, conflicting information for Location and not stated for Opening. Do not demand identical prompt wording if the requirements are clear.
teacher.support: Provide a frame with task, readers, evidence, output, missing/conflicting behaviour and checks. Let pupils mark an example output before writing their own prompt. Extension: propose a test that reveals whether a revision accidentally marks a present value as missing.
teacher.next: Week 27 examines the evidence behind individual claims and independently checks quantities and units.

ai-1/27.title: Verifying claims and quantities
goals: Separate an answer into claims and connect each claim to relevant evidence
Recalculate quantities with consistent units and a reasonableness check
Report supported, contradicted and unresolved claims without inventing missing evidence

prerequisite.prompt: A response follows the requested four-line format but invents a missing start time. Has it passed the task? Explain.
prerequisite.answer: No. Format and factual support are separate criteria. A correct layout cannot make an unsupported time acceptable.

vocabulary: A statement that can be examined against evidence
Checking whether a claim is supported by appropriate evidence
A reference that helps a reader locate a source
The agreed measurement scale attached to a quantity, such as centimetres
Additional evidence that supports a claim, with its origin checked

lesson.title: Split a polished answer into smaller claims

blocks.text: An answer can contain a mixture of correct, incorrect and unverified statements. Checking one sentence does not validate every other sentence. First separate the answer into individual claims. Then ask what evidence would support each one: a record, a measurement, a calculation or some combination.

Our fictional ribbon activity uses current materials card R. R states: four rolls of ribbon, each exactly 2 metres long; twelve pieces will each use 50 centimetres; no cutting loss is included in this paper model. One metre equals 100 centimetres. An old card Q describes a different activity with three rolls. These are provided classroom records, not instructions to cut real materials.

A draft says “R gives four rolls. The starting length is 8 metres. The pieces use 600 metres. Two metres remain. Every participant will enjoy the activity.” Do not approve or reject the whole paragraph at once. Inspect the roll count, starting length, used length, remaining length and enjoyment claim separately.

lesson.title: Follow the claim to the actual evidence

blocks.title: Different claims need different checks
blocks.caption: A correct source reference is a starting point. Read what the record actually says and check every derived quantity.

blocks.text: A citation is useful only if you can locate the source and confirm that it supports the specific claim. The title “Materials card R” beside a paragraph does not make the enjoyment claim part of R. If a cited card Z is not supplied or cannot be found, that citation cannot currently verify its claim. Record the gap rather than inventing Z’s contents.

Check whether the source covers the right activity, version, population or time. Q’s three rolls may be accurate for its own activity but irrelevant to the current four-roll task. In real work, also inspect who created the record, how they obtained the information and whether there is a correction or better source.

lesson.title: Carry units through the whole calculation

blocks.text: Convert to one length unit before subtracting. Two metres is 200 centimetres, so four rolls give 800 centimetres. The twelve pieces use 600 centimetres, leaving 200 centimetres, or 2 metres. Subtracting the bare numbers 8 − 600 would mix metres with centimetres and would not describe the remaining length correctly.

Use a second route as a check: 50 centimetres is half a metre, so twelve pieces use six metres. Eight minus six leaves two metres. A reasonableness check also asks whether the used length is at most the starting length and whether starting length equals used plus remaining. These checks can reveal mistakes; they do not replace checking the original inputs and assumptions.

lesson.title: Keep absence of evidence distinct from contradiction

blocks.text: The claim “600 metres used” conflicts with the stated inputs and calculation. The claim “everyone will enjoy it” is not supported by R or by any supplied enjoyment evidence. That does not establish that nobody will enjoy it. State “not verified from these records” rather than changing an unsupported positive claim into an unsupported negative claim.

blocks.label: Audit the draft from section one. For each of its five claims, state supported, contradicted or unresolved under the supplied evidence. Correct the used-length claim and explain why the correct remaining-length claim still needs its own calculation

blocks.text: Suppose three posters repeat the same number and each copied it from one unverified draft. That is three copies of one claim, not three independent measurements. Follow references back to their origin. A separate check of R and the arithmetic provides more useful evidence than counting copies that repeat the same mistake.

lesson.title: Write a correction that another reader can check

blocks.text: A useful correction names the original claim, relevant source, calculation with units and revised conclusion. For example: R lists four 2-metre rolls and twelve 50-centimetre pieces. The pieces use 600 centimetres, or 6 metres; the paper model leaves 2 metres when no cutting loss is included. This preserves the condition on which the result depends.

If the real activity loses ribbon at each cut, the no-loss result cannot simply be reused. Obtain that missing information or label the answer as a model with an explicit assumption. Similarly, if you cannot access a source, mark the claim unresolved and identify what evidence would settle it. Repeating a confident answer is not a new measurement.

blocks.label: In a changed paper model, each of the twelve pieces uses 50 cm and an extra 2 cm is lost for each piece. Calculate the total loss and the remaining ribbon from the same four rolls. State which assumption changed

workbook.title: Separate source facts from derived quantities
workbook.prompt: Using R, identify a directly stated fact and a quantity that must be calculated. Give the source or expression for each. Explain why a citation to R does not verify the claim that every participant will enjoy the activity.
workbook.answer: A directly stated fact is four rolls, 2 m per roll or twelve 50 cm pieces. A derived quantity is 8 m starting length, 6 m used or 2 m remaining, supported by the relevant calculation from R. R contains no enjoyment evidence, so citing it does not support everyone enjoying the activity.

workbook.title: Repair a unit error
workbook.prompt: A report calculates 12 × 50 = 600 and labels the result metres. Use R to correct the unit, convert the result to metres and calculate the remaining length. Give a second arithmetic route or a check using starting, used and remaining lengths.
workbook.answer: Each piece is 50 cm, so 12 × 50 cm = 600 cm = 6 m. Starting length is 4 × 2 m = 8 m; remaining is 8 − 6 = 2 m. A check is 6 m used + 2 m remaining = 8 m starting; alternatively twelve half-metre pieces use 6 m.

workbook.title: Do not count copied claims as separate evidence
workbook.prompt: Three posters say 600 metres were used, but all copied one draft. A fourth poster cites card Z, which is unavailable. Explain why these posters do not settle the quantity. Name the available evidence and check you would use instead.
workbook.answer: The first three are copies of one claim, not independent evidence. Z cannot be inspected, so the fourth citation cannot currently verify the result. Inspect supplied R and recompute twelve 50 cm pieces as 600 cm or 6 m; verify source, units and the no-loss assumption.

workbook.title: Audit a new model with mass units
workbook.prompt: Fictional craft card M states five sealed bags of modelling material at exactly 250 g per bag. Three models each use 300 g, with no other loss. A draft says “M supplies 1250 g; the models use 900 g; 350 kg remains; every model will win a prize.” Check all four claims, show the remaining mass in grams, and explain the status of the prize claim. Use 1 kg = 1000 g.
workbook.answer: 1250 g is supported by 5 × 250 g; 900 g is supported by 3 × 300 g. Remaining mass is 1250 − 900 = 350 g, so 350 kg is contradicted by the inputs and unit conversion: 350 kg would be 350000 g, greater than the starting mass. The prize claim is unresolved because M gives no prize evidence; it is not established true or false by the material counts.

workbook.title: State what a missing source prevents you from knowing
workbook.prompt: Another draft claims that the amount left in W4 accounts for all real-world waste, citing a missing instruction card. Explain which result can still be checked from M and which claim remains unresolved. What information would be needed before revising the no-loss model?
workbook.answer: The no-other-loss model in M can be checked: 350 g remains under its stated assumptions. The assertion that this includes all real-world waste is unresolved without relevant waste information. Obtain the actual instruction or measurement record specifying additional loss, its units and what stage it covers; do not invent a waste amount or subtract it twice.

teacher.background: Use the supplied fictional source cards to keep the activity accessible offline and separate evidence checking from internet search skill. Supported and contradicted are judgments relative to stated evidence and assumptions; unresolved is not a synonym for false. Emphasise that identical repeated claims may share one origin. This lesson checks exact paper models, not uncertain physical measurements.
materials: Current ribbon card R and old card Q details in the lesson
A metre strip marked into 100 centimetres or a paper drawing of one
The independent craft card M in W4 and paper for claim-by-claim audit notes
sessions: Retrieve format versus factual support from Week 26.
Split the ribbon draft into five claims and complete W1.
Trace the evidence diagram and work through centimetres and metres.
Complete W2 and check used plus remaining against starting length.
Retrieve why unresolved does not mean false.
Complete the guided audit and W3. Trace repeated claims to their common origin.
Collect W4 independently, requiring calculations, units and separate claim judgments.
Complete W5 and the changed-loss exit; retain the changed assumption.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Four rolls: supported by R. Starting 8 m: supported by 4 × 2 m. Used 600 m: contradicted; it is 600 cm = 6 m. Remaining 2 m: supported by 8 − 6, with no cutting loss. Everyone enjoys it: unresolved. Correctness of one number does not validate another; show each calculation. Exit: loss is 12 × 2 cm = 24 cm. Remaining is 800 − 600 − 24 = 176 cm. The no-cutting-loss assumption changed.
misconceptions: A citation proves every nearby claim
Inspect the actual source and the specific claim it supports.
The number is enough without a unit
600 cm and 600 m differ by a factor of 100.
An unsupported claim must be false
Unresolved means the supplied evidence does not settle it.
Three copied claims are three independent checks
Find the origin and seek an independent record or calculation.
teacher.assessment: W4 requires 1250 g, 900 g, 350 g remaining, rejection of 350 kg with a unit or size explanation, and an unresolved prize claim. After support change each model to use 350 g: require 1050 g used and 200 g remaining, still no evidence about prizes. Confirm that pupils change the affected quantities without changing unrelated claims.
teacher.support: Use a claim/evidence/decision frame and write units beside every number. Model the 100 cm to 1 m conversion before combining quantities. Extension: explain why a plausible-looking answer can pass a size check yet still be wrong, using a different incorrect remaining length.
teacher.next: Week 28 distinguishes checking whether an action is sensible from checking who has authority to approve it.

ai-1/28.title: Human authority and permission
goals: Distinguish a system’s capability, the correctness of its output and permission to take an action
Match an action to the person, version, audience and limits covered by an approval
Explain when to proceed within an existing permission and when a changed action needs review

prerequisite.prompt: You check every factual claim on a club announcement against the correct source. Does that alone establish permission to publish it? Explain.
prerequisite.answer: No. The checks establish factual support, not who may publish the announcement, where, or which version has been approved.

vocabulary: What a person or system is able to do
Responsibility and power to make a specified decision
An allowed action within stated limits
The boundaries of what a permission covers
A note of who approved which action and under what conditions

lesson.title: Ask three different questions before an action

blocks.text: A tool might be able to publish a message even when its user is only allowed to prepare a draft. A message might also contain correct facts but still be intended for a private group. Ask three separate questions: can the system do this, is the proposed result correct, and is this particular action allowed? Evidence for one question does not automatically answer the others.

Use this fictional paper exercise. A class is preparing an announcement about a model bridge exhibition. Version A says “Model bridge exhibition, Thursday, Room 6.” The teacher has checked those facts and is responsible for the class noticeboard. The teacher tells the class editor: “You may put exactly version A on our classroom noticeboard today, once. Do not post it online.” The editor has not yet posted it.

In the story, the editor’s tool has buttons for Save draft, Class noticeboard and Public website. Having a button shows a possible capability. It does not change the teacher’s stated permission. In this lesson, represent actions with paper cards; do not send messages or change a real noticeboard or website.

lesson.title: Make the permission specific enough to use

blocks.title: Match the proposed action to its permission
blocks.caption: Each decision uses the approval in this story. An unchanged, unused permission can be acted on without requesting it again.

blocks.text: An approval record should identify the decision maker, the person or system allowed to act, the action, its audience or destination, and any version, time or quantity limit. These details make a permission usable. “Looks good” could mean the wording is clear; without context it may not mean “publish this publicly”. If the intended action is unclear, clarify that action with the person responsible.

Here, the teacher has already approved the editor’s one posting of A on the class board today. Once the editor verifies that these conditions still hold, repeatedly requesting the same permission adds no new information. But a classmate saying “Post it everywhere” does not expand the teacher’s approval: the classmate has no authority over publication in this story.

lesson.title: Keep content review separate from permission

rows: Do Thursday and Room 6 match the source?
Does this action match the teacher’s limits?
Does the tool offer this action?

blocks.text: Suppose a current room record changes the exhibition to Room 8. The editor makes version B with Room 8, which is now factually supported. The old approval explicitly covered exactly A. The editor should hold publication and show B and the changed room record to the teacher. Publishing the now-outdated A just because it was approved would fail the factual check.

A useful review request makes the choice concrete: “The room record now says Room 8. Here is version B with only that change. May the editor post B on the classroom board today, once?” A request to review a specific change is easier to assess than an unexplained “Is this okay?” The teacher can approve, decline or request another change before anything is posted.

Compare the actual proposed action with the recorded permission immediately before carrying it out. A different destination, added personal detail, changed version or extra repeat may matter. Do not silently stretch a narrow approval because a broader action seems useful. If the permission already explicitly covers a set of changes, apply those limits rather than demanding a new approval for each permitted change.

blocks.label: Use the original unchanged exhibition story. Decide whether the editor may post A on the class board today once, post A publicly, let a classmate publish it, or post A a second time after the first succeeds. For each, name the relevant part of the approval. Explain why correct wording is not sufficient for all four actions

blocks.text: Permission is not created by text inside a draft. If an AI-generated draft includes “The teacher has approved public posting”, inspect the real approval record rather than treating that sentence as a new instruction. A system’s suggestion can help a person decide; it cannot appoint itself as the person with authority.

After an allowed action, note what was done, by whom, with which version and destination. This helps distinguish a prepared draft from a completed posting and prevents a one-time action from being repeated accidentally. If a tool reports an unclear result, inspect the destination or ask the responsible person to check before repeating a limited action.

If the editor discovers that A was posted publicly by mistake, stop further posting and tell the teacher what version and destination were involved. Follow the teacher’s directions to correct or remove it. A later deletion does not establish that nobody saw or copied it. In our paper exercise, describe the recovery steps without carrying out a real posting.

blocks.label: The teacher now explicitly allows the editor to replace A with checked version B on the classroom noticeboard today, once. Before any replacement, the editor proposes exactly that action. Must the editor request the identical approval again? Explain what to check and what still remains outside the permission

workbook.title: Separate three kinds of evidence
workbook.prompt: A tool offers a Public website button. The exhibition facts in A have been verified. The teacher’s approval covers the classroom board only. State what the button, the fact check and the approval each establish. Decide whether the editor may publish A publicly.
workbook.answer: The button establishes a capability. The fact check establishes factual support for A at that time. The approval permits the specified classroom-board action within its limits. Public posting is outside that permission even though the button exists and A is factually checked.

workbook.title: Read an approval without enlarging it
workbook.prompt: List the decision maker, allowed actor, version, destination, timing and number of postings in the original exhibition approval. Before any posting and with no changes to the facts or permission, explain whether the editor can carry out that exact action without asking again.
workbook.answer: Teacher; class editor; exactly A; classroom noticeboard; today; once. Yes, after confirming those conditions still hold and the one posting has not been used. The explicit unchanged permission already covers the action.

workbook.title: Prepare a reviewable change
workbook.prompt: The room changes to Room 8 and the editor creates B. Explain why publishing old A and publishing unapproved B each fail a different check. Write a specific request for the teacher to review B, keeping the original destination and one-posting limit.
workbook.answer: A now fails factual support because the room has changed. B has the supported room but is outside the exact-A approval. Show B and the updated source; ask whether the editor may post B on the classroom board today once. Do not infer public permission or approval from B’s correctness.

workbook.title: Transfer the permission check to a new case
workbook.prompt: In a fictional library, the librarian controls the internal shelf list. The librarian tells assistant Jo: “Replace the internal list with checked version L2 on Friday, once. Do not change the public catalogue.” It is Friday, L2 remains checked, and no replacement has occurred. A tool offers both destinations. Assess these proposals separately: Jo replaces the internal list with L2; Jo updates the public catalogue with L2; visitor Sam replaces the internal list with L2; Jo replaces the internal list with a changed L3. Identify the approval detail that settles each case.
workbook.answer: Jo using L2 internally on Friday once is within scope and needs no duplicate approval. The public catalogue is explicitly excluded. Sam is not the approved actor. L3 is not the approved version. These last three actions are not covered; hold them and refer any proposed change to the librarian rather than treating available buttons or correct text as permission.

workbook.title: Avoid an accidental second action
workbook.prompt: Jo attempts the permitted internal replacement, but the tool’s response does not show whether it succeeded. Explain why immediately repeating it is a poor choice under a once-only approval. What should Jo check? If Jo discovers a public change occurred instead, describe the first recovery steps.
workbook.answer: A repeat might perform the limited action a second time. Inspect the internal list or its change record, or have the librarian confirm the outcome, before retrying. If the public catalogue changed, stop further changes, tell the librarian what happened and follow their directions for correction. Do not claim that reversal proves nobody saw the public change.

teacher.background: Use the explicit rules of these fictional classroom and library scenarios. Keep capability, factual support and authority distinct. Learners should proceed within an existing clear permission and pause only when the proposed action is outside it or a necessary condition is unresolved. All publication and replacement actions are represented on paper.
materials: Paper cards labelled A, B, L2 and L3
Destination cards for class board, public website, internal list and public catalogue
The two fictional approval statements printed from the lesson and W4
sessions: Retrieve why a factual check does not establish publication permission.
Read the exhibition scenario and identify capability, correctness and authority. Complete W1.
Trace the permission diagram and record all six limits in W2.
Introduce the changed room, complete W3 and write a concrete review request.
Retrieve when an unchanged permission is sufficient.
Complete the guided decisions using paper action cards and the actual approval record.
Collect W4 independently; require a decision and the relevant limit for every proposal.
Complete W5 and the exit check; distinguish a prepared action from a confirmed result.
teacher.guidedAnswer: The editor’s first unchanged A posting on the class board today is allowed. Public posting is excluded. A classmate is not the allowed editor. A second posting exceeds once. Correct facts do not expand actor, audience or quantity limits. Exit: no identical approval is needed again if B remains checked, the actor and destination match, it is still today and the one replacement remains unused. Public posting, a different version, actor or extra replacement is not covered.
misconceptions: A working button grants permission
Capability does not establish who may use it or for what purpose.
A correct answer can always be published
Check the approved actor, action and audience as well as accuracy.
Always ask again even when nothing changed
Use an explicit, still-valid permission within its stated limits.
The draft can announce its own approval
Read the actual decision maker’s approval record.
teacher.assessment: W4 requires one allowed action and three uncovered actions, justified by destination, actor and version respectively. After support, give a new approval explicitly allowing Jo to replace either the internal list or the public catalogue with L2 on Friday, once total. Ask whether a first public replacement is covered and whether a subsequent internal replacement is covered. Expected: first yes, subsequent no because the one total replacement has been used.
teacher.support: Provide a frame with Who approved, Who acts, What version, Where, When and How many. Keep the permission card visible while sorting proposals. Extension: explain how an approval allowing a defined range of edits differs from an approval for one exact version, and give an edit inside and outside that range.
teacher.next: Week 29 uses these boundaries when choosing a problem worth solving for a small project.

ai-1/29.title: A problem worth solving
goals: Describe a specific user difficulty using supplied evidence without inventing its cause
Define a useful outcome and a way to observe it before choosing a solution
Choose a small project with clear boundaries, permitted information and a simple alternative

prerequisite.prompt: A teacher permits a paper prototype using fictional activity requests. Does this permit collecting real pupils’ names and publishing their choices? Explain.
prerequisite.answer: No. The permission covers a paper prototype and fictional requests. Collecting and publishing personal choices are different actions outside that scope.

vocabulary: Something a person needs to accomplish in a particular situation
A specific description of who faces a difficulty and what that difficulty is
The result experienced by the user
A condition that a proposed solution must respect
An observable quantity or result used to judge progress

lesson.title: Begin with the difficulty someone faces

blocks.text: For the final project sequence, we will develop a small activity recommender on paper. Its users are fictional pupils choosing a classroom activity that fits their available time and room conditions. We will decide what the recommender must do, build a traceable process, test it and explain its limits. A recommendation is a suggestion; the pupil can decline it.

Start before the solution. Our supplied observation log describes ten fictional requests made using an activity catalogue. Six first choices fit the request’s time and room conditions. Four did not and needed another choice. These invented classroom records give us a problem to investigate. They are not observations of your classmates and do not show how often this happens in other classes.

A useful problem statement is: “In the supplied ten-request exercise, four first choices did not fit the stated time or room conditions, so those users had to choose again.” “We need AI” names a possible technology but says neither who needs help nor what should improve. The log also does not establish whether unclear wording, missing information or another cause produced the mismatches.

blocks.title: From an observed difficulty to a testable goal
blocks.caption: The goal describes a useful result. Building a tool is an activity, not evidence that users benefited.

blocks.text: Our target outcome is a compatible suggestion when the catalogue contains one, and a clear no-match message when none fits. Compatibility means respecting the stated conditions; it does not mean that every pupil will enjoy the activity. We can check time and room conditions from a request and catalogue. Enjoyment would need different evidence.

Count compatible suggestions, incompatible suggestions and no-match messages separately. Otherwise a system could avoid every wrong suggestion by refusing to suggest anything. If a valid option existed, that refusal would still fail to provide the intended help. Record the total number of requests so a count has a clear denominator.

lesson.title: Keep the first project small enough to inspect

rows: Suggest an activity or report no match
Names, profiles, purchases and public posting
Not needed for this paper task

blocks.text: The teacher permits a paper prototype using fictional requests and an approved catalogue. We do not need names, home details or a history of a pupil’s choices. A request can say “10 minutes, quiet room required” without identifying anyone. Use only the request information needed to test the intended outcome.

A clear catalogue or a short checklist may solve this problem. We will compare a proposed recommender with a simple starting method instead of assuming a more complicated system is better. This project can use explicit rules; it does not have to fit a machine-learning model. The choice should follow the problem, available evidence and limits of the task.

lesson.title: Separate what you know from what you suspect

blocks.text: Suppose a team writes “All pupils hate the catalogue because it is too long.” The supplied log says nothing about every pupil’s feelings or the cause of the mismatches. A more careful note is “Four of ten first choices were incompatible; the cause is not yet known.” A hypothesis such as “the time information may be hard to find” is something to investigate, not an established finding.

blocks.label: Write a short project brief for the activity problem. Include the users and setting, the supplied evidence, the desired outcome, information needed, one boundary and a simple alternative. Name one claim the ten-request log does not establish

blocks.text: If we later investigate the cause, we could inspect where compatibility information appears in the catalogue or have a teacher organise a permitted comparison of clearer formats. Do not quietly collect real pupils’ data just because it might help. For this sequence, the supplied fictional records are enough to build and test a paper process.

lesson.title: Choose evidence that could change your decision

blocks.text: Before building, say what would count against your idea. If a clear catalogue already produces compatible choices for all supplied cases, adding a recommender might offer little benefit on those cases. If the recommender hides valid options or produces unexplained no-match messages, revise it or keep the simpler method. A project can succeed as an investigation even when the evidence favours a simpler solution.

Keep the ten-request observation log separate from later evaluation records. It motivates the problem; it is not a fair test result for a tool that has not been built. Later weeks will introduce explicit requirements and test cases, including a reserved final set. Label plans as plans and measured results as results.

blocks.label: A proposed system always says “Ask the teacher”. It never suggests an incompatible activity. Has this alone demonstrated the intended benefit? Explain which additional result you would need to check

workbook.title: Write the problem without prescribing a tool
workbook.prompt: Use the ten-request activity log to write a problem statement with a user, setting and observed difficulty. Explain why “Build an AI app” is not yet a problem statement.
workbook.answer: For example: fictional pupils choosing activities in the supplied classroom exercise had to choose again in four of ten requests because the first choice did not fit the time or room conditions. Build an AI app names a solution or construction task without specifying a user difficulty or evidence of need.

workbook.title: Identify claims beyond the evidence
workbook.prompt: A team says that the four mismatches prove every pupil dislikes the catalogue and that a recommender will fix the problem. Identify two unsupported conclusions and state what the log actually establishes.
workbook.answer: The log establishes four incompatible first choices out of ten supplied fictional requests. It does not establish every pupil’s opinion, the cause of the mismatches or that an untested recommender will improve outcomes. Accept any two of those unsupported conclusions with the bounded observation.

workbook.title: Choose information that serves the outcome
workbook.prompt: The paper project must suggest an activity compatible with available time and a quiet-room requirement. Choose relevant inputs from minutes available, quiet required, pupil name and home address. State the output and a simpler alternative to a recommender. Explain one boundary.
workbook.answer: Minutes available and quiet required are relevant. Name and address are unnecessary. Output a compatible activity suggestion or an explained no-match result. A clearer catalogue or compatibility checklist is a simple alternative. Keep requests fictional and the action advisory; do not extend the task to collecting personal profiles or publishing choices.

workbook.title: Frame a different problem independently
workbook.prompt: In a fictional equipment cupboard exercise, eight teams choose a box from a list. Three boxes do not contain the items required by the corresponding request; five do. The teacher permits a paper box-finder using fictional item requests and an inventory. Write a brief naming the user difficulty, evidence, desired outcome, necessary information, an excluded action and a simple alternative. Identify one cause or benefit that these counts do not establish.
workbook.answer: Teams selecting equipment in the supplied exercise had three mismatches out of eight and need a box whose listed contents meet the request, or a clear no-match result. Use requested items and the inventory; personal identities are unnecessary. Exclude real purchases, changing stock or public posting. A clearer inventory or item checklist is a simple alternative. The counts do not explain why teams chose mismatching boxes or prove that a box-finder will improve selection.

workbook.title: Measure help as well as avoided errors
workbook.prompt: For W4, a proposed box-finder never selects a wrong box because it always reports no match. Explain why counting only wrong suggestions would hide a failure. Name two results to record on test requests and explain why the original three-of-eight observation is not already an evaluation of the new tool.
workbook.answer: Always refusing misses useful matches when suitable boxes exist. Record compatible or incompatible suggestions and whether no-match outputs were justified by the inventory, along with total requests. The three-of-eight observation describes the earlier selection process; the proposed tool has not yet been tested under a comparison procedure.

teacher.background: This begins an eight-week project sequence culminating in an evidence-based defence. Use the activity recommender as a shared paper project; later weeks specify its catalogue and tests. The supplied counts are fictional motivation, not collected class data or a result of an AI system. Assess problem framing separately from enthusiasm for a particular technology. A justified decision to retain a simple method is a valid project conclusion.
materials: The fictional ten-request activity observation in the lesson
Paper for a brief with user, evidence, outcome, inputs and boundaries
The independent equipment-cupboard scenario in W4
sessions: Retrieve the limits of permission for a paper prototype.
Read the observation and distinguish difficulty, cause and proposed solution. Complete W1.
Trace the evidence-to-outcome diagram and complete W2.
Select relevant inputs and a simple alternative in W3.
Retrieve why four mismatches do not prove a cause or a solution.
Draft the guided project brief; challenge unsupported claims and excess data.
Collect W4 independently, checking the brief against the new scenario.
Complete W5 and the exit; discuss how a comparison could favour the simple method.
teacher.guidedAnswer: The brief should identify fictional pupils choosing classroom activities, four incompatible first choices out of ten, and the goal of a compatible suggestion where one exists or an explained no-match result otherwise. Inputs are minutes and quiet-room requirement. Boundaries include fictional requests, teacher-approved catalogue and suggestions only. A clear catalogue or checklist is a simpler alternative. The log does not establish causes, feelings or a future tool’s benefit. Exit: no; always asking avoids a wrong suggestion but may miss available compatible activities. Check useful matches and justified no-match cases, not only avoided errors.
misconceptions: Using AI is itself the outcome
State what improves for the user and how to observe it.
A mismatch count proves its cause
Separate observations from explanations that need further evidence.
No wrong suggestions means success
Check whether valid options were missed or every request was refused.
A prototype requires real personal data
This paper project uses permitted fictional requests and task-relevant inputs.
teacher.assessment: W4 must transfer the structure: three of eight mismatches, a compatible box or justified no-match outcome, requested items and inventory, one boundary, a simple alternative and a bounded claim. After support use a new scenario: six fictional room requests, two assigned rooms too small, four suitable; permit paper recommendations only. Require capacity and group size as relevant inputs, no real bookings, and no invented explanation for the two failures.
teacher.support: Use sentence starters: In this setting, these users need; the supplied evidence shows; we will check; we will not change. Allow an oral brief recorded by the teacher without supplying the choices. Extension: describe evidence that would make the team abandon its preferred solution.
teacher.next: Week 30 turns the activity problem into explicit requirements and a simple baseline for comparison.

ai-1/3.title: Sensors and measurement
goals: Describe a measurement using its quantity, value, unit and conditions
Distinguish a sensor reading from an interpretation or decision
Use repeated comparisons to investigate a measurement problem without inventing certainty

prerequisite.prompt: A record retains only the highest temperature of a day. Can it establish when that temperature occurred? Explain using two possible records.
prerequisite.answer: No. A maximum of 26 degrees C could occur at noon or at 3 pm. The retained number does not preserve time.

vocabulary: A device that responds to a physical quantity and helps turn it into a signal
A value obtained by comparing a quantity with a scale or standard
An agreed amount used to express a quantity, such as a second or a degree Celsius
Checking and, when appropriate, adjusting a measuring system against a reference

blocks.text: A garden display shows 24. Is that warm? We cannot interpret the number until we know what was measured and the unit. It might mean 24 degrees Celsius, 24 percent soil moisture according to a particular device, or 24 hours since watering. The screen alone does not supply the missing meaning.

A useful measurement record names the quantity, value, unit, time and relevant conditions. For air temperature, the location and exposure matter: a device in direct sunshine may warm differently from one in shade. Record the conditions rather than assuming that every nearby device measured the same situation.

Measurement is a way of representing part of the physical world. It does not capture everything about that world. One air-temperature reading does not tell us how dry the roots are, whether a plant is diseased or whether watering is permitted.

lesson.title: Follow the measurement into a decision

blocks.title: Three different stages in a garden system
rows: Written rule checks whether value exceeds 28
Gardener decides what action is appropriate
An action or a decision to wait
blocks.caption: Sensing, checking a rule and deciding what to do are separate stages. A correct rule can still receive an unsuitable measurement.

blocks.text: The sensor responds to a physical quantity. Electronics convert the response into a recorded value. A later program can compare the value with a threshold. Nothing about this path requires us to claim that the sensor understands plant health.

The rule uses exceeds 28, so a reading of exactly 28 does not trigger it. At 29 it does. This boundary is a property of the written rule; it is separate from the question of whether the measuring device is accurate enough for the intended purpose.

Two devices are placed side by side in a shaded room and allowed to settle. At three agreed times, device A reads 20, 21 and 20 degrees C; device B reads 22, 23 and 22 degrees C. B is 2 degrees higher on every comparison. That pattern is evidence of a consistent difference under these test conditions.

We cannot conclude from agreement patterns alone that A is correct and B is wrong. A suitable checked reference can help investigate. We also need to consider whether the devices have different response times, resolutions or placement. Three comparisons in one room do not prove performance in every temperature range.

Calibration is a reference check, sometimes followed by an adjustment. Do not simply subtract 2 from every future B reading because these three pairs happened to differ by 2. A correction needs support over the conditions where it will be used.

Suppose one classroom device reports 27 degrees C near a sunny window and another reports 22 degrees C in shade. The five-degree difference may reflect the locations. Calling one device faulty skips an alternative explanation. First write a prediction: if location explains the difference, placing both devices together after they settle should reduce it.

A fair comparison changes the suspected factor while keeping other relevant conditions as similar as practical. Record what was changed and what remained uncertain. Repeated results can strengthen or weaken an explanation, but a short classroom test is not a guarantee about all future measurements.

blocks.label: Two devices disagree near a window and a shaded wall. Describe a comparison that helps separate location from device differences

lesson.title: Keep the claim within the evidence

blocks.text: A warning based on one temperature reading can mean the recorded value crossed a threshold. It cannot automatically mean a plant needs water. That broader claim would need different evidence. When a system makes a surprising decision, check the units, time, location, measurement and rule in order.

For classroom investigations, use teacher-provided records or ordinary safe room conditions. The reasoning task does not require heating devices, opening electronics or testing people. A clear paper investigation can reveal the same distinction between a reading and an interpretation.

blocks.label: A display says 30 without a unit. State two questions needed before using it in a temperature-warning rule

workbook.title: Repair an incomplete record
