workbook.prompt: A notebook entry says 24 at lunchtime. Rewrite it as a useful air-temperature record by stating which missing fields must be collected. Do not invent values that were not observed.
workbook.answer: Keep the observed value 24 and approximate time lunchtime; mark the unit, exact time if needed, location, exposure and device identity as unknown or to be checked. A suitable completed record needs air temperature, value, unit and relevant conditions. Invented degrees C or shade is not an observation.

workbook.title: Trace a boundary
workbook.prompt: A warning rule is recorded temperature greater than 28 degrees C. State its output for 27, 28 and 29 degrees C. Explain why an off warning does not prove that the sensor is working correctly.
workbook.answer: 27 off, 28 off, 29 on. These outputs follow the comparison applied to the recorded values. A device could report an incorrect low value while the rule correctly stays off; measurement quality needs a separate check.

workbook.title: Compare without choosing a winner
workbook.prompt: At the same three times, A records 18, 19 and 18 degrees C and B records 21, 22 and 21 degrees C in the same location. Calculate the paired differences. What is established, and what further evidence would help judge accuracy?
workbook.answer: B minus A is 3, 3 and 3 degrees C. This establishes a consistent observed difference in these comparisons. It does not show which device is closer to the actual temperature. Use an appropriate checked reference, allow settling, record conditions and investigate across the intended range.

workbook.title: Investigate a new measurement dispute
workbook.prompt: A classroom sound display near a speaker reads higher than one near the door. A student declares the door device broken. Propose a safe comparison using normal classroom sound. Predict one result consistent with location explaining the difference and one result that would leave a device difference worth investigating.
workbook.answer: Place both devices side by side under the same normal sound conditions, using the same settings and reading times, or exchange positions and repeat. If readings become similar together or the higher reading follows the speaker location, location is a plausible explanation. If one device remains consistently lower side by side or after swapping, a device or setting difference remains plausible. Neither result alone proves a device broken; a checked reference and repeated observations help.

workbook.title: Limit a system's conclusion
workbook.prompt: An air-temperature sensor reports 29 degrees C and a rule turns on a warning. Someone writes The plant is thirsty. Explain the unsupported step and name information more directly relevant to deciding whether watering is needed.
workbook.answer: Crossing an air-temperature threshold does not establish root-zone dryness or a plant's watering need. Soil conditions, the kind of plant, recent watering and a gardener's inspection are more relevant. The warning can be correctly on while the thirst claim remains unsupported.

teacher.background: Separate physical quantity, recorded measurement and interpretation throughout. No hardware is required. Avoid describing every difference as error or every repeated value as accuracy. Consistent disagreement is a finding; deciding which device is accurate requires additional reference evidence. Keep units visible in both speech and written work.
materials: The paired-temperature table and two paper device labels
A sketch of a classroom with a window, shaded wall, speaker and door
Optional ordinary room thermometers used according to school procedures; paper data is sufficient
sessions: Retrieve information loss with the maximum-temperature prompt. Ask what time information disappeared.
Show only 24. Collect possible meanings, then build a measurement record with unknown fields.
Trace the garden diagram and test 27, 28 and 29. Separate sensing from the rule.
Pairs complete W1 and W2. Reject invented record details while accepting explicit unknowns.
Compute paired differences in the worked table. Ask whether consistent disagreement identifies the correct device.
Model a location comparison. Complete W3 and discuss what a reference adds.
Collect W4 independently. Ask for two predicted outcomes, not just a procedure.
Use W5 and the exit question to distinguish measurement from an unsupported plant-health claim.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Put the devices together, use comparable settings and times, allow settling and repeat, or swap positions while recording conditions. If the difference follows position, location is plausible; if it follows device, investigate the device or settings. For the exit: ask what quantity and unit 30 refers to, when and where it was measured, and whether that measurement is suitable for the rule.
misconceptions: The more stable device must be accurate
A device can repeatedly report an offset value. Stability and closeness to a reference answer different questions.
The warning proves the condition in the world
Trace the recorded number into the rule. An incorrect or irrelevant input can produce a correctly computed warning.
Missing details can be filled with sensible guesses
Keep unknown fields explicit until evidence supplies them. Guesses must be labelled as assumptions.
teacher.assessment: W4 is secure when it controls location or device identity in a meaningful comparison, keeps ordinary safe conditions, states two interpretable outcomes and avoids declaring certainty. If the learner only says try again, ask which factor will change and what each possible result would mean. Retest independently with light readings at a desk and window.
teacher.support: Give a record frame with quantity, value, unit, time and location boxes. Use a number line for paired differences. Extension: discuss why devices that round to whole degrees can differ at a boundary without either being grossly faulty.
teacher.next: Week 4 uses reliable recorded features to compare an explicitly written rule with a rule selected from labelled examples.

ai-1/30.title: Requirements and a simple baseline
goals: Turn the project outcome into precise input and output requirements
Apply a simple manual baseline to valid requests and record its results
Plan a fair comparison using the same catalogue, requests and judging rules

prerequisite.prompt: A recommender always reports no match. Why is a count of zero incompatible suggestions insufficient to show that it helps users?
prerequisite.answer: It may miss compatible options on every request where one exists. Check useful suggestions and whether no-match results are justified, as well as incompatible suggestions.

vocabulary: A precise condition that the solution must satisfy
A defined starting method used for comparison
Meeting all the stated conditions of the request
A stated way to choose when several options qualify
A check of whether a result satisfies a requirement

lesson.title: Specify what a correct result means

blocks.text: Last week we identified a difficulty: some fictional activity choices did not fit the available time or room conditions. Now define the task precisely enough that two reviewers can agree whether an output is correct. A requirement such as “suggest a good activity” is too vague. State which inputs are accepted, what counts as compatible and what to do when no option fits.

For this paper project, a valid request contains an available time from 0 to 30 whole minutes and a quiet-room requirement written Yes or No. Yes means the activity must be marked quiet. No means either quiet or non-quiet activities are permitted; it does not mean noise is required. A missing or invalid value needs clarification, not a guessed value or a no-match claim.

A compatible activity takes no more than the available minutes and meets the quiet-room condition. If several activities fit, suggest the first in catalogue order. If none fits a valid request, report no match. Give a brief reason. This is a suggestion only: it does not book resources, tell anyone to begin or guarantee enjoyment.

lesson.title: Use one catalogue for both methods

blocks.text: These four rows are the complete approved catalogue for the paper model. Treat their times as fixed task values, not measured guarantees about real pupils. All required materials are assumed available. The catalogue order B1, B2, B3, B4 is the tie rule; it is not a claim that B1 is everyone’s favourite.

For 10 minutes with quiet required, B1 fits because 10 is no more than 10 and B1 is quiet. B2 fails the quiet requirement. B3 and B4 take too long. For 8 minutes with quiet not required, B2 fits; B1 takes too long. A request for 7 minutes has no compatible activity in this catalogue, even when quiet is not required.

Check each condition. A fast activity can still fail the quiet requirement. A quiet activity can still take too long. Exact equality is allowed: an activity listed as 10 minutes fits 10 available minutes. A blank time is different from a valid time of zero.

lesson.title: Describe a baseline someone else can repeat

blocks.title: The manual checklist baseline
rows: Check minutes and Yes or No
Check time and quiet for each
blocks.caption: The baseline is a complete manual method. A prototype must be compared with this defined procedure, not an invented weak opponent.

blocks.text: Write the request at the top of a sheet. If it is invalid, record what needs clarification and stop. Otherwise mark each catalogue row as compatible or incompatible using both conditions. Circle the first compatible row in order, or write no match if every row fails. Record the output and its reason. This checklist is our baseline.

The baseline can be correct on all cases when applied carefully. A prototype that matches it has not demonstrated better compatibility. It may still be easier to use or faster to trace, but those are separate claims that need their own measures. Do not make the baseline skip a condition just to make the prototype look better.

lesson.title: Plan the comparison before seeing its outcome

blocks.text: Both methods must receive the same request values and the same catalogue version, and both must be judged by the same requirements. Record actual results, including errors, no-match outputs and clarification requests. A valid no-match result can pass; a no-match result that overlooks a fitting activity cannot. A guessed answer to invalid input fails the clarification requirement.

blocks.label: Apply the manual baseline to 12 minutes with quiet required and to 8 minutes with quiet required. Mark every catalogue row for each request, choose the required output and explain the tie rule. State what to do if the available-time field is blank instead

blocks.text: The cases used while designing are development cases. Keep the teacher’s reserved final cases unopened until the process is fixed and ready for evaluation. Do not change the requirements after seeing a poor result simply to count that result as a success. If a real need changes, record the new requirement and rerun the relevant checks.

lesson.title: Keep the project evidence ready for the next week

blocks.text: Your project record now needs the problem brief, this catalogue, the input rules, compatibility rule, tie rule and clarification behaviour. Add a baseline sheet with one row per request: supplied input, actual output, reason and whether the requirements were met. Record the method and catalogue version so a later reader can repeat the comparison.

For this week, complete the baseline before building a new process. Next week you will design the full decision path, including invalid input and no-match cases. Keep compatibility claims within the paper model. Real materials, changing room conditions and pupils’ preferences would require more information and a revised task.

blocks.label: Two methods both produce the required outputs on the same five valid requests. One team claims its prototype is more accurate because it uses an app. Is that conclusion supported? Name a separate benefit the team could investigate and what it would need to record

workbook.title: Make a requirement checkable
workbook.prompt: Replace “suggest a good activity” with the time condition, quiet condition and tie rule used in this project. Explain why Quiet required No permits B1 as well as non-quiet activities when their times fit.
workbook.answer: Time required must be no more than available time; when quiet is required the activity must be quiet. Choose the first compatible activity in B1 to B4 order. No means quiet is not required, not forbidden, so quiet B1 is permitted if 10 minutes fits.

workbook.title: Run the baseline on three requests
workbook.prompt: Using the catalogue, record the baseline output and reason for 10 minutes with quiet required, 8 minutes with quiet not required, and 7 minutes with quiet not required. Identify which no-match result is justified and why.
workbook.answer: 10 Yes gives B1: 10 fits exactly and it is quiet. 8 No gives B2: B1 is too long, B2 fits and non-quiet is permitted. 7 No gives no match: even the shortest activity requires 8 minutes. That no-match result is justified by the complete catalogue.

workbook.title: Separate invalid input from no matching option
workbook.prompt: Compare a request with blank minutes and Quiet required Yes to a request with 0 minutes and Quiet required Yes. What should the baseline record for each? Explain why these are different outcomes even though neither produces an activity suggestion.
workbook.answer: Blank minutes is invalid and requires clarification of the missing time. Zero is a valid whole number within 0 to 30; no activity takes 0 minutes or less, so no match is justified. The first lacks a usable input; the second has a usable input but no compatible option.

workbook.title: Build a baseline for a different catalogue
workbook.prompt: A paper room recommender uses R1 first, capacity 6, quiet Yes; then R2, capacity 10, quiet No. Valid requests give a whole group size from 1 to 12 and Quiet required Yes or No. A room fits when capacity is at least group size and the quiet condition is met; choose the first fitting room. Record outputs and reasons for 6 people Yes, 8 people No and 8 people Yes. Explain how a manual baseline can be compared fairly with a prototype. No real booking is allowed.
workbook.answer: 6 Yes gives R1: equality fits and it is quiet. 8 No gives R2: R1 is too small and R2 meets capacity with quiet not required. 8 Yes gives no match: R1 is too small, R2 is not quiet. Use the same room catalogue, request set and requirements for both methods and keep all results. Compare suggestions only; do not make bookings.

workbook.title: Challenge an unfair comparison
workbook.prompt: Team A tests a prototype on five easy requests and the manual baseline on five different requests, then reports only the prototype’s successful outputs. Identify two changes needed for a fair comparison. If both methods then meet all requirements, what can and cannot be concluded about compatibility?
workbook.answer: Use the same requests and catalogue for both with the same judging rules, and retain all outputs including failures and no-match or clarification results. If both meet the requirements on those cases, both pass those checks; the results do not demonstrate the prototype has better compatibility or prove either works on every possible case.

teacher.background: Use this catalogue and task contract unchanged through the shared project unless a later activity explicitly introduces a versioned change. The baseline is deliberately complete and credible: careful manual checking can satisfy the specification. The educational aim is a traceable, tested recommender and a defensible comparison, not a compulsory claim that automation wins. Minutes are exact paper-model values and resources are assumed available.
materials: The four-row B1 to B4 catalogue and fictional request cards
A baseline sheet with input, output, reason and pass or fail columns
Separate storage for teacher-reserved final cases, kept out of development work
sessions: Retrieve why zero incompatible suggestions is not sufficient evidence of help.
Define valid input and both compatibility conditions; complete W1.
Read the complete catalogue and run W2 by hand.
Complete W3 and distinguish blank input from a valid zero.
Retrieve the tie rule and the meaning of Quiet required No.
Complete the guided baseline and discuss a fair comparison plan.
Collect W4 independently, requiring reasons for each room result.
Complete W5 and the exit; save the contract and baseline for Week 31.
teacher.guidedAnswer: 12 Yes: B1 and B3 fit; B2 and B4 are non-quiet, and B4 is also too long. Choose B1 because it is first in catalogue order. 8 Yes: B1 and B3 are too long; B2 is not quiet; B4 fails both. Report no match. Blank time requires clarification, not a guessed number. Exit: equal successful outputs on five cases do not show better accuracy for the app. A separate claim such as faster completion needs recorded times under comparable conditions, with errors and help also recorded.
misconceptions: Quiet required No excludes quiet activities
No removes the quiet restriction; it does not reverse it.
Ten minutes does not fit a ten-minute limit
No more than includes equality.
Blank time means zero
Blank is missing; zero is a valid input with no matching activity here.
A baseline must be bad to make a comparison useful
Use a credible simple method and accept a tie or a baseline win.
teacher.assessment: W4 requires R1, R2 and no match with capacity and quiet reasons, plus matching inputs, catalogue and judging rules in the comparison. After support change R2 to quiet Yes and repeat 8 Yes: expected R2. Ask whether this revises a requirement or a catalogue value; it revises the catalogue, so record a new catalogue version and rerun affected checks.
teacher.support: Give one tick column for time or capacity and another for quiet. Require both ticks before circling a suggestion. Use a number line to distinguish equal to from greater than. Extension: explain why a fixed tie rule helps reproducibility but does not prove a preference ranking.
teacher.next: Week 31 designs the complete decision process using the same requirements and catalogue.

ai-1/31.title: Designing a complete decision process
goals: Design a decision process that covers valid, invalid and no-match requests
Trace changing state and explain why the search stops
Preserve both compatibility conditions and the agreed first-match rule

prerequisite.prompt: For the activity project, how does a blank time differ from a valid request for zero minutes?
prerequisite.answer: Blank time requires clarification because an input is missing. Zero is valid within 0 to 30, but no activity in the catalogue fits it, so the correct result is no match.

vocabulary: Checking an input against the agreed rules before using it
A path chosen according to a condition
Information that records the process’s current position or values
Reaching a point where the process stops

lesson.title: Turn the requirements into a complete path

blocks.text: A complete process says what happens for every kind of request in the task. It must handle a fitting activity, no fitting activity and unusable input. We will design a paper algorithm before building the prototype. Its decisions use the requirements from Week 30, so a different drawing should not silently change what counts as correct.

Keep the same catalogue order: B1 Bookmark drawing, 10 minutes, quiet Yes; B2 Story circle, 8 minutes, quiet No; B3 Pattern puzzle, 12 minutes, quiet Yes; B4 Tower challenge, 15 minutes, quiet No. These are fixed paper-model values with materials assumed available. Valid input is a whole number of minutes from 0 to 30 and Quiet required Yes or No.

A candidate fits when its required minutes are no more than the available minutes and either quiet is not required or the activity is quiet. Both parts must hold. The output is the first fitting activity in catalogue order, with a reason, or a clear no-match result. Invalid or missing input produces a clarification request. None of these outputs books materials or publishes a message.

lesson.title: Give every branch a next step

blocks.title: Four paths through the recommender
blocks.caption: Failing one candidate continues the search. No match is justified only after the valid request has no fitting candidate.

blocks.text: Begin by checking the request. If minutes are missing, outside 0 to 30 or not a whole number, ask for a whole number in that range. If the quiet field is not Yes or No, ask for one of those values. State the fields needing correction and stop this run. When a corrected request arrives, validate it as a new run rather than continuing with old candidate state.

For a valid request, start at B1. Check time and the quiet condition for the current candidate. If both pass, output that candidate and stop. If either fails, move forward exactly one row. After B4 fails, there is no next row, so output no match and stop. Never jump back to B1 within the same search.

lesson.title: Trace a request before trusting the design

headers: Stage for 9 minutes and Quiet required No
rows: 9 is a whole number in range; No is valid
8 is no more than 9; quiet is not required

blocks.text: The current candidate changes from B1 to B2. The request values stay the same. After B2 passes, the process stops: it does not replace B2 with a later fitting row. This early stop preserves the first-match rule and gives the same required suggestion as the manual baseline, which marked every row before selecting the first fit.

Termination needs a reason. There are only four rows, each failed check moves to the next row, and no row is revisited. A valid request therefore examines at most four candidates. A success can stop sooner. Invalid input stops before the search. Merely drawing an arrow around a loop is not enough; the state must make progress toward an end.

Consider the mistaken instruction “If B1 fails, report no match.” It would miss B2 on the 9-minute No request. Another mistake is “If time fits or quiet fits, suggest the activity.” That could allow an activity that takes too long merely because it is quiet. Use a concrete request to show which requirement a design breaks.

blocks.label: Trace 9 minutes with Quiet required Yes through every candidate. State the reason each fails and the final output. Then explain what would happen if a failed candidate were checked again without moving to the next row. Finally, state the first step for 31 minutes with Quiet required No

blocks.text: A process must also distinguish the meaning of No from a requirement for noise. When Quiet required is No, a quiet candidate can still pass. For 11 minutes No, B1 fits and comes first, even though B2 also fits. An instruction to reject all quiet activities when No is selected would change the task.

lesson.title: Keep the explanation tied to the decision

blocks.text: An explanation should identify the checks that actually justified the result. For example, B2 fits the 9-minute No request because its 8-minute duration fits and quiet was not required. Do not add “you will love it”, which was neither an input nor a tested condition. For no match, report that no catalogue row met both conditions; a trace can show why.

Save a labelled version of the process with its validation, candidate order, conditions, state changes and stopping points. A partner should be able to follow it without asking you to fill a missing step. Next week the paper prototype will turn this design into instruction cards and a trace record. Keep any final evaluation cases reserved while developing the design.

blocks.label: A design finds B1 compatible for 15 minutes No but keeps searching and returns B4 instead. Is B4 compatible? Does this output meet the full task requirements? Explain the difference and give the required output

workbook.title: Describe all possible kinds of ending
workbook.prompt: Name the three kinds of final output in the activity process and the condition that leads to each. Explain why a candidate failing its time check is not automatically a final no-match result.
workbook.answer: Clarification follows invalid or missing input. A suggestion follows the first candidate passing both compatibility conditions. No match follows a valid request after all candidates fail. A single failed candidate does not settle whether later candidates fit, so the process must advance.

workbook.title: Track the current candidate
workbook.prompt: Trace 9 minutes with Quiet required No. Record the current candidate, time result, quiet condition and next step until the process stops. Explain why the request values should not change as the candidate advances.
workbook.answer: B1 fails time because 10 is greater than 9; quiet is unrestricted. Advance to B2. B2 passes time because 8 is no more than 9 and quiet is not required, so suggest B2 and stop. Candidate state changes to search the catalogue; changing the request values would solve a different task.

workbook.title: Repair an incorrect branch
workbook.prompt: A design says “If the activity is quiet OR its time fits, suggest it.” For 5 minutes with Quiet required Yes it selects B1. Identify the failed requirement and replace the condition with a correct one. Give the correct result for this request.
workbook.answer: B1 is quiet but requires 10 minutes, exceeding 5. Require time to fit AND the quiet condition to hold. The quiet condition is either quiet not required or a quiet activity. No catalogue activity fits 5 minutes, so the correct output is no match after checking all candidates.

workbook.title: Design a complete room decision process
workbook.prompt: A new paper catalogue lists C1 first, capacity 4, quiet Yes; C2 second, capacity 8, quiet No. Valid requests give a whole group size from 1 to 10 and Quiet required Yes or No. A room fits if capacity is at least group size and the quiet condition is met; choose the first fit. Write a complete process with validation, search, state change and stopping rules. Trace 6 people No and explain the outcome for a blank quiet field. No booking takes place.
workbook.answer: Validate group size and Yes or No; request clarification and stop if invalid. Start C1; check capacity and quiet. If both pass, suggest and stop; otherwise advance to C2. If C2 also fails, report no match and stop. For 6 No, C1 fails capacity, C2 passes capacity with quiet unrestricted, so suggest C2. Blank quiet requires clarification before searching. Each failed row advances, so at most two candidates are checked.

workbook.title: Preserve the first compatible option
workbook.prompt: For the activity catalogue, 15 minutes with Quiet required No allows several activities. Explain why returning the last compatible row breaks the agreed rule even though it fits. Describe a stopping rule that preserves the first match, and one way to check that a loop cannot repeat forever.
workbook.answer: All four activities fit, but the tie rule requires B1 first. Returning B4 meets compatibility but not the full specification. Stop immediately after the first passing candidate. Check that every failure advances exactly one row, no row is revisited and exhaustion of B4 ends with no match.

teacher.background: Keep Week 30’s requirements separate from the algorithm that implements them. The manual baseline marked all rows; this design may stop at the first fit while preserving the required output. Check more than final labels: pupils must explain both conditions, validation and progress through the finite catalogue. This is an explicit-rule recommender, not a model fitted from examples.
materials: The unchanged B1 to B4 catalogue and Week 30 requirements
Four candidate cards and a marker for the current row
Paper for a process drawing and a trace with candidate, checks and next step
sessions: Retrieve blank input versus a valid zero and no match.
Identify all endings and branches using the diagram; complete W1.
Trace 9 No and complete W2 with visible candidate state.
Complete W3 and contrast both conditions with either condition.
Retrieve the first-match rule and the meaning of No.
Complete the guided no-match trace and demonstrate a loop without progress.
Collect W4 independently; ask a partner to follow the written process literally.
Complete W5 and the exit; save the versioned design for the prototype.
teacher.guidedAnswer: 9 Yes: B1 takes 10, too long; B2 takes 8 but is not quiet; B3 takes 12, too long; B4 takes 15 and is not quiet. After all four fail, output no match. Rechecking a failed row without advancing could repeat forever with unchanged state. 31 No is outside the accepted time range, so request a whole time from 0 to 30 and stop before searching. Exit: B4 is compatible for 15 No, but violates the first-match rule; the required output is B1.
misconceptions: One failed row proves no match
Later rows may fit; continue until a fit or catalogue exhaustion.
Passing either condition is sufficient
The time and quiet conditions must both hold.
Any compatible answer satisfies the task
The first-in-catalogue tie rule is also a requirement.
A loop stops because it should
Show a state change that advances toward a finite end.
teacher.assessment: W4 must contain input validation, both room checks, first-match stopping, advancement, exhaustion and the C2 trace for 6 No. Blank quiet must produce clarification. After support change the request to 6 Yes: both rooms fail different conditions, so no match after two checks. Require an explanation that this is different from invalid input.
teacher.support: Move a marker down the candidate cards while leaving the request card fixed. Use separate time and quiet ticks before combining them. Extension: compare the number of candidates examined by the early-stop process and the full manual checklist without claiming a measured time saving.
teacher.next: Week 32 builds a paper prototype from the decision process and records each step as a trace.

ai-1/32.title: Building and tracing a paper prototype
goals: Build a runnable paper prototype with explicit instructions and visible state
Record what actually happens without silently repairing the instructions
Use a trace to distinguish an instruction defect from an execution mistake

prerequisite.prompt: When one candidate fails, what must happen next, and when is no match justified?
prerequisite.answer: Advance to the next catalogue row. No match is justified only after valid input and failure of every row. A passing row produces the first suggestion and stops the run.

vocabulary: An early working version used to explore and test a design
A precise action or decision for the operator to follow
A record of the steps and state during one run
The result required by the agreed specification
What actually happened when this version was run

lesson.title: Build something a partner can run

blocks.text: This week you will turn the decision process into a paper prototype. One partner operates the instructions and another records the steps. A working prototype needs more than a polished drawing: someone else must be able to follow it without asking its author to supply missing rules. Keep the version you ran so the trace can be checked against it.

Copy this catalogue in order onto four cards: B1 Bookmark drawing, 10 minutes, quiet Yes; B2 Story circle, 8 minutes, quiet No; B3 Pattern puzzle, 12 minutes, quiet Yes; B4 Tower challenge, 15 minutes, quiet No. These are fictional paper-model values with materials assumed available. Label the catalogue B version 1.

Keep the Week 30 contract: input is a whole number of available minutes from 0 to 30, and Quiet required Yes or No. An activity fits when its time is no more than the available minutes AND either quiet is not required or the activity is quiet. No means either kind is allowed. Suggest the first fit with a reason; otherwise report no match. Missing or invalid input needs clarification. Suggestions do not book materials or publish anything.

lesson.title: Make the state and instructions visible

blocks.title: A paper run that can be checked
rows: First fit or end of list
blocks.caption: The request stays fixed while the marker advances. Keep the instruction version and trace together.

blocks.text: Make a request card with Available minutes and Quiet required fields, a marker for the current catalogue row, and a trace sheet. Head the sheet Run ID, prototype version, catalogue version and request. Below it use columns Step, current row, time check, quiet check and next action or output. Use not checked when validation stops the search.

Write instruction cards P1 version 1. Card 1: validate both fields; if invalid, name the field needing correction and stop; otherwise put the marker at B1. Card 2: check the marked row against both compatibility conditions; record both checks. If both pass, suggest that row with the reason and stop. Card 3: if either fails and another row remains, advance exactly one row and return to Card 2; if no row remains, report no match and stop. Begin each new request at Card 1 with a cleared output.

Before operating P1, use the full manual checklist to write the expected result for 9 minutes, Quiet required No. Then run the cards literally. Do not replace a surprising result with the expected one. Recording disagreement gives you something to investigate; hiding it removes useful evidence.

rows: Whole minutes in range; No accepted
8 is no more than 9; quiet unrestricted

blocks.text: This trace agrees with the expected B2 result. It shows that this run followed the instructions. One matching result does not prove that every request will work or that the prototype is faster than the manual checklist. This is a system of written rules, not a model trained on examples.

Suppose the operator starts a fresh 11-minute No request at B2 because the marker was left there. They return B2. The required first fit is B1, and Card 1 explicitly says to restart at B1. The trace therefore reveals an execution mistake. If the written instructions had omitted the reset, that would instead be an instruction defect. Inspect the saved version before deciding.

Preserve the first trace. For an execution mistake, rerun the same written version correctly and label the new run. For an instruction defect, save a corrected version with a new label, state what changed, and rerun. Never rewrite an old observed result to make a version appear successful.

blocks.label: Run P1 for 8 minutes with Quiet required Yes. Record every row, both checks and the final output. Then consider a blank Quiet required field: which card stops that run and how many candidates should be checked?

lesson.title: Hand over a small reproducible prototype

blocks.text: Swap roles and give your partner the request card, catalogue, instruction cards and blank trace sheet. Let them operate without extra hints from the author. Record any point where they cannot decide what to do from the written instructions. Label and save changes, then repeat the affected run. Keep development cases separate from any cases your teacher has reserved for a later evaluation.

Your handover should let someone repeat a run using the same inputs and versions and check why it stopped. Keep all results, including disagreements. Next week you will organise several routine cases into a test record. A neat interface is useful, but correctness depends on validation, both conditions, the first-match rule and a clear ending.

blocks.label: A saved trace says “P1 version 1; 11 minutes No; started at B2; suggested B2.” Explain the error using the written cards. State what evidence to keep and what should happen in a new correct run.

workbook.title: Assemble the runnable kit
workbook.prompt: Create P1 version 1 using the three instruction cards in the lesson. Copy catalogue B version 1 and make a request card, current-row marker and trace sheet. List what each item records. Explain which information stays fixed during one run and what changes.
workbook.answer: The kit contains labelled instructions and catalogue, request fields, a marker and a trace sheet with run and version labels. The request and catalogue stay fixed during the run; the current row and trace advance. The final output starts clear. The cards validate, check both conditions, return the first fit, advance after failure and stop with no match after exhaustion.

workbook.title: Run and record the first match
workbook.prompt: Use the manual checklist to predict P1’s output for 11 minutes No. Then ask a partner to operate your saved cards. Record the expected result separately from the observed steps and output, including the reason. Explain why the operator should stop without checking later rows.
workbook.answer: The expected output is B1: 10 is no more than 11, quiet is unrestricted and B1 is first. A correct observed trace validates, starts at B1, passes both checks and suggests B1 with this reason. Stop because the specification selects the first fit. If a pupil observes a different run, retain and investigate that evidence rather than replacing it with this expected trace.

workbook.title: Locate the source of a wrong result
workbook.prompt: Saved instructions P0 say “start at B1; if B1 fails, report no match.” For the valid request 9 minutes No, an operator follows P0 exactly and reports no match. Identify the instruction defect and write the changed step. Explain how to label the correction and what to retain from the failed run.
workbook.answer: P0 stops after one failure and misses B2, which fits 9 No. After failure, advance to the next row and continue; no match follows only after all rows fail. Save a new version with the change recorded. Keep the original P0 instructions, request, expected B2, observed no match and trace. Rerun the corrected version and record a new result.

workbook.title: Build a new route through a small catalogue
workbook.prompt: Independently make and trace instruction cards for this paper equipment catalogue: E1 first, capacity 3 people; E2 second, capacity 6. Valid input is a whole group size from 1 to 8. Suggest the first item whose capacity is at least the group size; no booking occurs. Include invalid input and no match. Write expected results, then operate your cards for groups of 5 and 7. Record both runs and explain every stopping point.
workbook.answer: Validate whole group size 1 to 8, otherwise clarify and stop. Start E1; if capacity is at least the group size, suggest and stop; otherwise advance to E2. If E2 fails, no match and stop. Expected 5: E1 fails 3 below 5; E2 passes 6 at least 5, suggest E2. Expected 7: both capacities too small, no match. Record actual runs separately and investigate any disagreement.

workbook.title: Make the evidence repeatable
workbook.prompt: A teammate keeps only a final “B2” answer and throws away the request and old instructions after editing them. Explain why another person cannot check this result. List what to save for each run and explain why an observed error must remain in the record.
workbook.answer: B2 alone does not identify the request, version or route taken, so its correctness cannot be checked. Keep run ID, exact request, instruction and catalogue versions, expected result, observed steps and output, and any change with its later rerun. Keeping errors allows the team to locate and verify repairs instead of showing only favourable results.

teacher.background: This session builds a runnable paper implementation of the existing rule-based recommender. A trace reports execution; the specification and manual baseline determine the expected result. Do not silently coach an operator through omitted instructions. Distinguish an instruction defect from a failure to follow a correct instruction by comparing the saved cards with the trace. A paper prototype can test logic and handover, but does not establish automated speed, real pupil satisfaction or general reliability.
materials: Paper for request, instruction and catalogue cards, using the exact B version 1 values in the lesson
A movable marker and trace sheets with version labels and check columns
The Week 30 requirements and manual checklist; a folder for unchanged runs and revisions
sessions: Retrieve the conditions for continuing a search and reporting no match.
Read the contract, build and label the P1 kit, and complete W1.
Model the 9 No trace, keeping expected and observed records separate.
Partners complete W2 with an unaided operator and retain any disagreement.
Compare the stale-marker execution mistake with the P0 instruction defect.
Complete W3 and the guided 8 Yes trace; record correction versions without altering old runs.
Collect W4 independently, including cards and two trace records. Offer support only after the first attempt.
Complete W5 and the exit; save the handover kit for routine tests next week.
teacher.guidedAnswer: 8 Yes is valid. B1 fails time 10 greater than 8 but passes quiet; B2 passes time 8 equal to 8 but fails quiet; B3 fails time 12 greater than 8 but passes quiet; B4 fails time 15 greater than 8 and fails quiet. After B4, no match. Blank quiet stops at Card 1 with clarification and zero candidate checks. Exit: starting at B2 violates P1’s reset instruction, so this is an execution mistake. Keep the original trace and run P1 again from validation and B1; for 11 No, suggest B1 because 10 fits 11 and quiet is unrestricted.
misconceptions: A correct-looking answer is enough
Inspect the request, versions and trace to check how it was reached.
The observer should repair missing instructions during a run
Record the ambiguity, revise a labelled version and rerun separately.
An observed result should be changed to match the expected one
Preserve disagreement as evidence and investigate its cause.
A successful paper run proves a trained AI works
These are explicit rules; one run supports only a limited claim about that implementation.
teacher.assessment: Assess W4 for a runnable validated process, first-match stopping, advancement, exhaustion and separate expected and observed records. The 5-person run should reach E2 and the 7-person run should exhaust both rows. After support, retry with group size 3, then blank: 3 selects E1 at equality; blank requests clarification before any capacity checks. Ask the pupil to explain the evidence rather than only name the result.
teacher.support: Provide trace column headings and let pupils move a marker while speaking each check aloud. Use not checked for candidates never examined. Extension: swap partners without author explanation and record whether any instruction needs clarification; do not turn one successful handover into a reliability claim.
teacher.next: Week 33 organises routine cases into a test record with expected and observed results, keeping the prototype version fixed during each test set.

ai-1/33.title: Testing routine cases
goals: Plan routine cases with expected results derived from the requirements
Compare a fixed prototype and manual baseline on the same requests
Report every result and explain what a small test set cannot establish

prerequisite.prompt: How does an expected result differ from an observed result, and why keep both when they disagree?
prerequisite.answer: The expected result comes from the requirements; the observed result records what the saved version actually did. Disagreement is evidence to investigate, so neither record should be silently changed to match the other.

vocabulary: A specified input with an expected result and a reason for testing it
A collection of cases used together to check a version
The requirement an observed result must meet to count as a pass
Which conditions or behaviours the selected tests examine
A simple comparison method tested under the same conditions

blocks.text: This week you will turn separate paper traces into a test record. Choose several ordinary requests, write the required answers first, then run the same saved prototype on every request. Testing is useful when it can reveal a mistake, so keep failures as carefully as successes. A demonstration chosen because it works is not a complete evaluation.

Use catalogue B version 1 in order: B1 Bookmark drawing, 10 minutes, quiet Yes; B2 Story circle, 8 minutes, quiet No; B3 Pattern puzzle, 12 minutes, quiet Yes; B4 Tower challenge, 15 minutes, quiet No. These fictional values assume materials are available. Inputs are whole minutes from 0 to 30 and Quiet required Yes or No. Time must fit AND either quiet is not required or the activity is quiet. No allows either kind. Select the first fit with a correct reason; otherwise report no match. Missing or invalid input requires clarification. No booking or publishing takes place.

Keep the P1 version 1 instructions from Week 32: validate and stop with clarification if input is invalid; otherwise start at B1, check both conditions, suggest the first passing row and stop. After a failure advance one row; report no match only after all rows fail. Reset to validation and B1 for each new valid request. The manual baseline marks every row against both conditions and selects the first fit. Both methods must follow the same contract.

lesson.title: Design a record that can reveal a failure

blocks.title: From a planned case to evidence
blocks.caption: Keep the catalogue, requests and pass criteria the same for the prototype and baseline.

blocks.text: Give each case an ID. Record its exact input, purpose, expected output and expected explanation before running it. Then add observed output, observed explanation, pass or fail, and a trace reference. Put the prototype version, catalogue version and baseline method at the top of the sheet. A pass needs the correct result and a reason supported by the checked conditions; the right activity with a false reason is not a full pass.

Our routine set R contains four valid requests. R1 is 11 minutes Yes, checking an early quiet match. R2 is 9 minutes No, checking that the search reaches a later fitting row. R3 is 6 minutes No, checking that a valid request can exhaust the list. R4 is 9 minutes Yes, checking that a time fit alone is insufficient. These cases do not cover every accepted input or validation error.

lesson.title: Compare two methods on the same cases

rows: B1; 10 fits 11 and B1 is quiet
B1 with the same correct reason; pass
B2; 8 fits 9, quiet unrestricted, B1 too long
B2 with the same correct reason; pass
No match; all activities take longer
No match with the same correct reason; pass
No match; B2 is not quiet and other rows take longer

blocks.text: This is an invented record for a comparison prototype Q version 0, not a claim about your P1 runs. Q ignores the quiet condition when searching. Its trace explains the R4 failure. In the same fictional comparison, the manual baseline produced the expected result and correct explanation on all four cases: 4 of 4 full passes. Q achieved 3 of 4. The denominator includes the failed case.

On this set Q has fewer full passes than the baseline. This supports investigating its quiet check; it does not establish performance on all requests. Do not claim a speed advantage because we did not measure time. Correct implementations of P1 and the baseline can both pass all four, in which case these results show no correctness advantage for either method.

lesson.title: Run the set without changing the evidence

blocks.text: Before testing your own cards, finish all four expected results and agree the pass criterion. Swap roles: one pupil operates and the other records. Keep the same version throughout the set and begin a fresh run for each request. Record what happened even if a card is ambiguous or the operator makes a mistake. A run that stops without a required answer is a failed run to investigate, not a row to delete.

Run the manual baseline on the same four requests and catalogue. Record its actual results too; a person can make an error in either method. If you find a defect, preserve this set’s results, save a new version and start a separately labelled set after the repair. Never combine the best result from each version into a score for one version.

blocks.label: In the fictional Q record, give the full-pass fraction for each method and explain the R4 failure. A teammate removes R4 and reports Q as 3 of 3. Explain how that changes the question being answered. Then state one condition that set R has not checked.

lesson.title: Report a useful but limited conclusion

blocks.text: A useful report names the version, catalogue, case set, full-pass count and total, then describes each failure and the requirement it breaks. Keep the trace so someone can reproduce the result. Say which conditions have not been tested. Four passing runs support a claim about those four runs; they do not prove that every possible request works.

For catalogue B, any request allowing B3 also allows the earlier quiet B1; any request allowing B4 also allows earlier B1 when quiet is not required. Therefore the first-match rule never selects B3 or B4 with this catalogue. Checking those rows in a no-match trace is different from testing a successful output from a later row. Next week we will deliberately examine boundaries and labelled catalogue variations while keeping the requirements explicit.

blocks.label: A team reports “Our prototype passed 4 of 4 routine cases, so it always works and is faster than the baseline.” Rewrite this as a claim supported by the evidence, and identify two further checks that would address different gaps.

workbook.title: Prepare the four cases
workbook.prompt: Create the test record for R1 11 Yes, R2 9 No, R3 6 No and R4 9 Yes. Before running anything, write each expected output, explanation and purpose using catalogue B version 1. Include blank places for observed output, observed reason, pass or fail and trace reference. State the version labels and pass criterion.
workbook.answer: R1 B1 because time fits and it is quiet; early match. R2 B2 because B1 is too long, B2 fits and quiet is unrestricted; later match. R3 no match because every time exceeds 6; exhaustion. R4 no match because B2 fails quiet while other rows exceed 9; both conditions. Record P1 version 1, B version 1 and the manual baseline. A full pass needs the required output and a correct explanation.

workbook.title: Run a fair comparison
workbook.prompt: Operate your saved P1 cards and the manual baseline on all four R cases. Record actual results and traces on your sheet. Summarise full passes over all attempted cases for each method, name any failures and explain why a tie would not prove the prototype improves correctness. Do not invent an observed run.
workbook.answer: A correctly executed P1 and baseline both produce B1, B2, no match, no match with correct reasons, giving 4 of 4 each. Accept an honest record of different observed results when the pupil identifies and investigates the disagreements. Both methods must use the same requests, catalogue and pass criterion. A tie establishes no correctness advantage on this set; an unperformed run must remain unperformed.

workbook.title: Keep the failed case in the total
workbook.prompt: Use the fictional Q version 0 record. Calculate its full-pass fraction and the baseline’s fraction. Explain why R4 fails and why dropping it to report 3 of 3 misrepresents the original four-case set. State what evidence you would inspect before changing Q.
workbook.answer: Q passes 3 of 4; the baseline passes 4 of 4. R4 returns nonquiet B2 when quiet is required, so time alone is insufficient. Removing R4 changes the tested set and hides its known failure; 3 of 3 is not the original set’s result. Inspect the saved Q instructions and R4 trace to locate the missing quiet check, then label any repair separately.

workbook.title: Audit a new test record
workbook.prompt: Independently audit this fictional equipment selector. Catalogue E has E1 first with capacity 4 and E2 second with capacity 8. Valid group sizes are whole numbers 1 to 10. Select the first item with capacity at least the group size, or no match; invalid input needs clarification. The saved prototype reports E1 for group 3 with reason “4 holds 3”; E1 for group 6 with reason “4 holds 6”; no match for group 9 with reason “both too small”. Write all expected results, mark full passes, calculate the fraction and explain the failure. Give one untested input category. No booking occurs.
workbook.answer: Expected group 3: E1 because 4 holds 3. Group 6: E2 because E1 is too small and 8 holds 6. Group 9: no match because both capacities are too small. The first and third pass; the second fails both output and reason, giving 2 of 3 full passes. The record suggests a capacity-check problem but the saved instructions and trace are needed to locate it. Missing, nonwhole or out-of-range input is untested, as is equality with a capacity.

workbook.title: State what the evidence leaves open
workbook.prompt: Explain why catalogue B cannot produce B3 or B4 as its first fitting output even if you try many ordinary requests. Distinguish checking a row during a failed search from successfully selecting it. Write a limited conclusion for a P1 run that passed all four R cases and name a useful next test category.
workbook.answer: B3 needs at least 12 minutes and is quiet, so earlier B1 at 10 also fits whenever B3 fits. B4 needs 15 and is nonquiet, so a compatible request permits earlier B1 as well. Both later rows may be checked in no-match runs but are never first fits in catalogue B. Report 4 of 4 full passes on set R with named versions; broader reliability is unestablished. Next examine boundaries, invalid inputs or an explicitly labelled catalogue variation.

teacher.background: The prototype remains an explicit rule system. This lesson focuses on prewritten expectations, repeatable conditions and honest records. Q version 0 and its comparison results are fictional worked examples. Pupils must record their own P1 observations, including operator errors, without copying invented successes. Judge both the output and its reason. Routine coverage is deliberately limited; boundary and variation tests follow next week.
materials: The saved P1 version 1 cards, catalogue B version 1 and manual checklist from Week 32
Paper test sheets with case ID, input, purpose, expected result, observed result, judgement and trace reference
A folder for all versions and results; keep any reserved final evaluation cases separate from development work
sessions: Retrieve expected versus observed results and why disagreement is retained.
Read the contract and diagram; prepare W1 expectations and agree the full-pass criterion.
Work through the fictional Q table and W3, including the denominator and failed quiet condition.
Begin W2 partner runs with fixed versions and one trace per request.
Finish W2 baseline comparison and audit whether any cases or failures were omitted.
Complete the guided explanation and discuss coverage gaps without claiming universal reliability.
Collect W4 independently before offering support; require reasons and the denominator.
Complete W5 and the exit; retain versioned records for boundary testing next week.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Q has 3 of 4 full passes and the fictional baseline 4 of 4. R4 selects B2 despite the quiet requirement. Dropping R4 answers how Q did on a selected three-case subset and conceals the failure in the original set. Gaps include missing or invalid fields, equality at thresholds, accepted range endpoints and successful later-row selection under a varied catalogue. Exit: this named version passed these four routine cases under the recorded conditions; all-input correctness and a speed advantage are not established. Two distinct useful checks could be invalid-input handling and equal-time boundaries. Measuring speed would require a separate fair timing comparison.
misconceptions: A correct label is always a full pass
The agreed criterion also requires a correct explanation.
Remove a failed run because something went wrong
Keep and investigate it; missing required output cannot count as success.
Four passes prove all inputs work
The conclusion is limited by the selected cases and conditions.
The prototype must beat the manual baseline
A correct simple baseline can tie or outperform a prototype; report the evidence.
teacher.assessment: W4 must independently produce E1, E2 and no match, identify the group-6 capacity failure and report 2 of 3 full passes without diagnosing unseen code. After support, use a fresh record: groups 2, 7 and 10 produce observed E1 with “4 holds 2”, E2 with “8 holds 7”, and E2 with “8 holds 10”. Expected E1, E2, no match gives 2 of 3. Require the pupil to identify the final failure and propose an untested validation case.
teacher.support: Provide blank column headings and a separate copy of the requirements. Ask pupils to check time and quiet separately before combining them. Permit a spoken explanation recorded by the teacher, while retaining the pupil’s independent first attempt. Extension: explain why repeated R1 runs do not add coverage of a missing condition.
teacher.next: Week 34 tests equality boundaries, accepted ranges, invalid inputs and explicitly labelled catalogue variations, then revisits what the evidence can support.

ai-1/34.title: Testing boundaries and varied conditions
goals: Choose tests just below, at and above a decision boundary
Distinguish valid no-match requests from invalid input
Use labelled catalogue variations to examine previously untested paths

prerequisite.prompt: Why can four successful routine cases leave a mistake undiscovered?
prerequisite.answer: They examine only the selected inputs and conditions. A mistake may affect equality, invalid input, another catalogue or a path that none of those cases reaches.

vocabulary: A value where an input changes category or a condition changes truth
Including the stated endpoint or equal value
A value that does not meet the agreed input rules
A documented change in the conditions used for a test
A relevant condition or behaviour the current tests have not examined

lesson.title: Test where an answer can change

blocks.text: Routine examples can miss a mistake at an exact limit. This week you will choose revealing cases around those limits and vary the paper catalogue to reach later successful outputs. Write expected results from the requirements before operating the prototype. Keep its saved instructions and each test record so a failure remains useful evidence.

Catalogue B version 1 is unchanged: B1 Bookmark drawing, 10 minutes, quiet Yes; B2 Story circle, 8 minutes, quiet No; B3 Pattern puzzle, 12 minutes, quiet Yes; B4 Tower challenge, 15 minutes, quiet No. Search in that order. These fictional paper values assume materials are available. Inputs are whole minutes from 0 to 30 inclusive and Quiet required Yes or No. No allows quiet or nonquiet activities.

Time fits when required minutes are no more than available minutes, including equality. The quiet condition must also hold. Select the first fitting row with a correct reason, or report no match after every row fails. Invalid or missing input requires clarification before searching. P1 validates, resets to the first row, checks both conditions, advances after failure and stops at the first fit or catalogue exhaustion. No output books or publishes anything.

lesson.title: Compare the two sides and the exact limit

blocks.title: Three requests around ten minutes
blocks.caption: Keep Quiet required Yes and catalogue B version 1 fixed while changing available time.

blocks.text: For quiet requests, 10 minutes is the first time a catalogue activity fits. Test 9, 10 and 11 with Yes so only the time changes. A faulty comparison S version 0 uses strictly less than instead of no more than for time, while keeping the other P1 rules. It rejects B1 at exactly 10. With quiet required, every later row also fails, so it incorrectly reports no match.

S can pass all four routine requests from Week 33: 11 Yes, 9 No, 6 No and 9 Yes. None has a fitting activity whose duration equals the request. The 10 Yes case reveals a gap those passes did not close. Another useful boundary is 8 minutes with No: equality should allow B2, while 7 No has no match. Keep both quiet values in your wider plan because No does not mean nonquiet only.

lesson.title: Separate validation limits from activity limits

rows: Zero is valid; every activity needs more time
30 is valid; B1 is the first fit
The accepted time must be a whole number
Choose Yes or No before searching

blocks.text: The accepted range and activity durations are different kinds of boundary. Zero belongs to the valid range even though no activity fits. Thirty also belongs to it. A negative time, such as minus one minute, is below zero and invalid. Do not change a blank to zero, round 10.5 to 10 or turn a blank quiet choice into No. Ask for the field to be corrected and start a new validated run.

A test record should say whether a search is expected to begin. Clarification should name the field needing correction; it should not claim the catalogue has no suitable activity. Test an unrecognised quiet value such as Maybe as well as a missing value. These check different forms of unusable input.

lesson.title: Vary the catalogue to reach a later success

blocks.text: In B version 1, earlier B1 always fits whenever B3 or B4 could be chosen. To test a successful later-row path, make a labelled copy of the catalogue. Keep the input rules, both compatibility conditions and first-match rule unchanged. Both the prototype and manual baseline must read the same test copy. Do not overwrite the original catalogue or reuse its expected answers for the changed data.

Test copy B version 2 changes only B1’s duration from 10 to 20 minutes. All other rows, quiet labels and order stay as in version 1. For 12 Yes, B1 is now too long, B2 is not quiet, and B3 fits exactly and is quiet. The expected first suggestion is B3. This checks a third-row success and equality under a documented variation.

blocks.label: Make test copy B version 3 with durations B1 20, B2 18, B3 17 and B4 15 minutes. Keep the original quiet labels and order. For 15 No, trace the rows and give the required output and reason. Then use 15 Yes with the same copy. Explain why the outcomes differ and what must be written on both test records.

blocks.text: Label each case by its purpose: time equality, accepted-range endpoint, invalid field or catalogue variation. Record the exact catalogue version and request, the expected output and explanation, and what actually happened. Compare the prototype with the manual baseline under identical conditions. Count every attempted case, retain failures, and distinguish cases not yet run from successful tests.

These are development tests that can guide repairs. Keep any final evaluation cases reserved by your teacher separate until the prototype version is fixed for evaluation. Even a broad development set does not establish real-world enjoyment, material availability or speed. Next week you will repair a located defect and check whether the change breaks behaviour that worked before.

blocks.label: S passes the four routine cases but fails 10 Yes by reporting no match. Explain which comparison to inspect and why changing the expected answer to no match would be wrong. Give one additional equality case and one invalid-input case, including their expected outcomes.

workbook.title: Plan the equality tests
workbook.prompt: For catalogue B version 1, write expected outputs and reasons for 9 Yes, 10 Yes and 11 Yes. Explain why keeping quiet and catalogue fixed helps examine the time boundary. Predict what the faulty strictly-less-than S comparison does for 10 Yes.
workbook.answer: 9 Yes has no match: B1 and B3 are too long and B2 is not quiet; B4 also fails. 10 Yes and 11 Yes select B1, which is quiet and fits at equality or with time left. Fixing the other conditions isolates the time comparison. S rejects equality at B1 and cannot find a later fit for 10 Yes, so incorrectly returns no match.

workbook.title: Check the validation boundary
workbook.prompt: Classify these requests before searching: 0 Yes, 30 Yes, 31 Yes, blank minutes with Yes, 10.5 Yes, and 10 Maybe. Give each expected output or clarification and explain whether any candidate should be checked. Why must zero not be treated like a blank?
workbook.answer: 0 Yes is valid and checks all rows before no match. 30 Yes is valid and selects B1 at the first row. 31, blank minutes and 10.5 require minutes clarification; 10 Maybe requires a Yes or No quiet choice. Invalid cases check zero candidates. Zero is a supplied whole number within range; blank is missing information.

workbook.title: Run a labelled catalogue variation
workbook.prompt: Copy B version 1 and change only B1’s duration to 20, labelling it B version 2. Write the expected result for 12 Yes, then run your saved P1 and the manual baseline on this copy. Record the actual traces separately. Explain why an answer checked against B version 1 would not be a fair judgement of this run.
workbook.answer: Expected B3: B1 takes too long, B2 fails quiet, B3 fits 12 exactly and is quiet. Correct P1 and baseline agree, but retain actual disagreements for investigation. Under version 1 the expected first fit is B1, so using that expectation with changed data would mix conditions. Save catalogue and instruction versions with both traces.

workbook.title: Find an independent capacity boundary
workbook.prompt: A new equipment selector lists E1 first, capacity 4; E2 second, capacity 8. Valid group size is a whole number from 1 to 10. Choose the first item whose capacity is at least the group size, or no match; invalid input needs clarification. A faulty version uses capacity strictly greater than group size. Independently give correct and faulty outputs for groups 3, 4 and 5, then for group 8. Explain the defect and give the correct response to group 0. No booking occurs.
workbook.answer: Correct outputs for 3, 4, 5 and 8 are E1, E1, E2 and E2. Faulty outputs are E1, E2, E2 and no match. Equality is wrongly excluded at capacities 4 and 8. Use capacity at least group size, including equality. Group 0 is outside the accepted 1 to 10 range and needs clarification before any search. This range differs from the activity time range.

workbook.title: Audit what changed in the test
workbook.prompt: A team runs 15 No on B version 3, gets B4, but records “B version 1” and calls B4 correct. Explain the documentation error and the expected result under each catalogue. State what must stay the same in a fair prototype-versus-baseline comparison and why a test not yet run cannot be counted as a pass.
workbook.answer: For version 3, B1 20, B2 18 and B3 17 are too long; B4 15 fits and quiet is unrestricted, so B4 is correct. Under version 1, earlier B1 fits and must be selected. Correct the catalogue label while preserving what was actually used and observed. Both methods need the same request, catalogue and pass criterion. An unrun case has no observed evidence, so cannot be counted as passing.

teacher.background: Boundary testing returns to inclusive comparisons and validation using the capstone context. S version 0 is a deliberately faulty comparison example, not the correct P1 implementation. It can pass the earlier routine set while rejecting exact duration fits. Catalogue variations test later successful paths that the original data cannot reach. Preserve the distinction between changing data, changing requirements and changing implementation; the variations here change only declared catalogue values.
materials: Saved P1 instructions and catalogue B version 1, plus separate labelled copies for versions 2 and 3
Test records with purpose, versions, input, expected result, observed result, judgement and trace
Paper cards for the independent equipment selector and a folder retaining every attempted run
sessions: Retrieve why routine-case success can leave coverage gaps.
Use the diagram and W1 to compare below, at and above ten minutes.
Complete W2; distinguish accepted range endpoints from activity duration limits.
Prepare B version 2 and begin W3 expected results and partner traces.
Finish W3 and verify both methods used the same catalogue copy.
Trace guided version 3 requests and discuss purpose and version labels.
Collect W4 independently before support; inspect both equality cases and validation.
Complete W5 and the exit; save the expanded development set for repair checks.
teacher.guidedAnswer: For B version 3 and 15 No, B1 20, B2 18 and B3 17 fail time. B4 15 fits exactly and quiet is unrestricted, so select B4 and stop. For 15 Yes, B4 fails quiet and all earlier rows fail time, so no match after all four. Record B version 3, the saved instruction version, exact request, expected and observed output with reasons, and trace. Exit: inspect strictly less than versus no more than; the specification includes equality, so expected 10 Yes remains B1. Another equality case is 8 No, expected B2. Invalid 31 Yes requires minutes clarification before searching.
misconceptions: At the limit means outside the rule
An inclusive rule accepts its endpoints and equality.
No match and invalid mean the same thing
No match follows valid input; invalid fields need clarification before search.
A catalogue change needs the same expected answer
Recompute expectations from the declared new data and unchanged requirements.
More routine repetitions close every gap
Choose cases that exercise a missing condition or path.
teacher.assessment: W4 should distinguish correct E1, E1, E2, E2 from faulty E1, E2, E2, no match for 3, 4, 5, 8. Require an inclusive-capacity explanation and clarification for zero, not the activity task’s valid-zero rule. After support, use a new catalogue F1 capacity 5 then F2 capacity 9 with the same 1 to 10 input range. For groups 5 and 9, correct F1 and F2; strict comparison gives F2 and no match. Require an independent explanation of both changes.
teacher.support: Draw a number line around each boundary and read at least or no more than aloud. Keep validation and candidate checks on separate cards. Provide version-label headings without filling expected results. Extension: contrast a catalogue reorder with a duration change and explain how the first-match requirement remains unchanged in both.
teacher.next: Week 35 repairs a documented defect, reruns revealing cases and checks earlier successful cases for regressions before fixing a version for final evaluation.

ai-1/35.title: Improving and checking regressions
goals: Repair a located defect without changing the agreed requirements
Check the repaired case and earlier successful behaviour
Preserve versioned evidence and fix a candidate before final evaluation

prerequisite.prompt: The faulty S comparison rejects an activity that takes exactly the available time. Which requirement does this break?
prerequisite.answer: Time fits when required minutes are no more than available minutes, including equality. Strictly less than wrongly excludes an exact fit.

vocabulary: A fault in the instructions or implementation that can cause incorrect behaviour
A change intended to correct a located defect
Previously correct behaviour that becomes incorrect after a change
A note of what changed, why, and which versions and tests support it
A saved version kept unchanged while a specified evaluation is run

lesson.title: Make a repair that follows the requirements

blocks.text: Finding a failure is useful only if you can explain and check the repair. This week you will locate an incorrect comparison, change it in a labelled version, and test both the revealing case and behaviour that worked before. A repair can solve one problem while introducing another, so one newly passing example is not enough.

Keep catalogue B version 1 in order: B1 Bookmark drawing, 10 minutes, quiet Yes; B2 Story circle, 8 minutes, quiet No; B3 Pattern puzzle, 12 minutes, quiet Yes; B4 Tower challenge, 15 minutes, quiet No. These fictional values assume materials are available. Inputs are whole minutes from 0 to 30 inclusive and Quiet required Yes or No. No allows either quiet or nonquiet activities.

A candidate fits when its duration is no more than the available minutes AND either quiet is not required or the activity is quiet. Return the first fit with a correct reason. Valid input with no fit gives no match after all rows fail. Invalid or missing input needs clarification before search. Each new run starts with validation and a cleared output, then the first row if valid. Suggestions do not book or publish anything. These written rules are not a model fitted from examples.

blocks.title: A repair with evidence
blocks.caption: A passing repair test checks the reported defect. Regression tests examine previously correct behaviour.

blocks.text: S version 0 follows the P1 process except that its time check uses strictly less than. On 10 Yes with catalogue B version 1, it reports no match. The expected result is B1 because 10 fits exactly and B1 is quiet. Compare the saved instruction with the trace: the cause is the exclusion of equality, not a need to change the catalogue or expected answer.

Create S version 1 by replacing only the time comparison with no more than. Keep validation, the quiet condition, catalogue order, advancement and stopping rules. Write a change record naming S0, S1, the failing 10 Yes case, the comparison changed and why equality belongs in the rule. Retain the old version and failed trace; do not overwrite them with the new result.

lesson.title: A tempting repair can cause a regression

blocks.text: Consider a different proposed repair, T version 1. It accepts equal times but accidentally removes the quiet check. It fixes 10 Yes, yet now returns B2 for 9 Yes. That second request correctly returned no match under S0 because B2 is not quiet. Previously correct behaviour has become wrong: this is a regression.

rows: S0 no match; T1 B1; S1 B1
No match with a valid reason
S0 no match; T1 B2; S1 no match
S0 no match; T1 B2; S1 B2
No match with a valid reason
S0 no match; T1 no match; S1 no match

blocks.text: These outputs are worked predictions from the described versions. Your own test record must contain the actual runs and their reasons. T1 should not replace the candidate merely because it passes the first row. For S1, check the revealing equality cases and rerun all four routine cases from Week 33, then validation and the labelled catalogue variations from Week 34. A full pass still needs both the required output and a correct explanation.

lesson.title: Run a repair and regression set

blocks.text: Write expectations before running S1. Use B version 1 for 11 Yes, 9 No, 6 No and 9 Yes; include the revealing 10 Yes and 8 No. Add 0 Yes, 30 Yes, 31 Yes, blank minutes with Yes, 10.5 Yes and 10 Maybe to check valid endpoints and invalid fields. Keep cases and results separated by version, and compare with the manual baseline under the same conditions.

Retain the catalogue variation tests: B version 2 changes only B1 time to 20, giving B3 for 12 Yes. B version 3 has times 20, 18, 17 and 15 for B1 to B4, with the original quiet labels and order; it gives B4 for 15 No and no match for 15 Yes. These cases check later successful paths and the quiet condition under changed data. Label each test with the catalogue it actually uses.

blocks.label: Explain why T1’s result on 9 Yes is a regression but S0’s result on 8 No is an existing defect. State the required result in each case and the instruction that explains the mistake. If S1 passes both, what further evidence should you keep before making a broader claim?

lesson.title: Prepare an honest candidate for evaluation

blocks.text: If your own P1 already passes the development set, do not introduce a defect just to claim an improvement. Use the supplied S example to practise repair, and report that no change was needed in your saved version for the tested cases. If your version fails, retain the evidence, locate the cause and label the next repair. A new label alone does not prove a better version.

Save a candidate with its complete instructions, required catalogue data, input rules, change history and development results. State unresolved failures and limitations. Keep this version unchanged during the final evaluation. Do not inspect reserved final cases to decide which repair to make. If you revise after seeing final results, retain those results as belonging to the old version and treat the seen cases as development evidence; they are no longer an unseen evaluation for the revision.

blocks.label: A team fixes 10 Yes, checks only that case and deletes S0’s failed trace. Explain two weaknesses in its evidence and give a better next action. Why should the candidate be fixed before reserved final cases are revealed?

workbook.title: Write the change record
workbook.prompt: Use S0’s failure on 10 Yes with catalogue B version 1. Record the expected and incorrect outputs, the faulty time comparison, the exact S1 correction and the other conditions that must remain. Explain what old evidence to preserve.
workbook.answer: Expected B1 with equality and quiet satisfied; S0 incorrectly returns no match because its time condition is strictly less than. S1 uses no more than, including equality. Preserve validation, quiet, first-match order, advancement, stopping and reset. Save S0, its failing trace and exact request/catalogue labels beside the new S1 change record and rerun.

workbook.title: Check the repair and earlier behaviour
workbook.prompt: Plan and operate the S1 repair and regression set described in the lesson, using the appropriate catalogue version for each case. Record expected and observed results separately with reasons and traces. Summarise full passes over all attempted cases, list unrun cases separately and identify any remaining failures. Do not replace observed mistakes with worked answers.
workbook.answer: Under B version 1 the listed requests yield B1, B2, no match, no match, B1, B2, no match, B1, then four clarifications for 31, blank minutes, 10.5 and Maybe. B version 2 with 12 Yes yields B3. B version 3 yields B4 for 15 No and no match for 15 Yes. There are 15 planned cases. Correct execution with correct reasons gives 15 of 15; accept honest different observations with investigation. Unrun cases are not passes and the attempted denominator must be stated.

workbook.title: Reject a repair that breaks quiet requests
workbook.prompt: T1 accepts equal times but omits the quiet check. Explain why it passes 10 Yes yet fails 9 Yes. Use S0’s earlier correct result for 9 Yes to justify the word regression. What should change in T1, and which two cases should be rerun first?
workbook.answer: At 10 Yes, first B1 fits and happens to be quiet, so the omission is hidden. At 9 Yes, T1 selects B2 on time despite its nonquiet label; required output is no match. S0 correctly gave no match on that request, so the new failure is a regression. Restore the quiet condition combined with inclusive time; rerun 10 Yes for the repair and 9 Yes for the regression, then the wider set.

workbook.title: Audit a different proposed repair
workbook.prompt: Equipment catalogue E lists E1 first with capacity 4 and E2 second with capacity 8. Valid whole group sizes are 1 to 10. Choose the first capacity at least the group size, or no match; invalid input needs clarification. Old U0 uses strictly greater capacity and stops at the first fit.
