Proposed U1 includes equality but keeps searching and returns the last fit. Independently compare U0, U1 and the requirement for groups 8 and 3. Identify the repair and regression, propose U2 and give one validation check. No booking occurs.
workbook.answer: For 8, U0 returns no match, U1 returns E2 and the requirement is E2: equality is repaired. For 3, U0 returns E1 correctly but U1 returns E2, violating first-fit order: a regression. U2 includes equality and stops immediately at the first fit, giving E2 for 8 and E1 for 3. Preserve both old traces and rerun both cases plus wider tests. Group 0 or 11, a blank or a nonwhole size needs clarification before searching.

workbook.title: Protect the meaning of final evaluation
workbook.prompt: After seeing a reserved final case fail, a team edits its candidate, reruns that same case and calls the result “a successful unseen test of the new version”. Explain what is wrong and what should be recorded instead. State what must be saved before an evaluation begins.
workbook.answer: The case informed the repair and is now seen development evidence for the new version. Preserve the original candidate and its final result, label the revision and describe the repeated case as a repair check. A fresh independent evaluation needs new reserved cases for the fixed revision. Save complete instructions, catalogue, requirements, version label, change history, development results and known limitations before evaluation.

teacher.background: Repair and regression testing concern the implementation of explicit rules, not fitting a model to examples. S0 and T1 are deliberately faulty instructional examples. Pupils whose P1 works should not invent a defect or claim an unneeded improvement. Assess the causal explanation and retained evidence, not only a favourable count. Final evaluation tests a fixed version; development success and a polished presentation cannot replace it.
materials: Saved P1 and the clearly labelled S0, S1 and T1 comparison instructions described in the lesson
Catalogue B versions 1, 2 and 3, the manual baseline and all earlier development records
Blank change records and an envelope or folder for the candidate; keep reserved final cases teacher-only
sessions: Retrieve the inclusive time requirement and S0 equality failure.
Read the repair diagram and complete W1 with a specific comparison change.
Trace S0, T1 and S1; complete W3 and distinguish old defects from new regressions.
Begin W2 partner repair checks using saved versions and prepared expectations.
Continue W2 with validation and catalogue variations; report attempted and unrun cases honestly.
Complete the guided explanation and organise the candidate evidence folder.
Collect W4 independently before support; check first-fit and equality reasoning.
Complete W5 and the exit, record unresolved issues and fix a candidate for final evaluation.
teacher.guidedAnswer: For 9 Yes, required no match; S0 met it but T1 newly returns nonquiet B2 because quiet was removed, so a regression. For 8 No, required B2; S0 already excluded equality and returned no match, so an existing defect. Keep saved versions, change records, exact inputs and catalogues, expected and observed reasons, traces and results for the remaining routine, validation and variation cases. Exit: one repaired case does not check earlier behaviour; deleting the old trace destroys evidence of the defect. Preserve the failure and rerun the wider development set with a new version. Fixing the candidate before reveal prevents tailoring that candidate to the reserved cases.
misconceptions: One repaired example proves improvement everywhere
Check the revealing case and previously successful behaviour under recorded conditions.
Any failure after editing is a regression
Show that the same behaviour was correct before the change; otherwise it may be an existing defect.
A good project must contain a repair
An unchanged correct version can be justified with honest evidence.
A seen final case becomes unseen after a new version label
Once it guides revision, it is development evidence for that revision.
teacher.assessment: W4 must identify U0 no match and U1 E2 for group 8, then U0 E1 and U1 E2 for group 3, with equality repaired but first-match stopping broken. U2 needs both inclusive capacity and immediate first-fit stopping. After support, retry with F1 capacity 5 then F2 capacity 9, same input range: group 9 exposes the equality defect and group 2 exposes the last-fit regression. Require fresh reasoning and one valid clarification test.
teacher.support: Use separate cards for time or capacity, quiet, and first-match stopping so pupils can point to the changed condition. Provide change-record headings without supplying the diagnosis. Partners may divide execution and recording, then swap; collect the independent audit before hints. Extension: explain why a higher total can still conceal a serious regression and why individual failures matter.
teacher.next: Week 36 evaluates a fixed candidate with reserved cases and asks pupils to defend their project using results, failures, a baseline and explicit limitations.

ai-1/36.title: Evaluating and explaining your project
goals: Evaluate a saved candidate and a manual baseline fairly
Defend a conclusion using results, failures and limits
Explain the rules, privacy choices and human control in your project

prerequisite.prompt: You change a candidate after seeing a final test fail. Can the same case be an unseen final test of the new version? Explain.
prerequisite.answer: No. It informed the change and is now development evidence for the revision. Keep the old candidate and its final result; a fresh evaluation of the revision needs new reserved cases.

vocabulary: Testing a saved candidate under stated conditions after development
A comparison method tested under the same conditions
Recorded observations that support or challenge a claim
A boundary on what a result or system can establish
An explanation of a decision using evidence and reasoning

blocks.text: This week you will evaluate your activity adviser and explain what its evidence supports. A project with an honestly reported failure can show strong understanding. Save your candidate instructions, version label, input rules, development records and known problems before your teacher reveals the final requests and catalogue. Keep the instructions unchanged during this evaluation.

The agreed rule remains: validate whole available minutes from 0 to 30 and Quiet required Yes or No. No allows quiet or nonquiet activities. Start at the first row and suggest the first activity whose time is no more than available time AND whose quiet label satisfies the request. Explain the choice. If all rows fail, report no match. Invalid or missing input needs clarification before searching. Clear the previous output for each run.

Your teacher will supply a fresh, labelled catalogue in the same format. Its values are test inputs, not permission to rewrite your instructions. All materials are assumed available. The manual baseline checks every row against the same requirements, then selects the first fit. Both methods advise only; neither books, publishes or chooses on a person’s behalf.

blocks.title: From saved version to supported claim
blocks.caption: Changing instructions during evaluation creates a different version. Keep evidence for the original version.

blocks.text: Use the same final requests, catalogue, requirements and full-pass rule for both methods. Record the candidate output and reason before looking at the expected answer. Record the baseline separately; do not copy the candidate result into it. Your teacher holds the answer key. A full pass needs both the required output and a valid reason, including why earlier rows fail when a later row is selected.

For each request record its ID, inputs, catalogue label, candidate label, candidate output and reason, baseline output and reason, and both results after checking. Keep a trace for any failure. Mark unrun cases explicitly. Do not silently correct an observation. If a person misreads an instruction, record that execution error separately from a defect in the written instruction.

lesson.title: Make a claim that matches the evidence

blocks.text: Here is a fictional example from a different project, not your class results. A candidate has 6 full passes from 8 attempted cases; the baseline has 8 from the same 8. Two more planned cases were not run. The candidate passed 75 percent of attempted cases; the baseline passed 100 percent. Neither has evidence for the two unrun cases. The candidate did not outperform the baseline on this measure.

rows: Six attempted cases met the full rule
Both methods pass the same cases
They tie on this measured result

blocks.text: Explain each failure and its consequence instead of hiding it inside a total. Even perfect results on a small reserved set do not establish reliability in every situation. Our paper adviser applies human-written rules; it has not learned a model from training examples. It checks compatibility, not enjoyment, popularity or real material availability.

blocks.label: In the fictional example, state the candidate and baseline results, explain how the two unrun cases should be reported, and give one useful next action. Why is “the adviser is ready for every classroom” unsupported?

lesson.title: Defend your decisions with a small evidence folder

blocks.text: Prepare a short explanation using your saved instructions, one complete trace, the final comparison, and a limitation. State the problem and whose choice the adviser supports. Explain validation, both matching conditions, first-fit order, reset and stopping. Show the exact instruction behind your trace. Describe any repair with its old evidence, or say honestly that no repair was needed.

Use only fictional requests and the two necessary input fields. Do not collect names, diagnoses or reasons a pupil prefers quiet. A quiet request is enough. A person may decline the suggestion; a teacher checks real materials and local rules before an activity. A successful output grants no permission to book or publish.

For a two-minute partner presentation, use this order: problem and rule; trace; candidate versus baseline results; failure or limitation; next action. Partners swap speaker and listener roles. Each person must explain one trace independently. The listener asks which recorded observation supports the main claim; attractive slides cannot substitute for that observation.

Archive the evaluated candidate and its original results. If you repair it after evaluation, give it a new version label and use revealed cases as development checks. Do not relabel them as unseen. Ask your teacher for fresh reserved cases only after the revision is fixed. Do not erase the first result.

Write one conclusion limited to the actual conditions tested and one specific next step. It may be better to keep the manual baseline. Grade 7 will turn carefully stated procedures into programs and examine data more closely. Carry forward the habits of validating inputs, recording evidence and keeping people in control.

blocks.label: Name one observation from your own evaluation, one limit on your conclusion and one next action. Explain why your adviser is a rule-based program design rather than a trained model, and why passing tests does not give it permission to book an activity.

workbook.title: Record the fixed candidate
workbook.prompt: Before final cases are revealed, record your version label, where its complete instructions are saved, the agreed input and matching rules, the manual baseline and any known limitation. Confirm that the instructions stay unchanged while the assigned catalogue is used as input.
workbook.answer: Require an identifiable saved version, complete instructions, valid whole minutes 0 to 30, Yes or No quiet input, inclusive time AND quiet compatibility, first-fit order, reset, stopping and clarification. The baseline checks all rows and selects the first fit under the same contract. Accept honestly stated known failures; do not award a stronger result for hiding them.

workbook.title: Keep the final evaluation record
workbook.prompt: Use a separate sheet for the teacher’s reserved cases. For every case record its ID and inputs, catalogue and candidate labels, both methods’ observed outputs and reasons, and results after checking. Preserve failure traces. Here summarise each method’s full passes over attempted cases and list unrun cases. State what the comparison supports.
workbook.answer: Use the reserved key in Preparation only after observations are saved. Full pass requires output and reason; no-match explanations must rule out all rows. Clarification must precede search. Report actual candidate and baseline counts over the same attempted cases, plus unrun cases. Never substitute the key for an observation or assume a baseline run was correct.

workbook.title: Prepare your evidence defence
workbook.prompt: Write a two-minute explanation of the problem, one trace, your actual comparison, a limitation and a next action. Explain why this is a written-rule design rather than a model trained on examples. State which personal information is unnecessary and who decides whether to act.
workbook.answer: Look for a saved trace connected to the actual instruction, accurate counts, a specific failure or limitation and a justified next step. The project applies explicit human-written rules, with no fitted model. Only minutes and quiet preference are needed; names and reasons for quiet are unnecessary. The person may decline and the teacher checks real conditions; the adviser does not book or publish.

workbook.title: Judge a different project independently
workbook.prompt: A fictional library adviser and its manual baseline face the same 6 reserved cases. The candidate has 4 full passes; the baseline has 5. One additional planned case is unrun by both. No speed data was collected. The team says “ours is faster and more reliable everywhere” and repairs it after seeing the failures. Explain what the counts support, two unsupported claims and how to label a rerun of the revealed cases.
workbook.answer: Report candidate 4 of 6 and baseline 5 of 6 full passes, with one unrun case for each. The baseline performed better on this measured set; neither result establishes reliability everywhere. Speed was not measured. A rerun after the failures informed a repair is development evidence for the revised version, not an unseen final test. Preserve the old results and label both versions.

workbook.title: Write your final conclusion
workbook.prompt: Use your own records to complete: Under these conditions, our saved version showed… The baseline showed… We still do not know… Our next action is… Include one privacy or human-control choice. If a case failed, explain its consequence without deleting the result.
workbook.answer: Accept different conclusions grounded in actual observations, including a decision to retain the baseline. Require stated conditions, honest comparison, a real uncertainty and a specific action. A quiet requirement does not require a diagnosis; an output does not authorise action. A failure remains part of the evaluated version’s record even after a repair.

teacher.background: This final week evaluates the saved paper candidate, not presentation polish or an imagined trained model. Fix instructions before revealing the new catalogue and requests. Keep the key below teacher-only until observations are recorded. If a pupil has already seen these cases, use a fresh teacher-checked set and record that substitution; do not call familiar cases unseen.
materials: Saved candidate, manual baseline, development folder and blank record sheets with the fields listed in W2. Provide the catalogue and requests without the answer key after candidates are fixed.

Reserved catalogue B version 4 keeps B1 to B4 order and names, with times 18, 14, 11, 7 minutes and quiet labels Yes, No, Yes, No. All materials are assumed available. Same input and matching rules as before.

Reserved requests and key: F1 7 No → B4; F2 11 Yes → B3; F3 14 No → B2; F4 18 Yes → B1; F5 6 No → no match; F6 7 Yes → no match; F7 0 No → no match; F8 30 Yes → B1; F9 31 No → clarify; F10 blank minutes Yes → clarify. For F1–F4, earlier rows fail time; the selected row fits with equality and satisfies quiet. F5 and F7 fail all times. F6 fits only nonquiet B4, which quiet excludes. F8 accepts first quiet B1. F9 and F10 fail validation before search.
sessions: Check the prerequisite and W1; collect or photograph each fixed instruction set before revealing any final inputs.
Reveal B version 4 and F1–F10 requests without the key. Explain W2 record fields and the unchanged full-pass criterion.
Run all ten cases with candidate and baseline. Partners swap operating and recording; preserve each output before comparison with the key. Record assistance and unrun cases.
Reveal the key, check reasons and summarise actual results in W2. Retain failure traces; do not edit the evaluated instructions.
Discuss the fictional 6-of-8 example and collect the guided explanation. Keep hypothetical results separate from class records.
Prepare W3 and run paired two-minute presentations with questions and role swaps. Sample individual traces; offer accessible spoken or written responses.
Collect W4 independently before hints. Assess evidence claims and the meaning of a rerun after revision.
Complete W5 and the exit. Archive the candidate, final results and next action; note support needs for Grade 7.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Fictional candidate 6/8 and baseline 8/8 attempted, with two unrun planned cases each; candidate 75 percent and baseline 100 percent on that set. Investigate retained failure traces before a versioned repair. Neither has evidence for all classrooms. Exit answers must use the pupil’s real record, limit the conclusion, name a next step and distinguish explicit rules from fitted models. Passing tests grants no booking authority.
misconceptions: A polished presentation proves the system works
Ask for the saved instruction, trace and actual result behind the claim.
Unrun cases count as passes
Report attempted denominators and unrun cases separately.
The baseline must lose
A tie or a better baseline can justify retaining the simpler method.
A repair erases the final failure
Preserve the evaluated version and results; revealed cases become development checks for the revision.
teacher.assessment: Assess four strands separately: faithful execution with traces; honest comparison including failures; independent explanation of rule-based mechanism and human control; justified limits and next action. Mark each secure, developing or not yet evidenced, with one cited observation. Do not infer individual mastery from group totals. W4 requires 4/6 versus 5/6, one unrun, unknown speed and a development rerun. After support, retry with candidate 3/5 and baseline 3/5, two unrun and no timing: a tie on observed passes, no universal or speed claim. Require fresh reasoning.
teacher.support: Provide a blank record grid, read instructions aloud and allow oral defence, while recording assistance. Keep independent W4 responses before feedback. Allow additional time for unrun cases with the same fixed version and record when they ran; do not manufacture completion. Extension: propose an additional test for a stated limitation and explain why it would help without claiming proof of every situation.
teacher.next: Grade 6 Foundations is complete. Grade 7 AI 2 begins programming and data. Carry forward versioned instructions, validation, tests, privacy and evidence-based conclusions; use the recorded assessment strands to plan support.

ai-1/4.title: Rules and learned patterns
goals: Execute a stated rule including its boundary
Select a rule by comparing errors on labelled examples
Explain why agreement with fitting examples does not establish performance on new cases

prerequisite.prompt: A warning uses temperature greater than 28 degrees C. What happens at exactly 28, and what must be checked before comparing a recorded number with 28?
prerequisite.answer: The warning stays off at exactly 28. Check that the reading is the intended quantity in degrees C and is relevant to the time and conditions.

vocabulary: A recorded property used as an input to a decision or model
A recorded category or target associated with an example
A boundary value used in a comparison
Choosing or adjusting a model using examples
The number of predictions that disagree with the comparison labels

lesson.title: The same rule can have different origins

blocks.text: A paper sorting task describes imaginary cards. Each card has a width in centimetres and a recorded label, narrow or wide. One person writes a rule from a design requirement: label a card wide when its width is at least 5 cm. Another person compares several candidate thresholds with labelled examples and chooses the one with fewest disagreements. Both may end up using the same threshold, but they selected it in different ways.

Executing a rule means applying it to an input. Fitting means using examples to select or adjust the rule or model. A fitted model can be very simple. We do not need a brain-like picture or a complicated computer to study the difference between selecting a rule and using it.

In this exercise the labels are supplied by the task designer. They are not a universal definition of wide, and a centimetre value alone would not determine every possible meaning of that word. State what the recorded labels mean in the task before counting disagreements.

blocks.title: How a threshold is selected and then applied
rows: Widths with supplied narrow or wide labels
Compare candidate rules by error count
Selected threshold and a new width
Prediction and a later comparison label
blocks.caption: The comparison label is available during fitting and later checking. A new prediction must be made before revealing that case's label.

blocks.text: For threshold t, our rule predicts wide when width is at least t and narrow otherwise. At least includes equality: with t=5, width 5 is wide. Changing at least to greater than changes the rule and may change the error count.

A fitting procedure also contains choices people made: the feature, candidate thresholds, label definition and way of counting errors. Calling a threshold learned does not remove human responsibility for those choices.

Apply threshold 3 to each width before checking the label. Only width 4 disagrees, so its error count is 1. Threshold 5 agrees on all four examples, so its error count is 0. Of these two candidates, this procedure selects 5. Zero disagreements here means it fits these four labels; it is not a guarantee about all future cards.

There can be ties. Threshold 6 also agrees on these four examples because 6 is included by at least. Thresholds 5 and 6 predict differently for width 5, which is absent from the fitting set. The available examples therefore do not uniquely determine how that width should be labelled. A procedure needs an explicit tie rule, and we should record the unresolved case.

Now use widths 1, 3, 5 and 7 with labels narrow, narrow, wide and wide. Compare candidates 3 and 5, using the same at least rule. Write all four predictions for each candidate before you count. This prevents a plausible-looking total from hiding a boundary mistake.

blocks.label: List the predictions and error count for each candidate. Select the lower-error candidate and state exactly what the result establishes

blocks.text: Keep this comparison separate from a final check on unseen cases. If we repeatedly choose a threshold after looking at the check answers, those cases have helped us fit the rule. They no longer provide an independent check of our finished choice.

lesson.title: A successful fit can still fail

blocks.text: Suppose a new card has width 5 and its supplied task label is narrow. The selected threshold 5 predicts wide, so it disagrees on this case. Do not erase the example to preserve a perfect score. Record the error and investigate whether the labels follow a different definition, whether measurement matters or whether width alone is insufficient.

For this week's paper task, a prediction is only a proposed category. It does not authorise a physical action. More consequential applications require additional checks and human decisions that a small fitting exercise cannot establish.

blocks.label: Explain the difference between choosing a threshold using examples and applying that threshold to a new card

workbook.title: Execute before fitting
workbook.prompt: Use wide when width is at least 5 cm. Predict the label for widths 4, 5 and 6. Then state what changes if the rule uses greater than 5 instead.
workbook.answer: At least 5 gives narrow, wide, wide. Greater than 5 gives narrow, narrow, wide. Only the equality case changes among these inputs.

workbook.title: Complete the supported comparison
workbook.prompt: Widths 1, 3, 5, 7 have labels narrow, narrow, wide, wide. For candidates 3 and 5, list all predictions using wide when width is at least the candidate. Count disagreements and select the lower-error candidate.
workbook.answer: Threshold 3: narrow, wide, wide, wide; one disagreement at 3. Threshold 5: narrow, narrow, wide, wide; zero disagreements. Select 5 among these candidates based on these examples only.

workbook.title: Make a tie visible
workbook.prompt: For the worked widths 2, 4, 6, 8 with labels narrow, narrow, wide, wide, compare thresholds 5 and 6. Give a width where they predict differently. Explain why the four fitting examples cannot decide that case.
workbook.answer: Both thresholds have zero disagreements. At width 5, threshold 5 predicts wide while threshold 6 predicts narrow. No fitting example is width 5 or otherwise distinguishes these thresholds; their equal fitting score does not establish a unique answer there.

workbook.title: Fit a new paper classifier
workbook.prompt: A fictional sorting task has lengths 2, 5, 7, 9 cm with labels short, short, long, long. Candidate rules predict long when length is at least 5 or at least 7. List predictions and errors for both, choose one, and predict a new length of 6 before any label is revealed. State one limit of your conclusion.
workbook.answer: Threshold 5 predicts short, long, long, long: one error at 5. Threshold 7 predicts short, short, long, long: zero errors. Choose 7 and predict short for 6. This fits these supplied labels among these two candidates; the new label, labels at other lengths and general performance are not established.

workbook.title: Keep the check honest
workbook.prompt: A learner sees that their final-check card was predicted incorrectly, changes the threshold to match it and reports the same card as an unseen test. Explain the problem and propose a valid next check.
workbook.answer: The revealed check label influenced the revised threshold, so it became part of development. Record the revision and use a different, unrevealed set after fixing the rule. Do not report the adapted-to case as an independent final test.

teacher.background: This is a genuine small fitting procedure: choose among candidate thresholds by empirical disagreement count. It is intentionally executable on paper. Do not equate all AI with machine learning or all handwritten rules with non-AI; the lesson isolates fitting versus execution. The fictional label convention avoids implying that size words have universal numerical definitions.
materials: Width and length cards with labels on a separate sheet
Two candidate-threshold cards for each exercise
A trace-table frame with input, prediction, supplied label and disagreement columns
sessions: Retrieve the equality boundary from the temperature rule. Compare greater than with at least.
Contrast a requirement-selected threshold with an example-selected threshold. Read the fitting and use diagram.
Work through all rows for candidates 3 and 5. Count errors only after writing predictions.
Pairs complete W1 and W2. Ask each learner to explain where the fitting decision occurs.
Show the tie between 5 and 6. Ask for an input that makes them disagree.
Complete W3 and discuss what the fitting data does not determine.
Collect W4 independently with comparison labels for the new case hidden.
Discuss W5 and the exit explanation. Save the selected rule and its known limitations.
teacher.guidedAnswer: For widths 1,3,5,7, threshold 3 predicts narrow,wide,wide,wide and has one error; threshold 5 predicts narrow,narrow,wide,wide and has zero. The choice establishes a lower fitting error among these candidates on these examples. The exit distinction is selecting a parameter using labelled examples versus keeping the parameter fixed while making a prediction on a new input.
misconceptions: A learned rule cannot be written simply
The selection procedure can fit a single threshold. Complexity is not the definition of fitting.
Zero fitting errors means the model is correct everywhere
Use thresholds 5 and 6, then input 5. Identical fitting scores leave different unseen predictions.
The label is available when predicting
Cover the new case's label until the prediction is recorded. Separate information available at fitting time from prediction time.
teacher.assessment: W4 is secure when both prediction lists and counts are correct, threshold 7 is selected, length 6 is predicted short and the learner limits the claim to available evidence. An arithmetic correction alone is insufficient if the fitting versus prediction distinction is missing. Retest with different lengths and thresholds after reteaching.
teacher.support: Use a number line with a closed dot at the threshold and arrows to the long or wide region. Permit oral explanation with a completed prediction table. Extension: ask learners to find every whole-number threshold tied for zero errors in the worked example and explain what a tie-breaking rule does.
teacher.next: Week 5 asks how an image becomes numerical input and what spatial information must be preserved before a model can use it.

ai-1/5.title: Images as numerical grids
goals: Encode and reconstruct a small image using an explicit grid convention
Explain why pixel counts alone cannot recover an arrangement
Distinguish numerical image data from a model's interpretation of that data

prerequisite.prompt: Two thresholds can agree on all fitting examples but disagree on a new input. Does zero fitting error identify one uniquely correct rule?
prerequisite.answer: No. The fitting examples may not distinguish the rules, and agreement on those examples does not settle every unseen case.

vocabulary: One position in a digital image grid with a recorded value or values
A convention for representing information with symbols or numbers
The number of positions in an image grid, often given as width by height
Where elements are located relative to one another
A meaning or category assigned to a representation using a rule, model or human judgment

lesson.title: Agree on the code before reading it

blocks.text: Imagine sending a small black-and-white sign using only numbers. We can divide the sign into a grid, record 1 for a black square and 0 for a white square, and read each row from left to right, starting at the top. The receiver needs the width, height and these conventions to reconstruct the same arrangement.

A pixel is a position with a recorded value. In our simplified binary image, one value selects black or white. Other image formats can record brightness levels or multiple colour channels. The convention 1 means black belongs to this exercise; it is not a universal rule for every digital image.

Encoding a picture does not recognise what it depicts. A program can store or display the numbers without calling the image a letter, an arrow or a person. Interpretation is another operation, just as displaying a book title was different from reading the entire book in Week 2.

lesson.title: Read a grid in a fixed order

blocks.title: A three by three binary image
blocks.key: Read rows top to bottom. Within each row read left to right. 1 is black and 0 is white.
blocks.caption: The image has width 3 and height 3, so it contains 9 pixels. Five are black. The row records preserve where those five black pixels occur.

blocks.text: The first row is 0,1,0, so only its middle pixel is black. The second row is 1,1,1, so all three are black. The third row repeats the first. This reconstructs the displayed cross-like pattern under our convention.

A flattened record would be 0,1,0,1,1,1,0,1,0. Without the grid dimensions, the same nine values could also be drawn in one row of nine. Keep the shape information with the values. Width times height counts pixels; it does not tell us their contents.

Suppose we discard the row records and retain only black pixel count=5. That count matches the cross, but it also matches rows 1,1,1 then 1,1,0 then 0,0,0. The second arrangement fills the top row and two positions below it. Both have five black pixels and nine pixels in total, yet they are different images.

rows: Five positions are black under this code
Dimensions and all three ordered rows
The full binary grid under this convention
What a viewer or model will call the picture

blocks.text: A pixel count can still be a useful feature for some tasks. For example, it can separate empty grids from grids with at least one mark. But it cannot separate every shape. To judge a feature, ask whether it retains the distinctions required by the task.

lesson.title: Reconstruct and check an unfamiliar image

blocks.text: Use width 3, height 2 and rows 1,0,1 then 0,1,0. Draw two rows of three squares and fill exactly the positions marked 1. Check by reading your drawing back into numbers. A round trip from code to drawing to code can reveal a swapped row or a missed pixel.

blocks.label: Draw the two by three image, write its black-pixel count and explain why saying only three black pixels would be insufficient

blocks.text: If an image classifier mislabels a picture, first inspect the input representation. Was the width correct? Were the rows reversed? Did the program use the intended colour convention? A later classifier cannot reliably repair every mistake in how its input was prepared.

lesson.title: More pixels do not settle every question

blocks.text: Higher resolution offers more positions for recording detail, but it does not guarantee a useful image. A larger blurry image can still hide a feature, and a cropped image can omit it entirely. A model's label also depends on what it was fitted to distinguish and the conditions represented in its examples.

Keep claims at the right stage. These nine values encode this grid is a reconstruction claim. This grid depicts a plus sign is an interpretation. This sign tells a person what to do adds context and authority. One does not automatically establish the others.

blocks.label: Can two different three by three images have the same black-pixel count? Explain with a specific arrangement change

workbook.title: Read and reconstruct
workbook.prompt: Using 1 for black and 0 for white, draw width 3, height 2 with rows 1,0,1 and 0,1,0. Read it back into numbers and count black pixels.
workbook.answer: The upper row has black, white, black; the lower row has white, black, white. Reading back gives the supplied two rows. There are three black pixels among six total positions.

workbook.title: Preserve the missing field
workbook.prompt: A message contains 1,0,0,1,1,0 but gives no dimensions. Show a one-row arrangement and a two-row arrangement using the same values. Name the extra information that would distinguish them.
workbook.answer: One row of width 6 is [1,0,0,1,1,0]. Two rows of width 3 are [1,0,0] and [1,1,0]. Specify width and height, plus reading order and colour convention. The values alone do not choose the shape.

workbook.title: Test a count feature
workbook.prompt: A classifier receives only the number of black pixels. Can it always distinguish the chapter's cross from every other three by three pattern? Construct a different pattern with the same count and explain.
workbook.answer: No. Rows [1,1,1], [1,1,0], [0,0,0] have five black pixels, as does the cross, but a different arrangement. The classifier receives identical input counts for the two, so that feature alone cannot distinguish them.

workbook.title: Design a new counterexample
workbook.prompt: Create two different images of width 4 and height 2, each with exactly three black pixels. Write both complete row encodings. Explain which fact their shared count retains and which difference it discards.
workbook.answer: One valid pair is A [1,1,1,0]/[0,0,0,0] and B [1,0,0,0]/[0,1,0,1]. Both have two rows of four values and three ones. Count retains the number of black positions but discards their locations. Other valid pairs are accepted if dimensions, counts and arrangements meet the constraints.

workbook.title: Locate an input problem
workbook.prompt: A program receives the correct grid but displays black wherever the code says 0 and white wherever it says 1. A student proposes collecting more classifier examples. Identify the earlier mismatch and the first check to perform.
workbook.answer: The display uses the opposite colour convention from the sender. Check and align the encoding/decoding convention, then reconstruct a known grid. More classifier examples would not be the first repair for this identified input/display mismatch.

teacher.background: The image is binary for transparency, not a claim that ordinary colour images contain only zeros and ones as pixel values. Distinguish bit-level storage from the image value convention. Grid reconstruction is assessed separately from interpretation. A learner may name the worked pattern differently while still reconstructing it correctly.
materials: Squared paper and a dark pencil for each learner
The worked grid with its explicit reading convention
Two empty two-row four-column grids for independent assessment
sessions: Recall the tied-threshold example. Ask why indistinguishable evidence can leave different answers possible.
Agree on colour and reading conventions. Reconstruct the worked grid row by row.
Flatten the values and show why dimensions matter. Compare the two five-black-pixel patterns.
Pairs complete W1 and W2, exchanging encodings and reading them back.
Show two equal-count grids and ask which input a count-only classifier would receive.
Complete W3 and diagnose a reversed convention. Require a specific counterexample.
Collect W4 independently. Check the dimensions and counts before evaluating the explanation.
Discuss W5 and the exit question. Distinguish stored values from assigned meaning.
teacher.guidedAnswer: The two rows are black-white-black and white-black-white, giving three black pixels. Other arrangements share that count, so it cannot recover positions. For the exit, move one black pixel to a previously white position while preserving the total; the image changes but the count does not.
misconceptions: The number one always means black
Our convention states that meaning. Other encodings use different scales or channels; read their specification.
A pixel count is the picture
Have students reconstruct two different arrangements with the same count.
Storing pixels recognises the object
A grid decoder only reconstructs the representation. A separate interpretation step assigns a category.
teacher.assessment: W4 is secure when both images are two by four, each has three ones, the patterns differ and the explanation identifies lost location information. If a learner draws valid pictures but mismatches their code, reteach the round-trip check, then assess with fresh patterns.
teacher.support: Provide large tactile or printed cells, with numbers as well as shading so colour is unnecessary. Let learners dictate row values. Extension: construct two grids with equal counts in every row but different arrangements, showing that row totals still lose information.
teacher.next: Week 6 transfers the idea of ordered numerical representations to sound, where the positions refer to times rather than image locations.

ai-1/6.title: Sound as sampled information
goals: Interpret an ordered sequence of sound-signal samples with a stated time interval
Explain why summaries or sparse samples can omit changes
Separate an audio recording, a transcript and an interpretation of meaning

prerequisite.prompt: Two image grids have the same number of black pixels. Why can their pictures differ?
prerequisite.answer: The total does not preserve positions. Different arrangements can contain the same number of black pixels.

vocabulary: A changing physical or recorded quantity that can carry information
A recorded value of a signal at a particular time in this lesson
The time between successive recorded samples
A representation of how a signal value changes over time
A text representation of spoken words, which may contain errors or omit sound details

blocks.text: Sound involves changing pressure in a medium such as air. A microphone responds to that variation and produces a changing signal. A digital recording stores measurements of the signal at successive times. The values are ordered: swapping their times changes the represented pattern.

We will use tiny invented sequences to study this idea on paper. Their values are arbitrary signal units, not decibels or a test of safe listening levels. Real audio uses many more samples, so our five-point examples should not be played as if they were a realistic recording of speech.

A recording must include enough information to interpret the values, including their time spacing and encoding. The sequence 0,2,0,2,0 does not by itself say how quickly the changes happened. This is similar to needing image dimensions as well as pixel values.

blocks.title: Three stages in a speech system
rows: Measure the changing signal at successive times
A transcript that may contain errors
A separate rule or model processes the text
blocks.caption: Recording, transcribing and interpreting are separate operations. A later stage can correctly process an incorrectly transcribed number.

blocks.text: There are five samples with four gaps between the first and last. Each gap is 1 millisecond, so the elapsed time from first to last is 4 milliseconds. If the same five values were spaced 2 milliseconds apart, they would span 8 milliseconds. Equal value lists with different timing do not describe the same time pattern.

The largest value in 0,2,0,2,0 is 2. The largest value in 0,0,2,0,0 is also 2. The first sequence reaches 2 twice at different times, while the second does so once. Keeping only the maximum loses that distinction, just as counting black pixels lost their arrangement.

Sparse measurements can also miss changes. If we inspect the first sequence only at times 0, 2 and 4 milliseconds, all retained values are 0. The two intervening values of 2 disappear from the record. It would be incorrect to conclude from these retained samples alone that the signal stayed at zero between them.

More frequent sampling can preserve faster changes under suitable recording conditions, but sampling frequency alone does not make every recording clear. Microphone placement, background sound, clipping and the recording format can also matter. We are studying one source of missing information, not a complete audio engineering specification.

A five-sample record has values 0,3,0,1,0 at times 0,2,4,6,8 milliseconds. Read the timing before answering. The first-to-last duration is the final time minus the initial time, not the sample count multiplied by the gap.

blocks.label: State the interval and first-to-last duration. If only times 0,4,8 are kept, list the retained values and identify a change the shorter record misses

blocks.text: To test a claim about the spaces between samples, construct another possible sequence that agrees at retained times but differs between them. If both match the stored record, that record alone cannot decide which intervening pattern occurred.

A transcript might record the words Fine, thank you while omitting a pause, a laugh or overlapping speech. It might also record the wrong words. Text can be useful for searching spoken content, but it is not the same representation as the audio. Do not infer a speaker's emotions with certainty from a short transcript.

In a voice calculator, audio saying sixteen can be transcribed as sixty. A calculator can then correctly divide sixty by four and return fifteen. Inspecting the intermediate transcript identifies the first mismatch. Confirming the interpreted numbers before acting can prevent this particular error from travelling into a later stage.

blocks.label: Explain one detail a transcript can preserve and one sound detail it may omit. Explain why a correct calculation does not prove the transcript was correct

workbook.title: Read samples and gaps
workbook.prompt: Five samples have values 0,3,0,1,0 at times 0,2,4,6,8 milliseconds. State the sample count, interval and elapsed time from first to last. Explain why there are four gaps.
workbook.answer: Five samples, a 2 ms interval, and 8 ms from first to last. Consecutive pairs make gaps 0-2, 2-4, 4-6 and 6-8: four gaps between five samples.

workbook.title: Inspect what was discarded
workbook.prompt: Retain only times 0,4,8 from W1. Write the retained values. Give one claim about the original signal that these retained values do not justify.
workbook.answer: The retained values are 0,0,0. They do not justify saying the signal was always zero or had no changes between those times; the original had values 3 and 1 at omitted times.

workbook.title: Compare equal summaries
workbook.prompt: Sequences A=0,2,0,2,0 and B=0,0,2,0,0 use the same time interval. State their maximum values and one difference the maximum discards. Name information that would preserve that difference.
workbook.answer: Both maxima are 2. A reaches 2 at two sample positions while B does so at one; their timing patterns differ. The full ordered samples with timing preserve the distinction. A maximum alone does not.

workbook.title: Construct a new hidden change
workbook.prompt: A record keeps values 0 at times 0,3,6 milliseconds. Construct two seven-sample sequences for every whole-millisecond time from 0 through 6 that agree with those retained values but differ at omitted times. Explain why the retained record cannot prove that nothing changed between measurements.
workbook.answer: One pair is [0,0,0,0,0,0,0] and [0,2,1,0,3,1,0]. Both have zero at indices/times 0,3,6, but the second changes at omitted times. The retained record is compatible with both, so it cannot establish an unchanged intervening signal. Any valid seven-value pair with those constraints is acceptable.

workbook.title: Check a speech pipeline
workbook.prompt: A recording says Set the timer for fourteen minutes. A transcript says forty minutes and the timer is set to 40. Name the first mismatch, propose a confirmation step and explain why the transcript cannot be treated as a complete copy of the recording.
workbook.answer: The first stated mismatch is fourteen becoming forty in transcription. Show or read back the interpreted duration and require correction/confirmation before starting the timer. A transcript may misstate words and omit tone, pauses and background sounds; correct handling of 40 does not validate the earlier transcription.

teacher.background: Keep the distinction between physical pressure variation, microphone signal and stored numerical samples. The examples use arbitrary nonnegative signal values to avoid introducing signed waveforms before they are needed; they do not model real speech faithfully. The lesson establishes ordering, time metadata and information loss. It does not teach a sampling theorem or make hearing-health claims.
materials: A time strip marked 0 through 8 milliseconds and paper sample-value cards
A cover sheet to hide omitted time positions
Printed fictional speech requests; recording students or opening accounts is unnecessary
sessions: Retrieve equal pixel counts with different arrangements. Replace position in space with position in time.
Trace the recording/transcript/processing diagram. Explain the invented units and times.
Count gaps physically between five sample cards. Compare the same values at two time intervals.
Complete W1 and W2, covering omitted positions and naming lost changes.
Compare the equal-maximum sequences. Require a specific difference, not only less information.
Complete W3 and practise constructing two records that agree at retained times.
Collect W4 independently, checking all seven positions and the three retained constraints.
Discuss W5 and the exit question. Close the unit by connecting evidence, representation, measurement, fitting, pixels and samples.
teacher.guidedAnswer: The interval is 2 ms and first-to-last duration 8 ms. Keeping 0,4,8 ms retains 0,0,0 and misses the 3 and 1 at 2 and 6 ms. A transcript can preserve estimated words but may omit pauses or background sounds. Correct arithmetic on a transcribed number does not establish that the number matches the recording.
misconceptions: Five samples make five gaps
Place five cards in a row and point to each space between them. The span ends at the last sample.
Equal recorded zeros prove the signal stayed zero
Reveal hidden sample cards between retained zeros. Construct both changing and unchanging originals.
A transcript is the recording in another file type
Compare the information each representation retains. Text estimates words and need not preserve sound details or exact wording.
teacher.assessment: W4 is secure when each proposed sequence has seven values, both satisfy the zero constraints at 0,3,6, at least one omitted position differs and the explanation identifies ambiguity between measurements. If positions are confused, reteach with labelled time boxes, then assess a fresh retained-time pattern.
teacher.support: Use large labelled boxes and tactile counters. Read values aloud while pointing to their time labels. No hearing-based task is required. Extension: ask whether doubling the interval changes the number of samples, the first-to-last duration or the stored values when the same list is replayed under the new timing convention.
teacher.next: Week 7 builds on this unit by defining categories operationally so different people can label the same evidence consistently.

ai-1/7.title: Categories and operational labels
goals: Apply a category definition using explicit evidence and boundary rules
Distinguish a known failure from information that is missing or unreadable
Use disagreement to improve a labelling guide without mistaking agreement for truth

prerequisite.prompt: A transcript leaves out an unclear word. Why should a later system not simply treat that missing word as a known value?
prerequisite.answer: The missing word is information the representation does not establish. Filling it without evidence adds an assumption; a later stage should preserve the uncertainty or request a check.

vocabulary: A group defined by stated membership criteria
A definition precise enough to tell someone what to observe or do when assigning a category
The category recorded for an example under a particular guide
A person who assigns labels to examples
A case where annotators assign different labels to the same example

lesson.title: A label needs a shared definition

blocks.text: Two students are sorting fictional event cards for a classroom calendar. Their first instruction is Put the good cards together. Mina calls a colourful card good. Theo calls a plain card good because its room is easy to read. They disagree even though both followed a reasonable interpretation of the word good.

A category is useful for a task when people can tell what evidence makes an example belong to it. An operational definition states the observations or checks to perform. For this paper exercise, we will check two printed fields: an event day and a room code. The task is to check the record against a classroom policy, not to judge the quality of the event or the person who wrote it.

Labels depend on the definition in use. A model fitted to labels can learn the distinctions those labels encode, including mistakes and inconsistencies. Before asking a model to copy a label, ask whether people have a clear, useful guide for assigning it.

lesson.title: Use a guide with an explicit order

blocks.text: Our fictional calendar accepts a whole-number day from 1 through 30, including both endpoints, and exactly one room code, A or B. The month is already fixed for this exercise. A blank or unreadable field counts as unknown. The categories are revise, review and ready. Use the checks in the order shown.

blocks.title: Three ordered checks for a calendar card
rows: Any known field fails its criterion
Revise even if another field is unknown
No known failure but a field is blank or unreadable
Day is 1 through 30 and room is A or B
blocks.caption: Stop at the first matching row. The order resolves a card with both a known failure and an unknown field. Ready describes the printed record under this policy; it does not confirm that the event exists or has permission to run.

blocks.text: Known failure and unknown are different. Day 31 is known and outside the accepted range, so the card needs revision. An unreadable day might be valid or invalid; without another known failure, it needs review. Never silently turn a blank into zero just to make a comparison possible.

rows: Revise because a known value fails
No known failure but the room is unknown
Review until the room is checked
The day already fails although the room is unknown
Revise because the first check has priority

blocks.text: For the last card, first read only what is known: day 31. Compare it with the allowed range and record a failure. The guide therefore selects revise before the missing-room check. Checking the room later could reveal another problem, but it cannot make day 31 satisfy this policy.

A clear explanation cites the particular criterion. Saying It looks wrong is not enough. Write Day 31 exceeds the accepted maximum of 30 instead. That explanation lets another person reproduce the check and challenge it if the recorded value or policy is different.

Mina labels day 30, room B as ready; Theo labels it revise because he thought the range stopped before 30. The disagreement points to a boundary interpretation. The guide says including both endpoints, so 30 passes. The appropriate repair is to clarify and practise the inclusive boundary, not to change the label merely because one student is more confident.

blocks.label: Label day 0 with room A and day 18 with a blank room. Cite the exact rule for each and explain why the two cards need different next steps

blocks.text: Ask annotators to label examples independently before comparing. If they copy one another, agreement no longer tells us whether the guide can be applied independently. Keep the original labels and reasons when discussing differences, then record any corrected labels separately.

If two annotators agree on four of six cards, we know that four assigned labels matched. We do not yet know whether those labels followed the guide. Both annotators might have made the same mistake. Check their reasoning against the criteria and, where necessary, the source record.

Even perfect agreement under our calendar policy would not prove that the room is really booked. It would only show agreement about whether the printed fields pass the specified checks. The policy itself may need changes for a real calendar. Record the policy version so examples labelled under different instructions are not mixed without review.

blocks.label: Two people label every card ready. Explain why their agreement alone does not establish correct labels or confirm the events

workbook.title: Apply the calendar guide
workbook.prompt: The calendar policy accepts whole-number days 1 through 30 inclusive and a room code A or B. Check known failures first, then unknown fields, then readiness. Label these cards and give evidence: day 30 room B; day 31 room A; day 14 room unreadable; day 31 room unreadable.
workbook.answer: In order: ready because both known fields pass; revise because 31 exceeds 30; review because the known day passes but the room is unknown; revise because the known day failure has priority over the unknown room. Equality at 30 is accepted.

workbook.title: Replace a vague instruction
workbook.prompt: A helper says Label a card ready if it looks nice. Explain why this can lead to inconsistent labels. Replace it with an instruction that another person can apply using the calendar policy, including what to do about a blank field.
workbook.answer: Looks nice has no agreed observable criterion and can invite different preferences. A usable replacement checks for a known day outside whole numbers 1 to 30 or a known room other than A/B and labels revise; otherwise any blank or unreadable required field gives review; otherwise label ready. Accept equivalent wording that preserves all criteria and priority.

workbook.title: Count and investigate disagreement
workbook.prompt: For the same four cards, Mina records ready, revise, review, ready. Theo records ready, review, review, revise. How many positions agree? Identify the disagreements. Can you decide which annotator is correct from these label lists alone? Explain what else you need.
workbook.answer: Positions 1 and 3 agree, so there are two agreements out of four. Positions 2 and 4 disagree. The lists alone do not show which labels are correct; inspect the corresponding card fields and the guide version, then compare each explanation with the criteria. Agreement at positions 1 and 3 does not itself prove correctness.

workbook.title: Transfer the method to a new record
workbook.prompt: A fictional equipment-request form accepts a whole-number borrowing duration of 1 through 7 days inclusive and one item code X or Y. Label revise if any known field fails; otherwise label review if a field is blank or unreadable; otherwise label ready. Classify these forms and justify each: 7 days X; 8 days Y; unreadable duration X; 8 days blank code. Explain whether ready alone grants permission to borrow.
workbook.answer: 7 days X is ready: both pass, including the endpoint. 8 days Y is revise: duration exceeds 7. Unreadable duration X is review: no known failure but duration is unknown. 8 days blank code is revise: the known duration failure has priority. Ready only means the printed fields satisfy this policy; borrowing still requires the actual availability and authorisation process.

workbook.title: Keep a policy change visible
workbook.prompt: Version 1 accepts calendar days 1 through 30. Version 2 accepts days 1 through 31. A card says day 31 room A. State its label under each version. Explain why mixing the two labels without recording the version could create a misleading training dataset.
workbook.answer: Under Version 1 the card is revise; under Version 2 it is ready. Both can be correct relative to their different policies. If the version is omitted, identical printed fields appear to have conflicting targets without explanation. Record which policy produced each label and review or relabel consistently for the intended task; do not erase the history.

teacher.background: This lesson establishes labels as task-dependent records produced under a guide. Use fictional event and equipment forms rather than categories about classmates. The three categories deliberately separate known failures from unknown information, with known failure taking priority. A ready label checks a representation; it does not establish truth, quality, safety or permission. Agreement is useful evidence about consistency, but shared mistakes can produce high agreement.
materials: Paper calendar cards with the four worked field combinations and the printed policy
A second set of cards labelled independently by partners before discussion
The equipment-request cases on a separate sheet for independent assessment; no accounts or personal data are required
sessions: Retrieve the missing-word example from Week 6. Ask what evidence a blank supplies and what it does not.
Give the vague good-card instruction and collect two different interpretations. Replace it with observable field criteria. Read the ordered checks aloud.
Trace all four worked cards. Emphasise the inclusive boundary and the priority of a known failure over an unknown field.
Pairs complete W1 and W2. Ask each learner to cite a criterion rather than a personal impression.
Label two fresh calendar cards independently before comparing. Keep original labels visible during discussion.
Complete W3. Distinguish counting agreement from checking correctness against source fields and policy.
Collect W4 independently. Require four labels with reasons and a statement about the limit of ready.
Use W5 to demonstrate a policy-version conflict. Discuss the exit question and preview choosing useful input features.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Day 0 room A is revise because 0 falls below the accepted minimum of 1; the known day needs correction. Day 18 with a blank room is review because the known day passes and the room is unknown; the missing evidence must be checked. Two people labelling everything ready establishes agreement only. They may share a mistake, ignore the criteria or work from inaccurate records. Correct field checks also do not confirm the event or its permission.
misconceptions: A blank is the same as a failing value
Contrast unreadable day with day 0. One is unknown; the other is known to violate the stated range.
Review must win whenever any field is missing
Trace the guide in order for day 31 with a blank room. The known failure already selects revise under this policy.
Agreement proves the labels are true
Give two annotators the same mistaken exclusive-boundary interpretation. Their agreement can coexist with incorrect labels.
A category describes the whole person or event
Return to the task scope. Ready checks two printed fields under one policy, not the worth of a person or the reality of an event.
teacher.assessment: W4 is secure when all four labels follow the new range and codes, the reasons cite the relevant evidence, the mixed failure/unknown case respects priority, and ready is not treated as authorisation. If only the labels are correct, ask for the reasoning before recording mastery. After support, use new forms with a different maximum and codes for an uncoached retry.
teacher.support: Provide a three-step checklist and highlight known versus unreadable fields using words as well as colour. Let learners explain orally while pointing to the criterion. Extension: ask how a different priority policy would label mixed cases, and why that change must be documented rather than silently merged into the old labels.
teacher.next: Week 8 examines features: which recorded properties retain the distinctions a task needs, and which attractive-looking inputs add little useful information.

ai-1/8.title: Features and useful distinctions
goals: Choose recorded properties that preserve distinctions needed for a stated task
Show why identical feature records can hide examples with different target labels
Reject an answer copied into the inputs and test a proposed feature with a new case

prerequisite.prompt: Two annotators agree that a calendar card is ready. What must you still check before treating that label as correct?
prerequisite.answer: Check the card fields against the same explicit policy and version. Agreement alone can preserve a shared mistake; it does not prove that an event exists or has permission.

vocabulary: A recorded property supplied as an input to a system
The answer a supervised learning task asks a model to predict
The selected input values for one example, in a defined order
An input property that helps make distinctions needed for the stated task
Information used during development that would not legitimately be available when making the intended prediction

lesson.title: Begin with the task before choosing inputs

blocks.text: Imagine a paper sorting task for a model delivery station. Each rectangular card has a length, width, colour and card number. The station labels a card fits if its length is at most 12 centimetres and its width is at most 8 centimetres. Both limits include equality. Cards stay flat in the marked orientation; turning, bending and thickness are outside this paper task. All measurements in the first examples are known positive whole numbers.

A feature is a recorded input property, such as width in centimetres. The target label is the answer we want to produce: fits or too large under this guide. Decide what the answer means before choosing the inputs. A card number can help us find a record, but knowing its number does not tell us its dimensions.

This guide already gives us a direct rule, so we do not need to train a model to solve it. We use the task to investigate the information that either a rule or a learned model would need. Later, when relationships are learned from examples, the same question remains: did we supply the distinctions the task requires?

Card A is 10 centimetres long and 7 centimetres wide. Card B is 10 centimetres long and 9 centimetres wide. A fits; B is too large because its width exceeds 8. Compare two ways of recording these cards.

blocks.title: The same cards under two feature choices
rows: A is 10 by 7 cm and fits
B is 10 by 9 cm and is too large
A is 10 by 7 cm and fits
B is 10 by 9 cm and is too large
blocks.caption: Length alone makes A and B look identical to the system. Retaining width preserves the difference needed by this task. The letters identify the examples here; they are not additional inputs.

blocks.text: A system receiving only the length cannot use the hidden width to tell these two cards apart. The same input, 10, is paired with two different correct answers. It may guess, return an uncertainty, or use a usual answer, but length alone cannot guarantee the right label for both. A more complicated model cannot reconstruct this missing distinction with certainty from that input alone.

A feature record needs a consistent order and units. Here we write length in centimetres first, then width in centimetres. The record 10, 7 means something different if someone silently switches the order or records millimetres. Write the definitions alongside the data.

lesson.title: Use contrasting cases to examine a feature

rows: Same length and colour but width changes the label
Same width and colour as the first card but length changes the label
Changing only colour does not change this guide

blocks.text: The first two cards show why width matters. The first and third show why length matters. The first and fourth show that colour has no part in this particular rule. That is a statement about our task, not a claim that colour is useless for every task. For sorting red and blue cards, colour would be essential.

Suppose every fitting card in a small practice set is blue and every oversized card is red. Colour would appear to predict the labels perfectly in that set. A red 10 by 7 card and a blue 13 by 7 card expose the shortcut. Check a proposed feature on deliberately different cases before trusting the practice score.

lesson.title: Separate available evidence from a copied answer

blocks.text: After measuring a card, a teacher adds a sticker saying fits or too large. A learner proposes using sticker text as an input to predict the label before that inspection. The sticker seems excellent in the completed records because it contains the answer. But it does not exist at the time of the intended prediction. This is leakage: development has used information the real task cannot provide.

Draw a line at the moment the system must answer. On the before side, put the permitted measurements available then. On the after side, put the final label sticker. Keep labels available for teaching and checking predictions, but do not feed the sticker back in as an input for this task.

blocks.label: A card is 12 cm long and its width is unreadable. Someone proposes using the label sticker that will be added after inspection. Which information is usable before inspection? Explain why it does not establish the label

blocks.text: Before adopting a feature set, state the task, name the inputs with units, and ask whether two different answers can share the same input record. Construct such a pair if you can. Then check that each input is available at the time the answer is needed. These checks can reveal a broken representation before any model is trained.

For our known measurements and fixed orientation, length and width are sufficient to apply the paper rule exactly. That does not establish whether a real parcel will fit through a real opening: thickness, shape and measurement error were excluded. If the task changes, review the features again. More columns are not automatically better; each one needs a reason to be collected and used.

blocks.label: Someone claims that a model using only card colour is reliable because it matches every practice label. Give a new card that challenges this claim and explain what should be checked instead

workbook.title: Separate inputs from the target
workbook.prompt: For the fixed-orientation card task, fits requires length at most 12 cm and width at most 8 cm, including equality. Choose the measurements needed as inputs from length, width, colour, card number and the final inspection sticker. State the target label and write the feature record for a 12 cm by 8 cm red card using a defined order.
workbook.answer: Use length and width measured before the decision. State the order as length in cm, then width in cm; the record is 12, 8. The target is fits or too large under the guide, and this card is fits because both equalities are included. Colour and card number are not needed for this rule; the final inspection sticker copies the answer and is unavailable before inspection.

workbook.title: Prove that one measurement is insufficient
workbook.prompt: Invent two cards with the same width but different correct labels under the card guide. Give both lengths and widths and justify the labels. Explain why a system receiving only width cannot always label both correctly.
workbook.answer: One valid pair is length 11 width 6, which fits, and length 13 width 6, which is too large. Both give the width-only input 6 but require different labels. Without length or other permitted distinguishing information, the system cannot guarantee correct labels for both. Accept any valid pair with positive measurements, equal widths at most 8, and lengths on opposite sides of 12.

workbook.title: Challenge an apparent colour shortcut
workbook.prompt: A practice set contains three blue cards that fit and three red cards that are too large. A helper uses blue means fits and red means too large. Create a new card that this helper mislabels. Explain why the perfect practice score did not establish that colour was a reliable feature for this task.
workbook.answer: A red 10 by 7 cm card fits but the helper says too large; alternatively a blue 13 by 7 cm card is too large but the helper says fits. The practice set paired colour with size and did not test cases that separate them. The stated guide depends on measurements, so compare predictions with that guide on cases where colour and size no longer follow the shortcut.

workbook.title: Design a record for a new task
workbook.prompt: A fictional display tray accepts a tile if its height is at most 9 cm and its thickness is at most 2 cm, including equality. Other dimensions are fixed. Before checking, you can record height, thickness and pattern name. A pass sticker is added afterward. Choose inputs with units. Construct two tiles with the same height but different labels. Then label a 9 cm high, 2 cm thick striped tile and explain why the sticker is unsuitable as an input before checking.
workbook.answer: Record height in cm and thickness in cm. A valid pair is height 8 thickness 1, which passes, and height 8 thickness 3, which fails: equal height hides the required thickness distinction. The 9 cm high, 2 cm thick tile passes both inclusive boundaries. Pattern name does not affect the stated rule. The pass sticker is created after checking and copies the target; using it to predict before checking is leakage.

workbook.title: Notice when the task changes
workbook.prompt: The delivery station now sorts cards into red and blue bins instead of checking dimensions. Which previously unneeded feature becomes useful? Explain why length and width alone may now be insufficient. Give two cards that support your explanation.
workbook.answer: Colour becomes useful because the new target is red or blue. A red 10 by 7 card and a blue 10 by 7 card have identical length-width records but require different bins. Feature relevance depends on the task; reusing the previous feature set without reviewing the target can discard the needed distinction.

teacher.background: Students investigate representation before fitting a model. Keep the paper rule explicit: positive known measurements, fixed orientation, no thickness in the card task, and both boundaries inclusive. Length and width suffice for that limited rule. A collision between feature records with different correct labels demonstrates lost information; it does not prove that every task needs these same inputs. Explain leakage through timing and the copied sticker, without requiring model training or statistics.
materials: Four cards matching the worked table, with dimensions, colour and identifying letters written as text
Two paper columns headed Before the decision and After inspection, plus removable label stickers
Blank records headed Length in cm and Width in cm, and the independent display-tray task from W4
sessions: Retrieve Week 7: agreement is not proof of a correct label. State the new target and check both inclusive boundaries.
Show cards A and B. Cover their widths and identifying letters. Ask what identical length-only inputs allow the system to distinguish, then reveal width.
Trace the four-row comparison table. Have students cite the pair showing each measurement matters and the pair showing colour does not enter this rule.
Complete W1 and W2 with partners. Require a constructed pair and reasons; do not accept only a list of feature names.
Retrieve the same-input problem using length 11 width 5 and length 11 width 10. Both length-only records are 11; the first fits and the second is too large.
Use W3 to break the colour shortcut. Place the sticker after the decision line and discuss why its apparent predictive success is misleading.
Collect W4 independently. Look for height and thickness, a valid equal-height pair, boundary reasoning and the timing explanation.
Use W5 and the exit response to revisit task-dependent relevance. Preview algorithms that update a recorded state one step at a time.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Length 12 cm is usable before inspection and passes its criterion. The unreadable width remains unknown, so it might be at most 8 or above 8; the available measurements do not establish fits or too large. The final sticker does not exist before inspection, so it cannot supply an input at the time the answer is needed. Using it would leak the later answer. The exit answer may use red 10 by 7 cm, which fits, or blue 13 by 7 cm, which is too large. Check the dimensions and use new cases that break the practice colour pattern.
misconceptions: A stronger model can always recover an omitted measurement
Cover width and all identifiers for two same-length cards with different labels. Ask which supplied value tells them apart. Guessing or using typical values cannot guarantee correctness for both.
A feature that matches practice labels must be useful
Use a red fitting card or a blue oversized card. Ask whether the feature preserves the stated distinction when the practice pattern changes.
The final label is the best input feature
Place the sticker after inspection on the timeline. It is a target for checking or teaching, not an available input for a prediction before inspection.
Useful features stay useful for every task
Change the target to red or blue bins. Identical dimensions can now require different answers, so colour matters.
teacher.assessment: W4 shows secure independent understanding when the learner selects height and thickness with units, supplies an equal-height pair on opposite sides of the thickness limit, labels the boundary tile correctly, and explains the sticker timing. Naming inputs without a counterexample is partial evidence. After support, retry with a new tray limit of height 7 cm and thickness 3 cm; ask for a fresh equal-height pair before confirming mastery.
teacher.support: Let students physically cover unselected columns and compare two records side by side. Provide the sentence frame Same input ___ but labels ___ and ___ because ___. Use written colour names so no task depends on colour vision. Extension: ask learners to prove the width-only input fails using a second valid pair, or explain how permitting card rotation would change the decision procedure even when the recorded dimensions stay the same.
teacher.next: Week 9 introduces algorithms and changing state. Students will trace ordered instructions and record how values change, keeping the initial conditions and the sequence visible.

ai-1/9.title: Algorithms and changing state
goals: Trace an ordered algorithm using the current value after every instruction
Explain how changing the initial state or instruction order can change the result
Locate the first incorrect update and distinguish copying a value from linking two variables

prerequisite.prompt: Two cards have the same recorded length but different widths and labels. Why can the length-only record fail to distinguish them?
prerequisite.answer: The selected record hides width, which this task needs. Identical length-only inputs can require different labels. We must retain the relevant information instead of expecting a later process to recover it with certainty.

vocabulary: A precise procedure for carrying out a task
A named place for a value that can be updated
The current values being tracked at a particular point in a process
The values before the first instruction is carried out
A record of the state as instructions are carried out in order

lesson.title: Instructions act on the current state

blocks.text: A classroom score display starts with the number 4. Its instructions are: add 3 to score; double score; subtract 2 from score; report score and stop. What number should it report? Before doing the arithmetic, name the value being tracked and write its starting value. Here the variable is score and the initial state is score 4.

An algorithm gives precise instructions for a task. In this chapter each instruction is carried out once, in the written order. An update replaces the current value. After adding 3, score is 7. The next instruction therefore doubles 7, not the original 4. Keeping only the starting value in mind is a common source of errors.

A variable name stays the same while its value may change. Think of score as the label on an erasable number box. Updating the box does not keep all earlier numbers inside it. A separate trace preserves those earlier states so we can explain how the result was reached. This score procedure follows fixed arithmetic instructions; it does not learn from examples.

lesson.title: Record every transition in a trace
