ai-2/5.title: Branching and boundary tests
goals: Trace the selected branch in an if elif else chain
Use indentation to identify which statements belong to a branch
Test values at and around a decision boundary

prerequisite.prompt: Does minutes <= 12 accept exactly 12? How does < differ?
prerequisite.answer: <= accepts equality; < excludes it. At 12 the two conditions produce different Boolean values.

vocabulary: A possible path through a program
An expression used to decide which path to take
Leading spaces that identify a Python code block
A value where a classification may change
A previous test rerun after an edit to detect a new failure

lesson.title: Choose one result for one input

blocks.text: A fictional activity sorter labels a supplied integer duration. Negative values are Invalid; values from zero through 12 are Short; larger values are Long. The labels describe duration only. Write this requirement before the program so that a test has an expected answer independent of the code.

An if statement selects a block when its condition is true. An elif is considered only if earlier conditions in the same chain were false. An else handles the remaining cases. Colons end the condition lines. Use four spaces for the indented statements and keep related branches aligned.

blocks.title: One chain chooses one label
blocks.caption: Later branches in this chain are skipped after a condition succeeds.

blocks.title: Python 3 code

blocks.text: The output is Short. For 12, the first condition is false and the second is true. The else block is skipped. print(label) is not indented, so it runs after the selected branch. Each path assigns label before this line reads it. Change only minutes and save before each fresh run.

These tests exercise every branch and the equality case. A change from <= 12 to < 12 is exposed by 12; testing 11 alone misses it. Branch coverage means every branch was exercised, but it does not prove every condition is correct.

blocks.label: Suppose the program uses < 12 instead of <= 12. What is printed for 12, why does that violate the written rule, and which earlier test should still pass after repair?

lesson.title: Separate a chain from two independent checks

blocks.title: Python 3 code

blocks.text: This faulty version prints Short. The second if starts a separate decision and overwrites Invalid. Its else belongs to that second if. Restoring elif makes the second test depend on the first test failing. Moving print inside one branch can also hide output on other paths; indentation affects behavior, not just appearance.

The script rejects negative integers, but it does not validate arbitrary types or check a measured duration. A supplied text value can raise an error during comparison. Keep the stated integer input contract and report the limitation honestly.

lesson.title: Keep a trace with the result

blocks.text: For each run, record input, expected label, conditions actually checked and observed label. Mark skipped conditions as skipped rather than pretending the program evaluated them. After a repair, rerun earlier cases as well as the failing one. Week 6 will repeat a block and track changes across iterations.

blocks.label: A learner tests -1, 2 and 20 and concludes the sorter is completely correct because all three branches ran. Explain what important case is missing and why branch coverage alone is insufficient.

workbook.title: Explain the chain
workbook.prompt: Describe the purpose of if, elif and else in the worked duration sorter. Explain why print(label) is outside the indented branches.
workbook.answer: if tests negative first; elif checks <= 12 only after that fails; else handles the rest. Unindented print runs after any selected branch, whose assignment gives label a value.

workbook.title: Trace the tested path
workbook.prompt: For -1, 12 and 13, record checked conditions, skipped conditions and the final label. Run each as a fresh script after predicting.
workbook.answer: -1: first True, second skipped, Invalid. 12: first False, second True, Short. 13: both False, else selected, Long. Retain observed results separately.

workbook.title: Repair the overwritten result
workbook.prompt: Trace the two-independent-if example for -1. Identify which assignment overwrites the earlier label and make the smallest repair.
workbook.answer: The first assignment sets Invalid; the second if also succeeds and changes label to Short. Replace the second if with elif. The repaired output is Invalid.

workbook.title: Build a new sorter independently
workbook.prompt: Use an integer tiles count. Label a negative value Invalid, zero Empty, 1 through 6 Small and values above 6 Large. Write an ordered if elif else script and predict -1, 0, 1, 6 and 7. Include one print after the chain.
workbook.answer: Use if tiles < 0, elif tiles == 0, elif tiles <= 6, else, assigning the respective labels and printing after the chain. Outputs Invalid, Empty, Small, Small, Large. Zero must be handled before the <= 6 branch.

workbook.title: Choose revealing regression tests
workbook.prompt: A repair changes the small-count condition from < 6 to <= 6. Name the case that exposes the original error and two different kinds of earlier cases to rerun.
workbook.answer: 6 exposes the original wrong Large label. Rerun zero for Empty and a negative count for Invalid, or 7 for Large. Passing only 6 does not check earlier branches.

teacher.background: Teach ordered selection and indentation using a written input contract. A script can cover all branches while missing an equality bug. Reference: https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/controlflow.html#if-statements. The new task requires one four-way chain; independently correct equivalent conditions are acceptable.
materials: Python 3 editor and branches.py
The written duration rule and boundary case cards
Blank trace table with a skipped marker
sessions: Retrieve inclusive comparison and collect the prerequisite.
Translate the duration rule and complete W1.
Trace the diagram and code, marking skipped branches.
Complete W2 with predicted and actual outputs.
Retrieve why equality needs a separate test.
Run the faulty two-if script and complete W3 and the guided question.
Collect the new sorter in W4 before hints.
Use W5 and the exit to distinguish coverage from correctness.
teacher.guidedAnswer: The faulty < 12 version prints Long for 12, contrary to the inclusive Short rule. Repair to <= 12 and rerun 11 or 13 as well as 12. Exit: exact 12 is missing. -1, 2 and 20 can visit all branches even when the equality comparison is wrong.
misconceptions: Every condition in the chain always runs
Once one condition succeeds, later alternatives are skipped.
Two if statements behave like if then elif
Independent if statements can both run and overwrite a result.
Indentation is cosmetic
Leading spaces define the branch body.
Every branch tested means every input correct
A missing equality case can hide a wrong comparison.
teacher.assessment: W4 must assign one correct label on all five cases and explain zero before the small branch. After support, retry a shelf-count sorter with Empty at zero, Few for 1 through 4, Many above 4 and Invalid below zero. Expected outputs at -1, 0, 4, 5 are Invalid, Empty, Few, Many.
teacher.support: Provide movable branch cards and align the four-space blocks on a ruled page. Permit an oral trace alongside the script and record help. Extension: swap the zero and <= 6 checks and find the smallest nonnegative counterexample.
teacher.next: Week 6 repeats a block with loops and records each change in state.

ai-2/6.title: Loops and trace tables
goals: Trace variable values before and after each loop iteration
Use the excluded stop value in range correctly
Explain initialization and test zero one and several iterations

prerequisite.prompt: Starting with total = 2, what does total = total + 3 store?
prerequisite.answer: It reads the old 2, adds 3 and stores 5. Assignment updates a value; it is not an algebraic equality.

vocabulary: A block of instructions that can run repeatedly
One execution of a loop body
A variable that keeps a running result
Giving a variable its starting value
A record of variable values as instructions execute

lesson.title: Repeat a block with a clear stopping point

blocks.text: Imagine adding numbered counters: first 1, then 2, then 3. A loop can repeat the same addition with a different number each time. This week you will predict each change before running a short Python script. Tracing repeated calculations prepares you to inspect the data processing used in larger AI applications.

In for turn in range(1, 4), Python supplies 1, 2 and 3 in order. The start is included and the stop is excluded. The indented body runs once for each supplied value. The colon and four-space indentation mark that body. This lesson uses integer range values with the default positive step of 1.

blocks.title: Python 3 code
blocks.text:
total = 0
for turn in range(1, 4):
    total = total + turn
print(total)

blocks.title: State after each addition
blocks.caption: Initialize total to 0 before the loop. The unindented print runs once afterward.

blocks.text: The output is 6. Before the first iteration, total is 0. Each assignment reads the previous total and adds the current turn. After turn 3, the range is exhausted, so execution continues after the loop. The table records state; it does not create extra instructions.

lesson.title: Test how many times the body runs

blocks.text: With one argument, range starts at zero. range(4) supplies four values but none is 4. If the worked script uses range(1, 1), the body never runs and the initialized total remains 0. Do not rely on a variable first assigned inside a loop: a zero-iteration run might never assign it.

blocks.label: Replace range(1, 4) with range(1, 3) in the worked script. Predict the supplied values and final total. What stop value is needed to include 3?

lesson.title: Find a reset hidden inside the loop

blocks.title: Python 3 code
blocks.text:
total = 0
for turn in range(1, 4):
    total = 0
    total = total + turn
print(total)

This faulty version prints 3. The extra reset discards earlier additions on every iteration. Remove the indented reset while keeping initialization before the loop. Then test zero, one and several iterations: the one-iteration case alone cannot reveal this reset bug.

Moving print(total) into the correct loop produces three lines, 1 then 3 then 6. Moving it out produces only the final 6. Trace both values and output events. A loop follows written instructions; repeating them does not make the program learn.

lesson.title: Use evidence to explain a repair

blocks.text: Write the expected range values and trace table before running. Keep predicted and observed output separate, then explain the first row where they differ. For a loop that should add a fixed amount repeatedly, zero iterations should preserve the initial amount. One iteration checks one update; several check accumulation.

blocks.label: A learner checks the reset bug using only range(1, 2) and sees the expected answer 1. Explain why this does not establish correctness, and give a revealing test with its expected correct output.

workbook.title: Explain the range
workbook.prompt: List the values supplied by range(2, 5) and explain why 5 is absent. How many times does its body run?
workbook.answer: 2, 3 and 4; the stop value is excluded. The body runs three times.

workbook.title: Trace before running
workbook.prompt: Copy the worked script. Change the range to range(2, 5). Record turn, total before and total after each iteration. Predict the single output, then run and compare.
workbook.answer: Rows are 2 / 0 / 2, 3 / 2 / 5, 4 / 5 / 9. Final output 9. Keep the observed result distinct from the prediction.

workbook.title: Repair the reset
workbook.prompt: For the faulty script with range(1, 4), record total after each addition. Explain the wrong final output and remove only the faulty reset.
workbook.answer: Faulty after-addition values are 1, 2, 3 because each starts from zero. Remove the indented total = 0. Correct after-addition values are 1, 3, 6; final output 6.

workbook.title: Build a repeated addition independently
workbook.prompt: A box starts with 5 counters. Each round adds 2 counters. Use rounds = 3, an initialized total and for turn in range(rounds). Print the final total once after the loop. Trace the totals and predict fresh runs with rounds 0, 1 and 3. Assume rounds is a nonnegative integer.
workbook.answer: Initialize total = 5 before the loop; add 2 inside it. For three rounds, turn values 0, 1, 2 give totals 7, 9, 11. Final outputs for 0, 1, 3 rounds are 5, 7, 11. Print is unindented.

workbook.title: Check a contract limitation
workbook.prompt: In your counter script, range(-2) performs no iterations. Does returning the initial 5 make negative rounds valid? Explain what the script checks and what it assumes.
workbook.answer: No. The written contract requires a nonnegative integer. The script assumes this and does not reject negative values. Empty range behavior does not validate the input; report the limitation or add an explicit check.

teacher.background: Teach for loops with finite integer ranges before adding more loop forms. Keep range values, body executions and output events separate. Reference: https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/controlflow.html#the-range-function. The examples use a positive default step and do not require lists or while loops.
materials: Python 3 editor and loops.py
Counters or numbered paper cards
Blank trace table with turn total before and total after columns
sessions: Model range with numbered cards and complete W1.
Trace each row of the worked addition and predict output.
Complete W2 and compare predicted and observed values.
Retrieve included start and excluded stop.
Trace the reset bug, complete W3 and discuss the guided response.
Collect independent W4 code and zero one and several iteration traces.
Use W5 and the exit to examine assumptions and revealing tests.
teacher.guidedAnswer: range(1, 3) supplies 1 and 2, giving total 3. Stop 4 includes 3. Exit: the reset bug agrees for one iteration because there are no earlier additions to lose. range(1, 4) should give 6; the faulty version gives 3.
misconceptions: The stop value is included
List the supplied values before tracing; range(1, 4) excludes 4.
Initialization belongs inside every iteration
Resetting the accumulator loses earlier work.
An unindented print repeats with the body
Indentation determines which statements repeat.
Zero iterations mean the entire program does nothing
Initialization and statements after the loop still execute.
teacher.assessment: W4 must preserve the initial 5, update by 2, trace three iterations and print once. Require outputs 5, 7, 11 for zero one and three rounds. After support, retry with an initial 4 and additions of 3 for zero one and two rounds: outputs 4, 7, 10. Record assistance before judging independence.
teacher.support: Use counters and let the learner move a pointer through one instruction at a time. Offer a blank trace grid and permit oral explanation. Extension: put print inside the correct loop and explain why zero rounds produces no output while an outside print still does.
teacher.next: Week 7 stores several values in a list and distinguishes an index from the value at that position.

ai-2/8.title: Functions and arguments
goals: Distinguish a function definition from a function call
Match positional arguments to parameters in order
Reuse one function and test that it uses the supplied values

prerequisite.prompt: A script sets capacity = 12 and used = 4. What does print(capacity - used) display?
prerequisite.answer: 8. Subtraction is ordered: reversing these values would produce -8.

vocabulary: A named block of reusable instructions that runs when called
Code that creates a function and specifies its body
An instruction that runs a function with supplied arguments
A name in a function definition that receives an argument
A value supplied when calling a function

lesson.title: Name a calculation you need again

blocks.text: A fictional supply cupboard records capacity and the number of occupied spaces. The remaining-space calculation is capacity minus used. Instead of copying the same instructions for every cupboard, define one function and call it with different values. A function makes a procedure reusable; its name alone does not guarantee that its instructions are correct.

Our input contract requires nonnegative integer counts with used no greater than capacity. The example assumes these conditions; it does not validate them. This week the function prints its result. Week 9 will show how to return a value for later calculations.

lesson.title: Define once and call with new values

blocks.title: Python 3 code
blocks.text:
def show_remaining(capacity, used):
    remaining = capacity - used
    print(remaining)

show_remaining(12, 4)
show_remaining(10, 7)

blocks.title: Arguments matched in order
blocks.caption: Each call runs the same body with the values supplied for that call.

blocks.text: def introduces the definition. The function name is followed by parameter names in parentheses and a colon. Four-space indentation marks the body. Executing the definition creates the function but does not run its body. The two unindented calls then run it, producing 8 and 3 on separate lines. A blank line helps readability; indentation determines the block.

lesson.title: Trace the call before running it

rows: Create the function; no output yet

blocks.text: In show_remaining(12, 4), 12 and 4 are arguments; capacity and used are parameters. Positional arguments match from left to right. show_remaining(4, 12) produces -8, showing why order matters; it also violates our written input contract. Use a fresh file with the definition before its calls.

blocks.label: Predict the output of show_remaining(9, 9) followed by show_remaining(9, 0). Name the parameter receiving each argument. What would be printed if both calls were removed?

lesson.title: Check whether the function uses its arguments

blocks.title: Python 3 code
blocks.text:
def show_remaining(capacity, used):
    remaining = 12 - 4
    print(remaining)

show_remaining(12, 4)
show_remaining(10, 7)

This faulty function prints 8 twice. Its fixed numbers ignore the arguments. Replace 12 - 4 with capacity - used, then rerun both calls. Testing only the first call would miss the bug because its expected answer happens to be 8.

For this two-parameter definition, show_remaining(12) raises TypeError because an argument is missing. Correct the call to supply both values. Naming a function without calling it does not execute the body: the parentheses in show_remaining(12, 4) are part of the call.

For each call, record the supplied arguments, expected printed output and observed output. Include different values that produce different answers, plus a valid zero-result case. Call order controls output order; it does not change the subtraction rule. These functions use supplied data and written instructions, not a pattern learned from examples.

blocks.label: A learner tests only show_remaining(12, 4) and says the function works for every cupboard. Give a second valid call that exposes the fixed-number bug, state its expected output and explain what passing two tests still cannot prove.

workbook.title: Label the parts
workbook.prompt: In def show_remaining(capacity, used), identify the function name and parameters. In show_remaining(15, 6), identify the arguments and their matching parameters.
workbook.answer: Name show_remaining; parameters capacity and used. Arguments 15 and 6 match capacity = 15 and used = 6. Expected printed result 9.

workbook.title: Follow the execution order
workbook.prompt: Using the correct definition, predict show_remaining(8, 3), show_remaining(8, 8) and show_remaining(8, 0) in that order. Explain what happens if the file contains only the definition.
workbook.answer: The calls print 5, 0 and 8 on separate lines. A definition alone creates the function but prints nothing because its body has not been called.

workbook.title: Repair ignored arguments
workbook.prompt: The faulty body calculates 12 - 4 regardless of the call. State the output and expected output for show_remaining(11, 2). Repair the expression and name an earlier call to rerun.
workbook.answer: Faulty output 8; expected 9. Use capacity - used. Rerun show_remaining(12, 4), expecting 8, as well as the revealing call.

workbook.title: Create a new function independently
workbook.prompt: Each sealed box contains 6 counters. Define show_stock(boxes, loose) to print the total counters using its two parameters. Assume nonnegative integer arguments. Call it with (3, 2), (0, 2) and (3, 0). Predict each output and explain why show_stock(2, 3) is a different case.
workbook.answer: The body prints boxes * 6 + loose. Outputs are 20, 2 and 18. show_stock(2, 3) gives 15 because boxes and loose have different roles. Define once and use three calls; do not hard-code one answer.

workbook.title: State the input assumption
workbook.prompt: The correct subtraction function prints -1 for show_remaining(4, 5). Does successful execution make this a valid cupboard record? Explain what the function assumes and what needs checking.
workbook.answer: No. used exceeds capacity and violates the contract. The function calculates with supplied values but does not check the contract. A separate validation check or guarded function is needed to reject invalid records.

teacher.background: Teach definition, call, parameter and positional argument as distinct ideas. Keep inputs scalar and avoid mutable-list aliasing in this first function lesson. Reference: https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/controlflow.html#defining-functions. These functions print results; reusable return values and local state are taught in Week 9.
materials: Python 3 editor and functions.py
Parameter cards labelled capacity and used
Call cards and a table for expected and observed output
sessions: Retrieve ordered subtraction with the prerequisite.
Read the contract and label the definition and calls for W1.
Match argument cards to parameters and trace the worked calls.
Complete W2 and the guided question before running the file.
Retrieve why a definition alone prints nothing.
Run the fixed-number bug, complete W3 and rerun the earlier case after repair.
Collect the independent W4 function and predictions before hints.
Discuss W5 and use the exit to assess the limits of passing tests.
teacher.guidedAnswer: The calls print 0 then 9. capacity receives 9 in both calls; used receives 9 then 0. Removing both calls leaves a definition with no printed output. Exit: show_remaining(10, 7) should print 3 but the faulty version prints 8. Passing two cases does not establish correctness for all allowed inputs or validate the input contract.
misconceptions: Writing def runs the body immediately
The definition creates the function; a call runs its body.
Arguments and parameters are interchangeable labels
Parameters are names in the definition; arguments supply values at a call.
Swapping arguments never matters
Different parameter roles can give different results when values are swapped.
A correct first example proves the function is reusable
Fixed numbers can match one case while ignoring later arguments.
teacher.assessment: W4 must define one function, use both parameters, call it three times and predict 20, 2, 18; the swapped case must give 15. After support, retry show_tiles(packs, singles) with 4 tiles per pack: calls (2, 3), (0, 3), (2, 0) print 11, 3, 8; swapped (3, 2) prints 14. Record assistance and collect new predictions before execution.
teacher.support: Use two labelled parameter spaces and place argument cards left to right. Permit an oral execution trace alongside code. Extension: add an if check inside show_remaining that prints Invalid when used exceeds capacity, otherwise prints the difference; test (4, 5) and (4, 4). This checks only that one constraint.
teacher.next: Week 9 returns results to the caller and explains local variables and fresh state on each call.

ai-3/1.title: The machine learning lifecycle
goals: Distinguish fitting a rule from applying a fixed rule
Trace a small learning lifecycle with separate data
Report test evidence with its limits

prerequisite.prompt: A fixed rule matches 3 labels out of 4 tested cases. What fraction is correct, and does that prove it works on all future cases?
prerequisite.answer: 3 of 4, or 75 percent, are correct in these cases. It does not prove correctness on future cases.

vocabulary: An input value used to make a prediction
An observed target value supplied for an example
Using examples to select or adjust a model
Examples reserved from fitting and model choices for evaluation

lesson.title: From a written rule to a fitted rule

blocks.text: In Grade 7 you programmed an activity chooser using a rule supplied by a person. This week you will choose a rule by comparing its predictions with labelled examples. This small supervised learning task makes the learning process visible: people define the task and possible rules; training data determines which candidate fits best.

Imagine fictional practice cards with a measured width x and a category label, 0 or 1. Width uses invented units. We want to predict the category of another card from its width. The labels are provided observations in this exercise, not values generated by our prediction code. These invented cards demonstrate a method; they provide no evidence about real objects or students.

Before fitting, set aside the final two cards. They are visible here so you can follow the complete example, but do not use them to choose a rule. Our candidates predict 1 when width is at least 2, 4 or 6, and 0 otherwise. Choose the candidate with the fewest training mistakes. If candidates tie, choose the smaller threshold; fix this rule before testing.

blocks.title: Python 3 code

blocks.text: int(True) is 1 and int(False) is 0. For threshold 2, the training predictions are 0, 1, 1, 1: the width 3 card is wrong. For threshold 4, they are 0, 0, 1, 1: none is wrong. For threshold 6, they are 0, 0, 0, 1: the width 5 card is wrong. The printed rows are 2 1, then 4 0, then 6 1. Select threshold 4 using this training evidence and record it. The loop reports errors; the learner makes and records the selection.

blocks.title: Keep fitting and testing separate
blocks.caption: Read down the stages. Test results may inform later development, but they must not silently change the rule being tested.

lesson.title: Freeze the rule and test it

blocks.text: Freeze means do not change the chosen threshold during this evaluation. With threshold 4, widths 2 and 6 receive predictions 0 and 1. Compare them with the held out labels: both match. Report 2 correct out of 2 held out cards. Training results and test results answer different questions: did the rule fit the examples used to select it, and how did that fixed rule perform on these separate examples?

blocks.label: Keep threshold 4 fixed. An additional card has width 4 and observed label 0. Predict its category, decide whether it is correct, and update the held out count from 2 of 2.

blocks.text: A learner sees the width 4 test error, changes the threshold to 5, and reports the same cards as a fresh final test. The test labels have now influenced the model. Keep the original 2 of 3 result for the original rule. Record the change as development, then reserve genuinely unused examples for a later evaluation. Do not delete the difficult card or rename reused cards as new evidence.

A lifecycle continues after fitting: define the intended use, prepare and separate data, fit, evaluate, review the limits, and monitor any approved use. Evaluation can send us back to development. That return needs an honest record and a new final evaluation; it does not erase the earlier error.

This threshold model learned only a choice among three candidate values. People supplied the feature, labels, candidate family and tie rule. Learning does not imply understanding, and perfect training performance does not guarantee good predictions. Two correct test cards are too few to establish reliable performance for a broader population. Even a larger score would depend on how examples were collected and what use was intended.

blocks.label: Your report says the fixed model matched 2 of 2 held out cards. Write one supported claim, one claim this does not support, and one sensible next step.

workbook.title: Identify the learning decision
workbook.prompt: For the worked cards, name the input, label, three candidate thresholds and the information allowed to select a threshold.
workbook.answer: The input is width x and the label is the observed category 0 or 1. Candidates are 2, 4 and 6. Selection uses mistakes on the four training cards only; held out labels must not guide it.

workbook.title: Trace one candidate
workbook.prompt: Use threshold 6 on the four training widths 1, 3, 5 and 7. Write all predictions, identify each error, and explain why threshold 4 is selected.
workbook.answer: Predictions are 0, 0, 0, 1. The width 5 card is wrong because its label is 1. Threshold 6 has one training mistake; threshold 4 has zero and is selected.

workbook.title: Repair the report
workbook.prompt: A learner fits on all six worked cards and then reports 6 of 6 as independent test performance. Explain what is wrong and what evidence is needed.
workbook.answer: All six cards influenced fitting, so none of those six provides an independent test. Report this as performance on fitting data. Freeze the rule and evaluate it on unused examples; do not claim a new split of the same reused cards repairs the earlier evaluation.

workbook.title: Fit and evaluate independently
workbook.prompt: New training cards are (width 2, label 0), (4, 0), (6, 1), (8, 1). Candidates are 3, 5 and 7. Predict 1 when width is at least the threshold. Count training mistakes, select the fewest with smaller threshold breaking ties, and record the choice before testing. Held out cards are (3, 0), (7, 1), (5, 0). Give each test prediction, the correct count and a limited conclusion.
workbook.answer: Training mistake counts for thresholds 3, 5 and 7 are 1, 0 and 1; select 5 before examining test results. Held out predictions are 0, 1, 1. The width 5 card is wrong, giving 2 correct out of 3. This supports the result on these three cards only, not universal reliability. Preserve threshold 5 for this evaluation.

workbook.title: Decide the next step
workbook.prompt: After W4, a team changes its threshold because of the test error. Can the same three cards be an untouched final test for the changed model? Explain how to proceed.
workbook.answer: No. Their labels have influenced the revision. Keep the first result, log the new threshold and use the old cases for development or regression checks. Use fresh reserved cases for an independent final evaluation.

teacher.background: Teach the first Grade 8 machine learning lesson as two 45-minute sessions. The central distinction is selection from labelled training examples versus evaluation of a fixed rule on separate examples. This is a deliberately small supervised classification exercise, not a deployed card recognition system. Students can complete it on paper; Python checks their trace. Do not add neural-network terminology or external accounts. The training loop reports candidate mistakes, and students explicitly select and record the winner.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook; six fictional worked cards
Paper to cover the held out rows until a threshold is recorded
Optional local Python 3 editor; no packages or personal data needed
Prepare a fresh retry card set from the assessment guidance
sessions: Retrieve the Grade 7 idea of testing a fixed rule. Ask the prerequisite question and require a denominator in the answer.
Define width, label and threshold. Read the card table. Cover the held out rows and agree the three candidate values and tie rule before fitting.
Trace every prediction for thresholds 2, 4 and 6. Use W1 and W2. Have students explain a wrong prediction rather than only counting errors. Optionally run the Python loop.
Record threshold 4, then uncover held out cards. Complete the guided additional width 4 case. Compare training and held out results with separate denominators.
Retrieve the sequence define, separate, fit, freeze and test. Ask which step may use training labels and which records test results.
Discuss the unfair evaluation and complete W3. Show why changing a model after seeing test labels changes the status of those examples.
Collect W4 independently. Have each learner record the training errors and threshold before revealing the test rows. Record whether support was needed.
Discuss W5 and the exit claim. Offer the fresh retry after support where needed. Preserve both the original result and later correction.
teacher.guidedAnswer: The prerequisite answer is 3 of 4, or 75 percent, for those four cases only. Guided case: width 4 produces 1 at threshold 4, but its label is 0, so it is wrong; the updated held out result is 2 of 3. Exit: a supported claim is that the fixed threshold matched both of these two cards. It does not show all future cards will be correct. A reasonable next step is to evaluate more unused examples chosen to represent the intended task, while recording the sampling limits.
misconceptions: The model wrote its own task
People chose the input, label meaning, candidate thresholds and selection rule. Learning here means choosing a parameter using the training examples.
Zero training mistakes means no future mistakes
Training performance measures the examples used to choose the threshold. The additional width 4 card shows how a fitted model can be wrong on a different example.
A better score makes reused test data independent
Once test labels influence a revision, the examples are part of development. Preserve the history and use unused cases for a later independent evaluation.
teacher.assessment: Require W4 training counts 1, 0, 1, selection 5, held out predictions 0, 1, 1 and result 2 of 3, plus an explanation of separation and limits. Assess the explanation before offering hints. Fresh retry: training (1,0), (5,0), (7,1), (9,1), candidates 4,6,8. Mistakes are 1,0,1; choose 6. Held out (2,0), (8,1), (6,0) produces 0,1,1 and 2 of 3. Ask why the final error must remain in the report. Correct arithmetic without keeping fitting and testing separate is not sufficient exit evidence.
teacher.support: Use a prediction grid with one row per card and one column per candidate. Cover held out rows until the choice is written. Read pairs aloud as width then label. Extension: candidates 4 and 5 both fit the worked training set with zero errors; the predeclared smaller-threshold tie rule chooses 4. Explain why the test labels must not break this tie.
teacher.next: Week 2 examines features, labels and which information exists at prediction time. Carry forward the recorded split, threshold and test result. Teacher reference for data separation and leakage: https://scikit-learn.org/stable/common_pitfalls.html#data-leakage (reviewed 2026-09-26).

ai-3/10.title: Nearest neighbours and distances
goals: Compute absolute distances and rank training neighbours
Apply a declared neighbour count and distance tie rule
Evaluate neighbour predictions without using validation labels as neighbours

prerequisite.prompt: What does a fitted depth-one tree store, and what does it do with a new example?
prerequisite.answer: It stores a root question and leaf predictions learned from training. A new example follows the appropriate branch to a stored leaf prediction.

vocabulary: A numerical measure of difference between selected feature values
A stored training example close under the chosen distance
The number of neighbours selected for a prediction
A contribution of a selected neighbour’s label to the predicted class

blocks.text: A nearest-neighbour classifier predicts using nearby training examples rather than following a fitted tree. This week we store labelled examples, measure how different their feature values are from a new query, and let selected neighbours vote. Nearby means close under our chosen feature and distance, not necessarily similar in every real-world way.

Our new fictional dataset has a distance reading in centimetres and a separately reviewed lane label. Each row comes from a distinct trip, and validation trips are separate. Only the numeric reading measures similarity. IDs identify rows and break distance ties; they are not numeric features. These invented readings are not a robot safety system.

For this one-dimensional feature, distance is abs(training reading minus query reading). abs removes the sign. Set k=3 and give each selected neighbour one vote. Order equal distances by ID alphabetically, declared before scoring. In this binary, three-vote exercise the label vote cannot tie, but the distances can.

blocks.title: Python 3 code
blocks.text:
train = [("A", 2, "blocked"), ("B", 4, "clear"),
         ("C", 8, "clear"), ("D", 10, "blocked"),
         ("E", 12, "clear")]
query = 3
ranked = sorted((abs(x - query), item_id, label)
                for item_id, x, label in train)
near = ranked[:3]
labels = [row[2] for row in near]
prediction = "clear"
if labels.count("blocked") > labels.count("clear"):
    prediction = "blocked"
print([row[1] for row in near])
print(prediction)

For query 3, distances to A through E are 1,1,5,7,9 cm. sorted orders tuples by distance first, then the unique ID. ranked[:3] takes the first three rows. The output is ['A', 'B', 'C'] then clear: one blocked vote and two clear votes.

If k were 1 under the same distance tie rule, A would win and predict blocked. Changing k can change a prediction. We declared k=3 for this exercise; do not choose k after seeing the desired answer and pretend the method was unchanged.

The code assumes unique IDs, numeric readings, only clear or blocked labels and at least three training rows. It does not validate those conditions. A larger k than the stored row count would not produce the promised number of votes. Keep unresolved review labels under a separate documented policy.

lesson.title: Separate feature distance from label evidence

blocks.title: Three selected neighbours for query 3
blocks.caption: Select neighbours by feature distance and the declared ID tie rule. Read their training labels to vote only after selecting them.

blocks.text: Store the training examples and the method settings. At prediction time, compare the query only with stored training examples. Do not add the query’s reference label or other validation labels to the neighbour pool. No cutoff or tree is fitted here, but retaining training examples is still part of the learning method.

blocks.label: Why do A and B tie for distance to query 3? Which wins for k=1 under our rule, and why does k=3 predict differently? Does the ID rule establish which label is true?

blocks.text: A vote share of two out of three describes these neighbours. It is not a verified two-thirds probability that the new scene is clear. A prediction can be wrong even when the nearest examples agree.

lesson.title: Score queries without changing the pool

blocks.text: Keep k=3 and the original five training rows. Validation queries with reference labels are (3,blocked), (9,blocked), (11,clear). Their selected neighbour IDs are A B C, C D E, and D E C respectively. Each group votes clear. Only the last prediction matches, so accuracy is 1/3, about 33.3 percent.

The training-majority baseline also predicts clear because three training labels are clear and two are blocked. It gets the same 1/3 on these validation rows. Record all distances, selected IDs and errors. Trying more k values is a development choice to document; preserve a separate final test for a final evaluation.

All distances here use one feature measured in the same unit. With multiple features, their units and scales affect which examples appear close. A large numerical range can dominate a distance calculation. Next week we will address scaling and learn any scaling values from training data only.

Identical readings from different trips can have different labels, and an exact match does not certify truth. Keep related examples grouped across splits as in Week 6. Testing an example against a pool containing itself can make a one-neighbour score misleadingly high; it does not show performance on a new trip.

blocks.label: A learner adds each labelled validation query to the stored pool, then uses k=1 and reports perfect predictions. Explain what the result fails to test and how to restore the intended comparison.

workbook.title: Calculate feature distances
workbook.prompt: For query 3 cm, calculate distances to all five training rows. Explain why A and B tie even though their labels differ.
workbook.answer: Distances to A,B,C,D,E are 1,1,5,7,9 cm. A and B are equally far from 3 on the numeric feature; their labels do not enter the distance calculation.

workbook.title: Apply neighbour and tie rules
workbook.prompt: For query 3, list the selected IDs and predictions for k=1 and k=3 using alphabetical ID order on equal distances. Explain what changes and what remains the same.
workbook.answer: For k=1 select A and predict blocked. For k=3 select A,B,C and predict clear from two clear votes. Training data, distance and ID tie rule stay the same; the number of voting neighbours changes.

workbook.title: Keep evaluation examples separate
workbook.prompt: Why must the three validation reference labels not enter the neighbour pool? Give the fixed k=3 score and baseline score on the worked validation examples.
workbook.answer: Adding validation labels uses evaluation answers to make predictions and changes the intended comparison with unseen trips. The fixed k=3 method predicts clear three times and gets 1/3. The training-majority clear baseline also gets 1/3.

workbook.title: Find neighbours independently
workbook.prompt: New training rows are P at 1 cm clear, Q at 5 blocked, R at 7 blocked, S at 11 clear, T at 13 blocked. For query 6, give all distances, order the IDs by distance then alphabetically, and predict with k=1 and k=3. Using the same training pool and k=3, score validation (6,blocked),(10,clear),(12,blocked). Compare the training-majority baseline.
workbook.answer: Query 6 distances P,Q,R,S,T are 5,1,1,5,7. Order Q,R,P,S,T. k=1 predicts blocked from Q; k=3 uses Q,R,P and also predicts blocked. For queries 6,10,12, selected triples are Q R P, S R T, S T R. All predict blocked, matching validation rows 1 and 3: 2/3. Training-majority blocked also scores 2/3.

workbook.title: Interpret a vote and a match
workbook.prompt: Two of three neighbours vote clear. Does that prove a two-thirds chance of a correct prediction? Does an exact feature match guarantee a correct label? Explain both limits.
workbook.answer: The vote fraction describes the selected training labels, not a verified probability of correctness. An exact match on one feature can still differ in omitted conditions or have a wrong or conflicting label. Separate evaluation and relevant features remain necessary.

teacher.background: Teach two 45-minute sessions. Use a single numeric feature to make distance arithmetic visible, then distinguish neighbour selection from voting. Store only training rows. Alphabetical IDs settle equal distances for this classroom method; explain that it is a convention and other implementations can use different tie behavior.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook
Number line from 0 to 14 cm and five labelled training markers
Optional Python 3 editor with no packages required
Blank table for distances ordered IDs votes and predictions
sessions: Retrieve tree storage and prediction. Introduce prediction from stored examples with a declared distance.
Place A through E on the number line. Calculate absolute distances to query 3 and complete W1.
Trace tuple sorting and list slicing. Complete W2; distinguish tied distances from a tied label vote.
Read the diagram and answer the guided question. Explain why ID order is not evidence of truth.
Retrieve the training-only neighbour pool. Ask why validation labels must remain outside it.
Compute the three validation predictions and complete W3. Compare the fixed training-majority baseline.
Collect W4 independently before support. Require ordered IDs, both k predictions and the full validation score.
Use W5 and the exit question. Offer the fresh retry after feedback and record support.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided: abs(2-3) and abs(4-3) both equal 1. For k=1 alphabetical tie order chooses A, blocked. k=3 adds B and C, whose clear votes win 2 to 1. ID order is a deterministic convention, not evidence of the query’s true label. Exit: using labelled validation examples in the neighbour pool leaks evaluation answers and may let a query select itself. Restore the original training-only pool and score every validation query without adding its label.
misconceptions: A negative difference is a negative distance
Take the absolute difference; in this example distance is nonnegative regardless of which reading is larger.
Odd k prevents every kind of tie
Three binary votes avoid a label tie, but neighbours can still tie in distance, including at the selection boundary.
An exact match proves the label
It matches the selected feature only. Other conditions, annotation errors or contradictory examples can remain.
teacher.assessment: Require W4 distances 5,1,1,5,7, order Q,R,P,S,T, both predictions blocked, and validation plus baseline scores 2/3. Fresh retry: L at 0 blocked, M at 4 clear, N at 6 clear, O at 10 blocked, P at 12 clear; query 5. Distances are 5,1,1,5,7; order M,N,L,O,P. k=1 is clear from M; k=3 is clear from M,N,L. Ask why L wins the third-place distance tie over O: alphabetical ID policy. Require a training-only pool and no probability claim.
teacher.support: Use physical steps on a number line before abs. Supply an empty distance table without the order. Extension: explain how renaming tied IDs can change a prediction under this policy while the measured features remain unchanged, and why the policy must be recorded.
teacher.next: Week 11 covers scaling without leakage. Carry forward training-only storage and explicit distance choices. Teacher reference: https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/neighbors.html (nearest-neighbour classification and tie considerations; reviewed 2026-09-27).

ai-3/12.title: A reproducible classifier pipeline
goals: Connect training-only scaling and neighbour prediction in one pipeline
Reproduce predictions from recorded data settings and fitted values
Audit a pipeline for refitting feature-order errors and evaluation leakage

prerequisite.prompt: Which values does min-max scaling learn, and which values should be reused for a validation query?
prerequisite.answer: It learns each feature minimum and range from training. Reuse the same minima, ranges, feature order and units to transform training and validation examples.

vocabulary: An ordered sequence of data transformations and prediction steps
The learned values and stored examples needed to make predictions
Obtain the same result using the same recorded inputs and procedure
The documented feature names order units and accepted values

blocks.text: A pipeline connects steps so a new query receives the same preparation as the training examples. This week combines the scale from Week 11 with a one-neighbour classifier. We will fit once, keep the fitted state, and call one prediction function for every raw query.

Use the same fictional trip data. Each feature pair is ordered (distance in cm, brightness in sensor units). Training IDs are A,B,C. Validation IDs V1,V2,V3 belong to separate trips; related trips were grouped before splitting. Use min-max scaling, sum of absolute scaled differences, k=1 and alphabetical ID order for exact distance ties.

The input contract requires two finite numeric features in the stated order and units, with no missing values. Training also needs unique IDs, known labels, at least one row and nonzero ranges. These assumptions must be checked before this short classroom program is used; its explicit guard only checks zero ranges.

blocks.title: Python 3 code

blocks.text: fit returns minima (10,100), ranges (10,100) and scaled training examples. predict transforms a raw query with that state, ranks distances, then returns the selected ID and label. zip pairs matching features; sum adds their absolute differences. sorted uses distance first and unique ID second.

Run the whole script in Python 3. It prints ('A', 'clear'), ('C', 'blocked'), ('B', 'blocked') on separate lines. No validation labels enter fit or predict. This is a small pipeline written with functions, not the scikit-learn Pipeline class.

lesson.title: Trace what is fitted and what is reused

blocks.title: Two stages with one fitted state
blocks.caption: Reference labels are used after prediction to score results. They do not enter the fitted scale or stored neighbour pool.

blocks.text: For raw query (11,120), scale gives (0.1,0.2). Distances to A,B,C are 0.9,1.1,1.7, so the function returns A and clear. It does not recalculate minima or add the query to stored rows. The returned ID is useful for checking the reasoning, but it is not evidence that the label is true.

blocks.label: Trace (11,120) through both functions. What does fit store, what does predict reuse, and at which point may a validation reference label be compared?

blocks.text: Store the fitted state together with the input contract and method settings. A model without its scale or feature order is incomplete. Swapping the raw pair to (120,11) produces B and blocked here; the function cannot detect that the caller swapped the meanings.

lesson.title: Record and reproduce the whole run

blocks.text: Record dataset and code versions, training IDs A B C, validation IDs V1 V2 V3, feature order and units, fitted minima and ranges, k=1, distance and tie policy, zero-range policy and the actual Python version. Save the predictions in validation ID order. This script has no random step; a seed would not fix changed data or swapped features.

References for V1,V2,V3 are clear,blocked,clear. The printed predictions clear,blocked,blocked match V1 and V2: 2/3. The training-majority blocked baseline matches only V2: 1/3. Rerunning the same code and inputs should reproduce these outputs, including the V3 mistake. Reproducibility does not establish correctness or performance on new data.

Changing the scaling, k or feature list creates a new development run to record. Keep a separate final test for the final evaluation. Next week a confusion matrix will show which kinds of label errors the predictions make.

lesson.title: Audit the boundaries before trusting the output

blocks.text: Check that fit receives training rows only, predict receives raw features in the correct order, and the fitted state stays unchanged during prediction. Do not scale a query twice, fit again on validation, or add labelled validation rows to the neighbour pool. A pipeline still leaks if the wrong rows are passed to its fit step.

The tuple state groups the learned numbers and stored examples. Keep the associated data and code versions with it, and compare stored values and outputs when repeating a run. Do not accept a matching score alone: two different prediction lists can have the same score.

blocks.label: A learner gets the same 2/3 score twice after fitting on training plus validation rows. They claim the pipeline must be valid because the result repeats. Explain why the claim fails and describe the repair.

workbook.title: Separate fit predict and evaluate
workbook.prompt: List what fit learns or stores, what predict takes as input, and what evaluation compares. State where the validation reference labels belong.
workbook.answer: fit learns training minima and ranges and stores scaled training rows with IDs and labels. predict takes a raw feature pair and the fitted state. Evaluation compares a prediction with its reference label afterward. Validation references belong only in evaluation, not in fitting or the neighbour pool.

workbook.title: Trace and score the saved run
workbook.prompt: Give the IDs and labels printed for V1,V2,V3. Use references clear,blocked,clear to calculate accuracy and the training-majority baseline. Which error should repeat in an unchanged rerun?
workbook.answer: V1 selects A clear, V2 C blocked, V3 B blocked. Accuracy is 2/3. The training-majority blocked baseline is correct only for V2, scoring 1/3. V3 is the repeatable error; repeated output does not turn it into a correct prediction.

workbook.title: Repair an incomplete run record
workbook.prompt: A classmate saves only k=1 and a score of 2/3. Name the information needed to reproduce this run. Explain why the same score alone is insufficient.
workbook.answer: Record the data and code versions, exact split IDs, feature names order and units, fitted minima and ranges, stored training rows, distance and tie policy, zero-range policy, runtime version and predictions linked to validation IDs. A score hides which examples were correct; different predictions can have equal accuracy.

workbook.title: Build and trace a fresh fitted state
workbook.prompt: Use P (0,60) blocked, Q (20,20) clear, R (20,60) clear as new training rows. Fit the same pipeline. Predict validation queries (2,28),(18,56),(4,12) with references blocked,clear,blocked. Give fitted minima and ranges, transformed queries, selected IDs, predictions, accuracy and training-majority baseline.
workbook.answer: Minima (0,20), ranges (20,40). Scaled queries are (0.1,0.2),(0.9,0.9),(0.2,-0.2). Selected IDs P,R,Q give blocked,clear,clear. Accuracy is 2/3; the training-majority clear baseline gets 1/3. The third query remains wrong. Validation rows do not change the fitted state.

workbook.title: Diagnose pipeline misuse
workbook.prompt: Explain and repair three mistakes: predict receives an already scaled query; fit receives training plus validation rows; a query uses brightness before distance. Does repeating each mistaken run make it valid?
workbook.answer: predict expects raw features, so a pre-scaled query is scaled again; pass the raw pair. Fitting on validation leaks evaluation information; refit on training only and reevaluate. Swapped features violate the input contract; restore distance then brightness in the stated units. Repeating a mistake shows repeatability, not validity.

teacher.background: Teach two 45-minute sessions. Assemble the two previous ideas into a complete runnable program, while keeping hand tracing available without devices. Distinguish a fitted state from settings and a run record. Require students to reproduce individual predictions, including errors, rather than merely quote a score.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook
Optional Python 3 editor with no packages required
Three cards labelled Fit Predict and Evaluate
Blank run record with split IDs feature order settings and outputs
sessions: Retrieve training-only scaling and the stored minima and ranges. State the input contract.
Use the three cards to place data and labels at the correct stage. Complete W1.
Run or trace the complete script. Unpack fitted state and explain zip sum and sorted.
Use the diagram and guided question, then complete W2 from the printed outputs.
Retrieve why predict must reuse the fitted state and receive raw feature pairs.
Complete W3 and compare two run records. Discuss why equal scores can hide different predictions.
Collect W4 independently before support. Require transformed queries and ID-linked predictions.
Use W5 and the exit question to audit misuse. Offer the fresh retry after feedback and record support.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided: fit stores minima (10,100), ranges (10,100) and A (0,1) clear, B (1,0) blocked, C (1,1) blocked. predict transforms (11,120) to (0.1,0.2), measures 0.9,1.1,1.7 and returns A clear. Compare the reference only afterward. Exit: reproducible leakage is still leakage. Restore the split, fit on training only, use the frozen state for every raw validation query, then score and record all outputs.
misconceptions: A pipeline prevents every leak automatically
Correct sequencing cannot fix a fit call that receives held-out rows or features unavailable at prediction time.
A seed is the whole reproducibility record
This program is deterministic. Data code split feature order settings and runtime still matter; a seed cannot repair changed inputs.
Same score means same predictions
Compare predictions by example ID. Different error patterns can produce the same accuracy.
teacher.assessment: Require W4 minima (0,20), ranges (20,40), scaled queries (0.1,0.2),(0.9,0.9),(0.2,-0.2), IDs P,R,Q, predictions blocked,clear,clear and scores 2/3 versus 1/3. Fresh retry: L (5,80) clear, M (15,40) blocked, N (15,80) blocked. Fit gives minima (5,40), ranges (10,40). Queries (6,48),(14,76) scale to (0.1,0.2),(0.9,0.9), selecting L clear and N blocked. Require the input contract and a statement that prediction does not refit.
teacher.support: Label each tuple field and use one query at a time. Provide a blank fit/predict/evaluate diagram without answers. Extension: use query (10,100) in the worked model. A and B both have scaled distance 1, C has 2; alphabetical ID order selects A clear. Explain why this convention must be recorded.
teacher.next: Week 13 introduces confusion matrices. Keep the ID-linked reference and prediction pairs from this week. Teacher reference: https://scikit-learn.org/stable/common_pitfalls.html (consistent preprocessing and training-only fitting; reviewed 2026-09-27).

ai-3/13.title: Confusion matrices
goals: Build a labelled confusion matrix from matched reference and prediction pairs
Distinguish false positives from false negatives using a declared positive class
Check matrix totals and explain why equal accuracy can hide different errors

prerequisite.prompt: Why should a reproducible run save predictions linked to example IDs rather than only an accuracy score?
prerequisite.answer: IDs preserve which reference belongs to each prediction and which examples were wrong. The same accuracy can come from different predictions and error patterns.

vocabulary: A table counting reference and prediction combinations
The class chosen as the condition of interest
A positive prediction when the reference is negative
A negative prediction when the reference is positive

lesson.title: Keep each prediction with its reference

blocks.text: A confusion matrix shows which labels a classifier mixes up. It counts examples after predictions are made; it does not fit or repair the classifier. Week 12 had reference/prediction pairs clear/clear, blocked/blocked, clear/blocked. A labelled table can preserve the type of that error as well as the total score.

This week uses eight new fictional evaluation records from a frozen classifier. They are not extra predictions from the Week 12 code. Each ID appears once with a reviewed reference and one prediction. The grouped table below lists every ID. Keep reference and prediction paired by ID before counting.

Use reference labels for rows and predicted labels for columns. On both axes the order is clear, then blocked. Declare blocked as the positive class and clear as negative. Positive means the condition of interest, not good or safe. A missed blocked case and a false alarm are different errors.

blocks.title: Python 3 code
blocks.text:
pairs = [("V1", "clear", "clear"),
         ("V2", "clear", "clear"),
         ("V3", "clear", "blocked"),
         ("V4", "blocked", "clear"),
         ("V5", "blocked", "clear"),
         ("V6", "blocked", "blocked"),
         ("V7", "blocked", "blocked"),
         ("V8", "blocked", "blocked")]
labels = ["clear", "blocked"]
index = {label: i for i, label in enumerate(labels)}
counts = [[0, 0], [0, 0]]
for item_id, reference, prediction in pairs:
    counts[index[reference]][index[prediction]] += 1
print(counts)
correct = counts[0][0] + counts[1][1]
print(correct, len(pairs))

index maps clear to 0 and blocked to 1. Each paired record adds one to its reference row and prediction column. The script prints [[2, 1], [2, 3]] then 5 8. It assumes unique IDs and only these two labels. Check IDs and missing or unresolved references before counting; the code does not validate all those conditions.

The diagonal cells count correct predictions: 2+3=5. Off-diagonal cells count mistakes: 1+2=3. Every record must contribute exactly once. This is a count matrix, not percentages or probabilities. Keep the axis labels even when copying the numbers.

lesson.title: Name each cell using the positive class

blocks.title: Blocked is the positive class
blocks.caption: Read reference first and prediction second. Here a false positive is a false blocked alarm; a false negative is a missed blocked case.

blocks.label: Place V3 and V4 in the matrix. Explain which is a false positive and which is a false negative when blocked is positive.

blocks.text: True means prediction agrees with the reference. It does not prove that the reference annotation is infallible. Resolve disputed labels with the documented review policy rather than silently changing them to match predictions.

Row totals are 3 reference-clear and 5 reference-blocked. Column totals are 4 predicted-clear and 4 predicted-blocked. All four cells sum to 8. Accuracy is the diagonal total divided by the total: 5/8, or 62.5 percent. The Week 12 three-record matrix was [[1,1],[0,1]] in this same axis order, giving 2/3.

Another classifier on these same eight reference-labelled records could have matrix [[3,0],[3,2]]. It also gets 5/8 correct, but has zero false positives and three false negatives. Our worked classifier has one false positive and two false negatives. Equal accuracy does not settle which error pattern is preferable; consider the task and evidence before choosing.

lesson.title: Preserve meaning when presenting a matrix

blocks.text: Always report the evaluated split, number of records, reference and prediction axes, label order and positive class. Reversing the axis order changes positions, not the underlying outcomes. Transposing rows and columns swaps the two kinds of error unless the labels are corrected. Read the headers before interpreting a diagram from another source.

A zero cell means no such event in this evaluated set, not that it is impossible. A confusion matrix does not show the cause of errors, label quality or performance on future data. Keep the ID-level records for investigation. Next week examines accuracy when class counts are unequal.

blocks.label: Two classifiers have accuracy 5/8. One misses two blocked records and the other misses three. Explain how both statements can be true and what must accompany their matrices for a fair comparison.

workbook.title: Build the count matrix
workbook.prompt: Use all eight worked IDs. Draw a matrix with reference rows and prediction columns, both ordered clear then blocked. Place the IDs in cells before writing the counts.
workbook.answer: Reference clear/predicted clear contains V1,V2: 2. Clear/blocked contains V3: 1. Blocked/clear contains V4,V5: 2. Blocked/blocked contains V6,V7,V8: 3. Matrix [[2,1],[2,3]].

workbook.title: Explain the two error types
workbook.prompt: Declare blocked positive. Give TP,TN,FP,FN counts and explain V3 and V4 in plain language. Does positive mean a desirable outcome?
workbook.answer: TP=3, TN=2, FP=1, FN=2. V3 predicts blocked for a reference-clear case, a false alarm or FP. V4 predicts clear for a reference-blocked case, a missed blocked case or FN. Positive names the chosen class; it does not mean desirable.

workbook.title: Audit totals and equal accuracy
workbook.prompt: Give the worked row totals, column totals, total count and accuracy. Compare its errors with [[3,0],[3,2]] using the same axes and eight reference records.
workbook.answer: Rows total 3,5; columns total 4,4; total 8; accuracy (2+3)/8=5/8=62.5 percent. The comparison matrix also scores 5/8, but has FP=0 and FN=3 rather than FP=1 and FN=2. Same accuracy can hide different error types.

workbook.title: Count a fresh evaluation independently
workbook.prompt: Each pair below is reference then prediction: R1 clear/clear, R2 clear/blocked, R3 clear/blocked, R4 blocked/blocked, R5 blocked/clear, R6 blocked/blocked. Use clear then blocked on both axes and reference rows. Build the matrix, give row and column totals, name TP,TN,FP,FN with blocked positive, and calculate accuracy.
workbook.answer: Matrix [[1,2],[1,2]]. Row totals 3,3; column totals 2,4; total 6. TP=2,TN=1,FP=2,FN=1. Accuracy (1+2)/6=3/6=50 percent. False alarms are R2,R3; the missed blocked case is R5.

workbook.title: Interpret a zero count carefully
workbook.prompt: A report gives zero false positives but omits the evaluated sample size, axes and class definitions. What information is missing, and why does zero not prove that future false alarms are impossible?
workbook.answer: Request split and sample size, labelled reference/prediction axes, class order and positive-class definition, plus the remaining counts. Zero describes only the observed evaluation cases; limited coverage or few negative cases may hide future errors. It is not a guarantee.

teacher.background: Teach two 45-minute sessions. Start with ID cards and a physical two-by-two table so students count matched pairs before learning abbreviations. Use blocked as positive consistently. Keep raw counts visible and postpone precision and recall formulas to later weeks.

Positive is the chosen condition of interest; blocked is positive in this exercise.
A matrix has one universal visual orientation
Check whether rows are references or predictions and inspect class order. Our convention uses reference rows and prediction columns.
Zero errors in a cell means no future risk
It is an observed count on one evaluation set. Coverage, sample size and future conditions still matter.

ai-3/14.title: Accuracy and class imbalance
goals: Explain why overall accuracy can hide failure on a less common class
Compare a training-majority baseline with class-specific results
Calculate an equal-class average and report its limits alongside the confusion matrix

prerequisite.prompt: With reference rows and prediction columns ordered clear then blocked, where are false negatives when blocked is positive?
prerequisite.answer: They are in the blocked-reference row and clear-prediction column: the lower-left cell. These are missed blocked cases.

vocabulary: Unequal numbers of examples in different classes
A rule that always predicts the most common training label
Correct predictions for one reference class divided by the number of examples of that class
The average of the class-specific correct fractions with equal weight for each class

lesson.title: Ask what the accuracy score leaves out

blocks.text: Accuracy counts all correct predictions and divides by all evaluated examples. Each example has equal weight, so a common class contributes more to the score. A high result can hide failure on a rare class. This week keeps the confusion matrix visible and checks both classes separately.

New fictional training data has 16 clear and 4 blocked labels. Its majority baseline predicts clear for every query; choose that rule from training, not evaluation labels. A separate evaluation set also contains 16 clear and 4 blocked cases. A frozen candidate and the baseline are evaluated on the same 20 records.

Rows are references and columns are predictions, ordered clear then blocked. Blocked is positive. Both methods get 16/20=80 percent accuracy. The baseline misses all four blocked cases. The candidate finds all four but falsely flags four clear cases. The same score conceals a different tradeoff.

lesson.title: Calculate two summaries from the same counts

blocks.title: Python 3 code
blocks.text:
def scores(counts):
    clear_n = sum(counts[0])
    blocked_n = sum(counts[1])
    if clear_n == 0 or blocked_n == 0:
        raise ValueError("Need evaluation examples of both classes")
    correct = counts[0][0] + counts[1][1]
    accuracy = correct / (clear_n + blocked_n)
    clear_fraction = counts[0][0] / clear_n
    blocked_fraction = counts[1][1] / blocked_n
    balanced = (clear_fraction + blocked_fraction) / 2
    return accuracy, balanced

baseline = [[16, 0], [4, 0]]
candidate = [[12, 4], [0, 4]]
for name, counts in [("baseline", baseline), ("candidate", candidate)]:
    accuracy, balanced = scores(counts)
    print(name, round(100 * accuracy, 1), round(100 * balanced, 1))

The output is baseline 80.0 50.0, then candidate 80.0 87.5. In each output line the first percentage is ordinary accuracy and the second is balanced accuracy. For the candidate, the clear-class correct fraction is 12/16=75 percent and the blocked-class fraction is 4/4=100 percent. Their equal average is 87.5 percent.

For the baseline, those fractions are 16/16=100 percent and 0/4=0 percent, averaging 50 percent. The code assumes a two-by-two table of nonnegative integer counts in the stated order. It stops when either reference class is absent. Then report the observed counts and the unavailable class result; do not invent a denominator or silently substitute zero.

lesson.title: Read the denominators before the percentage

blocks.title: Same overall score different class results
blocks.caption: Overall accuracy weights classes by their number of evaluation examples. Balanced accuracy gives the two class-specific fractions equal weight.

blocks.label: Both methods score 80 percent. Explain which cases the baseline fails, how the candidate changes the errors, and why their balanced accuracies differ.

blocks.text: Balanced accuracy is a metric choice, not a repair to the classifier or a guarantee of safety. It gives classes equal influence in this summary; it does not encode the actual consequences of false alarms and missed cases. Four blocked evaluation examples are also too few for a strong general claim.

Consider a separate illustrative set with 8 clear and 8 blocked cases. Suppose the same within-class fractions hold: the baseline matrix is [[8,0],[8,0]] and the candidate matrix is [[6,2],[0,8]]. Ordinary accuracy is now 50 percent versus 87.5 percent. Balanced accuracy remains 50 percent versus 87.5 percent. The class mix changed the overall score even though the within-class fractions stayed fixed.

This is an arithmetic comparison, not proof that a real classifier keeps the same behavior after a population change. Report sample size, class counts, full matrix and how the evaluation data was chosen. Do not remove inconvenient cases or duplicate rare evaluation cases just to improve a headline number. If training is resampled, keep that separate from evaluation and document it.

lesson.title: Make a comparison with honest limits

blocks.text: Compare methods on the same appropriate evaluation examples and report the training-derived baseline. Include ordinary accuracy, each class denominator, false positives and false negatives. An equal-class summary adds information but cannot choose the acceptable tradeoff for the task. Keep development decisions separate from a final test.

A result of 4/4 correct blocked cases is 100 percent on those four examples, not proof of perfect future detection. If the evaluated set contains no blocked cases, it cannot measure blocked-case performance at all. Next week separates precision and recall by asking which denominator answers each question.

blocks.label: A team advertises 80 percent accuracy but its classifier predicts clear on every record. What additional evidence would you request, and what can you already conclude about the four blocked cases in our worked evaluation?

workbook.title: Score the majority baseline
workbook.prompt: Training has 16 clear and 4 blocked labels. State the majority rule. On the worked evaluation, give its matrix, accuracy, false positives and false negatives with blocked positive. Explain why 80 percent is incomplete.
workbook.answer: The training-majority rule always predicts clear. Matrix [[16,0],[4,0]] gives 16/20=80 percent, FP=0,FN=4. It misses all four blocked cases, so the overall score hides complete failure on that evaluated class.

workbook.title: Compare both class fractions
workbook.prompt: For the worked candidate [[12,4],[0,4]], give ordinary accuracy, both class-specific correct fractions, balanced accuracy, false positives and false negatives. Compare with the baseline.
workbook.answer: Accuracy 16/20=80 percent. Clear fraction 12/16=75 percent; blocked fraction 4/4=100 percent; balanced accuracy (75+100)/2=87.5 percent. FP=4,FN=0. Baseline accuracy is also 80 percent but balanced accuracy is 50 percent with FP=0,FN=4.

workbook.title: Explain a changed class mix
workbook.prompt: For the illustrative 8-clear 8-blocked set, use baseline [[8,0],[8,0]] and candidate [[6,2],[0,8]]. Calculate ordinary and balanced accuracy for each. Explain what stayed fixed and what this example does not prove.
workbook.answer: Baseline ordinary 8/16=50 percent and balanced (100+0)/2=50 percent. Candidate ordinary 14/16=87.5 percent and balanced (75+100)/2=87.5 percent. Within-class fractions stayed fixed while class counts changed. This arithmetic assumption does not prove unchanged real-world behavior on a new population.

workbook.title: Assess a new comparison independently
workbook.prompt: New training labels have a clear majority. A separate evaluation has 18 clear and 2 blocked records. The always-clear baseline is [[18,0],[2,0]] and candidate is [[15,3],[1,1]], with reference rows and clear then blocked on both axes. Calculate ordinary accuracy, both class fractions and balanced accuracy for each. Give candidate FP and FN, then explain why the metrics do not choose an automatic winner.
workbook.answer: Baseline accuracy 18/20=90 percent; class fractions 100 percent and 0 percent; balanced accuracy 50 percent. Candidate accuracy 16/20=80 percent; clear fraction 15/18=5/6 about 83.3 percent, blocked fraction 1/2=50 percent; balanced accuracy (5/6+1/2)/2=2/3 about 66.7 percent. Candidate FP=3,FN=1. It finds one blocked case but adds three false alarms; task consequences and the small sample matter.

workbook.title: Limit claims from missing classes
workbook.prompt: An evaluation contains ten clear cases and no blocked cases. All predictions are clear. State ordinary accuracy, explain why blocked performance is unavailable, and describe how our code handles the missing class.
workbook.answer: Ordinary accuracy is 10/10=100 percent on the observed clear cases. The blocked-class fraction has denominator zero, so it cannot be measured. Our two-class summary function stops with ValueError; report the missing coverage instead of claiming perfect performance on both classes.

Introduce balanced accuracy as an equal average of two correct fractions, without treating it as a universal replacement for task-specific evaluation.

ai-3/15.title: Precision recall and denominators
goals: Choose the denominator that answers the question
Calculate precision and recall with a declared positive class
Report undefined ratios honestly

prerequisite.prompt: Why can 80 percent accuracy hide missed blocked cases?
prerequisite.answer: The common class can dominate the total; inspect the full confusion matrix and class counts.

vocabulary: True positives divided by all predicted positives
True positives divided by all reference positives
The group counted in the bottom of a fraction
A ratio with no valid value because its denominator is zero

blocks.text: Blocked remains positive. Precision asks: of the cases flagged blocked, how many were actually blocked according to the reference? Recall asks: of all reference-blocked cases, how many were found? Both use true positives, but they answer different questions. Keep reference rows and prediction columns ordered clear then blocked.

Use fictional classroom data throughout this investigation. Keep the task, units, reference labels and data split visible as you reason. Earlier weeks supplied the model-building process; this week examines precision recall and denominators.

For matrix [[12, 4],[1, 3]], TN=12, FP=4, FN=1, TP=3. There are seven predicted positives and four reference positives. Precision is 3/7, about 42.9 percent. Recall is 3/4=75 percent. Accuracy is 15/20=75 percent. A correct denominator matters more than memorizing a percentage.

blocks.title: Python 3 check
blocks.text:
tn, fp, fn, tp = 12, 4, 1, 3
precision = tp / (tp + fp) if tp + fp else None
recall = tp / (tp + fn) if tp + fn else None
accuracy = (tn + tp) / (tn + fp + fn + tp)
print(precision, recall, accuracy)
# None means unavailable, not zero or perfect.

Trace the calculation on paper before running this optional Python check. Use the stated fictional inputs and compare intermediate values. The code checks this example; your independent workbook case uses different evidence.

blocks.title: Precision recall and denominators at a glance
blocks.caption: Draw a box around the predicted-blocked column for precision and around the reference-blocked row for recall. Their overlap is TP. A model can flag nearly everything and find most blocked cases while producing many false alarms. Conversely, a model can flag very few cases accurately while missing many positives.

blocks.label: Calculate precision, recall and accuracy for the worked matrix. Explain the steps or evidence behind your response.

blocks.text: With [[16, 0],[4, 0]], there are no predicted positives. Precision is undefined because its denominator is zero; recall is 0/4=0. With [[16, 4],[0, 0]], recall is undefined because no reference positives were evaluated. Record counts and the undefined result instead of calling it perfect.

Ratios describe this evaluation set, not a guarantee for an individual case. Library zero-division policies differ; document yours. Do not select a metric only after seeing which one makes a model look best.

blocks.label: A team reports recall 100 percent but hides precision and counts. What is missing?

workbook.title: Calculate both ratios
workbook.prompt: Calculate precision, recall and accuracy for the worked matrix.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Precision 3/7 about 42.9 percent, recall 3/4=75 percent, accuracy 15/20=75 percent.

workbook.prompt: Explain precision and recall for [[16, 0],[4, 0]].
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Precision is undefined, with no flags; recall is 0/4=0. This does not mean excellent detection.

workbook.title: Apply independently
workbook.prompt: Use [[8, 2],[3, 6]]. Give TP, FP, FN, precision, recall and accuracy.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: TP=6, FP=2, FN=3. Precision 6/8=75 percent; recall 6/9 about 66.7 percent; accuracy 14/19 about 73.7 percent.

workbook.prompt: A team reports recall 100 percent but hides precision and counts. What is missing?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Request TP, FP, FN, sample size, positive class and precision. Finding every positive can coexist with many false alarms.
