ai-3/16.title: Thresholds and consequences
goals: Apply a declared score threshold including equality
Compare false alarms and misses at two thresholds
Separate validation choices from final testing

prerequisite.prompt: Which denominator defines recall?
prerequisite.answer: All reference positives, TP+FN.

vocabulary: A model output used to rank or decide
A boundary that converts a score to a label
A positive prediction for a negative reference
A declared way to value different mistakes

blocks.text: A classifier score is not automatically a probability. Declare blocked positive and predict blocked when score is at least the threshold. Changing this boundary changes decisions without necessarily retraining the model. Select it using development evidence and a task-relevant rule, not final-test answers.

Use fictional classroom data throughout this investigation. Keep the task, units, reference labels and data split visible as you reason. Earlier weeks supplied the model-building process; this week examines thresholds and consequences.

Six records have score/reference pairs A .9/blocked, B .7/clear, C .6/blocked, D .4/blocked, E .3/clear, F .1/clear. At threshold .5, TP=2, FP=1, FN=1, TN=2. At .3, TP=3, FP=2, FN=0, TN=1. Equality is positive, so E is flagged at .3.

blocks.title: Python 3 check
blocks.text:
scores = [0.9, 0.7, 0.6, 0.4, 0.3, 0.1]
actual = [True, False, True, True, False, False]
for threshold in [0.5, 0.3]:
    predicted = [s >= threshold for s in scores]
    fp = sum(p and not a for p, a in zip(predicted, actual))
    fn = sum(not p and a for p, a in zip(predicted, actual))
    print(threshold, fp, fn, fp + 4 * fn)
# Output rows: 0.5 1 1 5, then 0.3 2 0 2.

Trace the calculation on paper before running this optional Python check. Use the stated fictional inputs and compare intermediate values. The code checks this example; your independent workbook case uses different evidence.

blocks.title: Thresholds and consequences at a glance
blocks.caption: Lowering the threshold here finds D but adds E as a false alarm. The two accuracies are equal while consequences differ. Precision is 2/3 at .5 and 3/5 at .3; recall rises from 2/3 to 1. This behavior follows these fixed scores and records, not a promise of future performance.

blocks.label: Give TP, FP, FN, TN at both thresholds. Explain the steps or evidence behind your response.

blocks.text: Suppose the classroom cost is one point per false alarm and four per miss. Total costs are 5 at .5 and 2 at .3, so .3 wins among these two candidates under this rule. If false alarms cost four and misses cost one, costs are 5 and 8, reversing the choice.

These invented costs support arithmetic practice, not real robot deployment. Stakeholders must justify actual consequences. Record every tried threshold and retain a separate final test; a threshold is part of the selected method.

blocks.label: Why not select the threshold with the lowest final-test cost?

workbook.title: Apply the boundary
workbook.prompt: Which IDs are positive at .5 and .3?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: At .5: A, B, C. At .3: A, B, C, D, E, including equality.

workbook.title: Count the consequences
workbook.prompt: Give TP, FP, FN, TN at both thresholds.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: At .5: 2, 1, 1, 2. At .3: 3, 2, 0, 1.

workbook.title: Use the declared cost
workbook.prompt: Calculate costs with FP cost 1 and FN cost 4.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Costs are 1+4=5 and 2+0=2; .3 is preferred among these candidates.

workbook.title: Apply independently
workbook.prompt: Scores/references are .8/blocked,.5/clear,.2/blocked,.1/clear. Compare thresholds .5 and .2 using the same cost.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: At .5 TP 1 FP 1 FN 1 TN 1 cost 5. At .2 TP 2 FP 1 FN 0 TN 1 cost 1. Equality is positive at both boundaries.

workbook.title: Protect the final test
workbook.prompt: Why not select the threshold with the lowest final-test cost?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Selection uses the test answers, turning the test into development data and weakening its independent evaluation role.

Fresh retry .9/clear,.6/blocked,.4/clear,.2/blocked at threshold .4: TP 1 FP 2 FN 1 TN 0, cost 6 under FP 1 FN 4. Require equality and all counts. Mark each criterion as independent, supported or not yet demonstrated. Reassess the reasoning after feedback; do not replace the first attempt silently.

Use score and threshold in full sentences. Extension: alter one condition in the worked example and explain which conclusion changes and which remains supported.

ai-3/17.title: Calibration as a group property
goals: Interpret calibration using groups of forecasts
Compare average predicted probability with observed frequency
Distinguish calibration from individual correctness

prerequisite.prompt: Does a score necessarily represent a probability?
prerequisite.answer: No. Its interpretation must be established; a threshold can act on a score without making it a calibrated probability.

vocabulary: Agreement between predicted probabilities and outcome frequencies across comparable groups
Positive outcomes divided by cases in a group
A plot comparing group average prediction with observed frequency

blocks.text: If many comparable cases receive probability .8, a calibrated model should produce positives in roughly 80 percent of those cases over adequate data. It does not mean every case is 80 percent correct or that exactly eight of each next ten must be positive. Calibration is assessed across groups.

Use fictional classroom data throughout this investigation. Keep the task, units, reference labels and data split visible as you reason. Earlier weeks supplied the model-building process; this week examines calibration as a group property.

In a fictional held-out check, ten cases all have predicted probability .2 and two are positive. Another ten all have probability .8 and six are positive. Average predictions are .2 and .8; observed frequencies are 2/10=.2 and 6/10=.6. The second group is overconfident for positives in this sample.

blocks.title: Python 3 check

blocks.text: Trace the calculation on paper before running this optional Python check. Use the stated fictional inputs and compare intermediate values. The code checks this example; your independent workbook case uses different evidence.

blocks.title: Calibration as a group property at a glance
blocks.caption: Plot average prediction on the horizontal axis and observed frequency on the vertical axis. The two points are (.2,.2) and (.8,.6). Agreement lies along the diagonal. Use the average score within a bin, not automatically the bin midpoint. Small groups make frequencies uncertain.

blocks.label: Which worked group overstates positive frequency and by how much? Explain the steps or evidence behind your response.

blocks.text: If every case gets .5 and exactly half are positive, overall calibration can look good while the model cannot rank easy and difficult cases. Conversely, useful ranking can coexist with poor probabilities. Report discrimination and calibration separately. Fit any calibration adjustment on development data reserved for that purpose, then evaluate on separate data.

Bin boundaries, group sizes and dataset coverage affect the picture. Do not fit adjustments on the final test or claim certainty from a small bin. Real distributions can change, and a calibrated model on one population may not remain so elsewhere.

blocks.label: What is wrong with calibrating and reporting success on the same final-test records?

workbook.title: Compute frequencies
workbook.prompt: Give the observed frequencies for the two worked groups.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: 2/10=.2 and 6/10=.6.

workbook.title: Locate the discrepancy
workbook.prompt: Which worked group overstates positive frequency and by how much?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: The .8 group exceeds observed .6 by .2, or 20 percentage points in this sample.

workbook.title: Separate ranking
workbook.prompt: Why can constant .5 predictions look calibrated but rank poorly?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: When half the cases are positive, the overall fraction agrees, but every case has the same score and no ranking is provided.

workbook.title: Apply independently
workbook.prompt: Twenty cases all predict .3 with eight positives; ten all predict .7 with seven positives. Give plot points and interpret.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Points (.3,.4) and (.7,.7). The first understates observed frequency by .1; the second agrees on this sample. Group sizes still limit claims.

workbook.title: Protect evaluation
workbook.prompt: What is wrong with calibrating and reporting success on the same final-test records?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: The reported improvement reuses the answers used for adjustment; evaluate the frozen adjustment on separate data.

ai-3/18.title: Error analysis and controlled follow-up
goals: Categorize development errors using evidence
Design a controlled change with a stated hypothesis
Preserve failures and test boundaries

prerequisite.prompt: What does a confusion matrix omit?
prerequisite.answer: It counts outcome combinations but does not explain the causes of individual errors.

vocabulary: Inspection of mistakes to propose explanations
A comparison that changes one planned factor while holding relevant conditions fixed
A new failure introduced by a change

blocks.text: Error analysis begins with prediction IDs and reference labels. Inspect features, collection conditions and the labelling policy. Do not assume every surprising prediction proves the reference is wrong. Use development errors to propose a change and specify what outcome would support the explanation.

Use fictional classroom data throughout this investigation. Keep the task, units, reference labels and data split visible as you reason. Earlier weeks supplied the model-building process; this week examines error analysis and controlled follow-up.

A validation audit has 12 dim-light cases with 4 errors and 18 bright-light cases with 3 errors. Rates are 4/12=1/3 and 3/18=1/6. Dim lighting is a useful lead, not proof of causation: camera, route or labels may also differ. A planned change uses a training-fitted brightness normalization while keeping split and classifier settings fixed.

blocks.title: Python 3 check
blocks.text:
old_errors = [4, 3]
new_errors = [2, 4]
counts = [12, 18]
for old, new, n in zip(old_errors, new_errors, counts):
    print(old / n, new / n)
print(sum(old_errors), sum(new_errors))
# Total errors fall from 7 to 6; one group worsens.

Trace the calculation on paper before running this optional Python check. Use the stated fictional inputs and compare intermediate values. The code checks this example; your independent workbook case uses different evidence.

blocks.title: Error analysis and controlled follow-up at a glance
blocks.caption: After the change, the same validation groups have 2/12 and 4/18 errors. Total errors fall from 7 to 6, but bright-light errors increase from 3 to 4. Report both results. A net improvement does not mean every part improved, and repeated experiments can overfit validation.

blocks.label: Does the difference prove dim light causes model errors? Explain the steps or evidence behind your response.

blocks.text: Write a change record: hypothesis, exact code/data version, controlled factors, predicted effect, full before/after results and decision. Review disagreements using a consistent annotation policy. If labels are corrected, version the data and rerun all candidates on the same corrected evaluation set.

Do not delete difficult cases to raise the score or reuse final-test errors for an unreported revision. Once test feedback guides a change, treat it as development evidence and obtain a new independent evaluation for a fresh final claim.

blocks.label: A team removes all disputed records only from the new model report. Why is the comparison invalid?

workbook.title: Find the rates
workbook.prompt: Calculate the original error rates by lighting condition.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Dim 4/12 about 33.3 percent; bright 3/18 about 16.7 percent.

workbook.title: Explain the limit
workbook.prompt: Does the difference prove dim light causes model errors?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: No. Other conditions and label quality may differ; it motivates a hypothesis.

workbook.title: Track regressions
workbook.prompt: Summarize the changed results without hiding a regression.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Total errors 7 to 6; dim 4 to 2 improves, bright 3 to 4 worsens.

workbook.title: Apply independently
workbook.prompt: Old errors are 5/10 on route A and 2/20 on B. New errors are 3/10 and 5/20. State total and group changes and a justified next step.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Total worsens 7/30 to 8/30. A improves 50 to 30 percent, B worsens 10 to 25 percent. Investigate B and keep the original as a comparison; do not claim overall improvement.

workbook.title: Repair a misleading audit
workbook.prompt: A team removes all disputed records only from the new model report. Why is the comparison invalid?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: The models are evaluated on different selected records. Apply one documented review policy and compare both on the same versioned set.

ai-3/19.title: Regression and residuals
goals: Distinguish numeric prediction from classification
Calculate signed residuals with a stated convention
Use residual patterns to question a model

prerequisite.prompt: What does a class label predict?
prerequisite.answer: A category; regression predicts a numeric target instead.

vocabulary: Observed target minus predicted target in this course
A prediction below the observed value
A prediction above the observed value

blocks.text: A school garden example predicts plant height in cm from recorded conditions. The target is numeric, so a prediction can be too high or too low by different amounts. Define residual as observed minus predicted. Keep units and the sign convention visible; some software uses the opposite error convention.

Use fictional classroom data throughout this investigation. Keep the task, units, reference labels and data split visible as you reason. Earlier weeks supplied the model-building process; this week examines regression and residuals.

Observed heights [4, 7, 9] cm and predictions [5, 6, 9] cm give residuals [-1, 1, 0] cm. The first prediction is too high, the second too low and the third exact. Mean signed residual is zero, yet two predictions are wrong. Opposite errors can cancel.

blocks.title: Python 3 check
blocks.text:
observed = [4, 7, 9]
predicted = [5, 6, 9]
residuals = [y - p for y, p in zip(observed, predicted)]
print(residuals)
print(sum(residuals) / len(residuals))
# Output: [-1, 1, 0] and 0.0.
# Opposite signed errors can cancel.

Trace the calculation on paper before running this optional Python check. Use the stated fictional inputs and compare intermediate values. The code checks this example; your independent workbook case uses different evidence.

blocks.title: Regression and residuals at a glance
blocks.caption: To inspect a residual plot, place a feature or prediction on the horizontal axis and residual on the vertical axis. A trend can suggest a missed relationship. It does not by itself identify the cause or validate a new model. Use development data for analysis and preserve an independent final test.

blocks.label: Why does mean residual zero not imply perfect predictions? Explain the steps or evidence behind your response.

blocks.text: If predictions for early, middle and late growth have residuals -2, 0, 3 cm, the model moves from overpredicting to underpredicting across those records. Investigate whether a straight-line assumption or a missing condition could explain it. Check measurement consistency before adding complexity.

A residual of zero is an agreement with the measured target, not proof that the measurement is perfect. Do not compare errors measured in cm directly with errors measured in metres. Keep the same row pairing, unit and sign convention throughout.

blocks.label: A report combines 2 cm and .02 m as if they were different magnitudes. Repair it.

workbook.title: Calculate residuals
workbook.prompt: Compute the worked residuals and identify overprediction.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Residuals -1, 1, 0 cm; the first record is overpredicted.

workbook.title: Explain cancellation
workbook.prompt: Why does mean residual zero not imply perfect predictions?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Negative and positive residuals cancel even when individual errors are nonzero.

workbook.title: Read a pattern
workbook.prompt: Interpret residuals -2, 0, 3 ordered by growth stage.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: They shift from overprediction to underprediction; investigate a missed relationship without claiming a proven cause.

workbook.title: Apply independently
workbook.prompt: Observed [6, 10, 13], predicted [8, 9, 11] cm. Give residuals, mean residual and error directions.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Residuals [-2, 1, 2] cm; mean 1/3 cm. First overpredicted, others underpredicted.

workbook.title: Check units
workbook.prompt: A report combines 2 cm and .02 m as if they were different magnitudes. Repair it.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Convert to a shared unit; both represent 2 cm. Document units before comparing or aggregating errors.

ai-3/2.title: Features labels and prediction time
goals: Separate prediction inputs from observed targets
Check whether each feature exists at prediction time
Repair target leakage and state a feature contract

prerequisite.prompt: Why must held out labels not be used to choose the threshold in Week 1?
prerequisite.answer: They are reserved to evaluate the fixed choice. Using their labels to choose it makes them part of development.

vocabulary: A specification of input meaning units order and timing
The outcome a prediction aims to estimate
The moment when the prediction must be made
Predictor information that reveals the outcome but is unavailable at prediction time

blocks.text: Week 1 separated training examples from testing examples. This week asks a different question: could each input actually be known when a prediction is needed? A historical table may contain facts added after the event. A model trained with those facts can appear successful even though the inputs will be missing when it is used.

Use fictional library loans. At the instant a book is checked out, predict whether it will be returned more than 14 days later. For completed historical loans, label 1 means days_to_return is greater than 14; label 0 means it is at most 14. Exactly 14 days is on time. Assume no changed due dates in this exercise. All records and values are invented; do not collect classmates' borrowing histories.

queue_at_checkout is a saved count of waiting requests at that instant. It is not the queue when we later export the table. Candidate means available to consider, not proven useful or appropriate. Exclude the arbitrary loan identifier from this exercise; keep it separately to track records.

blocks.title: Python 3 code

blocks.text: The feature order is always pages first, queue count second. The first output is [120, 2]; the separate label is 1 because this historical loan took 18 days. The new loan produces [80, 0] even though its return outcome does not yet exist. The same feature function serves past and new records. It deliberately selects allowed fields rather than copying every column except returned_late.

blocks.title: Follow information through time
blocks.caption: The outcome may teach the model during training, but it cannot be an input to an earlier checkout prediction.

blocks.text: This code prepares inputs; it does not fit a model or predict lateness. It assumes the two feature fields contain valid nonnegative integer values and pages is positive. A missing required field raises KeyError. A real pipeline needs explicit validation and a missing-data policy.

For every proposed input, ask what it means, when it was recorded, and whether the same definition can be supplied at checkout. A field in the historical export is not automatically available at prediction time. An input calculated from later information is also unavailable, even if its name does not mention the outcome.

blocks.label: A completed loan has pages 200, queue_at_checkout 3 and days_to_return 14. Write the feature list and label. Someone adds overdue_fee calculated after return. Can it become a feature for the checkout prediction? Explain.

blocks.text: A learner removes returned_late but keeps days_to_return in the inputs. That still reveals the answer: compare days_to_return with 14. Remove both the target and the later return measurement from prediction inputs. Also exclude a fee calculated after return or a renewal made after checkout. These are examples of target leakage, where unavailable outcome information enters the predictors.

Moving rows into a test set does not repair this problem if each test row still contains the later return measurement. Rebuild the inputs to match checkout time and repeat development and evaluation honestly. If earlier test results influenced changes, obtain a new final evaluation set as well.

lesson.title: State the contract and its limits

blocks.text: A feature contract records field names, meaning, units, order and availability time. Here the inputs are pages in pages, then queue_at_checkout in requests, both captured at checkout. The target definition is returned more than 14 days later. Historical outcomes may be available for training, while new outcomes are unknown. Never fill an unknown label with 0 merely because the book has not yet been returned.

Availability alone does not establish predictive value, fairness, a causal effect or a reason to use a model. This lesson audits inputs; later lessons evaluate models. If an input cannot be collected at checkout, revise the design or specify a justified missing-input policy before use.

blocks.label: Write a two-sentence input contract for this checkout task. Include the feature order and timing, then explain why an unknown future outcome must not be recorded as an on-time return.

workbook.title: Assign the roles
workbook.prompt: For the worked loan table, identify the two candidate features, the target label and the tracking field. Explain why days_to_return is not a predictor.
workbook.answer: Candidate features are pages and queue_at_checkout. The target is returned_late and the tracking field is loan_id. days_to_return is known only after return and directly defines the target, so it must not enter checkout predictions.

workbook.title: Trace the feature contract
workbook.prompt: A completed loan has pages 96, queue_at_checkout 4 and days_to_return 14. Give the ordered feature list and target. Then state what changes if it took 15 days instead.
workbook.answer: The feature list is [96, 4]. At 14 days the target is 0. At 15 days the target becomes 1; the checkout feature list remains [96, 4].

workbook.title: Repair a misleading score
workbook.prompt: A model has every test prediction correct after using pages and days_to_return. A learner says a separate test set makes this valid. Explain the flaw and repair the inputs.
workbook.answer: The test rows contain future information that reveals the label. Separate rows do not make days_to_return available at checkout. Remove later outcome fields, use the checkout feature contract, and rerun development and evaluation with honest records.

workbook.title: Audit a new task independently
workbook.prompt: A fictional robot predicts at dispatch whether a parcel trip will take more than 10 minutes. Fields are route_steps and queue_at_dispatch captured at dispatch, trip_id for tracking, arrival_minutes measured after arrival, and slow = 1 when arrival_minutes > 10. Specify inputs, order, target and exclusions. For a past trip with steps 30, queue 2, arrival 10, give features and label. For a new trip with steps 24 and queue 0, give features and explain whether slow is known.
workbook.answer: Use [route_steps, queue_at_dispatch] in that order, measured in steps and queued trips at dispatch. slow is the target. Keep trip_id as tracking metadata; exclude arrival_minutes and slow from inputs. Past features are [30, 2] with label 0 because 10 is not greater than 10. New features are [24, 0]; slow is unknown until the outcome can be established.

workbook.title: Handle an unavailable input
workbook.prompt: For the robot task, a dataset stores queue_now at export time but has no saved queue_at_dispatch. Can you rename that field to make it usable? State a defensible next step.
workbook.answer: Renaming does not restore the missing dispatch-time value. Recover a reliable timestamped dispatch snapshot if available, or remove the feature and reevaluate the revised design. Do not invent a zero queue or copy the later count.

teacher.background: Teach features, labels and prediction time in two 45-minute sessions using fictional records. Students must define the decision moment before judging columns. The key distinction is that labels may be known for historical training but must not be fed into predictions for new cases. This lesson prepares inputs; it does not demonstrate a trained model or establish that loan prediction is useful. Use paper records or local Python, without accounts or personal borrowing data.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook
Two cards labelled checkout and later return
Optional Python 3 editor; no external packages
Blank field meaning unit availability role table
sessions: Recall why held out labels must not choose the Week 1 threshold. Connect separate examples to the separate question of input availability.
State the checkout moment and label boundary. Place each field on the timeline. Explain why an arbitrary identifier can stay as metadata without becoming an input.
Trace the feature function on past and new records. Complete W1 and W2. Require the correct order and the 14 versus 15 day distinction.
Complete the guided 200-page loan and fee question. Ask which fields are unknown on a new checkout and why unknown does not mean zero.
Retrieve the contract: names, units, order and availability time. Ask students to explain one later field without using only the word leakage.
Use W3 to challenge a perfect test score. Trace how days_to_return reveals the answer even on separate test rows.
Collect W4 independently. Require inputs, target, exclusions, boundary answer and unknown-outcome explanation before giving hints.
Discuss W5 and the exit contract. Use the fresh retry after support where needed and record the support given.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided: the ordered inputs are [200, 3] and the observed label is 0 at exactly 14 days. The fee is calculated later and cannot be used for an earlier checkout prediction. Exit example: use [pages, queue_at_checkout], in pages and requests, both recorded at checkout. An unknown future return outcome is not evidence of an on-time return and must not be silently labelled 0.
misconceptions: Every stored column is a feature
A historical export combines information from different times. Require a meaning and timestamp before treating a column as an input.
Removing the label column removes leakage
days_to_return and an outcome-based fee may still disclose the target. Audit how every field was created.
An unknown outcome is a negative label
Unknown means not established. In this exercise labels come from completed historical returns. Do not turn unavailable outcomes into on-time labels.
teacher.assessment: Require W4 features [30, 2], target 0, new features [24, 0], unknown new target, and the timing reason for exclusions. A column list without timing justification is insufficient. Fresh retry: at print-job submission, predict whether completion takes more than 5 minutes. Inputs are page_count then queue_at_submit. A completed job has 12 pages, queue 1, completion_minutes 6: inputs [12, 1], label 1. A new job has 8 pages, queue 0: inputs [8, 0], label unknown. Exclude completion_minutes and the label from inputs; keep job_id as metadata. Exactly 5 minutes would have label 0.
teacher.support: Place field cards before or after the prediction-time line. Supply an empty contract table, not completed answers. Extension: a queue measurement is recorded before checkout but overwritten at export. Explain why its current value is not necessarily the original snapshot, and propose retaining timestamped history.

ai-3/20.title: Constant prediction baselines
goals: Fit mean and median constant baselines on training targets
Compare constant predictions on separate records
Keep fitted constants independent of evaluation answers

prerequisite.prompt: Why can signed residuals hide error size?
prerequisite.answer: Opposite signs can cancel; a magnitude-based loss avoids that cancellation.

vocabulary: One fixed prediction for every query
Sum of training targets divided by their count
Middle value of sorted training targets

blocks.text: Before a complex regression model, fit a simple constant predictor. A mean baseline uses the training average. A median baseline uses the middle training target. They ignore features but provide a comparison that is easy to reproduce. Evaluation targets must not determine the constants.

Use fictional classroom data throughout this investigation. Keep the task, units, reference labels and data split visible as you reason. Earlier weeks supplied the model-building process; this week examines constant prediction baselines.

Training targets [2, 4, 6, 12] have mean 24/4=6 and median (4+6)/2=5. On separate targets [4, 8], the mean baseline predicts [6, 6] with absolute errors [2, 2], averaging 2. The median baseline predicts [5, 5] with errors [1, 3], also averaging 2.

blocks.title: Python 3 check
blocks.text:
from statistics import mean, median
training = [2, 4, 6, 12]
validation = [4, 8]
for name, value in [("mean", mean(training)),
                    ("median", median(training))]:
    mae = mean(abs(y - value) for y in validation)
    print(name, value, mae)
# Both validation MAEs are 2; constants differ.

Trace the calculation on paper before running this optional Python check. Use the stated fictional inputs and compare intermediate values. The code checks this example; your independent workbook case uses different evidence.

blocks.title: Constant prediction baselines at a glance
blocks.caption: Mean and median answer different training objectives. A mean minimizes total squared error among constants; a median minimizes total absolute error. This does not guarantee either wins on a new evaluation set. With extreme values, the mean can move much more than the median.

blocks.label: Calculate MAE for both baselines on [4, 8]. Explain the steps or evidence behind your response.

blocks.text: Replacing training 12 by 40 gives mean 13 and median 5. That change is a data change to record and investigate, not an instruction to delete an inconvenient observation. Decide whether the extreme value is valid using the measurement policy and provenance.

For an even number of values, this course averages the two middle values to report one median. Keep a frozen baseline across comparisons and show its evaluation score. A model that fails to beat it may still reveal a data or metric issue worth investigating.

workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Both score 2; their per-record absolute errors differ.

workbook.title: Inspect an extreme value

workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Mean becomes 13; median stays 5. Investigate validity before deciding treatment.

workbook.title: Apply independently
workbook.prompt: Training [1, 3, 5, 15], evaluation [3, 9]. Fit both constants and calculate MAE.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Mean 6 and median 4. Mean errors [3, 3] MAE 3; median errors [1, 5] MAE 3.

workbook.title: Prevent leakage
workbook.prompt: Why not predict the evaluation mean as the baseline?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: It fits using evaluation answers and makes the baseline unavailable for genuinely unseen cases.

ai-3/21.title: Absolute and squared loss
goals: Calculate MAE MSE and RMSE
Explain how squaring changes sensitivity to large errors
Match the loss and units to the task

prerequisite.prompt: Which constant minimizes training squared error?
prerequisite.answer: The training mean among all constant predictions.

vocabulary: Square root of mean squared error
A numerical penalty for prediction errors

blocks.text: A loss summarizes error magnitude without positive and negative cancellation. MAE averages absolute residuals. MSE averages squared residuals and penalizes large magnitudes more strongly. RMSE takes the square root of MSE so it returns to the target unit. These are different questions, not interchangeable labels.

Use fictional classroom data throughout this investigation. Keep the task, units, reference labels and data split visible as you reason. Earlier weeks supplied the model-building process; this week examines absolute and squared loss.

Residuals [-1, 2,-3] cm have absolute errors [1, 2, 3], so MAE=6/3=2 cm. Squared errors [1, 4, 9] sum to 14, so MSE=14/3 square cm and RMSE=sqrt(14/3), about 2.16 cm. Keep the square and the average in the correct order.

blocks.title: Python 3 check
blocks.text:
from math import sqrt
residuals = [-1, 2, -3]
mae = sum(abs(r) for r in residuals) / len(residuals)
mse = sum(r * r for r in residuals) / len(residuals)
print(mae, mse, sqrt(mse))
# About 2.0, 4.67, 2.16.
# MAE and RMSE: cm. MSE: square cm.

Trace the calculation on paper before running this optional Python check. Use the stated fictional inputs and compare intermediate values. The code checks this example; your independent workbook case uses different evidence.

blocks.title: Absolute and squared loss at a glance
blocks.caption: Model A has residuals [0, 0, 6]; model B has [2, 2, 2]. Both MAEs are 2, but MSEs are 12 and 4. Squaring distinguishes concentrated large errors from evenly spread smaller errors. Which pattern matters depends on the task and consequences.

blocks.label: Give MSE and RMSE with units. Explain the steps or evidence behind your response.

blocks.text: Changing cm to mm multiplies residuals and MAE/RMSE by 10, but MSE by 100. A loss decrease across reports is not meaningful unless units, evaluated rows and loss definitions match. Retain the per-record residuals for investigation.

Choose and document the comparison metric before reviewing final-test results. Neither MAE nor MSE reveals all subgroup patterns or proves safety. Do not remove a large valid error solely because it worsens squared loss.

ai-3/22.title: Fitting a line
goals: Fit a line from a declared training candidate set
Separate training loss from validation comparison
Interpret slope and intercept with units

prerequisite.prompt: How is MSE calculated?
prerequisite.answer: Square each residual, sum, then divide by the number of evaluated examples.

vocabulary: Change in predicted target per unit change in x
Predicted target when x is zero
Selecting model values using training evidence

blocks.text: A line predicts y as m*x+b. In this classroom search we compare a small declared set of slopes and intercepts; this is not a full least-squares solver over all possible lines. Use training error to choose a candidate, then freeze it before validation.

Use fictional classroom data throughout this investigation. Keep the task, units, reference labels and data split visible as you reason. Earlier weeks supplied the model-building process; this week examines fitting a line.

Training pairs are (0, 1),(1, 3),(2, 5). Candidate A has m 1 b 1, B m 2 b 0, C m 2 b 1. Predictions are A [1, 2, 3], B [0, 2, 4], C [1, 3, 5]. Training squared-error sums are 5, 3, 0 respectively, so choose C. Ties would use the earlier listed candidate.

blocks.title: Python 3 check
blocks.text:
training = [(0, 1), (1, 3), (2, 5)]
candidates = [(1, 1), (2, 0), (2, 1)]
def sse(line):
    m, b = line
    return sum((y - (m * x + b)) ** 2 for x, y in training)
chosen = min(candidates, key=sse)
print([sse(line) for line in candidates])
print(chosen)
# [5, 3, 0], then (2, 1); first candidate wins ties.

Trace the calculation on paper before running this optional Python check. Use the stated fictional inputs and compare intermediate values. The code checks this example; your independent workbook case uses different evidence.

blocks.title: Fitting a line at a glance
blocks.caption: For separate validation pairs (3, 6),(4, 10), C predicts [7, 9], giving residuals [-1, 1], MAE 1 and MSE 1. The training-mean constant baseline is 3 and gives residuals [3, 7], MAE 5 and MSE 29. The fitted line wins on this small evaluation, without proving performance elsewhere.

blocks.label: Predict at x 3 and x 4 and calculate MAE/MSE. Explain the steps or evidence behind your response.

blocks.text: If x measures days and y measures cm, slope 2 means two predicted cm per day and intercept 1 means one predicted cm at day zero. Predicting far outside the observed x range is extrapolation and may fail even when the training fit is exact.

Record candidates, training rows, tie policy and chosen parameters. Do not add a candidate after seeing validation and report it as if only the original search happened. A zero training loss can coexist with validation mistakes.

ai-3/23.title: Validation and model selection
goals: Select a model using a declared validation rule
Keep training, validation and test roles separate
Recognize repeated validation as development

prerequisite.prompt: Which data fitted the line last week?
prerequisite.answer: Training rows fitted parameters; separate validation rows compared performance.

vocabulary: Development evidence used to choose between options
A model setting chosen outside its fitted parameters
A declared method for choosing an option
Held-out evidence reserved for a final evaluation

blocks.text: Fitting and selecting answer different questions. Training adjusts parameters. Validation helps choose settings or model families. A final test estimates the performance of the frozen development process on held-out examples. Keep related records in the same split when separate rows could reveal the same source.

Use fictional classroom data throughout this investigation. Keep the task, units, reference labels and data split visible as you reason. Earlier weeks supplied the model-building process; this week examines validation and model selection.

Three candidates have training MAE A=1, B=0, C=2 and validation MAE A=3, B=5, C=3. The declared rule is smallest validation MAE, then simpler model, with A simpler than C. Choose A. B fits training perfectly but does worse on validation. The final test remains unopened.

Before continuing, underline the decision rule and circle the evidence that supports the conclusion. Explain the example to a partner without replacing the counts or conditions with a stronger claim. Keep the distinction between an observed result and a proposed next step.

blocks.title: Validation and model selection at a glance
blocks.caption: A tie policy prevents a convenient choice after inspecting results. Equal validation scores do not prove equal future performance. Record candidate settings, split identifiers, preprocessing and the full comparison, including rejected options.

blocks.label: Where should parameter fitting, setting selection and final reporting occur? Explain the steps or evidence behind your response.

blocks.text: If you inspect validation errors and invent candidate D, that is another development attempt. Log it. Repeated experiments can adapt to peculiarities of validation. Do not rename validation as an untouched test. More rows alone do not repair duplicated groups or future information leaking into inputs.

A low score is meaningful only with its unit, metric, evaluated population and baseline. Decide how to handle ties and missing predictions before comparison. If no appropriate final test exists, state that limitation and keep claims about validation.

ai-3/24.title: Final testing and honest claims
goals: Freeze the full evaluation procedure before testing
Report a held-out result with counts and limitations
Recognize when test feedback has become development

prerequisite.prompt: Why is validation not an untouched final test?
prerequisite.answer: It influenced choices during development.

vocabulary: Record a fixed model and procedure before testing
A record of where data and results came from
A statement whose scope must match its evidence

blocks.text: A final test is valuable because it did not guide model choices. Freeze the model, training preprocessing, threshold, metric, missing-prediction policy and test membership. Record the version before opening test labels. A classroom result is evidence about a small chosen set, not approval for deployment.

Use fictional classroom data throughout this investigation. Keep the task, units, reference labels and data split visible as you reason. Earlier weeks supplied the model-building process; this week examines final testing and honest claims.

A frozen classifier is tested on 20 fictional cases: TN 12 FP 2 FN 3 TP 3, blocked positive. Accuracy is 15/20=75 percent, precision 3/5=60 percent and recall 3/6=50 percent. Its previously fitted always-clear baseline gets 14/20=70 percent. The candidate improves accuracy here but misses half the blocked cases.

Before continuing, underline the decision rule and circle the evidence that supports the conclusion. Explain the example to a partner without replacing the counts or conditions with a stronger claim. Keep the distinction between an observed result and a proposed next step.

blocks.title: Final testing and honest claims at a glance
blocks.caption: The test comparison must use the same cases and consistent rules. Report the denominator, reference-label process and sampling limitations. If the software fails on one case, report that failure; do not silently drop the case and keep the original headline denominator.

blocks.label: Why does 75 percent versus 70 percent not settle deployment? Explain the steps or evidence behind your response.

blocks.text: After seeing three missed blocked cases, the team changes its threshold. The old test has now informed development. Preserve the first result and label later scores as post-test development. A new independent test is needed for a new untouched-test claim; repeatedly splitting the same inspected rows does not erase what was learned.

A report can honestly say 15 of 20 correct on this fictional held-out set. It cannot say the model is 75 percent reliable for every child, school or future input. Do not fabricate more examples to make a result sound decisive.

ai-3/25.title: Overfitting and model capacity
goals: Compare training and validation evidence for model capacity
Explain overfitting without assuming every gap proves it
Use a declared selection rule instead of perfect training fit

prerequisite.prompt: Can a zero training error guarantee good validation performance?
prerequisite.answer: No; it may fit peculiarities of the training sample.

vocabulary: Flexibility of a model to represent patterns
Learning details that fail to generalize well

blocks.text: A more flexible model can represent complicated relationships and accidental details. Capacity can help when there is enough relevant evidence, but perfect training performance is not the goal. Compare training and validation using the same metric while checking leakage and representativeness.

Use fictional classroom data throughout this investigation. Keep the task, units, reference labels and data split visible as you reason. Earlier weeks supplied the model-building process; this week examines overfitting and model capacity.

On the same regression split, a constant has training MAE 5 and validation 6, a line has training 2 and validation 3, and a highly flexible curve has training 0 and validation 8. Under smallest validation MAE, choose the line. The curve has the lowest training loss but the worst validation result.

Before continuing, underline the decision rule and circle the evidence that supports the conclusion. Explain the example to a partner without replacing the counts or conditions with a stronger claim. Keep the distinction between an observed result and a proposed next step.

blocks.title: Overfitting and model capacity at a glance
blocks.caption: The curve result is consistent with overfitting, but a gap alone does not prove its cause. A changed population, bad labels or a split error could also produce a gap. Inspect the procedure before claiming a diagnosis. The constant may miss useful structure, but these numbers alone do not identify the true relationship.

blocks.label: Does a training-validation gap alone prove overfitting? Explain the steps or evidence behind your response.

blocks.text: Change one development factor at a time: simplify the candidate, improve data coverage or adjust a declared regularization setting. Refit on training and compare on validation. Do not remove difficult valid examples or repeatedly search the test for a favorable result.

A simpler model is not always better. If a flexible candidate has better valid evidence under the declared rule, keep that evidence visible. Model capacity is one part of an experiment, alongside features, sample size, label quality and the split.

blocks.label: What extra evidence would you inspect before concluding a model memorized noise?

workbook.title: Select from evidence
workbook.prompt: Choose among the three worked candidates and explain the training trap.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Choose the line with validation MAE 3. The curve training MAE 0 does not compensate for validation MAE 8.

workbook.title: Interpret a gap
workbook.prompt: Does a training-validation gap alone prove overfitting?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: No. It is consistent with overfitting but may also reflect shift, data quality or split problems.

workbook.title: Propose a controlled change
workbook.prompt: Describe one fair next development comparison.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Compare a simpler curve against the current curve on the same validation rows, retaining the same metric and training-only fitting; log the change.

workbook.title: Apply independently
workbook.prompt: Models A training 4 validation 5, B training 1 validation 2, C training 0 validation 2. Lowest validation MAE then simpler; B is simpler than C. Choose and justify.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: B wins the validation tie by the declared simplicity rule. C is not selected merely for its zero training error.

workbook.title: Limit a diagnosis
workbook.prompt: What extra evidence would you inspect before concluding a model memorized noise?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Check data provenance, split grouping, label quality and repeated development results; inspect representative residuals without using final test feedback to tune.

ai-3/26.title: Learning curves and variability
goals: Read training-size learning curves
Describe variability across repeated development runs
Avoid unsupported guarantees from a trend

prerequisite.prompt: What does validation loss add to training loss?
prerequisite.answer: Evidence about examples that did not fit the model parameters.

vocabulary: Performance plotted against training sample size
Another run under a recorded procedure
How much results differ between runs
Maximum minus minimum of observed values

blocks.text: A learning curve asks how performance changes as the amount of training evidence grows. Keep the validation protocol, model settings and metric comparable. Use subsets of training only; never add validation rows into the training subsets. Multiple repeats reveal sensitivity to sample selection or model randomness.

Use fictional classroom data throughout this investigation. Keep the task, units, reference labels and data split visible as you reason. Earlier weeks supplied the model-building process; this week examines learning curves and variability.

At training sizes 10, 20, 40, validation MAEs across three declared repeats are [7, 9, 8], [5, 7, 6], [4, 6, 5]. Means are 8, 6, 5 and ranges 2, 2, 2. Mean training MAEs are 1, 2, 3. Validation improves as training grows, while training error rises because fitting more varied examples can be harder.

Before continuing, underline the decision rule and circle the evidence that supports the conclusion. Explain the example to a partner without replacing the counts or conditions with a stronger claim. Keep the distinction between an observed result and a proposed next step.

blocks.title: Learning curves and variability at a glance
blocks.caption: The decreasing gap is encouraging in this experiment. It does not establish that doubling again will halve error. A range from three repeats is a descriptive spread, not a confidence interval or a guarantee that future results fall inside it. Repeated runs can share records and therefore are not independent studies.

blocks.label: Why can training error rise while validation error falls? Explain the steps or evidence behind your response.

blocks.text: Record the actual subset identifiers and seeds for every repeat. If the validation population changes at the same time as training size, label that as a different experiment rather than attributing the difference only to more training data.

Collect additional data because it addresses a known coverage need, not merely to enlarge a count. When the curve stops improving, inspect labels, features and task suitability. Keep the final test reserved while planning these changes.

blocks.label: Why is an observed range not a confidence interval?

workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Mean(5+7+6)/3=6; range 7-5=2.

workbook.title: Read both curves
workbook.prompt: Why can training error rise while validation error falls?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: More varied training cases may be harder to fit exactly while giving a pattern that generalizes better.

workbook.title: Avoid extrapolation
workbook.prompt: Can the 40-row result guarantee a mean MAE of 2.5 at 80 rows?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: No. The observed trend does not establish a fixed proportional improvement.

workbook.title: Apply independently

workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Means 7 and 6; ranges 2 and 3. The larger condition improves the mean by 1 but has greater observed spread in these three repeats.

workbook.title: Explain the spread
workbook.prompt: Why is an observed range not a confidence interval?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: It only describes the smallest and largest observed repeats; no coverage-probability calculation or independent-sampling argument was supplied.

ai-3/27.title: Feature engineering
goals: Create features available at prediction time
Fit feature transformations using training evidence only
Compare a feature change without changing the evaluation set

prerequisite.prompt: Why must preprocessing be fitted on training only?
prerequisite.answer: Evaluation values must not influence the learned transformation.

vocabulary: Constructing model inputs from available measurements
An input computed from other inputs
Information entering a model that would not be available legitimately
Whether a value exists when a prediction is needed

blocks.text: A useful feature represents information available when the prediction is made. In a fictional parcel task, length and width are measured before packing, so area=length*width is available. The final delivery delay is not available when predicting dispatch time. A strong correlation cannot make a future value legitimate.

Use fictional classroom data throughout this investigation. Keep the task, units, reference labels and data split visible as you reason. Earlier weeks supplied the model-building process; this week examines feature engineering.

Training rectangles have lengths [2, 4, 6] and widths [3, 2, 1], so areas are[6, 8, 6] square cm. Training mean area is 20/3. A validation rectangle length 5 width 2 has area 10 and centered area 10-20/3=10/3. Freeze the training mean; do not recompute it with validation.

Before continuing, underline the decision rule and circle the evidence that supports the conclusion. Explain the example to a partner without replacing the counts or conditions with a stronger claim. Keep the distinction between an observed result and a proposed next step.

blocks.title: Feature engineering at a glance
blocks.caption: Area is a deterministic transformation; it adds a representation, not a new measured fact. It may help a limited model express a relationship, or may do nothing useful. Compare original versus extended features under the same split, metric and development policy.

blocks.label: Center the validation area using the frozen training mean. Explain the steps or evidence behind your response.

blocks.text: Build a feature log with name, units, source, time available, transformation and missing-value policy. If width is missing, follow a declared training-derived imputation or return a clear unavailable result. Do not silently use zero, which describes a zero-area object.

An identifier may appear predictive because related objects leak across splits. Inspect grouped records and proxy risks before adding it. Never include private student details for this exercise; use the supplied fictional measurements.

blocks.label: How would you test adding area without claiming it must help?

ai-3/28.title: Experimental records and seeds
goals: Record enough detail to reproduce a run
Distinguish reproducibility from validity
Report all planned seeds instead of selecting the best

prerequisite.prompt: What must accompany a reported validation score?
prerequisite.answer: The model version, split, metric, data provenance and development choices.

vocabulary: An initial value controlling a pseudo-random process
A saved account of inputs, settings and outputs
Ability to repeat a specified procedure
Reporting favorable results while hiding relevant others

blocks.text: A seed can help repeat a random split or initialization, but it is not a magic quality stamp. Save data version, split membership, code version, settings, preprocessing, seed and metric definition. Some software operations remain nondeterministic, so document tolerances and environment too.

Use fictional classroom data throughout this investigation. Keep the task, units, reference labels and data split visible as you reason. Earlier weeks supplied the model-building process; this week examines experimental records and seeds.

A team declares seeds 11, 22, 33 before running. Validation accuracies are 14/20, 16/20, 12/20:70, 80, 60 percent. Mean accuracy is 70 percent, with a 20-percentage-point range. Reporting only seed 22 as the model result hides the declared experiment.

Before continuing, underline the decision rule and circle the evidence that supports the conclusion. Explain the example to a partner without replacing the counts or conditions with a stronger claim. Keep the distinction between an observed result and a proposed next step.

blocks.title: Experimental records and seeds at a glance
blocks.caption: The seed is part of the procedure, not evidence that a split represents the target population. Reproducing leakage perfectly reproduces a mistake. Check group separation and legitimate features before celebrating identical outputs.

blocks.label: A file contains only seed 22 and 80 percent. Name four missing items. Explain the steps or evidence behind your response.

blocks.text: A small record can contain run ID, timestamp, dataset checksum, training and validation IDs, model settings, feature version, seed, predictions and notes. Keep personal information out of exported logs. Save failed runs with reasons instead of quietly removing them.

When comparing two methods, use the same declared splits or seeds where appropriate and compare paired results. A mean across reused samples does not automatically provide a statistical confidence claim. Report the procedure and observed variation plainly.

blocks.label: One planned seed fails before prediction. How should it appear in the record?

workbook.title: Separate two ideas

workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: No. A deterministic experiment can still contain leakage, invalid labels or an unrepresentative split.

ai-3/3.title: Classification and regression
goals: Identify a task from the meaning of its target
Distinguish category agreement from numerical error
Specify outputs and checks that match a user need

prerequisite.prompt: At dispatch, may the observed arrival duration be used as an input to predict that same trip duration? Explain.
prerequisite.answer: No. It is known later and is the outcome to predict, not an available dispatch-time input.

vocabulary: Predicting a category from a defined set
Estimating a numerical quantity with meaningful differences
A boundary used to turn a value into a decision
The nonnegative distance between an estimate and an observation

lesson.title: Choose the question before the model

blocks.text: At robot dispatch, we can ask two questions about the same fictional trip. Will it take more than 10 minutes? Or how many minutes will it take? The first asks for a category. The second asks for an amount with units. The target question determines the task, even if both models would use the same dispatch-time inputs.

rows: How long will the trip take?
Which route type will be used?

blocks.text: Classification predicts a category from a defined set. Regression estimates a numerical quantity for which differences have meaning. A category may be coded with numbers: 0 and 1 here are names for no and yes, not travel times. Conversely, a duration recorded as a whole number of minutes can still be a regression target. Decimal points do not decide the task.

Keep Week 2's prediction time: route length and the saved queue may exist at dispatch, while the observed duration is available later for training or evaluation. Do not feed that observed duration into an earlier dispatch prediction.

lesson.title: Compare two ways to judge a prediction

blocks.text: The following predictions are supplied for practice; no model is fitted here. Each estimate was written before revealing its matching observed duration. We compare duration error with a category decision made from that estimate. Predict slow when the estimated duration is greater than 10 minutes; exactly 10 is not slow. A classifier could also predict categories directly, but this example uses a threshold on estimates.

blocks.title: Python 3 code
blocks.text:
actual_minutes = [8, 10, 14]
estimated_minutes = [9, 11, 12]
correct = 0
errors = []
for actual, estimate in zip(actual_minutes, estimated_minutes):
    actual_slow = int(actual > 10)
    predicted_slow = int(estimate > 10)
    correct = correct + int(actual_slow == predicted_slow)
    errors.append(abs(estimate - actual))
print(correct, len(actual_minutes))
print(errors)

zip pairs the lists in order. They must have equal lengths and refer to the same trips; otherwise this loop is not a valid evaluation. abs gives the distance from zero, so both a one-minute overestimate and a one-minute underestimate have absolute error 1. The output is 2 3 followed by [1, 1, 2]. The mean absolute error is (1 + 1 + 2) / 3 = 4/3 minutes, about 1.33 minutes.

blocks.title: Read both kinds of evidence
blocks.caption: All three rows use the same greater-than-10 boundary. A small duration error can cross that boundary; a larger error can stay on the same side.

blocks.text: The 14-minute trip has the largest duration error in our example, yet its slow category is correct. The 10-minute trip has only a one-minute error but the category is wrong. These checks answer different questions. Report 2 correct out of 3 category decisions separately from a mean absolute error of about 1.33 minutes. Do not compare a fraction directly with minutes.

blocks.label: A trip actually takes 10 minutes and its estimate is 10.5 minutes. At the greater-than-10 boundary, give the actual category, predicted category and absolute duration error. Is the category decision correct?

blocks.text: A learner says that predicting route type is regression because indoor is encoded as 1 and outdoor as 2. The numbers are category codes: their difference does not measure travel time or another meaningful amount. Treat this as classification and judge the predicted category. Changing the codes must not change the meaning of the task.

Another learner puts durations into short and long bins, then claims to predict exact minutes. Binning creates a classification target and loses within-bin detail. If the user needs minutes, keep a quantity target and evaluate error in minutes. If the user needs a threshold decision, define the boundary and relevant consequences. Neither task is automatically better.

lesson.title: Match the evidence to the purpose

blocks.text: A task specification should name the prediction moment, permitted inputs, target meaning and how predictions will be checked. Classification checks compare category decisions with observed categories. Regression checks measure numerical error with stated units. Later weeks examine additional metrics and why the consequences of different errors matter.

A correct category does not imply an exact quantity, and low numerical error does not guarantee every threshold decision is right. Three supplied examples establish only these calculations. They do not establish a trained model's reliability or show that a robot should act without review.

blocks.label: A team needs an estimated arrival duration in minutes. State the task type and a suitable error check. Explain why reporting only the fraction of correct slow or not-slow decisions leaves its main question unanswered.

workbook.title: Classify the target meaning
workbook.prompt: At dispatch, identify the task for predicting route type coded 1 or 2, duration in whole minutes, and whether duration exceeds 10 minutes. Explain your choices.
workbook.answer: Route type is classification because 1 and 2 encode categories. Whole-minute duration is regression because numerical differences measure time. Exceeding 10 minutes is binary classification because the target is yes or no.

workbook.title: Trace both checks
workbook.prompt: For actual 14 minutes and estimate 12 minutes, calculate absolute error and both slow categories using greater than 10. Explain why a correct category does not mean an exact duration.
workbook.answer: Absolute error is 2 minutes. Both actual and predicted categories are 1, so the category matches even though the duration estimate is 2 minutes too low.

workbook.title: Repair a category average
workbook.prompt: Indoor is coded 1 and outdoor is coded 2. Someone averages predictions and reports route type 1.5 as an accurate halfway category. Explain the problem and name an appropriate check.
workbook.answer: The codes label categories, so 1.5 is not a defined route type. Predict one of the defined categories and compare it with the observed category. A numerical midpoint of arbitrary codes does not establish correctness.

workbook.title: Compare new evidence independently
workbook.prompt: For three fictional print jobs, actual completion times are 4, 5 and 9 minutes; estimates are 6, 5 and 8 minutes in matching order. Slow means more than 5 minutes. Write actual and predicted category lists, count correct categories, calculate each absolute error and the mean error in minutes. State what each result measures.
workbook.answer: Actual categories are [0, 0, 1]; predicted categories are [1, 0, 1], so 2 of 3 match. Absolute errors are [2, 0, 1] minutes; their mean is 1 minute. The fraction measures threshold-category agreement on these jobs, while mean absolute error measures average duration discrepancy.

workbook.title: Specify a useful output
workbook.prompt: A user needs the arrival duration in minutes, but a report gives only slow or not slow. What task should be specified, and what information was lost by the category output?
workbook.answer: Specify regression for duration in minutes and check numerical error, such as mean absolute error in minutes. The category omits the estimated duration and how far it is from the boundary; it cannot answer the requested quantity.

teacher.background: Use two 45-minute sessions to distinguish tasks by target meaning, not by input types or whether values contain decimals. Connect to Week 2 by keeping inputs available at dispatch and outcomes separate. Supplied duration estimates let students inspect category decisions and numerical errors without suggesting a model was trained. The threshold is fixed before evaluation. All examples are fictional.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook
Number line marked at 10 minutes and cards for no and yes
Optional Python 3 editor; no packages needed
Blank actual estimate category absolute error table
sessions: Retrieve the Week 2 rule that later outcomes cannot be dispatch inputs. Ask the prerequisite question and keep the prediction moment visible.
Compare the three target questions. Ask why numeric category codes remain categories and why whole-minute durations remain quantities.
Trace the three supplied estimates. Explain abs and zip, including equal lengths and matching record order. Complete W1 and W2.
Use the number line for the guided 10 versus 10.5 case. Separate category agreement from numerical closeness.
Retrieve task meaning and units. Ask for a numerical category code and a whole-number quantity as counterexamples to the decimal shortcut.
Complete W3 and discuss information lost by binning. Distinguish directly predicting a class from thresholding a quantity estimate.
Collect W4 independently, requiring category lists, denominator, absolute errors and the mean with units. Record hints or other support.
Use W5 and the exit to match outputs to a user need. Offer the fresh retry after support where necessary.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided: actual category 0, predicted category 1, absolute duration error 0.5 minutes; the category is wrong. Exit: specify regression for duration in minutes and use a numerical error check such as mean absolute error in minutes. Category agreement does not report how close the duration estimates are to observed times.
misconceptions: Numbers always mean regression
Category codes remain categories. Ask what a difference between the numbers would mean in the task.
Regression requires decimal observations
A quantity measured or rounded to whole minutes still has meaningful numerical distances. Target meaning decides the task.
A correct category means a precise estimate
The 14 versus 12 minute example has a correct category but a two-minute error. Conversely, a small error near the boundary can change the category.
teacher.assessment: Require W4 actual categories [0,0,1], predicted [1,0,1], 2 of 3 correct, absolute errors [2,0,1] and mean 1 minute. The learner must explain both meanings. Fresh retry: actual times 3,6,8 and estimates 4,5,10; slow means greater than 6. Actual and predicted categories are both [0,0,1], so 3 of 3 match. Absolute errors [1,1,2] have mean 4/3 minutes, about 1.33. Ask why perfect category agreement does not mean zero duration error.
teacher.support: Use a number line to mark actual and estimated times, then color which side of the boundary each lies on. Supply a blank table without answers. Extension: recode no and yes as 7 and 9. The classification task and matching count stay the same, while distances between those codes are not time errors.
teacher.next: Week 4 inspects datasets and documents their origin, units and limitations. Carry forward the target definition, prediction moment and measurement units. Teacher reference: https://scikit-learn.org/1.0/tutorial/basic/tutorial.html (classification and regression definitions; reviewed 2026-09-26).

ai-3/30.title: Subgroup evaluation
goals: Calculate subgroup results with sample sizes
Distinguish missing evidence from equal performance
Report differences without assigning causes from a table

prerequisite.prompt: What can a pooled error rate hide?
prerequisite.answer: Different error patterns in different evaluated conditions or groups.

vocabulary: A defined subset of the evaluated examples
Reporting results separately for defined groups
Which groups and conditions are represented
An observed difference between group results

blocks.text: A single overall score can hide different experiences. Define relevant groups before evaluation and report counts as well as rates. This classroom exercise uses fictional sensor conditions, not personal identities. Real evaluations involving people require appropriate permissions, privacy and contextual expertise.

Use fictional classroom data throughout this investigation. Keep the task, units, reference labels and data split visible as you reason. Earlier weeks supplied the model-building process; this week examines subgroup evaluation.

Sensor group A has 2 errors in 20 examples and group B has 3 in 5. Error rates are 10 and 60 percent; pooled error is 5/25=20 percent. The group difference is 50 percentage points. B has only five examples, so its rate is sensitive to each individual result.

Before continuing, underline the decision rule and circle the evidence that supports the conclusion. Explain the example to a partner without replacing the counts or conditions with a stronger claim. Keep the distinction between an observed result and a proposed next step.

blocks.title: Subgroup evaluation at a glance
blocks.caption: Changing one B error to a correct result changes its rate from 60 to 40 percent. Small samples can be unstable without making the observed errors unimportant. A missing group has no measured rate, not zero error. Intersections of conditions may be even smaller.

blocks.label: How does correcting one B error affect its rate? Explain the steps or evidence behind your response.

blocks.text: Choose group definitions for a reason connected to use and possible harm. Retain error types, reference-label quality and sampling method. Avoid searching many groupings merely to find a dramatic or reassuring number. Report exploratory checks as exploratory.

Equal error rates alone do not establish fairness, and unequal rates alone do not identify discrimination or a cause. Groups may differ in base rates, label quality or conditions. Use results to ask better questions and plan review rather than label a group as inherently difficult.

blocks.label: Why does equal accuracy not settle whether use is fair?

workbook.title: Calculate group rates
workbook.prompt: Calculate the worked group and pooled rates.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: A 2/20=10 percent; B 3/5=60 percent; pooled 5/25=20 percent, a 50-point group gap.

workbook.title: Check sensitivity
workbook.prompt: How does correcting one B error affect its rate?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: B becomes 2/5=40 percent, a 20-percentage-point change from one case.

workbook.title: Report missing coverage
workbook.prompt: Group C has no evaluated cases. What is its measured error rate?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Unavailable because the denominator is zero; report missing coverage and do not substitute zero.

workbook.title: Apply independently
workbook.prompt: Groups X 1 error/10 and Y 2/4: calculate separate and pooled rates, then state one limit.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: X 10 percent; Y 50 percent; pooled 3/14 about 21.4 percent. Y has only four examples, and the table does not establish a cause.

workbook.title: Avoid a fairness shortcut
workbook.prompt: Why does equal accuracy not settle whether use is fair?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Error types, consequences, access, labels and context can differ; a single equality does not establish acceptable treatment.

ai-3/31.title: Proxy features and fairness
goals: Identify possible proxy features
Explain why removing one field does not guarantee fairness
Propose a contextual review with concrete evidence

prerequisite.prompt: Does equal overall accuracy prove fair treatment?
prerequisite.answer: No; examine errors, consequences, data and context.

vocabulary: A variable that can stand in for another characteristic
An observed association, not proof of cause
A characteristic requiring particular care in a context
A comparison that removes a feature or component

blocks.text: An input can carry information about a characteristic without naming it. In a fictional school-device dataset, device code may be associated with building or access to newer equipment. Removing a building field does not remove all related information. Do not infer a real student identity or protected characteristic in this exercise.

Use fictional classroom data throughout this investigation. Keep the task, units, reference labels and data split visible as you reason. Earlier weeks supplied the model-building process; this week examines proxy features and fairness.

Fictional records show device code X on 8 of 10 north-building examples and 2 of 10 south-building examples. Device and building are associated in this sample. This does not prove device causes model errors or that every X device comes from north. The remaining cases contradict such a universal rule.

Before continuing, underline the decision rule and circle the evidence that supports the conclusion. Explain the example to a partner without replacing the counts or conditions with a stronger claim. Keep the distinction between an observed result and a proposed next step.

blocks.title: Proxy features and fairness at a glance
blocks.caption: A feature may be legitimate for one purpose and inappropriate for another. Ask what is measured, when it is available, why it predicts and who might be disadvantaged. A correlation alone neither authorizes use nor proves harm. Talk through the intended decision and available alternatives.

blocks.label: Why might removing building but keeping device code leave related information? Explain the steps or evidence behind your response.

blocks.text: Compare versions with and without device code on the same validation cases, while checking subgroup errors and useful task performance. This ablation measures a change in that experiment; correlated inputs may still carry similar information. Retain group definitions and denominators, and avoid using the final test for repeated feature decisions.

Do not advertise fairness through unawareness merely because names or a sensitive field were removed. A classroom audit should state unresolved questions, intended non-use and a human review path. Never collect sensitive student information simply to fill this exercise.

blocks.label: Does unchanged accuracy after removing a proxy prove fairness?

workbook.title: Read an association
workbook.prompt: What do the device counts support, and what do they not support?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: X occurs 8/10 north and 2/10 south in this sample. This supports an association, not a deterministic identity rule or a causal explanation.

workbook.title: Find a proxy risk
workbook.prompt: Why might removing building but keeping device code leave related information?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Device code is associated with building in the sample and may carry some of that information indirectly.

workbook.title: Plan an ablation
workbook.prompt: Describe a controlled with/without-code comparison.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Use the same validation rows and metric, fit both versions only on training, and report overall and relevant subgroup errors with denominators.

workbook.title: Apply independently
workbook.prompt: A team removes postcode but retains school code and claims all location-related information is gone. Evaluate the claim and request evidence.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: The claim is unsupported: school code may be associated with location. Review provenance and associations, compare ablations and group errors, and state unresolved proxy risks.

workbook.title: Limit the result
workbook.prompt: Does unchanged accuracy after removing a proxy prove fairness?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: No. Other features can retain information and accuracy can hide different errors and consequences.
