ai-3/32.title: Model cards and review
goals: Write a model card whose claims match evidence
Separate intended use from unsupported use
Review a card for missing evaluation details

prerequisite.prompt: What should remain visible after an evaluation?
prerequisite.answer: Data provenance, model version, full results, limitations and decision history.

vocabulary: A concise structured account of a model and its limits
The purpose and conditions the evidence supports
A purpose for which the model is not supported
The current state of checks and unresolved issues

blocks.text: A model card helps another person understand what was built and what evidence exists. It is a record, not a certificate of safety. Link statements to saved data and run records. Use unknown or not evaluated where evidence is absent instead of filling gaps with optimistic language.

Use fictional classroom data throughout this investigation. Keep the task, units, reference labels and data split visible as you reason. Earlier weeks supplied the model-building process; this week examines model cards and review.

Example card: classroom parcel classifier v 1; purpose: compare toy classification methods on fictional clear/blocked labels. Training 40, validation 20, test 12 with separate record groups. Frozen test TN 7 FP 1 FN 2 TP 2, blocked positive: accuracy 9/12, precision 2/3, recall 2/4. Always-clear baseline scores 8/12. No real parcel or student decision is supported.

Before continuing, underline the decision rule and circle the evidence that supports the conclusion. Explain the example to a partner without replacing the counts or conditions with a stronger claim. Keep the distinction between an observed result and a proposed next step.

blocks.title: Model cards and review at a glance
blocks.caption: The model card should name feature availability, preprocessing fitted on training, model settings, reference-label rules and test date. Include subgroup coverage if evaluated; otherwise say it was not assessed. Describe relevant failure examples without exposing personal information.

blocks.label: Verify the worked accuracy, precision and recall. Explain the steps or evidence behind your response.

blocks.text: A peer reviewer traces one headline number back to the saved predictions, checks denominators and looks for mismatches between intended use and evidence. Record requested changes and whether each was resolved. A card must be updated when its model, data or intended use changes.

Do not claim a synthetic classroom dataset represents every school or age group. Missing calibration, subgroup or shift evidence must remain explicit. A useful card may conclude that the model should stay a classroom demonstration.

blocks.label: What should change in a card after a threshold revision?

workbook.title: Draft a purpose
workbook.prompt: Write an intended-use and non-use statement for the worked card.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Intended: compare toy classifiers on the documented fictional task. Not supported: real parcel handling, student assessment or decisions outside the evaluated setup.

workbook.title: Check arithmetic
workbook.prompt: Verify the worked accuracy, precision and recall.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: TN 7 TP 2 give 9/12 accuracy; TP 2/(TP 2+FP 1)=2/3 precision; TP 2/(TP 2+FN 2)=2/4 recall.

workbook.title: Find missing evidence
workbook.prompt: A card says fair and reliable but provides only accuracy. Request three additions.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Request full error counts and denominators, relevant subgroup coverage/results, data provenance and limits; remove unsupported fairness/reliability claims.

workbook.title: Apply independently
workbook.prompt: Review this card: model v 2, 90 percent accurate, works for every school. No dataset size, split or baseline is given. Write a correction request with a bounded replacement claim.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Request evaluated counts, split history, reference labels, baseline, errors and supported use. Replace the universal claim with: performance scope is not established from the supplied evidence; the reported 90 percent cannot yet be audited.

workbook.title: Maintain the record
workbook.prompt: What should change in a card after a threshold revision?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Record a new version, threshold, reason, affected evaluations and review status; retain prior results and distinguish new independent evidence from reused development data.

ai-3/33.title: Capstone data and requirements
goals: Define a feasible capstone question and acceptance criteria
Create a data and split plan before modelling
Specify evidence, privacy and a fallback

prerequisite.prompt: Which evaluation choices should precede model selection?
prerequisite.answer: Task, data roles, metric, baseline, tie policy and intended use.

vocabulary: A concrete condition the project must meet
Evidence that decides whether a requirement is met
Definitions and units for dataset fields
A review point with a stated deliverable

blocks.text: The capstone is a classroom investigation, not a product launch. Choose the supplied fictional clear/blocked parcel task or an equally bounded teacher-approved synthetic task. Write a question that can be answered by comparing a simple model against a baseline. Do not use private student records or real safety decisions.

Use fictional classroom data throughout this investigation. Keep the task, units, reference labels and data split visible as you reason. Earlier weeks supplied the model-building process; this week examines capstone data and requirements.

Example proposal: can a small classifier improve validation accuracy over the training-majority baseline on fictional parcel measurements? Before modelling, assign 40 training, 20 validation and 12 final-test records, with related parcel groups kept together. Define blocked as positive, keep a fixed label rule, and reserve test labels with the teacher until Week 35.

Before continuing, underline the decision rule and circle the evidence that supports the conclusion. Explain the example to a partner without replacing the counts or conditions with a stronger claim. Keep the distinction between an observed result and a proposed next step.

Your teacher can prepare the 72-record fictional grid described in the teacher guide, or approve another documented synthetic dataset. Each supplied record has an ID, group ID, width and height in cm. Training and validation labels are released for development; final-test labels stay with the teacher until the model is frozen. The numerical results in later worked examples are illustrative and are not expected scores for your project.

blocks.title: Capstone data and requirements at a glance
blocks.caption: The data dictionary lists record ID, group ID, width in cm, height in cm and reference class. IDs track provenance and splitting; they are not automatic predictive inputs. Check uniqueness, units, missing values, class coverage and group separation. Fit imputation or scaling only on training.

blocks.label: Explain why record ID, group ID and measured width have different roles. Explain the steps or evidence behind your response.

blocks.text: Acceptance criteria describe the process even if the model loses: no split leakage; predictions for every planned case or documented failures; the same metric for baseline and candidate; precision/recall with denominators; a model card with limits. Improvement is a research outcome, not a grade requirement.

Submit a one-page proposal, data dictionary, split-membership record and risk/limitations note. The teacher approves feasibility and synthetic-data scope before modelling. If there are too few valid records for an independent test, use a clearly labelled demonstration and explicitly limit the claim rather than inventing evidence.

blocks.label: What should the team do if it cannot obtain a valid untouched final test?

workbook.title: State a question
workbook.prompt: Write a bounded question and a non-use statement for the supplied task.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Compare a simple classifier with a training-majority baseline on the fictional parcel evaluation; no real handling or student decisions are supported.

workbook.title: Define fields
workbook.prompt: Explain why record ID, group ID and measured width have different roles.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Record ID tracks rows, group ID keeps related records together, and width is a potential measured feature available before prediction; IDs are not automatic inputs.

workbook.title: Set criteria
workbook.prompt: Name three acceptance criteria that do not require the candidate to win.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Examples: no group overlap, all planned predictions accounted for, matched baseline comparison and documented limitations with denominators.

workbook.title: Apply independently
workbook.prompt: A proposed 80-row dataset has 40 related pairs, and the team splits individual rows randomly then uses pair ID as a feature. Revise its plan.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Keep both members of each pair in one split, exclude pair ID from predictive inputs, check group/class coverage and record split membership before training. Reserve final-test labels.

workbook.title: Prepare a fallback
workbook.prompt: What should the team do if it cannot obtain a valid untouched final test?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Label the work as development or a demonstration, report the limitation and avoid an untouched-test claim; do not fabricate test data or results.

teacher.background: Teach two 45-minute sessions. This week focuses on capstone data and requirements. Model the worked example first, collect the new W 4 case independently before feedback, and use the fresh retry to check transfer. Award credit for traceable reasoning and bounded claims, including justified uncertainty.
materials: Printed student lesson and workbook
Paper, pencils and a calculator for fractions
The fictional examples and a blank evidence table
Saved classroom project records for critique; no personal student dataset required

Optional reproducible data kit: create IDs i=0 through 71, width=2+(i mod 9) cm, height=2+floor(i/9) cm, and group ID equal to i. Each record is a distinct fictional parcel. Reference label is blocked when width+height is at least 12, otherwise clear. These are invented operational labels, not real parcel safety labels.

Split by (5*i) mod 18: values 0–9 go to training, 10–14 to validation, 15–17 to final test. This gives 40/20/12 rows. Prepare the kit before class, check both classes in each split, and distribute final-test features without labels. Keep the final key in teacher materials. The constructed split is not a random sample; students must report that limitation.
sessions: Use the prerequisite question: Which evaluation choices should precede model selection? Check the explanation before proceeding.
Model the worked proposal, then introduce the prepared fictional dataset and its data dictionary. Students choose the supplied task or a bounded approved alternative.
Teams draft their question, non-use statement and three process acceptance criteria. Use W1–W3 as prompts while preparing the proposal.
Teams check IDs, units, missing values and split membership. Collect the proposal and identify repairs before any model fitting.
Retrieve the distinction between requirement and acceptance criterion. Invite a counterexample to an overconfident claim.
Complete the independent W4 split critique first. Then teams revise their own data plan and document group separation.
Review each team proposal and data dictionary for feasibility. Confirm synthetic-data scope, task metric and baseline; reserve final-test labels before approving modelling.
Use W 5 and the exit response to assess limits. Give targeted feedback, then the fresh retry. Save evidence of independent understanding.

The independent task changes the evidence. Require a fresh explanation: Keep both members of each pair in one split, exclude pair ID from predictive inputs, check group/class coverage and record split membership before training. Reserve final-test labels.
teacher.assessment: For independent W 4, require: Keep both members of each pair in one split, exclude pair ID from predictive inputs, check group/class coverage and record split membership before training. Reserve final-test labels. Fresh retry: three images of the same fictional parcel must stay in one split. Ask the learner to identify the group and record a split-level check before modelling. Mark each criterion as independent, supported or not yet demonstrated. Reassess the reasoning after feedback; do not replace the first attempt silently.
teacher.support: Provide a blank evidence table and allow a verbal explanation before writing. Highlight the given conditions without supplying the W 4 conclusion. Use requirement and acceptance criterion in full sentences. Extension: alter one condition in the worked example and explain which conclusion changes and which remains supported.
teacher.next: Next week: Capstone models and baselines. Carry forward the saved evidence and the distinction between development choices and justified claims.

ai-3/35.title: Capstone evaluation and revision
goals: Run a frozen final evaluation with complete accounting
Separate error analysis from an untouched-test claim
Document revisions and their evidence status

prerequisite.prompt: What changes after final-test labels inform a revision?
prerequisite.answer: The inspected set becomes development evidence for the revised version.

vocabulary: Assessment of the frozen procedure on held-out evidence
A documented inspection of mistakes and missing predictions
A record of changes, reasons and affected evidence
Whether a result is development, untouched test or post-test reuse

blocks.text: The teacher releases final-test labels only after checking the freeze record. Score baseline and candidate on the same planned rows. Save every prediction, denominator and failure. Do not edit a model while reading labels and then present only the edited version as the original test.

Use fictional classroom data throughout this investigation. Keep the task, units, reference labels and data split visible as you reason. Earlier weeks supplied the model-building process; this week examines capstone evaluation and revision.

Illustrative frozen test has 12 rows: candidate[[7, 1],[2, 2]], baseline[[8, 0],[4, 0]], blocked positive. Candidate accuracy 9/12=75 percent, precision 2/3 and recall 2/4; baseline accuracy 8/12 about 66.7 percent. The candidate adds one false alarm and misses two rather than four blocked cases.

Before continuing, underline the decision rule and circle the evidence that supports the conclusion. Explain the example to a partner without replacing the counts or conditions with a stronger claim. Keep the distinction between an observed result and a proposed next step.

blocks.title: Capstone evaluation and revision at a glance
blocks.caption: Compare the result with validation without claiming they should be identical. Check error types and coverage. A one-case accuracy difference on twelve rows supports a cautious classroom comparison, not a general reliability guarantee. Keep the original prediction ledger unchanged.

blocks.label: What does the one-correct-case improvement establish? Explain the steps or evidence behind your response.

blocks.text: If dim examples account for both misses, record that observation and inspect collection conditions. It is a hypothesis for investigation, not proof that lighting caused the failures. A proposed feature or model change creates version 2. Scores on the same inspected test must be labelled post-test development.

Submit the frozen test report, error audit, revision proposal and updated model card. A revision proposal may conclude that more appropriate data or a simpler baseline is preferable. If no fresh test is available, stop at a transparent proposal instead of claiming the revision has been independently validated.

blocks.label: What must remain visible when version 2 is proposed without a fresh test?

workbook.title: Score the frozen test
workbook.prompt: Compute the worked candidate metrics and baseline accuracy.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Candidate accuracy 9/12=75 percent, precision 2/3, recall 2/4; baseline 8/12 about 66.7 percent, with all four blocked cases missed.

workbook.title: Audit a difference
workbook.prompt: What does the one-correct-case improvement establish?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: It establishes a difference on these 12 examples under the saved procedure, not reliable improvement for every future population.

workbook.title: Label a revision
workbook.prompt: A threshold changes after test errors are read. Label its score on the same rows.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Post-test development or reused-test evidence for the revised version, not an untouched final test.

workbook.title: Apply independently
workbook.prompt: Frozen candidate[[6, 2],[1, 3]] and baseline[[8, 0],[4, 0]] on 12 cases. Compute candidate metrics and compare error types.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Candidate accuracy 9/12=75 percent, precision 3/5=60 percent, recall 3/4=75 percent. Baseline FP 0 FN 4 versus candidate FP 2 FN 1; baseline accuracy 8/12.

workbook.title: Update the card
workbook.prompt: What must remain visible when version 2 is proposed without a fresh test?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Version 1 frozen results, reason for change, reused-evidence status and the fact that version 2 has no new independent final evaluation.

teacher.background: Teach two 45-minute sessions. This week focuses on capstone evaluation and revision. Model the worked example first, collect the new W 4 case independently before feedback, and use the fresh retry to check transfer. Award credit for traceable reasoning and bounded claims, including justified uncertainty.
materials: Printed student lesson and workbook
Paper, pencils and a calculator for fractions
The fictional examples and a blank evidence table
Saved classroom project records for critique; no personal student dataset required
sessions: Use the prerequisite question: What changes after final-test labels inform a revision? Check the explanation before proceeding.
Verify each team freeze record before releasing final labels. Review the worked example and separate illustrative numbers from actual project evidence.
Teams run or trace frozen baseline and candidate predictions on all planned test cases. Save the unchanged prediction ledger and account for failures.
Teams calculate metrics and inspect error types. Use W1–W3 to check calculations and evidence status before writing claims.
Retrieve the distinction between final evaluation and error audit. Invite a counterexample to an overconfident claim.
Teams write an error audit and propose one follow-up tied to an observed limit. Keep version1 results unchanged.
Collect W4 independently. Teams then update their model card and clearly mark any revision as untested or supported only by reused development evidence.
Use W 5 and the exit response to assess limits. Give targeted feedback, then the fresh retry. Save evidence of independent understanding.

Exit response: Version 1 frozen results, reason for change, reused-evidence status and the fact that version 2 has no new independent final evaluation.
misconceptions: A final answer is enough

Ask for the relevant counts, units, procedure or saved record. For this week: Candidate accuracy 9/12=75 percent, precision 2/3, recall 2/4; baseline 8/12 about 66.7 percent, with all four blocked cases missed.
A stronger claim makes a stronger project
Version 1 frozen results, reason for change, reused-evidence status and the fact that version 2 has no new independent final evaluation.
The new case can be copied from the example

The independent task changes the evidence. Require a fresh explanation: Candidate accuracy 9/12=75 percent, precision 3/5=60 percent, recall 3/4=75 percent. Baseline FP 0 FN 4 versus candidate FP 2 FN 1; baseline accuracy 8/12.

Baseline FP 0 FN 4 versus candidate FP 2 FN 1; baseline accuracy 8/12. Fresh retry candidate[[5, 1],[2, 2]] on 10 cases: accuracy 7/10, precision 2/3, recall 2/4. Require a test-status statement before any proposed tuning. Mark each criterion as independent, supported or not yet demonstrated. Reassess the reasoning after feedback; do not replace the first attempt silently.

Use final evaluation and error audit in full sentences. Extension: alter one condition in the worked example and explain which conclusion changes and which remains supported.

ai-3/36.title: Machine learning project defense
goals: Defend the project using traceable evidence
Explain errors and limits to a non-specialist audience
Respond to critique and propose an evidence-based next step

prerequisite.prompt: What is the difference between a result and a claim?
prerequisite.answer: A result describes observed evidence; a claim must not extend beyond what that evidence supports.

vocabulary: An explanation of decisions supported by inspectable evidence
Ability to follow a claim back to its source
A boundary on interpretation or supported use
An account of learning and justified next steps

blocks.text: The final defense tells a coherent story: question, data, method, comparison, errors and limits. A strong project may conclude that the baseline is preferable or evidence is insufficient. The aim is sound reasoning and a reproducible investigation, not an impressive headline or polished unsupported claim.

Use fictional classroom data throughout this investigation. Keep the task, units, reference labels and data split visible as you reason. Earlier weeks supplied the model-building process; this week examines machine learning project defense.

Example opening: We compared a simple classifier with an always-clear training baseline on fictional parcels. We froze the procedure before a 12-case test. Candidate accuracy was 9/12 versus baseline 8/12; candidate FP 1 FN 2. These small synthetic results support a classroom comparison, not real parcel decisions. We would next investigate dim-condition coverage using new development data.

Before continuing, underline the decision rule and circle the evidence that supports the conclusion. Explain the example to a partner without replacing the counts or conditions with a stronger claim. Keep the distinction between an observed result and a proposed next step.

blocks.title: Machine learning project defense at a glance
blocks.caption: Prepare a five-minute presentation with a one-page evidence summary and linked project files. Include the data dictionary, split record, run record, prediction ledger, model card and revision history. Demonstrate one prediction or arithmetic calculation live so the audience can follow the reasoning.

blocks.label: Name the files needed to audit one reported accuracy figure. Explain the steps or evidence behind your response.

blocks.text: Peers ask three questions: what influenced model selection, which cases failed, and what evidence would change the conclusion? Respond using saved records. If an answer is unknown, say so and name the evidence needed. Record feedback as resolved, deferred with reason, or requiring new data.

The teacher rubric has four dimensions scored 0, 1, 2: valid data/splits, reproducible method, complete evaluation, and honest communication. Two means evidence is complete and explainable; one means partial evidence with identified gaps; zero means absent or materially incorrect. Report dimensions separately; a serious leakage problem cannot be hidden by presentation points.

blocks.label: Write one next investigation tied to an observed limitation, and identify what must stay held out.

workbook.title: Write an opening
workbook.prompt: Draft a three-sentence opening with purpose, a result and a limit.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: A valid response names the fictional task, reports an auditable baseline/candidate comparison with denominator, and restricts the claim to the evaluated setup.

workbook.title: Trace evidence
workbook.prompt: Name the files needed to audit one reported accuracy figure.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Prediction ledger with references and outputs, split membership, frozen model/run record and metric definition; count correct rows over all scored rows under the saved policy.

workbook.title: Answer critique
workbook.prompt: A peer asks whether your model works for every school. Give a supported response.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: No universal conclusion is supported. State the actual synthetic dataset and conditions, missing coverage and what additional appropriate evidence would be needed.

workbook.title: Apply independently
workbook.prompt: Review a defense claiming 95 percent success on 20 cases but omitting the baseline, split history and errors. Give three revision requests and explain why polish is insufficient.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Request the baseline on the same cases, split/development history and full error counts/limits. A polished presentation cannot establish validity or supported use without auditable evidence.

workbook.title: Plan the next step
workbook.prompt: Write one next investigation tied to an observed limitation, and identify what must stay held out.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: A valid response links a documented limitation to new development evidence, records any revised version, and reserves fresh independent final-test evidence for a later frozen evaluation.

teacher.background: Teach two 45-minute sessions. This week focuses on machine learning project defense. Model the worked example first, collect the new W 4 case independently before feedback, and use the fresh retry to check transfer. Award credit for traceable reasoning and bounded claims, including justified uncertainty.

Paper, pencils and a calculator for fractions
The fictional examples and a blank evidence table
Saved classroom project records for critique; no personal student dataset required
sessions: Use the prerequisite question: What is the difference between a result and a claim? Check the explanation before proceeding.
Review the four rubric dimensions. Use W1–W3 to prepare a bounded opening and an auditable evidence summary.
Teams prepare a five-minute defense and one-page summary. Check every claim against the saved project files and rehearse one prediction trace.
Run peer rehearsals in pairs. Each reviewer records a question about data roles, a failure and the claim limits.
Complete W4 independently as a short critique of unsupported claims. Use the result to target final feedback.
Begin defenses in parallel small groups: five minutes presenting plus two minutes of questions per team. Teacher samples evidence and collects all records.
Continue defenses and record scores separately for data/splits, reproducibility, evaluation and communication. Use written evidence as well as the live explanation.
Complete W5 as an individual reflection. Resolve or record peer feedback, identify a justified next step and use the fresh retry for learners who confuse model improvement with project success.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided response: Prediction ledger with references and outputs, split membership, frozen model/run record and metric definition; count correct rows over all scored rows under the saved policy. Exit response: A valid response links a documented limitation to new development evidence, records any revised version, and reserves fresh independent final-test evidence for a later frozen evaluation.
misconceptions: A final answer is enough

Ask for the relevant counts, units, procedure or saved record. For this week: A valid response names the fictional task, reports an auditable baseline/candidate comparison with denominator, and restricts the claim to the evaluated setup.
A stronger claim makes a stronger project
A valid response links a documented limitation to new development evidence, records any revised version, and reserves fresh independent final-test evidence for a later frozen evaluation.
The new case can be copied from the example

The independent task changes the evidence. Require a fresh explanation: Request the baseline on the same cases, split/development history and full error counts/limits. A polished presentation cannot establish validity or supported use without auditable evidence.

A polished presentation cannot establish validity or supported use without auditable evidence. Fresh retry: a learner says our baseline won, so the project failed. Ask for a defense explaining the valid comparison, retained baseline, limits and an evidence-based next investigation; do not reward invented improvement. Mark each criterion as independent, supported or not yet demonstrated. Reassess the reasoning after feedback; do not replace the first attempt silently.

ai-3/4.title: Dataset inspection and cards
goals: Inspect row meaning missing values and repeated records
Document dataset source schema and limitations
Separate observed quality flags from justified corrections

prerequisite.prompt: Why is elapsed trip duration in minutes a regression target even when recorded as whole numbers?
prerequisite.answer: It is a numerical quantity whose differences measure time. Whole-number formatting does not turn it into a category.

vocabulary: Where data came from and how it was created
The stated meaning types units and rules for fields
An unknown or unavailable value rather than a measured zero
A concise record of dataset contents creation intended use and limitations

blocks.text: A dataset can look like a neat table and still contain missing outcomes, repeated records or impossible values. Before fitting a model, inspect what one row represents and document where the table came from. A dataset card is a short record of its purpose, contents, collection, changes and limits. It helps another person decide whether the data suits a proposed use.

Our source is a teacher-authored fictional export called Robot practice v1, created for this lesson. Each row is intended to describe one trip, with one unique trip ID and elapsed duration in minutes. Durations may be zero or positive; None means unknown. All trips are described as indoor practice trips. No real robot measurements or personal records were collected, and there is no evidence about outdoor performance.

Keep this raw version unchanged. At this stage a flag means investigate, not automatically delete or replace. A repeated ID might be a copied row or a problem with the supposed one-row-per-trip definition. We need evidence before deciding what happened.

blocks.title: Python 3 code
blocks.text:
rows = [("A", 8), ("B", None), ("B", None),
        ("C", -2), ("D", 12)]
ids = set()
missing = 0
negative = 0
for trip_id, minutes in rows:
    ids.add(trip_id)
    if minutes is None:
        missing = missing + 1
    elif minutes < 0:
        negative = negative + 1
print(len(rows), len(ids), missing, negative)

A set stores each distinct ID once. The output is 5 4 2 1: five rows, four distinct IDs, two rows with unknown duration and one row with a negative duration. There is one extra occurrence beyond the four distinct IDs. This is not a count of all rows in repeated-ID groups: both B rows belong to that group.

blocks.title: Turn an observation into a documented action
blocks.caption: Flags can overlap: both rows with ID B also have missing duration. Do not add flag counts as if they were separate groups.

blocks.text: The code assumes every row is a pair and each duration is a number or None. It is a small audit, not full schema validation. It does not check text values, units, source truth or whether IDs refer to real unique events. A successful run does not certify data quality.

lesson.title: Write a card another person can use

blocks.text: For Robot practice v1, record the purpose as practising inspection, the source as teacher-authored fictional data, and the row meaning as an intended single indoor trip. Record the five-row count, the ID field, minutes as the duration unit and None as unknown. List the duplicate-ID and invalid-duration findings. State that no cleaning has occurred, no train/test split is assigned, and no model has been evaluated.

Add intended use, excluded uses, known gaps, version and a contact or owner. Here the lesson teacher maintains the practice copy; its allowed classroom purpose is inspection practice. Do not describe it as validated navigation data. For a real external dataset, also verify its actual permission or licence and collection context; an absent field in the documentation is an unanswered question, not permission to invent a value.

blocks.label: What fraction of the five raw rows has unknown duration? Can you subtract two missing rows, one negative row and one extra ID occurrence from five to count distinct usable trips? Explain using the B rows.

lesson.title: Repair a claim without hiding the raw data

blocks.text: A learner replaces both None values with 0 and removes the negative sign from -2. The table now passes a simple nonnegative check, but those edits invent durations. Keep the original values, record the reason for each flag, and check the source. If a correction is supported, save a new version with the original value, corrected value and reason. If not, keep the uncertainty visible.

Another learner says all robot trips are covered because every row says indoor. A dataset card should instead state that outdoor trips are absent and that the data is fictional. Extra copies of existing rows do not create new conditions or new independent evidence.

A complete-looking card does not prove the table is accurate or suitable for a model. It makes claims and unanswered questions reviewable. Report raw counts separately from any later accepted subset, with explicit rules for missing, invalid and repeated records. Do not silently change denominators after cleaning.

For this exercise, zero is allowed and unknown is not zero. That is a stated schema choice, not a universal rule for all duration datasets. In a real task, measurement resolution and event definitions determine which values make sense. Dataset inspection also does not replace protecting held out data from model choices.

blocks.label: A card says the dataset is ready because it has no empty cells. Name two checks that claim misses, then write a more accurate statement about Robot practice v1.

workbook.title: Define the row and source
workbook.prompt: For Robot practice v1, state what one row is intended to represent, the source, the unit and the meaning of None.
workbook.answer: One row is intended to represent one indoor practice trip. The source is a teacher-authored fictional export for this lesson, duration uses minutes, and None means unknown rather than zero.

workbook.title: Interpret the audit counts
workbook.prompt: Explain each number in 5 4 2 1. How many extra ID occurrences are there, and how many rows belong to a repeated-ID group?
workbook.answer: The numbers mean 5 raw rows, 4 distinct IDs, 2 missing durations and 1 negative duration. There is 1 extra ID occurrence; 2 rows belong to the repeated-ID group B. These are different counts.

workbook.title: Reject an unsupported correction
workbook.prompt: A learner changes None to 0 and -2 to 2, then reports a clean dataset. Explain why this is not a justified repair and what record should be kept.
workbook.answer: Those edits invent outcomes without source evidence. Preserve the raw version, flag the affected rows and investigate. Record any supported correction with old value, new value, reason and version; unresolved values remain uncertain.

workbook.title: Inspect and document independently
workbook.prompt: A new fictional indoor trip export has (P,4), (Q,None), (Q,None), (R,-1), (S,6), (T,0), with durations in minutes and the same schema. Count raw rows, distinct IDs, missing durations, negative durations and extra ID occurrences. Identify overlap. Draft a short dataset card stating source, row meaning, unit, findings, unchanged version and one excluded use.
workbook.answer: There are 6 rows, 5 distinct IDs, 2 missing durations, 1 negative duration and 1 extra ID occurrence. Both Q rows are missing, so the duplicate and missing flags overlap. Zero for T is allowed by the stated schema. The card should identify the supplied fictional indoor export, one intended row per trip, minutes, all findings, raw unchanged version and no evidence for real or outdoor navigation use.

workbook.title: State an evidence gap
workbook.prompt: Someone duplicates each row ten times and claims the export now covers more kinds of trips. Explain what changed and what did not.
workbook.answer: The row count increased but no new trip conditions or independent observations were added. Coverage remains limited to the same supplied fictional indoor cases; the larger count does not establish broader usefulness.

teacher.background: Teach inspection before modelling in two 45-minute sessions. Use fictional data only. Emphasize the unit of observation, provenance, units, unknown values and overlapping audit flags. The dataset card is a concise classroom documentation exercise inspired by datasheets for datasets, not a claim to implement every part of a research framework. Students must distinguish observations from unsupported repairs and from evidence of model fitness.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook
Cards for the five raw rows including both B rows
Optional Python 3 editor; no packages required
Blank card headings: purpose source row schema findings changes limits version owner
sessions: Retrieve regression target meaning and why later outcomes are separate from prediction inputs. Establish that this week inspects data before fitting.
Read the source description and schema. Count physical rows and distinct trip IDs separately. Ask whether a repeated ID proves the reason for duplication.
Trace the code with row cards. Explain set, None and negative checks. Complete W1 and W2 with named denominators.
Use the guided question to show overlap: place both B cards in missing and repeated-ID groups. Do not subtract all flag counts independently.
Retrieve raw version versus corrected version. Ask what evidence could justify changing a recorded value.
Read the card example and complete W3. Distinguish a documented fact, an unknown and an assumption.
Collect W4 independently. Require counts, overlap and a concise card with source and limitations before offering hints.
Discuss W5 and the exit claim. Use the fresh retry after support and record the support given.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided: 2 of 5 raw rows have unknown duration, or 40 percent. No: the extra B occurrence is already among the missing rows, so subtracting all three flag counts double-counts it. A distinct usable-trip count requires a stated resolution policy and source review. Exit examples include duplicate IDs, impossible values, units, provenance and coverage. A defensible statement is that this five-row fictional export has documented quality flags and is suitable for inspection practice, with no model-readiness claim.
misconceptions: A complete card certifies data quality
The card records evidence and gaps; its claims still need checking. Documentation does not prove suitability.
Missing means zero
None is unknown; zero is a specific allowed value in this exercise. Substitution without evidence changes the meaning.
Flag counts can always be added
The same row can have multiple flags. Count rows or unique events under an explicit policy and retain the raw denominator.
teacher.assessment: Require W4 counts 6,5,2,1,1 in the stated order, the Q overlap, acceptance of zero under this schema, and a card with source, unit, raw version and excluded use. Fresh retry: rows (L,3), (M,None), (N,-2), (N,-2), (O,0). Counts are 5 raw, 4 IDs, 1 missing, 2 negative and 1 extra ID occurrence. The negative and repeated-ID flags overlap on N. Do not infer whether the two N rows describe one event without checking the source.
teacher.support: Use physical row cards and overlapping circles for flags. Supply blank card headings but no completed findings. Extension: explain how to record an evidenced seconds-to-minutes conversion while preserving the raw value, unit and version, and why a unit guess is not enough.
teacher.next: Week 5 examines label definitions and disagreement. Carry forward the dataset card, source questions and explicit distinction between unknown and observed values. Teacher reference: https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.09010 (Datasheets for Datasets; reviewed 2026-09-26).

ai-3/5.title: Label definitions and disagreement
goals: Write an observable label rule with boundaries and a review option
Measure agreement using matched items and an explicit denominator
Investigate disagreement and record justified label decisions

prerequisite.prompt: Why should an unknown duration remain different from zero in a dataset card?
prerequisite.answer: Unknown means the measurement is unavailable. Zero is a recorded value permitted by that schema; replacing unknown with zero invents evidence.

vocabulary: A written definition for assigning an outcome to an example
A person who assigns labels using a stated rule
How often annotators assign the same label to the same items
Reviewing evidence and rules to resolve a disputed label or retain uncertainty

blocks.text: A model learns from examples with recorded targets. If two people interpret a target differently, their labels can mix different tasks. This week you will write a label rule, compare independent labels and keep a record of disputed cases. We use invented corridor descriptions, not real images or a system for controlling a robot.

The classroom task is to label whether a marked practice lane is blocked in a supplied description. Rule v1 says blocked means an object touches or crosses either lane boundary or lies inside the lane; clear means all objects are outside both boundaries and the entire lane is visible. Use review if visibility or position is insufficient to decide. Review is a workflow status for a person to inspect, not a third physical condition of the lane.

rows: A box lies inside a fully visible lane
A wheel touches the boundary line
All objects are outside and the lane is fully visible
A curtain hides part of the lane

blocks.text: These are exercise definitions, not real robot safety rules. Do not infer that a lane is physically safe from this label. The label describes only the supplied evidence under this version of the rule.

lesson.title: Compare independent labels on matched items

blocks.text: Two annotators used an earlier vague instruction, mark an obstructed lane, on four invented items. Their labels are shown in the code. A and D match; B and C differ. Compare the same item IDs, not merely the first row in two differently ordered files.

blocks.title: Python 3 code
blocks.text:
pairs = [("A", "blocked", "blocked"),
         ("B", "clear", "blocked"),
         ("C", "review", "clear"),
         ("D", "clear", "clear")]
agree = 0
for item_id, first, second in pairs:
    if first == second:
        agree = agree + 1
print(agree, len(pairs))

The output is 2 4: two matching labels among four paired items, so observed exact agreement is 2/4 or 50 percent. Here review is included as a label value in the comparison: review versus clear is a disagreement. This simple count is not model accuracy and does not establish which labels are correct.

blocks.title: Follow a disagreement back to evidence
blocks.caption: Preserve independent labels before discussion. Shared mistakes can produce agreement, and missing evidence can prevent a justified final label.

blocks.text: The code assumes one valid pair per unique item ID and allowed label strings. It does not validate IDs or spelling. Use a nonempty paired set before calculating a fraction; zero paired items gives no agreement estimate.

For B, the full lane is visible and a wheel touches its boundary. One annotator treated touching as clear; the other treated it as blocked. Rule v1 explicitly includes touching, so the reviewed label is blocked. Preserve both original labels and record the item, rule version, evidence, decision and reviewer. Do not silently overwrite the originals.

For C, a curtain hides part of the lane. One annotator guessed clear; the other requested review. Rule v1 requires full visibility for clear. The justified status remains review until sufficient evidence is available. More votes cannot reveal the hidden area.

blocks.label: Using rule v1, explain the decisions for B and C. If you exclude C from the original comparison, what is agreement among the remaining pairs? Why must you still report the exclusion?

blocks.text: A decision log could say: B, original clear/blocked, wheel touches line, v1, blocked after review by the teacher. For C it could say: original review/clear, lane partly hidden, v1, unresolved review. Add the labeling method and rule version to the dataset card.

lesson.title: Improve the rule without changing the question

blocks.text: A useful rule names the object of judgment, allowed labels, observable evidence, boundaries and an uncertainty route. Include a typical example and a boundary example. Pilot the rule independently on a few new items, compare labels, discuss causes, revise the wording and label new items again. Record which rule produced each set of labels.

Do not change the rule simply to improve a score or make a model look correct. A rule revision can change the target itself. If touching is changed from blocked to clear, document the changed task, review all affected examples consistently and keep versions separate. Consult task evidence when interpreting a disagreement; a majority vote alone cannot prove truth.

lesson.title: Make a claim the comparison supports

blocks.text: Report the paired-item count, agreement count, handling of review and the rule version. For the original four-item comparison, say two of four pairs match, including review statuses. If you report a subset, name its selection rule and denominator. This tiny invented set says nothing about reliability on other scenes.

Keep practice for writing label rules separate from final model testing. Resolving labels needs a documented process; reviewing model predictions to choose convenient labels would undermine a fair evaluation. Next week you will separate related examples when designing data splits.

blocks.label: Two annotators agree on every item but both ignore the boundary rule. What does perfect agreement establish, and what does it fail to establish? Give one evidence check to perform next.

workbook.title: Use the boundary and review rules
workbook.prompt: Under rule v1, label a wheel touching the boundary, an object entirely outside a fully visible lane, and a partly hidden lane. Explain the evidence for each.
workbook.answer: Touching is blocked. An object entirely outside is clear only when all objects are outside and the entire lane is visible. A partly hidden lane requires review because clear cannot be established from the available description.

workbook.title: Interpret agreement
workbook.prompt: Explain the output 2 4 for A through D. State the fraction and percent, whether review is included, and why this is not model accuracy.
workbook.answer: Two of four matched items have identical annotator labels: 2/4 or 50 percent. Review is included in this exact comparison. Neither annotator is established as a correct reference, and no model predictions are being scored.

workbook.title: Write a decision log
workbook.prompt: For B and C, record original labels, visible evidence, rule version and reviewed decision. Explain why the original labels should remain available.
workbook.answer: B: clear/blocked, wheel touches boundary, v1, blocked. C: review/clear, partly hidden lane, v1, unresolved review. Record the reviewer as well. Originals preserve the independent disagreement and let another person audit how a decision was made.

workbook.title: Apply the process independently
workbook.prompt: New pairs are P blocked/blocked, Q clear/blocked, R review/review, S clear/clear, T blocked/clear. P has an object inside; Q touches the line; R is partly hidden; S has all objects outside a fully visible lane; T has an object inside. Count agreement including review. Apply v1 to all five. Then report agreement on the original pairs excluding any review status, with its denominator and limitation.
workbook.answer: Three of five pairs match, or 60 percent. Reviewed results are P blocked, Q blocked, R review, S clear, T blocked. Excluding R leaves two matches among four pairs, or 50 percent. The subset omits the uncertain case and does not establish correctness or general reliability. Preserve original labels separately from reviewed decisions.

workbook.title: Draft and test a label rule
workbook.prompt: Write a short v1 labeling instruction covering blocked, clear, the touching boundary and review. Add one boundary example. Explain why three people voting clear cannot settle a hidden lane.
workbook.answer: A suitable instruction specifies the marked lane: inside or touching either boundary means blocked; clear requires all objects outside and full visibility; insufficient position or visibility means review. A wheel touching the line is blocked. Votes supply no missing visual evidence, so a hidden lane remains review under v1.

teacher.background: Teach two 45-minute sessions using invented scene descriptions. The target is applying a stated observation rule, not certifying real robot safety. Keep original independent labels separate from reviewed decisions. Exact agreement includes review in the main exercise; review is a workflow status, not a physical lane class. Avoid calling annotator agreement accuracy.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook
Scene cards for the four worked examples and five independent cases
Optional Python 3 editor with no extra packages
Blank decision log with item originals evidence rule decision reviewer
sessions: Retrieve unknown versus zero. Ask why a label needs an explicit meaning before it becomes training data.
Read v1. Apply inside, boundary, outside and hidden examples. Establish that these are fictional descriptions, not robot safety advice.
Have pairs label fresh verbal examples independently before talking. Trace the supplied four-item code and complete W1 and W2.
Compare B and C using evidence. Complete the guided denominator question and preserve the original pair list.
Retrieve agreement versus correctness. Show a shared mistake on a touching-boundary example.
Model a decision-log entry without erasing original labels. Complete W3 and discuss a genuine rule revision.
Collect W4 independently before support. Require both denominators, rule-based decisions and the unresolved review case.
Use W5 and the exit response. After feedback, offer the fresh retry and record any support used.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided: B is blocked because touching counts; C stays review because the lane is partly hidden. Excluding C leaves the original pairs A, B and D: 2 matches out of 3, about 66.7 percent. Report the exclusion because this is a different subset from the four-item comparison, not newly correct labels. Exit: perfect agreement establishes matching labels on these items only. Both people can share a rule error. Check their labels against the boundary evidence and v1 before making a correctness claim.
misconceptions: Agreement is accuracy
Agreement compares annotators. Accuracy would require predictions and an appropriate reference; shared mistakes can still match.
Review means clear
Review preserves insufficient evidence. It is neither a negative label nor proof of a physical condition.
Voting removes uncertainty
Votes may select a decision policy but cannot create missing evidence. Preserve unresolved cases and document the policy.
teacher.assessment: Require W4 counts 3/5 including review and 2/4 excluding review, all five v1 decisions, and an explicit subset limitation. Fresh retry: U clear/clear with all objects outside a fully visible lane; V blocked/clear with an object touching the boundary; W blocked/blocked with an object inside; X review/blocked with part of the lane hidden. Original agreement is 2/4 or 50 percent; excluding X gives 2/3 or about 66.7 percent. Reviewed v1 decisions are clear, blocked, blocked, review. Require evidence for V and X before accepting the retry.
teacher.support: Use lane drawings and movable object cards for touching versus outside; cover part of the drawing for review. Provide blank log headings without decisions. Extension: construct two annotators who agree perfectly while both break v1 and explain why the agreement fraction does not reveal the error.
teacher.next: Week 6 covers splits and related examples. Carry forward item IDs, rule versions, original labels and review status so that related cases and labeling decisions remain traceable.

ai-3/6.title: Splits and related examples
goals: Choose a split unit that matches the intended prediction claim
Keep related examples together and audit group overlap
Record split roles counts and limits before model evaluation

prerequisite.prompt: Why does agreement between two annotators not prove their labels are correct?
prerequisite.answer: They can share the same mistake or use an unclear rule. Agreement counts matching labels; correctness requires checking the rule and evidence.

vocabulary: Examples used to fit a model
Separate examples used to compare choices during development
Held out examples used for final evaluation after choices are fixed
Related examples that must stay together for a stated evaluation goal

lesson.title: Ask what should be new at evaluation

blocks.text: A model may seem successful when its test examples closely resemble examples it already learned from. Imagine several pictures taken seconds apart during one robot trip. They have different picture IDs but share a route, lighting and objects. This week you will assign entire trips to separate sets and explain what the resulting evaluation could measure. No model is fitted in this lesson.

Our invented twelve-row dataset contains frame descriptions from six trips. Each row is one frame; the group is its trip ID. The proposed claim concerns new trips on the same practice route under similar conditions. We therefore keep all frames from a trip in one set. To claim success on new routes, grouping only by trip would not be enough.

This small fictional assignment is for learning split design, not evidence of real performance. Each frame belongs to one group and one set. Store frame and trip IDs as metadata for auditing; do not assume an ID is an appropriate prediction input.

lesson.title: Check every pair of group sets

blocks.text: Training data fits the model. Validation data helps compare choices such as candidate rules. Keep the test set for a final check after those choices are fixed. A learner who repeatedly changes the model after seeing test results has used that set for development; its score is no longer an untouched final check.

blocks.title: Python 3 code

blocks.text: The first line of output is []: no trip ID is shared between any pair of sets. The second is 3 1 2: training, validation and test contain three, one and two trip groups. The symbol & finds shared values and | combines sets. These are group counts, not frame counts.

blocks.title: Keep each trip in one role
rows: A B C with all frames
blocks.caption: Keep related frames together. Separate group IDs prevent this form of overlap; they do not prove that every other source of leakage is absent.

blocks.text: This audit assumes the lists correctly describe every frame assignment. It cannot find an omitted frame, a wrong trip ID, a copied image with a different ID or a feature containing the answer. Check the assignment table and source records too.

lesson.title: Repair a split at the group level

blocks.text: Suppose A1 and A2 are in training while A3 is in test. The frame IDs differ, but A appears in both sets. Shuffling the rows does not remove this relationship. For our new-trip claim, move all A frames to one chosen role and record the revised assignment before evaluating a model. Do not copy A3 into both roles.

Audit that every source frame occurs exactly once, no group crosses roles and the assigned counts sum to the source count. In our worked plan the row counts are six training, two validation and four test: twelve total. A fixed random seed can reproduce a random split, but it cannot make a flawed grouping choice fair.

blocks.label: A learner moves D2 from validation to training but leaves D1 in validation. Give the new row counts and shared trip ID. Explain why different frame IDs and a fixed seed do not repair the overlap.

blocks.text: A split record names the prediction goal, source version, group definition, exact assignments, row and group counts, date and any random method or seed used. For this hand-assigned example, record that there was no random sampling. Keep label-rule versions and unresolved review statuses traceable as in Week 5.

lesson.title: Choose the split for the intended use

blocks.text: For new trips on a familiar route, holding out whole trips addresses within-trip similarity. For new routes, hold out entire routes so all their trips stay together. For forecasting future events, a time-respecting split may be needed: training on later events to predict earlier ones would not represent that intended use. The evaluation question determines the separation.

There is no universal percentage that makes a split valid. Large groups can make row counts unequal. Check that the sets can support the intended comparison, including enough relevant cases and labels, without moving individual related frames just to hit a percentage. This twelve-row example is too small to justify a reliable performance claim.

Fit learned preprocessing, such as scaling values using an average, on training data and apply the stored transformation to the other sets. Using the full dataset to learn such values would let held out information influence development. We will implement preprocessing later; group separation alone does not solve that issue.

Record exclusions and label-review policies before scoring. Do not remove difficult test cases because they reduce the score. If a genuine data error requires repair, document it and its effect on the evaluation rather than claiming the old test stayed untouched. Next week you will build a simple baseline using these split roles.

blocks.label: All trip IDs are separate, but every trip uses the same route. Can you claim the model works on unseen routes? Explain the limitation and propose a split unit for that new claim.

workbook.title: Explain the three roles
workbook.prompt: Explain what training, validation and test sets are used for. What changes if you repeatedly choose a model using its test score?
workbook.answer: Training fits the model; validation compares development choices; test evaluates after choices are fixed. Repeatedly selecting by the test score uses that set for development, so it is no longer an untouched final evaluation.

workbook.title: Distinguish frames from groups
workbook.prompt: For the worked A through F plan, give training, validation and test counts first in groups and then in rows. Interpret [] from the code and state one problem it cannot detect.
workbook.answer: Group counts are 3,1,2; row counts are 6,2,4. The empty list means no trip ID overlaps between any pair of the listed sets. The code cannot detect wrong metadata, an omitted frame, a disguised duplicate or an outcome feature.

workbook.title: Repair a related example leak
workbook.prompt: A1 and A2 are in training and A3 is in test. Explain why unique frame IDs and a fixed random seed do not fix this. Propose a repair and what to record.
workbook.answer: The frames share trip A, so the test contains a trip already represented in training. Unique frame IDs do not remove similarity; a seed only reproduces the assignment. Put every A frame in one role, keep each frame once and record the revised assignments and counts before model evaluation.

workbook.title: Audit and repair independently
workbook.prompt: Eight frames come from trips P (P1 P2 P3), Q (Q1 Q2), R (R1), S (S1 S2). A proposed split is training P1 Q1 R1; validation P2 S1; test Q2 P3 S2. Identify shared groups for each pair of sets. Repair it by assigning P and Q to training, R to validation and S to test. List all frames in each role and give row and group counts. State one limit of the repaired plan.
workbook.answer: Training/validation share P; training/test share P and Q; validation/test share P and S. Repaired training is P1 P2 P3 Q1 Q2 (5 rows,2 groups), validation R1 (1 row,1 group), test S1 S2 (2 rows,1 group). Every frame appears once and groups are disjoint. This tiny plan does not establish reliable performance, correct metadata, label coverage or success on new routes.

workbook.title: Match separation to the claim
workbook.prompt: A model will be evaluated on new routes. Route North has trips A and B; route South has C and D. A proposed split trains on A and C and tests on B and D. Explain the problem and give a route-based alternative. Is this enough for a strong performance claim?
workbook.answer: Both routes occur in training and test, so the plan does not hold out a new route. For illustration, keep A and B together for training and C and D together for test, or reverse the route roles. With only two routes there is too little evidence for a strong general claim and no separate route left for validation; obtain more routes for a fuller design.

teacher.background: Teach two 45-minute sessions with fictional frame cards. Focus on the evaluation goal and unit of separation before percentages. The worked plan separates trips for an intended new-trip claim on a familiar route. It neither trains a model nor establishes performance. Distinguish frames, groups and sets, and retain Week 5 label-rule and review records.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook
Twelve frame cards A1 A2 A3 B1 B2 C1 D1 D2 E1 E2 F1 F2
Three trays or paper areas named training validation and test
Optional Python 3 editor with no extra packages
sessions: Retrieve why matching labels can share an error. State the new-trip evaluation goal and define one row and one group.
Use the frame cards to build the worked split. Count rows and groups separately and explain the three roles.
Trace the intersection audit. Complete W1 and W2; ask which metadata problems an empty overlap list could miss.
Move D2 into training and complete the guided question. Repair it by moving it back, then record the before and after counts.
Retrieve why shuffling and fixed seeds do not remove relationships. Ask what must stay together for a new-route claim.
Complete W3 and discuss group-based, route-based and time-respecting evaluation goals. Explain why percentages cannot decide the goal.
Collect W4 independently before hints. Require all three overlap checks, exact repaired frame lists and both count units.
Discuss W5 and the exit question. Use the fresh retry after support and record what help was needed.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided: the row counts become 7 training, 1 validation and 4 test. D is shared by training and validation because D1 and D2 are related frames from one trip. Unique frame IDs and a seed do not remove the shared trip. Return D2 to validation to recover the worked plan. Exit: separate trip IDs on one route do not test unseen routes. Hold out whole routes with all their trips, and collect enough routes and relevant conditions for the intended evaluation.
misconceptions: Different row IDs mean independent examples
Different frames may share a trip or source. Choose group metadata based on the claim and verify it against the source.
A fixed percentage guarantees a fair test
Percentages do not remove overlap or ensure enough groups and relevant cases. The goal and dependencies determine the split.
An empty overlap list proves there is no leakage
The audit checks listed group IDs only. Wrong metadata, copied content, outcome features or preprocessing fitted on all sets can still invalidate evaluation.
teacher.assessment: Require W4 overlaps P; P and Q; P and S, in pair order, then exact repaired lists with rows 5,1,2 and groups 2,1,1. Fresh retry: U1 U2 belong to U, V1 to V, W1 W2 to W. Proposed training U1 V1, validation W1, test U2 W2 has shared U between training/test and W between validation/test; training/validation share none. Repair to all U in training, V in validation and all W in test: rows 2,1,2 and groups 1,1,1. Require an explicit small-sample limitation.
teacher.support: Keep a coloured border shared by cards from the same trip. Supply blank assignment tables without the correct roles. Extension: explain why a new-route evaluation with many frames but only two routes has limited evidence and cannot obtain three nonempty disjoint route sets.
teacher.next: Week 7 introduces a baseline before a model. Carry forward the split record and keep the final test protected while comparing choices. Teacher reference: scikit-learn cross-validation documentation, grouped data section, https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/cross_validation.html (reviewed 2026-09-27).

ai-3/7.title: A baseline before a model
goals: Fit a majority label baseline using training labels only
Score fixed predictions on the same validation examples
Explain what a baseline comparison does and does not establish

prerequisite.prompt: Why should frames from the same trip stay in one set when evaluating on new trips?
prerequisite.answer: Related frames can share conditions and objects. Keeping the trip together prevents that trip from appearing in both development and evaluation sets.

vocabulary: A simple reference method used to judge a more complex approach
The label with more examples than the other label in this binary task
Correct predictions divided by the number of scored examples
A unit for the difference between two percentages

lesson.title: Give a score a useful comparison

blocks.text: A learner reports that a classifier gets 80 percent correct. Is that useful? We need to know the task, the examples and what a simple method achieves on those same examples. A baseline is a reference method. This week our baseline ignores each scene and always predicts the label that is most common in the training set.

Use a new teacher-authored fictional dataset for predicting clear or blocked lanes. Each listed row describes one frame from a different trip on a familiar route; training and validation trips do not overlap. This is a new practice set, not the twelve-frame table from Week 6. All supplied labels have been resolved under the classroom rule. There are no review cases in this exercise, and no real navigation claim is made.

rows: clear clear blocked clear blocked clear

blocks.text: The training counts are four clear and two blocked. Our stated method therefore predicts clear for every new example. A baseline can still learn a value from training data; simple does not mean it uses no data. If the two training counts tie, our rule chooses clear, declared before scoring.

lesson.title: Fit once and score the fixed prediction

blocks.title: Python 3 code
blocks.text:
train = ["clear", "clear", "blocked",
         "clear", "blocked", "clear"]
valid = ["blocked", "clear", "blocked", "clear"]
prediction = "clear"
if train.count("blocked") > train.count("clear"):
    prediction = "blocked"
correct = 0
for label in valid:
    if prediction == label:
        correct = correct + 1
print(prediction, correct, len(valid))

The output is clear 2 4. The fixed prediction matches two of the four validation labels, so accuracy is 2/4 or 50 percent. The training majority share, 4/6, is not the validation accuracy. The baseline does not inspect the validation labels to decide which constant to predict.

blocks.title: Keep fitting separate from scoring
blocks.caption: The baseline uses training labels to choose its constant. Validation labels are used to score that fixed constant, not to refit it.

blocks.text: The code assumes nonempty training data with only clear and blocked labels. It counts matches on the supplied validation list; a percentage also requires a nonempty validation set. Do not run it on empty training data and describe the default clear value as learned evidence. Other labels and unresolved review statuses need an explicit policy.

Suppose a candidate method supplies blocked, clear, clear, clear for the four validation rows in the table. These are supplied predictions for a comparison exercise; we have not fitted that candidate. It gets three of four correct, or 75 percent. The baseline gets two of four, or 50 percent. The candidate is ahead by one correct example and 25 percentage points on this set.

Use identical row IDs, reference labels, exclusions and metric for both methods. Match predictions to their rows even if files are reordered. A score on easier examples is not a fair comparison. Neither this four-row result nor beating one baseline proves that the candidate will perform well on future trips.

blocks.label: The candidate misses the third validation row. Which rows does the baseline miss? Explain how the candidate changes the number correct. Why is the improvement 25 percentage points rather than a claim of 25 percent relative improvement?

blocks.text: Record training counts, the fixed prediction and tie rule, validation IDs and labels, prediction lists and correct/total counts. Keep the final test separate from development decisions. Next week we will search candidate rules using training evidence, then compare choices carefully.

A learner sees that blocked is common in a new validation set and changes the baseline to always blocked. That is not the original training-majority baseline. Its parameter was selected from evaluation labels. Restore the training-derived constant for that comparison and document any separate method honestly.

Another learner compares a candidate on ten easy rows with a baseline on four difficult rows. The difference could come from the examples. Score both on the same intended set with the same treatment of missing predictions and unresolved labels; report exclusions rather than silently dropping mistakes.

Imagine ten validation cases with nine clear and one blocked, while the training-derived constant is clear. The baseline gets 9/10 or 90 percent accuracy but misses the only blocked case. Overall accuracy counts all rows equally; it does not describe every kind of error or its consequences. Later weeks will examine those errors in detail.

A majority baseline is a useful first comparison, not a guarantee of the best simple method. It can be weak when validation label proportions differ from training. Keep the declared baseline, report what happened and consider other justified reference methods during development. Do not tune a final test result into a better-looking claim.

blocks.label: A candidate and the clear baseline both get 90 percent on ten cases. Does that prove they make the same mistakes or are suitable for use? State what additional evidence you would inspect.

workbook.title: Choose from training evidence
workbook.prompt: Count clear and blocked in the worked training list. State the constant prediction and the declared tie rule. Explain why the validation majority does not choose this baseline.
workbook.answer: Training has four clear and two blocked, so the constant is clear. A tie chooses clear under the declared classroom rule. Validation labels score the stored prediction; using their majority to choose it would change the fitting procedure.

workbook.title: Calculate the validation score
workbook.prompt: List the four baseline predictions and mark which validation rows are correct. Give correct/total and accuracy. Explain why 4/6 is not the answer.
workbook.answer: Predictions are clear, clear, clear, clear. Rows 2 and 4 match, giving 2/4 or 50 percent. The fraction 4/6 describes clear labels in training, not correct predictions on the four validation rows.

workbook.title: Make the comparison fair
workbook.prompt: A candidate is scored on ten easy rows and the baseline on four difficult rows. Describe a fair comparison and two details you must record.
workbook.answer: Score both methods on the same intended validation examples with matched IDs, reference labels, metric and exclusion policy. Record predictions, correct/total counts and the training-derived baseline rule. Different example sets do not isolate a method difference.

workbook.title: Fit and compare independently
workbook.prompt: New training labels are blocked, clear, blocked, blocked, clear. New validation labels are clear, blocked, clear, blocked. Fit the same baseline rule and list its four predictions. A supplied candidate predicts clear, blocked, blocked, blocked. Score both on these rows and state the difference in correct examples and percentage points. What claim remains unsupported?
workbook.answer: Training counts are three blocked and two clear, so predict blocked four times. The baseline matches rows 2 and 4: 2/4 or 50 percent. The candidate matches rows 1,2,4: 3/4 or 75 percent. It gains one correct example and 25 percentage points. This tiny validation comparison does not prove future performance or readiness for use.

workbook.title: Explain the hidden error
workbook.prompt: A training-derived clear baseline gets nine of ten validation cases correct; the labels are nine clear and one blocked. State its accuracy and missed case. If a candidate also gets nine correct, must it miss the same case? Explain.
workbook.answer: Accuracy is 90 percent, and the baseline misses the sole blocked case. A candidate could also score 90 percent by correctly identifying blocked but missing one clear case. Equal totals do not imply identical errors; inspect predictions by row and error type.

teacher.background: Teach two 45-minute sessions. Fit a binary majority-label baseline from training labels and freeze its prediction before scoring. The invented set uses one frame per distinct trip; it is separate from Week 6 data. Supplied candidate predictions are comparison examples, not an implemented fitted model. Treat this as a first benchmark and evidence lesson, not a readiness test.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook
Six training label cards and four validation cards kept in order
Optional Python 3 editor with no extra packages
Blank comparison table with row reference baseline candidate and matches
sessions: Retrieve the split roles and related-trip issue. Ask what a score means without a reference method.
Count training labels and write the constant before revealing validation labels. State the tie rule before any comparison.
Trace the code. Complete W1 and W2, separating training share from validation accuracy.
Build a row-by-row comparison for the supplied candidate. Complete the guided percentage-point question.
Retrieve what changes if the baseline constant is chosen using validation labels.
Discuss the two unfair comparisons and complete W3. Require common rows, labels and scoring policy.
Collect W4 independently before hints. Require the training counts, both prediction lists, scores and restrained claim.
Use W5 and the exit question to compare error patterns. Give the fresh retry after feedback and record support.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided: the baseline misses rows 1 and 3; the candidate misses only row 3, adding one correct example. The difference is 75 minus 50 = 25 percentage points. Relative improvement in accuracy would be (75 minus 50)/50 = 50 percent; keep the measure explicit. Exit: equal accuracy does not establish identical mistakes or suitability. Inspect predictions by row, missed blocked cases, false blocked predictions, sample coverage and consequences, then evaluate using an appropriate held out process.
misconceptions: A simple baseline does not need training data
This method learns its constant from training label counts, although it ignores input features.
Training majority share is validation accuracy
Fit using training labels, then count matches separately on validation rows. Their label proportions can differ.
Beating a baseline proves the system is ready
It is one comparison on specified examples. Error types, coverage, uncertainty and final evaluation remain relevant.
teacher.assessment: Require W4 blocked from counts 3 versus 2, baseline 2/4, candidate 3/4, one extra correct and 25 percentage points. Fresh retry: training clear, blocked, blocked, clear is tied, so choose clear by the declared rule. Validation blocked, clear, blocked, blocked gives baseline 1/4 or 25 percent. Candidate blocked, clear, clear, blocked gives 3/4 or 75 percent: two extra correct and 50 percentage points. Require the tie rule and explain why validation majority blocked cannot replace the stored constant.
teacher.support: Use labelled cards and matching ticks before fractions. Supply a blank row-aligned comparison table without predictions. Extension: construct two different prediction lists with identical accuracy but different missed rows, and explain how to report both.
teacher.next: Week 8 searches candidate rules. Carry forward a frozen training-derived baseline and a fair comparison record. Teacher reference: scikit-learn DummyClassifier documentation, most_frequent strategy, https://scikit-learn.org/dev/modules/generated/sklearn.dummy.DummyClassifier.html (reviewed 2026-09-27).

ai-3/9.title: Fitting a decision tree
goals: Fit a root question and leaf predictions from training examples
Trace a new example through the learned tree
Compare a shallow tree with a baseline and state its limits

prerequisite.prompt: Why does a cutoff with zero training errors still need validation on separate examples?
prerequisite.answer: The cutoff was selected using training labels. Matching those examples does not establish performance on new examples; validation can expose mistakes and support a baseline comparison.

vocabulary: The first question asked by a tree
A path selected by the answer to a question
An endpoint that stores a prediction
The largest number of question steps from root to leaf

lesson.title: Learn the question and its answers

blocks.text: A decision tree asks a feature question and follows a branch to a prediction. A tree with one question has depth one and is sometimes called a stump. Unlike Week 8, where the two output labels were fixed in advance, this week we fit both the question and the label stored at each leaf.

Our six fictional training rows have two binary sensor flags available before prediction: near and tall. A value of 1 means that flag is present; 0 means absent. The reviewed scene label is separate. Each row represents a different trip on a familiar route, including rows with identical values. Similar readings can have different scene labels. These are teaching examples, not robot control instructions.

Try near first and tall second. For each question, group the training rows by 0 and 1, then predict each group’s majority label; choose clear for tied label counts. Count all training mistakes and keep the first question if scores tie. Stop after one question. This is our stated classroom fitting procedure.

lesson.title: Fit the root and both leaves

blocks.title: Python 3 code
