blocks.text: Feature 0 is near; feature 1 is tall; row[2] is the label. Output is 0 1, then 1 2, then 0 clear blocked. Near makes one training mistake: near=0 contains two clear labels and one blocked, so that leaf predicts clear. Near=1 contains three blocked labels. Tall makes two mistakes because both its groups have a blocked majority.

The stored tree contains the chosen feature and its two learned leaves. The code assumes nonempty data, binary flags, allowed labels and examples on both branches of each candidate. An empty branch would need a declared fallback; this small example does not implement one. The score is total training mistakes, not an average giving small and large branches equal weight.

This is an explicitly limited depth-one learner. General tree algorithms can repeat split selection within branches and often use impurity criteria such as Gini. Our code does not implement that full procedure. Keeping the scope small lets you inspect every decision.

lesson.title: Trace the fitted tree on new rows

blocks.title: Two paths through the learned tree
blocks.caption: Both paths start at the same root. Tall is not used by this fitted tree; the leaf labels came from training counts.

blocks.text: Validation rows are (near=1,tall=1,blocked), (0,0,clear), (0,1,blocked), (1,0,clear). Follow only near: predictions are blocked, clear, clear, blocked. Two of four match. The training-majority baseline predicts blocked, since training has four blocked and two clear; it also matches two of four validation labels.

blocks.label: Which validation rows does the tree miss, and which does the baseline miss? Explain why the tall value cannot change this tree’s prediction.

blocks.text: Keep the fitted root and leaves unchanged while scoring. Equal accuracy does not mean identical errors, and five correct training predictions out of six is not the validation result.

lesson.title: Distinguish a learned leaf from a fixed label

blocks.text: Do not assume near=1 must always predict blocked. If a new training set gives that branch a clear majority, this same learner will store clear there. A feature name is not the answer. Use the training labels belonging to that branch.

Adding more questions can fit finer training details but does not guarantee better new-case performance. Record any depth choice made during development, and keep final test data separate. A leaf majority describes this training group; it is not a promise about every future example.

lesson.title: Explain the model you actually fitted

blocks.text: Record the two candidate questions, branch label counts, total errors, tie rules, depth limit, stored tree and validation predictions. Retain all rows, including the blocked example in the near=0 branch; removing a disagreement would change the evidence.

Our tree uses a single feature because that question scored better under this procedure. This neither establishes that near causes blockage nor that tall is useless in every dataset. Next week a nearest-neighbour method will predict by comparing examples instead of following learned questions.

blocks.label: A learner says the tree is reliable because near=1 has only blocked training labels. Rewrite this claim using the leaf evidence, validation score and one limitation.

workbook.title: Name the parts and decisions
workbook.prompt: Identify the root, its two branches, leaf predictions and depth of the worked fitted tree. Which parts were selected using training labels?
workbook.answer: The root asks near, with branches 0 and 1. Leaves predict clear for 0 and blocked for 1. Depth is one. Training labels determined both leaf majorities and the error comparison that selected near rather than tall.

workbook.title: Verify the candidate scores
workbook.prompt: For each near branch and each tall branch, count blocked and clear labels and choose a leaf. Give the total errors for each candidate question.
workbook.answer: Near=0 has 1 blocked and 2 clear, predicts clear with 1 error; near=1 has 3 blocked and 0 clear, predicts blocked with 0 errors. Tall=0 has 2 blocked and 1 clear; tall=1 also has 2 blocked and 1 clear. Both tall leaves predict blocked with 1 error each. Totals are near 1 and tall 2.

workbook.title: Separate fitting from prediction
workbook.prompt: A learner sees a blocked validation case with near=0 and changes that leaf to blocked before reporting the score. Explain what changed and how to report the original fitted tree fairly.
workbook.answer: The leaf was changed using validation evidence, so it is no longer the original training-fitted tree. Score the original stored leaves on all the same validation rows and record any later development change separately. Preserve a separate final test for final evaluation.

workbook.title: Fit a new tree independently
workbook.prompt: New training rows (near,tall,label) are (1,0,clear),(1,1,clear),(1,0,clear),(0,1,blocked),(0,0,blocked),(0,1,clear). Use the same candidate order and tie policies. Give both candidates’ leaves and errors, then select the tree. Validation rows are (1,1,clear),(0,0,blocked),(0,1,clear),(1,0,blocked). List tree predictions and compare accuracy with the training-majority baseline.
workbook.answer: Near=0 predicts blocked from 2 blocked and 1 clear; near=1 predicts clear from 3 clear. Near has 1 error. Both tall groups have 2 clear and 1 blocked, so both leaves predict clear and total errors are 2. Choose near with reversed leaf labels compared with the worked example. Validation predictions clear,blocked,blocked,clear match rows 1,2: 2/4. Baseline clear matches rows 1,3: 2/4. Both are 50 percent but errors differ.

workbook.title: Audit a tie and a claim
workbook.prompt: If near and tall make the same training error count, which question does this code retain and why? Does retaining that question prove it will be better on future trips?
workbook.answer: It retains near because near is tried first and strict < replaces only for fewer errors. This is a declared tie convention, not evidence of better future performance. Separate evaluation and relevant examples are still needed.

teacher.background: Teach two 45-minute sessions. Students fit a depth-one decision tree by learning branch majorities and selecting the question with the fewest total training mistakes. This transparent classroom algorithm is not a claim to reproduce CART or a library default. Explain tuple positions, list comprehension and the leaves dictionary; offer the full paper route for students who need it.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook
Six training row cards and four validation cards
Two branch areas labelled 0 and 1
Optional Python 3 editor with no packages required
sessions: Retrieve training search versus validation. Introduce root, branch, leaf and depth with one question.
Sort the six cards by near. Count labels within each branch and assign its majority without using validation.
Repeat for tall and complete W1 and W2. Add branch mistakes to score the full training set.
Trace code and the diagram. Predict all four validation rows, complete the guided question and compare the baseline.
Retrieve why a leaf label is learned rather than dictated by the feature name.
Complete W3 and discuss depth limits, tied questions and the assumptions required by the short code.
Collect W4 independently before hints. Require branch counts, both candidate scores, learned leaves and validation comparison.
Use W5 and the exit claim. Give the fresh retry after feedback and record support.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided: tree predictions blocked,clear,clear,blocked miss rows 3 and 4. Baseline blocked misses rows 2 and 4. Both get 2/4 or 50 percent. Tall cannot affect prediction because the stored root uses near only. Exit: the near=1 leaf contains three blocked training examples, but the whole tree gets 2/4 on this tiny validation set and misses one near=1 validation case. This does not establish reliability on future trips.
misconceptions: A near branch must predict blocked
The branch label is learned from its training labels; W4 deliberately reverses that relationship.
Every feature is used during prediction
Only questions in the stored tree are followed. Candidate questions rejected during fitting do not affect this tree’s output.
A deeper tree must work better
More questions can fit training detail. Future performance needs separate evaluation; depth choices must be documented.
teacher.assessment: Require W4 near error 1, tall error 2, near=0 blocked and near=1 clear, with both validation scores 2/4. Fresh retry: training (0,0,clear),(0,1,blocked),(1,0,clear),(1,1,blocked). Near branches each tie and predict clear, giving 2 errors. Tall=0 predicts clear and tall=1 blocked with 0 errors; choose tall. Validation (0,1,blocked),(1,0,clear),(1,1,clear) gives blocked,clear,blocked: 2/3. The tied training baseline predicts clear and also gets 2/3, with different missed rows. Require the learned feature and both tie policies.
teacher.support: Use physical sorting before code. Explain row[feature] as selecting a flag and row[2] as reading its label. Supply empty branch-count tables. Extension: explain why an empty branch needs a fallback, and why this code would silently return clear if given an empty label list.
teacher.next: Week 10 introduces nearest neighbours and distances. Carry forward the training/validation split and baseline. Teacher reference: https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.tree.DecisionTreeClassifier.html (reviewed 2026-09-27); its library criteria differ from our stated classroom mistake-count procedure.

ai-4/1.title: Representing inputs as vectors
goals: Encode a record using a fixed feature order and units
Distinguish a vector dimension from the number of examples
Detect missing values and target leakage before computation

prerequisite.prompt: A parcel classifier uses width and height to predict a class. Why must its final class label stay outside the input features?
prerequisite.answer: The class is the target being predicted. Supplying that answer as an input leaks information that would not be available for a new prediction.

vocabulary: An ordered list of numerical components
One value at a specified position in a vector
The number of components in a vector
The recorded feature order, units and validity rules

blocks.text: A neural network receives numbers in a specified order. Before learning how it computes, we need to represent one example without losing the meaning of its fields. A vector is an ordered list: [4, 2] can mean width 4 cm and height 2 cm if that is the declared order. Reversing the two numbers describes a different rectangle under the same schema.

For this fictional parcel investigation, use [width in cm, height in cm]. Width and height must both be present and greater than zero. The vector has dimension 2 because it contains two components. Record IDs identify examples; they do not measure the parcel. The target class is stored separately.
There are three examples, each with two features. Stacking their vectors makes a table with three rows and two columns. Do not confuse the number of rows with the dimension of one input.

Read fields by name, convert to the declared units, validate, and only then write the vector. Parcel D has width 50 mm and height 30 mm. Because 10 mm equals 1 cm, its encoded vector is [5, 3]. Writing [50, 30] would preserve the numbers while changing the physical meaning by a factor of ten.

blocks.title: Optional Python check

blocks.text: This short function assumes each supplied value is a number in mm or None for missing. It is a classroom example, not a complete input validator. Trace the conversion before running it. The function represents data; it does not fit a model or predict a class.

lesson.title: Read the same record through three stages

blocks.title: An input vector keeps an agreed order
blocks.caption: Read each row left to right, then assemble the final ordered pair. The schema explains the numbers; the vector alone does not.

blocks.label: Parcel E has width 20 mm and height 70 mm. Encode it and explain why [7, 2] is not the same input under this schema.

lesson.title: Repair a representation before using it

blocks.text: A missing height is unknown, not zero. Under this schema zero is also invalid, so reject the incomplete record and request the measurement. A different project might use a documented training-fitted replacement plus a missingness flag; that would be a different schema that must be applied consistently.

A changed field order must also change every consumer that reads positions. A vector can have the expected length and still be wrong because its order, units or meaning changed. A class label appended as a third component causes target leakage even if the software accepts three values.

lesson.title: Recognise the limits of an encoding

blocks.text: Two parcels can share width and height yet differ in material or weight. Their vectors are identical in this representation, so a deterministic model receiving only these features cannot distinguish them. Adding a feature changes the schema and dimension; it does not automatically improve predictions. Keep data splits and evaluation discipline from Grade 8.

blocks.label: Two records both encode as [4, 2] but have different target classes. What can this representation reveal, and what can it not reveal?

blocks.text: Next week, we will multiply each component by a matching weight and add the results. The computation is meaningful only if the feature order stays fixed.

workbook.title: Encode the records
workbook.prompt: Write A, B and C as ordered pairs from the lesson. State the dimension of each and the shape of the stacked table.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: A [4, 2], B [2, 4], C [3, 3]. Each has dimension 2. The table has 3 rows and 2 columns.

workbook.title: Convert before encoding
workbook.prompt: A new record has width 60 mm and height 10 mm. Give its vector in the agreed cm schema, and name one error in [60, 10].
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: The vector is [6, 1]. [60, 10] uses mm numbers where cm numbers are expected, scaling both measurements tenfold.

workbook.title: Handle missing information
workbook.prompt: Width is 4 cm and height is missing. A teammate writes [4, 0]. Explain why this is invalid and give the action required by this schema.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Missing is not measured zero. Height must be present and positive; reject the record and request a valid measurement before encoding.

workbook.title: Apply a new schema independently
workbook.prompt: A new toy battery task uses [temperature in degrees C, voltage in V, age in days]. Record K has voltage 5, age 12, temperature 18. Record L has temperature 20, voltage 4, age 0. Encode both; state the vector dimension and table shape. Age zero is valid. The future failure label is also supplied in the data file: should it be appended?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: K [18, 5, 12], L [20, 4, 0]. Dimension 3, table 2 rows by 3 columns. Age zero is a valid known value. Exclude the future failure target from inputs; it is not available at prediction time.

workbook.title: Explain a collision
workbook.prompt: Two parcels have the same width and height but different material and target class. Explain why adding more examples alone cannot let this deterministic two-feature model tell these two inputs apart.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: The two input vectors are identical, so the fixed deterministic computation returns the same output. Additional rows do not create a missing distinction in these two vectors; a relevant available feature or an explicit uncertainty policy may be needed.

teacher.background: Begin Grade 9 by connecting the Grade 8 feature table to an ordered numerical input. Students should name every component before calculating. Use two 45-minute sessions. Avoid treating a vector as a mysterious neural object: the learning target is a precise data contract, including order, units, missing values and the distinction between inputs and targets.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook; paper and pencil
Calculator and optional local Python 3 editor; no packages or AI accounts needed
Use the fictional examples supplied; prepare the fresh retry before class
sessions: Ask the prerequisite question. Retrieve the distinction between a feature and a target; require a prediction-time explanation.
Place A, B and C on paper. Students label horizontal width and vertical height, then write vectors with the schema above them.
Complete W1 and W2. Contrast three examples with two components per example. Model the mm-to-cm conversion explicitly.
Trace the Python function or its paper equivalent. Complete the guided E case and compare the swapped vector.
Retrieve the schema without looking. Ask how two correctly sized vectors can have different meanings.
Use W3 and the identical-input example. Discuss valid zero in another schema without changing the parcel rule.
Collect W4 independently before giving hints. Check field order, dimensions, valid age zero and the excluded future target.
Use W5 and the exit response. Give targeted feedback, then administer the fresh retry and retain both attempts.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided E: [2, 7]. The reversed [7, 2] means width 7 cm and height 2 cm, a different measurement pair. Exit: [4, 2] reveals only width and height under the schema. It cannot reveal the omitted distinction causing different labels; the same deterministic input receives the same output.
misconceptions: Order does not matter
A and B use the same numbers but assign them to different features. Read each position by name.
More rows increase vector dimension
Rows count examples; components count features of one example.
A missing value is zero
Whether zero is valid depends on the field. Missing means unknown, and is not interchangeable with a measured zero.
teacher.assessment: Assess W4 for named order, all values retained, dimension 3, two-row shape and exclusion of the future label. Fresh retry: schema [mass in g, length in cm]; two records (length 4, mass 12) and (mass 9, length 6) encode as [12, 4] and [9, 6], dimension 2, table 2 by 2. Ask why an absent mass must not become zero without a declared policy.
teacher.support: Provide empty boxes labelled with feature names and units. Accept a correct spoken explanation before written notation. Extension: propose two different real objects that share the same two-feature vector, then identify an additional measurable feature available before prediction.
teacher.next: Week 2 uses the ordered components in dot products. Revisit order and signed multiplication before introducing weights.

ai-4/10.title: Gradients with a numerical check
goals: Estimate one partial derivative while other parameters stay fixed
Assemble a gradient in a declared parameter order
Compare numerical and formula based gradients with a tolerance

prerequisite.prompt: Why is the symmetric-slope denominator twice the step?
prerequisite.answer: The two evaluation points lie one step on either side of the centre, so their separation is two steps.

vocabulary: A local slope with respect to one parameter while others are held fixed
The ordered vector of partial derivatives of a scalar function
An estimate of change computed from nearby function values
A stated allowance for numerical disagreement

lesson.title: Vary one parameter at a time

blocks.text: Use one example with input x = 2 and target t = 3. The model predicts y = wx + b, and loss L(w, b) = (2w + b - 3) squared. At w = 1, b = 0, prediction is 2, residual is -1 and loss is 1. There are two parameters in order [w, b].

To estimate the partial slope for w, change w only and keep b = 0. To estimate the partial slope for b, change b only and keep w = 1. Moving both at once measures change along a combined direction; it does not isolate either partial derivative.
The gradient is [-4, -2] in order [w, b]. Both entries refer to the same original parameter vector, not to a partially updated model.

blocks.title: Optional Python check
blocks.text:
def loss(w, b):
    return (2 * w + b - 3) ** 2

def gradient_check(w, b, step=0.001):
    dw = (loss(w + step, b) - loss(w - step, b)) / (2 * step)
    db = (loss(w, b + step) - loss(w, b - step)) / (2 * step)
    residual = 2 * w + b - 3
    formula = [4 * residual, 2 * residual]
    numerical = [dw, db]
    assert all(abs(a - n) < 1e-6
               for a, n in zip(formula, numerical))
    return numerical

print([round(g, 6) for g in gradient_check(1, 0)])
# [-4.0, -2.0]

The helper assumes finite numerical inputs and a positive nonzero step. The formula follows the squared-loss rule: local loss change is twice the residual times the prediction sensitivity. Changing w by a small amount changes prediction twice as much here; changing b changes prediction by the same amount.

Exact floating-point equality is not required. Record the step and a tolerance, then try more than one parameter setting. A passing numerical check supports agreement for those tested points; it does not prove all possible inputs.

blocks.title: Two separate probes at one parameter vector
blocks.caption: The first two rows are independent local probes, not successive parameter updates. The final row records both results in the declared order.

blocks.label: At w = 0, b = 1, find prediction, residual, loss and the gradient using [4 times residual, 2 times residual].

lesson.title: Choose checks away from sharp corners

blocks.text: ReLU is not differentiable exactly at zero. A symmetric difference across that corner can average two different behaviours. When checking a network gradient, use points whose relevant scores are safely away from zero, and check that the small perturbations do not cross a corner. Document any derivative convention used at zero.

At the centre of the simple scalar ReLU function, [ReLU(0.1) - ReLU(-0.1)] / 0.2 equals 0.5. This symmetric number does not make the function differentiable at zero. Also avoid assuming an ever-smaller step is always better: subtraction and rounding can spoil numerical differences.

lesson.title: Use the gradient as local evidence

blocks.text: The gradient describes how the stated loss changes near the current parameters. For a differentiable function, moving a sufficiently small distance opposite a nonzero gradient decreases the function locally. The gradient alone does not choose a safe finite step, establish a global minimum or demonstrate generalisation.

blocks.label: A numerical checker moves w and b together, gets one slope and copies it into both gradient entries. What is wrong with this check?

blocks.text: Next week combines a gradient with an explicit learning rate to update parameters together.

workbook.title: Recover a gradient
workbook.prompt: For the lesson model at w = 1 and b = 1, calculate prediction, residual, loss and gradient.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Prediction 3, residual 0, loss 0, gradient [0, 0].

workbook.title: Catch a denominator error
workbook.prompt: A w probe has losses 1.44 and 0.64 at 0.9 and 1.1 with b fixed. A learner divides their difference by 0.1. Correct the result.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: The interval is 0.2. (0.64 - 1.44) / 0.2 = -4, not -8.

workbook.title: Separate a direction from a coordinate
workbook.prompt: Starting at [w, b] = [1, 0], both coordinates move by plus or minus 0.1 together. Compute the symmetric slope and explain why it is not either partial derivative.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Residuals are -1.3 and -0.7; losses 1.69 and 0.49. Slope is -6. It measures the combined direction [1, 1], equal here to the sum of partials -4 and -2.

workbook.title: Check a new example independently
workbook.prompt: Use x = 3, target 2 and y = wx + b at w = 0, b = 1. With step 0.1, calculate both numerical partials. Compare with [2 times residual times x, 2 times residual].
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Residual -1 and loss 1. w probes give predictions 0.7 and 1.3, losses 1.69 and 0.49, partial -6. b probes give predictions 0.9 and 1.1, losses 1.21 and 0.81, partial -2. Formula gradient is [-6, -2].

workbook.title: Recognise a corner
workbook.prompt: Compute the symmetric difference of ReLU at zero with step 0.1. Explain why this does not prove a derivative exists there.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: The value is 0.5. The left slope is 0 and right slope is 1, so the slopes disagree and the derivative at zero does not exist.

teacher.background: Use two 45-minute sessions to separate coordinate probes from combined changes. The first gradient check is deliberately an affine model with squared loss, avoiding hidden-layer calculus. Introduce the chain-rule reasoning in words before showing the compact formula.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook; paper and pencil
Calculator and optional local Python 3 editor; no packages or AI accounts needed
Use the fictional examples supplied; prepare the fresh retry before class
sessions: Retrieve the symmetric denominator and compute the initial prediction and residual.
Probe w alone with b fixed; record the two losses and slope.
Probe b alone and assemble [-4, -2]. Complete W1 and W2.
Trace the optional numerical checker and the guided [0, 1] case.
Use W3 to distinguish a combined direction from two partial derivatives.
Discuss the ReLU corner in W5 and a stated numerical tolerance.
Collect W4 independently, requiring both pairs of losses and coordinate order.
Use the exit response and fresh retry, then connect local gradient evidence to next week.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided: prediction 1, residual -2, loss 4, gradient [-8, -4]. Exit: changing both parameters measures a directional change; each partial must vary just its own coordinate while holding the others fixed.
misconceptions: The gradient is one scalar
It has one entry per parameter for a scalar loss, in a stated order.
Use the updated weight for the bias probe
Both entries must refer to the same current parameter vector.
A symmetric value defines the derivative at any corner
Left and right slopes can differ; the ReLU example exposes this.
teacher.assessment: W4 requires numerical and formula gradients [-6, -2] with losses shown. Fresh retry: x = 1, target 4, w = 2, b = 1 gives residual -1 and gradient [-2, -2]. Step 0.1 in either coordinate gives losses 1.21 and 0.81. Require the fixed coordinate to be named.
teacher.support: Provide separate w-probe and b-probe tables. Extension: at the lesson model [1, 0], test steps 0.1, 0.01 and 0.001 and report absolute disagreements from [-4, -2], without claiming universal tolerance guarantees.
teacher.next: Week 11 applies gradients to simultaneous parameter updates.

ai-4/11.title: Updating parameters
goals: Apply a learning rate to an ordered gradient
Update all parameters from the same saved state
Verify the new loss and identify overshooting

prerequisite.prompt: For x = 2, target 3, w = 1 and b = 0, what is the squared-loss gradient in order [w, b]?
prerequisite.answer: The residual is -1 and the gradient is [-4, -2].

vocabulary: A multiplier that controls the size of a gradient update
Updating parameters in the direction opposite the gradient
Computing all new parameter values from the same old state
A step that moves too far and can increase the objective

blocks.text: Gradient descent uses new parameter = old parameter - learning rate times its gradient entry. The minus sign chooses the locally downhill direction for a positive learning rate. A negative gradient therefore increases the corresponding parameter.

Keep the Week 10 example: x = 2, target 3, y = 2w + b and L = (y - 3) squared. At [w, b] = [1, 0], the loss is 1 and gradient is [-4, -2]. With learning rate 0.1, new w = 1 - 0.1 times -4 = 1.4 and new b = 0 - 0.1 times -2 = 0.2.
This particular step reaches zero loss on one example. It does not establish a unique parameter solution, successful learning on other examples or a generally ideal learning rate.

lesson.title: Save the old state before assignment

blocks.title: Optional Python check

blocks.text: Predict the rows: unchanged parameters and loss 1 at rate 0; [1.2, 0.1] and loss 0.25 at rate 0.05; [1.4, 0.2] and loss 0 at rate 0.1; [2.2, 0.6] and loss 4 at rate 0.3. The helper performs one step on this fixed example; it assumes numeric inputs and does not choose a learning rate for you.

blocks.title: Use one gradient for one parameter snapshot
blocks.caption: Read top to bottom. All gradient entries come from the same old model. The final row evaluates the fully updated model rather than mixing old and new coordinates.

blocks.label: Starting again from [1, 0], use learning rate 0.05. Show both new parameters, the new prediction and the new loss.

blocks.text: Suppose a program first changes w to 1.4, then recomputes the bias gradient using new w and old b. Its residual is now -0.2, so its bias gradient is -0.4 and new b becomes 0.04. Prediction becomes 2.84 and loss 0.0256. That is a different procedure from the declared simultaneous step, even though it also lowered this loss.

An excessive rate can increase loss. At rate 0.3, both coordinates move in the locally suggested direction but prediction jumps to 5 and loss rises from 1 to 4. Always evaluate and record the result. Later lessons compare learning-rate behaviour across repeated updates.

A lower loss after a step supports progress on the objective and examples used for that step. It does not show that a model is safe, calibrated or better on unseen data. Keep the data split fixed and never use final-test labels to compute training gradients.

blocks.label: A teammate says any update that lowers loss is a correct implementation of simultaneous gradient descent. Use the mixed-state example to evaluate that claim.

blocks.text: Next week repeats the forward, loss, gradient and update cycle in a small network with a clearly stated stopping budget.

workbook.title: Apply a negative gradient
workbook.prompt: Starting with parameter a = 2, gradient -3 and learning rate 0.2, calculate the new a.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: New a = 2 - 0.2 times -3 = 2.6.

workbook.title: Detect overshooting
workbook.prompt: For the lesson start [1, 0], apply rate 0.3 and calculate prediction and loss.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Gradient [-4, -2] gives [2.2, 0.6], prediction 5 and loss 4, larger than the starting loss 1.

workbook.title: Preserve one snapshot
workbook.prompt: Explain why recomputing the bias gradient after changing w is not the simultaneous update specified here.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: The two gradient entries then belong to different parameter vectors. Save the full old gradient and use it for both assignments.

workbook.title: Update a new model independently
workbook.prompt: Use x = 1, target 4, w = 1, b = 1, squared loss and learning rate 0.1. Compute prediction, residual, gradient [2 times residual times x, 2 times residual], new parameters and new loss.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Prediction 2, residual -2, gradient [-4, -4]. New parameters [1.4, 1.4] give prediction 2.8, residual -1.2 and loss 1.44, down from 4.

workbook.title: Evaluate a zero gradient
workbook.prompt: At a point with gradient [0, 0], what does this update do? Does that alone prove a global minimum on any loss surface?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: It leaves parameters unchanged for a finite learning rate. Zero gradient alone does not establish a global minimum; stationary points can have other meanings.

teacher.background: Use two 45-minute sessions and keep old and new parameter boxes separate. This lesson checks one update, not a full optimiser. Treat the mixed-state procedure as different from the stated algorithm, rather than claiming all sequential methods are invalid.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook; paper and pencil
Calculator and optional local Python 3 editor; no packages or AI accounts needed
Use the fictional examples supplied; prepare the fresh retry before class
sessions: Retrieve the Week 10 gradient and write the update rule with parentheses around negative entries.
Calculate the rate 0.1 worked step and recompute the loss from the new parameters.
Complete W1 and the guided rate 0.05 calculation.
Run or trace all four code rows and complete W2.
Rebuild the old-state snapshot and compare it with the mixed-state example.
Complete W3 and discuss zero gradient with W5.
Collect W4 independently, including old loss, both new parameters and new loss.
Use the exit response and a fresh retry. Keep the model-quality claim separate from implementation correctness.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided: [1.2, 0.1] gives prediction 2.5, residual -0.5 and loss 0.25. Exit: no. The mixed-state procedure lowers this loss but does not implement the specified simultaneous gradient step; compare states and gradients, not just whether loss decreased.
misconceptions: Subtracting a negative gradient decreases the parameter
Subtracting a negative adds a positive amount; show the signed calculation.
A downhill direction allows any rate
A finite step can overshoot and increase loss.
Recompute each gradient after its assignment
For this algorithm, all entries are computed at the same saved state.
teacher.assessment: W4 requires gradient [-4, -4], parameters [1.4, 1.4] and loss 1.44. Fresh retry: x = 1, target 1, w = 1, b = 1, rate 0.25 gives residual 1, gradient [2, 2], new parameters [0.5, 0.5] and loss 0. Require both updates to use the original residual.
teacher.support: Use separate old, gradient and new columns. Extension: for the lesson example, show that the new residual is the old residual multiplied by (1 - 10 times rate). Explain why rates 0 and 0.2 preserve loss while 0.3 raises it for a nonzero residual.
teacher.next: Week 12 repeats the training cycle for a small network.

ai-4/12.title: Training a small network
goals: Trace repeated forward loss gradient and update steps
Keep frozen parameters distinct from the trained parameter
Report training results with their evaluation limits

prerequisite.prompt: Why should all parameters in one simultaneous update use the same saved gradient?
prerequisite.answer: The gradient describes one parameter snapshot. Mixing snapshots changes the stated update procedure.

vocabulary: A repeated sequence of prediction, loss calculation, gradient calculation and parameter update
A model value intentionally held fixed during fitting
A declared limit on updates or other training resources
A record of a performance measure across training steps or time

lesson.title: Start with a deliberately small training problem

blocks.text: Use one hidden ReLU unit h = ReLU(x) and an output y = vh. The hidden input weight is fixed at 1, its bias is fixed at 0, and the output bias is fixed at 0. Only output weight v is trained. This is a restricted two-layer network, not training every parameter of a general network.

Training pairs are (x, target) = (1, 2) and (2, 4). Both x values are positive, so hidden activations are 1 and 2. Define ordinary MSE over both rows. Start at v = 0 and use learning rate 0.1 for exactly four full-data updates. The declared budget prevents stopping only when a preferred result appears.

Each row evaluates the parameter value after that many updates. Row zero records the starting model. The loss decreases in this specific experiment; that pattern is not a promise for all networks or rates.

Let errors be v - 2 and 2v - 4. MSE is their squared sum divided by 2, which simplifies to 2.5 times (v - 2) squared. Its gradient with respect to v is 5 times (v - 2). At v = 0 the gradient is -10, so the first update gives v = 0 - 0.1 times -10 = 1.

blocks.title: Optional Python check
blocks.text:
train = [(1.0, 2.0), (2.0, 4.0)]
v = 0.0
rate = 0.1
for step in range(5):
    hs = [max(0.0, x) for x, target in train]
    errors = [v * h - target
              for h, (x, target) in zip(hs, train)]
    loss = sum(e * e for e in errors) / len(train)
    print(step, v, loss)
    if step == 4:
        break
    gradient = 2 * sum(e * h for e, h in zip(errors, hs)) / len(train)
    v = v - rate * gradient

The factor 2 comes from squared error; division by the number of rows makes this the gradient of the mean, not the sum. The code uses every training row for each update. It prints five states but performs only four updates. All data are supplied fictional numbers.

blocks.title: One full-data update from v is 1
blocks.caption: Each row depends on the preceding calculation. Recompute predictions and loss on the next iteration; do not keep using the first gradient after parameters change.

blocks.label: Starting from v = 1.5, calculate both training predictions, errors, MSE, gradient and the next v.

blocks.text: After four updates, freeze v = 1.875. A reserved demonstration pair (3, 6), not used in the updates, receives prediction 5.625 and squared error 0.140625. Report it separately from training MSE 0.0390625. One synthetic held-out example is a small demonstration, not evidence of broad real-world reliability.

The frozen representation has a limit: for any negative x, ReLU gives h = 0 and the output is always 0. If the intended task were y = 2x for all real inputs, x = -1 would need target -2, so this model would fail there regardless of v. Training cannot recover distinctions that the fixed hidden representation removes.

Save the model formulas, frozen values, trained parameter, initial value, data pairs, loss definition, learning rate, update budget and the printed trace. State that these numbers are a classroom experiment. Changing a setting after seeing reserved outcomes makes those outcomes development evidence for that revision.

blocks.label: A team reports that its training MSE fell each step and concludes the network learned y = 2x for every real x. Give one numerical counterexample and a more accurate conclusion.

blocks.text: Next week separates an update, a batch and an epoch when training uses more than one group of examples.

workbook.title: Trace the first update
workbook.prompt: At v = 0, calculate both predictions, errors, MSE and gradient, then update at rate 0.1.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Predictions [0, 0], errors [-2, -4], MSE 10, gradient -10 and new v = 1.

workbook.title: Check the mean convention
workbook.prompt: At v = 1, the sum of squared errors is 5. A learner uses gradient -10 with rate 0.1. Explain the mismatch with this lesson and give the next v under MSE.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: The stated objective averages two rows. Its gradient is -5, giving v = 1.5. Gradient -10 corresponds to the sum objective and changes the effective update size.

workbook.title: Freeze before checking
workbook.prompt: At final v = 1.875, calculate the prediction and squared error on reserved pair (3, 6). May its target be included in the four reported training updates?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Prediction 5.625, residual -0.375, squared error 0.140625. Its target must stay outside those updates if the pair is described as reserved evaluation.

workbook.title: Run a new training case independently
workbook.prompt: Keep h = ReLU(x), train only v, and use one pair (2, 2), v = 0 and rate 0.125. Use squared error and gradient 2 times (2v - 2) times 2. Perform two updates, reporting each new v and loss. Explain why the second update changes nothing.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: At start loss 4 and gradient -8. First update gives v = 1 and loss 0. The next gradient is 0, so second update keeps v = 1 with loss 0. This is an exact fit on the one training pair, not proof for every input.

workbook.title: Expose a frozen representation limit
workbook.prompt: For the lesson architecture at x = -1, give h and prediction for any finite v. If target is -2, calculate squared error and explain why changing v cannot fix it.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: h = 0, prediction 0, squared error 4. Every v is multiplied by zero. A representation or architecture change is needed for that target at this input.

teacher.background: Use two 45-minute sessions to connect earlier ideas into one reproducible training loop. Be explicit that only the output weight is trained; backpropagation through all hidden parameters is not implemented here. Keep the reserved pair outside training and do not oversell its evidential value.

Calculator and optional local Python 3 editor; no packages or AI accounts needed
Use the fictional examples supplied; prepare the fresh retry before class
sessions: Retrieve the simultaneous update rule and identify fixed versus trained values.
Compute hidden activations for both training rows, then W1 and the first update.
Trace the next iteration with the diagram; use W2 to distinguish mean from sum.
Run or trace the code, marking five printed states and four actual updates.
Complete the guided v = 1.5 iteration and reconstruct the learning curve.
Freeze the final model, complete W3 and discuss the negative-input limit in W5.
Collect W4 independently with both iterations and the reason for no second change.
Use the exit response and fresh retry; save the experiment record for the next week.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided: predictions [1.5, 3], errors [-0.5, -1], MSE 0.625, gradient -2.5, next v = 1.75. Exit: x = -1 produces 0 rather than -2 for every v. The recorded training loss fell on two positive synthetic pairs; the model did not establish the rule over all real inputs.
misconceptions: Every parameter was trained
Only v changes. Hidden weight, hidden bias and output bias were explicitly frozen.
Five printed rows mean five updates
The initial state is row zero; the loop performs four updates.
Falling training loss proves generalisation
Report reserved evidence and representation limits separately.
teacher.assessment: W4 requires v values 1 and 1, both losses 0, and a zero second gradient. Fresh retry: one pair (1, 3), v = 1, rate 0.25. First residual -2 and gradient -4 give v = 2 with loss 1. Next gradient -2 gives v = 2.5 with loss 0.25. Require a recomputed gradient on the second step.
teacher.support: Provide the hidden activations so students can focus on errors and updates; allow a calculator for decimals. Extension: show that v - 2 is halved each step at rate 0.1, so MSE is quartered. Explain why this is a property of this particular quadratic training problem.
teacher.next: Week 13 introduces batching and epochs with explicit update counts.

ai-4/13.title: Batching and epochs
goals: Distinguish an example a batch an update and an epoch
Trace parameter changes across successive batches
Calculate update counts and aggregate unequal batch losses correctly

prerequisite.prompt: Week 12 printed states numbered 0 to 4. How many parameter updates occurred?
prerequisite.answer: Four updates occurred. State zero was the initial model before training.

vocabulary: A group of training examples used together to calculate one gradient here
One application of the gradient and learning rate to the current parameters
One pass through all training examples under the stated sampling rule
The intended number of examples in each batch with a possible smaller final batch

blocks.text: In Week 12 every update used both training examples. We now keep the same network h = ReLU(x), y = vh, with only v trained, and divide the data into batches. In this lesson each nonempty batch produces exactly one update. An epoch visits every training example exactly once, without replacement. These rules make the counts unambiguous.

Imagine five fictional records A through E in fixed order. With batch size 2, the groups are [A, B], [C, D] and [E]. Keep the smaller last batch. One epoch has three batches and three updates; two epochs have six updates and ten example visits.

When the last batch is retained, updates per epoch equal the row count divided by batch size rounded up. A program that drops the final incomplete batch follows a different rule and omits examples in that pass. Record the rule instead of silently changing the denominator.

Use the two fictional pairs A = (1, 2) and B = (2, 4), start v = 0 and rate 0.1. For one pair with hidden value h, squared-error gradient is 2 times (vh - target) times h. For a batch, average these gradients at the same current v. Apply one update, then recompute for the next batch.

blocks.title: Optional Python check
blocks.text:
def epoch(v, rows, size, rate):
    if not rows or size < 1:
        raise ValueError("Need rows and positive batch size")
    trace = []
    for start in range(0, len(rows), size):
        batch = rows[start:start + size]
        hs = [max(0.0, x) for x, target in batch]
        gradient = sum(2 * (v * h - target) * h
                       for h, (x, target) in zip(hs, batch)) / len(batch)
        v = v - rate * gradient
        trace.append(v)
    return trace

rows = [(1.0, 2.0), (2.0, 4.0)]
print([round(v, 6) for v in epoch(0.0, rows, 1, 0.1)])  # [0.4, 1.68]
print([round(v, 6) for v in epoch(0.0, rows, 2, 0.1)])  # [1.0]

Assume finite numeric pairs, integer size and finite rate. With size 1, A gives gradient -4 and new v = 0.4. B then uses 0.4, giving prediction 0.8, residual -3.2 and gradient -12.8, so v becomes 1.68. With size 2, both gradients are evaluated at v = 0; their mean is -10, producing v = 1.

blocks.title: One pass can contain different numbers of updates
blocks.caption: All three passes visit two examples. The reversed order happens to end at the same value for these proportional targets; that coincidence is not a general order-invariance rule.

blocks.label: For B then A separately, show both gradients and new parameter values. Why does one epoch still contain two updates?

lesson.title: Compare losses at a shared snapshot

blocks.text: Batch losses observed during training can refer to different parameter values and different examples. They are not automatically the full training loss of the final model. To compare final models, freeze each one and evaluate every training example again. Here full training MSE is 2.5 times (v - 2) squared: at v = 1 it is 2.5, and at v = 1.68 it is 0.256. These are training results only.

Even at one fixed model, averaging batch means without their sizes gives the wrong dataset mean when batches have different lengths. Suppose the squared errors on A to E are [1, 1, 4, 4, 9]. Batch means for lengths 2, 2, 1 are [1, 4, 9]. Full MSE is (2 times 1 + 2 times 4 + 1 times 9) / 5 = 3.8, not (1 + 4 + 9) / 3. Use example counts as weights.

Equal epochs mean equal example visits under our rule, but changing batch size changes the number of updates. A comparison should report both counts, starting values, order, learning rate and the rule for the last batch. Neither smaller batches nor more updates guarantee better independent performance.

blocks.label: Two teams train on five rows for two epochs. One uses size 2 and the other size 5, retaining every row. Are their example visits and update counts equal? Explain what to record.

blocks.text: Next week holds the batch rule fixed while comparing learning rates.

workbook.title: Count a partial batch
workbook.prompt: For 10 rows, batch size 4 and three epochs, retaining the final batch, list batch lengths and count total updates and example visits.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Batch lengths 4, 4, 2; three updates per epoch, nine total updates and 30 example visits.

workbook.title: Repair a stale gradient
workbook.prompt: For A then B separately in the lesson, a learner computes both gradients at v = 0, then applies them to get v = 2. Explain the error and give the correct final value.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: The second gradient must use v = 0.4. Using -16 from the old state is stale; the current B gradient is -12.8 and the final v is 1.68.

workbook.title: Combine unequal batches
workbook.prompt: At one frozen model, batches of sizes 3 and 1 have mean squared errors 2 and 10. Find the full MSE and explain why the average of 2 and 10 is wrong.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Full MSE is (3 times 2 + 10) / 4 = 4. The unweighted average 6 gives the single-row batch too much weight.

workbook.title: Test order on a new case independently
workbook.prompt: Use A = (1, 1), B = (2, 0), h = ReLU(x), y = vh, v = 0 and rate 0.1. Train with size 1 for one epoch in A then B order, then restart at 0 and reverse the order. Show gradients and parameter values. Compare the final values.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: A then B: A gradient -2 gives v = 0.2; B residual 0.4 gives gradient 1.6 and v = 0.04. B then A: B gradient 0 keeps v = 0; A gradient -2 gives v = 0.2. Both see the same rows but finish differently.

workbook.title: Audit an epoch claim
workbook.prompt: A program processes 11 rows using size 4 and drops the last incomplete batch. How many examples did it visit and how many updates occurred? What must its report disclose?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: It visits eight rows in two batches and performs two updates. Three rows are omitted; it did not complete a full pass under this lesson definition. Report the drop rule and actual visits.

teacher.background: Use two 45-minute sessions to separate counting from numerical training. Keep the frozen hidden layer from Week 12. Have students move paper record cards into batches before doing arithmetic. The coincident final values for the proportional-target example require the independent counterexample; do not teach that ordering is generally irrelevant.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook; paper and pencil
Calculator and optional local Python 3 editor; no packages or AI accounts needed
Use the fictional examples supplied; prepare the fresh retry before class
sessions: Retrieve states versus updates, then arrange five cards into batches of two.
Count batches, updates and visits for the table and W1; discuss retaining the final group.
Trace A then B at current v. Complete W2 and identify exactly where the stale gradient arose.
Run or trace the code and compare the full-batch update with the two singleton updates.
Complete the guided reverse-order trace and mark its coincidental equal endpoint.
Calculate fixed-model loss and use W3 to weight unequal batch means.
Collect W4 independently, requiring a fresh reset for the reverse-order run.
Discuss W5 and the exit response, then assess the fresh retry after targeted feedback.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided: B at v = 0 gives gradient -16 and v = 1.6. A then gives residual -0.4, gradient -0.8 and v = 1.68. Two batches each cause one update. Exit: both teams visit ten examples. Size 2 produces six updates; size 5 produces two. Record both budgets and all training settings.
misconceptions: One epoch always means one update
Only a full-data batch gives one update per epoch in this procedure.
Reuse all gradients from the start of an epoch
Recompute at the parameter value before each batch update.
Average batch means equally
At one fixed model, weight each batch mean by the number of examples in that batch.
