A then B gives gradients -4 and 2, values 1 and 0.5. Reverse order gives gradients 0 and -4, values 0 and 1. Ask students to name the reset and explain the order effect.
teacher.support: Provide separate boxes for old v, batch gradient and new v; allow calculators. Extension: at a fixed v, prove that the row-count-weighted mean of batch gradients equals the full-data mean gradient. Explain why successive updates with changed v are a different procedure.
teacher.next: Week 14 compares learning rates under one fixed batch rule.

ai-4/14.title: Learning rate experiments
goals: Run a controlled comparison of learning rates
Explain slow progress oscillation and increasing loss in a toy model
Report the limits of a training experiment

prerequisite.prompt: Why can equal epochs give different update counts when batch size changes?
prerequisite.answer: An epoch visits the data once, but each batch causes an update. More batches mean more updates under the stated rule.

vocabulary: The multiplier controlling the size of a gradient update
An experiment changing a named factor while holding other stated conditions fixed
Repeated movement from one side of a value to the other
Movement away from a target solution with growing error in this experiment

lesson.title: Change one setting at a time

blocks.text: Use the same restricted network h = ReLU(x), y = vh, with only v trained. Keep the fictional training pairs (1, 2) and (2, 4), start v = 0, and use one full-data batch per update. Compare rates 0.05, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4 and 0.5 for exactly four updates each. Restart at zero for every run.

The training objective is ordinary MSE: L(v) = 2.5 times (v - 2) squared. Its gradient is 5 times (v - 2). A step is new v = v - rate times 5 times (v - 2). This small quadratic lets us explain each result rather than treating the rate as a magic setting.
The same rate need not behave this way for another model, input scale, loss convention or batch rule. Rate 0.2 is an exact one-step solution here because of this particular gradient formula.

lesson.title: Predict the trajectory before running it

blocks.text: Write d = v - 2, the signed distance from this objective minimum. Substituting the update gives new d = (1 - 5 times rate) times old d. At rate 0.05 the factor is 0.75: distance shrinks without changing sign. At rate 0.3 it is -0.5: distance changes sign and halves. Both can reduce loss.

blocks.title: Optional Python check
blocks.text:
def run(rate, updates=4):
    v = 0.0
    history = [v]
    for _ in range(updates):
        gradient = 5 * (v - 2)
        v = v - rate * gradient
        history.append(v)
    losses = [2.5 * (value - 2) ** 2 for value in history]
    return history, losses

for rate in [0.05, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4, 0.5]:
    values, losses = run(rate)
    print(rate, values, losses)

The helper assumes a finite rate and nonnegative integer update count. Its five logged states include the initial value. At 0.3 the parameter sequence is [0, 3, 1.5, 2.25, 1.875] and loss is [10, 2.5, 0.625, 0.15625, 0.0390625]. Crossing the minimum does not itself mean training failed.

lesson.title: Relate a factor to a loss pattern

blocks.title: The update factor explains three behaviours
blocks.caption: For this objective, loss is 2.5 times squared distance. Therefore the loss multiplier is the square of the distance multiplier.

blocks.label: For rate 0.4, calculate its distance multiplier, the first two new v values and both losses. Does a changing parameter guarantee progress?

blocks.text: For a nonzero starting distance, loss strictly decreases on each step of this quadratic when the absolute value of 1 - 5 times rate is below 1. For positive rates this means 0 < rate < 0.4. At 0 the model does not move. At 0.4 it oscillates with unchanged loss. Above 0.4 its distance grows. These bounds belong to this model and objective, not to neural networks generally.

If we switch from mean squared error to the sum over the same two examples, the gradient doubles from 5(v - 2) to 10(v - 2). Keeping the old rate changes the update. To reproduce the original steps, halve the rate. Likewise, rescaling features can change gradient magnitudes. Record the loss and units alongside the rate.

lesson.title: Report the result within its limits

blocks.text: Record the initial state, data, frozen values, objective, batch rule, update budget, candidate rates, parameter traces and loss traces. These runs compare training behaviour on two examples. They do not establish which setting performs best on independent data. Keep the final test set out of rate selection; later lessons use validation curves to make development choices.

blocks.label: A team says rate 0.2 is the best rate for every neural network because it reached zero training loss here. Replace this claim with a precise experimental conclusion and one limitation.

blocks.text: Next week compares training and validation curves, including when their trends disagree.

workbook.title: Trace slow progress
workbook.prompt: For rate 0.05, start v = 0 and compute two updates and their training MSE values using the lesson objective.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: First v = 0.5 with MSE 5.625. Second gradient -7.5 gives v = 0.875 and MSE 3.1640625. Distance is multiplied by 0.75 each step.

workbook.title: Explain a crossing
workbook.prompt: At rate 0.3 the first update gives v = 3, past the minimum at 2. Calculate the next v and loss. Has the first crossing proved divergence?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Next gradient 5 gives v = 1.5 and loss 0.625. No. Signed distance changes side but shrinks by half each update; loss decreases.

workbook.title: Preserve an update after rescaling loss
workbook.prompt: Replace MSE by the sum of squared errors on the two training pairs. Which rate reproduces the MSE run at rate 0.3? Explain using gradients.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: The sum gradient is twice the mean gradient, so rate 0.15 reproduces the original steps. Rate 0.3 would double each step from the same state.

workbook.title: Compare a new objective independently
workbook.prompt: Use J(a) = (a - 1) squared with gradient 2(a - 1), start a = 0 and two updates. Restart for each rate 0.25, 0.5 and 1. Compute the two new a values and losses for each run. Identify the result supported after two updates.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: At 0.25: a = 0.5 then 0.75; losses 0.25 then 0.0625. At 0.5: a = 1 then 1; losses 0 then 0. At 1: a = 2 then 0; losses 1 then 1. Rate 0.5 attains the lowest objective in this comparison. The useful rate differs from the lesson model.

workbook.title: Find an unfair comparison
workbook.prompt: Run A starts v = 0 with full-data batches for four updates. Run B starts at the final A value, changes both rate and batch size, then compares final training losses. Can the difference be attributed only to rate? Propose a repair.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: No. Initial state and batch rule also changed. Restart every run at the same v, hold data, loss, batch rule and update budget fixed, and vary only rate. Report the traces and separate any later experiment with a different factor.

teacher.background: Use two 45-minute sessions and connect signed distance to squared loss before introducing the factor formula. This is a fully explained quadratic experiment with a frozen hidden representation. Avoid general prescriptions about rate values. Students should distinguish an oscillating parameter from increasing loss.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook; paper and pencil
Calculator and optional local Python 3 editor; no packages or AI accounts needed
Use the fictional examples supplied; prepare the fresh retry before class
sessions: Retrieve epoch and update counts; agree on one full-data batch and four updates per run.
Calculate the first row of each rate run and keep all resets visible.
Derive new d from the update rule using substitution; complete W1.
Run or trace Python and compare rate 0.3 with W2, marking sign and magnitude separately.
Complete the guided rate 0.4 example and explain why changing values can leave loss unchanged.
Use W3 to connect the loss scale with the gradient and an equivalent rate.
Collect the three independent W4 traces with a fresh reset before each.
Use W5 and the exit response, then administer the fresh retry and record the experimental limits.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided: multiplier -1; v becomes 4 then 0, with MSE 10 at both states. Parameter change does not guarantee decreasing loss. Exit: for the fixed two-example objective, start and four-update budget, rate 0.2 reached zero training MSE after one update. This does not demonstrate an optimal rate or generalisation for other networks or data.
misconceptions: Crossing the minimum means divergence
Compare distance magnitudes or losses; alternating sides can converge.
A larger rate is always faster
The tested 0.5 rate increases this objective; 0.4 keeps it unchanged.
The best rate is independent of loss scaling
Scaling the loss scales its gradient and changes the step at a fixed rate.
teacher.assessment: W4 must include all six new states and losses with no carry-over between runs. Fresh retry: J(c) = 2(c - 3) squared, gradient 4(c - 3), start c = 1. At rate 0.125, c becomes 2 then 2.5 with losses 2 then 0.5. At rate 0.25, c becomes 3 then 3 with losses 0 then 0. Ask for a conclusion limited to these runs.
teacher.support: Provide a number line with the minimum marked and a table for old value, gradient, new value and loss. Extension: derive 0 < rate < 1 for strict loss decrease on J(a) = (a - 1) squared away from the minimum, and compare with the lesson bound 0.4.
teacher.next: Week 15 separates training and validation curves.

ai-4/15.title: Training and validation curves
goals: Compute comparable training and validation losses at saved checkpoints
Choose among observed checkpoints using a declared validation rule
Distinguish development evidence from final test evidence

prerequisite.prompt: Why does the lowest training loss in a learning-rate experiment not establish the best performance on new examples?
prerequisite.answer: Training loss measures fit to the examples used for updates. Independent performance needs suitable separate evidence, and settings selected using validation must not be presented as independent final testing.

vocabulary: Saved model parameters and the information needed to identify a training state
A record of a training measure at successive saved states
A record of a development measure on separate examples at those states
A declared procedure for choosing among candidate models or checkpoints

lesson.title: Evaluate both splits at one saved state

blocks.text: Keep the restricted network h = ReLU(x), y = vh, with only v trained. Training pairs remain (1, 2) and (2, 4). Start v = 0 and make four full-data updates at rate 0.1. Save states v = 0, 1, 1.5, 1.75 and 1.875. At each saved state, evaluate both splits without changing v during evaluation.

For this deliberately constructed demonstration, validation pairs are (3, 4.5) and (4, 6). Their targets follow a different slope from the training pairs. This makes the two trends disagree visibly; it is not evidence that these few rows represent a real population. Validation labels do not enter the gradient.

Both columns use ordinary MSE in the same target units, evaluated on their own fixed rows. Training MSE is 2.5(v - 2) squared; validation MSE is 12.5(v - 1.5) squared. Different input values and target rules affect the loss levels. A gap alone does not identify its cause.

For checkpoint 3, v = 1.75. Training predictions are [1.75, 3.5], residuals [-0.25, -0.5], and MSE 0.15625. Validation predictions are [5.25, 7], residuals [0.75, 1], and MSE 0.78125. All four predictions must use the same saved value.

blocks.title: Optional Python check
blocks.text:
def mse(v, rows):
    if not rows:
        raise ValueError("Need evaluation rows")
    return sum((v * max(0.0, x) - target) ** 2
               for x, target in rows) / len(rows)

train = [(1.0, 2.0), (2.0, 4.0)]
valid = [(3.0, 4.5), (4.0, 6.0)]
checkpoints = [0.0, 1.0, 1.5, 1.75, 1.875]
validation_losses = []
for step, v in enumerate(checkpoints):
    validation_losses.append(mse(v, valid))
    print(step, mse(v, train), mse(v, valid))
best = min(range(len(checkpoints)),
           key=lambda i: (validation_losses[i], i))
print("Selected checkpoint", best)  # 2

The code evaluates supplied checkpoints; it does not train on validation data. It assumes finite numeric pairs and selects the lowest observed validation MSE, breaking exact ties in favour of the earlier checkpoint. The rule is chosen before inspecting the values.

lesson.title: Follow each curve on a shared scale

blocks.title: Later updates improve only one split
blocks.caption: This chart shows checkpoints 2 to 4 only, on one MSE scale from 0 to 2. Circles and a solid line mark training; squares and a dashed line mark validation. Lines connect measured checkpoints, not additional evaluations. The full table includes checkpoints 0 and 1.

blocks.label: Using the table, calculate the training and validation loss changes from checkpoint 2 to checkpoint 4. Which saved parameter does the selection rule choose?

blocks.text: Falling training loss with rising validation loss can be consistent with overfitting, but it is not a complete diagnosis. In this example the split-specific target rules are known to differ. In another dataset, inspect representativeness, preprocessing, leakage, label quality and evaluation settings before attributing the pattern to model capacity alone.

Evaluate comparable quantities: do not compare a training sum with a validation mean, or a training objective containing a penalty with unpenalised validation MSE. Keep the row sets fixed across checkpoints. Do not mix losses recorded before each batch update with a full-split evaluation of the final checkpoint.

Restore checkpoint 2, v = 1.5, if following the declared rule. Its zero validation MSE is a result on two constructed development examples. Choosing this checkpoint using those examples makes them part of model selection. After all choices are frozen, a separate untouched test set can provide final evidence within its own coverage limits.

blocks.label: A team calls checkpoint 2 independently proven because its validation MSE is zero, then uses the test results to choose another checkpoint. Identify both reporting problems and propose a clean procedure.

blocks.text: Next week adds a weight penalty and an early-stopping policy, keeping their roles distinct.

workbook.title: Recover a plotted point
workbook.prompt: At v = 1, compute both validation predictions, residuals and MSE on (3, 4.5) and (4, 6).
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Predictions [3, 4], residuals [-1.5, -2], squares [2.25, 4], MSE 3.125.

workbook.title: Use the declared rule
workbook.prompt: Observed validation MSE at checkpoints 0 to 4 is [5, 2, 1, 1, 1.2]. Lowest loss wins with earlier exact ties. Which checkpoint is selected? What if training loss is lowest at checkpoint 4?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Select checkpoint 2. The tie at 3 does not replace the earlier checkpoint. Lower training loss at 4 does not change a validation-based rule.

workbook.title: Repair incompatible measures
workbook.prompt: A training report shows sum of squared errors 12 over six rows. Validation shows mean squared error 3 over two rows in the same target units. A learner says training error is four times larger. Repair the comparison.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Training MSE is 12 / 6 = 2. Compare 2 with validation MSE 3, not sum 12 with mean 3. The split sizes and examples still limit interpretation.

workbook.title: Evaluate new checkpoints independently
workbook.prompt: Use h = ReLU(x), y = vh, candidate v values 1, 1.5 and 2. Training pairs are (1, 2), (2, 4); validation pairs are (1, 1), (2, 2). Calculate both MSE columns and select by minimum validation MSE. Explain the disagreement with selection by training loss.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: For v = 1, train MSE 2.5 and validation MSE 0. For v = 1.5, both MSE values are 0.625. For v = 2, train MSE 0 and validation MSE 2.5. Validation chooses v = 1; training chooses v = 2. These constructed splits favour different slopes.

workbook.title: Limit a curve diagnosis
workbook.prompt: Training loss falls while validation loss rises. Give two checks before declaring model complexity the cause, and explain why repeatedly selecting with validation makes it development evidence.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Possible checks include comparable loss definitions, unchanged preprocessing and evaluation settings, split representativeness, leakage and label quality. Repeated selection uses validation outcomes to guide choices, so final evaluation needs separate untouched examples.

teacher.background: Use two 45-minute sessions. Have students draw checkpoint number horizontally and MSE vertically, using one clearly labelled scale for both curves. Explicitly name the differing target rules in this synthetic example so the picture is not misrepresented as proof of a single overfitting mechanism. Keep checkpoint selection separate from parameter updates.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook; paper and pencil
Calculator and optional local Python 3 editor; no packages or AI accounts needed
Use the fictional examples supplied; prepare the fresh retry before class
sessions: Retrieve why training performance alone cannot select for independent performance.
Identify the two fixed splits and trace checkpoint 1; complete W1.
Calculate checkpoint 3 by hand and plot all supplied points on one MSE scale.
Run or trace the evaluation code, then use W2 to practise the exact tie rule.
Complete the guided comparison of checkpoints 2 and 4; identify the parameter to restore.
Use W3 and W5 to examine metric comparability and alternative causes of a widening gap.
Collect W4 independently with both loss columns and the explicit selection rule.
Use the exit question and fresh retry; require a distinction between selection and untouched final testing.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided: training changes by 0.0390625 - 0.625 = -0.5859375; validation changes by 1.7578125 - 0 = 1.7578125. Select checkpoint 2 with v = 1.5. Exit: zero on selected validation examples is limited development evidence, and choosing with test results turns that test into development data. Freeze choices using training/validation, then evaluate once on suitable untouched test examples and report the scope.
misconceptions: The last checkpoint is always best
Choose by the stated validation criterion and restore the saved parameters.
A gap proves one specific cause
Check split composition, metrics and evaluation procedures; this demonstration has deliberately different target rules.
Validation is untouched final evidence
Once used to choose settings or checkpoints, it is development evidence.
teacher.assessment: W4 requires all six MSE values and the validation choice v = 1. Fresh retry: candidates v = 0.5, 1, 1.5 and validation pairs (2, 2), (4, 4). MSE values are 2.5, 0 and 2.5, so choose v = 1. Ask what the result establishes and why it is not final test evidence after selection.
teacher.support: Provide squared-error columns and labelled axes, allowing calculators. Extension: derive the two quadratic loss expressions and locate their different minima. Explain why this constructed mismatch makes the validation optimum occur before the training optimum.
teacher.next: Week 16 introduces a weight penalty and a precise early-stopping policy.

ai-4/16.title: Regularisation and early stopping
goals: Separate a weight penalty from prediction error
Trace a regularised update under a stated objective
Apply a stopping rule and restore the best observed checkpoint

prerequisite.prompt: If validation chooses an earlier checkpoint, which parameters should be used after selection?
prerequisite.answer: Restore the parameters saved at the chosen checkpoint. The last parameters produced by training may have a different validation loss.

vocabulary: A constraint or training procedure intended to limit fitting choices and improve generalisation
An added objective term that discourages specified large parameter values
The allowed run of consecutive non-improving evaluations before stopping under a stated rule
Reload the parameters saved at the selected checkpoint

lesson.title: State exactly what receives a penalty

blocks.text: Keep h = ReLU(x), y = vh, train only v on (1, 2) and (2, 4), and freeze all hidden parameters and the zero output bias. Training MSE is L(v) = 2.5(v - 2) squared. Define J(v) = L(v) + lambda times v squared, with lambda nonnegative. Only this one output weight is penalised here.

For lambda = 0.5, the penalty at v = 1.5 is 0.5 times 2.25 = 1.125. Prediction MSE is 0.625, so total objective J is 1.75. Keep these quantities separate in logs. A smaller total objective does not automatically mean a smaller prediction error.

Among these three candidates, the smallest penalised objective is at v = 1.5, whereas the smallest training MSE is at v = 2. Penalising a weight changes the tradeoff. It does not guarantee better validation performance or fair outcomes.

The data gradient is 5(v - 2). The penalty gradient is 2 times lambda times v, giving total gradient 5(v - 2) + 2 lambda v. At v = 1.5 and lambda = 0.5, these contributions are -2.5 and 1.5, so total gradient is -1. A rate 0.1 step gives v = 1.6.

blocks.title: Optional Python check
blocks.text:
def terms(v, penalty):
    data_loss = 2.5 * (v - 2) ** 2
    weight_cost = penalty * v * v
    gradient = 5 * (v - 2) + 2 * penalty * v
    return data_loss, weight_cost, data_loss + weight_cost, gradient

v = 1.5
penalty = 0.5
old = terms(v, penalty)
v = v - 0.1 * old[3]
print(round(v, 6))  # 1.6
print([round(x, 6) for x in terms(v, penalty)])
# [0.4, 1.28, 1.68, -0.4]

Assume finite numeric values and nonnegative penalty. At the new v, data loss is 0.4, penalty 1.28 and total 1.68. Choose penalty strength using a declared validation prediction metric, not by comparing total objectives with different lambdas as if they were the same measure.

lesson.title: Make the stopping policy executable on paper

blocks.title: Patience two with strict improvement
blocks.caption: Initial checkpoint is epoch 0. Evaluate once after each epoch. A strict decrease is improvement; an exact tie is a miss. Reset the miss count after improvement and stop at two consecutive misses. Restore epoch 4, the best observed checkpoint.

blocks.label: At epochs 3, 4, 5 and 6, record the miss count after evaluation. Which epoch stops training, and which epoch supplies the restored parameters?

lesson.title: Distinguish stopping time from selected state

blocks.text: Early stopping limits the training duration using development evidence; it does not add a weight term to the objective. For this policy, initialise the best checkpoint to epoch 0 and the miss count to zero. After each later evaluation, save and reset only on a strict improvement; otherwise increment the count. Stop as soon as the count reaches patience, then reload the best checkpoint.

Suppose a pre-recorded demonstration also lists epoch 7 loss 1.3. A live run following the rule has already stopped at 6 and does not observe 7. Do not use future values to rewrite the stopping decision. The policy can miss a later improvement; patience balances waiting against a training budget and must be specified in advance.

Save actual model parameters with the checkpoint, not just its epoch number or loss. With a fixed maximum epoch budget, stop when either limit is reached and restore the best observed state. An exact tie keeps the earlier checkpoint under our rule. Different minimum-improvement thresholds are possible, but would be different declared policies.

lesson.title: Evaluate the choices as development decisions

blocks.text: Weight penalties and early stopping can be used together, but they act differently. Record which weights receive penalties, the objective convention, lambda, learning rate, checkpoint frequency, patience, tie rule and maximum budget. For this classroom model there are no extra learned preprocessing or running statistics; larger models may require more state to reproduce evaluation.

blocks.label: A team stops at epoch 6, uses its final parameters instead of the saved best state, and chooses patience by looking at final test losses. Identify the two mistakes and explain how to repair the experiment.

blocks.text: Select these settings using validation, freeze the complete procedure, and reserve untouched final test data for reporting. Neither regularisation nor stopping makes a weak validation set representative. Next week studies initialisation and reproducibility.

workbook.title: Separate the objective terms
workbook.prompt: At v = 2 and lambda = 0.5 in the lesson, compute prediction MSE, penalty, total objective and total gradient. Does zero training MSE make this gradient zero?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: MSE 0, penalty 2, total J 2, total gradient 2. Zero data gradient does not remove the penalty gradient.

workbook.title: Trace the next update
workbook.prompt: Start v = 1.6 with lambda = 0.5 and rate 0.1. Calculate both gradient contributions, new v and new prediction MSE.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Data gradient -2, penalty gradient 1.6, total -0.4. New v = 1.64; prediction MSE is 2.5 times 0.36 squared = 0.324.

workbook.title: Apply patience without peeking
workbook.prompt: Validation MSE at epochs 0 to 7 is [4, 2, 1.5, 1.6, 1.4, 1.45, 1.46, 1.3]. Apply the lesson policy with patience 2. Give the stop epoch, restored epoch and why the listed epoch 7 cannot change this decision.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Stop at epoch 6 after misses at 5 and 6; restore epoch 4 with MSE 1.4. A live run has stopped before observing epoch 7; hindsight cannot be included in that policy decision.

workbook.title: Transfer both rules independently
workbook.prompt: For a new objective J(a) = (a - 2) squared + a squared, gradient 4a - 4, start a = 0 and take one step at rate 0.25. Give new a, prediction error term, penalty and total J. Separately apply patience 2 with strict improvement to validation values [3, 2, 2, 2, 1] at epochs 0 to 4; report the stop and restored epochs.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: The update gives a = 1. Prediction error 1, penalty 1, total J 2. For the separate curve, epoch 1 is best at 2; ties at 2 and 3 are two misses, so stop at epoch 3 and restore epoch 1. Epoch 4 is not observed by that live policy.

workbook.title: Compare penalties fairly
workbook.prompt: A team compares lambda 0 and lambda 0.5 by choosing whichever has the smaller penalised training objective. Explain why this does not establish the better prediction model and name a suitable development comparison.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: The objectives use different penalties, and both are training quantities. Compare the candidates on the same fixed validation examples using the same declared prediction metric, such as ordinary MSE. Reserve final test examples from setting selection.

teacher.background: Use two 45-minute sessions. Keep prediction error, penalty and total objective in separate columns. Teach early stopping as a second mechanism with a precise state machine on paper. Cover future curve values until a decision is made; do not reward retrospective selection as if it were a live stopping rule.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook; paper and pencil
Calculator and optional local Python 3 editor; no packages or AI accounts needed
Use the fictional examples supplied; prepare the fresh retry before class
sessions: Retrieve checkpoint restoration and introduce the named penalised weight.
Calculate the objective table and W1, identifying the nonzero penalty gradient at v = 2.
Trace the worked regularised update and use W2 for the next step.
Run or trace the code and distinguish objective reduction from validation evidence.
Reveal the validation sequence one epoch at a time; complete the guided miss counts.
Complete W3 before revealing the future value; compare stopping and restored epochs.
Collect W4 independently, scoring the arithmetic and the tied-loss policy separately.
Discuss W5 and the exit response, then use the fresh retry and record the complete policy.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided: miss counts at epochs 3, 4, 5, 6 are 1, 0, 1, 2. Stop at 6 and restore 4. Exit: using final parameters ignores restoration; selecting patience with test losses uses test data for development. Restore the selected checkpoint, choose policy using validation, then freeze it before evaluating suitable untouched final examples.
misconceptions: Zero prediction error means no regularised update
The penalty gradient can remain nonzero.
Early stopping adds a weight penalty
It limits training duration using a validation rule; a weight penalty changes the objective.
Restore the epoch where stopping happened
Restore the best observed checkpoint under the declared rule, which can be earlier.
teacher.assessment: W4 requires a = 1 and terms 1, 1, 2 plus stop epoch 3 and restored epoch 1. Fresh retry: J(b) = (b - 3) squared + 0.5b squared, gradient 3b - 6; start b = 0, rate 0.25. New b = 1.5, data term 2.25, penalty 1.125, total 3.375. On validation [5, 3, 3.2, 3.1] with patience 2, stop at 3 and restore 1.
teacher.support: Use a ledger with columns epoch, metric, best epoch and miss count; cover future rows. Extension: solve 5(v - 2) + 2 lambda v = 0 to obtain v = 10 / (5 + 2 lambda). For nonnegative lambda, discuss why the optimum moves toward zero without claiming this always improves prediction.
teacher.next: Week 17 investigates initialisation and reproducibility.

ai-4/17.title: Initialisation and reproducibility
goals: Trace how starting values affect a fixed training budget
Explain a simple hidden-unit symmetry
Record enough information to replay and audit a classroom experiment

prerequisite.prompt: Why must an early-stopping report identify both the stop epoch and the restored checkpoint?
prerequisite.answer: The stopping state can differ from the best observed state. Reproducing the reported model requires the actual saved parameters selected by the declared rule.

vocabulary: The procedure that assigns model parameter values before training
A value used to initialise a pseudorandom generator
An equivalence between parts of a model that can keep their computations identical
Saved data settings code and results that let another person check how an experiment was performed

lesson.title: Compare starts under the same budget

blocks.text: Return to h = ReLU(x), y = vh, training pairs (1, 2) and (2, 4), ordinary MSE and a frozen hidden unit. Only v is trained. Keep full-data updates, learning rate 0.1 and exactly two updates. Compare initial v values 0, 1 and 3. This experiment changes only the start.

The gradient is 5(v - 2), so each step gives new v = 0.5v + 1. Signed distance from 2 halves on every update. Different starting distances therefore produce different losses after this finite budget, even though all three runs approach the same minimum if this exact procedure continues.

The equal losses for starts 1 and 3 arise because they are equally distant from 2. They do not have equal final parameters. This simple convex example does not show the multiple solutions or inactive units that can occur in larger networks.

A pseudorandom generator produces a sequence determined by its state. In the same Python setup, recreating a local generator with the same seed and making the same calls reproduces the sequence below. Saving the generated values also removes ambiguity about which draw became which parameter.

blocks.title: Optional Python check
blocks.text:
from random import Random

def initial_values(seed):
    rng = Random(seed)
    return [rng.uniform(-1.0, 1.0) for _ in range(4)]

def train(v):
    states = [v]
    for _ in range(2):
        v = v - 0.1 * 5 * (v - 2)
        states.append(v)
    return states

first = initial_values(17)
second = initial_values(17)
assert first == second
print(first)
for start in [0.0, 1.0, 3.0]:
    print(start, train(start))

The four random numbers illustrate a saved initialisation sequence; they are not used in the three separate scalar training runs. The range [-1, 1] is a classroom choice, not a general recommendation for network initialisation. An extra random draw before assigning weights shifts which value is used, even if the seed stays the same.

blocks.title: Identical units receive identical updates
blocks.caption: In this separate two-unit example there are no biases. At x = 1, output is 2 and target is 1. Each of the four squared-error partial gradients equals 2. A simultaneous update at rate 0.1 changes every weight from 1 to 0.8 and keeps the units identical.

blocks.label: For x = 1, calculate the two-unit output and squared error before and after the shown simultaneous update. Have the units become different?

blocks.text: For the two-unit example, y = a ReLU(ux) + b ReLU(vx). At x = 1, u = v = a = b = 1, output is 2 and target is 1. Because both ReLUs are in their positive region, changing any one parameter slightly changes y at rate 1. Squared-error gradient is twice residual times that sensitivity, so each gradient is 2. Students can check it with the symmetric numerical probe from Week 10.

With identical initial weights, identical data and deterministic symmetric updates, these units remain copies and cannot learn distinct roles through those updates alone. Different hidden weights can break the symmetry. For example, u = 1 and v = -1 give hidden activations [1, 0] at x = 1 and [0, 1] at x = -1. This demonstrates different responses, not a guarantee of successful training.

Zero is not always an invalid start: v = 0 worked in our single trained-output-weight model. But setting all four weights to zero in the two-unit product model leaves every single-coordinate loss probe unchanged, because each path still contains a zero factor. Do not generalise the success of one scalar start to every architecture.

Save actual initial parameters, their order, data and split IDs, preprocessing rules, model formulas, loss convention, learning rate, batch order, update budget, selection policy, code version, software environment and final checkpoint. A seed helps replay one source of randomness; it does not specify all of these choices or guarantee identical results across different numerical environments.

blocks.label: Two runs use seed 17 but have different final losses. One run made an extra random draw and used a different batch order. Is either difference evidence that the network is broken? Describe a useful investigation.

blocks.text: Repeatability alone cannot prove correctness: a program can repeat the same mistake. Preserve hand-calculated checks as well as logs. When comparing starts, report every planned run instead of selecting a lucky result using final test outcomes. Next week locates shape and gradient errors.

workbook.title: Trace a fresh starting value
workbook.prompt: For the scalar lesson model, start v = -2 and apply two updates at rate 0.1. Give all three v values and the final training MSE.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: States are -2, 0 and 1. Final training MSE is 2.5. Each step halves the signed distance from 2.

workbook.title: Distinguish equality of loss and parameters
workbook.prompt: The lesson runs starting at 1 and 3 finish with the same training MSE. Give their final v values and explain the equality without calling the models identical.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: They finish at 1.75 and 2.25. Both are distance 0.25 from 2, so both have MSE 0.15625. Their predictions for nonzero positive inputs differ.

workbook.title: Audit a seed claim
workbook.prompt: Both runs use the same seed and generator. Run A assigns the first four draws to its weights. Run B draws a preview number first, then assigns the next four. Must the initial weight arrays match? What should be saved?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: No. Their positions in the generated sequence differ, though coincidental equality is not logically impossible. Save the actual initial arrays, parameter order and random-call procedure as well as the seed.

workbook.title: Transfer the starting-value experiment independently
workbook.prompt: Use J(a) = (a - 3) squared, gradient 2(a - 3), rate 0.25 and two updates. Restart from a = 1, then restart from a = 5. Calculate both traces and final losses. Explain what can be concluded about these two runs.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Start 1 gives 1, 2, 2.5 and final loss 0.25. Start 5 gives 5, 4, 3.5 and final loss 0.25. Equal initial distances yield equal final losses under this rule, but the final parameters differ.

workbook.title: Test repeated correctness
workbook.prompt: A forward-pass program returns the same wrong answer every run with a fixed seed. Has repeatability verified the implementation? Name two stronger checks.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: No. Compare intermediate values with independent hand calculations, test shapes and boundary cases, or compare analytical gradients with numerical probes away from activation corners. Repeating the same result only checks consistency.

teacher.background: Use two 45-minute sessions. Keep the scalar initial-value experiment separate from the four-parameter symmetry example. No full-network training library is needed. Derive the local gradients verbally from residual and output sensitivity, or verify them with numerical probes. Do not teach that all zero values are forbidden or that a seed proves correctness.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook; paper and pencil
Calculator and optional local Python 3 editor; no packages or AI accounts needed
Use the fictional examples supplied; prepare the fresh retry before class
sessions: Retrieve checkpoint state and agree on the fixed two-update experiment.
Trace the three starts in the table and complete W1 with signed distances.
Use W2 to distinguish equal loss from identical model parameters.
Run or trace the local generator example and use W3 to discuss random-call order.
Trace the separate symmetric two-unit model and complete the guided output calculation.
Compare activations for hidden weights 1 and -1, then discuss the all-zero product example.
Collect W4 independently, requiring a reset and a complete trace for each start.
Use W5 and the exit response to build an experiment record, then administer the fresh retry.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided: initially output 2 and squared error 1. After all four weights become 0.8, hidden activations are [0.8, 0.8], output 1.28, residual 0.28 and squared error 0.0784. Both units still match. Exit: differing random-call and batch orders are changed conditions, not automatic proof of a defect. Compare saved initial arrays and intermediate traces under matched settings, then check against independent expectations.
misconceptions: The same seed specifies the entire experiment
Data, call order, batching, code and numerical environment also matter.
Every parameter should start at zero
The scalar example permits zero, but identical or all-zero multi-unit initialisations can create different limitations.
Equal loss means equal models
Different parameters can be equally far from a minimum or give the same scalar loss.
teacher.assessment: W4 requires traces ending at 2.5 and 3.5, both with loss 0.25. Fresh retry: J(c) = 2(c - 1) squared, gradient 4(c - 1), rate 0.125 and two updates. Start -1 gives -1, 0, 0.5; start 3 gives 3, 2, 1.5. Both final losses are 0.5. Require a conclusion restricted to the declared runs.
teacher.support: Provide a number line and a ledger for start, gradient and updated value. Save concrete arrays instead of relying on seed vocabulary alone. Extension: use symmetric differences with step 0.001 to check all four initial gradients in the positive-region two-unit example, then explain why identical computations preserve symmetry.
teacher.next: Week 18 debugs dimension contracts, gradient order and update direction.

ai-4/18.title: Debugging shapes and gradients
goals: Check dimension contracts before computing a layer
Locate the first wrong value in a forward or gradient trace
Verify a repair with independent checks and limited claims

prerequisite.prompt: Why does running the same code twice and getting the same answer not establish correctness?
prerequisite.answer: A deterministic error can repeat perfectly. Independent expected values and checks of intermediate computations are needed.

vocabulary: The sizes of an array along its declared axes
A stated condition that inputs and outputs must satisfy
The change rate of a scalar loss with respect to one parameter while others are fixed
A saved check rerun after a repair to detect the return of a defect

blocks.text: For this lesson, a dense layer stores one output unit per weight-matrix row. If an input has two features and the layer has three units, W has three rows and two columns, b has length 3, and one input x has length 2. Compute z for each unit, then apply ReLU to each component.

Use W rows [1, 0], [0, 1], [1, -1] and b = [0, 0, 1]. For x = [1, 2], the scores are [1, 2, 0] and the activations are [1, 2, 0]. A batch stores examples in rows: inputs [[1, 2], [3, 1]] have shape 2 by 2, and outputs have shape 2 by 3.

rows: Three units each reading two features
Two examples each with three activations

blocks.text: Other software may use a transposed weight convention. The key is to record and follow one contract. An array with the right number of values can still be wrong if features or axes are swapped.

Python zip stops when its shortest input ends. Without a length check, a missing feature can silently remove a contribution. Reject malformed dimensions before computing: do not pad, truncate or reshape a mismatched input just to make the calculation run.

blocks.title: Optional Python check

blocks.text: The function assumes finite numeric values; it checks dimensions, not every possible input fault. Evaluate the two batch rows independently and stack their outputs. Retain tests that reject a missing input feature, a short weight row and an incorrect bias count.

blocks.title: Repair from the first disagreement
rows: x length 2 W 3 by 2 b length 3
blocks.caption: The submitted third score omits bias 1. ReLU hides the error for this input, so matching final activations are not enough. At x = [3, 1], the same omission changes the third activation from 3 to 2.

blocks.label: Trace x = [0, 2] with the correct layer. Then omit the third bias. Which scores differ, and why do the activation vectors still agree?

blocks.text: Use a separate scalar diagnostic model y = 2w + b, target 3, loss (y - 3) squared, and parameter order [w, b]. At [1, 0], prediction is 2, residual -1 and gradient [-4, -2]. A submitted gradient [-2, -4] has the correct length but swapped meanings.

With symmetric step 0.1, probe w while b stays 0: losses at w = 0.9 and 1.1 are 1.44 and 0.64. Their difference divided by 0.2 is -4. Probe b while w stays 1: losses at b = -0.1 and 0.1 are 1.21 and 0.81, giving -2. Use original parameters for both probes and compare by coordinate with a stated tolerance.

A gradient check must include the actual loss convention and any penalty. For ReLU, avoid probes crossing its corner at zero; a symmetric value there need not be a derivative. A passing numerical check at selected points is evidence about those points, not a proof for every input.

lesson.title: Verify update direction and retain the repair

blocks.text: At [w, b] = [1, 0], use the verified gradient [-4, -2] and rate 0.05. Subtracting rate times gradient gives [1.2, 0.1], prediction 2.5 and loss 0.25. A sign bug that adds it gives [0.8, -0.1], prediction 1.5 and loss 2.25. Recompute loss after the complete update instead of trusting an intended direction.

blocks.label: A repair makes one final output match but leaves the third score wrong. Another repair makes loss decrease but has swapped gradient entries. Are either of these sufficient implementation checks? Describe the evidence needed.

blocks.text: Lower loss alone cannot prove a correct gradient or update; some wrong steps also improve loss. Retain shape rejections, hand-computed intermediate traces, numerical coordinate checks and update checks. Next week investigates the representations produced by hidden layers.

workbook.title: Reject a shape mismatch
workbook.prompt: The layer expects W shape 3 by 2, b length 3 and x length 2. A submitted x has length 3. Should the last feature be silently ignored? State the failed contract and repair process.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: No. Each weight row must have the same length as x. Confirm the intended feature schema, then supply a valid two-feature input or deliberately redesign and retrain the layer; do not silently discard a value.

workbook.title: Expose a hidden bias error
workbook.prompt: Compute scores and activations for x = [3, 1] with the lesson layer, then omit the third bias. Identify the first discrepancy and the resulting activation error.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Correct scores and activations are [3, 1, 3]. Omitting the third bias produces [3, 1, 2]. The third score is the first discrepancy and now survives ReLU.

workbook.title: Check an update sign
workbook.prompt: For the diagnostic model at [1, 0], gradient [-4, -2] and rate 0.05, calculate the correct new parameters and loss. Compare with adding the gradient step.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Correct subtraction gives [1.2, 0.1], prediction 2.5 and loss 0.25. Addition gives [0.8, -0.1], prediction 1.5 and loss 2.25, compared with starting loss 1.

workbook.title: Debug a new gradient independently
workbook.prompt: Use y = 3a + c, target 2, loss (y - 2) squared, at [a, c] = [0, 1]. A program returns gradient [-2, -6] in order [a, c]. Use symmetric step 0.1 to check each coordinate, then update both with the corrected gradient and rate 0.05. Report new parameters and loss.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: For a, losses at -0.1 and 0.1 are 1.69 and 0.49, giving -6. For c, losses at 0.9 and 1.1 are 1.21 and 0.81, giving -2. The entries were swapped. Correct update gives [0.3, 1.1], prediction 2 and loss 0.

workbook.title: Keep independent regression checks
workbook.prompt: A program passes only the x = [1, 2] final-activation test. Propose one intermediate-value check, one malformed-input check and one additional input that exposes the bias omission.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Check scores [1, 2, 0] before ReLU; reject a wrong input length or bias count; test x = [3, 1], whose third activation must be 3. These checks address different defects rather than repeating the same final output.

teacher.background: Use two 45-minute sessions. Start with an axis contract and a deliberately wrong intermediate value. Keep the dense-layer example separate from the scalar gradient diagnostic. The central assessment is locating the first error and preserving meaningful regression checks, not merely getting a program to execute.
