Calculator and optional local Python 3 editor; no packages or AI accounts needed
Use the fictional examples supplied; prepare the fresh retry before class
sessions: Retrieve the difference between repeated and independently checked results; label all axes.
Trace both batch examples and use W1 to reject a dimension mismatch.
Run or trace the guarded dense-layer function and test invalid dimensions.
Use the visual and W2 to show how ReLU can hide a bias omission on one input.
Complete the guided x = [0, 2] trace, comparing scores with activations.
Probe w and b separately in the scalar diagnostic, then complete W3.
Collect W4 independently with four probe losses, ordered gradients and the corrected update.
Use W5 and the exit response to retain a regression checklist; administer the fresh retry.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided: correct scores [0, 2, -1], activations [0, 2, 0]. With the third bias omitted, scores become [0, 2, -2], but activations stay [0, 2, 0]. Exit: neither check is sufficient. Verify the intermediate score, coordinate meanings and expected update, use multiple independent inputs and retain malformed-dimension checks.
misconceptions: Matching output shape guarantees the computation
Correct dimensions can hide swapped features, missing biases or wrong axis meanings.
Matching final activations proves all scores
ReLU can map different negative scores to the same zero.
Decreasing loss proves a correct gradient
An incorrect direction can still improve one case; compare coordinate probes and exact update expectations.
teacher.assessment: W4 requires partials [-6, -2], new parameters [0.3, 1.1] and loss 0. Fresh retry: y = 2p + q, target 4, at [1, 1]. With step 0.1, p losses 1.44 and 0.64 give -4; q losses 1.21 and 0.81 give -2. Rate 0.1 gives [1.4, 1.2], prediction 4 and loss 0. Require parameter ordering to remain explicit.
teacher.support: Provide labelled columns for inputs, scores, activations and parameter coordinates; allow calculators. Extension: test several positive and negative inputs against an independent explicit formula and explain why a test at a ReLU corner needs different reasoning from a smooth gradient check.
teacher.next: Week 19 explores learned representations and the distinctions hidden activations preserve.

ai-4/19.title: Learned representations
goals: Trace an input through a hidden representation and a decision rule
Identify distinctions that a representation preserves or loses
Separate a useful constructed feature from evidence of successful learning

prerequisite.prompt: Why should a debugging trace inspect scores before ReLU as well as final activations?
prerequisite.answer: Different negative scores all become zero. Matching activations can hide an earlier error, so intermediate values need independent checks.

vocabulary: An encoding of an example used by another computation
A value produced inside a network after applying an activation function
Two different inputs receiving the same representation
A feature whose computation depends on parameters adjusted using training data

blocks.text: Consider fictional rectangles with input [width, height] in cm. The task is to identify rectangles whose width is strictly greater than height. The target is 1 for wider rectangles and 0 otherwise. A square therefore has target 0. This is an arithmetic teaching task, not a claim that a network is needed to measure rectangles.

Define two hidden units: h1 = ReLU(width - height) and h2 = ReLU(height - width). Their weight rows are [1, -1] and [-1, 1], with zero biases. The representation h = [h1, h2] records excess width or excess height. Predict 1 when h1 > 0; otherwise predict 0.

These weights were chosen by the lesson author. They demonstrate a representation that could be implemented by a network, but no training run has established that a model learned it. Learning would require adjusting parameters using training data and recording the procedure.

lesson.title: Trace the representation separately from the head

blocks.text: A prediction head is the computation that reads the hidden vector and produces an output. Keeping it separate lets us inspect what information is available before making a decision. This example assumes two finite, positive measurements in cm; it is not a general input validator.

blocks.title: Optional Python check

blocks.text: The raw difference width - height can be recovered as h1 - h2. The original width and height cannot in general be recovered: many rectangles share a difference. Two hidden components do not guarantee preservation of two input components.

lesson.title: See a collision and its consequences

blocks.title: Different rectangles can share a hidden vector
blocks.caption: The representation preserves the wider-than-height answer for these examples but discards information needed to recover their different areas. A deterministic head receiving only this vector must give both examples the same output.

blocks.label: Encode [6, 4] and [7, 5]. Give their wider-than-height predictions and areas. Can a head that sees only h always recover the exact area? Explain using this pair.

lesson.title: Match the representation to the question

blocks.text: A representation can be sufficient for one task and insufficient for another. Our hidden vector supports the wider-than-height rule for every valid input under the stated formula. It fails to identify exact area for all rectangles because a collision can contain different areas. No more complicated deterministic head can recover information that is absent from its input.

Compare a second encoding s = width + height. Rectangles [4, 2] and [2, 4] both give s = 6 but have different wider-than-height targets. A head receiving only s must fail on at least one of them. Useful features depend on the question, not just the number of encoded values.

One repair for area is to retain the original measurements. Another is to append s to h. Since d = h1 - h2, width = (s + d) / 2 and height = (s - d) / 2. This works with exact valid measurements; it does not mean every added feature improves generalisation on noisy data.

In a trained network, hidden features depend on fitted weights and may not have simple human names. A strong output result does not by itself show that a unit represents a concept such as shape or fairness. Inspect activations on deliberately varied examples, compare with a baseline, and limit conclusions to the evidence.

blocks.label: A teammate calls the hand-chosen rectangle layer a learned area detector because all four wider-than-height predictions are correct. Identify two problems with this claim and propose one decisive area check.

blocks.text: When testing a learned representation, fit preprocessing and parameters on training data, use validation data for choices, and reserve the final test for the declared final evaluation. Compare representations with matched data, head rules and training budgets, and report collisions and failures. Next week makes the axis and channel meanings of image tensors explicit.

workbook.title: Trace new inputs
workbook.prompt: Encode [8, 3], [3, 8] and [4, 4] with the lesson layer. Apply its prediction rule and explain the square boundary.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: The vectors are [5, 0], [0, 5] and [0, 0]. Predictions are 1, 0 and 0. Equal width and height does not satisfy strictly greater.

workbook.title: Prove an information loss
workbook.prompt: Give the hidden vectors and areas for [4, 2] and [5, 3]. Explain why increasing only the complexity of a deterministic area head cannot make both exact predictions correct.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Both hidden vectors are [2, 0], while areas are 8 and 15 square cm. Identical inputs to a deterministic head yield identical outputs, so the head cannot return both required values.

workbook.title: Compare another encoding
workbook.prompt: The alternative representation is s = width + height. Use [4, 2] and [2, 4] to decide whether s alone always supports the wider-than-height task.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Both have s = 6, but their targets are 1 and 0. This collision prevents any deterministic head using only s from getting both right.

workbook.title: Audit a new representation independently
workbook.prompt: A different layer uses g = [ReLU(width - height - 1), ReLU(height - width - 1)]. Encode [4, 3] and [3, 4]. State their targets for width strictly greater than height. Can any deterministic head receiving only g classify both correctly?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Both encode as [0, 0]: the scores are [0, -2] and [-2, 0]. Targets are 1 and 0. No deterministic head receiving only this shared vector can distinguish the pair. The added threshold erased a distinction required by this task.

workbook.title: Repair and qualify a claim
workbook.prompt: For h = [2, 0] and s = 8, recover width, height and area. Does this algebra prove that a training program learned the representation or that it will work well on noisy measurements?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Difference d is 2. Width is (8 + 2) / 2 = 5 and height is (8 - 2) / 2 = 3; area is 15 square cm. The algebra establishes recovery under the formula, not a training history or performance with noisy measurements.

teacher.background: Use two 45-minute sessions. Begin with rectangle measurements and the explicit strict comparison. Distinguish the constructed layer from a genuinely fitted layer throughout. The key reasoning is the collision argument: identical representations force identical deterministic outputs. No calculus, external AI account or full training framework is required.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook; paper and pencil
Calculator and optional local Python 3 editor; no packages or AI accounts needed
Use the fictional examples supplied; prepare the fresh retry before class
sessions: Retrieve how ReLU can hide distinctions and establish the rectangle schema and target.
Trace the four lesson examples, including a square, before naming the hidden features.
Complete W1 and trace the optional code, separating the representation from its head.
Use the visual and W2 to explain why identical hidden inputs cannot yield two exact areas.
Complete the guided pair and compare the sum-only encoding using W3.
Derive recovery from sum and difference, then discuss the limited conclusion in W5.
Collect W4 independently, requiring both score vectors, hidden vectors and target labels.
Use the exit response and fresh retry to distinguish learning evidence from an authored formula.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided: [6, 4] and [7, 5] both encode as [2, 0], predict 1 and have areas 24 and 35 square cm. A deterministic head using only h cannot recover both exact areas. Exit: hand-chosen weights are not evidence of learning, and correct comparison labels do not establish area prediction. Test the collision [4, 2] versus [5, 3], with areas 8 and 15.
misconceptions: Two hidden values preserve both input measurements
Dimension alone does not guarantee recovery; distinct inputs can collide.
A more complex head can always fix lost information
A deterministic head cannot distinguish identical representations without additional input.
Correct outputs prove human concepts were learned
The layer here was constructed, and a task score alone does not establish a hidden concept.
teacher.assessment: W4 requires scores [0, -2] and [-2, 0], hidden vector [0, 0] for both, targets 1 and 0 and an impossibility explanation. Fresh retry: use g = [ReLU(width - height - 2), ReLU(height - width - 2)] for [5, 3] and [3, 5]. Scores are [0, -4] and [-4, 0]; both hidden vectors are [0, 0], but targets are 1 and 0. No deterministic head using only g can classify both correctly.
teacher.support: Provide paper rectangles and columns for signed difference, two scores, activations and target. Allow calculators and ask for verbal collision explanations before algebra. Extension: show that adding the same positive amount to width and height preserves h while changing area; derive exact recovery when the sum is also retained.
teacher.next: Week 20 introduces image tensors and channels, with explicit axis order and value scales.

ai-4/2.title: Dot products and weighted sums
goals: Calculate a dot product by matching feature positions
Explain how a weight changes a score with other inputs fixed
Distinguish a weighted score from a probability or trained model

prerequisite.prompt: Under schema [width, height], why must [4, 2] and [2, 4] remain distinct?
prerequisite.answer: Their components assign different values to width and height. A calculation using different weights for those features can produce different results.

vocabulary: A numerical coefficient multiplying one input component
The sum of products of corresponding vector components
The product of one input component and its matching weight
A numerical output whose interpretation must be specified

lesson.title: Match a weight to each input

blocks.text: A small model can combine several measurements into one score. Let x = [4, 2] contain fictional width and height measurements in cm. Set weights w = [2, -1]. Multiply matching positions, then add: s = (2 times 4) + (-1 times 2) = 6. The letter x names the input vector.

We call this calculation a dot product, written w dot x. The vectors must have the same number of components. Each weight belongs to one named feature. These hand-selected weights demonstrate a computation; no training has happened. The result 6 is a score, not a probability or a claim that this parcel is safe.
The coefficients carry score-per-cm units in this example, making both contributions compatible score units. A weighted sum needs a consistent definition of units.

lesson.title: Compare inputs with a fixed computation

blocks.text: Keep w = [2, -1] fixed. For A = [4, 2], the score is 6. For B = [2, 4], it is 4 - 4 = 0. For C = [3, 3], it is 6 - 3 = 3. Swapping input positions without swapping their matching weights changes the computation. A zero score can come from cancellation, even when neither input is zero.

blocks.title: Optional Python check

blocks.text: The length check matters: Python zip alone stops at the shorter list and could silently omit a feature. The function assumes numeric inputs already validated under the schema. First predict the three printed values on paper, then compare.

blocks.title: Multiply matching components then add
blocks.caption: The first two rows are separate contributions. The last row combines them; multiplying the final input sum by the final weight sum would be a different operation.

blocks.label: Keep w = [2, -1]. Change [4, 2] to [4, 3]. Compute both contributions and explain the score change.

blocks.text: Holding other inputs fixed, raising width by 1 cm raises this score by 2; raising height by 1 cm lowers it by 1. A negative weight reverses the direction of that feature contribution. It does not label the feature as bad, and its sign alone does not explain cause in the world.

Unit changes affect coefficients. If height is written in mm instead of cm while width remains in cm, use height weight -0.1 instead of -1 to preserve the same scores. For [4 cm, 20 mm], 2 times 4 plus -0.1 times 20 still gives 6. Raw coefficient magnitudes cannot establish feature importance when units differ.

A weighted sum can combine evidence, but it discards information: [4, 2] and [5, 4] both produce score 6 under these weights. A downstream rule receiving only that score cannot recover which of these vectors was used. To classify, we would also need a stated decision rule and labelled evaluation examples.

blocks.label: A teammate calls score 6 a 60 percent chance of class 1. What is missing from that claim?

blocks.text: Next week adds an offset called a bias and states exactly how a score becomes a class prediction.

workbook.title: Calculate contributions
workbook.prompt: For w = [2, -1] and x = [3, 5], write both contributions and their sum.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Contributions are 6 and -5, so the score is 1.

workbook.title: Explain cancellation
workbook.prompt: For w = [2, -1] and x = [2, 4], explain why score zero does not mean the input contains no information.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Contributions 4 and -4 cancel. The input still contains width 2 and height 4; zero is the combined score.

workbook.title: Preserve a unit change
workbook.prompt: Width stays in cm and height changes to mm. For the worked parcel [4 cm, 20 mm], give the revised weights and score.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Use [2, -0.1]. Contributions 8 and -2 give score 6, preserving the original measurement meaning.

workbook.title: Compute a new dot product independently
workbook.prompt: Use x = [3, 1, 2] and w = [-2, 4, 0.5]. Give each contribution and the total. Increase only the second component from 1 to 2 and compute the new total. Explain why a two-weight list is invalid for this input.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Contributions -6, 4, 1 give -1. With second component 2, contributions -6, 8, 1 give 3, a rise of 4. Three input components need three matching weights; silently dropping the final component changes the computation.

workbook.title: Find lost information
workbook.prompt: Verify that [4, 2] and [5, 4] both score 6 with w = [2, -1]. Can a later step receiving only this score distinguish those two records?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: The scores are 8 - 2 = 6 and 10 - 4 = 6. A deterministic later step receiving only 6 receives identical information and cannot distinguish them.

teacher.background: Teach the dot product as a traceable sum of signed contributions in two 45-minute sessions. Keep weights fixed throughout each comparison and separate hand-chosen parameters from training. Students should explain a score change using the corresponding coefficient, while retaining the limits of that interpretation.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook; paper and pencil
Calculator and optional local Python 3 editor; no packages or AI accounts needed
Use the fictional examples supplied; prepare the fresh retry before class
sessions: Ask the prerequisite question. Check signed multiplication with -1 times 2 before introducing a dot product.
Lay out the contribution table. Students draw a connection between each named input and its own weight.
Complete W1 and W2. Trace A, B and C with the same weights; discuss cancellation rather than calling zero an empty input.
Run or trace the guarded Python function. Try a missing weight and explain the error. Complete the guided change.
Retrieve the two contributions for A. Ask what changes if height increases while width stays fixed.
Complete W3, converting only height to mm. Show why weight magnitude depends on units.
Collect W4 independently. Require the three signed contributions, original and changed totals, and the dimension error explanation.
Complete W5 and the exit response. Use the fresh retry after targeted feedback; keep first attempts for assessment.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided: [4, 3] gives 8 and -3, total 5, down 1 from 6 because height rose by 1 with coefficient -1. Exit: the score has no supplied probability mapping, fitted probability model or calibration evidence. Multiplying it by ten does not create a supported probability.
misconceptions: Multiply the sums instead
The operation is 2 times 4 plus -1 times 2, not (2 - 1) times (4 + 2). That shortcut happens to match for some inputs but is not the rule.
Negative means unimportant
A negative coefficient changes direction. Units, data and the rest of the model affect interpretation.
The weights have been learned
These values were supplied. Training would require data, an objective and a fitting procedure.
teacher.assessment: W4 requires contributions -6, 4, 1 and total -1, changed total 3 and a dimension check. Fresh retry: w = [1, -3, 2], x = [2, 1, 4] gives 2 - 3 + 8 = 7. If only the third input falls to 3, the score is 5. Ask for the two-point decrease explanation.
teacher.support: Provide three labelled contribution boxes and a number line for signed addition. Extension: permute both inputs and matching weights together and show that the sum is preserved; then permute only one to expose a schema mismatch.
teacher.next: Week 3 adds a bias after the dot product and uses an explicit decision boundary.

ai-4/20.title: Image tensors and channels
goals: Read a pixel using declared row column and channel axes
Convert channel layout without changing pixel meaning
Distinguish fixed value scaling from information losing transformations

prerequisite.prompt: Why does a representation with two components not necessarily preserve two original measurements?
prerequisite.answer: Different inputs can map to the same representation. The number of components alone does not guarantee that the original values can be recovered.

vocabulary: A numerical array with a declared set of axes
One component plane of an image such as red green or blue
The sequence of meanings assigned to array dimensions
A declared numerical conversion applied to stored values

lesson.title: Give every image axis a meaning

blocks.text: A small fictional RGB image has height 2 pixels, width 2 pixels and three channels ordered red, green, blue. Store it as image[row][column][channel], abbreviated HWC. Use zero-based indices: the top row is 0, the left column is 0, and red, green and blue are channels 0, 1 and 2. Each stored component is an integer from 0 to 255.

The shape is 2 by 2 by 3. There are four pixels and twelve channel values. The blue component of the bottom-left pixel is image[1][0][2] = 255. A single channel is a plane of values across positions; it is not a separate photograph or a label.

Shape needs a schema. A grayscale image might be stored as H by W or H by W by 1. An RGB image uses three channels here; other formats can include additional channels. Declare the format instead of assuming every three-dimensional array means the same thing.

A channel-first layout uses image[channel][row][column], abbreviated CHW. Our image then has shape 3 by 2 by 2. A correct conversion preserves the rule chw[c][r][k] = hwc[r][k][c]. The code assumes a nonempty rectangular image with exactly three values per pixel.

blocks.title: Optional Python check
blocks.text:
hwc = [
    [[255, 0, 0], [0, 255, 0]],
    [[0, 0, 255], [255, 255, 255]],
]
height, width = len(hwc), len(hwc[0])
chw = [[[hwc[r][k][c] for k in range(width)]
        for r in range(height)] for c in range(3)]
for channel in chw:
    print(channel)
assert chw[2][1][0] == hwc[1][0][2] == 255
restored = [[[chw[c][r][k] for c in range(3)]
             for k in range(width)] for r in range(height)]
assert restored == hwc

Reading nested values in order and merely regrouping them into a new shape does not perform this axis conversion. The first four flattened HWC values are [255, 0, 0, 0]. A naive regrouping makes these the first channel plane, but the correct red plane is [[255, 0], [0, 255]]. Shape agreement alone cannot detect this mistake.

blocks.title: The same pixels in three channel planes
blocks.caption: Each row describes one channel plane. Within a plane the first listed row is the image top and the second is the bottom. Combining the three values at the same position recovers its RGB triplet.

blocks.label: Use the planes to reconstruct the top-right and bottom-right RGB pixels. Give both HWC and CHW indices for the top-right green value.

lesson.title: Scale values under a stated contract

blocks.text: For this lesson, divide every channel value by 255 to obtain floating-point values from 0 to 1. Thus [255, 128, 0] becomes [1, 128/255, 0], with the middle value approximately 0.502. This fixed conversion does not fit a statistic from data. Apply the same conversion during training and later use, and record whether an input is already scaled.

Dividing twice makes a raw value of 255 become 1/255, approximately 0.00392, instead of 1. Integer rounding after scaling can also erase distinctions. In exact arithmetic the declared division is reversible by multiplication; finite precision or deliberate rounding can limit exact recovery.

Averaging RGB channels is a different operation. The classroom mean gives red [255, 0, 0] and green [0, 255, 0] the same value 85, losing their colour distinction. It is a simple illustration, not a perceptual brightness formula. If preprocessing instead estimates means or spreads from a dataset, fit those statistics using training data only.

Stacking five same-size HWC images adds a leading example axis N. This batch has shape 5 by 2 by 2 by 3 and contains 60 channel values. With channel-first images, its shape is 5 by 3 by 2 by 2. The example axis is not another colour channel. Every axis must keep its meaning through the model.

blocks.label: A loader returns the expected shape, but red and blue channels were exchanged and already scaled values were divided by 255 again. Does the shape check establish correctness? Name an exact pixel check and a value check that expose these faults.

blocks.text: Use a tiny known image, named axis meanings and expected channel values to check a pipeline. Keep original images when testing transformations. Flattening can be reversed if shape and traversal order are retained; averaging colours generally cannot. Next week reads small neighbourhoods with a convolution operation.

workbook.title: Read a pixel precisely
workbook.prompt: For the lesson image, give image[1][0], image[1][0][2], the HWC shape, pixel count and number of channel values.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: The RGB pixel is [0, 0, 255]; its blue value is 255. Shape is 2 by 2 by 3, with four pixels and twelve channel values.

workbook.title: Audit an axis conversion
workbook.prompt: A program flattens the lesson HWC array and groups the first four values into a 2 by 2 red plane. Give that incorrect plane and the correct plane. Identify a position where they disagree.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: The incorrect plane is [[255, 0], [0, 0]]. The correct red plane is [[255, 0], [0, 255]]. They disagree at row 1 column 1. Regrouping consecutive values does not transpose axes.

workbook.title: Check scaling and lost colour
workbook.prompt: Scale [255, 128, 0] by 255, keeping the middle value as a fraction. Then calculate the classroom RGB means of pure red and pure green. Which operation loses the distinction between those colours?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Scaling gives [1, 128/255, 0]. Both RGB means are 85, so averaging loses the red versus green distinction. Exact fixed scaling preserves the triplet distinction.

workbook.title: Convert a new image independently
workbook.prompt: A one-row two-column RGB image has pixels [10, 20, 30] then [40, 50, 60]. State its HWC shape and all three CHW planes. Give the green value at row 0 column 1 in both layouts. A batch contains four copies: give its NHWC shape and total channel-value count.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: HWC shape is 1 by 2 by 3. CHW planes are [[10, 40]], [[20, 50]], [[30, 60]], giving shape 3 by 1 by 2. hwc[0][1][1] and chw[1][0][1] both equal 50. Batch shape is 4 by 1 by 2 by 3, containing 24 values.

workbook.title: Design revealing pipeline checks
workbook.prompt: The lesson image is loaded with red and blue exchanged, then scaled twice. Give two expected checks that would expose these errors even though the shape is correct.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Before scaling, the top-left pixel must be [255, 0, 0], not [0, 0, 255]. A known raw component of 255 must become 1 after scaling once; approximately 0.00392 indicates division twice. Test named values and positions as well as dimensions.

teacher.background: Use two 45-minute sessions. Draw the four-pixel image and label row, column and channel before writing nested brackets. Keep RGB ordering, zero-based indices and the 0 to 255 contract explicit. Distinguish an axis permutation from regrouping, and fixed scaling from fitted preprocessing. No external image files or student photographs are needed.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook; paper and pencil
Calculator and optional local Python 3 editor; no packages or AI accounts needed
Use the fictional examples supplied; prepare the fresh retry before class
sessions: Retrieve information loss and label the four image positions with zero-based indices.
Count pixels and components, then use W1 to read a full pixel and one channel.
Trace the three channel planes and run or hand-trace the optional code.
Use W2 to expose naive regrouping with the bottom-right red component.
Reconstruct the guided pixels and locate the same green value in both layouts.
Use W3 to compare fixed scaling with colour averaging and discuss double scaling.
Collect W4 independently, checking the non-square shape and the leading batch axis.
Use W5 and the exit response to plan exact-value checks, then administer the fresh retry.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided: top-right is [0, 255, 0] and bottom-right is [255, 255, 255]. The top-right green value is hwc[0][1][1] or chw[1][0][1], both 255. Exit: shape alone misses both errors. Check the top-left RGB pixel is red before scaling and that a raw value 255 becomes exactly 1 under one declared division, rather than approximately 0.00392.
misconceptions: Three channels mean three images
Channels are component planes at matching spatial positions in one image.
Reshaping automatically changes axis meanings correctly
Axis permutation must preserve coordinate correspondence; regrouping a flattened list can mix positions and colours.
Every conversion to a smaller number preserves information
Exact fixed scaling differs from rounding and channel averaging, which can collapse distinct values.
teacher.assessment: W4 requires three planes, both coordinate references to value 50, NHWC shape 4 by 1 by 2 by 3 and 24 values. Fresh retry: a two-row one-column image contains [3, 6, 9] above [12, 15, 18]. HWC shape is 2 by 1 by 3. CHW planes are [[3], [12]], [[6], [15]], [[9], [18]]. The bottom blue component is hwc[1][0][2] = chw[2][1][0] = 18. A batch of three has NHWC shape 3 by 2 by 1 by 3 and 18 values.
teacher.support: Use three labelled paper grids and a coordinate ledger; provide colour names so success does not depend on colour vision. Allow fraction answers for scaling. Extension: convert a rectangular image HWC to CHW and back, checking every coordinate, then construct two different colours with the same classroom channel mean.
teacher.next: Week 21 introduces convolution as a local operation with explicit neighbourhoods and boundary rules.

ai-4/21.title: Convolution as a local operation
goals: Compute a local weighted sum at each valid image position
Explain shared weights and predict output dimensions
Check how stride boundaries and activation affect the result

prerequisite.prompt: Why must an image schema record axis order as well as shape?
prerequisite.answer: The same dimensions can describe different coordinate meanings. A correct computation must know which axis is row, column or channel.

vocabulary: A small array of weights applied to a local input neighbourhood
The spatial array of outputs produced by applying a filter
The distance between successive window starting positions
Values added around an input boundary under a declared rule

lesson.title: Reuse one local rule across an image

blocks.text: Use a fictional single-channel image with rows [1, 2, 0], [0, 1, 3] and [2, 0, 1]. Coordinates are zero-based row then column. Our kernel has rows [1, -1] and [0, 1]. At each position, multiply matching entries of a 2 by 2 window and the kernel, then add the four products. Use bias 0, stride 1 and no padding.

At the top-left window, the sum is 1 times 1 plus 2 times -1 plus 0 times 0 plus 1 times 1 = 0. Slide the same kernel right, then down. Only use windows that fit entirely inside the image; this is the valid boundary rule.

The feature map has rows [0, 5] and [-1, -1]. This neural-network convention keeps the kernel orientation fixed; mathematically it is cross-correlation. Mathematical convolution reverses the kernel along both spatial axes. We use the fixed-orientation convention throughout, so every hand calculation and program agrees.

The following function assumes nonempty rectangular numeric arrays and a positive integer stride. It rejects a kernel larger than the image. It computes one input channel, one output map, zero bias and no padding; no activation is applied inside the function.

blocks.title: Optional Python check
blocks.text:
def local_filter(image, kernel, stride=1):
    h, w = len(image), len(image[0])
    kh, kw = len(kernel), len(kernel[0])
    if kh > h or kw > w:
        raise ValueError("Kernel does not fit")
    out = []
    for r in range(0, h - kh + 1, stride):
        row = []
        for c in range(0, w - kw + 1, stride):
            value = sum(image[r+i][c+j] * kernel[i][j]
                        for i in range(kh) for j in range(kw))
            row.append(value)
        out.append(row)
    return out

x = [[1, 2, 0], [0, 1, 3], [2, 0, 1]]
k = [[1, -1], [0, 1]]
assert local_filter(x, k) == [[0, 5], [-1, -1]]
assert local_filter(x, k, 2) == [[0]]

The kernel weights are reused at all four positions. There are four kernel parameters, not sixteen separate weights. If we add one shared bias for this output map, there are five parameters. The number of multiply operations grows with the number of windows even though the parameter count stays fixed.

lesson.title: Separate the window from the output position

blocks.title: One shared kernel produces four local sums
blocks.caption: Read windows in row order. Each output summarizes one neighbourhood. With stride 1, adjacent windows overlap, but their output values occupy separate cells.

blocks.label: Change only input[0][0] from 1 to 4. Which valid windows include it? Compute the changed feature map and explain why the other three outputs stay the same.

lesson.title: State the stride and boundary rule

blocks.text: For no padding and a kernel that fits, output height is floor((H - Kh) / s) + 1 and width is floor((W - Kw) / s) + 1, where s is the positive integer stride. Floor means round down. Count allowed start positions before using the formula. With a 3 by 3 image, 2 by 2 kernel and stride 2, the only row and column start is 0, so the output is 1 by 1.

Padding changes which windows exist and what they contain. Adding one border of zeros on every side changes this 3 by 3 input to 5 by 5. At stride 1 with our 2 by 2 kernel, output shape becomes 4 by 4. Its top-left window is [[0, 0], [0, 1]] and its output is 1. Zero padding is a chosen boundary assumption, not a measured black region outside the picture.

If ReLU is applied after the unpadded sums, the feature map becomes [[0, 5], [0, 0]]. Negative responses are valid weighted sums before activation; they are not necessarily a software error. Keep raw sums available when debugging so ReLU does not hide a mistake.

These kernel weights were chosen for arithmetic practice, not fitted from data. A response of 5 is neither a probability nor proof that an object was recognised. A trainable convolutional layer adjusts shared parameters using training examples. Additional channels require summing contributions across channels; that is beyond this single-channel calculation.

blocks.label: A teammate reports a 3 by 3 output for the unpadded lesson image and calls its largest number a probability. Identify the missing or incorrect assumptions and give the expected shape and meaning under our declared setup.

blocks.text: Sharing weights applies the same local rule at each allowed position. It does not guarantee that a whole image classifier ignores object location, especially when strides, boundaries or later layers change the result. Next week studies pooling and the spatial information it can discard.

workbook.title: Trace a local sum
workbook.prompt: Use the lesson image and kernel at window start [0, 1]. List the window rows, four products and output before activation.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Window rows are [2, 0] and [1, 3]. Products are 2, 0, 0 and 3, giving output 5.

workbook.title: Separate parameters and operations
workbook.prompt: How many shared kernel weights does the lesson use? How many products are computed over all four valid windows? What changes if one shared bias is added?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: There are four shared weights and sixteen products across four windows. One shared bias raises the parameter count to five and adds the same bias once to each output.

workbook.title: Check stride and padding
workbook.prompt: For the lesson image and kernel, give the output shape with no padding and stride 2. Then give the shape with one zero border on each side and stride 1, and calculate that padded map’s top-left output.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Stride 2 without padding gives shape 1 by 1. The padded input is 5 by 5, giving output 4 by 4. Its top-left window [[0, 0], [0, 1]] gives output 1.

workbook.title: Filter a new image independently
workbook.prompt: Use image rows [2, 1, 0], [1, 3, 2] and kernel rows [0, 1], [-1, 2]. Use no padding, stride 1 and bias 0. Give the output shape, both four-product sums and the feature map. Then add a shared bias of -5 and apply ReLU.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Shape is 1 by 2. First products are 0, 1, -1, 6, summing to 6. Second products are 0, 0, -3, 4, summing to 1. Map is [[6, 1]]. Bias gives [[1, -4]]; ReLU gives [[1, 0]].

workbook.title: Test a convention error
workbook.prompt: A program reverses both axes of the lesson kernel to [[1, 0], [-1, 1]]. Compute the top-left output. Does it agree with our declared convention? Explain what the test checks.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: The top-left output becomes 1 + 0 + 0 + 1 = 2 instead of 0. It does not follow the declared fixed-orientation convention. The asymmetric kernel and known window expose a kernel-orientation mismatch.

teacher.background: Use two 45-minute sessions. Prepare a 2 by 2 paper window and a labelled 3 by 3 grid. Keep kernel orientation fixed and distinguish raw sums, bias and ReLU. Explain that neural-network convolution commonly uses cross-correlation; the exercise explicitly declares this convention. Technical reference: https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.modules.conv.Conv2d.html . No library installation is needed.

teacher.next: Week 22 explores pooling and spatial information, including distinct inputs that share a pooled output.

ai-4/22.title: Pooling and spatial information
goals: Compute max and mean pooling under an explicit window rule
Use collisions to explain lost spatial information
Test boundary and movement claims with revealing examples

prerequisite.prompt: For a 3 by 3 input and a 2 by 2 window with stride 2 and no padding, how many valid window positions exist?
prerequisite.answer: Only the start at row 0 column 0 fits. The output shape is 1 by 1 under the complete-window rule.

vocabulary: Replacing each window by its largest value
Replacing each window by the arithmetic mean of its values
Information about where values occur and how positions relate
Different inputs producing the same pooled values

blocks.text: A fictional single-channel feature map has rows [1, 4, 2, 0], [3, 2, 5, 1], [0, 6, 1, 3] and [2, 4, 2, 7]. Use a 2 by 2 window, stride 2, no padding and only complete windows. Coordinates are zero-based. The four starts are [0, 0], [0, 2], [2, 0] and [2, 2].

Max pooling keeps the largest value in each window. Mean pooling adds the four values and divides by 4. Neither operation learns weights in this lesson. These are fixed summaries of the incoming feature map, unlike the trainable kernel parameters introduced last week.

The max output is [[4, 5], [6, 7]], and the mean output is [[2.5, 2], [3, 3.25]]. Both have shape 2 by 2. Sixteen values become four, but the four outputs still preserve the coarse arrangement of the four regions.

This code assumes a nonempty rectangular numeric map at least 2 by 2. It uses only complete 2 by 2 windows, stride 2 and no padding. It returns two separate summaries of the same map; it does not apply one pooling operation after the other.

blocks.title: Optional Python check
blocks.text:
def pool2(image):
    h, w = len(image), len(image[0])
    if h < 2 or w < 2:
        raise ValueError("Need a complete 2 by 2 window")
    maxima, means = [], []
    for r in range(0, h - 1, 2):
        max_row, mean_row = [], []
        for c in range(0, w - 1, 2):
            values = [image[r+i][c+j]
                      for i in range(2) for j in range(2)]
            max_row.append(max(values))
            mean_row.append(sum(values) / 4)
        maxima.append(max_row)
        means.append(mean_row)
    return maxima, means

x = [[1, 4, 2, 0], [3, 2, 5, 1],
     [0, 6, 1, 3], [2, 4, 2, 7]]
assert pool2(x) == ([[4, 5], [6, 7]],
                    [[2.5, 2], [3, 3.25]])

For this complete-window rule the output shape is floor((H - 2) / 2) + 1 by floor((W - 2) / 2) + 1. A 3 by 3 map produces just one output; its last row and last column are not read. Do not silently invent a partial-window rule or pad missing positions.

lesson.title: Find different inputs with the same summary

blocks.title: A maximum does not identify its location
blocks.caption: The first two windows differ in the position of their nonzero value yet have the same maximum and mean. The third has the same maximum but a different mean. Each summary retains some distinctions and discards others.

blocks.label: Compare windows [[0, 0], [6, 0]] and [[0, 0], [0, 6]]. Compute both summaries. Can a deterministic head receiving only either scalar distinguish bottom-left from bottom-right?

blocks.text: Within one isolated window, rearranging its values preserves both its maximum and mean. But moving a value across a window boundary can change the output map. In a 2 by 4 map of zeros, put a single 8 at row 0 column 1. Max pooling gives [[8, 0]]. Move that 8 one column right to column 2, replacing the old position with zero: the output becomes [[0, 8]]. Pooling therefore does not guarantee that a classifier ignores every small movement.

Negative values are valid inputs. For [[-4, -2], [-7, -3]], the maximum is -2 and the mean is -4. Starting a maximum calculation at zero would incorrectly return 0. Adding a zero to the window would also change its maximum: padding choices matter. Our examples use no padding.

Returning the position of a maximum can preserve extra location information, but it still does not restore the discarded values. For example, [[5, 1], [2, 3]] and [[5, 0], [0, 0]] have the same unique maximum 5 at the top-left position. Even the maximum plus its position cannot tell which original window was used.

Pooling can reduce the amount of data processed by later layers. Whether the lost information is acceptable depends on the task. A task about whether any large response exists in a region may benefit from a maximum; a task requiring exact positions may need the unpooled map or another representation. Do not assume smaller always means better.

blocks.label: A teammate says a 2 by 2 max-pooled map lets them reconstruct the original 4 by 4 map exactly and guarantees unchanged predictions after any one-pixel shift. Use one collision and one boundary example to challenge those claims.

blocks.text: Compare pooling choices with matched data splits and a declared evaluation rule. Fit model parameters on training data and choose alternatives using validation data, leaving final tests reserved. Next week combines these components in a small image-model experiment.

workbook.title: Calculate both summaries
workbook.prompt: For the lesson window starting at [2, 2], list the four values, sum, maximum and mean. State the complete pooled output shape.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Values are 1, 3, 2 and 7. Sum is 13, maximum 7 and mean 3.25. Each pooled output has shape 2 by 2.

workbook.title: Prove that location can be lost
workbook.prompt: Give two different 2 by 2 windows containing exactly one 4 and three zeros that have the same maximum and mean. Explain why either scalar alone cannot identify the position of the 4.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: For example, [[4, 0], [0, 0]] and [[0, 4], [0, 0]] both give maximum 4 and mean 1. A deterministic head receiving the same scalar must give the same output, so it cannot distinguish those positions.

workbook.title: Audit an omitted border
workbook.prompt: Apply the lesson complete-window rule to [[1, 2, 99], [3, 4, 99], [99, 99, 99]]. Give the output shape and both outputs. Explain why neither output includes 99.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Shape is 1 by 1. Only [[1, 2], [3, 4]] is read, giving maximum 4 and mean 2.5. The final row and column lie outside the only complete stride-2 window.

workbook.title: Pool a new map independently
workbook.prompt: Use rows [-4, -1, 2, 6], [-3, -2, 4, 0], [5, 1, -8, -2], [3, 7, -4, -6]. Under the lesson rule, give all four sums, the max map and the mean map. Explain why replacing a negative maximum by zero is an error here.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Window sums in row order are -10, 12, 16 and -20. Max map is [[-1, 6], [7, -2]]. Mean map is [[-2.5, 3], [4, -5]]. Zero is not in either all-negative window; pooling is not ReLU and must return the largest actual value.

workbook.title: Check the movement boundary
workbook.prompt: A 2 by 4 map is zero except for 8 at row 0 column 1. Move the 8 to column 2 and set its old position to zero. Give the max and mean maps before and after. What claim does this refute?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Before: max [[8, 0]], mean [[2, 0]]. After: max [[0, 8]], mean [[0, 2]]. Crossing a pooling boundary changes the output, refuting guaranteed invariance to every one-pixel movement.

teacher.next: Week 23 trains and evaluates a small image model with a declared baseline and data split.

ai-4/23.title: Training a small image model
goals: Trace a complete image model with fixed features and one trained weight
Select a checkpoint using a declared validation rule
Evaluate a frozen model against a baseline and limit the conclusion

prerequisite.prompt: Why could pooling all four pixels of a 2 by 2 image hide whether the bright pixels are on the left or right?
prerequisite.answer: Moving the same values between left and right can preserve the maximum and mean. A summary of all four positions may discard the distinction the task needs.

vocabulary: A feature computation whose parameters are kept unchanged during training
Saved model parameters at a particular training stage
The quantity used under a declared rule to choose a model
A simple comparison method evaluated on the same cases

lesson.title: Declare the image task and the split

blocks.text: Use fictional 2 by 2 binary images, stored as two rows. Predict class 1 when the left column sum exceeds the right column sum; otherwise predict class 0. Equal sums belong to class 0. This known arithmetic task makes every step checkable; it does not establish real-world image recognition.

Apply the fixed kernel [[1, -1], [1, -1]] to the entire image to obtain d. Its negative gives -d. ReLU produces h1 = max(0, d) and h2 = max(0, -d). The output score is a(h1 - h2) = ad. Only the shared scalar a is trained; both kernels stay frozen and there is no bias or pooling.

For squared-error training, map class 1 to target t = 1 and class 0 to t = -1. Predict class 1 only when score > 0; otherwise class 0. The score is not a probability. Keep the teacher-held final cases unseen until the checkpoint is selected and recorded.

lesson.title: Train with a fixed update budget

blocks.text: Start a = 0. Use all four training examples in each update, ordinary mean squared error and learning rate 0.1. Save checkpoints at updates 0, 1 and 2. The training loss is 2.5a squared - 3a + 1, with gradient 5a - 3. Subtract learning rate times gradient; this gives a = 0.3 then a = 0.45.

blocks.title: Optional Python check

blocks.text: The code assumes valid 2 by 2 numeric images and nonempty labelled lists. It prints update, weight, training MSE and validation MSE. Validation examples are scored but never used in the gradient. A single-channel filter spanning the whole image produces one value here, so no further spatial pooling is needed.

blocks.title: Compare the saved checkpoints
blocks.caption: Before training, declare selection by lowest validation MSE among these three checkpoints, with the earliest checkpoint winning an exact tie. Checkpoint 2 is selected. Training loss alone does not define the selection rule.

blocks.label: At a = 0.3 and a = 0.45, compute the validation scores for E and F and their predicted classes. Why can validation accuracy stay the same while validation MSE changes?

lesson.title: Freeze the model and compare a baseline

blocks.text: Save a = 0.45, both fixed kernels, the input schema, target mapping, strict decision threshold, split IDs, learning rate, update budget and selection rule. The baseline always predicts class 0: training classes are tied, and the declared tie rule chooses 0. It gets 2 of 4 training cases and 1 of 2 validation cases correct. The selected model gets all of those cases correct.

The teacher now supplies the three reserved final images. Record each score and prediction before comparing with the supplied labels. Report correct count and denominator for both the frozen model and the same constant baseline. Do not tune the threshold or retrain after viewing final errors and still call that same set unseen.

Because the images and target rule were constructed for this small exercise, even perfect results support only a narrow claim. Validation images differ from training pixels but reuse differences 1 and -1. This is a deliberately simple check of a procedure, not evidence of broad generalisation.

Training adjusted one weight in a model with hand-chosen features. It did not discover the left-versus-right kernel. The arithmetic rule itself would solve the declared task exactly; the trained model helps us study fitting and evaluation, not demonstrate that learning is necessary here.

blocks.label: A teammate claims the model learned its own image features and that choosing the best score on the final test would improve the experiment. Correct both claims and name the evidence needed in the final report.

blocks.text: Report the fixed and trained components separately, selected checkpoint, per-case final predictions, baseline results and limitations. If a final case fails, preserve that failure and design a new experiment with new reserved evaluation data. Next week examines augmentation and leakage between related images.

workbook.title: Trace features and a prediction
workbook.prompt: For Train B, compute d, h1, h2 and the score at a = 0.45. Give the class prediction and squared error against its signed target.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: d = 2, h1 = 2 and h2 = 0. Score is 0.9, prediction class 1 and squared error (0.9 - 1) squared = 0.01.

workbook.title: Check both updates
workbook.prompt: Starting at a = 0, use gradient 5a - 3 and rate 0.1 for two updates. Give each gradient, new weight and training MSE.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: First gradient -3 gives a = 0.3 and MSE 0.325. Second gradient -1.5 gives a = 0.45 and MSE 0.15625. Each gradient is computed at the current weight before the update.

workbook.title: Apply the selection rule
workbook.prompt: Select among the three saved lesson checkpoints using validation MSE, with earliest update breaking a tie. Is selecting by training accuracy the same declared procedure?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Select update 2 with a = 0.45 and validation MSE 0.3025. Training accuracy is a different selection metric; both trained checkpoints have perfect training accuracy, so it does not establish the same choice.

workbook.title: Choose a checkpoint independently
workbook.prompt: A separate model scores bd. Its training examples have d = 1 and -1 with signed targets 1 and -1. Start b = 0; gradient is 2(b - 1), rate 0.25 and budget two updates. Validation differences are 2 and -2 with targets 1 and -1. Calculate all three weights and their validation MSEs, then select by lowest validation MSE.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Weights are 0, 0.5 and 0.75. Validation scores are [0, 0], [1, -1] and [1.5, -1.5], so validation MSEs are 1, 0 and 0.25. Select update 1 with b = 0.5, even though a later update exists. Training MSE falls from 1 to 0.25 to 0.0625.

workbook.title: Audit a final evaluation
workbook.prompt: After inspecting the final cases, a team changes the decision threshold and reports the best result as an unseen test score. Explain the problem and list two things the original report should preserve.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Final outcomes influenced the revised model, so that set is no longer unseen evidence for the revision. Preserve the original frozen checkpoint and threshold, per-case predictions and errors, baseline results, and split IDs. Evaluate the revision on new reserved cases.

teacher.next: Week 24 examines augmentation and leakage, including how related image variants should remain in the same split.

ai-4/24.title: Augmentation and leakage
goals: Check whether a transformation preserves the task label
Keep related examples in one split using source groups
Compare augmentation fairly without inflating independent evidence

prerequisite.prompt: Why must a checkpoint be chosen before inspecting final evaluation results?
prerequisite.answer: Using final outcomes to choose parameters or settings makes that set part of model selection rather than unseen evidence for the selected model.

vocabulary: Creating transformed training examples under a declared procedure
A transformation leaving the correct target unchanged for the stated task
An identifier joining records that must stay together when splitting
Information crossing an evaluation boundary in a way that undermines the intended independent check

lesson.title: Ask what the label means before transforming

blocks.text: Return to the binary image task: class 1 means the left column sum is strictly larger than the right column sum; equal sums belong to class 0. Let d be left sum minus right sum. An augmentation is useful only under a stated task and transformation rule. More image files do not automatically mean more independent evidence.

Swapping rows preserves each column sum, so it preserves this task label for every valid image. Swapping columns changes d to -d. For nonzero d the class changes; for d = 0 it stays class 0. Blindly copying the original label after every flip would create incorrect training targets.

A transformation may be valid for one task and invalid for another. A crop can remove the evidence needed for a label. Choose allowed transformations using the task definition and training evidence, document the assumptions, and evaluate the choice on validation data.

This code assumes valid 2 by 2 binary lists. It constructs new lists instead of changing the input. The label function encodes the classroom task rule, not a general method for recovering unknown real-world labels.

blocks.title: Optional Python check

blocks.text: If an allowed transformation changes a known target, the transformed example needs a justified new label. Do not invent labels for ambiguous cases. Keep the source ID, transformation and resulting label with every derived image so a teacher can audit what happened.

lesson.title: Split source groups before making variants

blocks.title: Every variant stays with its source group
rows: A original and A row swap
blocks.caption: Assign source groups before generating training variants. A new filename does not make a derived image independent. Evaluation examples follow a fixed declared protocol, not random training augmentation.

blocks.label: A training image has source ID A. Its row-swapped copy is called A2 and placed in validation. No filenames match across splits. Is the split valid for evaluating unseen source images? Describe the repair.

lesson.title: Audit both lineage and duplicate content

blocks.text: Week 23 used deliberately constructed toy images. Its validation E is exactly a row-swapped version of training A, and F is a row-swapped version of C. They had different pixel arrays, but the transformation relation means they are a weak independence test for an experiment that trains on row-swapped variants. If those variants are added, they become exact training-validation duplicates. Preserve the original narrow claim and design a new grouped split for the augmentation experiment.

Source groups should match the evaluation question. If the goal is generalisation to new objects or people, several photographs of the same object or person may need one group even when they have different original file IDs. A lineage audit catches recorded relationships; an exact-pixel audit catches duplicates with inconsistent IDs. Neither audit alone proves that all dependence has been removed.

When a leak is discovered after validation has influenced choices, repair the split and rerun training and selection. Do not merely rename or remove the overlapping files and keep claiming the old score evaluates the repaired experiment. Final data that influenced decisions is no longer reserved.

lesson.title: Count sources and control the comparison

blocks.text: Suppose 12 training source images each produce an original plus two variants. That creates 36 records but still only 12 source groups. Keep validation and final groups separate. Report source counts as well as record counts; repeated variants are correlated observations, not new independent subjects.

blocks.label: An augmented run uses 36 records for five epochs while a baseline uses 12 records for five epochs. Both use one-example batches. Are their update budgets matched? Propose a controlled comparison and explain what 36 records does not establish.

blocks.text: With one-example batches the runs use 180 and 60 updates. A declared comparison could give both 180 updates, cycle the baseline data and record the exposure policy. Keep starting parameters, architecture and evaluation cases matched where possible. Select augmentation settings using validation evidence and report the limits of the chosen budget. Next week moves from images to sequence representations.

workbook.title: Check the label after a transformation
workbook.prompt: For rows [0, 1], [0, 1], compute d and class before and after swapping rows and after swapping columns.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Original d = -2 and class 0. Row swapping leaves d = -2 and class 0. Column swapping gives rows [1, 0], [1, 0], d = 2 and class 1.

workbook.title: Keep the equality boundary
workbook.prompt: For rows [1, 0], [0, 1], compute d and class before and after a column swap. Why is always replacing a label by 1 minus the label incorrect?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Both differences are 0 and both labels are class 0. Complementing class 0 would give class 1, which is wrong for ties.

workbook.title: Audit related records
workbook.prompt: Training contains P original and Q original. Validation contains P crop and R original. Final test contains S original. P crop is derived from P original. Identify the overlap and explain what must be rerun if this validation set already selected a model.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Source P crosses training and validation. Keep all P records in one split and choose distinct evaluation groups. Rerun training and model selection on the corrected plan; the old validation score does not describe the repaired experiment.

workbook.title: Design a grouped split independently
workbook.prompt: Six fictional source groups J, K, L, M, N and O each have one original and three derived records. Assign J, K and L to training, M to validation and N, O to final test. Keep all four records per training group but only originals for evaluation. Give source and retained-record counts per split, total retained records and excluded derived records.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Training: 3 groups and 12 records. Validation: 1 group and 1 record. Final test: 2 groups and 2 records. Total retained records are 15. Nine derived evaluation records are excluded. No group crosses splits; the small group counts still limit evaluation evidence.

workbook.title: Match a training budget
workbook.prompt: Eight source images each have an original plus two variants. Compare four epochs of these 24 records with four epochs of the eight originals, using one-example batches. Give both update counts and one way to match budgets without using final outcomes.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Augmented run uses 96 updates; original-only run uses 32. Predeclare 96 updates for both, equivalent to 12 passes over the originals for the baseline. Record repetition and augmentation policies, use validation for choices and keep final evaluation reserved.

teacher.background: Use two 45-minute sessions. This chapter explicitly revisits Week 23: different pixel arrays do not guarantee independent augmentation evaluation. Keep its original toy-domain claim narrow and use a new grouped plan for the new experiment. Use fictional source IDs rather than student photos. No new training framework is needed.

ai-4/25.title: Sequence representations
goals: Encode an ordered sequence with an explicit vocabulary
Use padding and a mask without inventing real events
Identify information lost by counts unknown symbols and truncation

prerequisite.prompt: Why can two different image regions have the same pooled maximum?
prerequisite.answer: Pooling discards detail. A maximum can preserve the largest value while losing its location and the other values; identical summaries do not imply identical inputs.

vocabulary: An ordered list of elements in which positions can matter
A numerical identifier assigned to a symbol by a vocabulary
Placeholder positions added to make stored sequences the same length
A list marking which stored positions are real inputs and which are placeholders

blocks.text: Use fictional robot event logs whose symbols are GO, TURN and STOP. The task asks whether the final real event is STOP. This is a representation exercise, not a claim that an event log proves a robot is safe. GO then STOP and STOP then GO contain the same symbols but have different final events.

headers: Counts in GO TURN STOP order

blocks.text: A count vector discards order, so no deterministic rule using only the first two count vectors can distinguish their answers. A sequence of IDs preserves order if we retain each position. Declare the vocabulary: PAD = 0, UNK = 1, GO = 2, TURN = 3 and STOP = 4. PAD is reserved for added storage positions; UNK represents a real but unrecognised symbol.

IDs are names, not measured amounts. STOP having ID 4 does not make it twice as much as GO with ID 2. Changing the vocabulary requires changing every consumer consistently. Do not interpret numerical distance between IDs as semantic similarity.

Store each log in four positions, padding on the right. A mask value 1 marks a real position and 0 marks padding. The encoder rejects empty logs, logs longer than four, and literal reserved markers. Other unrecognised symbols become UNK and still receive mask 1.

blocks.title: Optional Python check

blocks.text: The code assumes a list of symbol strings and uses exact spelling. It does not fit a vocabulary from data. If a future project fits vocabulary choices or frequency cutoffs, derive those choices from training data and apply the saved encoding consistently to validation and final cases.

lesson.title: Read the mask before the final position

blocks.title: A padded log still has two real events
blocks.caption: The final stored slot is padding. For this right-padded contiguous mask, the real length is the mask sum, and the final real event is at length minus one. A different masking layout would need a different indexing rule.

blocks.label: Encode TURN STOP, give its mask and real length, then identify the final real position and its ID. Why would reading stored position 3 give the wrong event?

lesson.title: Use masks in the actual computation

blocks.text: A mask must affect a calculation to protect it from padding. Suppose real sensor values are [2, 4], stored as [2, 4, 0, 0] with mask [1, 1, 0, 0]. The masked mean is (2 + 4) / 2 = 3. Averaging all four slots gives 1.5. Unlike arbitrary token IDs, these sensor values are measurements for which a mean is meaningful.

Measured zero must remain real: values [0, 4, 0, 0] with mask [1, 1, 0, 0] have mean 2. Removing every zero would incorrectly give 4. The mask distinguishes a measured zero from a storage placeholder. An all-zero mask has no real values; reject it or follow an explicitly defined empty-input policy instead of dividing by zero.

Storing ordered IDs makes order available but does not guarantee a later model uses it. A computation that sums token counts or averages position-independent vectors can lose order again. Trace what the whole procedure reads, not just what the input format could preserve.

WAIT STOP and PAUSE STOP both become [1, 4, 0, 0] with the same mask. UNK retains a real position but loses the identity of the unrecognised symbol. The final-event task can still answer Yes for both because the last real ID is STOP. A final real UNK would require an unknown result or another documented policy when the intended event cannot be determined.

blocks.label: A log GO TURN GO TURN STOP is cut to its first four events before encoding. What happens to the final-event answer? Explain why the lesson encoder rejects the original log instead of silently truncating it.

blocks.text: The full log ends in STOP, while the retained prefix ends in TURN. Truncation changes the evidence needed for this task. Save the original length and any truncation policy in a real experiment, and test the consequences. Next week introduces embeddings while preserving the distinction between identifiers and learned vectors.

workbook.title: Encode and recover the final event
workbook.prompt: Encode GO TURN STOP using the lesson vocabulary and four positions. Give its mask, real length and final real event.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: IDs are [2, 3, 4, 0], mask [1, 1, 1, 0], real length 3 and final real event STOP at position 2.

workbook.title: Expose an order collision
workbook.prompt: Give two logs made of exactly GO, TURN and STOP once each that have equal count vectors but different answers to whether the final event is STOP.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: For example GO TURN STOP and STOP TURN GO both have count vector [1, 1, 1]. The first answer is Yes and the second No. Counts alone cannot distinguish them.

workbook.title: Separate unknown from padding
workbook.prompt: Encode WAIT GO. Which positions are real? Compare it with PAUSE GO, and state what information the encoding loses.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Both encode as [1, 2, 0, 0] with mask [1, 1, 0, 0]. Positions 0 and 1 are real. UNK at position 0 loses whether the symbol was WAIT or PAUSE; padding is only at positions 2 and 3.

workbook.title: Apply a fresh schema independently
workbook.prompt: Use PAD = 0, UNK = 1, OPEN = 2, CLOSE = 3, CHECK = 4 and five stored positions. Encode OPEN CHECK CLOSE and give its mask and final real position. Separately, sensor values [0, 6, 3, 0, 0] have that same mask. Calculate their masked mean and the incorrect mean over all five slots.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: IDs [2, 4, 3, 0, 0], mask [1, 1, 1, 0, 0]; final real position 2 contains CLOSE. Masked sensor mean is (0 + 6 + 3) / 3 = 3. Unmasked mean is 9 / 5 = 1.8. The measured zero must count in the denominator.

workbook.title: Audit length and empty input
workbook.prompt: The encoder receives five events ending in STOP, then an empty log. What should it do under the lesson contract? Why should a program not simply crop the first and assume a final event for the second?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: It rejects both: one exceeds four real events and the other has none. Cropping can remove the final event and change the task answer. An empty log has no final real position; the program needs an explicit policy rather than an invented event.

teacher.background: Use two 45-minute sessions. Arrange event cards physically before using IDs. Keep token identifiers separate from the sensor measurements used for meaningful mean calculations. The encoder is a fixed classroom schema, not a learned language model. All indexing is zero-based and all masks in the examples are contiguous right-padding masks.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook; paper and pencil
Calculator and optional local Python 3 editor; no packages or AI accounts needed
Use the fictional examples supplied; prepare the fresh retry before class
sessions: Retrieve representation collisions and compare GO STOP with STOP GO.
Declare the vocabulary and task, then complete W1 and W2.
Trace the encoder, including a real unknown event and its mask.
Use W3 to distinguish lost unknown identity from artificial padding.
Complete the guided final-position calculation and compare stored versus real length.
Calculate masked sensor means, including a measured zero, and explain the empty-mask boundary.
Collect W4 independently, checking the new vocabulary and five-position layout.
Use W5 and the exit response to audit truncation, then administer the fresh retry.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided: TURN STOP becomes IDs [3, 4, 0, 0] and mask [1, 1, 0, 0]. Length is 2, so final real position is 1 with ID 4, STOP. Position 3 is PAD. Exit: the full five-event log answers Yes, but its first four events end in TURN and answer No. Rejection makes the unsupported length visible and avoids silently changing the question.
misconceptions: Larger token IDs mean more of a concept
IDs identify symbols; their arithmetic sizes have no declared semantic meaning.
Zero always means missing data
A measured zero can be real; the mask determines which positions contribute.
A mask automatically fixes every model computation
The relevant operation must actually use the mask, and later aggregation can still discard order.
teacher.assessment: W4 requires IDs [2, 4, 3, 0, 0], mask [1, 1, 1, 0, 0], final index 2, masked mean 3 and unmasked mean 1.8. Fresh retry: use the same five-position vocabulary for CHECK OPEN. IDs are [4, 2, 0, 0, 0], mask [1, 1, 0, 0, 0], final index 1 is OPEN. Sensor values [8, 0, 0, 0, 0] with that mask have mean 4, not 8 or 1.6.
teacher.support: Provide a ledger with position, original symbol, ID and mask. Use separate coloured or labelled cards for real unknowns and placeholders without relying on colour alone. Extension: enumerate all logs of length one through four over GO, TURN and STOP, verify encode-and-decode recovery, and find count-vector collisions with different final-event answers.
teacher.next: Week 26 explores embeddings and neighbourhoods, including why a vector representation is different from an arbitrary token ID.

ai-4/26.title: Embeddings and neighbourhoods
goals: Look up a vector using a token ID and preserve sequence shape
Calculate nearest neighbours with an explicit distance and tie rule
Distinguish constructed vectors from learned features and limit similarity claims

prerequisite.prompt: Why should numerical differences between token IDs not be treated as differences in meaning?
prerequisite.answer: IDs are assigned identifiers. Their numerical order and spacing have no declared semantic meaning; a consistent relabelling can change those differences without changing the symbols.

vocabulary: A table assigning a fixed-length numerical vector to each token ID
The number of components in each embedding vector
Nearby candidates under a stated representation and distance rule
The sum of squared component differences between two vectors

lesson.title: Use an ID to select a vector

blocks.text: Continue the fictional robot vocabulary and add WAIT as ID 5. Use the table below, chosen by the lesson author for arithmetic practice. These coordinates are not measured robot properties and were not learned from data. Each token ID selects one row; the resulting two-component vector is its embedding in this example.

The table shape is 6 by 2: six vocabulary entries and embedding dimension 2. The ID sequence [2, 4, 0, 0] becomes [[2, 0], [0, 2], [0, 0], [0, 0]], with shape 4 by 2. Its mask remains [1, 1, 0, 0]. The vector dimension is not the sequence length or vocabulary size.

A zero PAD vector does not remove the need for masking. Averaging all four vectors above gives [0.5, 0.5]; averaging only the two real vectors gives [1, 1]. UNK is a real position when it replaces an unknown symbol, so its vector is not automatically excluded.

Use squared Euclidean distance: square each component difference and add. From GO [2, 0] to TURN [1, 1], the distance is (2 - 1) squared + (0 - 1) squared = 2. To STOP it is 8; to WAIT it is 5. TURN is therefore the nearest of those three under this table and metric.

blocks.title: Optional Python check

blocks.text: The candidate set excludes PAD, UNK and the query token itself. Otherwise a query would normally retrieve itself at distance zero. This code assumes finite numeric components and uses exact ties, appropriate for these integer examples. Floating-point comparisons in other experiments need a declared precision policy.

blocks.title: One query can have two closest candidates
blocks.caption: The nearest set is GO and TURN. Alphabetical display order does not break the mathematical tie or make one candidate more similar.

blocks.label: Using STOP [0, 2] as the query, calculate distances to GO, TURN and WAIT. Exclude STOP itself and both reserved entries. Which candidate is nearest?

blocks.text: An embedding table can be trainable: an optimisation procedure adjusts its entries to reduce a declared objective. To isolate one update, let the GO row e start at [2, 0] and use the classroom loss J(e) = (e1 - 0) squared + (e2 - 2) squared. The target vector [0, 2] is chosen for this arithmetic demonstration, not discovered evidence about the word GO.

The gradient at the start is [4, -4]. With learning rate 0.25, subtract the step to obtain e = [1, 1]. Loss decreases from 8 to 2. Keep every other table row frozen in this isolated example. GO now has the same vector as TURN, so a downstream rule receiving only this vector cannot distinguish those two tokens.

This update proves only that the declared objective decreased. It does not prove that the new neighbourhood reflects useful meaning. Learned neighbourhoods depend on the training data, objective and model. A nearby token need not be a safe substitute, have the same label, or be interchangeable in a sentence or command.

In the original table, the masked average for GO STOP is [1, 1], and STOP GO has the same average. It also equals the single TURN vector. Averaging discarded order and can collide across different sequence lengths unless additional information is retained. Keeping the sequence of vectors makes order available; a later model must still use it.

blocks.label: A teammate says TURN must mean the same as GO because it is the closest candidate, and says a lower embedding-training loss proves this. Explain what the calculations establish and what evidence is missing.

blocks.text: Save the vocabulary-to-row mapping, table version, mask convention, distance rule and candidate policy with the model. Compare embedding choices using training and validation discipline, and keep final evaluation reserved. Next week examines how normalisation and similarity measures can change neighbour rankings.

workbook.title: Trace the lookup shape
workbook.prompt: Using the original table, embed TURN WAIT STOP with one right-padding slot. Give the vector sequence, mask and shape.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Vectors are [[1, 1], [0, 1], [0, 2], [0, 0]], mask [1, 1, 1, 0] and shape 4 by 2.

workbook.title: Calculate distances and a tie
workbook.prompt: For query [1, 0], compute squared distances to GO, TURN, STOP and WAIT in the original table. Return all nearest candidates.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Distances are 1, 1, 5 and 2 respectively. The nearest set is GO and TURN; ordering their names does not remove the tie.

workbook.title: Trace a trainable row
workbook.prompt: For the isolated GO-row update, give the gradient, updated vector, starting loss and new loss. Which other token now shares the vector?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Gradient [4, -4], updated vector [1, 1], loss 8 before and 2 after. TURN already has [1, 1]. This collision does not establish equivalent meaning.

workbook.title: Find a neighbourhood independently
workbook.prompt: A separate table contains A [0, 0], B [2, 0] and C [1, 2]. For query [1, 0], give all squared distances and every nearest candidate. Then calculate the mean of A and B and compare it with the query. Can that mean identify which ordered pair produced it?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Distances to A, B and C are 1, 1 and 4. A and B tie. Their mean is [1, 0], equal to the query. Reversing A B to B A gives the same mean, so the mean alone cannot identify the order.

workbook.title: Keep the lookup consistent
workbook.prompt: A developer swaps the IDs of GO and STOP but leaves the embedding rows unchanged. What goes wrong, and what must be saved or changed together?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Each token now selects the other token’s old row, changing the encoded input. Save and update the vocabulary-to-row mapping and table together, along with version and downstream model. ID relabelling is harmless only when every lookup and consumer stays consistent.

teacher.background: Use two 45-minute sessions. Begin with the difference between an identifier and its looked-up vector. The original table is authored, not learned; the separate one-row update demonstrates optimisation under a stated artificial objective. Do not attach invented semantic labels to the two coordinate axes. Keep original and updated table versions separate.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook; paper and pencil
Calculator and optional local Python 3 editor; no packages or AI accounts needed
Use the fictional examples supplied; prepare the fresh retry before class
sessions: Retrieve arbitrary IDs and label vocabulary size, sequence length and vector dimension.
Trace table lookups and masks, then complete W1.
Compute GO distances by hand and run or trace the nearest-neighbour code.
Use W2 and the visual to preserve ties under an explicit candidate policy.
Complete the guided STOP query before changing any table row.
Trace the isolated learning update and complete W3, noting the resulting collision.
Collect W4 independently, requiring distances, the full nearest set and an order-loss explanation.
Use W5 and the exit response to audit interpretation and version consistency, then administer the fresh retry.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided: STOP distances to GO, TURN and WAIT are 8, 2 and 1, so WAIT is nearest. Exit: the original table and squared Euclidean rule place TURN nearest to GO among the stated candidates. That is not proof of equivalent meaning or substitutability. A lower artificial training objective only supports improvement on that objective; useful task behaviour requires appropriate independent evaluation and error analysis.
misconceptions: Token ID differences define embedding distances
The ID selects a row; distances are computed between row vectors.
