Nearest always means interchangeable
Closeness depends on representation, metric and candidates, and need not preserve task labels or meaning.
A learned embedding cannot lose identity
Two rows can coincide, and sequence aggregation can create additional collisions.
teacher.assessment: W4 requires distances 1, 1, 4, both A and B, mean [1, 0] and a reversed-order collision. Fresh retry: query [0, 1], candidates D [0, 0], E [0, 2], F [3, 1]. Distances are 1, 1, 9; D and E tie. Their mean is [0, 1], and swapping their order leaves it unchanged.
teacher.support: Provide separate columns for token, ID and vector. Use a distance ledger with two differences, two squares and a sum; allow calculators. Extension: consistently permute all table row IDs and show that token-level neighbour results stay unchanged, then deliberately omit the table permutation to expose the mismatch.
teacher.next: Week 27 explores similarity and normalisation, including changes in neighbour ranking.

ai-4/27.title: Similarity and normalisation
goals: Calculate vector length and normalise a nonzero vector
Compare squared distance with cosine similarity and explain a changed ranking
Handle zero vectors explicitly and justify what information a comparison keeps

prerequisite.prompt: For query [3, 4] and candidate [3, 0], calculate squared Euclidean distance. Does a smaller distance prove equivalent meaning?
prerequisite.answer: The squared distance is (3 - 3) squared + (4 - 0) squared = 16. It describes closeness under this representation and rule; it does not prove equivalent meaning.

vocabulary: The square root of the sum of squared components, also called the L2 norm
Dividing every component of a nonzero vector by its length
The dot product of two nonzero vectors divided by the product of their lengths

blocks.text: Last week, a neighbourhood depended on a chosen distance rule. This week, compare the same fictional vectors in two ways. Squared distance rewards nearby coordinates. Cosine similarity compares direction and ignores positive changes in length. Neither rule is automatically right for every task.

For Q, length = square root of (3 squared + 4 squared) = square root of 25 = 5. Divide both components by 5 to get its unit vector [0.6, 0.8]. Its length is one because 0.6 squared + 0.8 squared = 1. A becomes the same unit vector. C becomes [-0.6, -0.8], pointing in the opposite direction.

These supplied coordinates are for arithmetic practice. They are not learned language embeddings. Normalising each row keeps its direction but removes its original length unless that length is saved separately.

Multiply matching components and add to obtain the dot product. Cosine similarity equals dot(Q, candidate) divided by (length(Q) times length(candidate)). Higher cosine means a closer direction. For A, the dot product is 3 times 6 + 4 times 8 = 50, so cosine = 50 / (5 times 10) = 1. For B it is 9 / 15 = 0.6; for C it is -25 / 25 = -1.

blocks.title: Optional Python check

blocks.text: Trace before running: A gives 1, B gives 0.6 and C gives -1. This classroom code assumes finite, moderate numeric inputs. It rejects empty, unequal-length and zero vectors. Keep full precision for decisions; rounding here is only for display. Cosine lies between -1 and 1 in exact arithmetic and is not a probability.

blocks.title: Compare the same candidates using two rules
blocks.caption: For Q [3, 4], raw squared distance selects B by minimising the score. Cosine selects A by maximising the score. The candidates stayed the same; the comparison rule changed.

blocks.text: After normalising both Q and every candidate, squared distances to A, B and C are 0, 0.8 and 4. For unit vectors, squared distance = 2 - 2 times cosine. Thus the smallest normalised distance and largest cosine produce the same ranking, including ties, in exact arithmetic.

blocks.label: Add candidate D [0, 5]. Calculate its raw squared distance and cosine from Q [3, 4]. Compare D with A under each rule.

blocks.text: Suppose [3, 4] records counts of two event types, while [6, 8] records twice as many of each. Both have the same proportions and direction, but totals are 7 and 14. Normalisation makes their vectors identical. That may suit a question about proportions, but it removes information needed to compare total activity. For learned embeddings, the usefulness of length must be tested for the task.

The zero vector [0, 0] has no direction, so its cosine is undefined. Do not silently assign zero similarity: zero cosine already means perpendicular nonzero vectors. This lesson rejects a zero query and excludes zero candidates with an explicit report. If no valid candidates remain, return no comparison. PAD entries stay excluded by the mask; a real zero input needs its own policy.

Positive scaling preserves cosine: Q and 2 times Q have the same direction. Negative scaling reverses direction; Q and -Q have cosine -1. Candidate labels, self-exclusion and a stated floating-point tie tolerance are still required when retrieving neighbours.

L2 normalisation divides each individual vector by its own length; it does not estimate a mean or scale from a dataset. Feature standardisation is a different operation and must fit its statistics on training data only. Choose between raw distance and cosine using the task, training and validation evidence. Do not repeatedly change the rule after seeing final evaluation results.

blocks.label: A teammate says a cosine of 1 proves two records mean the same thing, and normalisation always improves a model. Use A and Q to challenge both claims. What must be checked before adopting the rule?

blocks.text: Record the representation version, comparison rule, normalisation, zero-vector handling, candidate set and tie tolerance. Preserve a baseline and evaluate on the same reserved examples. Next week, transfer learning asks when a representation learned for one task can help another.

workbook.title: Trace the unit vectors
workbook.prompt: For Q [3, 4], A [6, 8] and C [-3, -4], give each length and unit vector. Explain one distinction that normalisation removes and one that it preserves.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Lengths are 5, 10 and 5. Unit vectors are [0.6, 0.8], [0.6, 0.8] and [-0.6, -0.8]. The length difference between Q and A disappears; the opposite direction of C is preserved.

workbook.title: Compare the rankings
workbook.prompt: For query Q, write the raw squared distances and cosines to A, B and C from the lesson. Name the winner under each rule. Calculate squared distances after normalising both sides and check the relationship to cosine.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Raw squared distances are 25, 16, 100, so B wins. Cosines are 1, 0.6, -1, so A wins. Unit-vector squared distances are 0, 0.8, 4, matching 2 - 2 times each cosine and selecting A.

workbook.title: Handle a vector without direction
workbook.prompt: A candidate set contains Z [0, 0] and B [3, 0]. With nonzero query Q, what happens under this lesson’s zero-vector policy? What if Q is zero, or Z is the only candidate? Explain why replacing an undefined cosine with zero is misleading.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Exclude Z and report it; compare B normally. Reject a zero query. If only Z exists, report no comparison. Zero cosine represents perpendicular nonzero directions, whereas the zero vector has no direction.

workbook.title: Compare a new case independently
workbook.prompt: Use query [5, 0] and candidates P [10, 0], R [4, 3] and S [0, 5]. Calculate all raw squared distances and cosines, name each winner, and give squared distances after normalising both query and candidates. Explain the changed ranking.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Raw squared distances to P, R and S are 25, 10, 50, selecting R. Cosines are 1, 0.8, 0, selecting P. Normalised squared distances are 0, 0.4, 2. P shares the query direction despite its greater length; raw distance also reflects that length difference.

workbook.title: Audit a proposed improvement
workbook.prompt: For event-count vectors [3, 4] and [6, 8], what useful information can normalisation remove? A team chooses cosine because it improves results on the final evaluation set, then calls that same set independent evidence. Explain how to repair the evaluation plan.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Normalisation removes magnitude: totals 7 and 14 become indistinguishable in the unit vectors. Choose the rule using task needs and training/validation evidence, preserving a baseline. A final set used to choose the rule is no longer independent final evidence; reserve new untouched evaluation data or explicitly report the limitation.

teacher.background: Use two 45-minute sessions. Supply calculators and connect vector length to the right-triangle calculation 3 squared plus 4 squared equals 5 squared. Students should justify a rule by the information it retains. The supplied vectors are constructed examples; no semantic or accuracy claim is established by their geometry.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook; paper and pencil
Calculator and optional local Python 3 editor; no packages or AI accounts needed
Use the fictional examples supplied; prepare the fresh retry before class
sessions: Retrieve squared distance and explain why a geometric score alone does not establish meaning.
Compute lengths and unit vectors. Complete W1 with both positive and opposite directions.
Trace the cosine formula and optional code, checking which score is maximised.
Use the diagram and W2 to contrast raw and normalised distance rankings.
Complete the guided D comparison, retaining the same query and candidate A.
Discuss event counts and zero vectors. Complete W3 and require an explicit no-comparison outcome.
Collect W4 independently, including raw scores, cosines, normalised distances and an explanation.
Complete W5 and the exit response. Give feedback before administering the fresh retry.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided: D has squared distance 9 + 1 = 10 and cosine 20 / 25 = 0.8. Raw distance prefers D over A (10 versus 25); cosine prefers A (1 versus 0.8). Exit: Q and A share direction but have different lengths and may represent different totals. Cosine 1 proves aligned nonzero vectors, not equivalent meaning. Check the task, retained information, zero and tie policies, and validation performance against a baseline; reserve final evaluation.
misconceptions: Cosine is a probability
Its possible negative values and geometric definition show that it is not a calibrated probability.
Normalisation keeps all information
Positive multiples collapse to the same unit vector; preserve length separately if the task needs it.
Any scaling leaves cosine unchanged
Positive scaling preserves direction. Multiplying only one vector by a negative number reverses the cosine sign; zero scaling makes it undefined.
teacher.assessment: W4 requires raw scores 25, 10, 50; cosines 1, 0.8, 0; normalised distances 0, 0.4, 2; and winners R then P. Fresh retry: query [0, 5], candidates D [0, 10], E [3, 4], F [5, 0]. Raw squared distances are 25, 10, 50; cosines 1, 0.8, 0; unit distances 0, 0.4, 2. Raw distance selects E; cosine selects D. Ask students to explain why a zero query is rejected.
teacher.support: Provide a ledger for squared components, length, unit components and score. Allow a calculator and separate lower-is-better distance from higher-is-better similarity. Extension: expand the squared distance between two unit vectors to derive 2 - 2 times their dot product. For floating-point retrieval, declare a tolerance and retain all scores within it of the best; show that rounding first can create false ties.
teacher.next: Week 28 examines transfer learning, comparing a reused representation with a baseline and testing what can transfer to a new task.

ai-4/28.title: Transfer learning
goals: Trace a reused feature extractor and a newly fitted output head
Fit a small target-task head using training data and compare a baseline
Identify when a frozen representation cannot support a new task

prerequisite.prompt: If two different records become the same feature vector, can a deterministic output head receiving only that vector distinguish them?
prerequisite.answer: No. Identical inputs to a fixed deterministic head produce identical outputs. Information lost by the representation cannot be recovered from that representation alone.

vocabulary: Reusing knowledge learned on a source task or dataset to help a target task
The part of a model that maps an input to a representation
The part that maps a representation to the current task’s output
Training some or all previously learned parameters on the target task

lesson.title: Reuse a representation for a new task

blocks.text: A source model may learn useful features before we have many labels for a new target task. Transfer learning reuses those learned features or parameters. One approach freezes the feature extractor and fits a new output head. Fine tuning instead updates some or all of the reused parameters, usually together with the head.

Use a transparent stand-in for a source-trained extractor: f(x) = ReLU(x1 + x2), with supplied weights [1, 1] and bias 0. ReLU keeps a positive value and replaces a negative value with zero. Here x1 and x2 are nonnegative fictional event counts, so f(x) is their sum. We did not train this extractor on a source dataset; this exercise demonstrates the mechanics of reuse, not measured transfer benefits.

rows: Fit the threshold on target training data

blocks.text: The target is a high-activity label. The extractor returns a single number h, not a class label or probability. A new head converts h into the target prediction.

lesson.title: Fit the target head on training data

blocks.text: Use target training records T1 [1, 1] with label 0, T2 [1, 3] with label 0, T3 [4, 2] with label 1 and T4 [5, 3] with label 1. Their extracted values are 2, 4, 6 and 8. Fit the head by trying thresholds 3, 5 and 7 and counting training mistakes. Fitting can use a small search; it need not use gradients.

blocks.title: Optional Python check

blocks.text: The tie rule prefers the smaller threshold if training mistake counts match; there is no tie here. The extractor remains unchanged. The code assumes finite numeric counts and valid binary labels. A constant baseline predicts the most frequent training label; with two of each, our declared tie rule chooses 0.

lesson.title: Compare on held out target examples

blocks.title: Freeze the fitted head before validation
blocks.caption: The fitted head is correct on 2 of 2 validation records; the constant-0 baseline is correct on 1 of 2. This tiny constructed comparison is not evidence of general transfer performance.

blocks.text: Use the same validation records for both methods. These records were not used to fit the threshold. If validation guides later choices, reserve separate untouched final evaluation data. We have not compared with a full model trained from scratch or measured training time, so this result cannot establish either advantage.

blocks.label: A new input [2, 3] uses the fitted threshold 5. Give h and the predicted class, including the equality rule. Which parameters changed during fitting?

lesson.title: Find a task that the features cannot solve

blocks.text: Now change the target: predict 1 when the first count is greater than the second, otherwise 0. U [1, 3] has label 0 and V [3, 1] has label 1, but both become h = 4. Every fixed deterministic head receiving only this h must give both the same prediction. At least one of the two will be wrong, regardless of how many extra head parameters we add.

Fine tuning could change the extractor to retain relevant distinctions; it does not guarantee success. To see a possible change, hand-set the weights to [1, -1], keep bias 0 and use threshold 1. U then gives ReLU(-2) = 0 and predicts 0; V gives ReLU(2) = 2 and predicts 1. This hand-chosen repair is not a trained result or an independent evaluation.

Keeping the original input alongside h is another possible representation change. Any such change needs a new training and evaluation plan. Normalising the inputs also changes the pipeline; last week showed why that can remove useful magnitude information.

For a real source-trained model, record the checkpoint version, source task and data provenance, permitted use, input order and preprocessing, frozen and trainable parts, target splits, baseline and resource budget. Check for source-data overlap with target evaluation records; a different filename is not proof of independence. If source history is unknown, report that limitation.

blocks.label: A team says its reused extractor must outperform training from scratch because it scored 2 of 2 here. Give two reasons this conclusion is unsupported and propose a fair next comparison.

blocks.text: Evaluate methods on the same target examples under a declared training budget, with choices made before final evaluation. Record errors as well as totals. Next week examines uncertainty and failure analysis, including confident predictions that can still be wrong.

workbook.title: Trace the reused pipeline
workbook.prompt: For input [4, 2], compute h using the original extractor and the class at threshold 5. Identify the frozen weights and bias, the fitted quantity, and why h is not a probability.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: The extractor gives h = 6 and the head predicts 1. Weights [1, 1] and bias 0 stay frozen; only the threshold is fitted. h is a nonnegative sum of counts, with no probability mapping or calibration.

workbook.title: Fit and compare
workbook.prompt: For the four target training records, give the number of mistakes at thresholds 3, 5 and 7 and choose the fitted threshold. Then score that head and the declared constant baseline on V1 and V2. Explain which data fitted the head.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Training mistake counts are 1, 0 and 1, selecting threshold 5. Validation predictions are 0 and 1, so the head scores 2 of 2. The constant-0 baseline scores 1 of 2. Only T1 through T4 fit the head; validation evaluates the fitted choice.

workbook.title: Diagnose a lost distinction
workbook.prompt: For the first-count-greater target, explain why the original extractor cannot distinguish U [1, 3] from V [3, 1]. Trace the hand-chosen [1, -1] extractor and threshold 1. Does this show that fine tuning has been trained and independently validated?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Both original features are 4, so a deterministic head must give the same answer despite labels 0 and 1. The changed features are 0 and 2, giving predictions 0 and 1. This is a hand-chosen change on the examples being inspected, not training or independent validation.

workbook.title: Fit a new head independently
workbook.prompt: A separate frozen extractor is h = 2*x1 + x2. Training inputs [1, 0], [1, 2], [2, 1], [3, 1] have labels 0, 0, 1, 1. Compare thresholds 2, 4 and 6 using prediction 1 when h >= threshold; choose the fewest mistakes, breaking ties toward the smaller threshold. Score it on validation [2, 0] with label 1 and [0, 2] with label 0. Compare with the training-majority baseline, whose tie rule chooses 0.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Training features are 2, 4, 5 and 7. Mistakes at thresholds 2, 4 and 6 are 2, 1 and 1, so the tie rule selects 4. Validation features are 4 and 2, predictions 1 and 0, scoring 2 of 2. The constant-0 baseline scores 1 of 2. Equality at threshold 4 gives class 1.

workbook.title: Plan credible evidence
workbook.prompt: A report omits the source checkpoint and preprocessing, claims faster learning without timing, and repeatedly chooses settings using the final evaluation set. Name the missing records and propose a fair comparison with a model trained from scratch.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Record source version, provenance and permitted use, preprocessing, frozen/trainable parts, splits, baseline and resource budget. Measure time or computation before claiming speed. Use training/validation for choices and new untouched final evaluation after repeated final-set tuning, or report that independent evidence is unavailable. Compare both methods on the same target cases and declared budget.

teacher.background: Use two 45-minute sessions. Keep three claims separate: real transfer reuses previously learned knowledge; this supplied extractor is a transparent stand-in; the reported scores concern tiny constructed target examples. No external model, student account or personal dataset is needed. Require students to mark frozen versus fitted quantities before computing.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook; paper and pencil
Calculator and optional local Python 3 editor; no packages or AI accounts needed
Use the fictional examples supplied; prepare the fresh retry before class
sessions: Retrieve the collision principle: a head cannot reconstruct distinctions absent from its input.
Trace the input, extractor and head. Complete W1 and label frozen weights and fitted threshold.
Count training mistakes for each threshold. Trace the optional code and declared tie rule.
Use the validation visual and W2 to compare with the constant baseline on identical records.
Complete the guided boundary example and check equality at the threshold.
Use W3 to expose the new-task collision. Distinguish a hand-chosen repair from fine tuning.
Collect W4 independently; require the training tie and its declared resolution before validation.
Use W5 and the exit response to audit evidence. Give feedback, then administer the fresh retry.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided: h = 5 and prediction is 1 because equality is included. The threshold was fitted; weights [1, 1] and bias 0 stayed frozen. Exit: two constructed validation cases provide limited evidence, the extractor was supplied rather than source-trained here, and no from-scratch comparison was run. Compare both methods on the same target cases with a declared training budget and untouched final evaluation after all choices.
misconceptions: Frozen means the whole model cannot learn
The extractor stays fixed while the new head is fitted on target training examples.
A larger head can undo any lost information
Identical representations remain indistinguishable to a fixed deterministic head, regardless of its size.
Transfer guarantees better or faster results
The source representation may not suit the target. Accuracy and resource benefits require fair measured comparisons.
teacher.assessment: W4 requires features 2, 4, 5, 7; mistake counts 2, 1, 1; tie-selected threshold 4; and validation scores 2 of 2 versus 1 of 2. Fresh retry: frozen h = x1 + 2*x2; training inputs [0, 1], [2, 1], [1, 2], [1, 3], labels 0, 0, 1, 1. Thresholds 2, 4, 6 again give 2, 1, 1 mistakes, selecting 4. Validation [0, 2] label 1 and [2, 0] label 0 yield features 4 and 2 and both correct; constant 0 gets one correct. Ask which parameter was fitted.
teacher.support: Provide separate input, feature, threshold and prediction boxes. Allow calculators and mark frozen parameters with a lock symbol on the board. Extension: on U and V, consider thresholds at or below 4 and thresholds above 4; show that neither case classifies both correctly. Discuss why source performance does not establish target suitability.
teacher.next: Week 29 studies uncertainty and failure analysis, using specific errors and limitations rather than assuming a confident output is correct.

ai-4/29.title: Uncertainty and failure analysis
goals: Distinguish a predicted class, confidence score and observed correctness
Calculate accuracy and coverage for a review policy
Investigate failure patterns without claiming an untested cause

prerequisite.prompt: Last week a model was correct on two constructed validation examples. Why did that not prove it would work reliably on new examples?
prerequisite.answer: Two constructed cases provide very limited evidence. New inputs can differ, and validation used to choose settings is not untouched final evaluation. Performance needs representative independent testing.

vocabulary: The model’s score for its selected class, which may not match observed reliability
Agreement between predicted probabilities and observed frequencies across many comparable cases
Withholding an automatic prediction and following a declared alternative process
The fraction of all cases on which a system makes an automatic prediction

lesson.title: Read a score without treating it as proof

blocks.text: A model can be confidently wrong. Use these supplied outputs for a fictional image classifier: class 1 means a triangle is present; class 0 means it is absent. The values p1 are probability estimates for class 1, invented for this exercise rather than produced by a trained model. Predict 1 when p1 >= 0.5 and 0 otherwise. The selected-class confidence is max(p1, 1 - p1).

A predicts 1 with confidence 0.95 and is correct. F predicts 0 with confidence 0.90 and is wrong: p1 = 0.10 is not low confidence in the selected class. Reference labels are supplied for this exercise; real investigations must check their quality too.

A score alone cannot establish reliability. Calibration asks whether, across many comparable cases, predictions assigned a probability such as 0.90 are correct about 90 percent of the time. One correct or incorrect case cannot answer that question.

The predictions for A through F are 1, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0. A, C and E are correct, so overall accuracy is 3 / 6 = 50 percent. There are two false positives (B and D), one false negative (F), two true positives and one true negative. Different errors can matter differently; a single accuracy number hides that distinction.

blocks.title: Optional Python check

blocks.text: The function returns overall accuracy, coverage and accuracy among accepted cases. It assumes numeric scores and binary labels. None means no cases were accepted, so accepted-case accuracy is undefined, not zero or perfect. Keep counts with proportions and declare the comparison at the boundary.

blocks.title: Confidence does not remove every error
blocks.caption: The policy accepts confidence at least 0.80. Coverage is 4 / 6 and accepted-case accuracy is 2 / 4. The confident errors B and F remain.

blocks.text: Deferred cases are not automatically repaired. A review workflow needs an assigned reviewer, suitable evidence, a decision record and an outcome check. Report review workload and the final system’s results separately; we have no reviewer outcomes here. Do not erase deferred cases from the report or count them as correct.

blocks.label: Raise the cutoff to 0.95 for the same six cases. Which cases are accepted, what are coverage and accepted-case accuracy, and why does that result not guarantee perfect future predictions?

lesson.title: Turn a failure pattern into a testable question

blocks.text: All three clear images are correct; all three blurred images are wrong in this constructed set. Blur is a candidate explanation, not an established cause: other differences, reference-label errors or preprocessing bugs could be involved. Record case ID, input conditions, model and preprocessing version, score, prediction and checked reference label.

First inspect B, D and F and check input order, resizing and label quality. Then plan new examples that vary blur while keeping the underlying image and label fixed. Keep related versions of the same source image in one data split; compare both versions within the reserved group. Do not repair cases and report scores on those same cases as independent evidence.

Uncertainty can arise from ambiguous inputs, limited training evidence or unfamiliar conditions. A single confidence score does not identify the cause and may stay high on unfamiliar inputs. Collect evidence before selecting a remedy.

lesson.title: Report the limits of a confidence rule

blocks.text: Choose review thresholds and model changes using training and validation evidence, before final evaluation. Report total cases, overall errors, accepted errors, coverage, deferred workload and subgroup results. For tiny groups, give counts and avoid strong claims about future rates. Higher cutoffs do not guarantee higher observed accuracy or safe decisions.

blocks.label: A teammate reports “100 percent accurate” after accepting only A at cutoff 0.95. Rewrite the claim honestly and name the evidence still needed before trusting this policy.

blocks.text: Keep a baseline and record unsuccessful changes too. Next week examines dataset shift: performance can change when the inputs or relationships encountered in use differ from those seen during development.

workbook.title: Separate confidence from correctness
workbook.prompt: For B, E and F, give the predicted class, selected-class confidence and correctness. Explain why p1 = 0.10 does not mean F has low confidence in its predicted class.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: B predicts 1 with confidence 0.90 and is wrong. E predicts 0 with confidence 0.55 and is correct. F predicts 0 with confidence 0.90 and is wrong. F’s low score for class 1 corresponds to a high score for class 0, the class selected.

workbook.title: Count both types of error
workbook.prompt: For all six cases, list false positives and false negatives, count true positives and true negatives, and calculate overall accuracy. Why might a single accuracy hide useful information?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: False positives are B and D; the false negative is F. A and C are the two true positives; E is the one true negative. Accuracy is 3 of 6, or 50 percent. It hides which errors occur and how their consequences differ.

workbook.title: Audit the review policy
workbook.prompt: At cutoff 0.80, list accepted and deferred cases, coverage and accepted-case accuracy. Can you calculate final accuracy after human review from the supplied data? What does the report function return for accepted-case accuracy at cutoff 0.99?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Accepted cases are A, B, C, F; deferred cases are D and E. Coverage is 4 of 6 and accepted accuracy is 2 of 4. No reviewer outcomes are supplied, so final system accuracy is unknown. At 0.99 no case is accepted; accepted accuracy is undefined and the function returns None.

workbook.title: Analyse new outputs independently
workbook.prompt: Four new cases have (p1, reference label): K (0.85, 0), L (0.70, 1), M (0.30, 0), N (0.05, 0). Give predictions and confidences, overall accuracy, and accepted cases at cutoff 0.80. Calculate coverage and accepted-case accuracy. Does this policy improve accuracy on the accepted subset here?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Predictions are 1, 1, 0, 0; confidences are 0.85, 0.70, 0.70, 0.95. L, M and N are correct, so overall accuracy is 3 of 4. K and N are accepted; coverage is 2 of 4 and accepted accuracy is 1 of 2. Accepted accuracy is lower than overall accuracy in this example.

workbook.title: Design a failure investigation
workbook.prompt: All three blurred cases are wrong. A team claims blur caused the errors and plans to put clear images in training and their blurred copies in final evaluation. Identify the unsupported claim and the split problem; propose a better investigation.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Three failures show a pattern, not a proven cause. Related clear and blurred copies across splits can leak source-image information. Check labels and preprocessing, then hold related versions together in reserved source groups and compare controlled blur variants within those groups. Choose changes before new final evaluation and report the small sample limitation.

teacher.background: Use two 45-minute sessions. These are supplied classifier outputs for arithmetic and reasoning, not calibrated probabilities from a trained model. Keep overall accuracy, accepted-case accuracy and coverage visible together. Do not imply that review guarantees correction or that model confidence diagnoses the cause of uncertainty.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook; paper and pencil
Calculator and optional local Python 3 editor; no packages or AI accounts needed
Use the fictional examples supplied; prepare the fresh retry before class
sessions: Retrieve the limits of the two-case validation result from Week 28. Define the triangle-present label.
Trace A and F, then complete W1 with selected-class confidence distinct from p1.
Build the error tally and complete W2. Trace the report function and its three returned quantities.
Use the visual and W3 to retain deferred cases in workload reporting and handle an empty accepted set.
Complete the guided cutoff 0.95 case and critique a perfect-accuracy claim.
Inspect the blur pattern and design a controlled comparison with source-grouped splits.
Collect W4 independently, including denominators and the worse accepted-subset result.
Use W5 and the exit response to evaluate causal and reliability claims. Give feedback, then the fresh retry.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided: only A is accepted. Coverage is 1 of 6; accepted accuracy is 1 of 1. This single constructed success, selected by a rule examined on these data, does not establish future reliability. Exit: report one correct automatic prediction out of one accepted, with five of six deferred and no reviewer outcomes. Require representative untouched evaluation, subgroup and calibration evidence, measured reviewer outcomes and workload, and a comparison with a declared baseline.
misconceptions: A low p1 always means low confidence
For a binary model, p1 = 0.10 selects class 0 with confidence 0.90.
Reviewing uncertain cases fixes all errors
B and F remain confidently wrong; deferred outcomes also need measurement.
A shared condition proves the cause
A small error pattern motivates investigation; label checks, controlled examples and independent evaluation are still needed.
teacher.assessment: W4 requires predictions 1, 1, 0, 0; confidences 0.85, 0.70, 0.70, 0.95; accuracy 3 of 4; accepted K and N, coverage 2 of 4 and accepted accuracy 1 of 2. Fresh retry: (p1, label) values (0.90, 1), (0.65, 0), (0.35, 1), (0.10, 0). Predictions are 1, 1, 0, 0; confidences 0.90, 0.65, 0.65, 0.90. Overall accuracy is 2 of 4. At cutoff 0.80 accept first and fourth: coverage 2 of 4 and accepted accuracy 2 of 2. Require a limitation despite the perfect accepted subset.
teacher.support: Provide separate boxes for p1, predicted class, confidence, reference label and correctness. Use fractions before percentages. Extension: for A, B, C and F, mean confidence is 0.8875 while observed accuracy is 0.5. Discuss why this small grouped discrepancy motivates calibration study but cannot establish a population-wide calibration rate.
teacher.next: Week 30 studies dataset shift, comparing development and new-use conditions without assuming a familiar confidence score implies familiar data.

ai-4/3.title: Bias terms and decision boundaries
goals: Calculate a weighted score with a bias term
Locate and test a two-feature decision boundary
Explain how changing the bias shifts a boundary without training

prerequisite.prompt: For w = [2, -1] and x = [3, 5], what are the contributions and dot product?
prerequisite.answer: The contributions are 6 and -5, giving dot product 1.

vocabulary: An additive parameter applied after a weighted sum
Input locations where the declared classification rule changes class
A weighted sum plus a constant offset
A stated comparison that converts a score into a class

lesson.title: Add an offset to a weighted score

blocks.text: Use the fictional parcel schema [width in cm, height in cm]. Our model computes z = 2 times width - height - 3. The weights are [2, -1]; the bias b is -3. Compute the weighted sum first, then add the bias once. The result is an affine score: a weighted sum plus a constant offset.

Now declare a classification rule: predict class 1 when z is at least 0, and class 0 when z is below 0. Equality belongs to class 1. These are invented categories for arithmetic practice, not a real parcel decision. The weights and bias are supplied, so this is a forward calculation, not training.
A bias is a mathematical parameter. It is not the same use of the word as unfair treatment; numerical offset alone does not establish whether a system is fair.

Set z to zero to locate the boundary: 2 times width - height - 3 = 0, so height = 2 times width - 3. Plot width on the horizontal axis and height on the vertical axis. Boundary points include (2, 1), (3, 3) and (4, 5). Join them with a straight line and label the axes in cm.

At width 3, height 2 gives score 1 and class 1; height 3 gives score 0 and class 1; height 4 gives score -1 and class 0. Under this axis convention class 1 lies on or below the boundary. One point on each side checks that orientation.

blocks.title: Optional Python check

blocks.text: The code assumes valid numerical measurements in the agreed units. Changing >= to > changes the equality case, even though the drawn line remains in the same place.

lesson.title: Track the effect of the bias

blocks.title: Hold the weights fixed while shifting the boundary
blocks.caption: The boundary moves parallel to itself because the weights stay fixed. An increased score does not always change a class: only inputs crossing the declared threshold change.

blocks.label: For [3, 4], compare z and prediction with bias -3 and bias -1. Explain which parameter changed.

lesson.title: Separate a parameter change from evidence

blocks.text: Without a bias, this score would be z = 2 times width - height and its zero line would pass through (0, 0). The offset lets the boundary move away from the origin. In this parcel schema zero dimensions are invalid measurements; the origin is still useful as a point on the extended mathematical graph.

Changing bias from -3 to -1 increases every score by 2, but does not rotate the line. Changing a weight can rotate or otherwise change the boundary. Neither change is automatically an improvement. To compare models, retain labels, a declared metric, the same evaluation records and the separate training, validation and test roles.

The boundary states what this particular formula predicts. It does not establish the true classes of all possible inputs. A point very far from the line need not have a reliable prediction when the model, features or data are inappropriate. The raw score is not calibrated confidence or a physical distance from the line.

blocks.label: A team changes b after seeing final-test mistakes and reports the same cases as an untouched test of the new model. Explain the error and the next step.

blocks.text: Next week, we transform scores with activation functions before discussing layers.

workbook.title: Trace the bias once
workbook.prompt: Use z = 2 times width - height - 3 at [5, 4]. Give the weighted sum, bias, final score and prediction under z >= 0.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Weighted sum 10 - 4 = 6; bias -3; score 3; prediction 1. Add the bias once after summing.

workbook.title: Plot and label the boundary
workbook.prompt: For the worked model, find boundary points at width 2 and width 4. Test [4, 4] and [4, 6] to identify the class on each side.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Boundary points (2, 1) and (4, 5). [4, 4] has z = 1 and class 1; [4, 6] has z = -1 and class 0. With height vertical, class 1 is on or below the line.

workbook.title: Check the equality rule
workbook.prompt: At [3, 3], compare prediction under z >= 0 with prediction under z > 0. Does changing this comparison move the zero line?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Score is zero. The >= rule predicts 1; the > rule predicts 0. The zero line remains height = 2 width - 3, but its assigned class changes.

workbook.title: Analyse a new model independently
workbook.prompt: A new model has w = [-1, 2], b = -2, inputs [u, v] and class 1 when z >= 0. Calculate scores and classes for [2, 1], [2, 2], [2, 3]. Write the boundary as v in terms of u. Then change only b to 0 and recompute [2, 1].
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Scores -2, 0, 2 give classes 0, 1, 1. Boundary -u + 2v - 2 = 0 gives v = u/2 + 1. With b = 0, [2, 1] scores 0 and class 1. The score rose 2 and the boundary moved to v = u/2.

workbook.title: Require evidence of improvement
workbook.prompt: A teammate says that raising b must improve the model because all scores rise. What information is needed before accepting an improvement claim?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Higher scores can fix some missed class-1 cases while creating false alarms. Compare with observed labels on the same valid evaluation set under a declared metric, keeping fitting and model choices separate from final testing.

teacher.background: Use two 45-minute sessions to connect signed arithmetic, linear equations and graph regions. Require the explicit equality policy each time. The classroom formula is hand-selected; it demonstrates prediction and parameter effects, not evidence of successful training.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook; paper and pencil
Calculator and optional local Python 3 editor; no packages or AI accounts needed
Use the fictional examples supplied; prepare the fresh retry before class
sessions: Retrieve the dot product in the prerequisite question and review adding a negative constant.
Trace all three table rows. Students circle the one addition of b and identify the equality case.
Complete W1 and derive height = 2 width - 3. Plot the three boundary points on labelled axes.
Use W2 and the guided bias comparison. Check both sides numerically before shading a class region.
Retrieve the rule z >= 0. Run or trace the optional code and compare it with the plotted points.
Complete W3. Distinguish moving the boundary from changing the class assigned at equality; discuss the extended origin.
Collect W4 independently. Check scores, classes, rearranged equation and the effect of changing only b.
Complete W5 and the exit response. Offer the fresh retry after feedback to assess the same ideas with a new boundary.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided [3, 4]: with b = -3, z = -1 and class 0; with b = -1, z = 1 and class 1. Only b changed. Exit: test labels influenced the new bias, so the reused cases are development evidence for the revision. Preserve the original result and evaluate a frozen revision on fresh independent cases.
misconceptions: Add bias to each contribution
Compute the dot product, then add one b. Adding b twice implements a different formula.
Higher scores mean more correct
Correctness also needs target labels. A shifted boundary can trade one error type for another.
The bias term measures unfairness
This b is an additive parameter. Evaluating unfairness requires context and evidence about outcomes and use.
teacher.assessment: W4 should include all three scores and the equality class, with v = u/2 + 1 before the change. Fresh retry: z = u + v - 5, class 1 if z >= 0. [2, 2], [2, 3], [2, 4] give -1, 0, 1 and classes 0, 1, 1; boundary v = 5 - u. With b changed from -5 to -4, [2, 2] reaches zero and class 1.
teacher.support: Provide graph paper and a partially labelled contribution table. If rearranging equations is difficult, find three zero-score points by substitution first. Extension: multiply all weights and b by positive 2 and explain why scores double while classifications under >= 0 stay the same.
teacher.next: Week 4 compares identity, ReLU and sigmoid transforms of the score.

ai-4/30.title: Dataset shift in neural models
goals: Explain how a changed input mix can change overall accuracy
Calculate group and overall results with the correct denominators
Plan a shift investigation while preserving independent evaluation

prerequisite.prompt: Can a high confidence score establish that a new input resembles the development data or that its prediction is correct?
prerequisite.answer: No. Confidence is a model output, not a guarantee of familiarity or correctness. Check input conditions and independently verified outcomes rather than treating confidence as proof.

vocabulary: A change in the distribution of inputs, labels or their relationship between settings
A declared subset of examples sharing a relevant condition
The proportions of examples belonging to different groups
Repeatedly checking recorded inputs, outputs and available outcomes against a reference

lesson.title: Keep the model fixed while the setting changes

blocks.text: A neural image classifier developed using mostly clear pictures may later receive mostly dim pictures. Its learned weights can stay unchanged while its overall results change. Dataset shift concerns changes in the data encountered, including inputs, label frequencies or the relationship between inputs and labels. A shift does not always reduce accuracy, and an accuracy change alone does not identify its cause.

Use the fictional audit below. Clear and dim are disjoint groups defined before the audit, and every case belongs to exactly one group. The same model checkpoint, preprocessing and prediction threshold are used throughout. Counts are constructed teaching data, not results from a deployed model. Both cohorts have checked reference labels.

Clear accuracy is 72 / 80 = 90 percent in development and 18 / 20 = 90 percent in new use. Dim accuracy is 10 / 20 = 50 percent and 40 / 80 = 50 percent. The observed group rates are unchanged, but the group proportions are different.

lesson.title: Combine counts before computing a rate

blocks.text: Development accuracy is (72 + 10) / (80 + 20) = 82 percent. New-use accuracy is (18 + 40) / (20 + 80) = 58 percent. The drop is 24 percentage points. Taking the unweighted mean of 90 and 50 gives 70 percent, which is not either cohort’s overall accuracy because neither cohort has equal group sizes.

blocks.title: Optional Python check
blocks.text:
def accuracy(groups):
    if not groups:
        raise ValueError("Need at least one group")
    total = correct = 0
    for n, k in groups:
        if n <= 0 or not 0 <= k <= n:
            raise ValueError("Invalid group counts")
        total += n
        correct += k
    return correct / total

development = [(80, 72), (20, 10)]
new_use = [(20, 18), (80, 40)]
old = accuracy(development)
new = accuracy(new_use)
print(round(100 * old, 1))  # 82.0
print(round(100 * new, 1))  # 58.0
print(round(100 * (old - new), 1))  # 24.0

Each pair is (cases, correct), and the function assumes integer counts for non-overlapping groups. It rejects empty inputs, groups with no cases and impossible correct counts. A group with no observed cases has an undefined empirical accuracy, not zero accuracy. Do not count the same example in two groups when forming an overall total.
Equivalently, weight each group accuracy by its share of cases: development is 0.80 times 0.90 + 0.20 times 0.50 = 0.82; new use is 0.20 times 0.90 + 0.80 times 0.50 = 0.58.

lesson.title: Read the mix and the errors together

blocks.title: The same group rates meet a different mix
blocks.caption: The weaker group becomes more common. Overall mistakes rise from 18 of 100 to 42 of 100 without any change in these observed within-group accuracy rates.

blocks.text: The arithmetic explains this constructed aggregate difference. It does not prove that dim lighting caused each real error or that these group rates will stay fixed in future samples. Report group counts and uncertainty about generalisation. Review specific errors and reference labels as in Week 29.

blocks.label: If a new cohort has 50 clear and 50 dim cases, and exactly 90 percent and 50 percent are correct respectively, how many correct cases and what overall accuracy result? State the assumption behind this calculation.

blocks.text: Start with model and input-pipeline version checks. A changed resize operation, channel order or unit conversion is an implementation change, not evidence that the input population itself shifted. Compare image conditions, missing values, source groups and label definitions. A neural network may have learned a shortcut tied to a background or capture condition; that is a hypothesis to test, not a conclusion from a histogram.

Input monitoring without new reference labels can reveal a changed group mix. It cannot calculate current accuracy or prove that the relationship between inputs and labels stayed the same. Conversely, stable input summaries can miss a changed labelling policy. Obtain a representative, correctly labelled audit sample and document unresolved label quality.

For a controlled lighting study, keep scene identity and the label fixed while varying lighting. Keep related images together in one split. If new data guide retraining or threshold choices, they are development data; reserve separate source groups or a later appropriate time period for final evaluation. More data alone do not guarantee that a shortcut is removed.

lesson.title: Evaluate a response under the new conditions

blocks.text: Possible responses include fixing a confirmed pipeline bug, gathering missing training coverage, changing a representation or routing some cases for review. Choose a response based on evidence. Compare the original and revised model on identical reserved cases, report both group and overall results, and measure review workload if a review policy is used. Preserve the original checkpoint for comparison.

blocks.label: A team sees more dim images but has no new reference labels. It announces accuracy has fallen, retrains, and claims success using the same cases that guided its changes. Identify what is known, what is missing and how to repair the evaluation.

blocks.text: Record the reference period, group definitions, model and pipeline versions, counts, available labels, decisions and follow-up outcomes. Avoid silently replacing the baseline or the evaluation set. Next week measures efficiency and resource use alongside model quality.

workbook.title: Audit the two cohorts
workbook.prompt: From the table, calculate clear and dim accuracy in each cohort and the clear/dim proportions. Which observed quantities change, and which remain the same?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Clear accuracy is 90 percent in both cohorts; dim accuracy is 50 percent in both. Development has 80 percent clear and 20 percent dim; new use has 20 percent clear and 80 percent dim. The mix changes while observed group rates remain the same.

workbook.title: Use the right denominator
workbook.prompt: Calculate overall correct counts, accuracy and errors in both cohorts, plus the percentage-point drop. Explain why averaging 90 percent and 50 percent without weights gives the wrong overall result here.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Development has 82 correct and 18 errors out of 100, or 82 percent accuracy. New use has 58 correct and 42 errors out of 100, or 58 percent. The drop is 24 percentage points. An unweighted mean gives 70 percent and ignores the unequal group sizes.

workbook.title: Separate an alert from an outcome
workbook.prompt: New-use monitoring shows more dim images but reference labels have not arrived. What can you report now, what can you not calculate, and what checks should precede blaming the neural network?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Report the observed change in group proportions with counts and period. Current accuracy and error patterns need verified outcomes. Check checkpoint and preprocessing versions, group definitions, input quality and label policy; collect a representative labelled audit sample before concluding how performance changed.

workbook.title: Analyse a new mixture independently
workbook.prompt: A separate audit has development groups P: 60 cases, 48 correct and Q: 40 cases, 20 correct. New-use groups are P: 20 cases, 16 correct and Q: 80 cases, 40 correct. Compute each group rate, both overall accuracies, and the percentage-point change. Under the same group rates, what accuracy would equal-sized P and Q groups have?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: P is 80 percent correct and Q is 50 percent correct in both cohorts. Development accuracy is 68 of 100, or 68 percent; new-use accuracy is 56 of 100, or 56 percent. The drop is 12 percentage points. Equal-sized groups at those rates give 65 percent accuracy.

workbook.title: Protect the comparison
workbook.prompt: A team retrains using new-use errors, then evaluates on those same images and their brightened copies. Explain why the score is not independent evidence and propose a comparison that includes the original model.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: The evaluated cases influenced training, and transformed copies share source content. Keep related images in one split and reserve untouched source groups or an appropriate later period. Evaluate original and revised models on identical reserved examples, with checked labels, group counts and rates, overall accuracy, and documented preprocessing.

teacher.background: Use two 45-minute sessions. Work from counts before percentages and keep the frozen model separate from the changing sample mix. The exact equal group rates are constructed for arithmetic; they do not establish a population law. A monitoring alert should lead to evidence gathering rather than an automatic causal claim or retraining decision.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook; paper and pencil
Calculator and optional local Python 3 editor; no packages or AI accounts needed
Use the fictional examples supplied; prepare the fresh retry before class
sessions: Retrieve Week 29’s warning that confident outputs can be wrong on unfamiliar inputs.
Read the cohort table and complete W1. Mark fixed checkpoint and pipeline versus changed mix.
Compute totals and W2. Compare the weighted result with the tempting unweighted average.
Trace the optional count function and the visual; explain why group sizes affect overall accuracy.
Complete the guided balanced cohort and name the fixed-rate assumption.
Complete W3 and discuss missing labels, pipeline changes and possible learned shortcuts.
Collect W4 independently, requiring counts, group rates, both totals and percentage points.
Use W5 and the exit response to protect independent evaluation. Give feedback, then a fresh retry.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided: 45 clear plus 25 dim cases are correct, giving 70 of 100 or 70 percent. This assumes exactly the stated group rates hold in that cohort. Exit: the mix change is observed, but accuracy is unknown without checked labels. Gather a labelled audit and check model/pipeline versions. Cases used to choose or fit a change cannot also provide independent final evidence. Reserve new appropriate cases and compare original and revised models on the same cases with group and overall results.
misconceptions: Average the percentages regardless of group sizes
Overall accuracy is total correct divided by total cases; group accuracies need weights proportional to group size.
A shift alert proves a loss of accuracy
Input changes may help, hurt or leave accuracy unchanged; verified outcomes are needed to measure performance.
An unchanged input summary proves nothing changed
A summary can miss relevant differences, and the input-label relationship or labelling policy can change without an obvious input shift.
teacher.assessment: W4 requires group rates 80 and 50 percent, overall accuracies 68 and 56 percent, a 12-percentage-point drop, and equal-group accuracy 65 percent. Fresh retry: development P has 75 cases with 60 correct; Q has 25 with 10 correct. New use P has 25 with 20 correct; Q has 75 with 30 correct. Group rates are 80 and 40 percent in both. Overall accuracy changes from 70 to 50 percent, a 20-percentage-point drop. Equal-sized groups at those rates give 60 percent.
teacher.support: Provide separate columns for cases, correct, errors and group share. Use 100 counters or a drawn 100-cell grid to change the mix while keeping group rates fixed. Extension: with clear share s and fixed rates 0.90 and 0.50, overall accuracy is 0.50 + 0.40*s. Test s = 0, 0.5 and 1, and explain why observed data need not keep those rates fixed.
teacher.next: Week 31 measures efficiency and resource use while keeping task quality, hardware and comparison conditions explicit.

ai-4/31.title: Efficiency and resource measurement
goals: Calculate throughput and amortised time per example from repeated timings
Count dense-network parameters and distinguish storage from peak memory
Compare resource use under fixed quality and measurement conditions

prerequisite.prompt: Why should two models be evaluated on the same examples and subgroup mix before comparing their accuracy and speed?
prerequisite.answer: Different examples or group proportions can change accuracy and workload. Shared cases and declared conditions help isolate model differences rather than differences in the evaluation sample.

vocabulary: Elapsed time for one request from a declared start to completed response
The number of completed examples processed per unit time
The bytes used to store model weights and biases at a declared precision
The largest amount of memory in use during a measured operation

lesson.title: Define the measurement before comparing models

blocks.text: A neural model can be faster yet fail the task’s accuracy requirement. Training cost and prediction cost are different: training updates parameters, while inference uses the fitted model. Compare quality and resources together under a declared test, rather than calling a model efficient from one small number.

Use these invented classroom timings for models A and B. Each timed pass processes the same 100 preprocessed examples sequentially, one at a time, on the same device and precision. Start before the first prediction and stop after the final prediction completes. Loading and preprocessing are excluded for both. One untimed warm-up pass precedes three timed passes; the warm-up work must still be reported.

The validation cases are the same for both models and are scored once each; repeating timing passes does not create 300 independent quality examples. No actual benchmark was run to produce this table.

Sort each set of three times and take the middle value. A’s median is 2.0 seconds per 100 examples; B’s is 1.2 seconds. Dividing by 100 gives amortised times of 0.020 and 0.012 seconds per example, or 20 and 12 milliseconds. Median-pass throughput is 100 / 2.0 = 50 examples per second for A and about 83.33 for B.

blocks.title: Optional Python check
blocks.text:
from math import isfinite
from statistics import median

def timing_summary(seconds, count):
    if count <= 0 or not seconds:
        raise ValueError("Need examples and timed passes")
    if any(not isfinite(t) or t <= 0 for t in seconds):
        raise ValueError("Times must be finite and positive")
    middle = median(seconds)
    ms_per_example = 1000 * middle / count
    examples_per_second = count / middle
    return middle, ms_per_example, examples_per_second

print(timing_summary([2.0, 2.2, 1.8], 100))
print(timing_summary([1.2, 1.1, 1.3], 100))

The code assumes a positive integer example count and numeric times. A outputs (2.0, 20.0, 50.0); B outputs approximately (1.2, 12.0, 83.33). Retain full precision until display. The time reduction is (20 - 12) / 20 = 40 percent, while throughput rises by about 66.67 percent. These are different denominators.

Amortised time does not reveal the slowest request or a latency percentile. In a batched or concurrent workload, total time divided by count is not an individual request’s waiting time. Record per-request timings if the requirement concerns latency; keep batch size and concurrency explicit.

blocks.title: A faster result can miss the requirement
blocks.caption: For this declared validation rule, only A meets both requirements. The time requirement uses amortised time from the median pass, not a per-request latency guarantee.

blocks.text: The requirements were set before inspecting these results. B is faster under this measurement but is not eligible under the quality rule. One hundred validation cases do not establish future accuracy; reserve independent final evaluation after choosing a model, and inspect relevant subgroup results.

blocks.label: If the quality requirement had instead been set in advance to at least 90 correct, with the same time limit, which models would qualify? Which would you choose if lower measured amortised time is the declared tie-breaker?

lesson.title: Count what parameters can tell you

blocks.text: A fully connected layer with m inputs and n outputs has m times n weights and n biases, assuming every output has one bias. A network with dimensions 4 to 3 to 2 has (4 times 3 + 3) + (3 times 2 + 2) = 23 parameters. At four bytes per parameter, its raw parameter payload is 92 bytes.

That is not the saved file size or peak runtime memory. A file can contain metadata, and inference also needs activations and buffers. Training may additionally store gradients and optimiser state. Record whether a memory measurement refers to the model, the process, an accelerator or the whole device. Parameter count alone does not establish speed.

Runtime alone does not establish energy use or carbon emissions either. Those require additional measurements and declared assumptions, such as power over time and the electricity source. Report what you measured rather than converting fewer parameters into an unsupported energy claim.

Record model and code versions, input size, device, precision, batch size, concurrency, warm-up, timed boundary, repetitions and raw results. Alternate model order where practical, check background load and wait for computation to finish before stopping a timer; queued accelerator work may finish after the host call returns. Report cold-start behaviour separately when it matters.

blocks.label: A report calls B “best and greener” because it is faster, compares B’s batched device run with A’s unbatched run on a different device, and omits B’s quality result. Name the unsupported claims and design a fair comparison.

blocks.text: Keep training and inference costs separate, and include unsuccessful trials in the total experiment budget. Changes chosen using validation need untouched final evaluation. Next week assembles a network experiment record so another person can understand and repeat the comparison.

workbook.title: Summarise repeated timings
workbook.prompt: For A and B, calculate median pass time, amortised milliseconds per example and median-pass throughput. State the measured boundary and one latency claim these numbers cannot support.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: A: 2.0 seconds, 20 ms per example, 50 examples per second. B: 1.2 seconds, 12 ms per example, about 83.33 examples per second. The boundary covers 100 completed sequential predictions on preprocessed inputs, excluding loading and preprocessing. It does not establish worst-case or percentile request latency.

workbook.title: Compare under requirements
workbook.prompt: With at least 91 correct out of 100 and at most 25 ms amortised time required, which model qualifies? Calculate B’s time reduction relative to A and explain why the percentage throughput increase differs.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Only A qualifies; B misses the quality requirement. B reduces time by 8 / 20 = 40 percent. Throughput rises from 50 to about 83.33, an increase of about 66.67 percent relative to 50. Time and throughput use different baseline denominators and are reciprocal for this fixed workload.

workbook.title: Separate storage and memory
workbook.prompt: Count weights, biases and total parameters in the 4 to 3 to 2 network. Calculate raw parameter bytes at four bytes each. Explain why this cannot be reported as peak training memory or an energy measurement.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: There are 12 + 6 = 18 weights and 3 + 2 = 5 biases, totalling 23 parameters and 92 bytes. Activations, buffers, gradients, optimiser state and overhead can require additional memory. Energy needs power-and-time evidence; parameter bytes alone provide neither peak training memory nor energy.

workbook.title: Evaluate a new case independently
workbook.prompt: For 50 shared validation cases, P has times 0.6, 0.5, 0.4 seconds and 47 correct; Q has 0.3, 0.4, 0.5 seconds and 45 correct. Require at least 92 percent accuracy and at most 12 ms amortised time. Give median times, amortised times, throughput, accuracy and eligible models. A separate dense network has dimensions 3 to 2 to 1 with one bias per output: find its parameter count and raw bytes at four bytes each.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: P: median 0.5 s, 10 ms, 100 examples/s, accuracy 47 / 50 = 94 percent. Q: median 0.4 s, 8 ms, 125 examples/s, accuracy 45 / 50 = 90 percent. Only P qualifies. The separate network has (3*2 + 2) + (2*1 + 1) = 11 parameters, or 44 raw bytes.

workbook.title: Repair an unfair benchmark
workbook.prompt: A runs on one device with batch size 1; B runs on another with batch size 32. Only B’s fastest trial and the winning training run are reported. Explain how to compare and report the results fairly.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Control device, precision, workload, batch size, concurrency and timed boundary for a model-only comparison, or explicitly compare whole systems without attributing the result to the model alone. Use the same quality cases, report repetitions and raw timings rather than one best trial, and count all training trials and warm-up work in their appropriate budgets.

teacher.background: Use two 45-minute sessions. The timings are invented for arithmetic and do not describe a particular device or trained model. Keep units and denominators visible. Separate a validation choice from a general performance claim, and separate raw parameter payload from file size, runtime memory and energy.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook; paper and pencil
Calculator and optional local Python 3 editor; no packages or AI accounts needed
Use the fictional examples supplied; prepare the fresh retry before class
sessions: Retrieve why shared examples and group proportions matter for comparisons.
Read the timing protocol and table. Label training, warm-up and inference work separately.
Complete W1 and trace the timing code, including milliseconds and examples per second.
Use W2 and the visual to apply the quality and time requirements before choosing a model.
Complete the guided alternative requirement without retroactively changing the original rule.
Count weights and biases and complete W3; discuss what memory and energy require beyond counts.
Collect W4 independently, requiring units, accuracy fractions, eligibility and parameter bytes.
Use W5 and the exit response to repair benchmark claims. Give feedback before the fresh retry.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided: under the alternative rule set in advance, A and B both qualify. B wins the declared lower-amortised-time tie-breaker, 12 versus 20 ms. Exit: best depends on requirements and B fails the original quality rule; greener is unsupported without energy evidence. Use identical workload and declared conditions or label a whole-system comparison, measure completed work, repeat timings, retain raw results and quality outcomes, and reserve final evaluation after selection.
misconceptions: Fewer parameters always means faster
Hardware, operations, memory access, precision and implementation affect runtime; measure the declared workload.
Total time divided by count is every request’s latency
It is an amortised quantity. Individual requests can vary, and batching or concurrency changes waiting time.
Only the winning run consumed resources
Unsuccessful trials and warm-up also consume resources; record them in the appropriate experiment budget.
teacher.assessment: W4 requires P: 0.5 s, 10 ms, 100/s, 94 percent; Q: 0.4 s, 8 ms, 125/s, 90 percent; only P eligible; 11 parameters and 44 bytes. Fresh retry: 40 shared cases, R times 0.8, 1.0, 0.6 seconds with 38 correct; S times 0.4, 0.6, 0.5 with 36 correct. Require 95 percent accuracy and at most 25 ms. R gives 0.8 s, 20 ms, 50/s and 95 percent; S gives 0.5 s, 12.5 ms, 80/s and 90 percent. Only R qualifies. A 2 to 3 to 1 dense network has 13 parameters and 52 bytes at four bytes each.
teacher.support: Use a units ledger: seconds per pass, examples per pass, milliseconds per example and examples per second. Draw every dense connection and one bias per output. Extension: compare median-pass throughput with total examples divided by total elapsed time; explain why these can differ when pass durations vary. Neither alone measures a latency percentile.
teacher.next: Week 32 documents a network experiment, preserving methods, data splits, versions, raw results, resource measurements and limitations.

ai-4/32.title: Documenting a network experiment
goals: Record a network experiment with enough detail to replay its calculations
Trace reported metrics to data roles and saved parameters
Write a bounded conclusion and identify missing evaluation evidence

prerequisite.prompt: Why is “the model was fast and accurate” insufficient as an experiment record?
prerequisite.answer: It omits the task, data and splits, model and code versions, quality counts or loss definition, hardware, timing boundary and raw results. Another person cannot check what was measured or repeat the comparison.

vocabulary: A unique label linking one experiment’s settings, outputs and records
Saved model parameters at a specified stage of training
An inventory connecting named artifacts with versions, roles and integrity information
Repeating a recorded procedure to check whether its outputs agree

lesson.title: State a question and preserve the inputs

blocks.text: A useful experiment record explains what was asked, what was done, what happened and what remains unknown. Use run NN32-A: does fitting one positive ReLU weight reduce validation mean squared error compared with its initial value? This tiny constructed regression task teaches record keeping; it cannot establish performance on real-world data.

The network predicts max(0, a*x), with one weight a and no bias. Start at a = 1, use learning rate 0.1, two full-batch training updates and mean squared error, the mean of squared prediction errors. There is no normalisation, random initialisation or shuffling. Use Python float arithmetic and record the actual Python version when replaying.

Before running, set the selection rule: choose the checkpoint with the smaller validation MSE, breaking a tie toward the earlier update. The initial model is the baseline. Validation V1 chooses a checkpoint but never contributes to the training gradient. Final evaluation has not been run; its result must be recorded as not measured.

lesson.title: Keep a record of every update

blocks.text: For these two training cases, MSE = 2.5*(a - 2) squared and its gradient is 5*(a - 2). At a = 1 the gradient is -5, so the first update is 1 - 0.1*(-5) = 1.5. The next gradient is -2.5, giving a = 1.75. All preactivations in this run stay positive, so ReLU’s derivative is one; this is not a general backpropagation implementation.

blocks.title: Optional Python check

blocks.text: The code assumes the supplied nonempty numeric datasets and positive preactivations. Each record stores update number, weight, training MSE and validation MSE after the update. Keep both records, the initial weight and the rule; saving only the best score erases how the choice was made.

lesson.title: Link a conclusion to its evidence

blocks.title: Read each checkpoint against the same validation case
blocks.caption: The baseline validation MSE is 9. The predeclared rule selects update 2 with validation MSE 0.5625 on one validation case. This is not a final-test score.

blocks.text: A defensible conclusion is: in run NN32-A, update 2 reduced MSE on the single constructed validation case from 9 to 0.5625 compared with the initial model. This checkpoint was selected using that same validation case; generalisation is untested. No timing, peak-memory or energy measurements are provided.

blocks.label: Using the selected weight, calculate the prediction for V1 and its squared error. Explain why the result must be labelled validation rather than independent final evaluation.

lesson.title: Package a record another person can inspect

blocks.text: Keep a manifest for the data with IDs and split membership, the exact code, settings, every checkpoint, raw prediction rows and metric calculations. Add run ID, author/date, environment versions, known data provenance and permitted use, failed attempts, decisions and limitations. A descriptive filename helps navigation, but does not prove that file contents stayed unchanged.

When saving artifacts, record their content hashes and keep the exact versions used. Hashes help detect content changes; they do not prove label correctness or experiment quality. Retain the input order, any training-fitted preprocessing, model architecture and numeric precision. Randomised experiments must also record seeds and the relevant random operations; a seed alone does not guarantee identical results across environments.

Ask a partner to replay from the record rather than from memory. If results differ, check inputs, split membership, preprocessing, configuration, code, parameters and environment. Document the discrepancy and the repair instead of overwriting the old record. A rerun on the same data checks the procedure; it does not add new independent evaluation cases.

lesson.title: Separate evidence from the next experiment

blocks.text: Report missing measurements as not measured, not as zero. If a final set has influenced a change, document that use and reserve new untouched evaluation before making an independent performance claim. A polished report cannot fix leakage or missing evidence. For larger experiments, preserve denominators, subgroup results and resource conditions from Weeks 29 to 31.

blocks.label: A report says “final accuracy 0.5625, low energy” but includes only the selected weight and no data or code. Repair its claim and name the minimum evidence needed to check this run.

blocks.text: Finish with a next action that follows from the limitations, such as planning a broader reserved evaluation without claiming it has already succeeded. Next week begins the capstone by defining a hypothesis and baseline before controlled experiments.

workbook.title: Write the replay settings
workbook.prompt: For NN32-A, record the prediction rule, initial weight, bias policy, learning rate, update count, loss, training/validation IDs, data order or shuffling policy, and checkpoint selection rule. Name one environment field still to record when you run it.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Predict max(0, a*x); start a = 1 with no bias; rate 0.1; two full-batch updates; MSE is mean squared prediction error. T1 and T2 train, V1 validates; no shuffling or normalisation. Select lower validation MSE, ties to earlier update. Record the actual Python version, alongside the code and Python float arithmetic.

workbook.title: Trace the selected result
workbook.prompt: Calculate both weight updates and give each training and validation MSE. Name the selected checkpoint and baseline validation MSE. How many independent validation examples support the comparison?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Weights are 1.5 then 1.75. Training MSE values are 0.625 and 0.15625; validation MSE values are 2.25 and 0.5625. Update 2 is selected; baseline validation MSE is 9. There is one validation example, not two examples created by evaluating two checkpoints.

workbook.title: Audit the artifact record
workbook.prompt: A folder contains only best-model.json and a screenshot of 0.5625. Identify four missing artifacts or records and explain what a content hash can and cannot verify.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Missing items include exact data with IDs and splits, code/configuration, earlier checkpoints, raw predictions and metric definitions, selection rule, and environment details. A hash can detect changes relative to recorded content; it cannot establish correct labels, sound splits or a valid conclusion.

workbook.title: Audit a new record independently
workbook.prompt: A separate run R17 records baseline a = 1 and checkpoints a = 1.5 and a = 1.75. It uses prediction max(0, a*x) and one validation case V9 with x = 4, y = 8. Compute baseline and checkpoint predictions and squared errors, choose by lowest validation MSE, and write a bounded conclusion. Final evaluation and runtime have not been measured.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Predictions are 4, 6 and 7; squared errors are 16, 4 and 1. Choose a = 1.75. In R17, that checkpoint lowers MSE on V9 from 16 to 1 relative to the baseline, but V9 also selects it. This is one-case validation evidence; final performance and runtime are not measured.

workbook.title: Investigate a replay mismatch
workbook.prompt: A partner gets different results after changing preprocessing and replacing the validation file. They keep the old run ID and overwrite the old score. Explain what should be preserved and how the revised work should be recorded.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Preserve the original data, preprocessing, settings, outputs and run ID. Compare exact artifact versions to identify the mismatch. Record changed preprocessing and data under a new run or explicit version, including reasons and results. A changed validation set is a different comparison; do not overwrite it as though it were the same run.

teacher.background: Use two 45-minute sessions. Treat the tiny ReLU model as a fully inspectable experiment, not a claim about real-world accuracy. The code trains one scalar on two rows and selects using one validation row. Require students to label metrics, denominators and data roles before judging the result; no final evaluation or resource measurement is supplied.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook; paper and pencil
Calculator and optional local Python 3 editor; no packages or AI accounts needed
Use the fictional examples supplied; prepare the fresh retry before class
sessions: Retrieve the missing details in a vague performance claim and introduce run NN32-A.
Read the data roles and configuration. Complete W1 with a replay settings record.
Trace the two gradient updates, optionally run the code, and complete W2.
Use the visual to connect parameters, predictions, metrics and the selection decision.
Complete the guided V1 calculation and distinguish replay from independent evidence.
Build an artifact manifest and complete W3, including the limits of hashes and seeds.
Collect W4 independently, requiring raw predictions, errors and a bounded validation claim.
Use W5 and the exit response to repair records. Give feedback, then administer the fresh retry.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided: 1.75*3 = 5.25, error 5.25 - 6 = -0.75, squared error 0.5625. V1 selected the checkpoint and is validation, not untouched final evaluation. Exit: replace final accuracy with validation MSE 0.5625 on one constructed case selected using that case. Energy is not measured. Supply data and splits, exact code, settings, baseline and both checkpoints, raw predictions, metric definition, selection rule and environment information.
misconceptions: A smaller MSE is an accuracy percentage
MSE is an average squared error in squared target units; it is not classification accuracy or a percentage.
A replay adds new evaluation evidence
Reusing the same rows checks procedure consistency, not performance on new independent cases.
A seed or hash proves the experiment is sound
Seeds and hashes help track execution or integrity; they cannot repair bad labels, leakage or an unsupported claim.
