teacher.assessment: W4 requires predictions 4, 6, 7 and squared errors 16, 4, 1; choose a = 1.75 and label the result one-case validation with final evaluation and runtime not measured. Fresh retry: R18 has the same baseline and checkpoints but validation x = 5, y = 10. Predictions are 5, 7.5, 8.75; squared errors are 25, 6.25, 1.5625. Choose a = 1.75. Require a validation-only conclusion and a record of which validation data version was used.
teacher.support: Provide a record frame with question, fixed settings, data roles, raw results, selection, limitations and next action. Allow a calculator and compare predictions before squared errors. Extension: rename a data file without changing its bytes, then edit a value; explain why only the content change alters its content hash. Use copies of fictional classroom data.
teacher.next: Week 33 starts the capstone by recording a hypothesis, baseline, evaluation plan and success criteria before running controlled experiments.

ai-4/33.title: Capstone hypothesis and baseline
goals: Write a testable capstone hypothesis and a credible baseline
Specify data roles and a selection rule before inspecting results
Calculate baseline MSE and distinguish a success criterion from a result

prerequisite.prompt: Why must a checkpoint chosen using validation data still face an untouched final test?
prerequisite.answer: Validation influences selection, so its score is not independent final evidence. Freeze the chosen procedure before opening the final test.

vocabulary: A testable expectation with a stated comparison and outcome
A specified reference procedure evaluated on the same cases
A rule written before evaluation for judging the measured result
Cases kept out of fitting, tuning and selection

lesson.title: Turn a broad aim into a question

blocks.text: A capstone needs a question that evidence can answer. “Build a better network” leaves better undefined. Here the question is: does two-update full-batch fitting of one scalar ReLU weight reduce validation mean squared error relative to the initial-weight baseline on a constructed positive-input task? Predict max(0, a*x), with no bias. The baseline has a = 1. The trained candidate starts at a = 1, uses learning rate 0.1 and exactly two updates. These choices are written before results are inspected.

The hypothesis is that the trained candidate has lower validation MSE. The plan does not guarantee that result. This task tests training and record keeping, not whether neural networks are preferable to every other model. A stronger comparison may also include an ordinary fitted line.

lesson.title: Assign roles and calculate the baseline

blocks.text: Training rows determine updates. Validation rows compare the prespecified candidate with the baseline. The final-test inputs and targets remain sealed until the procedure and reporting plan are frozen. MSE = sum of squared prediction errors divided by the number of evaluated rows. Baseline predictions on V1 and V2 are 3 and 4. Errors are -3 and -4, squared errors 9 and 16, and validation MSE is 25/2 = 12.5. There are two validation cases.

blocks.title: Keep the evidence roles separate
blocks.caption: Each arrow preserves a distinct data role. Opening final rows to choose a learning rate changes their role.

blocks.text: The validation criterion is candidate MSE strictly below baseline MSE on V1 and V2. Equality does not pass. The final criterion is lower MSE than the same baseline on the sealed final rows. Report both scores and every raw prediction whether or not the criterion passes. Record the rule, training rows, update count, learning rate, loss, data versions and code version. A criterion specifies how to judge a future result; it is not evidence that the result already happened.

Keep validation and final criteria separate. Do not silently add epochs or change preprocessing after seeing a weak result. A changed plan is a new version and needs an honest account of what evidence informed it.

Supported example: a separate baseline predicts 2 and 4 for validation targets 5 and 7. Its errors are -3 and -3 and MSE is 9. A proposed plan says to train one fixed candidate and report both MSE values on those same two rows. It supplies no candidate predictions, so no improvement can yet be claimed.

blocks.label: Guided: compute that baseline MSE, name the missing evidence, and state whether the hypothesis has been confirmed.

lesson.title: Plan without contaminating the final test

blocks.text: Before running, exchange a plan with a partner. The partner should be able to identify what is changed, what stays fixed, what metric is computed, which rows select the procedure and when the final test may be opened. A file name alone does not protect a split; record who can inspect it and how related examples were separated.

blocks.label: Exit: someone opens the final targets to choose between learning rates, then calls the winning score independent final evidence. Explain the change of role and the next honest step.

workbook.title: Write the hypothesis
workbook.prompt: State the prediction rule, baseline, candidate learning rate and update count, comparison data and metric. Write a testable hypothesis.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Predict max(0, a*x) without bias; baseline a = 1; candidate starts at 1, learning rate 0.1, two full-batch updates on T1/T2. Hypothesis: candidate validation MSE on V1/V2 is strictly below the baseline MSE.

workbook.title: Calculate the reference score
workbook.prompt: Compute baseline predictions, errors, squared errors and MSE on V1 and V2. State the denominator.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Predictions 3 and 4; errors -3 and -4; squared errors 9 and 16; MSE 12.5 over two rows.

workbook.title: Audit the plan
workbook.prompt: A proposal says “try models until the test score looks good”. Identify the missing fixed choices and explain why that test is not independent.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: It omits architecture, baseline, training settings, metric, stopping/selection rule and split policy. Repeated choices based on the test use it for development; reserve new independent final data after freezing the revised procedure.

workbook.title: Plan a new case independently
workbook.prompt: A new task predicts max(0, a*x), with baseline a = 1. Training rows are (1,3) and (2,6); validation rows are (3,9) and (4,12); final rows are sealed. Specify a candidate starting at 1 with learning rate 0.1 and two full-batch updates. Calculate baseline validation MSE and write a strict improvement criterion. Has the candidate succeeded yet?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Baseline predictions 3 and 4, errors -6 and -8, squared errors 36 and 64, MSE 50 over two rows. Candidate is fixed at two updates with rate 0.1 on training only; success means candidate validation MSE < 50. No candidate results have been supplied, so success is unknown.

workbook.title: Preserve the reserved evidence
workbook.prompt: A partner inspects final labels and changes the learning rate. Explain how to document this and obtain independent evidence.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Record the inspection and changed plan. Those rows informed selection and cannot honestly serve as untouched final evidence. Freeze the revised procedure and use newly reserved independent cases; retain the earlier result as development evidence.

teacher.background: Use two 45-minute sessions. This capstone uses constructed scalar ReLU regression so every calculation is inspectable. It is an experiment in training and evidence, not a real-world deployment. Preserve written plans, data roles and raw predictions. Optional local Python requires no external packages or AI account. Do not expose independent-task solutions before collecting work.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook; paper and pencil
Calculator; optional local Python 3 interpreter

ai-4/34.title: Capstone controlled experiments
goals: Trace matched two-update learning-rate experiments
Select a candidate using a prespecified validation rule
Explain the limits of a one-factor comparison

prerequisite.prompt: What must stay fixed when comparing learning rates?
prerequisite.answer: Data and splits, initial parameters, architecture, loss, update count and evaluation procedure must stay fixed; change only the intended learning rate.

vocabulary: A comparison holding specified conditions constant while changing an intended factor
An update whose gradient uses all training rows
A rule for choosing a candidate using development evidence
A differing condition that prevents isolating the intended explanation

lesson.title: Change one setting with matched inputs

blocks.text: Continue with training (1,2) and (2,4), validation (3,6) and (4,8), and prediction max(0, a*x). Compare learning rates 0.1 and 0.2. Each run starts at a = 1, has no bias and takes two full-batch updates. Keep the loss, data order and arithmetic fixed. This toy model has no randomness; repeating the exact run checks replay, not variation across seeds.

Record the comparison as an explicit revision to the one-candidate Week 33 plan before viewing new results. Validation may guide selection; sealed final data must not. Select lower validation MSE, with a tie going to learning rate 0.1.

For positive weights and these positive inputs, the ReLU is active. Training MSE is ((a-2)^2 + (2*a-4)^2)/2 = 2.5*(a-2)^2. Its gradient is 5*(a-2). Update a to a - rate*5*(a-2). At rate 0.1, weights are 1.5 then 1.75. At rate 0.2, weights are 2 then 2. The formula assumes the active region; do not extend it blindly to nonpositive weights.

blocks.title: Keep the evidence roles separate
blocks.caption: The selected run fits this exact constructed relationship. Its zero error does not establish universal reliability.

blocks.text: At a = 1.75, validation predictions are 5.25 and 7. Errors -0.75 and -1 square to 0.5625 and 1, giving MSE 0.78125. At a = 2 the predictions equal 6 and 8, so MSE is zero. Rate 0.2 wins the written validation rule. This selection uses two validation cases, not four independent cases because two runs used them.

If one run used extra epochs or different training rows, the comparison would mix factors. Either rerun a matched experiment or report the differences and avoid claiming an isolated learning-rate effect. A zero validation score is also compatible with a very simple task and says nothing about a new distribution.

Supported example: rate 0.3 starts at a = 1. The first gradient is -5, giving a = 2.5. The next gradient is 2.5, giving a = 1.75. This two-update run finishes at the same weight as rate 0.1 although its path differs.

blocks.label: Guided: calculate the second update and its validation MSE. Explain why equal final scores do not mean identical trajectories.

blocks.text: Save run IDs, settings, each checkpoint, predictions and metric calculations. Report the losing run as well as the winner. Freeze the selected rate, architecture and update count before the final evaluation. Any change after opening final data requires a new development record and fresh reserved evidence.

blocks.label: Exit: one run receives six updates and the other two. What can the score comparison establish, and what must be rerun to isolate the learning rate?

workbook.title: Name the controls
workbook.prompt: List six settings held fixed and the single intended changed factor.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Hold training and validation rows, initial a, architecture/bias policy, loss, update count and evaluation metric fixed. Change learning rate.

workbook.title: Trace both runs
workbook.prompt: Compute both updates for rates 0.1 and 0.2 using gradient 5*(a-2).
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Rate 0.1: 1 -> 1.5 -> 1.75. Rate 0.2: 1 -> 2 -> 2. Gradients are -5 then -2.5 for the first run and -5 then 0 for the second.

workbook.title: Select without extra evidence
workbook.prompt: Recompute validation MSE for the final weights and apply the written selection rule. How many distinct validation rows were used?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: MSE 0.78125 for a = 1.75 and 0 for a = 2, so select rate 0.2. There are two distinct validation rows; re-evaluation does not add cases.

workbook.title: Run a new comparison independently
workbook.prompt: For training (1,3),(2,6) and validation (3,9),(4,12), start a = 1. Compare rates 0.1 and 0.2 for two updates. Gradient is 5*(a-3). Compute final weights and validation MSE, then select lower MSE; ties go to 0.1.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Rate 0.1: gradients -10,-5; weights 2,2.5. Validation errors -1.5,-2 give MSE 3.125. Rate 0.2: weights 3,3, errors 0,0 and MSE 0. Select 0.2, with only validation evidence on two constructed rows.

workbook.title: Audit a mixed comparison
workbook.prompt: Run A uses rate 0.1 for two updates; run B uses rate 0.2 for six updates and different training rows. Can the difference be attributed to rate alone? Propose a repair.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: No: update count and training data also differ. Rerun both rates with the same initial parameters, architecture, rows, loss, two-update budget and evaluation procedure; preserve and label the earlier mixed comparison.

The largest rate must be best

ai-4/35.title: Capstone limitations and revision
goals: Evaluate a frozen candidate and baseline on final rows
Identify a distribution limitation from raw errors
Distinguish revision checks from new independent evaluation

prerequisite.prompt: After selecting rate 0.2, may you change it after viewing final scores and keep calling those scores untouched?
prerequisite.answer: No. Once final results influence changes, those rows become development evidence for the revised procedure.

vocabulary: A recorded procedure fixed before final evaluation
A documented change informed by earlier evidence
A condition or group missing or poorly represented in the evidence

blocks.text: Freeze the Week 34 candidate: max(0, a*x), initial a = 1, rate 0.2, two full-batch updates on (1,2),(2,4), no bias. The final weight is 2. The baseline is unchanged at a = 1. Now open final rows F1=(5,10), F2=(6,12), F3=(-1,-2), F4=(-2,-4). These fictional rows deliberately include a condition absent from the positive training and validation inputs. Opening them is an evaluation event, not permission to tune on them while retaining an independent-test claim.

Write raw predictions for both procedures before summarising. A low overall error can hide a systematic problem in a condition. These four constructed examples do not estimate prevalence or real-world performance.

Baseline squared errors are 25,36,4,16, so MSE is 81/4 = 20.25. Candidate squared errors are 0,0,4,16, so MSE is 20/4 = 5. The candidate passes the strict lower-MSE final criterion on these four rows. On the two negative-input rows its MSE is (4+16)/2 = 10; on the positive rows it is zero.

blocks.title: Keep the evidence roles separate
blocks.caption: A passed aggregate criterion and a known structural failure can both be true.

lesson.title: Explain a failure before proposing a repair

blocks.text: The ReLU output cannot be negative. When targets are negative, no choice of this scalar weight can produce the required negative output. More epochs do not remove that output constraint. A proposed signed linear output a*x would represent negative targets, but it changes the architecture. It needs a new version, appropriate fitting and selection, and fresh reserved evaluation.

Running that proposal on F3 and F4 checks the revealed failures. It does not create new independent final evidence. Preserve the original test result and label later scores as revision or regression checks. Do not replace the earlier failure report with a score from a new model on already inspected rows.

Supported example: for a = 2 on x = -3 with target -6, the ReLU prediction is 0, residual 6 and squared error 36. The signed proposal predicts -6 on this revealed case. This demonstrates that the alternative can represent the case; it does not establish how well a newly trained model will perform elsewhere.

blocks.label: Guided: calculate both predictions and errors and explain which claim the comparison supports.

blocks.text: A revision record names the observed failure, proposed mechanism, changed rule, preserved earlier results and new evaluation plan. Reserve fresh cases spanning the relevant input conditions. Include regression checks for earlier successes, and keep independent evaluation separate. Record any cases still missing from coverage.

blocks.label: Exit: write one sentence reporting the original final result and one sentence describing what remains unverified after the proposed architecture change.

workbook.title: Trace final predictions
workbook.prompt: For F1–F4 calculate candidate residuals and squared errors.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Residuals 0,0,2,4; squared errors 0,0,4,16. The ReLU predictions for both negative inputs are zero.

workbook.title: Compare with the baseline
workbook.prompt: Compute both overall MSE values and the candidate negative-input MSE. Apply the strict final criterion.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Baseline MSE 20.25; candidate MSE 5. Candidate negative-input MSE 10 over two rows. Candidate passes the lower-overall-MSE criterion but has a structural negative-output limitation.

workbook.title: Explain the architecture limit
workbook.prompt: Why cannot extra training alone make this ReLU output negative? Name a proposed change and the evidence it would require.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: max(0,a*x) is always nonnegative, regardless of a. A signed linear output can represent negative values; treat it as a changed architecture and run a recorded fitting/selection procedure with fresh reserved final evidence.

workbook.title: Evaluate new evidence independently
workbook.prompt: A frozen ReLU candidate with a = 3 is compared with baseline a = 1 on final rows (2,6),(4,12),(-1,-3),(-2,-6). Compute both MSE values and candidate MSE on negative inputs. Write a bounded conclusion.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Baseline squared errors 16,64,9,36 total 125, MSE 31.25. Candidate squared errors 0,0,9,36 total 45, MSE 11.25. Negative-input MSE 22.5 over two rows. Candidate improves overall on these four constructed cases but still cannot represent negative outputs.

workbook.title: Label a revision honestly
workbook.prompt: After inspecting F1–F4, a student changes to prediction 2*x and reports “new final MSE 0”. Explain the accurate label and the next evaluation step.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: The score is a revision check on already inspected final rows. Preserve the original final MSE 5 and the architectural change. Freeze the revised training and selection procedure and evaluate on fresh reserved cases; also retain regression checks.

ai-4/36.title: Neural network experiment defense
goals: Defend a network experiment using traceable evidence
Separate selection, final evaluation and revision claims
Answer a challenge with a calculation and a bounded conclusion

prerequisite.prompt: Can a revised model reuse inspected final rows as new independent evidence?
prerequisite.answer: No. They may support regression checks, but a revised procedure needs fresh reserved cases for independent evaluation.

vocabulary: An explanation of methods and claims supported by inspectable evidence
The connection from inputs and procedure through raw outputs to a reported claim
A condition restricting what evidence can establish
Repeating the documented procedure to check reported outputs

lesson.title: Assemble a claim that can be checked

blocks.text: A defense is not a sales pitch. Assemble the original question and criterion, data roles, baseline, model equation, settings, raw checkpoints, validation selection, frozen final predictions, limitations and revision history. Someone reading the record should be able to recompute a reported MSE and see which decisions each dataset informed.

For this capstone, two rates were compared under matched conditions. Rate 0.2 selected a = 2 with validation MSE 0 versus 0.78125 for rate 0.1. The frozen candidate then achieved final MSE 5 versus baseline 20.25 on four constructed cases. These are different comparisons and must not be collapsed into “the network was 100% accurate”.

rows: Lower MSE than initial-weight baseline on these rows
Nonnegative output fails to represent negative targets
A possible representational repair, not new final evidence

blocks.title: Keep the evidence roles separate
blocks.caption: Every claim has an evidence source and a limit. A complete record is not a substitute for broader data.

blocks.text: Challenge: “Your validation error was zero, so why did the final test fail on negative targets?” Response: validation contained only positive inputs; the output max(0,a*x) cannot be negative. The final negative cases expose a coverage and architecture limitation. The overall criterion still passed, but that does not remove the failure.

Challenge: “Is a neural network better than linear regression?” Response: the supplied baseline was a fixed initial weight, not a fitted line. The evidence establishes improvement relative to that baseline only. A fitted signed line is a relevant additional comparison and needs a documented, fair evaluation. Challenge: “Was the candidate faster?” Response: no timing evidence was collected, so speed is unmeasured.

Supported case: another experiment reports baseline MSE 8 and candidate MSE 2 on four untouched final rows after freezing the candidate. The reduction is 6 MSE units, or 75% of the baseline MSE. That percentage is a relative reduction in MSE, not 75% classification accuracy. It cannot establish deployment performance.

blocks.label: Guided: calculate the absolute and relative MSE reduction, then write a sentence preserving the metric and four-row scope.

lesson.title: Close with limitations and next questions

blocks.text: Use a short presentation: question; method and controls; selection; final result; failures; revision; next question. State the small constructed sample, absent real-world coverage, limited baseline and unmeasured resource use. A useful next question is whether a signed-output procedure improves on a fitted-line baseline under newly reserved evaluation conditions. Passing this capstone means explaining the evidence correctly, including an unsuccessful or limited result.

blocks.label: Exit: correct “our network is universally reliable, 100% accurate, faster than every baseline and repaired on the final test”. Give measured claims and identify the missing evidence.

workbook.title: Build the evidence inventory
workbook.prompt: Name eight items needed to check the capstone from question through final result.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Question/criterion, data and split IDs, baseline rule, architecture, initial values and learning rates, update count/loss, checkpoints and raw predictions, validation selection rule, frozen final record, limitations and revision history are acceptable items.

workbook.title: Defend the result
workbook.prompt: State the validation selection and frozen final comparison using their correct metrics and scopes.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Rate 0.2 selected a = 2 with validation MSE 0 versus 0.78125 on two positive rows. Frozen final MSE was 5 versus baseline 20.25 on four constructed rows; negative-input candidate MSE was 10 on two rows.

workbook.title: Challenge an unsupported claim
workbook.prompt: A presenter claims the experiment proves neural networks beat fitted lines and use less energy. What evidence is missing?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: No fitted-line comparison or energy measurement was supplied. The initial-weight baseline comparison supports neither claim; specify a fair fitted-line procedure and measured resource boundary before comparing.

workbook.title: Defend a new record independently
workbook.prompt: A separate experiment compares candidates C1 and C2 on two validation rows: MSE 1.5 and 1.0. The written rule selects lower MSE. After freezing C2, four fresh final rows give baseline squared errors 4,9,1,2 and C2 squared errors 1,1,2,0. Compute final MSE and relative reduction. Two condition-B rows are the last two rows; compare baseline and candidate MSE there. State what this record supports and what is unmeasured.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Select C2. Baseline final MSE 16/4 = 4; candidate MSE 4/4 = 1; absolute reduction 3 and relative reduction 75%. Condition B baseline MSE (1+2)/2 = 1.5 and candidate MSE (2+0)/2 = 1, though one condition-B row worsened from 1 to 2. The record supports lower MSE on these four final rows, not universal reliability or a classification-accuracy percentage. Speed and energy are unmeasured.

workbook.title: Record the next investigation
workbook.prompt: Propose a fair next comparison with a fitted signed line. State how to preserve previous evidence and reserve new evaluation.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Keep the original plans, outputs and failures. Define and fit the signed-line baseline with development data, match task and evaluation metric, freeze both procedures, and use fresh reserved cases with positive and negative input coverage. Record revised settings and report all outcomes.

ai-4/4.title: Activation functions
goals: Trace identity ReLU and sigmoid on a numerical score
Explain how a nonlinear activation changes a computation
Distinguish an activation output from a final class or verified probability

prerequisite.prompt: For z = 2 times width - height - 3 at [3, 3], what are the score and class under z >= 0?
prerequisite.answer: The score is zero and the class is 1 because equality is included.

vocabulary: A function applied to a computed score
The function max(0, z), retaining positive scores and replacing negative scores with zero
The function 1 / (1 + exp(-z)), mapping finite real scores into the interval between 0 and 1
A function that cannot be represented by one fixed slope and offset over its entire domain

lesson.title: Transform the score with a stated function

blocks.text: First compute an affine score z = w dot x + b. An activation then returns a = f(z). In a network this value may become an input to another layer; it is not automatically a class prediction. We will compare three functions using the same incoming scores so that only the activation changes.

Identity returns z unchanged. ReLU, pronounced ree-loo, returns the larger of zero and z. Thus ReLU(-2) = 0, ReLU(0) = 0 and ReLU(2) = 2. Positive scores keep their magnitude; ReLU does not turn every positive value into 1.
These are fixed arithmetic functions. Selecting a function or changing its input is not itself a training procedure. Later weeks will introduce losses and parameter updates.

Sigmoid is 1 / (1 + exp(-z)). Here exp(t) means e raised to power t, where e is approximately 2.718. A calculator or the supplied Python code can evaluate it; no calculus is required this week. For z = -2, 0 and 2, sigmoid outputs are approximately 0.1192, 0.5 and 0.8808.

For every finite mathematical input, sigmoid is strictly between 0 and 1, though computer rounding can produce an endpoint for extreme scores. Negative inputs produce values below 0.5, zero gives 0.5, and positive inputs give values above 0.5. A class rule still needs to be stated: if class 1 means sigmoid(z) >= 0.5, these three predictions are 0, 1 and 1.

blocks.title: Optional Python check

blocks.text: The two algebraically equivalent branches avoid taking exp of a large positive number. A value within [0, 1] is not automatically a reliable probability: its interpretation depends on the fitted task and evaluation evidence.

lesson.title: Compare transformations without mixing the rules

blocks.title: Three functions receive the same score
blocks.caption: Each row starts again from the same score -2 and applies one function. The functions are alternatives here, not successive steps. These outputs are activation values, not class labels.

blocks.label: For z = -1 and z = 1, give identity and ReLU outputs. Using sigmoid(-1) = 0.2689 and sigmoid(1) = 0.7311, give classes under the rule a >= 0.5.

blocks.text: An affine function has one fixed slope. ReLU has slope zero on the negative side and slope one on the positive side, so no single straight line fits the whole function. For a concrete check, inputs -2, 0, 2 give outputs 0, 0, 2. The average of the endpoint outputs is 1, but the output at the midpoint 0 is 0. This differs from an affine function, which preserves midpoints.

For a one-input chain with identity between stages, h = 2x + 1 followed by y = 3h - 2 collapses to y = 6x + 1. Insert ReLU instead: h = max(0, 2x + 1), y = 3h - 2. At x = -1, the identity chain gives -5 while the ReLU chain gives -2. At x = 1, both give 7. The nonlinear step can change the overall family of functions.

A nonlinear activation allows a network to represent relationships that a chain of affine operations alone cannot express. It does not guarantee that training will find a useful model or that more layers will help. ReLU can erase differences between negative scores; sigmoid can compress very large scores into nearly identical values. The architecture, data and training procedure still matter.

blocks.label: A learner reports sigmoid(2) is about 0.8808 and concludes the system will be correct 88 percent of the time for every future case. What does the calculation establish, and what evidence is still missing?

blocks.text: Next week, we will compose layers while keeping every intermediate value and its role visible.

workbook.title: Trace three activations
workbook.prompt: For scores -2, 0, 2, list identity and ReLU outputs. Explain why ReLU(2) is not 1.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Identity gives -2, 0, 2; ReLU gives 0, 0, 2. ReLU retains the positive score itself; it is not a step classifier.

workbook.title: Apply a declared class rule
workbook.prompt: Use the lesson sigmoid values for -2, 0, 2. Predict classes under a >= 0.5, then explain the zero-score case.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Classes are 0, 1, 1. Sigmoid(0) equals 0.5 and the declared >= comparison includes equality.

workbook.title: Check the midpoint
workbook.prompt: Compare ReLU at inputs -2, 0, 2. Give the average of the two endpoint outputs and the output at the midpoint; explain what this shows.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Endpoint outputs 0 and 2 average to 1; the midpoint input 0 produces 0. The mismatch shows ReLU is not one affine function over these inputs.

workbook.title: Trace a new chain independently
workbook.prompt: Let z = x - 2, a = ReLU(z), y = 2a + 1. For x = 0, 2, 5, record every z, a and y. Then replace ReLU with identity and give all three y values. Which inputs have the same ReLU output, and why?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: For x = 0, 2, 5: z = -2, 0, 3; a = 0, 0, 3; y = 1, 1, 7. Identity gives y = -3, 1, 7. Inputs 0 and 2 both give a = 0 because ReLU maps negative and zero scores to zero.

workbook.title: Limit a probability claim
workbook.prompt: A model returns a sigmoid value 0.9 on one case. Does the numerical range alone establish a calibrated 90 percent probability? Explain what needs checking.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: No. It establishes only the computed activation value. Probability interpretation requires a suitable fitted model and evaluation, including checking predicted probabilities against outcome frequencies on relevant separate data; one value does not establish calibration.

teacher.background: Use two 45-minute sessions to compare activation functions before network training. Students should trace z, activation a and any later output separately. Sigmoid arithmetic may use the supplied approximations. Focus on the change in function shape and the distinction between an activation, class decision and probability claim.

Trace identity and ReLU for -2, 0 and 2. Complete W1, checking that positive values keep magnitude.
Introduce the sigmoid formula and supplied values. Trace or run the stable code; complete W2 using the explicit equality policy.
Compare the visual rows and complete the guided -1 and 1 case. Keep activation values separate from classes.
Retrieve ReLU at one negative and one positive input. Ask whether one line covers both sides.
Complete W3 and trace the two worked chains at x = -1 and x = 1. Show the identity-chain simplification by substitution.
Collect W4 independently, requiring a three-stage table. Do not award full credit for final y values without the intermediate trace.
Complete W5 and the exit response. Use the fresh retry after feedback; connect to composing layers next week.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided: identity outputs -1 and 1; ReLU outputs 0 and 1. Sigmoid class predictions under >= 0.5 are 0 and 1. Exit: the computation establishes an activation of about 0.8808 for score 2. It does not establish calibrated probabilities, correctness on this individual case or reliability on future populations.
misconceptions: ReLU returns a class label
Positive scores retain magnitude, so ReLU(2) is 2. A final class rule is separate.
A bounded number is a calibrated probability
A range restriction comes from the formula. Calibration needs appropriate evidence.
Nonlinearity guarantees a better result
It changes which functions can be represented; data, fitting and valid evaluation still determine model quality.
teacher.assessment: Assess W4 for z values -2, 0, 3, ReLU values 0, 0, 3, final outputs 1, 1, 7 and identity outputs -3, 1, 7. Fresh retry: z = 2x - 3, a = ReLU(z), y = a - 1 at x = 1, 1.5, 3. The triples (z, a, y) are (-1, 0, -1), (0, 0, -1), (3, 3, 2). Require an explanation of which distinctions were erased.
teacher.support: Use a number line and a three-column z, a, y table. Supply sigmoid values rather than requiring exponent calculations from memory. Extension: use several inputs to verify that sigmoid(z) and sigmoid(-z) sum to 1 within rounding error, while noting that this symmetry is not evidence of calibration.
teacher.next: Week 5 composes layers and traces how activations become inputs to the next computation.

ai-4/5.title: Composing layers
goals: Trace how one layer supplies the next layer inputs
Check that connected layer dimensions and feature order agree
Explain why intermediate activations are not automatically class predictions

prerequisite.prompt: For z = -2 and z = 3, what does ReLU return? Does this operation itself assign a class?
prerequisite.answer: ReLU returns 0 and 3. It transforms a numerical score. A class prediction requires a separate declared output rule.

vocabulary: A group of computations that maps an input vector to an output vector
An intermediate value computed inside a network
Applying one function to the output of another
Computing successive values from an input using fixed parameters

lesson.title: Connect computations with an explicit contract

blocks.text: A network connects layers so that the output vector of one layer becomes the input vector of the next. Use a fictional numerical input x = [x1, x2]. The first layer computes z1 = x1 - x2 and z2 = x1 + x2 - 2, then applies ReLU separately: h1 = max(0, z1), h2 = max(0, z2). Its output is the ordered vector h = [h1, h2].

The next layer computes y = 2h1 - h2 + 1. It receives h, not the original x. It uses weights [2, -1] and bias 1, with identity as its output activation. This is a two-layer computation when counting the layers with weights; an input placeholder is not counted here. All parameters are supplied, so this lesson performs no training.
The two first-layer units both receive the same original x. They can be calculated in either order. Only after both activations are available do we evaluate the output layer.

Take x = [3, 1]. First compute z1 = 3 - 1 = 2 and z2 = 3 + 1 - 2 = 2. ReLU gives h = [2, 2]. The output layer receives exactly this ordered pair and returns y = 2 times 2 - 2 + 1 = 3. Record z, h and y separately so that a correct final number cannot hide an incorrect intermediate step.

blocks.title: Optional Python check
blocks.text:
def forward(x):
    if len(x) != 2:
        raise ValueError("Expected two input components")
    x1, x2 = x
    z = [x1 - x2, x1 + x2 - 2]
    h = [max(0, value) for value in z]
    y = 2 * h[0] - h[1] + 1
    return z, h, y

print(forward([3, 1]))  # ([2, 2], [2, 2], 3)
print(forward([1, 3]))  # ([-2, 2], [0, 2], -1)

The code assumes numeric inputs with the agreed meaning. Its length check does not validate units or field order. Python indices 0 and 1 correspond to the first and second hidden components. There is no feedback from y into h during this forward calculation.

blocks.title: Complete each stage before using its output
blocks.caption: Read the rows from top to bottom. The first two rows together form the hidden layer; the final row is the output layer. Each row shows the values actually passed to the next stage.

blocks.label: Trace x = [1, 1]. Record z1, z2, h1, h2 and y. Explain why using x directly in the output formula would be a different model.

blocks.text: The output layer expects two inputs because its two weights match h1 and h2. If the hidden layer is redesigned to return three activations, the output layer needs a compatible three-input definition. Silently dropping an activation or inventing a third weight does not preserve the stated model.

Order matters even when lengths match. For x = [4, 1], h = [3, 3] happens to be unchanged by swapping, so that case cannot reveal an order bug. For x = [3, 0], h = [3, 1] gives y = 6. Swapping only those hidden values gives 2 times 1 - 3 + 1 = 0. Swapping both the values and their matching weights would preserve the dot product.

Keeping the output layer fixed, replacing ReLU with identity changes the model. For x = [1, 3], identity gives h = [-2, 2] and y = -5; ReLU gives h = [0, 2] and y = -1. More layers or a different activation do not establish better predictions without valid evaluation.

The computed y is a numerical output, not a verified probability or a class by itself. If we separately declare class 1 when y >= 0 and class 0 otherwise, the worked inputs [3, 1] and [1, 3] receive classes 1 and 0. Their true labels are not supplied, so these calculations do not measure accuracy.

A hidden value is a computed feature. We should not name h1 as confidence or h2 as danger without evidence for that interpretation. Distinct inputs may also produce the same hidden vector: [0, 1] and [0, 2] both give h = [0, 0] and y = 1. A later deterministic layer seeing only h cannot recover the lost distinction.

blocks.label: A team says its output is correct because all layers connect and its code runs. Which claim has it checked, and what evidence is still missing?

blocks.text: Next week uses longer forward-pass tables to locate the first incorrect intermediate value and check complete network calculations.

workbook.title: Trace the second worked case
workbook.prompt: For x = [1, 3], write both scores, both ReLU activations and y using the lesson model.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Scores are -2 and 2; activations are 0 and 2; y = 0 - 2 + 1 = -1.

workbook.title: Repair a dimension mismatch
workbook.prompt: A revised hidden layer returns [h1, h2, h3]. The output layer still has weights [2, -1]. Explain the mismatch and what must be specified before calculation.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Three hidden values need three matching weights under this dense output definition. Specify all three coefficients and the bias or explicitly design a documented selection operation. Do not silently drop the third value.

workbook.title: Use a revealing order check
workbook.prompt: Compare hidden vectors for x = [4, 1] and x = [3, 0]. Which input reveals a bug that swaps h1 and h2 but keeps output weights unchanged? Give correct and swapped outputs for that input.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: The first gives [3, 3] and cannot expose a swap. The second gives [3, 1]; correct output 6 becomes 0 when values alone are swapped.

workbook.title: Compose a new network independently
workbook.prompt: A new model takes [u, v]. Compute a = ReLU(u + v - 3), b = ReLU(u - v), then q = a + 2b - 1. Trace both inputs [2, 1] and [1, 2], including scores before ReLU. Apply class 1 when q >= 0. State the hidden and output vector sizes.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: For [2, 1], scores 0 and 1 give [a, b] = [0, 1], q = 1 and class 1. For [1, 2], scores 0 and -1 give [0, 0], q = -1 and class 0. Hidden dimension is 2; output dimension is 1. The equality at hidden score zero produces activation zero, not an automatic final class.

workbook.title: Explain information loss
workbook.prompt: Use the lesson model to verify h and y for [0, 1] and [0, 2]. Could a fixed later layer receiving only h distinguish the two original inputs?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Scores are [-1, -1] and [-2, 0]. Both produce h = [0, 0] and y = 1. A deterministic later computation given the same h produces the same result; additional original-input information would require a changed architecture.

teacher.background: Teach composition through explicit numerical traces in two 45-minute sessions. Keep the layer definition, order and activation visible. The aim is to understand which values each computation receives, not to memorise a network drawing or claim successful training.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook; paper and pencil
Calculator and optional local Python 3 editor; no packages or AI accounts needed
Use the fictional examples supplied; prepare the fresh retry before class
sessions: Retrieve ReLU at negative, zero and positive scores. Ask students to distinguish an activation from a class.
Write both first-layer formulas side by side. Draw arrows from the same x to both; label the ordered hidden output.
Trace [3, 1] together, then use W1. Require scores before ReLU and output contributions after ReLU.
Run or trace the optional Python and complete the guided [1, 1] case. Ask why directly substituting x into the output formula is incorrect.
Retrieve the two layer input/output sizes. Let students describe composition in one sentence.
Complete W2 and W3. Compare a swap-insensitive case with a revealing case before discussing bug coverage.
Collect W4 independently before hints. Check both pre-activation scores, both activations, q and class under the declared threshold.
Complete W5 and the exit response. Give targeted feedback and the fresh retry without replacing the original assessment record.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided: x = [1, 1] gives z = [0, 0], h = [0, 0], y = 1. Using x directly would give 2, skipping the hidden transformation. Exit: compatible shapes and execution check whether the specified computation can run, not whether predictions match real labels. Accuracy requires appropriate labelled examples, a metric and independent evaluation.
misconceptions: The second hidden unit receives the first hidden unit output
Both units in this hidden layer receive x. The next layer receives the pair of activations after both are computed.
Two numbers mean the connection must be correct
Matching lengths do not establish matching order or meaning. Trace a case with unequal hidden activations.
A hidden unit is already a class prediction
Its activation is an intermediate numerical feature. A declared output rule assigns the final class.
teacher.assessment: W4 requires both complete traces, correct classes and sizes. Fresh retry: a = ReLU(u - 1), b = ReLU(v - 2), q = 2a - b. Inputs [0, 3] and [2, 2] give pre-activation scores [-1, 1] and [1, 0], hidden vectors [0, 1] and [1, 0], and q values -1 and 2. Under q >= 0 their classes are 0 and 1. Ask which vector the output layer actually receives.
teacher.support: Provide a five-column trace table labelled x, z, h, output contributions and y. Allow arithmetic support while requiring the student to name each connection. Extension: replace hidden ReLU with identity and simplify the lesson network to y = x1 - 3x2 + 3. Test [1, 3] to show that the simplified affine model differs from the ReLU model.
teacher.next: Week 6 develops forward passes by hand and systematic checking of intermediate values.

ai-4/6.title: Forward passes by hand
goals: Record scores and activations in dependency order
Locate the first incorrect value in a forward trace
Separate a final output from evidence of model accuracy

prerequisite.prompt: In Week 5, what does the output layer receive?
prerequisite.answer: It receives the ordered hidden activation vector, rather than the original input or the scores before activation.

vocabulary: A record of intermediate values in a computation
A weighted score before an activation function
An earlier value needed to compute a later value
A retained test rerun after a change to detect a new error

blocks.text: Use a new one-input network with two hidden units. Its scores are z1 = 2x - 1 and z2 = -x + 2. Apply ReLU to obtain h1 and h2. The output is y = h1 - 2h2 + 1. Parameters stay fixed while the input changes. The input x is an abstract number; these are arithmetic examples, not measurements of children.

A forward pass evaluates this network in dependency order. Compute both scores from x, then both activations, then the output contributions h1 and -2h2, and finally add bias 1. A trace table makes an omitted bias or a sign error easier to locate than a final answer alone.
At x = 1 the output is exactly zero. If we later declare class 1 for y >= 0, equality belongs to class 1. Applying ReLU in the hidden layer does not make the final output nonnegative.

For x = 0, the first score is -1, which ReLU changes to 0. The second score is 2, which ReLU leaves at 2. Therefore y = 0 - 4 + 1 = -3. Negative output is allowed because this output layer uses identity.

blocks.title: Optional Python check
blocks.text:
def trace(x):
    z = [2 * x - 1, -x + 2]
    h = [max(0, value) for value in z]
    y = h[0] - 2 * h[1] + 1
    return z, h, y

for x in [0, 1, 3]:
    print(x, trace(x))

This optional Python uses only numeric inputs. Compare every returned component against the table. The same code being run twice is a repeatability check; comparing it with a separately calculated expectation is a stronger check of correctness.

blocks.title: Correct a trace from the earliest error
blocks.caption: The columns compare expected and submitted traces. The first disagreement is the activation of -1, not the final addition. Recompute all dependent values after repairing it.

blocks.label: Trace x = 2, recording both scores, both activations and y. What happens to the second unit at its zero-score boundary?

lesson.title: Choose checks that can reveal a defect

blocks.text: A test where both scores are positive cannot reveal a missing ReLU. Include x = 0, where the first score is negative, and x = 3, where the second score is negative. Include x = 0.5 and x = 2 to exercise each hidden zero-score boundary. Neither a few examples nor an attractive diagram proves every implementation case is correct.

A missing output bias shifts every output by -1. A swapped hidden order may pass a case where h1 equals h2; x = 1 has this limitation. Keep several checks with different intermediate values, and retain them when repairing code.

lesson.title: Report the claim that was checked

blocks.text: A forward trace verifies what specified parameters calculate for one input. It does not show how those parameters were learned or whether the output is useful. Classification accuracy also needs a declared class rule, true labels and suitable independent examples.

blocks.label: A program matches y at x = 1 but its hidden activations are wrong. Is the implementation verified? Explain what evidence to retain after fixing it.

blocks.text: Next week separates the network architecture from its numerical parameters and counts the values that training could change.

workbook.title: Complete a fresh row
workbook.prompt: Trace x = -1 through the lesson network. Record z, h and y.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: z = [-3, 3], h = [0, 3], y = -5.

workbook.title: Locate a bias omission
workbook.prompt: At x = 3 a trace gives z = [5, -1], h = [5, 0] and y = 5. Identify the first incorrect stage and repair it.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Scores and activations are correct. The output omitted bias 1; y should be 6.

workbook.title: Check both boundaries
workbook.prompt: Trace x = 0.5 and x = 2. Which hidden score is zero in each case?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: At 0.5, z = [0, 1.5], h = [0, 1.5], y = -2. At 2, z = [3, 0], h = [3, 0], y = 4. Zero maps to zero under ReLU.

workbook.title: Audit a different network independently
workbook.prompt: Use z1 = x + 1, z2 = 2 - 2x, h = ReLU(z) component by component, and y = 2h1 + h2 - 3. Trace x = 0 and x = 2. A submitted x = 2 trace uses h = [3, -2] and y = 1. Find its first error and correct all later values.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: At 0: z = [1, 2], h = [1, 2], y = 1. At 2: z = [3, -2], h = [3, 0], y = 3. The first submitted error is h2 = -2 rather than 0; the corrected output is 3.

workbook.title: Limit a passing test
workbook.prompt: Explain why testing only x = 1 in the lesson model may miss a hidden-order swap.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Both hidden values equal 1, so exchanging them changes nothing. Use unequal hidden values, such as x = 0, and compare intermediate values as well as y.

teacher.background: Use two 45-minute sessions to build a habit of recording intermediate values. Students should identify the first disagreement, then propagate the correction. Do not award full credit for a correct final value supported by an incorrect trace.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook; paper and pencil
Calculator and optional local Python 3 editor; no packages or AI accounts needed
Use the fictional examples supplied; prepare the fresh retry before class
sessions: Retrieve the distinction between scores, hidden activations and output inputs.
Trace x = 0 on the board. Label every column and identify the output bias.
Complete W1 and compare the x = 1 and x = 3 worked rows. Discuss negative final outputs.
Run or trace Python; complete the guided x = 2 case and W2.
Reconstruct a trace from memory, then check its dependencies against the formula.
Complete W3 and discuss which cases detect missing activation and which detect order errors.
Collect W4 independently, including the first erroneous stage and corrected descendants.
Use W5 and the exit question, then offer the fresh retry after feedback.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided: x = 2 gives z = [3, 0], h = [3, 0], y = 4; the zero score remains zero. Exit: no; final agreement can hide compensating errors. Retain correct intermediate expectations and varied regression cases, not only the single final output.
misconceptions: ReLU means the output cannot be negative
Only the hidden scores receive ReLU here. The output formula can be negative.
Fix just the final number
Repair the earliest incorrect operation and recompute every dependent value.
One passing case proves the network
Cases with equal activations or positive scores can hide specific defects.
teacher.assessment: Assess W4 for both full traces and the activation error. Fresh retry: h = ReLU(x - 2), y = -3h + 2. For x = 1 and x = 4, preactivations are -1 and 2, activations 0 and 2, outputs 2 and -4. A submitted x = 1 activation -1 is the first error, even if later arithmetic compensates.
teacher.support: Provide blank trace columns and allow a calculator for signed arithmetic. Extension: show that for 0.5 <= x <= 2 the lesson output is 4x - 4; verify both endpoints without applying that expression outside its stated interval.
teacher.next: Week 7 names architectural choices and counts dense-layer parameters.

ai-4/7.title: Parameters and architecture
goals: Distinguish architectural choices from parameter values
Count weights and biases in a small dense network
Explain why parameter count alone cannot establish quality

prerequisite.prompt: In the Week 6 network, which quantities change when x changes while the model stays fixed?
prerequisite.answer: Scores, activations and outputs may change. The weights, biases, connections and activation choices stay fixed.

vocabulary: A numerical model value that a fitting procedure may adjust
The arrangement of layers, connections and activation choices
A layer in which each output unit has a weight for every input component
A setting chosen for a model or training procedure rather than fitted as an ordinary weight

lesson.title: Separate the plan from its numbers

blocks.text: Consider a dense network with 2 inputs, 3 hidden units using ReLU, and 1 output unit using identity. We call its widths 2 to 3 to 1. These widths, connectivity and activation choices describe its architecture. The weights and biases supply the numerical values used by that architecture.

A fully connected hidden unit receiving 2 inputs needs 2 weights plus 1 bias. Three such units need 6 weights and 3 biases. The output receives 3 activations and needs 3 weights plus 1 bias. Total: 13 parameters. Input values and computed activations are not additional parameters.
This counting rule assumes one separate bias per output unit and no shared or tied weights. Other architectures can use different rules.
For a dense layer with n input components and m output units, each output has n weights and one bias. The count is n times m plus m, or (n + 1) times m. Count each layer separately before adding.

blocks.title: Optional Python check
blocks.text:
def dense_count(inputs, outputs):
    return inputs * outputs + outputs

print(dense_count(2, 3))   # 9
print(dense_count(3, 1))   # 4
print(dense_count(2, 3) + dense_count(3, 1))  # 13
The helper assumes positive integer widths and the bias convention stated above. It is a counting aid, not a model trainer. A ReLU has no fitted numerical parameters in this example.

blocks.title: Decide what a change alters
blocks.caption: Each row is a separate proposed change. A parameter value, an architectural choice and a training setting answer different questions about the system.

blocks.label: For a dense 2 to 4 to 1 network with one bias per unit, count each layer and the total. How many more parameters does it have than 2 to 3 to 1?

blocks.text: Two networks can share an architecture and still make different predictions because their parameter values differ. Conversely, two architectures can happen to produce identical outputs on the few cases tested. A count describes the model, not how well it has learned.

When comparing widths, keep the task, feature schema, training data, validation cases and evaluation rule fixed. Record the training budget and seed as well. More parameters can increase flexibility, but they can also increase resource use and overfitting risk. Neither outcome follows from counting alone.

A reproducible description needs ordered input features, layer widths, connections, activations and the exact parameter values or a way to recover them. A description of training also needs the data split and training settings. The label small neural network does not specify a computation.

blocks.label: Two teams both report 13 parameters. What would you request before claiming they built the same model?

blocks.text: Next week defines a loss so that we can measure how a particular set of parameters performs on labelled examples.

workbook.title: Count a single layer
workbook.prompt: A dense layer has 4 inputs and 2 outputs with one bias per output. Count weights, biases and total.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: There are 8 weights and 2 biases, total 10.

workbook.title: Sort the quantities
workbook.prompt: Classify hidden activation 0.7, weight -2, hidden width 3 and learning rate 0.1 as computed value, parameter, architecture choice or training setting.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Activation 0.7 is computed; weight -2 is a parameter; width 3 is an architecture choice; learning rate 0.1 is a training setting.

workbook.title: Change the bias convention
workbook.prompt: Recount the 2 to 3 to 1 model if every bias is omitted. State what the original count assumed.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: There are 6 + 3 = 9 weights and no biases. The original 13 assumed three hidden biases plus one output bias.

workbook.title: Count a new architecture independently
workbook.prompt: A dense 3 to 2 to 2 network uses ReLU in the hidden layer and identity in the output layer, with one bias per unit. Give each layer count and the total. If hidden width becomes 4, recount and explain why activation values are excluded.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Original: 3 times 2 + 2 = 8, then 2 times 2 + 2 = 6, total 14. Wider: 3 times 4 + 4 = 16, then 4 times 2 + 2 = 10, total 26. Activations are computed from inputs and parameters, not separately fitted values.

workbook.title: Limit a size claim
workbook.prompt: A team says its 26-parameter model must outperform a 14-parameter model. Give a fair check and one reason the claim is unsupported.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Compare on the same valid evaluation task and cases after a documented fitting process. Count alone does not establish suitable features, successful optimisation or generalisation.

teacher.background: Teach counting through one drawn unit before using a formula. Explicitly state the dense connectivity and bias assumptions. Architecture is chosen by a designer; this does not imply it can never be selected using a separate search procedure.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook; paper and pencil
Calculator and optional local Python 3 editor; no packages or AI accounts needed
Use the fictional examples supplied; prepare the fresh retry before class
sessions: Retrieve fixed parameters versus changing activations from a forward pass.
Draw three hidden units, each with two input weights and a bias. Count without a formula first.
Complete W1 and the 13-parameter worked table. Derive (n + 1) times m.
Trace the optional counting code, classify changes and complete W2.
Recall the assumptions behind the count, then discuss omitted biases in W3.
Complete the guided 2 to 4 to 1 count; compare size without assuming quality.
Collect W4 independently with separate layer totals and the wider variant.
Use W5 and the exit response to define the evidence needed for a model comparison.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided: hidden layer 12, output layer 5, total 17, four more than 13. Exit: ask for architecture, activations, ordered input schema and exact weights/biases; equal parameter counts do not establish matching computations.
misconceptions: Count one bias per input
Here each output unit has its own bias. A layer with m outputs has m biases.
Count the activation values as parameters
Activations change with the input; the network computes them.
More weights prove better learning
Capacity and performance differ. Compare measured outcomes with controlled conditions.
teacher.assessment: W4 must show 8 + 6 = 14 and 16 + 10 = 26. Fresh retry: dense 2 to 2 to 3 with biases has 6 + 9 = 15 parameters. Without biases it has 4 + 6 = 10. Require the bias convention explicitly.
teacher.support: Use a connection grid and a separate bias box per output. Extension: for 2 to h to 1, derive 3h + h + 1 = 4h + 1; test h = 1 and h = 5. Explain why this rule is specific to the stated architecture.
teacher.next: Week 8 introduces losses for comparing predictions with targets.

ai-4/8.title: Loss functions
goals: Calculate per-example squared error and mean squared error
Distinguish residual cancellation from a low loss
Separate training loss from independent evaluation

prerequisite.prompt: Does knowing a network output tell us whether it is accurate?
prerequisite.answer: No. We also need a target or other evaluation criterion and appropriate examples.

vocabulary: The recorded value a model is intended to predict
Prediction minus target under the sign convention used here
The square of a numerical residual
The average squared error over the evaluated examples

lesson.title: Measure a prediction against a target

blocks.text: A loss assigns a numerical penalty to a prediction compared with a target. For this regression lesson, residual e = prediction - target, and squared error is e squared. Squaring makes both positive and negative residuals contribute nonnegative penalties. We use ordinary mean squared error without a one-half factor.
The mean squared error, or MSE, is (1 + 1 + 4) / 3 = 2. It summarises these three examples, not every possible future input. If targets use cm, residuals use cm and MSE uses square cm.

lesson.title: Do not let signs cancel mistakes

blocks.text: For targets [1, 3] and predictions [2, 2], the mean residual is zero because 1 and -1 cancel. MSE is 1, correctly recording that both predictions miss. A mean residual can describe directional tendency, but it is not a substitute for an error magnitude.

blocks.title: Optional Python check

blocks.text: The guard prevents silently ignoring an unmatched example or dividing by zero. It still assumes paired, numeric, valid records. Wrong row alignment produces a meaningless comparison even when list lengths agree.

lesson.title: Compare two candidates on the same cases

blocks.title: Use the same targets and denominator
blocks.caption: Each row evaluates a separate candidate against targets [1, 3, 2]. Q has the lowest MSE on these three cases. The comparison alone does not establish performance on unseen examples.

blocks.label: Candidate R predicts [0, 3, 3] for targets [1, 3, 2]. Calculate residuals, squared errors and MSE. Compare R with the baseline.

lesson.title: Choose a loss for the stated purpose

blocks.text: Squaring gives larger residuals more influence: residual 4 contributes 16, four times the penalty of residual 2. This can be useful when large misses matter, but it can also make outliers influential. Mean absolute error uses absolute residuals instead; it can rank candidates differently.

MSE is appropriate here because targets are numerical quantities. A class identifier such as 0, 1 or 2 may merely name a category; its numeric gap does not automatically measure error severity. Later classification models need a loss suited to their outputs and task.

Training loss measures the cases used to adjust parameters. Validation loss can guide choices, so repeated use makes it development evidence. A reserved final test supports a separate evaluation claim only while it remains outside those choices. Always report the split, number of cases and loss definition.

blocks.label: A model reports MSE zero on its training rows. What has this shown, and why is it insufficient to claim perfect future predictions?

blocks.text: Next week studies local changes in a loss, preparing us to choose a direction for a parameter update.

workbook.title: Calculate a loss
workbook.prompt: For targets [2, 4] and predictions [1, 6], record residuals, squares and MSE.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Residuals are -1 and 2, squares 1 and 4, MSE 2.5.

workbook.title: Expose cancellation
workbook.prompt: Targets [0, 4] have predictions [2, 2]. Compare mean residual and MSE.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Residuals 2 and -2 average to 0; squares 4 and 4 give MSE 4. Both predictions are wrong despite zero mean residual.

workbook.title: Check the denominator
workbook.prompt: A learner totals squared errors 1, 0, 9 and divides by 2 because there are two nonzero errors. Correct the MSE.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: All three evaluated examples count. MSE is 10 / 3, not 5. A zero-error example is still an example.

workbook.title: Compare an unfamiliar evaluation independently
workbook.prompt: Targets are [0, 2, 4]. Model A predicts [1, 2, 3]; model B predicts [0, 2, 2]. Calculate both MSEs and identify the better model under MSE on these cases. Calculate mean absolute errors too. State what changes in the conclusion.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: A residuals [1, 0, -1] give MSE 2/3; B [0, 0, -2] gives MSE 4/3, so A is better under MSE. Both mean absolute errors are 2/3, giving a tie under that metric. Neither ranking establishes future performance.

workbook.title: Protect final testing
workbook.prompt: A team tries ten models and picks the one with the lowest final-test MSE. Can that same result be presented as an untouched final evaluation?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: No. The test informed selection and became development evidence. Preserve the result with that disclosure, freeze the chosen process and use fresh independent evaluation for a new final claim.

teacher.background: Keep paired prediction and target rows visible in both 45-minute sessions. Require residuals, per-row penalties and the denominator before accepting an average. This week uses regression and ordinary MSE; do not introduce a different scaling convention midway.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook; paper and pencil
Calculator and optional local Python 3 editor; no packages or AI accounts needed
Use the fictional examples supplied; prepare the fresh retry before class

Calculate A, B and C row by row. Explain the sign convention and units.
Complete W1 and W2, showing how cancellation hides error.
Run or trace the guarded MSE code; try unequal and empty lists.
Use W3 to recover the full denominator, then compare the visual candidates.

misconceptions: Average residual is the loss
Signed residuals can cancel. Apply the specified penalty before averaging.
Ignore perfect predictions in the average
The denominator includes every valid evaluated pair, including zero-error cases.
One metric gives the universal winner
Different losses express different penalties. Choose and disclose the criterion.
teacher.assessment: W4 requires MSEs 2/3 and 4/3, tied MAEs 2/3, and limited claims. Fresh retry: targets [1, 5], predictions [3, 4] give residuals [2, -1], MSE 2.5 and MAE 1.5. Reject averaging the residuals to 0.5 as an error magnitude.
teacher.support: Provide a residual and squared-error table and permit a calculator for fractions. Extension: if both targets and predictions are converted from cm to mm, explain why residuals multiply by 10 and MSE by 100 while candidate ranking stays the same.
