ai-2/9.title: Return values and local state
goals: Use a returned value in a later calculation
Trace local variables separately for each function call
Detect a missing return and test repeated calls

prerequisite.prompt: A function show_remaining(capacity, used) prints capacity - used. What does calling it with (9, 4) display? Does defining it alone display that result?
prerequisite.answer: The call prints 5. The definition alone creates the function without running its body.

vocabulary: A value a function sends back to its caller
The code that calls a function
A name assigned inside a function and used in that function call
The region of code in which a name can be looked up
A Python value representing no result value in this lesson

lesson.title: Keep a result for another calculation

blocks.text: Two fictional cupboards have spare spaces. We want to add their spare spaces without copying numbers from the screen. Last week a function printed each answer. This week a function returns its answer so the calling code can store it, combine it or choose to print it.

Assume nonnegative integer counts and used no greater than capacity. This calculation does not validate those assumptions. Work in a Python script so a call does not automatically display its return value as it might in an interactive console.

lesson.title: Follow the result back to the caller

blocks.title: Python 3 code
blocks.text:
def remaining(capacity, used):
    spaces = capacity - used
    return spaces

first = remaining(12, 4)
second = remaining(10, 7)
print(first + second)

blocks.title: Two calls return two values
blocks.caption: The caller adds the returned values. Only print(first + second) displays 11.

blocks.text: return spaces ends the current function call and sends the value of spaces back. The assignment first = remaining(12, 4) waits for that value and stores 8. The next call stores 3 in second. Neither call prints. The final statement prints 11. A statement after an executed return in the same call is not reached.

lesson.title: Give each call its own local names

rows: Not accessible by this local name

blocks.text: capacity, used and spaces belong to the current call. The second call gets new parameter values and calculates its own spaces; it does not overwrite first. In a fresh script with no outside variable called spaces, adding print(spaces) after the calls raises NameError. Use the returned value stored in first or second instead.

blocks.label: Change the calls to remaining(9, 9) and remaining(9, 0). What values are stored and what does their sum print? What happens if only the final print statement is removed?

lesson.title: Repair a function that only prints

blocks.title: Python 3 code
blocks.text:
def remaining(capacity, used):
    spaces = capacity - used
    print(spaces)

answer = remaining(12, 4)
print(answer)

This faulty version displays 8 and then None. It reaches the end of its body without a return statement, so the call returns None. Printing 8 inside the function does not make 8 its return value. None is not zero. Trying answer + 1 raises TypeError in this example.

Replace print(spaces) inside the function with return spaces. Keep print(answer) in the caller. The repaired script prints 8 once, and the caller can calculate answer + 1. Test the stored value as well as what appears on screen.

lesson.title: Test fresh state and a usable result

blocks.text: For a function that only calculates from these integer arguments, repeat the first call after a different call. remaining(12, 4), remaining(10, 7), remaining(12, 4) should return 8, 3, 8. Store each result and compare it with a prediction. These examples create fresh local variables each time; do not assume every possible function is independent of earlier calls.

blocks.label: A learner says that a function is correct because it prints 8. Explain how you would check that its caller actually receives 8. Include a second call and say why two passing tests are limited evidence.

workbook.title: Separate returning from displaying
workbook.prompt: Using the correct worked definition, execute result = remaining(15, 6), then doubled = result * 2. State both stored values and what the script displays before a print statement is added.
workbook.answer: result is 9 and doubled is 18. Nothing is displayed by these assignments or the returning function. print(doubled) would display 18.

workbook.title: Trace separate calls
workbook.prompt: Using the correct definition, store a = remaining(8, 3), b = remaining(8, 8), c = remaining(8, 3). State a, b and c. In a fresh script, explain why print(spaces) outside the function fails.
workbook.answer: a is 5, b is 0, c is 5. Each call has its own local spaces. That name has not been defined outside the function, so print(spaces) there raises NameError. Print a, b or c to use the saved results.

workbook.title: Repair the returned value
workbook.prompt: Use the faulty printing version with answer = remaining(11, 2). State the displayed number and the value stored in answer. Explain why print(answer + 1) fails, then repair the function and predict the repaired output.
workbook.answer: The call displays 9 but stores None. None + 1 raises TypeError. Replace the internal print(spaces) with return spaces. The repaired call itself displays nothing; print(answer + 1) displays 10. Rerun (12, 4) and check that the stored value is 8.

workbook.title: Build a reusable calculation independently
workbook.prompt: Each tray holds 5 counters. Define stock(trays, loose) to return the total using a local variable total. Assume nonnegative integer arguments. Store results for (2, 3), (0, 3) and (2, 0). Print the sum of the first two stored results. Predict that output and all three stored values. Call (2, 3) again to check fresh state.
workbook.answer: Define stock(trays, loose) with total = trays * 5 + loose followed by return total. Store values 13, 3 and 10. The sum of the first two is 16. The repeat returns 13. The function should not print; the caller prints 16.

workbook.title: Locate a statement that never runs
workbook.prompt: A function body has spaces = capacity - used, then return spaces, then print("done"), all at the same indentation. What does answer = remaining(4, 4) store and display? Explain whether the final print can run.
workbook.answer: The call stores 0 and displays nothing. return ends this call, so the following print("done") is not reached. Zero is a valid returned value here and is different from None.

teacher.background: Use integer inputs, explicit return and simple local assignments. Avoid global variables, mutable defaults and shared objects in this introduction. Python reference: https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/controlflow.html#defining-functions. A call has its own local names; return sends a value to the caller. Examples assume valid counts and do not validate them.
materials: Python 3 editor and returns.py
Separate paper spaces for each call and the caller
Expected return value and observed return value table
sessions: Retrieve the Week 8 distinction between definition and call.
Trace the worked example and move returned-value cards to first and second.
Complete W1 and trace local names separately for W2.
Predict the guided case, run it and explain why assignments do not print.
Recall where the caller stores a return value.
Run the printing bug, record None and repair it for W3.
Collect independent W4 code and predictions before offering hints.
Use W5 and the exit to check return control flow and test evidence.
teacher.guidedAnswer: first stores 0, second stores 9, and the final print displays 9. Removing only that print leaves the calculations and stored values but no displayed output. Exit: assign answer = remaining(12, 4), then print(answer) and check it is 8 rather than None. Repeat with (10, 7), expecting 3. Passing two tests does not establish all-input correctness or verify the input assumptions.
misconceptions: Printing a value returns that value
print displays a value. Without an explicit return, these functions return None.
A second call overwrites the first saved answer
These integer results are stored separately in the caller. A later call creates new local bindings.
A local name is available anywhere
spaces is assigned inside remaining. In our fresh script it cannot be looked up outside that function.
Zero means the function returned nothing
Zero is a number and supports arithmetic. None is a different value.
teacher.assessment: W4 must use both arguments, return its local total, store 13, 3, 10 and print 16 in the caller. Repeating (2, 3) must return 13. After support use fresh retry tiles(packs, singles), with 4 tiles per pack: (3, 2), (0, 2), (3, 0) return 14, 2, 12; print the sum of the first two, 16; repeat (3, 2) to obtain 14. Record help used and collect predictions before running.
teacher.support: Use separate boxes on paper labelled caller and current call. Move the value card at return, not the local name. Offer the definition header as a hint and record it. Extension: set spaces = 100 outside the correct worked function, call remaining(9, 4), then print the returned result and outside spaces separately. Expect 5 and 100. Explain why the two assignments use different scopes; do not generalize this to mutation of shared objects.

ai-2/10.title: Dictionaries and records
goals: Read and update named dictionary fields
Connect a record to a function call
Distinguish missing fields from zero values

prerequisite.prompt: What does remaining(8, 3) return when its body returns capacity - used?
prerequisite.answer: 5; the caller may store or print it.

vocabulary: A mapping from unique keys to values
A name used to look up a value
The error from looking up an absent dictionary key

blocks.text: A fictional cupboard record has a name, capacity and used count. A list asks us to remember positions. Named fields make the intended meaning visible. Our schema requires name as text and capacity and used as nonnegative integers, with used no greater than capacity.

blocks.title: Python 3 code
Follow the evidence
blocks.caption: Read each row from left to right and connect the evidence to the stated rule.

blocks.text: Square brackets look up the value for a key. The quoted key "used" is text; its value is an integer. Assigning to an existing key replaces that field. Other fields remain the same. Dictionary syntax does not enforce our schema: the programmer must check it.

blocks.label: Set used to 12. Predict the returned spaces. Does a used value of 0 mean the field is missing?

blocks.text: cupboard["Used"] raises KeyError here because keys are case sensitive. Correct it to "used". Adding a new field called "Used" would create a second key and leave the original unchanged; it would not repair the intended lookup.
Named fields reduce position mistakes but do not prove that a record is accurate. A capacity of 2 with used of 5 is representable in a dictionary and violates this schema.

blocks.label: A record has capacity 3 and used 4. It gives -1 spaces without an error. Should it be accepted? Explain.

workbook.title: Identify fields
workbook.prompt: For {"name": "Red", "capacity": 9, "used": 2}, state the keys, value of used and remaining spaces.
workbook.answer: Keys name, capacity, used; used is 2; remaining spaces 7.

workbook.title: Trace an update
workbook.prompt: Change the Red record used to 9. State remaining spaces and whether capacity changes.
workbook.answer: Spaces 0; capacity remains 9.

workbook.title: Repair a lookup
workbook.prompt: The code reads record["Used"] from the Red record. Explain the error and repair it without adding a field.
workbook.answer: KeyError because Used is absent. Use record["used"].

workbook.title: Build a record independently
workbook.prompt: Create a Green record with capacity 15 and used 6. Pass its fields to remaining and store the result. Update used to 10 and repeat. Predict both results.
workbook.answer: Use a dictionary with name Green, capacity 15, used 6; results are 9 and then 5. The second call must read the updated field.

workbook.title: Check the contract
workbook.prompt: A record has capacity 3 and used 4. It gives -1 spaces without an error. Should it be accepted? Explain.
workbook.answer: No. The used count exceeds capacity. Successful arithmetic does not validate the record.

teacher.background: Teach Week 10 as a two-session investigation using fictional data. A fictional cupboard record has a name, capacity and used count. A list asks us to remember positions. Named fields make the intended meaning visible. Our schema requires name as text and capacity and used as nonnegative integers, with used no greater than capacity. Assess the three stated outcomes through the independent task, not by copying the worked result.

misconceptions: A successful run proves the conclusion
Named fields reduce position mistakes but do not prove that a record is accurate. A capacity of 2 with used of 5 is representable in a dictionary and violates this schema.
Matching the example is enough

Require the new W4 case, explicit predictions and an explanation. Fresh retry: create a Gold record with capacity 11 and used 3; return 8, update used to 11 and return 0. Require field lookups rather than copied literal arguments.
A convenient shortcut preserves meaning

Record whether the learner needed no help, a hint or explanation. Fresh retry: create a Gold record with capacity 11 and used 3; return 8, update used to 11 and return 0. Require field lookups rather than copied literal arguments.

ai-2/11.title: Reading structured data
goals: Process a list of records consistently
Compute a total from named fields
Preserve record meaning while tracing a loop

prerequisite.prompt: Which key stores the occupied count in {"capacity": 8, "used": 3}?
prerequisite.answer: The key "used" stores 3.

vocabulary: One named part of a record
A variable updated to keep a running result

blocks.text: Two fictional cupboards are stored as a list of dictionaries. Each record uses the same keys and units. We want the total spare spaces. Treat the records as a dataset, and trace one record at a time before trusting a total.

blocks.title: Python 3 code
blocks.text:
rows = [{"capacity": 8, "used": 3},
        {"capacity": 6, "used": 6}]
total = 0
for row in rows:
    spare = row["capacity"] - row["used"]
    total = total + spare
print(total)

blocks.title: Follow the evidence
blocks.caption: Read each row from left to right and connect the evidence to the stated rule.

blocks.text: The loop variable row refers to each record in turn. We calculate spare from that record, then add it. total starts before the loop. An empty list produces 0 because there are no updates; it does not tell us whether no cupboards exist or records were not collected.

blocks.label: Add a third record with capacity 10 and used 4. Predict the total and list each contribution.

blocks.text: Putting total = 0 inside the loop discards earlier contributions. With the original rows it finishes at 0, the second contribution. Move the initialization before the loop and rerun both the original and reversed row order.
This loop assumes every record has the required integer fields. A missing used field causes KeyError. Do not silently treat a missing count as zero; that would invent unused capacity.

blocks.label: An empty dataset produces total 0. Can you conclude that every cupboard is full?

workbook.title: Read a row
workbook.prompt: In the worked dataset, state the number of records and the spare spaces in the second record.
workbook.answer: There are 2 records. The second has 0 spare spaces.

workbook.title: Trace all updates
workbook.prompt: For spare contributions 2, 4 and 1, trace total starting at 0.
workbook.answer: Running totals 2, 6, 7.

workbook.title: Repair initialization
workbook.prompt: A loop resets total to 0 on each pass over contributions 2, 4, 1. What final total appears and how should it be fixed?
workbook.answer: It ends at 1. Initialize total once before the loop; repaired total 7.

workbook.title: Process new records independently
workbook.prompt: Write a loop for records (capacity 9, used 2), (capacity 5, used 1), and (capacity 4, used 4). Predict the total. Reverse the order and test an empty list.
workbook.answer: Contributions 7, 4, 0 give 11 in either order. Empty list gives 0. The loop must use both fields for every row.

workbook.title: Interpret an empty result
workbook.prompt: An empty dataset produces total 0. Can you conclude that every cupboard is full?
workbook.answer: No. No records were processed; the result provides no evidence about actual cupboards.

ai-2/15.title: Units conversions and data provenance
goals: Convert compatible units before comparing
Retain original values and provenance
Avoid inventing missing measurements

prerequisite.prompt: How many minutes are 180 seconds?
prerequisite.answer: 3 minutes, since 60 seconds make one minute.

vocabulary: The origin and processing history of data
Expressing a quantity in another unit
A value calculated from recorded data

blocks.text: Two fictional activity logs use different duration units. Log A records 180 seconds and Log B records 4 minutes. Keep the raw values, units and source labels; derive a shared unit so another learner can reproduce the comparison.

blocks.title: Python 3 code
Follow the evidence
blocks.caption: Read each row from left to right and connect the evidence to the stated rule.

blocks.text: The script prints [3.0, 4]. The slash operator returns a floating-point result. The original dictionaries are unchanged. Assume nonnegative numeric raw values have already been validated. An unsupported unit produces None here and must be reported for review rather than included in arithmetic.

blocks.label: Convert 90 seconds and 0 seconds. Which is longer: 90 seconds or 2 minutes?

blocks.text: Comparing raw 180 to raw 4 ignores their units. Dividing 4 by 60 without checking its unit is also wrong: it was already minutes. Branch on the documented unit and keep a conversion note.
Correct conversion does not establish that the sources measured the same activity, used the same start and stop rules, or are accurate. Provenance helps someone investigate those differences.

blocks.label: A record contains value 8 and unit ticks with no conversion rule. Should you assume seconds?

workbook.title: Retain the source
workbook.prompt: Name four pieces of information to keep for Log A and its conversion.
workbook.answer: Source A, raw 180, unit seconds and derived 3.0 minutes; also record divide by 60.

workbook.title: Convert precisely
workbook.prompt: Convert 150 seconds and 30 seconds to minutes without rounding to whole numbers.
workbook.answer: 2.5 and 0.5 minutes.

workbook.title: Repair a comparison
workbook.prompt: A report claims 120 seconds exceeds 3 minutes because 120 > 3. Correct it.
workbook.answer: 120 seconds is 2 minutes, so 3 minutes is longer.

workbook.title: Normalize independently
workbook.prompt: Create records for 240 seconds, 1.5 minutes and 60 seconds. Derive minutes while keeping raw data. State the values and their total.
workbook.answer: 4.0, 1.5 and 1.0 minutes; total 6.5 minutes. Retain original units and values.

workbook.title: Handle an unknown unit
workbook.prompt: A record contains value 8 and unit ticks with no conversion rule. Should you assume seconds?
workbook.answer: No. Mark it unresolved and ask for the unit definition. Do not include it as a known duration.

ai-2/16.title: Summaries with counts and proportions
goals: Count categories with a stated denominator
Compute proportions from eligible records
Report excluded and unknown responses

prerequisite.prompt: If 3 of 12 responses are Yes, what fraction are Yes?
prerequisite.answer: 3/12, which is 1/4.

vocabulary: The total number used in a fraction
A part divided by its relevant whole

blocks.text: A fictional poll asks whether a short activity was useful. Responses are Yes, No or Unknown. We will report Yes among known responses and also disclose unknown responses. Choosing a denominator changes the question being answered.

Follow the evidence

blocks.text: The printed proportion is 0.75, or 75 percent, among four known responses. Yes among all five supplied responses is 0.6, or 60 percent. Both calculations are correct when labelled; they describe different denominators. Unknown must not silently become No.

blocks.label: For Yes, No, Unknown, Unknown, calculate Yes among known and Yes among all supplied.

blocks.text: Dividing by known when it equals 0 causes ZeroDivisionError. Test known > 0 before division and report no known responses if none exist. Reporting 0 percent would wrongly suggest known responses with no Yes answers.
A percentage from a few volunteers is not automatically representative of the whole class. Report counts, the question, who responded and exclusions alongside the percentage.

workbook.title: Repair zero division

workbook.answer: No known responses, with 3 unknown. Do not divide by zero or report 0 percent as a measured proportion.

workbook.prompt: Process Yes, Yes, No, Unknown, No, Yes. Report Yes count, known count, unknown count and Yes proportion among known.
workbook.answer: 3 Yes, 5 known, 1 unknown; 3/5 = 0.6 = 60 percent.

workbook.title: Avoid overclaiming
workbook.prompt: Three of five known volunteers said Yes. Can you say 60 percent of all students agree?
workbook.answer: No. The denominator is known volunteers, and participation may not represent all students.

The starting reference value on a scale
A graph using bar lengths to compare categories
The mapping from values to positions or lengths

ai-2/21.title: Relationships and confounding
goals: Describe associations without claiming cause
Suggest a plausible confounder
Propose a fairer comparison

prerequisite.prompt: Can a survey of only one club establish the preference of all students?
prerequisite.answer: No; selection and coverage limit the claim.

vocabulary: Two variables vary together in observed data
A change in one factor produces a change in another
A factor related to both the proposed cause and outcome

blocks.text: In a fictional log, groups that practiced longer also scored higher: 1 hour with 4 points, 2 hours with 6 and 3 hours with 8. This pattern is an association. Prior experience could affect both practice choices and scores. The table alone cannot establish the effect of adding practice time.

blocks.title: Python 3 code
blocks.text:
rows = [{"hours": 1, "score": 4},
        {"hours": 2, "score": 6},
        {"hours": 3, "score": 8}]
for row in rows:
    print(row["hours"], row["score"])

blocks.title: Follow the evidence
blocks.caption: Read each row from left to right and connect the evidence to the stated rule.

blocks.text: The numbers rise together in these three invented records. A description such as higher practice hours went with higher scores is supported. A claim that one extra hour guarantees two more points goes beyond the observations. No statistical calculation is required to see this limit.

blocks.label: Name one factor besides practice duration that could influence both time chosen and score.

blocks.text: A chart title Practice causes success overstates the evidence. Replace it with Practice time and scores in three fictional records, and describe the possible confounder. Better wording does not repair the study, but it makes the report honest.

A fairer comparison could offer the same task, instructions and assessment and randomly assign fictional groups to practice conditions. In real classrooms, a teacher must approve any activity and protect equal learning opportunities; this lesson uses a paper plan.

blocks.label: Even a better comparison has only four fictional groups. What should be reported?

workbook.title: Describe the evidence

workbook.answer: Higher recorded practice hours are associated with higher scores in these three records.

workbook.prompt: Explain how prior experience could relate to both practice time and score.
workbook.answer: Experienced learners may choose different practice amounts and also score higher even without additional practice.

workbook.prompt: A learner predicts every student gains 2 points per extra hour. Explain why that is unsupported.
workbook.answer: The three observations do not establish a universal causal rule or predict every individual; other factors and variation are unmeasured.

workbook.prompt: A fictional dataset links more hints used with lower scores. Give a noncausal explanation and plan a fairer comparison of whether hints help.
workbook.answer: Learners finding tasks harder may use more hints and score lower. Use comparable tasks and starting skill, a teacher-approved or paper random-assignment plan, same outcome measure and report uncertainty; do not deny needed support.

workbook.prompt: Even a better comparison has only four fictional groups. What should be reported?
workbook.answer: Small size, constructed data, conditions and measured outcome; do not generalize broadly or claim classroom effectiveness.

ai-2/25.title: File input and output
goals: Read a small local data file
Close files reliably with a context manager
Separate raw text from parsed numbers

prerequisite.prompt: Is "12" immediately usable as an integer count?
prerequisite.answer: It is text; conversion and validation are needed.

vocabulary: Stored data with a name and location
A location used to find a file
A rule for representing text as bytes
A with block that manages a resource such as closing a file

blocks.text: Use a teacher-provided local sandbox folder, never a real personal file. Create durations.txt with two lines: 12 and 8. The goal is to read the text, convert it to integers and report the total. Keep the original file unchanged for this activity.

blocks.title: Python 3 code
blocks.text:
with open("durations.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
    lines = handle.read().splitlines()
values = []
for line in lines:
    values.append(int(line))
print(sum(values))

blocks.title: Follow the evidence
blocks.caption: Read each row from left to right and connect the evidence to the stated rule.

blocks.text: The mode r means read. with closes the file when the block finishes, including when an error occurs. splitlines separates lines without retaining newline characters. This example assumes each line is a valid integer text; an empty line or twelve raises ValueError during int conversion.

blocks.label: If the file contains 0, 3 and 7 on separate lines, predict the values and total.

blocks.text: If Python cannot find durations.txt, it raises FileNotFoundError. Check the current working folder and exact filename. Do not switch to write mode to solve a missing input: opening an existing file with w would replace its contents.

File reading does not establish that the values are valid durations. After conversion, apply the schema and record any rejected lines. Do not upload personal records to an external tool for this exercise.

blocks.label: The file contains twelve on one line. Why should the program not silently turn it into zero?

workbook.answer: The parsed values sum to 5 + 0 + 2 = 7.

workbook.answer: Use the correct path to class-data/durations.txt or run from the intended folder. Keep read mode and do not overwrite the input.

workbook.prompt: In a fresh sandbox file counters.txt put 4, 6 and 0 on separate lines. Adapt the reader, print the number of values and total. State the expected results.
workbook.answer: Read counters.txt as UTF-8 text, convert three lines to integers; count 3 and total 10. Keep the raw file unchanged.

workbook.answer: It is a parse failure, not a measured zero. Flag the line and report the problem; silently substituting changes the evidence.

ai-2/27.title: Exceptions and recovery
goals: Handle expected exceptions specifically
Keep parse failures distinct from valid zero
Return a clear outcome for every input path

prerequisite.prompt: Which error can int("twelve") raise?
prerequisite.answer: ValueError.

vocabulary: A signal that an operation could not complete normally
Code that responds to a specified exception
A defined next step after a failure
A label stating the outcome of a processing step

blocks.text: A small parser receives duration text. Its contract permits a string representing a nonnegative integer up to 60. Invalid numeric text should return a clear status rather than crash or pretend that the duration was zero. Test both the successful and failing paths.

blocks.title: Python 3 code
Follow the evidence
blocks.caption: Read each row from left to right and connect the evidence to the stated rule.

blocks.text: try covers the operation expected to fail; except ValueError handles that known conversion failure. Returning early ends the failing path. This contract expects a string: it does not claim to handle every possible object. Spaces around an integer are accepted by int, and that behavior should be documented.

blocks.label: Predict statuses and values for "-1", " 5 " and "3.5".

blocks.text: A bare except that returns 0 hides unrelated programming errors and corrupts missing values. Catch the expected exception, preserve an error status and keep the unknown value as None. If file reading is added, handle FileNotFoundError separately with an actionable message.

Recovery must fit the task. A caller may ask for corrected input or exclude the row with a recorded reason. It must not use None as a number or claim that rejected records were successfully processed.

blocks.label: A batch has 8 valid and 2 invalid lines. What should its report include?

workbook.answer: abc gives invalid text/None; 70 gives out of range/None. Both fail but for different reasons.

workbook.answer: It confuses failure with observed zero and may hide unrelated bugs. Catch ValueError, return an explicit status and None, then validate range.

ai-2/28.title: Versioned experiments
goals: Record a reproducible experiment version
Change one factor deliberately
Keep development checks separate from final evaluation

prerequisite.prompt: Why should expected test results be written before running the function?
prerequisite.answer: To avoid changing expectations simply to match a bug.

vocabulary: An identified state of code or rules
Cases used while choosing or improving a method
Cases reserved for an evaluation after choices are fixed

blocks.text: A fictional activity scoring experiment compares two weight settings on the same development records. Save code version, input version, weights, tie rule and outputs. A label such as v2 is useful only when it refers to an identifiable saved state.

blocks.title: Python 3 code
blocks.text:
items = [{"name": "A", "fun": 4, "learning": 1},
         {"name": "B", "fun": 2, "learning": 4}]
for version, fun_weight, learning_weight in [("v1", 2, 1), ("v2", 1, 2)]:
    scores = []
    for item in items:
        scores.append(fun_weight * item["fun"]
                      + learning_weight * item["learning"])
    print(version, scores)

blocks.title: Follow the evidence
blocks.caption: Read each row from left to right and connect the evidence to the stated rule.

blocks.text: The ranking changes because the preference weights changed. That is a policy comparison, not proof that v2 is more accurate. Keep the same data and constraints when comparing weights, and record why a policy better fits the stated goal.

blocks.label: If the data also changes between v1 and v2, can the ranking change be attributed only to weights?

blocks.text: Overwriting a file called latest removes the ability to reproduce earlier results unless versions are retained elsewhere. Save identifiable versions and a run log. Avoid editing a reserved final test after seeing its output to make the chosen version look better.
Once holdout results guide another change, those cases have become development evidence. A later independent evaluation needs new reserved cases. Small holdouts still provide limited evidence.

blocks.label: You revise the policy after reading final-case failures. Are those cases still untouched holdout evidence?

workbook.title: Record a run
workbook.prompt: List five items needed to reproduce a scoring run.
workbook.answer: Code version, input version, configuration weights, tie/eligibility rules and outputs; also record date and method as useful context.

workbook.prompt: A has fun 3 and learning 2. Score it under weights (2,1) and (1,2).
workbook.answer: Scores 8 and 7.

workbook.prompt: A learner changes weights, input ratings and the time limit together. Why is attribution difficult?
workbook.answer: Multiple factors changed. Compare one deliberate change while holding the others fixed, or explicitly describe a multi-change experiment without attributing it to one cause.

workbook.prompt: Plan two versions for C (fun 5, learning 1) and D (fun 2, learning 5), using weights (2,1) and (1,2). Record expected scores, ranks, fixed data and a separate final-case plan.
workbook.answer: v1 C 11, D 9 selects C; v2 C 7, D 12 selects D. Preserve the same records and other rules; reserve unseen cases until the policy is fixed.

workbook.title: Protect evaluation
workbook.prompt: You revise the policy after reading final-case failures. Are those cases still untouched holdout evidence?
workbook.answer: No. They now informed development. Report that use and seek fresh cases for a new independent check.

ai-2/29.title: Privacy and least privilege
goals: Collect only necessary information
Give each role only needed access

prerequisite.prompt: Does a duration summary need student names to calculate a total?

vocabulary: Keeping only data needed for the stated purpose

blocks.text: A fictional class activity dashboard needs category counts, not names or personal messages. Design its data and role permissions before collection. This exercise uses invented data and policy cards; do not change the Academy's actual authentication settings.

Follow the evidence

blocks.text: The toy code prints True, False, False. It models a permission decision, not a complete security system. A real server must verify identity and enforce authorization on every protected request; hiding a button in a page is insufficient.

blocks.label: If a student manually requests the review endpoint, should hiding its menu link be enough?

blocks.text: A form asks for names, birthdays and comments to count activity preferences. Remove fields not needed for the purpose. Aggregated counts can still expose information in very small groups; choose reporting rules with the responsible teacher.

workbook.title: Limit the toy model

workbook.answer: No. It omits authentication, server integration, session protection and many other controls; it demonstrates only a policy lookup.

ai-2/30.title: A reproducible data investigation
goals: Write a reproducible data question
Connect cleaning decisions to conclusions
Report results with coverage and uncertainty

prerequisite.prompt: What should happen to an invalid duration instead of silently making it zero?
prerequisite.answer: Record the rejection and reason; preserve the raw value for authorized review.

vocabulary: A documented process for answering a question with evidence
An ordered sequence of processing steps
A record of inputs, decisions and changes
A reason a conclusion has restricted scope

blocks.text: Investigate the fictional question: among supplied sessions with valid duration records, what is the mean duration? Inputs are 10, 0, 20, None and -2 minutes. Our schema accepts exact integers 0 through 60. The wording deliberately limits the answer to accepted records.

blocks.title: Python 3 code
Follow the evidence
blocks.caption: Read each row from left to right and connect the evidence to the stated rule.

blocks.text: The result is 3 accepted, 2 rejected, and mean 10.0 minutes. A reproducible report states the question, raw input version, schema, exclusion reasons, calculation and scope. Someone else should obtain the same result from the same inputs and rules.

blocks.label: If another valid value 30 is added, calculate the new accepted count and mean.

blocks.text: Dividing the accepted total 30 by all five records gives 6 and answers no clear observed-duration question. Use the accepted count for this mean, disclose exclusions, and never describe it as the average for every supplied session.

Missing or invalid durations might belong to unusually long sessions. The accepted mean may therefore differ from the full group's mean. Do not make a causal claim from this descriptive investigation.

blocks.label: A report gives only mean 9. What additional evidence lets a peer reproduce it?

workbook.title: State the question
workbook.prompt: Write the worked investigation question so its population of records is clear.
workbook.answer: What is the mean duration among supplied sessions with valid integer minutes from 0 through 60?

workbook.title: Trace exclusions
workbook.prompt: Classify 0, None, -2 and 60 under the schema.
workbook.answer: 0 and 60 accepted; None missing/unknown and -2 out of range are rejected.

workbook.prompt: A report divides a valid total of 24 by six supplied rows, though only three are valid. Correct the valid-record mean.
workbook.answer: 24/3 = 8. Report 3 accepted and 3 rejected; do not use all six as the valid-record denominator.

workbook.answer: Accepted [6, 12, 0, 18], 2 rejected, total 36, mean 9. State 4 of 6 accepted; missing/invalid records may differ. Preserve the raw list and rules.

workbook.title: Support reproduction
workbook.prompt: A report gives only mean 9. What additional evidence lets a peer reproduce it?
workbook.answer: Input records/version, schema, excluded rows and reasons, accepted count, calculation and code/configuration version.

Build a small pipeline from tested parts

prerequisite.prompt: What are the steps between raw records and a recommendation?

vocabulary: One part of a processing pipeline
A function that decides whether an input meets a schema
Keeping different responsibilities in distinct parts

ai-2/33.title: Testing functions and interfaces
goals: Test functions and their connections
Keep expected results independent of the implementation
Check invalid and empty inputs

prerequisite.prompt: Why can testing only valid_item miss a pipeline bug?
prerequisite.answer: The later pipeline might still pass rejected rows to selection or mishandle its result.

vocabulary: A check of one small component
A controlled input used in a test
An independent source of the expected result

blocks.text: Test the chooser at two scales. A unit test checks one validator or score calculation. An integration test runs validation through selection and reporting. Write expected outcomes from the specification, not by calling the same function twice.

blocks.title: Python 3 code
blocks.text:
def score(item):
    return 2 * item["fun"] + item["learning"]

cases = [( {"fun": 0, "learning": 0}, 0),
         ( {"fun": 3, "learning": 2}, 8),
         ( {"fun": 5, "learning": 5}, 15)]
for item, expected in cases:
    assert score(item) == expected
print("3 score cases passed")

blocks.title: Follow the evidence
blocks.caption: Read each row from left to right and connect the evidence to the stated rule.

blocks.text: The code prints its success message only if all assertions pass. It checks the scoring component but says nothing about duration filtering, malformed records, ties or reporting. Add focused cases for those requirements. Use the production functions from earlier weeks rather than rewriting a second copy just for tests.

blocks.label: A test computes expected = score(item) then compares score(item) to expected. Why is it weak?

blocks.text: A test suite that only checks the winner name can miss wrong rejection counts. Check the full expected report: supplied, accepted, rejected, eligible, selected and reason. Avoid relying on dictionary display order when the contract concerns values.

Test results establish only the executed cases on the tested version. Retain failures and version information. Use explicit expected rejection behavior for invalid data instead of assuming every exception is acceptable.

workbook.answer: Use a controlled fixture and an independently specified expected winner, plus relevant report counts and reason.

workbook.prompt: What expected result should an empty-input integration case specify?
workbook.answer: 0 supplied/accepted/rejected/eligible, no selected item and a clear no-data or no-eligible explanation, without crashing.

ai-3/8.title: Searching candidate rules
goals: Fit a threshold rule by comparing training errors
Apply an explicit boundary and tie rule consistently
Compare the frozen rule with a baseline on validation data

prerequisite.prompt: How does a training-majority baseline choose its prediction, and where is its validation accuracy measured?
prerequisite.answer: It chooses its constant from training label counts, using a declared tie rule. Accuracy is then measured by matching the fixed prediction to validation labels.

vocabulary: One possible prediction rule in a declared search
A numerical boundary used to choose between outcomes
A mismatch between a prediction and its reference label in training data
Using training examples to choose a model value or rule

lesson.title: Turn a rule template into a search

blocks.text: Last week the baseline ignored scene features. This week a small fitting algorithm will choose a rule that uses one feature. We supply the rule form: predict blocked when a distance reading is at or below a cutoff, otherwise predict clear. The algorithm will try three cutoffs and keep the one making the fewest training mistakes.

The teacher-authored fictional rows contain a sensor distance in centimetres and a separate reviewed lane label, blocked or clear. The reading is available before prediction; the label comes from the scene review. A single distance need not describe every obstruction. These numbers are for learning, not real robot control. Each row comes from a different trip, and training and validation trips are separate.

Before scoring, declare cutoffs 3, 5 and 7 cm in ascending order, predict blocked at equality, and keep the smaller cutoff if training errors tie. This search tests only these three rules with this direction. It does not find the best possible model or prove that distance causes the label.

blocks.title: Python 3 code
blocks.text:
train = [(2, "blocked"), (4, "blocked"),
         (6, "clear"), (8, "clear")]
best_errors = len(train) + 1
best_cutoff = None
for cutoff in [3, 5, 7]:
    errors = 0
    for distance, label in train:
        guess = "clear"
        if distance <= cutoff:
            guess = "blocked"
        if guess != label:
            errors = errors + 1
    print(cutoff, errors)
    if errors < best_errors:
        best_errors = errors
        best_cutoff = cutoff
print("chosen", best_cutoff)

The output lines are 3 1, 5 0, 7 1, then chosen 5. Cutoff 3 misses the blocked row at 4 cm. Cutoff 5 matches all four training labels. Cutoff 7 wrongly marks the 6 cm clear row as blocked. Fitting stores cutoff 5; prediction then applies that stored rule to a new distance.

blocks.title: Separate search from later scoring
blocks.caption: The supplied search chooses a cutoff using training errors. A perfect training fit does not establish performance on new examples.

blocks.text: best_errors starts above any possible mistake count. The strict < keeps the first tied candidate; ascending order makes that the smaller cutoff. The code assumes nonempty training data, numeric distances and the two allowed labels. Validate those assumptions before using another dataset.

Now reveal four validation rows in order: (3, blocked), (5, clear), (7, clear), (9, blocked). With the stored cutoff 5, predictions are blocked, blocked, clear, clear. Rows 1 and 3 match, so validation accuracy is 2/4 or 50 percent despite zero training mistakes.

The training labels tie at two blocked and two clear. Carry forward Week 7’s baseline tie rule, choose clear. That baseline matches validation rows 2 and 3, also 2/4 or 50 percent. The fitted rule has not improved total accuracy on this set, and the two methods make different mistakes.

blocks.label: For the validation distance exactly 5 cm, what does the fitted rule predict and why? Which rows are wrong for the rule and the baseline? State their difference in percentage points.

blocks.text: Keep the rule and baseline fixed for this comparison. Do not secretly choose a different cutoff after seeing validation labels and call that a training-only choice. Validation can guide later development, but record those choices and reserve an untouched final test. No final test is supplied here.

lesson.title: Repair a search that changes its own rules

blocks.text: A learner uses distance < cutoff instead of distance <= cutoff during prediction. That changes the boundary: at 5 cm the stored cutoff now predicts clear. Recheck code against the declared rule before interpreting the score. A small symbol can change which examples match.

Another learner uses <= when deciding whether a candidate has fewer errors. That replaces an earlier candidate on a tie. The prediction boundary <= and the search comparison < have different jobs. Use the declared tie policy; a tied training score gives no evidence that one tied rule will be better on new cases.

Humans chose the feature, labels, candidate cutoffs, direction and scoring method. The program used training examples to select the cutoff. That is a small example of fitting a model; writing a loop alone does not make a method learn. Choosing the cutoff in advance without consulting training examples would instead be a fixed rule.

Record the source and split, rule form, candidate list, all training error counts, tie policy, selected cutoff and both validation prediction lists. Do not discard a difficult row to improve a score. Next week a decision tree will extend the idea of feature-based decisions, while the need for honest evaluation stays the same.

blocks.label: A learner reports that cutoff 5 is perfect because training error is zero. Rewrite the claim using the training result, validation comparison and the limits of this small search.

workbook.title: State the search before running it
workbook.prompt: Write the rule direction, equality behavior, candidate cutoffs and tie policy. Identify what humans supplied and what fitting selects.
workbook.answer: Predict blocked for distance <= cutoff and clear otherwise. Try 3,5,7 cm; choose the smaller cutoff on tied training errors. Humans supplied the feature, rule form, candidates and policy; fitting selects the cutoff using training labels.

workbook.title: Trace the training mistakes
workbook.prompt: List errors for cutoffs 3, 5 and 7 on the worked training rows. Identify the mistaken row for each imperfect candidate. Which cutoff is stored?
workbook.answer: Errors are 1,0,1. Cutoff 3 misses row 2 at 4 cm; cutoff 7 misses row 3 at 6 cm. Cutoff 5 has no training mistakes and is stored as the best of these three candidates.

workbook.title: Audit the boundary and comparison
workbook.prompt: What happens at distance 5 if prediction uses < instead of <= with cutoff 5? Explain why the search uses a strict < for error counts even though prediction uses <= for distance.
workbook.answer: The changed prediction would be clear instead of blocked at 5 cm. Prediction <= includes equality in blocked. Search < replaces a candidate only for fewer mistakes, preserving the first tied candidate; with ascending candidates that implements the smaller-cutoff policy.

workbook.title: Search and evaluate independently
workbook.prompt: New training rows are (1,blocked), (3,clear), (5,blocked), (7,clear). Try cutoffs 2,4,6, using the same direction and smaller-cutoff tie policy. Give every training error count and select a cutoff. Validation rows are (2,blocked), (4,blocked), (6,clear), (8,clear). List the selected rule’s predictions and score. Compare with the training-majority baseline using clear on ties.
workbook.answer: Training errors for 2,4,6 are 1,2,1. Choose 2 under the declared tie policy. Validation predictions are blocked,clear,clear,clear, matching rows 1,3,4: 3/4 or 75 percent. Training labels tie, so baseline clear matches rows 3,4: 2/4 or 50 percent. The selected rule gains one correct example or 25 percentage points on this small set only.

workbook.title: Limit the claim
workbook.prompt: The worked rule fits training perfectly but ties the baseline on validation accuracy. Explain why neither result proves it is the best possible model. Name two details to keep in the experiment record.
workbook.answer: Perfect training fit describes the examples used for selection; the four-row validation score is only 50 percent and ties the baseline. Only three candidates of one form were searched. Keep the candidates, all error counts, tie policy, chosen cutoff, split and row-aligned validation predictions; none proves general superiority.

teacher.background: Teach two 45-minute sessions using fictional sensor readings and reviewed labels. This is a small supervised fitting algorithm with a supplied rule form, not a complete decision-tree implementation. Separate the prediction boundary from the candidate replacement rule. The same split and baseline principles apply, and a zero training error must never be described as proof of generalization.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook
Four training cards and four validation cards with distance and reference label
Optional Python 3 editor with no extra packages
Blank table for cutoff predictions errors and selected rule
sessions: Retrieve training-majority fitting and validation scoring. Establish the distinct-trip fictional data and distance unit.
State candidates, direction, equality and tie policy before counting. Predict all four training rows for cutoff 3 by hand.
Trace the loop and complete W1 and W2. Name the stored parameter and distinguish fitting from later prediction.
Reveal validation and compute both methods on the same rows. Complete the guided boundary and error-pattern question.
Retrieve the difference between the prediction <= and search < comparisons.
Complete W3 and inspect both bug examples. Explain that a tie policy is a convention, not evidence of future superiority.
Collect W4 independently before hints. Require every candidate count, selected cutoff, predictions and baseline comparison.
Use W5 and the exit claim. Give the fresh retry after feedback and record support.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided: at 5 cm the selected rule predicts blocked because equality is included. The rule misses validation rows 2 and 4; baseline clear misses rows 1 and 4. Both score 50 percent, a zero percentage-point difference. Exit: cutoff 5 has zero mistakes on four training rows among the three supplied candidates, but scores 2/4 on validation and ties the baseline. This small comparison does not prove broad performance or global optimality.
misconceptions: Zero training error means perfect predictions
The rule was selected using those labels. New examples can disagree, as the two validation mistakes show.
Every comparison should include equality
Prediction and candidate replacement serve different purposes. Follow the specified boundary and tie policy separately.
The best tested rule is the best possible model
The search covers only the declared candidates and rule form, evaluated on a small set. Other forms and future cases remain unknown.
teacher.assessment: Require W4 training errors 1,2,1, cutoff 2, validation 3/4 and baseline 2/4 with a 25 percentage-point difference. Fresh retry: training (2,blocked),(4,clear),(6,blocked),(8,clear), candidates 3,5,7. Errors are 1,2,1; select 3. Validation (3,clear),(5,blocked),(7,clear),(9,clear) gives rule blocked,clear,clear,clear: 2/4. Baseline clear gives 3/4, so the rule is one correct example or 25 percentage points worse. Require correct equality handling and a restrained claim.
teacher.support: Use a number line and move a cutoff marker; place equality on the blocked side. Give a blank prediction grid but no error counts. Extension: reverse tied candidate order in the supplied code and explain why the retained cutoff changes unless the tie policy is implemented explicitly.

ai-3/11.title: Scaling without leakage
goals: Calculate feature scales from training data only
Apply the same stored transformation to training and new examples
Explain how scaling changes distance and how leakage invalidates evaluation

prerequisite.prompt: What determines the nearest training neighbour, and which examples belong in the stored neighbour pool?
prerequisite.answer: The selected features, distance measure and declared tie rule determine the nearest neighbour. Only training examples belong in the stored pool; validation reference labels must not enter it.

vocabulary: The largest training value minus the smallest for one feature
Learn and store values from training data
Apply a stored calculation to feature values
Use information that should be unavailable while developing or evaluating a prediction method

blocks.text: Last week we compared one numeric feature. With two features, their numerical ranges can give one feature much more influence. Scaling changes those contributions. We will learn a minimum and range for each feature from training only, then reuse them for every example.

These fictional trips have a distance reading in cm, a brightness reading in sensor units and a reviewed lane label. Features are available before prediction; labels are separate evidence. Related trips have already been grouped before splitting. For this exercise use k=1, add absolute differences across the two features, and break equal distances by alphabetical ID.

For query (11,120), raw distances to A,B,C are 1+80=81, 9+20=29 and 9+80=89. B wins and predicts blocked. Adding these different units is an unscaled numerical choice; the large brightness range strongly affects it. Scaling offers another explicit distance choice, not proof of which features matter.

lesson.title: Fit once and reuse the same calculation

blocks.title: Python 3 code
blocks.text:
train = [(10, 200), (20, 100), (20, 200)]
low = [min(row[j] for row in train) for j in range(2)]
span = [max(row[j] for row in train) - low[j]
        for j in range(2)]
if 0 in span:
    raise ValueError("Review a constant training feature")

def transform(row):
    return tuple((row[j] - low[j]) / span[j]
                 for j in range(2))

scaled_train = [transform(row) for row in train]
query = (11, 120)
print(low, span)
print(scaled_train)
print(transform(query))

For each feature use scaled value = (value minus training minimum) divided by training range. range(2) visits feature positions 0 and 1. The code prints [10, 100] [10, 100], then [(0.0, 1.0), (1.0, 0.0), (1.0, 1.0)], then (0.1, 0.2). Each minimum becomes 0 and each maximum becomes 1.

The first calculations fit low and span from train. transform uses those stored values without learning new ones. The code assumes nonempty training rows with exactly two finite numeric features; it does not check all inputs. Its explicit zero-range guard stops division by zero so a constant feature can be reviewed. This is a classroom policy, not a claim that every library stops this way.

blocks.title: One stored scale for every split
blocks.caption: Only training examples determine the scale. Transform validation and new examples using the same stored feature order, minima and ranges.

blocks.text: The scaled query is (0.1,0.2). Distances to scaled A,B,C are 0.1+0.8=0.9, 0.9+0.2=1.1 and 0.9+0.8=1.7. A now wins and predicts clear. We changed feature contributions; we did not change any reference label. Compare scaled queries with scaled training rows, never with raw training rows.

blocks.label: Show why raw distance selects B but scaled distance selects A for (11,120). Which stored numbers must remain fixed when the next query arrives?

blocks.text: Equal training ranges after scaling do not establish equal real-world importance. Outliers affect minima and ranges. Scaling does not repair wrong labels, missing information or an unsuitable distance measure.

Keep the training scale and k=1 fixed. Validation rows are (11,120,clear), (19,190,blocked), (12,80,clear). Their scaled feature pairs are (0.1,0.2), (0.9,0.9), (0.2,-0.2). Nearest IDs are A,C,B, so predictions clear,blocked,blocked score 2/3. The training-majority blocked baseline gets 1/3. These three examples do not establish general superiority.

The last brightness value scales to -0.2 because 80 is below the training minimum 100. New values can fall outside 0 to 1; do not refit or silently clip them. Including validation features in minima or ranges leaks evaluation information even without labels. Fitting a separate scale on validation also changes coordinates and breaks the intended comparison.

Record the split, feature names and units, feature order, minima, ranges, constant-feature policy, distance, k and tie rule. Keep the scale with the stored training examples. New data uses the same calculation. If development choices change, document them and reserve a separate final test. Next week combines these steps into one reproducible classifier pipeline.

If a feature is constant in training, its range is zero. This example stops for review. One documented option is to omit that feature everywhere and update the recorded feature list; do not divide by zero or invent a scale using validation values. Library policies differ, so inspect and record the one actually used.

blocks.label: A learner finds minima and ranges using all rows, then splits them and says there is no leakage because labels were never used. Explain the error and give the correct order of operations.

workbook.title: Learn the scale from training
workbook.prompt: Using A,B,C, give the minimum, maximum and range for each feature. Transform all three training rows and query (11,120). Explain which rows supplied the scale.
workbook.answer: Distance minimum 10 maximum 20 range 10; brightness minimum 100 maximum 200 range 100. A becomes (0,1), B (1,0), C (1,1), and query (0.1,0.2). Only A,B,C supplied the scale; the query did not.

workbook.title: Trace the changed prediction
workbook.prompt: For query (11,120), calculate raw and scaled distances to A,B,C. Give both k=1 predictions. Does this prove that scaling always improves predictions?
workbook.answer: Raw distances 81,29,89 select B blocked. Scaled distances 0.9,1.1,1.7 select A clear. The feature contributions changed. This single changed prediction does not establish better performance; evaluate separately and report limits.

workbook.title: Keep one coordinate system
workbook.prompt: Transform (12,80) using the stored training scale. Explain the negative value and why validation must not fit its own scale. Give the worked validation and baseline scores.
workbook.answer: (12,80) becomes (0.2,-0.2). Brightness is below the training minimum, so the negative result is valid under this formula. Refitting validation creates different coordinates; use the stored training transformation. Scaled k=1 scores 2/3 and the blocked baseline 1/3.

workbook.title: Scale a fresh dataset independently
workbook.prompt: New training rows are P (20,1000) clear, Q (40,600) blocked, R (40,1000) blocked. Fit minima and ranges. For query (22,680), show transformed features, raw and scaled distances to P,Q,R, and both k=1 predictions. Transform new row (50,520) with the same scale.
workbook.answer: Minima (20,600), ranges (20,400). P,Q,R become (0,1),(1,0),(1,1); query becomes (0.1,0.2). Raw distances 322,98,338 select Q blocked. Scaled distances 0.9,1.1,1.7 select P clear. New row (50,520) becomes (1.5,-0.2); keep the fitted scale and do not silently clip.

workbook.title: Repair two preprocessing mistakes
workbook.prompt: A learner fits scales using training plus validation features but no labels. Another divides by a zero training range. Explain both problems and give a recorded repair for each.
workbook.answer: Evaluation features influenced the first learned transformation, causing leakage even without labels. Split first, fit only on training and reuse those values for validation. A zero range causes division by zero. This code stops for review; one documented repair is to omit that feature consistently from every split and update the feature list.

teacher.background: Teach two 45-minute sessions. Keep the two feature columns distinct and require students to state which rows supplied each fitted number. First compare hand calculations, then trace optional Python. Explain that min-max scaling is one preprocessing choice; a small demonstration cannot establish the best method for a real task.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook
Two coloured number lines for the feature columns
Optional Python 3 editor with no packages required
Blank table for minima ranges transformed pairs and distances
sessions: Retrieve k=1 prediction and training-only neighbour storage. Introduce two features with different ranges.
Calculate raw distances and discuss how units affect contributions. Complete W1 minima and ranges.
Transform A,B,C and the query. Trace fit versus transform in code and finish W1.
Complete W2 and the guided question. Use the diagram to follow the same stored scale across splits.
Retrieve the stored feature order, minima and ranges without recalculating from validation.
Transform and score all three validation rows. Complete W3 and explain values outside 0 to 1.
Collect W4 independently before giving support. Require raw and scaled arithmetic plus the new row.
Discuss W5 and the exit question. Use the fresh retry after feedback and record support.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided: raw distances A,B,C are 81,29,89 so B predicts blocked; scaled distances are 0.9,1.1,1.7 so A predicts clear. Keep minima (10,100), ranges (10,100), feature order and method settings fixed. Exit: even unlabelled evaluation features affected the fitted transformation. Split first, fit minima and ranges on training, transform every split with those values, then evaluate frozen predictions.
misconceptions: Every transformed value must lie between 0 and 1
Only the fitted training range maps to 0 through 1. New values outside that range can transform below 0 or above 1.
No labels means no leakage
Held-out feature values can leak into a learned transformation. Fit preprocessing on the training split only.
Scale each split separately
Separate fits create different coordinates. Apply the same stored scale to training examples and queries.
teacher.assessment: Require W4 minima (20,600), ranges (20,400), query (0.1,0.2), raw distances 322,98,338 and scaled distances 0.9,1.1,1.7. Predictions Q blocked and P clear; new row (1.5,-0.2). Fresh retry: L (5,80) blocked, M (15,40) clear, N (15,80) clear; query (6,48). Minima (5,40), ranges (10,40), query (0.1,0.2). Raw distances 33,17,41 select M clear; scaled distances 0.9,1.1,1.7 select L blocked. Require training-only fitting and consistent transformation.
teacher.support: Colour each feature column separately and supply the formula with spaces for the training minimum and range. Let students use fractions before decimals. Extension: convert one entire feature to a different positive unit, refit on training only, and explain why the scaled values remain the same.
teacher.next: Week 12 builds a reproducible classifier pipeline. Carry forward the fitted scale, feature order and distance settings. Teacher reference: https://scikit-learn.org/stable/common_pitfalls.html (consistent preprocessing and leakage; reviewed 2026-09-27).

ai-3/29.title: Distribution shift
goals: Recognize changes between development and later data
Compare errors across conditions with denominators
Plan monitoring and a response without tuning on an old test

prerequisite.prompt: Why does a test score need a population description?
prerequisite.answer: Performance may differ when inputs, labels or conditions change.

vocabulary: A change in the data-generating conditions
Repeated checks of inputs, outputs and later outcomes
The labels used to evaluate predictions
A planned alternative when the model is unsuitable

blocks.text: A model trained on one set of conditions may encounter another. Lighting, measuring tools, class frequency and the relationship between inputs and labels can change. A shift does not automatically imply failure, but it challenges the assumption that old evidence represents current use.

Use fictional classroom data throughout this investigation. Keep the task, units, reference labels and data split visible as you reason. Earlier weeks supplied the model-building process; this week examines distribution shift.

On development-like bright images, a frozen classroom classifier makes 2 errors in 20 cases:10 percent. On a separate dim set it makes 6 errors in 20:30 percent. The pooled result is 8/40=20 percent error. The pooled score hides a 20-percentage-point difference between conditions.

Before continuing, underline the decision rule and circle the evidence that supports the conclusion. Explain the example to a partner without replacing the counts or conditions with a stronger claim. Keep the distinction between an observed result and a proposed next step.

blocks.title: Distribution shift at a glance
blocks.caption: The comparison identifies an observed weakness, not its cause. Check how images and labels were collected and whether other factors changed with lighting. An input shift can be detected before labels arrive, but performance cannot be measured from predictions alone.

blocks.label: Why is 8/40 incomplete by itself? Explain the steps or evidence behind your response.

blocks.text: For a supervised classroom prototype, define a review trigger before use, such as a new unsupported input range or a documented increase in labelled error. Pause the affected use, provide a human or non-model fallback, and investigate with new development evidence. Version any revision.

Do not normalize away a shift by silently changing preprocessing during evaluation. Treat a revised transformation or retrained model as a new version. Use fresh appropriate evidence for its claims and retain earlier results.

blocks.label: State a safe classroom response to inputs outside the supported range.

workbook.title: Compare conditions
workbook.prompt: Calculate each worked error rate and the difference.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Bright 2/20=10 percent; dim 6/20=30 percent; dim is 20 percentage points higher.

workbook.title: Read pooled evidence
workbook.prompt: Why is 8/40 incomplete by itself?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: It combines conditions and hides the higher observed dim-condition error.

workbook.title: Wait for labels
workbook.prompt: Can changed predictions alone prove an accuracy drop?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: No. Prediction patterns can change without known correctness; valid reference labels are needed to measure error.

workbook.title: Apply independently
workbook.prompt: Old-like data has 3 errors/30 and new-condition data 5/10. Give both rates and the pooled rate.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Rates 10 percent and 50 percent; pooled 8/40=20 percent. Report both denominators and the 40-point condition gap.

workbook.title: Plan a response
workbook.prompt: State a safe classroom response to inputs outside the supported range.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Flag unsupported inputs, pause the affected model decision, use the declared human or non-model fallback, and gather appropriate evidence before revision.

teacher.background: Teach two 45-minute sessions. This week focuses on distribution shift. Model the worked example first, collect the new W 4 case independently before feedback, and use the fresh retry to check transfer. Award credit for traceable reasoning and bounded claims, including justified uncertainty.

Ask for the relevant counts, units, procedure or saved record. For this week: Bright 2/20=10 percent; dim 6/20=30 percent; dim is 20 percentage points higher.
A stronger claim makes a stronger project
Flag unsupported inputs, pause the affected model decision, use the declared human or non-model fallback, and gather appropriate evidence before revision.
The new case can be copied from the example
The independent task changes the evidence. Require a fresh explanation: Rates 10 percent and 50 percent; pooled 8/40=20 percent. Report both denominators and the 40-point condition gap.

Fresh retry condition A 1/10 errors and B 3/10:10 and 30 percent, pooled 4/20=20 percent. Require separate counts and no causal claim from the table alone. Mark each criterion as independent, supported or not yet demonstrated. Reassess the reasoning after feedback; do not replace the first attempt silently.

ai-3/34.title: Capstone models and baselines
goals: Fit and compare a baseline and a simple candidate
Keep an auditable validation prediction table
Freeze a justified choice without requiring improvement

prerequisite.prompt: What must be fixed before the capstone comparison?
prerequisite.answer: Task, features, group-aware splits, metric, baseline and selection policy.

vocabulary: A simple reference method fitted or chosen from training
A per-record table of reference and predicted outputs
A saved model and procedure that will not change during testing
A written reason for a development choice

blocks.text: Build the baseline before the candidate. For classification, use the most common training class, with a declared tie policy. Choose one simple candidate using techniques already learned, such as k-nearest neighbours with training-only scaling and a fixed k. Record every development attempt; complexity earns no automatic credit.

Use fictional classroom data throughout this investigation. Keep the task, units, reference labels and data split visible as you reason. Earlier weeks supplied the model-building process; this week examines capstone models and baselines.

Illustrative training has 30 clear and 10 blocked cases, so the baseline always predicts clear. On 20 validation cases with 14 clear and 6 blocked, its matrix is[[14, 0],[6, 0]], accuracy 70 percent. Candidate matrix[[12, 2],[2, 4]] gives accuracy 80 percent, precision 4/6 and recall 4/6. These are example results, not the student team results.

blocks.title: Python 3 check
blocks.text:
# A check of the illustrative validation matrix.
# Replace with your own saved counts; do not invent results.
tn, fp, fn, tp = 12, 2, 2, 4
n = tn + fp + fn + tp
print("accuracy", (tn + tp) / n)
print("precision", tp / (tp + fp))
print("recall", tp / (tp + fn))
# Compare with the training-majority baseline: 14 / 20.

Trace the calculation on paper before running this optional Python check. Use the stated fictional inputs and compare intermediate values. The code checks this example; your independent workbook case uses different evidence.

blocks.title: Capstone models and baselines at a glance
blocks.caption: The candidate gains two correct cases while introducing two false alarms and reducing misses from six to two. Whether that tradeoff is acceptable depends on the predeclared classroom criteria. Do not choose a threshold or metric after the final test. If using a regression alternative, compare with a training-derived constant and report MAE in target units.

blocks.label: Compute the worked candidate accuracy, precision and recall. Explain the steps or evidence behind your response.

blocks.text: Save the data version, feature order, preprocessing values, model settings, tie policy and predictions. A prediction ledger includes row ID, split, reference, baseline output, candidate output and error type. Test labels remain held by the teacher. A peer should be able to reproduce one row by hand.

The deliverable is a runnable or fully traceable baseline/candidate comparison, a validation table and a signed-off freeze record. If the baseline wins, retain it and explain why. If a pipeline fails, record the failure and fix it on development data before requesting final testing.

blocks.label: List what must be saved before the teacher releases final-test labels.

workbook.title: Build the baseline
workbook.prompt: State the worked training-majority rule and validation accuracy.

workbook.title: Evaluate the candidate

workbook.title: Explain the tradeoff
workbook.prompt: Compare errors rather than only headline accuracy.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Baseline FP 0 FN 6; candidate FP 2 FN 2. Candidate finds four more blocked cases while falsely flagging two clear cases.

workbook.title: Apply independently
workbook.prompt: Training 18 clear/6 blocked; validation baseline[[9, 0],[3, 0]], candidate[[8, 1],[1, 2]]. Calculate accuracy for each and candidate precision/recall.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Baseline 9/12=75 percent; candidate 10/12 about 83.3 percent; precision 2/3 and recall 2/3. Candidate FP 1 FN 1 versus baseline FP 0 FN 3.

workbook.prompt: List what must be saved before the teacher releases final-test labels.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Model and preprocessing version, settings, feature order, split IDs, prediction/scoring rules, validation comparison, metric and decision record.

ai-5/5.title: Embeddings and position
goals: Look up token embeddings and add explicit position vectors
Trace how token order changes a representation
Explain what a toy position scheme does and does not establish

prerequisite.prompt: Do adjacent vocabulary IDs prove that their tokens have similar meanings?
prerequisite.answer: No. IDs are indices. Similarity must refer to the embedding vectors and a defined comparison, not numerical ID distance.

vocabulary: A vector associated with a token under a specified model
A vector carrying information about a sequence position
The number of components in each vector

blocks.text: Use a two-token vocabulary: ID 1 means red with embedding [1,0]; ID 2 means blue with embedding [0,1]. This lookup table is constructed, not trained. The input red blue has embedding rows [1,0] and [0,1], so its shape is two sequence positions by two components. Reversing the text reverses the rows. ID 2 is not “twice as blue” as ID 1 is red.

A model needs a way to use order. A collection of vectors without any order-sensitive procedure may lose that distinction. We introduce one explicit toy scheme: add position vector [0,0] at position 0 and [2,0] at position 1. These invented values teach arithmetic; they are not a recommended production encoding.

The same red token now has [1,0] at position 0 and [3,0] at position 1. Both token identity and position affect the represented row. Addition requires equal widths; adding a three-component position vector to a two-component embedding violates the input contract. Record the position numbering and embedding-table version.

blocks.title: Keep the evidence roles separate
rows: Do not infer meaning from ID gaps
blocks.caption: The position contribution changes a token representation according to its location.

blocks.text: The elementwise sum of the represented rows is [3,1] for both red blue and blue red. This aggregate loses the row-order distinction despite the position additions. A later computation must actually use the represented rows appropriately; merely adding position vectors does not guarantee that every summary preserves order.

A position scheme may use learned values or a deterministic construction. The original Transformer added positional information to embeddings. Modern architectures can use other order-sensitive schemes. Our two-vector example demonstrates one possible mechanism and one information-loss failure, not all architecture choices.
Supported case: embeddings A=[2,1], B=[1,3], positions [0,0] and [1,-1]. Sequence A B becomes [2,1] and [2,2]. Sequence B A becomes [1,3] and [3,0]. Both sums are [4,3].

blocks.label: Guided: compute both ordered representations and compare their sums. Explain which operation discarded the difference.

blocks.text: State whether a vector is a token embedding, a position vector or their combination before calculating distances. Position changes can affect numerical similarity even for the same token. An unknown token or a sequence beyond the toy position table needs explicit handling. This two-position contract rejects a third position; it does not silently wrap back to position 0.

blocks.label: Exit: a program compares vocabulary IDs instead of vectors and silently repeats its two-position table for a longer sequence. Identify both contract errors.

workbook.title: Look up vectors
workbook.prompt: For red blue name the IDs, embedding rows and shape before adding positions.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: IDs [1,2]; rows [1,0],[0,1]; shape two positions by two components.

workbook.title: Add positions
workbook.prompt: Compute representations for red blue and blue red under the stated position table.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: red blue rows [1,0],[2,1]; blue red rows [0,1],[3,0]. Addition is component by component.

workbook.title: Audit the sum
workbook.prompt: Sum the rows for both sequences. Does the sum establish that the original text had the same order?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Both sums [3,1]. Summing discards the ordered-row difference; equal summaries do not prove equal source sequences.

workbook.title: Trace new vectors independently
workbook.prompt: Embeddings A=[1,2], B=[3,0], position 0=[0,1], position 1=[1,0]. Compute represented rows and sums for A B and B A. Explain what the equal sums mean.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: A B rows [1,3],[4,0]; B A rows [3,1],[2,2]. Both sums [5,3]; the summaries lose the ordering difference while the ordered row representations differ.

workbook.title: Handle a shape failure
workbook.prompt: An embedding has width two but its position vector has width three. The input also contains a third position absent from the table. Specify honest handling.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Reject mismatched vector widths and unsupported position explicitly. Do not truncate, wrap or invent values unless a separate documented contract defines that transformation.
